units.la: ANNI sunt sedecim plus minus, candide lector, cum hanc historiam auditoribus meis publice enarrare. Quo tempore nonnulla observavi quae digna luce videbantur hominibus minime invidis, cujusmodi paucos fert haec aetas. Nolui tamen ea publicare ob certas causas. Superiore anno cum affulgeret benignius astrum abOrdinum Delegatis hujus provinciae cię[?] mutavi sententiam. Nam ecce di-vulgo jam, quod antea fieri quidă voluissent. Tantum potest potentiorum favor. Scimus, inquit Symmachus præfectus urbi, sub Theodosio imperatore, bonas artes honore nutriri, atq; hoc specimen esse florentis reipub.ut disciplinarum Professoribus præmia ampla pendantur. Qua de re alias: nunc scire te volo, quid a nobis in hoc opere præstitum sit. Ante omnia damus textum cum iis notis marginalibus, quæ in editione Plantini. paucas delevimus. Adjecimus quoque correctiones doctorum virorum, & aliquas etiam nostras. In nominibus propriis hominum aut urbium spectavimus non quid scribi debeat, sed quid ipse Severus olim scripserit. Nam ævū illud in nominibus Ebraicis potius Græcam consuetudine sequebatur, quam Ebręam, hoc est veram. Nos in notis utramque indicavimus. Si-mul historiam universam, quantum in nobis fuit, revocavimus ad ipsam veritatem, a qua Sulpicius non semel exorbitavit. Quod ea fide ac diligentia fecimus, ut nihil aut parum admodum desiderari possit. Quicquid ejus fit, fruere; & si fructum aliquem inde percipis, age gratias, primum Deo optimo maximo, cui debemus, quicquid habemus: deinde viris honora-tis, quibus haec historia dedicata & in-scripta; quorum favore atq; auxilio ea-dem nunc emendatior & cōmenta-rio auctior ad manus tuas pervenit. Vale & fave lingua.
units.tr: It is some sixteen years, more or less, kind reader, since I began to expound this history publicly to my hearers. In that time I noticed a number of things that seemed worth bringing to light for men who are not ill-disposed, of whom this age has few. Yet for certain reasons I did not want to publish them. Last year, when a kinder star shone on me from the Delegates of the Orders of this province, I changed my mind. For behold, what some had wished to have done before is now already being made public. So much can the favour of the powerful achieve. "We know," said Symmachus, prefect of the city, under the emperor Theodosius, "that the liberal arts are nourished by honour, and that this is a sign of a flourishing commonwealth, when generous rewards are paid to the teachers of the disciplines." But on that matter another time. Now I want you to know what we have accomplished in this work. First of all, we give the text with those marginal notes which were printed in the Plantin edition, though we have removed a few. We have also added the corrections of learned men, and some of our own as well. In the proper names of persons and cities, we looked not to what ought to be written but to what Severus himself wrote. For that age, in its Hebrew names, followed Greek usage rather than Hebrew, that is, the true form. In the notes we have indicated both. At the same time, as far as lay in us, we have restored the whole history to the truth itself, from which Sulpicius has not once strayed. We did this with such fidelity and care that little or nothing can be found wanting. Whatever its worth, enjoy it; and if you derive any profit from it, give thanks first to God, best and greatest, to whom we owe whatever we have; then to the honourable men to whom this history has been dedicated and inscribed, by whose favour and help it now comes into your hands, more correct and enlarged with commentary. Farewell, and wish well to the language.

units.la: Tu, frater dilectissime, ad Dominum miraculo majore conversus es, quia atate[?] florentior, laudibus abundantior, oneribus patrimonii levior, substantia facultatum non egentior & in ipso adhuc mundi theatro, id est fori celebritate diversans, & fa-cundi nominis palmam tenens repentino im-petu discussisti servile peccati jugum, & lethalia carnis & sanguinis vincula rupisti. Neque te divitiae de[?] matrimonio familiae consularis adgesta[?] neque post conjugium pecandilitcentia & caelebs juventus ab angusto salutis introitu & arduo itinere virtutis in mollem illam & spaciosam multorum viam revocare potuerunt. ITEM: Christum secutus nec minoris domesticis opibus ingenii facultatis laudem ab hominibus non accipiens, & inanis gloriae sublimiter negligens, piscatorum praedicationes Tullianis omnibus & tuis litteris praetulisti.
units.tr: You, most beloved brother, were converted to the Lord by a greater miracle, because you were in the flower of your age, richer in praise, lighter in the burdens of your inheritance, not poorer in means, and still living in the very theatre of the world, that is, in the bustle of the forum, and holding the palm of a famous orator's name. With sudden force you shook off the servile yoke of sin and broke the deadly bonds of flesh and blood. Neither the riches gathered from a marriage into a consular family, nor your unmarried youth after your wedding, could recall you from the narrow entrance to salvation and the steep road of virtue to that soft and broad way trodden by many. LIKEWISE: Following Christ, and not accepting the praise of men, which was no less than your family's wealth and the gifts of your talent could bring, and disdaining empty glory on high, you preferred the preaching of fishermen to all the writings of Tully and your own.

units.la: Idem epistola 5. ad eundem.
units.tr: The same, letter 5, to the same.

units.la: Neq; sat habeas occasionibus cunctis re-visere, nisi & pueros tuos mittas: nec solum de famulis, sed & de filiis sanctis, quorum benedicta in Domino prole laetaris, eligas ta-bellarios, quorum oculis nos videas & ore contingas, speciosi nobis pedes illorum tanquam euangelizantium bona. Nuciant enim nobis & afferunt ea, quae ad pacem sunt de te, cum praeferunt opera Domini, quae aut operaris in verbo Dei, aut scribis in spiritu verbi.
units.tr: Nor do you think it enough to visit us on every occasion unless you also send your servants. Choose messengers not only from your household servants but also from your holy sons, in whom you rejoice over a blessed offspring in the Lord, so that we may see them with our eyes and touch them with our mouths; their feet are beautiful to us, like those of men who bring good tidings. For they bring us and announce what concerns peace about you, when they show forth the works of the Lord, which you perform in the word of God or write in the Spirit of the word.

units.la: Idem Epistola eadem.
units.tr: The same, in the same letter.

units.la: Te vero vincla[?] lege membrorum & exte-riore riore corrupto puram conspersionem parare et sine fermento azymum Christo confici, eloquia tua tam facunda quam casta testantur. Neque enim tibi donatum fuisset enarrare Martinum, nisi dignum os tuum sacris lavaribus mundo corde fecisses. Benedictus igitur tu DOMINO, qui tanti sacerdotis & manifestissimi confessoris historiam tam digno sermone, quam justo affectu percensuisti beatus & ille pro meritis, qui dignum fide & vita sua meruit historicu, qui & ad divinam gloriam suis meritis, & ad humanam memoriam tuis litteris consecratur.
units.tr: Your eloquence, as chaste as it is eloquent, bears witness that you prepare a pure offering, with the limbs of the body in order and the outward man corrupted, and that unleavened bread is made for Christ without leaven. For it would not have been granted to you to recount Martin, unless you had made your mouth, which is worthy, clean through holy washings and a pure heart. Blessed, therefore, are you before the Lord, who have set forth the history of so great a priest and most manifest confessor in a discourse as worthy as it is righteous in feeling. Blessed too is he, according to his merits, who has deserved a historian worthy of his faith and life, and who is consecrated both to the divine glory by his merits and to human memory by your writings.

units.la: Gennadius in Catalogo virorum illustrium.
units.tr: Gennadius, in the Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

units.la: Severus presbyter, cognomento Sulpicius, Aquitanica provincia, vir genere & litteris nobilis, & paupertatis atque humilitatis amore conspicuus: charus etiam sanctorum virorum Martini Turonensis episcopi, & Paulini Nolani, scripsit non contemnenda opuscula. Nam epistolas ad amorem Dei & contemptum mundi exhortatorias scripsit sorori sue multas, qua & nota sunt. Scripsit & ad supradictum Nolanum duas, et ad alios alias. Sed quia in aliquibus etiam fami-liaris necessitas inserta est, non digeruntur. Composuit & Chronica. Scripsit & ad multorum profectum vitam B. Martini monachi & episcopi signis & prodigiis & virtutibus illustris viri, & Collationem Posthumiani & Galli, se mediante & judice, de conver-satione monachorum Orientalium & ipsius Martini, habitam in specie dialogi, duabus incisionibus comprehendit: in quarum priore refert suo tempore apud Alexandrinam synodum episcoporum decretum, Originem & cautius a sapientibus pro bono legendum, & a minus capacibus pro malo repudiandum. Hic in senectute sua a Pelagianis deceptus, & agnoscens loquacitatis culpam, silentium usque ad mortem tenuit, ut peccatum, quod loquendo contraxerat, tacendo penitus emē-daret.
units.tr: Severus, a presbyter, surnamed Sulpicius, of the province of Aquitaine, a man distinguished by birth and learning, and conspicuous for his love of poverty and humility. He was also dear to the holy men Martin, bishop of Tours, and Paulinus of Nola, and he wrote works that are not to be despised. He wrote many letters to his sister urging the love of God and contempt of the world, and these are well known. He also wrote two letters to the aforementioned Paulinus of Nola, and others to other people. But since some of them contain private family matters, they are not collected here. He also composed a Chronicle. For the benefit of many he wrote the life of the blessed Martin, monk and bishop, a man illustrious for signs, wonders and virtues. He also set down, in the form of a dialogue and in two books, the conference held between Posthumianus and Gallus, with himself as mediator and judge, concerning the way of life of the Eastern monks and of Martin himself. In the first book he reports that at the time, at the synod of Alexandria, the bishops decreed that Origen should be read cautiously by the wise for good, and rejected by the less capable for harm. In his old age Severus was deceived by the Pelagians, and, recognising the fault of his loquacity, he kept silence until his death, so that by silence he might fully make amends for the sin he had incurred by speaking.

units.la: Guibertus abbas Gemblacensis.
units.tr: Guibert, abbot of Gembloux.

units.la: Quod autem a Pelagianis seductus in aliquo a regula orthodoxa fidei exorbitaverit, nusquam omnino, nisi in solo Gennadio legi, qui nescio utrum hoc alicubi & ipse legerit, an ex sola fama, quae facta infectaque loqui-tur, didicerit. Illud tamen fideliter credo, hunc ejus errorem gloriam sanctitatis ejus non obscurasse; cum autor idem, qui referit deceptum, testetur & correctum.
units.tr: As for his having strayed from the rule of orthodox faith in some point, being seduced by the Pelagians, it is nowhere to be read at all except in Gennadius alone. I do not know whether he himself read this somewhere, or learned it only from rumour, which speaks of things made and falsified. Yet I faithfully believe that this error did not obscure the glory of his holiness, since the same author who reports that he was deceived also testifies that he was corrected.

units.la: Collegit vitam hujus Sulpicii, quam Plantinus vulgavit, in qua sacram hanc historiam, vel si Chronicon appellare quis malit, his verbis commendat:
units.tr: He gathered the life of this Sulpicius, which Plantin published, and in it he commends this sacred history (or, if anyone prefers to call it a Chronicle) in these words:

units.la: Quo opusculo, non sane magno, aliud ab ullo unquam seculo Reipub. Christianae utilius ac praestabilius editum sit, iis, quorum illud est judicium, judicandum relinquo. De elegantia vero praestare ausim & affirmare me posse confido, nulli idem omnium scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum quicquam concedere; alia vero omnia, quae in eodem genere ver-santur fantur, tanto intervallo omnimodis superare, ut ne sint quidem ad hoc comparanda. Magnum est quod dico & fortasse plurimis incredibile. Sed ejusmodi tamen, quod non tam dicenti mihi, quam testificanti promeritati creditum iri confidam, quibus opera pretium erit Orosium, Florum, Eutropium, aliosque epitomatum autores cum hoc nostro omnibus partibus contendere. Eam vero palmam sola, ut mihi videtur, C. Sallustii, rerum Romanarum autoris florentissimi, imitatione consecutus est. In quo cum multa viri, tutis locum obtinere videret, quae tamen sub imitationem vix caderent, abruptum dico sermonis genus, quod audientem lectore trahit, volat, nec, dum repetatur, exspectat: sive, ut loquitur Seneca, amputat sententias, & verba ante expectatum cadentia; eas virtutes, utpote Sallustio suas, integras reliquit. a verbis item antiquis ex Catonis, ut volebat Augustus, Originibus excerptis, confulto se abstinuit. At concinnam illam brevitatem, lectissimis ac significantibus verbis temperas tam, suo institutio cumprimis accommodam, tanta arte expressit, ut propemodum quis dicat non imitatum eum, sed amulatum. Neque enim fatis habuit eodem, quo ille, modo orationem ducere, secare, circumscribere, colligare, ac denique a re una ad aliam transire; nisi & principiis isdem libros suos ordiretur, ita tamen, ut qua ille, teste Fabio, nihil voluit ad historiam pertinere, hic paullo propius ad rem accommodarit. Quae omnia in sacra saltem historia praeclare elucere, vel primo oculorum injectu facile quivis animadvertit. confecta est enim, ut dixi, in primo aetatis flore, cum flagrans eloquentiae studium severa Turonensis contubernii disciplina nondum restinxisset. ejus operis semel tantum meminit Paullinus epist. ix. qua, rogatus si quas de regnorum sive annorum non congruente calculo hiantis historiae causas observasset, se respondet eadem de re Rufinum consuluisse, & siquid opis attulerit, facturum[?] certiorem.
units.tr: I leave it to those whose judgement it is to decide whether any work of a not particularly large size has ever been published in any age more useful and more excellent for the Christian commonwealth. As for elegance, I dare to claim and confidently affirm that I can show that no one among all ecclesiastical writers can match it, and that all the other works in the same genre, to whatever extent they are current, surpass it by such a distance that they are not even to be compared with it for this purpose. What I say is great, and perhaps incredible to very many. Yet I trust it will be believed, not so much because I say it as because those who bear witness to it have the merit to be believed; for those who will find it worth their while to set Orosius, Florus, Eutropius and other epitomists against this work of ours in every respect will see. Indeed, he won that palm, as it seems to me, by imitating alone Sallust, the most flourishing author of Roman history. In this, when he saw that many things of Sallust's had a place that were nevertheless scarcely fit for imitation, I mean the abrupt style of speech, which carries the hearer along, flies, and does not wait to be repeated, or, as Seneca puts it, cuts off sentences and words that fall before they are expected, he left these virtues whole, as belonging to Sallust. Likewise he deliberately abstained from the archaic words excerpted from Cato's Origines, as Augustus wished. But that neat brevity, tempered with most choice and expressive words, most suited to his own purpose, he expressed with such art that one might almost say he did not imitate Sallust but vied with him. For he was not content to conduct, cut, circumscribe and connect his discourse in the same way as Sallust, and to pass from one matter to another; he also began his books with the same openings, yet in such a way that, where Sallust, as Fabius bears witness, wished nothing to pertain to history, he has here fitted things somewhat more closely to the subject. All these qualities shine out brilliantly in this sacred history at least, as anyone will readily notice at the first glance. For it was composed, as I said, in the first flower of his age, when a burning zeal for eloquence had not yet been quenched by the strict discipline of the Turonian community. Paulinus alone recalls this work once, in letter ix, where, asked whether he had observed any causes for the gap in the history arising from the non-matching reckoning of the reigns or years, he replies that he had consulted Rufinus on the same matter, and that if he brings any help he will let him know.

units.la: B. Severus Sulpitius, Bituricensis episcopus, homo ut sanctus, sic[?] disertus imprimis & eruditus.
units.tr: Blessed Severus Sulpitius, bishop of Bourges, a man as holy as he was eloquent and learned.

units.la: Scaliger
units.tr: Scaliger

units.la: Sulpitium Severū nemo hactenus Aqui-tanum fuisse dubitavit: sed patria ignoratur, cum tamen ipse Nitiobrigem se ipse manifesto prodat, cum Servationem Tungrorum, Phœbadium autem suum episcopū fuisse scribit. Phœbadius autem erat Nitiobrigum episcopus. Iste[?] Sulpitius Ecclesiasticorum pu-rissimus scriptor, post transitum Martini, recepit sese Elufonem, quo tempore ad eum scribebat Paulinus.
units.tr: No one until now has doubted that Sulpitius Severus was from Aquitaine, but his homeland is unknown, although he himself clearly reveals that he was a Nitiobrigan. He writes that Servatio was bishop of the Tungri, but that his own bishop was Phoebadius, and Phoebadius was bishop of the Nitiobriges. This Sulpitius, the purest of the ecclesiastical writers, after Martin's death withdrew to Elusa, at the time when Paulinus was writing to him.

units.la: Idem paullo post,
units.tr: The same, a little later:

units.la: Mei Nitiobriges pro Sulpitio Supplicium dicunt, quomodo & Bituriges suum illum vocant, quem eundem cum hoc faciunt per-peram, cum inter transitum Martini, cuius noster Sulpitius discipulus fuit, & ordinationem Sulpitii episcopi Bituricensis sub Guntchramno rege, intercedant plus minus anni centum nonaginta.
units.tr: My Nitiobriges say Supplicius for Sulpitius, just as the Bituriges also call their own man by that name, and they wrongly identify him with this man. For between Martin's death, whose disciple our Sulpitius was, and the ordination of Sulpitius as bishop of Bourges under king Guntchramn, lie roughly one hundred and ninety years.

units.la: Clarissimo viro D. IOHANNI DRVSIO, Juper curis ejus Historicis.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, Mr. JOHN DRUSIUS, on his historical labours.

units.la: QUicunque Sacrae praestitem Scientiae Olim audiisti Drusium; Quicunque linguas pluribus non cognitas Docente discis Drusio; Qua voce jura dixerit Deus sua Seris Isaci posteris; Quibusque verbis invias rerum vias, Et si quid oculis abditum est, Alumna VERI, prisca doctrinae parens Chaldaea gens descripserit; Huc, huc adesto. Divus, en, Divus Senex Meliora mentis pignora Sacrabit ævo, quae nec Invidentia, Nec Momus ipse lancinet. Ille, ille partis sat beatus laudibus, Privaque claritudine Non ante curis terminum tamen suis Metamque ponit ausubus,
units.tr: You who once heard Drusius lecture on sacred learning, you who learn from Drusius as teacher the languages unknown to most, by what voice God pronounced his laws to the posterity of Isaac's seed, and in what words he has described the trackless paths of things and whatever lies hidden from our eyes, the Chaldean race, nursling of truth and ancient parent of doctrine: come here, come here. Behold, the godlike old man will consecrate to the ages better pledges of his mind, which neither envy nor Momus himself can tear to pieces. He, blessed enough in his praise and his own renown, does not yet set an end to his cares or a goal to his labours.

units.la: Quàm per vetusta seculorum scrinia Hiante oberrans lumine Minúta, magna spectet, atque casuum Notet vicissitudines. Hic prima Sanctæ jacta Gentis femina, Ritusque & actus explicat: Hic æstuosam Cæsarum impotentiam, SOLYMASQUE monstrat dirutas; Cum pingue victor hinc & hinc eques solum Sonante tundit ungula; Facesse livor. Drusius probris tuis Aut major, aut intactus est. Tibi, Serari, tabidæ Stygis Deæ Fumosa rumpant ilia. Stupes, & ora pallor ambit luteus, Mentemque percitus furis. Insane, vera quæ fit Eruditio, Quæ litterata, discito. Mirare summis Drusium parem viris, Ast æmulari desine. Haut esse vobis eruditis contigit Quotcunque rosis unguibus Barbáque sapitis. IPSA SAPIENTVM SACRA PROCVL VIDETIS INVIDI.
units.tr: Than to wander through the ancient chests of the centuries with gaping eyes, surveying small and great things and noting the changes of fortune. Here he sets out the first woman of the holy nation, and its rites and deeds; here he shows the scorching impotence of the Caesars and Jerusalem laid waste, while the victor's horse on either side pounds the rich soil with ringing hoof. Begone, envy! Drusius is either greater than your reproaches or untouched by them. Serarius, may the smoking entrails of the wasting Stygian goddess burst for you. You stand stupefied, your face pale and sallow, and your mind is driven mad by fury. Madman, learn what true erudition is and what it means to be learned. Marvel at Drusius, a peer of the greatest men, but cease to try to rival him. It has not fallen to you learned men, however many of you with rosy nails and beards are thought wise, to... You see the sacred things of the wise, far beyond the reach of the envious.

units.tr: Carolus Sigonius.

units.la: Hortor omnes qui se aut sacris aut profanis studiis dediderunt adolescentes, ut Severum hunc eo animo legant, ut plurimum se non tam imprudentia, quam in religionis & innocentia studio profecturos esse confidant. Addo etiam latina eloquentia[?], quam ille tanta industria coluit, ut Sallustianam dictionem nobis magna ex parte expresserit.
units.tr: I urge all young men who have devoted themselves to sacred or profane studies to read this Severus in the confident expectation that they will make great progress, not so much through imprudence as through their zeal for religion and innocence. I add also his Latin eloquence [?], which he cultivated with such diligence that he has reproduced the style of Sallust for us to a great extent.

units.la: LIB. I.
units.tr: BOOK I.

units.la: RES a mundi exordio sacris literis editas breviter constringere, & cum distinctione temporum usq; ad nostram memoriam carptim dicere aggressus sum: multis id a me studiose efflagitantibus{a}, qui divina, compendiosa lectione, cognoscere properabant. Quorum ego voluntatem secutus, non peperci labori meo, quin ea, quæ permultis voluminibus perscripta continebantur, duobus libellis concluderem: ita brevitati studens, ut poene nihil gestis subduxerim. Visum autem mihi est non absurdū, cum usq; ad Christi crucem, Apostolorum q; actus per sacram historiam cucurrissem, etiam post gesta cōvertere{*}: excidium Hierosolymæ, {b}vexationes populi Christiani, & mox pacis{3} tempora, ac rursum ecclesiarum intestinis periculis turbata omnia locutu-rus. Ceterum illud non pigebit fateri, me, sicubi ratio exegit, ad distinguenda tepora, continuandamq; feriem, usum esse historicis ethnicis, atque ex * his quæ ad supplementum cognitionis deerant ut-furpasse,ut & imperitos docerem, & lite-ratos convincerem. Veruntamen ea,quæ de sacris voluminibus breviata digesi-mus, non ita legentibus auctor accesse-rim, ut prætermissis illis, unde hæc deri-vata sunt, appetatu nisi cum illa quis fa-miliariter noverit, hic recognoscat, quæ ibi legerit. Etenim universa divinarū re-rum mysteria non nisi ex ipsis fontib. hau-riri queunt. Nunc initiū narrandi faciam,
units.tr: I have set out to briefly condense the events recorded in the sacred letters from the beginning of the world, and to relate them selectively, with a distinction of times, down to our own memory. Many people eagerly demanded this of me, since they were anxious to learn divine matters through a short reading. Following their wishes, I did not spare my labour, but compressed into two small books what was set out in very many volumes, aiming at such brevity that I omitted almost nothing of the events. It did not seem unfitting to me, however, having run through the acts of the Apostles as well as sacred history up to the cross of Christ, to also turn back and treat what came after: the destruction of Jerusalem, the persecutions of the Christian people, then the times of peace, and again the churches thrown into confusion by internal dangers. I will not be ashamed to confess that wherever reason required, in order to mark out the times and keep the sequence continuous, I have made use of pagan historians and borrowed from them what was lacking to complete the knowledge, both to instruct the unlearned and to convince the learned. Nevertheless, I have not so presented myself as the author of this digest of the sacred books that a reader, neglecting those sources from which these things were derived, should come here to recognise what he has read there, unless he already knows those sources intimately. For the whole mysteries of divine things can be drawn only from the fountains themselves. Now I will make a beginning of the narrative.

units.la: MUNDUS A DOMINO constitu-tus est abhinc annos iam pæne sex millia, licut processu voluminis istius digere-mus: quanquam inter se parum consentiant, qui rationem temporū investigaram ediderunt. Quod cum vel Dei nutu, vel vitio vetustatis eveniat, calumnia carere debebit. Mundo autem condito, homo factus est: viro Adam, mulieri Eua nomen fuit. Sed constituti in paradiso, cum inter dicta sibi arborem degustassent, in nostrā, velut exsules, terram ejecti sunt. Deinde ex his Cain atq; Abel nascitur. Sed Cain impius, fratrem interemit. Filium Enoch habuit, a quo primum civitas condita est, auctoris nomine vocitata. Ex hoc Irad{a} atque ex eo Maviael nascitur. Hic Mathusalam{b} filium habuit, ilq; Lamech genuit, a quo {c}juvenis quidam occisus traditur, nec tamen nomē refertur occili, quod quidem futuro mysterio fuisse praemissum a prudentibus aestimatur. Igitur Adam post necem filii minoris. Seth filium pro-creavit, cum jam tricesimum & ducentesi.mum[?] annum aetatis implesset. Vixit autē annos DCCCCXXX. Seth vero Enos, Enos Cainā, Cainan{d} Malaleel Iared, Iared Enoch genuit: qui ob{e} justitia translatus a Deo traditur. Hujus filius Mathusala dictus est, qui Lamech genuit: ex quo Noë natus, justitia egregius, & praeceteris mortalibus Domino carus acceptusque.
units.tr: THE WORLD was established by the Lord almost six thousand years ago, as we shall set out in the course of this volume, although those who have published investigations of chronology do not agree closely among themselves. Since this happens either by the will of God or through the corruption of antiquity, it ought to be free from calumny. Once the world was created, man was made: the man was called Adam, the woman Eve. But placed in paradise, after they had tasted the tree forbidden to them, they were cast out like exiles into our land. Then Cain and Abel were born to them. But Cain, being impious, killed his brother. He had a son Enoch, by whom the first city was founded, named after its founder. From him Irad was born, and from Irad Mehujael. He had a son Methuselah, who begot Lamech, by whom a certain young man is said to have been killed; yet the name of the slain man is not recorded, which the wise judge to have been sent forward as a foreshadowing of a future mystery. So Adam, after the death of his younger son, begot Seth when he had completed his two hundred and thirtieth year. He lived nine hundred and thirty years. Seth begot Enos, Enos begot Cainan, Cainan Mahalalel, and Mahalalel Jared; Jared begot Enoch, who, because of his righteousness, is said to have been taken up by God. His son was called Methuselah, who begot Lamech, from whom Noah was born, outstanding in righteousness and dear and acceptable to the Lord beyond other mortals.

units.la: Qua tempestate cum jam humanū genus abundaret, angeli, quibus cælū sedes erat, speciosarū forma virginum capti, illicitas cupiditates appetierunt: ac naturæ suę originisq; degeneres, relictis Superiobus, quorū incolæ erant, matrimoniis se mortalibus miscuerūt. Hi paulatim mores nō-xios conferentes, humana corrupere pro geniem, ex quorū coitu Gigates editi esse dicuntur,cum diversę inter se naturę per-mixtio monstra gigneret. Quibus rebus offensus Deus, maximéq; malitia hominum,quæ ultra modum processerat,dele-re penitus humanum genus decreverat. Sed Noë, virum justum, vita innocens de- stinatæ exemit sententiæ. Idem admonitus a Domino, diluvium terris imminere,arcam immensæ magnitudinis ex lignis co-texuit:acbitumine illitam impenetrabile aquis reddidit, qua ille cum uxore, ac fi-liis tribus,& totidem nuribus est clausus: volucrum etiam paria, itidemque diversi generis bestiarum,eodem claustro recep-ta,reliqua omnia diluvio absumpta. Igi-tur Noë, cum jam imbrem destitisse, ac quieto in salo arcam circumferri, intelli-geret, ratus id quod erat, aquas decedere, corvum primum explorandæ rei gratia, eoq; non revertente,(ut ego conjicio,ca-daveribus detéto) emisit columbam:quæ cum consistendi locum non reperiisset, reversa est. Rursu{*} remissa,folium olivæ retulit, manifestum indicium, nudari ca- cumina arborum. tertio demum emissa non rediit,unde animadversum aquas de-stitisse.Ita Noë arcam egressus est.id gestu amuna mundi exordio, post annos (ut ego comperio) ii. cc. duos & quadraginta. Ac primum Noë aram Domino statuit, hostiasq; ex volucribus immolavit. Mox a Domino cum filiis benedicitur: præceptumq; accepit, ne sanguine vescerētur, aut sanguinem hominū effunderet: quia mundi primordia, mandati istius liber, Cain maculaverat. Igitur vacuo tum sæculo, ex filiis Noë Sem fuit. Tres enim habuit, Sem, Cham, Iapheth. Sed Chā, quod sopitū vino patre riserat, maledictum a patre meruit. hujus filius, Chus nomine, Nebrod gigante genuit: a quo Babylon civitas constructa traditur. Pleraq; etiam opida ea tempestate condita memorantur, quæ nominatim persequi animus non fuit. Sed cum multiplicaretur humanū genus, diversaq; loca, atq; insulas mortales haberet, una tantū omnes lingua utebantur: donec se in unum, dispergenda per totum orbem, multitudo cōtraxit. His more humani ingenii consilium fuit, insigni aliquo opere famā quærere, priusquam a se invicem deducerētur. Ita turrim facere aggressi, quæ cælo accederet, nutu Dei, ut officia operā-tiū præpedirentur, inassueto sermonis genere, multa diverso, neq; ulli invice intel-lecto linguarum ritu loquebantur: quo promtius dispersi sunt, cum alter alterū velut alienigenam facile relinquebat. Sed filiis Noë ita divisus orbis fuit, ut Sem intra Orientem, Iapheth Occidentem, Cham mediis contineretur. Ita usque{a} ducta successio, nihil sane infigne aut memorabile in fe habuit. Abram autem patre Thara natus est, post diluvium anno millesimo & septuagesimo. Abram uxor Sara dicta est, primaq; eis in regione Chaldaeorum habitatio fuit. Inde apud Charras una cum patre diversatus est. Qua tepestate admonitus a Domino, domum, patriam ac patrem relinquens, assumpto Lot fratris filio, in terram Chanæorū{b} nanæorū profectus, in loco {b}eui Sichem nomen est, consedit. Mox annonæ inopia Aegyptum concessit, ac rursum reversus {c}Lot, præ multitudine familiæ a patruo digressus, ut laxioribus vacuæ tum regionis spatiis uteretur, in Sodomis consedit. Id opidum infame incolis, viris in viros irruentibus, atque ob id invisum Domino fuisse traditur. Ea tempestate Reges vi-cinarum gentium in armis erant: cum an-
units.tr: At the time when the human race was already growing numerous, the angels, whose dwelling was heaven, were captivated by the beauty of the maidens and pursued forbidden desires; and, degenerate from their nature and origin, they left the higher places where they dwelt and mingled with mortal women in marriage. Gradually these beings introduced harmful customs and corrupted the human race, and from their union the Giants are said to have been born, since the mixing of such different natures produced monsters. Offended by these things, and above all by the wickedness of men, which had gone beyond all measure, God decided to utterly destroy the human race. But Noah, a just man of innocent life, was exempted from the sentence decreed. Warned by the Lord that a flood was about to fall upon the earth, he wove an ark of immense size from timber, smeared it with bitumen and made it impervious to the waters. He was shut into it with his wife, his three sons and as many daughters-in-law; pairs of birds and pairs of beasts of every kind were also received into the same enclosure, while all else was swept away by the flood. Then Noah, understanding that the rain had stopped and that the ark was being carried about on the calm sea, supposed that the waters were receding, which was indeed the case. First he sent out a raven to explore the matter; when it did not return (as I suppose, it was detained by the carcasses), he sent out a dove. Finding no place to settle, the dove came back. Sent out again, it brought back a leaf of olive, a plain sign that the tops of the trees were uncovered. Sent out a third time, it did not return, from which it was perceived that the waters had withdrawn. Thus Noah left the ark. This took place, as I find, two hundred and forty-two years after the beginning of the world. And first Noah set up an altar to the Lord and offered sacrifice of birds. Soon the Lord blessed him with his sons, and he received the command not to eat blood nor to shed human blood, because Cain, the first breaker of this commandment, had defiled the beginnings of the world. So the age was then unpeopled, and among the sons of Noah there was Shem. For he had three: Shem, Ham and Japheth. But Ham, because he mocked his father when he lay sleeping off the wine, earned a curse from him. His son, named Cush, begot Nimrod the giant, and by him Babylon is said to have been built. Many other towns are also recorded as founded at that time, which I do not intend to list by name. But as the human race multiplied and mortals held different places and islands, all used one language, until the multitude gathered together into one place, though they were to be scattered over the whole earth. In keeping with the nature of the human mind, they planned to win fame by some remarkable work before they were led away from one another. So they set about building a tower that would reach to heaven. By the will of God, so that the work of the builders might be hindered, they spoke in an unaccustomed kind of speech, with many different tongues, none understood by another; and so they were scattered the more quickly, since each easily left the other behind as a foreigner. Thus the world was divided among the sons of Noah: Shem held the East, Japheth the West, and Ham the regions between. The succession then proceeds, having nothing especially notable or memorable in it. Abram, however, was born to his father Terah in the year one thousand and seventy after the flood. Abram's wife was called Sarai, and their first dwelling was in the region of the Chaldeans. From there he stayed with his father at Haran. At that time, warned by the Lord, he left his home, his country and his father, took Lot, his brother's son, with him, set out for the land of the Canaanites, and settled in a place called Shechem. Soon, because of a shortage of food, he withdrew into Egypt, and when he came back again, Lot, because of the size of his household, separated from his uncle so as to use the wider spaces of the then empty region, and settled in Sodom. That town was infamous for its inhabitants, who rushed upon men with men, and for this it is said to have been hateful to the Lord. At that time the kings of the neighbouring peoples were under arms, and

units.la: a Vs ad Par. [?] tea nullum inter mortales certamen fuisset. Sed adversum hos,qui bello vicina tentabant, reges Sodomorum, Gomorrhæorum vicinarumq; regionum in prælium erumpunt: primoq; impetu fusi,victoriam concessere. Tum a victoribus Sodoma direpta, prædæ hostibus fuit, ductufq; Lot in captivitatem. Quod cum Abram comperiflet, propere armatis fervis suis,numero trecentis,decem & octo, reges victoria feroces, exutos prædaarmifq; in fugam compulit. Tum a Melchifedec sacerdote benedictus est, eidemq; decimas prædæ dedit. Reliqua his,quibus ereptæ erant, reddidit. Peridem tempus Abrae Dominus locutus est, multiplicans dumq; femen ejus,sicut arenas maris ftellafq; cæli, spopondit: peregrinumq; ejus femen prædictum futurum, ac posteros in hostili solo per quadringentos annos laturos servitium, postea libertati restituendos. Tum ei atq; uxori ejus, adjectione unius litteræ nomen immutatum:ita nunc ex Abram Abraam, ex Sara Sarra discitur. Cujus quidem rei non inane mysterium non est hujus operis exponere. Eodem tempore Abraæ lex circumcisionis imposita cft.erat ei autem{*}ex an-cilla filius Ismael: & cum ipse esset annorum centum, uxor autem ejus nonaginta, futurum eis filium Isaac, Dominus pollicetur, qui cum duobus angelis ad eum venerat. Inde Sodomam misi angeli, Lot in porta sedentem reperierunt. Quos cum ille, homines existimans, hospitio receptos, coenatosque domi haberet: juventus improba ex opido, novos hospites ad stuprum flagitabant. Lot pro hospitibus filias offerens, non acquiescentibus, quibus illicita potius desiderio erant, ipse ad stuprum trahebatur. Quem angeli propere ab injuria vindicantes, luminibus impudicorum caecitatem offuderunt. Tum Lot, ab hospitibus edoctus perdendi opidum, propere cum uxore, & filiabus est egressus: interdictum tamen eis est, ne retrorsum conspicerent. Sed mulier paru dicto audiens (humano malo, quo aegrius veritis abstinetur) reflexit oculos, statimque in molem conversa traditur. At Sodomadi-vinis ignibus conflagravit. Lot autem filiae existimantes humanum genus interiisse, concubitu inebriati patris appetiverunt: unde Moab & Ammon nati sunt. Per idem idem tempus fere, cum Abraam esset etiam centum annorum, Isaac filius natus est. Tum ancillam, de qua Abraam filium susceperat, Sarra expulit: quæ habitasse in deserto una cum filio, & præsidio Domini defensa, traditur. Non multo post, Domi-nus Abrae fidem tentans, immolandum sibi a patre Isaac filium poscit. Quem ille non cunctatus offerre, cum arae puerum su-perpofuiffet, gladiumq; educeret, vox missa[?] de caelo est, puero ut parceret: victimæ aries præsto fuit. Consummatoq; sacrificio, Abrae Dominus locutus est, promittens ea quæ jam spoponderat. At Sarra, cum septimum & vicesimum supra centesimum annum ageret, decessit: corpus cura viri sepultum in Hebron, Chananaeorum opido. Etenim illic Abraam commoraba-tur. Tum Abraam Isaac filium juvenilis ætatis videns, siquidem tum quadragesimum annum ætatis agebat, servo suo imperavit, uxorem ei quæreret: ex ea tamen tribu atque terra, de qua ipse oriundus videbatur: modo ut inventam puellam in regionem Chananaeorum deduceret, nec putiret eum causa conjugis in solum patrium reditururum. Atque ut ea strenue mandamandata exsequeretur, contacto domini femine, sacramentum dedit. Ita servus profectus in Mesopotamiam, ad opidum Nachor, Abraami fratris, devenit: tuccesfitque in domum Bathuelis Syri, Nachore patre geniti: hujus filiam Rebeccam, speciosam virginem, conspicatus, poposcit atque ad dominum adduxit. Post id Abraam accepit uxorem Cetiram nomine, quae in Paralipomenis concubina dicitur: suscepit quoque ex ea filios. Sed Isaac Sarra edito substantiam tradidit: his autem, quos ex concubinis susceperat, dona distribuit, atque ita ab Isaac separati sunt. Abraam diem functus est, impletis annis centum & quinque & septuaginta: corpus sepulchro Sarrae uxoris appositum. At Rebecca diu sterilis, assiduis maritia ad Dominum precibus, a die matrimonii vicesimo fere anno geminos edidit: qui in matris alvo exsultasse saepius traduntur. dictumque responso Domini est, duos in his populos praenuntiari, & majorem minori subdendum esse principio. Sed prius edi-tus a sper fetis Esau vocatus: minori Iacob nomen fuit. Ea tempestate gravis annonae inopia terras incesserat. Qua necessitate Isaac in Geraris ad regem Abimelech cessit, admonitus a Domino ne in Aegyptum descenderet: eidemque universæ illi-us terræ possessio promittitur, ibiqué benedicitur, multiplicatusque pecore atque omni substantia, agente invidia, ab incolis pel-litur: pulsus apud Puteum iurameti consedit. Igitur annis gravior, luminibus obductis, cum Esau filium benedicere pararet, consilio Rebeccæ matris, Iacob se benedicendum pro fratre obtulit. Ita Iacob adorādus principibus & getib. fratri præponitur. Queis rebus Esau accesus fratri necé moliebatur. Quo metu Iacob, hortate matre, in Mesopotamiá confugit: admonitus a patre, ut ex domo Laban fratris Rebeccæ, uxorem acciperet. Tara illis cura fuit, cum in alienis terris consisterer, genustamen intra familiam suam ducere. Ita Iacob profectus in Mesopotamiá, per soporem Dominum vidisse traditur: atque ob id locum somnii sacratum habens, lapidem ex eo sumpsit: vovitque si rebus prosperis revertisset, titulum sibi domus Domini futurum; decimasque omnium quæ acquisita sibi forent, Domino daturum. Inde se ad Laban fratrem matris contulit: quem ille sororis filium ag-nitum, in hospitium benigne receepit. E-rant Laban duæ filiæ, Lia & Rachel. Sed Lia oculis deformior, Rachel pulchra su-isse traditur. Cujus specie Iacob captus, amore virginis conflagrabat: eamq; sibi in matrimonio a patre postulans, septem annorum servitio se mancipavit. Sed im-pleto tempore, Lia ei supponitur: ac rursum septe in servitio subditur, atq; ei Rachel traditur. Sed hanc diu sterilem, Liam fecundam fuisse accepimus. Filiorum quos ex Lia Iacob habuit, hæc sunt nomina; Ruben, Simeon, Levi, Iudas, Isachar, Za-bulon, Dina. Ex ancilla vero Liæ, Gad & Aser. Ex ancilla Rachel, Dan & Nephtalim nati sunt. At Rachel, desperato jam partu, Ioseph edidit. Tum Iacob redire ad patrem cupiens, cum ei Laban socer partem pecorum mercede servitii dedisset, ob quæ parū sibi eū æquū gener Iacob ratus, dolū ab eo suspectas, clam profectus est vicesi-mo primo fere anno, quam advenerat. Ra-chel, viro inscio, patris idola furto abstulit, qua injuria Laban generū persecutus, nō repertis idolis, pace facta, regressus est: multum obtestatus generū, ne uxores filiabus suis lupinduceret[?]. Inde digressus la-cob, vidisse angelos & castra Domini, tradi-tur. Sed cum praeter regione Edom, quam Esau frater incolebat, iter deflinaret misis prius legatis & muneribus, suspectum sibi fratrem exploravit. Tum ille obvia fratri processit: nec tamen Iacob se ultra fratri credidit. Sed pridie, quam inter se fratres convenirent, Dominus humana specie assumpta, colluctatus cum Iacob refertur. Et cum adversus Dominum praevaluisset, ta-men non esse mortale non ignoravit: benedici sibi ab eo flagitabat. Tum a Deo illi immutatu nomen est, ut ex Iacob Israel diceretur. Sed cum ille vicissim a Domino nomen Domini quaereret, Non esse quaerendum (quia admirabile esset) respondit. Ex colluctatione aut, latitudo femoris Iacob obtorpuit. Igitur Israel declinas fratris domum, promovit agmen in Sale Si-cimorum opidum: atque ibi loco pretio accepto, tabernaculu statuit sibi. Huic opido Emor, Chemoreus * princeps, praerat. huius filius Siche[?], Dinam filiam Iacob ex Lia genitam, stupro subdidit. Quo coperto, Simeo, & Levi, Dinae fratres, omnes in opido sexus virilis dolo peremerut, ac im-pigre pigre sororis ulti sunt injuriam : opidum a filiis Iacob direptum, prædaq; omnis est abducta. Id factum ægre admodum tulif- fe Iacob traditur. Mox a Domino monitus, Bethleem petiit, ibiq; altare Domino statuit. Inde in parte turris Gader tabernaculum fixit. Rachel ex partu obiit, puer Benjamin vocatus est. Isaac decessit annos natus centum & octoginta. At Esau potens divitiis erat, uxoribus sibi etiam e Chananæorū gente assumtis; cuius progeniem in hoc tam precifo opere inferendā non putavi. Siquis studiosior erit, ad ori-gines revertatur. Post excessum patris, Iacob in solo eo, in quo Isaac vixerat, com-morabatur. Filii ejus aliquantū ab eo, pa-scui gratia, cum gregibus secesserant: Ioseph tamen ac Benjamin parvus domi re-manserant. Carus admodum Ioseph patri, obq; id invisus fratribus: simul, quia frequentib. ejus somniis majorem cum omnibus futurum portēdi videbatur. Igitur ad insipiciendos greges, revisendo fratres a patre missus, opportunus injuriæ fuit. Namq; viso fratre, consilium necis ejus ceperunt. Sed obsistente Ruben, cuius tanto facinore abhorrebat animus, in lacum demisdemisus, mox suadente Iuda deduĉti ad mitius consilium, negotiatoribus eum, qui tum Aegyptum petebant, vendiderunt, atque ab his Potifari praeposito Pharaonis traditus est. Per idem tempus Iudas, Iacob filius, Suam Chananaeam in matrimonium assumsit. Ex qua tres filios sustulit, Her, Onan, Selam. Sed Her Thamar connubio sociatur. Quo mortuo, Onā fratris uxorem accepit. Qui, quia spermatain terram effuderet, extinctus a Domino refertur. Tum Thamar meretricio habitu af- sumpto socero mistaest, exque eo gemi-nos edidit. In partu autem illo mirabile fuit, quod cum prodeunti puero ad dignoscendum, qui prius nasceretur, obstetrix manum ejus cocco illigasset, reduĉtus in alvum matris puer, postero die editus est. Nomen infantibus Phares & Zara inditum. At Ioseph, cum benigne a curatore regio, qui eum pretio acceperat, haberetur, domumque ejus & familiam procuraret, decorus ipse insigni specie uxoris domini oculos in se converterat. Cumque amore ipsius deperiret, appeti-tum saepius nec acquiescentem sibi, falso scelere infamat: ac viro quaeritur stuprum sibi intentatum. Ita Ioseph in carcerem est coniectus. Erant in eadem custodia minis-tri regis duo, qui cum somnia sua Ioseph retulissent, futura ex somnio coniectans, unum eorum poenas capite luiturum, alium absolvendum pronuntiavit. Atq; ita accidit. Igitur post biennium somnium regi obiectum est. Quod cum a prudentibus Aegyptiorum non posset absolvi, mi-nifter regis ille carcere exemptus, regem admonet, Ioseph esse mirum somniorum interpretem. Ita Ioseph solvitur. Interpretatusque est regi somnium: septem annis proximis maximam frugum ubertatem futuram, consequentibus inopiam. Quo metu rex perculsus, videns divinum in Ioseph spiritum, rei eum annonariae praefecit, aequato secum imperio. Tum Ioseph abundantibus per totam Aegyptum frumentis, magnam copiam congessit: multiplicatisq; horreis, adversus futuram famem consuluerat. Ea tempestate ipsius atq; salus Aegypti in illo sita erat. Per idem tempus vero duos ex Asenech filios genuit, Manassen & Ephrem. Ipse autem, cum summam a rege potestatem accepit, erat annorum xxx. Nam a fratribus se-ptendeprendecim annos natus, venundatus est. Interea rebus in Agypto aduersus famem bene compositus, orbem terrae gravis fru-menti inopia quatiebat. Qua necessitate compulsus Iacob, filios in Aegyptum misit, Benjamin tantum secum domi retento. Igitur Ioseph rerum potentem, penes quem annonae arbitrium erat, fratres adeunt & more regio adorant. Quibus ille visis, calide agnitionem dissimulas, hostiliter eos venisse, & subdole loca explorare arguebat. Angebatur autem quod Benjamin fratrem non videbat. Res ergo in id deduc-ta, ut præsentiam ejus pollicerentur: nimirum ut ex eo quæreretur, an isti exploran-di causa Aegyptum intrassent. Ad promissi autem fidem Simeo obses traditur, ipsis frumentum gratis datum. Rursum igitur reuertentes, Benjamin, ut convenerat, deduxerunt. Tum se cognoscedum[?] lo-seph fratribus præbuit, non sine pudore male merentium. Ita eos oneratos frumen-to multisque donatos domum remisit, præmonens quinque adhuc annos famem futuram: cum patre atque omni progenie ac familia ad se commigrarent. Igitur Iacob in Aegyptum descendit, Aegyptiis admodum lætantibus, gaudente rege, benigne a filio susceptus. Id gestum anno ætatis iacob centesimo & tricesimo: a diluvio autem anno Mccc & lx. Cæterum ab eo tempore quo Abrahã in terra Chanaanæorum consedit, in id quod Iacob Ægyptum ingressus est, referuntur anni CCxv. Igitur Iacob septimo & decimo anno quâ Ægypto advenerat, urgente morbo, Ioseph filium obtestatur, corpus sepulcro suo redderet. Tum Ioseph patri benedicendos filios suos obtulit: quibus benedictis cum tamē benedictionis merito maiori minorem præposuisset, filios omnes benedictione lustravit. Decessit autē annos natus cxLvii. Funus magnifice curatum. Corpus in sepulcro maiorū Ioseph condidit. Fratres post patris obitum pro conscientia paventes, benigne habuit. Decessit autem Ioseph ipse ætatis anno decimo & centesimo. Hebræi igitur qui in Ægyptum devenerant, incredibile memoratu est, quam cito numero auctifint, multiplicataque progenie Ægyptum repleverint. Sed defuncto rege, qui eos ob meritū Ioseph benigne fovebat, succes-tium regū imperio deprimebantur. Nam &c. & opus durum aedificandarum civitatum eis impositum: & quia jam multitudo abundans metuebatur, ne quandoq; libertatem armis vindicarent, parvulos recens editos aquis mergere edicto regio cogebatur. Nec dissimulare cruentum imperium licebat. Qua tepestate filia Pharaonis infantem in flumine repertum nutriedum pro filio curavit: nomē puero Moyses dedit. Moyses hic, cum viriles annos ageret, conspicatus Hebraeu ab Aegyptio pulsari, permotus dolore, fratre ab injuria vindicans, Aegyptium calce percussum interemit. Mox supplicium e facto metuens, in terra Madian profugit: & apud Iethro sacerdotem regionis illius diversatus, filia ejus Sephoram in matrimonium accepit, exq; ea duos filios Gerlom & Eliefer suscepit. Hoc tractu temporum Iob fuit, legem naturæ & agnitione Dei, & omnem justitiam complexus, praedives opibus: atque eo illustrior, quod his neq; integris corruptus, neque amissis depravatus est. Nam cum per diabolum exutus bonis, filiis etiam esset orbatus, ad extremum diris ulceribus affectus, non potuit vinci, ut præ doloris impatientia aliqua in parte peccas Mercedem deniq; divini testimonii consecutus, sanitati redditus, omnia quæ amiserat, in duplum recepit. At Hebræi multiplicato servitutis malo pressi, que telis in cælum cõversi, spem auxilij a Deo exspectabant. Tum Moysi pascenti oves, repere rubus ardere visa: flammis tamen, quod erat mirabilius, innoxiis. Qua novitate obstupefactus, rubo propriusaccessit, statimque ad eum istiusmodi fere verbis Deus locutus est; Dominum se esse Abra-am, Isaac & Iacob: quorum progeniem, Aegyptiorum dominatione depressam, ereptam malis cupiat, iter ergo suscipe-ret ad regem Aegypti, ducemq; se populi in libertatem restituendi præstaret. Cun-ctantem potestate confirmat, virtutem ei signorum faciendorum impertiens. Ita Moyses in Aegyptum profectus, signis prius apud suos editis, assumpto fratre Aaron, regem adiit, missum se a Deo prodit, verbisq; se Dei dicere, populum Hebræum uti dimitteret. At ille negas se Dominum nosse, parere imperio abnuebat. Cumq; Moyses in testimonium mandatorum Dei, ex virga draconem fecisset, mox aquas omnes in sanguinem convertisset, tetamq; terram ranis opplesset: facientibus similia Chaldæis, magicas esse artes, quæ- cunq; per Moysen fierent, potius quaDei[?] virtute, pronunciabat, donec superductis ciniphibus terra oppleta est, Chaldæis fa- tentibus majestate divina ista fieri. Tum rex malo coactus, advocato ad se Moyse & Aaron, dat populo discedendi potestatem, modo ut superductam cladem averterent. Sed ubi clades exempta est, impotens sui animus, in se reversus, exire, ut cō-venerat, Israelitas non patiebatur. Ad extremum, decē plagis corporis & regni sui contusus & evictus est. Sed prius quam Aegypto populus est egressus, mandatis Domini instruitur, rudis adhuc temporum, mensem illum, qui tum erat, primum omnium mensium esse recognosceret: sacrificium autem diei illius in solennitatem consequentium saeculorum ita esse celebrandum, ut quartadecima die mensis agnus immaculatus anniculus victima cedere- tur: ejusdem sanguine postes illinerētur: carnem penitus exedēdam, os autem non conterendum: septem diebus fermento abstinerent, azymis uterentur, ritumque hunc posteris tradērent. Ita populus eGreslus,dives suis copiis,& Aegypti spoli-is cumulatior, cujus numerus ex quinq; & septuaginta Hebræis, qui primum Ae-gyptum descederat, ad millia virorum sex-centa pervenerant: ab eo autem quo pri-mum Abraham terram Chananæorū ac-cesserat, anno tricesimo & quadringente-simo: a diluvio aut, mille quingentis qui-q; & septuaginta. Igitur propere egressis, columna nubis interdiu, noctu columna ignis præferebatur. Sed cum obinterje-ctum sinum rubri maris, præter terrā Phi-listim viaduceret, ne postea Hebræis {*}ere-mum aspectantibus[?] redeundi in Aegy-ptum continentibus terris noto itinere fa-cultas panderetur, nutu Dei aversi,in ru-brum[?] mare illati sunt, castraq;ibi cunctan-tes constituerunt. Quod ubi regi nuncia-tum est, Hebræum populū viæ errore {b}in objectum mare devenisse, nullum ei esse exitum obsistente elemēto, furens animi, quo angebatur, tot hominū millia regno suo & potestati decedere, exercitum pro-pere educit, jamque eminus arma signaq; & protentæ patentibus late campis acies visebantur:cum Hebræis metu trepidis & cælum aspectatibus, Moyses a Deo moni-tus, tus,percussum virga mare discidit. Ita po-pulo cedentibus in latere aquis, velut in continenti,iter pervium fuit. Nec cunctatus rex AEgyptius cedetes insequi,mare,qua patebat,ingressus: mox coeuntibus aquis, cum omni exercitu deletus est. Tunc Moyses incolumitate suorum, exitio ho-stium virtuteque exultans canticum Do-mino cecinit: idemq; omnis turba virilis ac muliebris sexus fecit. {a}Sed ingressus e-remũ,cum jam per triduum iter agerent, aquae penuria urgebat, repertaq; ob ama-ritudinem usui non erat. At tum primum impotentis populi contumacia apparuit, jamq; in Moysen ferebatur cum edoctus a Deo,lignum aquis intulit,cujus hæc vis fuit, ut dulcem saporem fluentis redderet. Exin promotum agmen,apud Elim duodecim fontibus aquarum & septua-ginta arboribus palmarum repertis, con-sedit. Rursum populus famem conquerens,Moysen increpabat, AEgypti servi-tiū cum saturitate ventris desiderans,tum grex coturnicum superne missus castra opplevit.Postero autè dic animadvertunt, qui extra castra processerant, parvis qui- bufdam siliquis oppletum solum: quarū species in modum coriandri feminis gla- cialialbedine[?] erat, ut crebro hybernis mę- sibus superductis pruinis tegi terram vi- demus. Tum per Moysen populus admo- netur, panem hunc eis munere missum Dei, unumquemq; in id paratis vasculis tantum usurpare debere, quantum in dię[?] unū pro numero singulis fatis esset; sexto tamen die, quia Sabbato colligi non lice- ret, duplum præsumerent. Verum popu-lus, ut semper parum dicto addiens, more humani ingenii, non refrenavit cupidita. tem, ex reconditis in posterum quoq; di- em consulens. Sed reposita, fœtore diro, in vermes effervescebat; cum die sexto in Sabbatum reservata, integra permaneret. Hoc Hebraei per xl. annos cibo sunt usi, cujus sapor melli proximus. nomen Ma- na traditur. In testimonium autem divini muneris, reservasse Moyses gomor ple- num in vase aureo dicitur. Inde progres- sus populus, cum aquę penuria tetaretur, ægre ab exitio ducis temperabat. Tum Moyses mandante Domino, apud locum, cui Oreb nomen est, yirga petram percuti- ens, large aquæ copiam fecit. Sed ubi Ra- phidim perventum, Amalechitæ populū incursiincursionibus vastabant. Moyses suis in prælium eductis, cum Iesum bellantibus præfecisset, assumpto Aaro & Vr, specta-tor pugnæ futurus, simul precandi Deum gratia monte conscendit. Sed cum dubio eventu acies concurrissent, Moysi precibus victor Iesus, hostes in noctē cecidit. Peridem tempus, Iethro Moysi locer, cum filia Sephora, quæ Moysi nupta, proficiscente in Aegyptum viro, domi resederat liberisq; ejus, cognitis rebus quæ per Moy-sen gerebantur, ad eum venit. Hujus con-filio Moyses ordines populi distribuit tri-bunos centurionesq; & decuriones præ-ficiens, necessarium disciplinæ ritum po-steris tradidit. Iethro in patriam regressus, Exin ad Sinam montem perventum, ibi Moyses a Domino monetur, populus ut sanctificaretur, auditurus Dei voces, idq; sollicite curatum. Sed ubi Deus monti in-stitit, validis tubarum clangoribus aer quatiebatur, crassæq; nubes crebris cum fulminibus advolvebantur. Sed Moyses & Aaro in montis cacumine Dominum propter, populus circa montis ima cósti-tit. Ita lex lata multiplex & copiosa Dei verbis, & sæpe repetita: cujus siquis erit curiosior, fontem ipsum adeat, nos eam breviter perstringimus. Non erit, inquit, tibi Dei alieni praeter me: Non facies tibi idolum: Non sumes nomen Dei tui in vanum: Sabbato nullum opus facies: Honorifica patrem tuum, & matrem tuam: Non occides: Non moechaberis: Non furtum facies: Non falsum testimonium dices adversus proximum tuum: Non concupisces quidquam proximi tui. His a Deo dictis, cum tabernacula circumstreperent, lampades ardescerent, montem fumus obtegeret, populus prae timore inhorruit, verba Dei non sustinens: poposcitque [?] a Moyse, ut ipsi tantum loqueretur Dominus, atque ita audita ad populum referret. Edicta autem Dei ad Moysen istiusmodi sunt: He-braeus puer pecunia emptus, sex annis serviet, post haec liber erit: Sponte autem permanenti in servitute, auris forabitur. Qui hominem occiderit, capite poenas luet: Qui imprudens, rite exul erit. Qui patrem matremve pulsaverit, convitiumque eis dixerit, capitali supplicio afficitor. Si quis Hebraeum subreptum vendiderit, morti dabitur. Si quis servum proprium fer-vamve percusserit, exque eo ictu obierit, reus judicio fiet. Si quis partum non deformatum mulieri excusserit,{*} neci dabi-tur. Si quis servo oculum aut dentem ex-torserit, servus vindicta liberabitur. Tau-rus si hominem occiderit, lapidabitur. Si dominus sciens bestiæ vitiū, non consuluerit,&ipse lapidabitur: aut pretio se redimet: in quantum accusator poposcerit.
units.tr: Before this there had been no fighting among mortals. But the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah and of the neighbouring regions rose up in arms against those who were attacking their neighbours. In the first charge they were routed and gave up the victory. Then the victors plundered Sodom, the spoils went to the enemy, and Lot was led off into captivity. When Abram learned of this, he quickly armed his servants, three hundred and eighteen in number, and pursued the kings, who were elated by their victory, and drove them in flight, stripping them of their spoils and arms. Then he was blessed by the priest Melchizedek, and he gave him a tithe of the spoils. He restored the rest to those from whom it had been taken. At the same time the Lord spoke to Abram, promising to multiply his seed like the sand of the sea and the stars of heaven, and foretold that his seed would be sojourners, and that his descendants would serve for four hundred years in a land not their own and afterwards be restored to freedom. Then the name of Abram and of his wife was changed by the addition of one letter, so that Abram is now called Abraham and Sarai Sarah. I do not intend in this work to set out the hidden meaning of this. At the same time the law of circumcision was imposed on Abraham. He had a son, Ishmael, by his maidservant; and when he was ninety-nine years old and his wife ninety, the Lord, who had come to him with two angels, promised that they would have a son, Isaac. Then the angels were sent to Sodom, and they found Lot sitting in the gate. When he, supposing them to be men, had received them as guests and had them to supper at his house, the wicked young men of the town demanded the new guests for immoral purposes. Lot offered his daughters in place of the guests, but they would not agree, since their desire was rather for what was unlawful, and Lot himself was being dragged towards the outrage. The angels quickly rescued him from the injury and struck the eyes of the shameless men with blindness. Then Lot, having been told by the guests that the town was to be destroyed, quickly left it with his wife and daughters; yet it was forbidden to them to look back. But the wife, not obeying the command (a human fault, which is with difficulty avoided), turned her eyes back and was at once changed into a pillar. But Sodom was burned with fires from heaven. Lot's daughters, thinking that the human race had perished, made their father drunk and lay with him, and from this Moab and Ammon were born. At about the same time, when Abraham was a hundred years old, Isaac was born. Then Sarah drove out the maidservant by whom Abraham had had a son; she is said to have lived in the desert with her son, protected by the Lord's care. Not long after, the Lord, testing Abraham's faith, demanded that his son Isaac be offered to him as a sacrifice by his father. Abraham, without hesitation, laid the boy on the altar and drew out his knife, when a voice was sent from heaven telling him to spare the boy, and a ram was at hand as the victim. When the sacrifice was completed, the Lord spoke to Abraham, promising what he had already pledged. Sarah died at the age of a hundred and twenty-seven and was buried by her husband's care in Hebron, a town of the Canaanites, for Abraham was then living there. Then Abraham, seeing that his son Isaac was of a young age (for he was then forty years old), ordered his servant to seek a wife for him, but from that tribe and land from which he himself seemed to come; only, he was to bring the girl he found into the land of the Canaanites, and not to take her back to the homeland for the sake of a wife. And so that the servant might carry out these commands diligently, he gave an oath, the servant touching his master's thigh. So the servant set out for Mesopotamia and came to the town of Nahor, Abraham's brother; he came into the house of Bethuel the Syrian, the son of Nahor, and seeing his daughter Rebekah, a beautiful maiden, he asked for her and brought her to his master. After this Abraham took a wife named Keturah, who in Chronicles is called a concubine; he also had sons by her. But to Isaac, the son of Sarah, he gave his property; and to the sons he had by his concubines he gave gifts, and so they were separated from Isaac. Abraham died when he had completed a hundred and seventy-five years, and his body was laid in the tomb beside his wife Sarah. But Rebekah, long barren, through her husband's constant prayers to the Lord, bore twins about twenty years after the day of her marriage; they are said often to have leapt about in the mother's womb. And by the Lord's answer it was said that two peoples were foretold in them, and that the greater would be made subject to the lesser. The first-born was called Esau, the younger was named Jacob. At that time a severe famine had come upon the land. Under this necessity Isaac went to Abimelech, king of Gerar, having been warned by the Lord not to go down into Egypt; and the possession of that whole land was promised to him, and there he was blessed. But when he had multiplied in flocks and all his property, envy stirring, he was driven out by the inhabitants; driven away, he settled at the Well of the Oath. Then, when he was old and his eyes were dim, and he was about to bless his son Esau, at the counsel of his mother Rebekah, Jacob offered himself to be blessed in place of his brother. Thus Jacob was set before his brother, to be worshipped by the princes and peoples. Esau, enraged by these things, plotted his brother's death. Through fear of this, Jacob, urged by his mother, fled into Mesopotamia; he was told by his father to take a wife from the house of Laban, his mother's brother. They cared that, while living in foreign lands, he should nonetheless take a wife from his own family. So Jacob set out into Mesopotamia, and he is said to have seen the Lord in a dream; and therefore, holding that place of the dream sacred, he took a stone from it and vowed that if he returned in prosperity it would be a house of the Lord for him, and that he would give the Lord a tenth of all that should be acquired for him. From there he went to Laban, his mother's brother; Laban, recognising him as his sister's son, received him kindly into his house. Laban had two daughters, Leah and Rachel. But Leah was said to be uglier in the eyes, and Rachel beautiful. Jacob, captivated by her beauty, burned with love for the maiden, and asking her from her father in marriage, he bound himself to seven years of service. But when the time was fulfilled, Leah was put in his place, and again he was made to serve seven years, and Rachel was given to him. But we are told that Rachel was long barren and Leah fruitful. The names of the sons Jacob had by Leah are these: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah. By the maidservant of Leah came Gad and Asher. By the maidservant of Rachel, Dan and Naphtali were born. And Rachel, her hope of childbirth now gone, bore Joseph. Then Jacob, wishing to return to his father, when his father-in-law Laban had given him a share of the flocks as wages for his service, and thinking his father-in-law no longer fair to him on account of these things, and suspecting deceit from him, departed secretly about the twenty-first year after he had come. Rachel, without her husband's knowledge, stole her father's household idols; for this injury Laban pursued his son-in-law, but when he did not find the idols, peace was made and he returned, having first earnestly pleaded with his son-in-law not to bring wives over his daughters. From there Jacob went on, and he is said to have seen the angels and the camp of the Lord. But when he intended to pass by the region of Edom, which his brother Esau inhabited, he first sent messengers and gifts, and he sought to find out about his brother, whom he suspected. Then Esau came out to meet his brother; yet Jacob did not trust himself further to his brother. But on the day before the brothers were to meet, the Lord, having taken on a human form, is said to have wrestled with Jacob. And although he had prevailed against the Lord, he did not fail to know that he was not mortal; he begged to be blessed by him. Then his name was changed by God, so that from Jacob he was called Israel. But when the other in turn asked the Lord's name, he answered that it should not be asked (because it was wonderful). From the wrestling, too, the hollow of Jacob's thigh was numbed. Therefore Israel, turning aside from his brother's house, moved his company on to Shechem, a town of the Shechemites; and there, having bought a plot for a price, he set up a tent for himself. Hamor, the prince, ruled over this town, and his son Shechem subjected Dinah, the daughter of Jacob born of Leah, to rape. When this was concealed, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, killed all the males of the town by treachery, and bravely avenged their sister's injury; the town was plundered by the sons of Jacob, and all the booty was carried off. It is said that Jacob took this very hard. Soon, warned by the Lord, he went to Bethel, and there he set up an altar to the Lord. From there he pitched his tent in a part of the tower of Eder. Rachel died in childbirth, and the boy was called Benjamin. Isaac died at the age of a hundred and eighty. But Esau was powerful in riches, having also taken wives from the Canaanite people; I have not thought it right to set out his progeny in this very brief work. If anyone is more eager, let him go back to the origins. After his father's death, Jacob stayed in the same place where Isaac had lived. His sons had gone off some distance from him with the flocks, for the sake of pasture; but Joseph and the little Benjamin had remained at home. Joseph was very dear to his father, and for that reason hated by his brothers; also, because by his frequent dreams it seemed to be foretold that he would be greater than all of them. So, sent by his father to look after the flocks and to visit his brothers, he became an opportunity for injury. For when they saw him, they plotted to kill him. But Reuben, whose mind shrank from so great a crime, resisted; he let him down into a pit; soon Judah, persuading them to a milder plan, sold him to merchants who were then going to Egypt, and by them he was handed over to Potiphar, the captain of Pharaoh. About the same time Judah, Jacob's son, took a Canaanite woman as his wife. From her he had three sons, Er, Onan, and Shelah. Er was joined in marriage to Tamar; when he died, Onan took his brother's wife. Because he spilled his seed on the ground, he is said to have been killed by the Lord. Then Tamar, taking the appearance of a prostitute, lay with her father-in-law, and from him she bore twins. In that birth there was something wonderful: when the midwife had tied a scarlet thread on the hand of the boy who was coming forth, so that it could be known which was born first, the boy was drawn back into the mother's womb, and was born the next day. The infants were named Perez and Zerah. But Joseph, while he was kindly treated by the royal steward who had bought him for a price, and while he managed his master's house and household, had turned the eyes of his master's wife upon himself by his outstanding looks and handsome appearance. And when she was consumed with love for him, and often sought his favours, and he would not consent, she slandered him with a false crime, accusing him to her husband of an attempted rape. So Joseph was thrown into prison. There were two royal servants in the same prison, who, when they had told Joseph their dreams, he interpreted them from the dreams: one of them, he declared, would pay the penalty with his head, the other would be acquitted. And so it came about. Then, after two years, the king's dream was brought to his notice. When the wise men of the Egyptians could not explain it, that royal servant, released from prison, reminded the king that Joseph was a wonderful interpreter of dreams. So Joseph was released. He interpreted the king's dream for him: that for the next seven years there would be the greatest abundance of crops, and that after them there would be scarcity. Struck with fear by this, the king, seeing the divine spirit in Joseph, placed him in charge of the grain supply, with power equal to his own. Then, with grain abundant throughout all Egypt, Joseph gathered a great store, and having multiplied the granaries, he provided against the coming famine. At that time the well-being and very survival of Egypt depended on him. About the same time he had two sons by Asenath, Manasseh and Ephraim. He himself was thirty years old when he received supreme power from the king. For he had been sold at the age of seventeen by his brothers. Meanwhile, while affairs in Egypt were well arranged against the famine, a grievous shortage of grain was shaking the whole world. Under this necessity Jacob sent his sons into Egypt, keeping only Benjamin at home. So they came before Joseph, the man in power, in whose hands the decision on the grain supply lay, and they bowed to him in royal fashion. When he saw them, he cunningly hid his recognition of them, and charged them with having come as enemies, and with spying out the country by stealth. But he was troubled that he did not see his brother Benjamin. The matter was therefore brought to this point, that they promised to produce him: namely, that from him it might be asked whether those men had entered Egypt for the purpose of spying. As a pledge of their promise, Simeon was handed over as a hostage, while grain was given to them free. So, returning again, they brought Benjamin, as had been agreed. Then Joseph made himself known to his brothers, not without shame for those who had deserved ill. So he sent them home laden with grain and given many gifts, warning them that there would still be five more years of famine; they were to move with their father and all their offspring and household to join him. So Jacob went down into Egypt, the Egyptians rejoicing greatly, and the king glad, and he was kindly received by his son. This happened in the hundred and thirtieth year of Jacob's life; and from the Flood it was the year 1660. Moreover, from the time when Abraham settled in the land of the Canaanites to when Jacob entered Egypt, two hundred and fifteen years are counted. So Jacob, in the seventeenth year after he came to Egypt, pressed by illness, adjured Joseph his son that he would return his body to his tomb. Then Joseph brought his sons to their father to be blessed; and when, although by the merit of the blessing, he had placed the younger before the elder, he blessed all the sons. He died at the age of a hundred and forty-seven. His funeral was celebrated with great honour. Joseph laid his body in the tomb of his ancestors. After their father's death, the brothers, fearing for their conscience, were treated kindly by him. Joseph himself died in the hundred and tenth year of his life. Therefore the Hebrews who had come into Egypt multiplied in number, it is incredible to relate, how quickly, and filled Egypt with their multiplied offspring. But when the king who had kindly favoured them on account of Joseph's merit had died, under a successor's rule they were oppressed. For both the hard labour of building cities was laid upon them, and since their growing multitude was feared, lest one day they should avenge their freedom by arms, they were compelled by royal edict to drown their newly born infant sons in the waters. Nor was it permitted to disguise this bloody rule. At that time the daughter of Pharaoh, having found an infant in the river, cared for him to be nursed as her own son; she gave the boy the name Moses. This Moses, when he had reached manhood, seeing a Hebrew being struck by an Egyptian, moved by grief, defended his brother from the injury and killed the Egyptian by striking him down. Soon, fearing punishment for the deed, he fled into the land of Midian; and staying with Jethro, the priest of that region, he took his daughter Zipporah in marriage, and by her he had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. About this time lived Job, who embraced the law of nature and the knowledge of God and all righteousness, very rich in resources; and he was the more distinguished because he was neither corrupted when he possessed these things nor depraved when he lost them. For although, stripped of his goods by the devil, and bereaved even of his sons, and at last afflicted with dreadful ulcers, he could not be overcome, so that through impatience of pain he sinned in any respect. At last, having received the reward of the divine testimony, he was restored to health and received back twice over all that he had lost. But the Hebrews, pressed by the multiplied evil of their slavery, and turning their eyes to heaven with groans, awaited the help of God. Then to Moses, as he was tending the sheep, a bush appeared to burn; yet, what was more wonderful, it was not harmed by the flames. Astonished by this strange sight, he drew nearer to the bush, and at once God spoke to him in words of about this kind: that he was the Lord of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; that he desired to rescue from evils their descendants, who were oppressed by the domination of the Egyptians; so he was to take his way to the king of Egypt and to undertake to lead the people back into freedom. When he hesitated, God strengthened him with authority, granting him the power of performing signs. So Moses went into Egypt, and after first doing signs among his own people, taking his brother Aaron with him, he approached the king, declared that he had been sent by God, and said in God's words that he should let the Hebrew people go. But the king denied that he knew the Lord and refused to obey his command. And when Moses, as a token of God's commands, had turned a rod into a serpent, and soon afterwards had turned all the waters into blood, and had filled the whole land with frogs, the Chaldeans, doing similar things, declared that whatever was done through Moses was magic arts rather than the power of God; until, when lice had been brought over and covered the land, the Chaldeans confessed that these things were being done by the divine majesty. Then the king, forced by the plague, summoned Moses and Aaron and gave the people permission to depart, provided they would avert the disaster that had been brought on. But when the calamity was removed, his unrestrained spirit, coming to itself again, did not allow the Israelites to leave as had been agreed. At last he was worn down and defeated by ten plagues on his body and his kingdom. But before the people went out of Egypt, they were instructed by the Lord's commands—the people being still rough in their understanding of time—to recognise that the month then current was the first of all months; and that the sacrifice of that day was to be celebrated in solemn observance for all following ages in this way: on the fourteenth day of the month an unblemished lamb of one year was to be offered as the victim; its blood was to be smeared on the doorposts; its flesh was to be eaten entirely, but its bones were not to be broken; for seven days they were to abstain from leaven and eat unleavened bread, and they were to hand down this rite to their descendants. So the people went out, rich in their resources and loaded with the spoils of Egypt, and their number, from the seventy-five Hebrews who had first gone down into Egypt, had grown to six hundred thousand men. And this was in the four hundred and thirtieth year from when Abraham first came to the land of the Canaanites; from the Flood, it was two thousand five hundred and seventy-five years. So, the people being hurried out, a pillar of cloud went before them by day, and a pillar of fire by night. But when God led them round by the bay of the Red Sea, past the land of the Philistines, lest afterwards a way back into Egypt should be opened to the Hebrews by a known route, if they were looking at the desert and had continuous land to return by, they were turned aside by God's nod and brought to the Red Sea, and there they set up camp, hesitating. When this was reported to the king, that the Hebrew people had come by a mistake of their way to the sea which lay before them, that there was no way out because the element barred the path, he, raging in mind, and grieving that so many thousands of men should depart from his kingdom and power, quickly led out his army; and now the weapons and standards, and battle lines spreading over the wide-open plains, could be seen from afar. While the Hebrews, trembling with fear and gazing at the sky, were in alarm, Moses, warned by God, struck the sea with his rod and divided it. So, with the waters standing up on either side, a passable way opened, as if on dry land. And the Egyptian king did not hesitate to pursue them as they went, entering the sea where it lay open; but soon, as the waters closed back, he was destroyed with his whole army. Then Moses, exulting in the safety of his own people and the destruction of their enemies and their virtue, sang a song to the Lord, and every crowd of men and women did the same. But when they had entered the desert, and had already been travelling for three days, a lack of water pressed them; and the water they found was bitter and so not useful. Then for the first time the obstinacy of the unrestrained people appeared, and complaints were already being made against Moses; but, instructed by God, he put a piece of wood into the waters, and its power was this: that it made the flowing water sweet to taste. Thereafter, the column moved on; and at Elim, where twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees were found, it settled.
