Again the people, complaining of hunger, rebuked Moses, longing for the slavery of Egypt together with the fullness of their bellies; then a flock of quails sent down from above filled the camp. On the next day those who had gone outside the camp noticed that the ground was covered with small seed-pods, whose form, like coriander seeds, was white like frost, as we often see the earth covered with frost when it has been spread over it in the winter months. Then the people were instructed through Moses that this bread had been sent to them as a gift from God, and that each person should gather only as much of it, in vessels prepared for the purpose, as was enough for each for one day, according to the number in each family; but on the sixth day, since it was not lawful to gather it on the Sabbath, they were to take double. But the people, as always adding little to what was said, in the manner of the human mind did not restrain their greed, and gathered from the stores for the following day too. But what was kept over bred vermin with a dreadful stench; whereas what had been kept for the Sabbath on the sixth day remained intact. The Hebrews ate this food for forty years; its taste was closest to honey. It is called by the name manna. As a memorial of the divine gift, Moses is said to have kept a full omer in a golden vessel. Then the people moved on, and when they were tormented by lack of water, they were scarcely restrained from destroying their leader. Then Moses, at the Lord's command, struck a rock with his rod at the place called Horeb, and made a large supply of water flow. But when they came to Rephidim, the Amalekites attacked the people with raids and laid waste. Moses, leading his men out to battle, placed Joshua in command of the fighters, and taking Aaron and Hur with him, he went up a mountain to watch the battle and at the same time to pray to God. But when the battle lines had clashed with a doubtful outcome, by Moses' prayers Joshua was victorious, and he drove the enemy to the night. At the same time Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, came to him with Zipporah, the wife whom Moses had married, who had stayed at home when her husband set out for Egypt, and with her sons, having learned what had been done through Moses. At his counsel Moses arranged the orders of the people, appointing tribunes, centurions, and decurions, and he handed down to posterity the necessary forms of discipline. Jethro returned to his homeland. Then they came to Mount Sinai, and there Moses was warned by the Lord that the people should be sanctified, that they might hear God's voices, and this was carefully carried out. But when God came down upon the mountain, the air was shaken by the loud blasts of trumpets, and thick clouds rolled in with frequent flashes of lightning. But Moses and Aaron stood near the Lord on the peak of the mountain, and the people stood round the foot of the mountain. So the law was given, manifold and full, in God's words, and often repeated; if anyone is more curious about it, let him go to the source itself; we will touch on it only briefly. "You shall have no other gods before me." "You shall not make for yourself an idol." "You shall not take the name of your God in vain." "On the Sabbath you shall do no work." "Honour your father and your mother." "You shall not kill." "You shall not commit adultery." "You shall not steal." "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour." "You shall not covet anything that belongs to your neighbour." When these things had been spoken by God, the tents resounded, the lamps blazed, smoke covered the mountain, the people shuddered with fear, not able to endure God's words; and they asked Moses that the Lord should speak only to him, and that he should then report to the people what he had heard. The commands of God to Moses are of this kind: "A Hebrew boy bought for money shall serve for six years; after this he shall be free. But if a man willingly remains in servitude, his ear shall be bored through." "Whoever kills a man shall pay with his life; but whoever kills by accident shall properly be an exile." "Whoever strikes his father or mother and speaks abusively to them shall be punished with death." "If anyone steals a Hebrew and sells him, he shall be put to death." "If anyone strikes his own male or female slave, and the slave dies from the blow, he shall be liable to judgment." "If anyone knocks out a woman's unformed child, he shall be given to death." "If anyone knocks out the eye or tooth of a slave, the slave shall be freed as compensation." "If an ox kills a man, it shall be stoned." "If its owner, knowing the beast's vice, has not taken precautions, he shall himself be stoned, or he shall redeem himself with a payment, as much as the accuser demands."

units.la: Si servū taurus occiderit, in trigita{b} drag-mis pecunia domino numerabitur. Si quis defossum lacū non cooperuerit, pe-cufq; in lacum ceciderit, pretium pecudis domino dabit. Si taurus alterius taurum occiderit pecus venundabitur, pretiumq; domini partietur, peremtum etiam divi-dent. Quod si dominus vitium tauri sci-ens non consuluerit, tauro dabit. Si quis{c} vitulum subripuerit, quinque restituet.
units.tr: If a bull gores a manservant, thirty drachmas shall be counted out to the master. If anyone leaves a pit uncovered, and an animal falls into it, he shall pay the beast's price to its owner. If one bull gores another bull, the living bull shall be sold and the price divided between the owners; the dead one they shall divide as well. But if the owner knowingly failed to guard against the bull's vice, he shall give ox for ox. If anyone steals a calf, he shall restore five.

units.la: Si ovē[?] subripuerit, quadrupli poena erit. Si viva penes abactorem pecora reperien-tur,dupla restituet. Nocturnū furem occi-di licet, diurnū non licet. cuius pecora alterius fata depaverint, dominus pecoris eversa restituet. Si depositū perierit, is penes quem depositum fuit, jurabit nihil se dolo{d}egisse. Fur inventus duplū dabit.
units.tr: If he steals a sheep, the penalty is fourfold. If the sheep are found alive in the thief's keeping, he shall restore double. A thief may be killed at night, but not by day. Whose beasts have eaten up another's fields, the owner of the beasts shall make restitution for what was ruined. If a deposit has perished, the one with whom it was deposited shall swear that he has not acted fraudulently. A thief who is caught shall pay double.

units.la: Commodatum pecus a bestia interceptū, non restituetur. Si quis virginem corruperit, dotabit puellam & ita eam uxorem accipiet. Si pater puellae nuptias recusaverit, dotem raptor dabit. Si quis se pecudi miscuerit, mortи dabitur. Sacrificas idolis pereat. Viduam & orphanum non premendos: pauperem debitorem non perurgendum: nec ulram poscendam: Vestimentum pauperis pro pignore non accipiedum: Principem populi non increpandum, primogenita omnia Domino offerenda. Carnem a fera raptam non edendam. Coitiones in testimonium falsum, aut in quacumque malitia, non esse faciendas. Inimici pecus errans non praeteribis, sed reduces. Si animal inimici succubuisse oneri inveneris, erigere debebis. Innocentem & justum non occides. Non justificabis impiu pro muneribus. Munera non accipienda. Advenam benigne habendum. Sex diebus opus faciendum. Sabbato requiescendu. Fructus septimi anni non metendos, sed pauperibus & egenis relinquendos. Haec fere Moyses ad populu verba Dei retulit; altariuq; ex duodecim lapidibus sub monte constituit. Ac rursum montem, in quo Dominus consistebat; conscenditque adhibito secum Aaron, Nabad & Abiud, majoribus natu septuaginta. Sed hi non vocentes Dominum intueri, locum tamen, in quo Dominus stabat, viderunt; cujus mirabilis forma & claritudo eximia referetur.
units.tr: An animal lent out and killed by a wild beast shall not be restored. If anyone seduces a virgin, he shall endow the girl and take her as his wife. If the girl's father refuses the marriage, the seducer shall still give the dowry. If anyone lies with a beast, he shall be put to death. He who sacrifices to idols shall perish. The widow and the orphan are not to be oppressed; the poor debtor is not to be pressed hard, nor is interest to be demanded from him; a poor man's garment shall not be taken as a pledge; the prince of the people is not to be reviled; all firstborn are to be offered to the Lord. Flesh torn by a beast is not to be eaten. Conspiracies to bear false witness, or to do any kind of mischief, are not to be made. You shall not pass by your enemy's straying flock, but shall bring it back. If you find your enemy's animal collapsed under its burden, you must help raise it up. The innocent and the just you shall not kill. You shall not justify the wicked for gifts. Gifts are not to be accepted. The stranger is to be treated kindly. Work is to be done for six days. On the Sabbath one shall rest. The fruits of the seventh year are not to be reaped, but left for the poor and the needy. Moses delivered these words of God to the people more or less in this way, and he set up an altar of twelve stones beneath the mountain. Then he climbed the mountain again, where the Lord stood, taking with him Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders. But these did not dare to look upon the Lord, yet they did see the place where the Lord stood; its wondrous form and extraordinary brightness are reported.

units.la: Moyses autem accersitus a Domino, interiore nube, quæ circum Dominum fleterat, ingressus, quadraginta diebus totidemque noctibus ibi fuisse traditur. Quo tempore super ædificando tabernaculo atque arca, rituque sacrificandi edoctus verbis Dei est,
units.tr: Moses, however, summoned by the Lord, entered the inner cloud which had surrounded the Lord, and he is said to have been there forty days and as many nights. At that time he was instructed by God's words concerning the building of the tabernacle and the ark, and the rite of sacrifice.

units.la: Quæ ego, quia prolixa admodum videbantur, inferenda huic tam præcisio operi non putaui. Sed immorate diutius Moyse, quippe qui XL. dies apud Dominum duceret, populus desperato ejus reditu, Aaron compulit simulacra facere. Tunc ex metallis conflatis vituli caput extitit. Cui cum populus, Domini immemor, holocausta obtulisset, vinoque & vetri dediitet, despectas hæc justo dolore Deus, improbum populum, nisi a Moyse fuisset exoratus, deleret. Sed regressus Moyses, cum duas ex lapide tabulas manu Domini scriptas detulisset, populumque luxui & sacrilegio dedito deprehendisset, tabulas confregit: indignam esse gentē existimans, cui lex Domini traderetur. Multis tamē{a} increpitis, crepitos. Levitas ad se aggregavit eisdemq; praece-pit ut districtis gladiis populum cęderent. Quo impetu *xxxiii[?]. millia virorum per-empta traduntur. Tum Moyses taberna-culum extra castra constituit: quod quo-tiens fuisset ingressus, columna nubis a-stare pro foribus visebatur, coramque ad Moysen Dominus loquebatur. Poscente autem Moyse, ut Dominum in majestate propria videret: responsum, Formam Dei mortalibus oculis perspici non posse, po-steriora tamen ejus videre concessum: tabulęque, quas Moyses prius cōfregerat, refectæ. Sed in hoc colloquio Dei xl. die-bus diversatus apud Dominum Moyses traditur. Cumq; de monte descenderet, tabulas præferens, tanta claritudine faci-es ejus renidebat, ut intueri eum popu-lus non valeret. Sed cum mandata Dei re-laturus esset, vultum velamento obtexit, atque ita ad populum verbis Domini lo-cutus est. Hoc in loco tabernaculi interi-orum quę ejus ædificatio refertur. Quo consummato, nubes superne decidit, atq; ita tabernaculum obumbravit, ut ipsum Moysen aditu excluderet. Hæc fere duo-bus libris, Genesi atque Exodo, continen-tur. Exin Leviticus liber sequitur, in quo litandi præcepta traduntur: mandata etiam latæ superius legis adduntur, plena omnia sacerdotalibus institutis. Quæ si quis cognoscere volet, perfectius inde capiet: nos enim suscepti operis modum custodientes, solam historiam persequimur. Igitur Levi tribu in sacerdotium se-gregata, reliquæ tribus dinumeratæ, reper-ta; hominum DC & III M. Cum ergo po-pulus mannæ cibo, ut supra retulimus, u-teretur, tot tantisque beneficiis Dei, ut semper ingratus, viles, quibus in AEgypto af-sueverat, dapes desiderabat.
units.tr: Since these matters seemed very lengthy, I have not thought fit to include them in a work so concise as this. But Moses lingered longer, since he was spending forty days with the Lord; the people, despairing of his return, forced Aaron to make images. Then a calf's head emerged from the molten metals. When the people, forgetful of the Lord, had offered burnt offerings to it and given themselves over to wine and gluttony, God, indignant with a just anger at these things, would have destroyed the wicked people had Moses not appeased him. But Moses, returning, brought down the two tablets written by the hand of the Lord from the rock, and finding the people given over to luxury and sacrilege, he broke the tablets, judging the nation unworthy to receive the law of the Lord. Yet after rebuking many, he gathered the Levites to himself and ordered them to strike down the people with drawn swords. In that onslaught thirty-three thousand men are said to have been slain. Then Moses set up the tabernacle outside the camp; whenever he entered it, a pillar of cloud was seen standing before the doors, and the Lord spoke to Moses there. When Moses asked to see the Lord in his own majesty, the answer was that the form of God cannot be seen by mortal eyes, though his hinder parts might be seen; and the tablets which Moses had broken earlier were restored. But Moses is said to have stayed forty days with the Lord in this conversation. And when he came down from the mountain carrying the tablets, his face shone with such brightness that the people could not bear to look upon him. But when he was about to relay God's commands, he covered his face with a veil, and so he spoke to the people in the words of the Lord. At this point is related the inner part of the tabernacle and its construction. When this was finished, a cloud came down from above and overshadowed the tabernacle, so that it shut Moses out from entering. These things are contained in the first two books, Genesis and Exodus. Next follows the book of Leviticus, in which the precepts of sacrifice are handed down; the commands of the law already given are also added, all full of priestly institutions. Whoever wishes to learn these will get a fuller account there; for we, keeping to the scope of the work we have undertaken, pursue only the history. Therefore, when the tribe of Levi had been set apart for the priesthood and the other tribes had been numbered, there were found to be six hundred and three thousand men. Now while the people were feeding on manna, as we related above, despite so many and great benefits of God, they, ever ungrateful, longed for the cheap dishes to which they had been accustomed in Egypt.

units.la: Tum Dominus immensam copiam coturnicum castris intulit: quas cum avi-de diriperent, primoribus labiis admotis carnibus, interibant. Magnaque eo die cla-des in castris fuit, adeo ut xx. & iii. virorum millia periisse tradantur. Ita populus eo, quem desiderabat, cibo punitus est. In-de promotum agmen, & in Pharan ven-tum est, edoctusque a Domino Moyses vicinam esse terram, cujus possessionem eis promiserat Dominus: exploratoribus in eam mißis, renunciatur, felicem omni copia esse regionem: sed gentes validas, & munita ingentibus muris opida. Quod ubi populo comperrum, magna mentes omnium formido incesserat: eoque mali venrum[?], ut spreto Moysi imperio, ducem sibi constituere parárent, cujus ductu[?] in Aegyptum reverterentur. Tunc {a}Iesus & Chaleb, qui inter exploratores terræ fuerant, conscisis vestibus flentes, populum obtestantur, ne exploratoribus credant, formidolosa referentibus: se quoque una cum his fuisse, nihil metuendum in solo illo repperisse, promissis illos Dei confidere oportere, hostes prædas potius quam exitio fore. Sed gens indomita, sanis con-filiis male renitens, in perniciem {b}eorum ferebatur. Queis rebus commotus Domi-nus, partem populi hostibus cædenda ob-jecit. Exploratoribus interfectis ad vulgi formidinē, secura est eorum contumacia qui se, Dathan & Abiron ducibus, adversum Moysen & Aaro erigere conati sunt. Sed eos vivos hiatu suo terra absorbuit. Nec multo post, totius populi in Moysen & Aaron orta seditio est, adeo ut tabernaculum (quod etiam[?] nefas, nisi sacerdotibus, introire)irrumperent. Tum vero caterva-tim in eos graflata[?] mors est: momentoq; omnes interiffent, nisi Moysi precibus placatus Dominus cladem averteret. Numerus tamen peremptorum leptingenti & xiiii.[?] millia fuit. Nec multo post, ob aquae penuriā, ut jam saepius populi exorta seditio est. Tunc Moyses a Domino monitus, ut petram virga feriret, familiari sibi experimento (si quidem id jam ante fe-ciset) semel atq; iterum petram percusit, atque ita aqua effluxit. In quo quidem notatus a Domino Moyses refertur, quod per diffidentiam non nisi iterato actu aquam eduxerit. Deniq; ob hoc peccatum promissam sibi terram non ingressus est, sicut inferius ostendam. Igitur Moyses ex eo loco promovetur, cum praeter Edom agmen educere pararet, misis[?] ad regem legatis, transeundi copiam poposcit, ob jus sanguinis bello abstinendum ratus. Etenim gens illa Esau progeniesterat[?]. Sed rex supplices aspernatus transitum negavit, paratus armis contendere. Tum Moyses in Or monte iter convertit, vetita via abstinens, ne quam inter cosanguineos caulam belli praeberet. In eo quoque cursu regem gentis Chananæorum delevit. Seon quoque regem Amorrhæorum perculit, omniu- q; eorum opidis potitus est . Balan etiam & Balac reges devicit, & castra superlor- danè haud longe ab Hiericho molitus est. Tunc adversus Madianitas certatu,vi&iqs & lubacti sunt. Moyses mortuus est,cum xL.in deserto annos populo præfuisset.
units.tr: Then the Lord brought an immense flock of quails into the camp. While they greedily tore them apart, with the first bites of meat still at their lips, they perished. That day there was a great slaughter in the camp, so that twenty-three thousand men are said to have died. Thus the people were punished with the very food they desired. From there the army set out and came to Paran, and Moses, instructed by the Lord, learned that the land nearby was the one whose possession the Lord had promised them. Spies were sent into it, and they reported that the region was blessed with every abundance, but that its nations were strong and its towns fortified with huge walls. When the people learned this, great terror seized the minds of all, and it came to such a pass that, scorning Moses' command, they prepared to set up a leader for themselves, under whose guidance they might return to Egypt. Then Joshua and Caleb, who had been among the spies of the land, tore their clothes and, weeping, implored the people not to believe the spies who brought back frightening reports. They themselves had been with them, they said, and had found nothing to fear in that land; the people ought to trust in God's promises, and the enemies would be plunder rather than destruction. But the untamed people, badly resisting sound counsel, rushed on to their own ruin. Moved by this, the Lord allowed a part of the people to be cut down by the enemy. The spies were killed, and to the common dread, the rebellion of those who had risen up against Moses and Aaron under the leadership of Dathan and Abiram did not go unpunished. But the earth swallowed these men alive in its gaping mouth. Not long afterward a rebellion of the whole people against Moses and Aaron arose, so that they burst into the tabernacle, which it was a sin for anyone but the priests to enter. Then death fell upon them in droves; in a moment all would have perished, had not the Lord, appeased by Moses' prayers, turned away the plague. The number of those slain, however, was fourteen thousand seven hundred. Not long after, because of the lack of water, a rebellion of the people arose, as had happened many times before. Then Moses, warned by the Lord to strike the rock with his staff, struck the rock once and again, as he had already done before by familiar experience, and so water flowed out. In this incident Moses is reported to have been rebuked by the Lord, because through lack of faith he drew water only by a repeated action. Finally, on account of this sin, he did not enter the land promised to him, as I shall show below. Therefore Moses moved on from that place, and when he was about to lead the army past Edom, he sent envoys to the king and asked for passage, thinking that because of kinship war must be avoided. For that nation was the offspring of Esau. But the king rejected the suppliants and refused passage, ready to contend with arms. Then Moses turned his course to Mount Hor, avoiding the forbidden way, so that he would not give cause for war among his kinsmen. On that journey too he destroyed the king of the Canaanite people. He also struck down Sihon, king of the Amorites, and gained possession of all their towns. He conquered the kings Balaam and Balak as well, and set up his camp beyond the Jordan, not far from Jericho. Then he fought against the Midianites, and they were conquered and subdued. Moses died after he had led the people for forty years in the wilderness.

units.la: XL Caeterum Hebræi ob hanc causam tanto tempore in eremo fuisse traduntur, donec omnes, qui verbis Dei non credi- derant, interirent. Excepto enim Iesu & Chaleb,nemo ultra xx.annos natus Ægy- pto profectus,Iordane transiit.Ipse Moyses, ut terram promissam videret tantum nec contingeret,peccato ejus adscribitur: quod eo tempore, quo saxum ferire & a- quam producere præceptus est, post tot virtutum suarum experimenta,dubitave- rit. Decessit autem anno ætatis vicesimo & centesimo, de sepulchri loco parum compertum.
units.tr: XL Moreover, the Hebrews are said to have stayed in the wilderness for so long for this reason: until everyone who had not believed God's words had died. For apart from Joshua and Caleb, no one who had set out from Egypt after the age of twenty crossed the Jordan. Moses himself is charged with a sin, so that he saw the promised land only from afar and did not enter it. At the time when he was commanded to strike the rock and bring forth water, after so many proofs of his virtues, he doubted. He died in the hundred and twentieth year of his life, and the place of his burial is little known.

units.la: XLI Moyse mortuo, summa rerum penes Ie- (ü Nave filium erat.Etenim illū sibi Moy- ses successore constituerat, virum virtutib. suis simillimus. Pricipio autem suscepti im- perii,dimissis per castra nuntiis,populum certiorem facit, frumentum uti pararent: tri* duoq; proximo iter pronunciat. Sed Iordanis, flumen validissimum, transitu prohibebat: quia neq; navium copia pro tempore erat, neq; vadari fluvius poterat, qui tum pleno alveo ferebatur. Igitur arcam præferri a sacerdotibus, eosdemq; adverso flumine consistere jubet. Quo facto, incisus Iordanis traditur: ita per siccum copiæ traductę. Erat in his locis opidum, no- mine Hiericho, muris validissimis munitum, neq; expugnationi neque obsidioni facile. Sed Iesus Domino fretus, non armis aut viribus urbem aggressus, ferri arcam Dei circa muros iubet: sacerdotes q; præire arcam & tuba canere. Sed cum arca septies circulata esset, muri ac turres conciderunt: direptum oppidum atq; incensum. Tum Iesus Dominum traditur {a}. In- de adversus Gæ ductus exercitus: locatisq; a tergo urbis insidiis, Iesus metum simu- las terga hosti dedit. Quo viso qui in oppido erant patentibus portis cedentibus intare. Ita si qui insidiis fuerant, vacuam urbem ceperunt: cæsiq; omnes absque ullius effugio. Rex captus, summoq; supplicio affectus. Quod ubi vicinarum gentium regibus cō pertum est, in bellum confpi-rant Hebreos armis depellere. Verum Gaa-baonitæ, gens valida, ex urbe opulenta, ul-tro le Heoraeis[?] dederunt, iussa facturos pollicentes: receptiq; in fidem, ut ligna & aquam conveherent imperatum. Sed regibus proximarum urbium deditio eorum tras conciverat. Itaq; admotis copiis oppidum eorum, Gabaon nomine, obsidi-one circumsiftûr. Igitur oppidani arctis rebus suis nuntios ad lefum mittunt, obses-sis uti succurreret. Ita ille maturato itinere inopinantibus supervenit, caesaq; ad internecionem multa hostium millia, cum dies cedentes deficeret, noxq; victis futura præsidio videretur, merito fidei dux Hebræus[?] noctē avertit, dies perseveravit: ita nullum hostibus effugiū fuit. Quinque reges capti interfecti sunt. Eodem impetu vicinæ quoque urbes imperio adiectæ, regesque earum perempti. Verum quia omnia hæc in ordinem persequi non fuit consilium, dum brevitati studemus, id modo annotandum curavimus, xx. & novem regna imperio Hebræorum subiecta: quorum terra per undecim tribus viritim distributa est. Levitis enim in sacerdotium assumptis, nulla portio data, quo liberius servirent Deo. Equidem hoc exemplum non tacitus praeterierim, legendum q; mi-nistris Ecclesiarum libenter ingesserim. Etenim praecepti huius non solum immemores, sed etiam ignari mihi videntur, tanta hoc tempore animos eorum habendi cupido veluti tabes incessit: inhiant pos-sessionibus, praedia excolunt, auro incubant, emunt venditantq; quaestui per omnia student. At si qui melioris propositi videntur neque possidentes neq; negotiantes, quod est multo turpius, sedentes munera exspectant, atq; omne vitae decus mercede corruptum habent, dum quasi venalem praeferunt [illegible, ~3 letters]. Sed longius quam volui egressus sum, dum me temporum nostrorum piget taedetque. Ad incep-tum redeo. Igitur, ut supra dixi, diuiso per tribus captiuo solo, pace summa Hebraei perfruebatur, finitimis bello territis, tot victoriis nobiles, armis nemine audente tare[?]. Eodem tractu Iesus mortuus est anno aetatis decimo & cetesimo, de imperii autem ejus tempore parum definio. Frequens tamen opinio est, xx. & vii. annis eum Hebraeis praefuisse. Quod si ita est, a munadi exordio in excessum ejus anni sunt ᵃM. DCCC. LXXX ,& ᵇ 1111. Iesu mortuo populus fine duce agebat. Sed cum adversus Chanaæos bellandū esset, dux belli Iudas af- iumptus est. Hujus duĉtu res profperege. stæ domi militiæq; summū otium, popu- lus aut subactis aut per deditione accep- tis gentibus, imperitabat. Inde ut semper fieri secundis rebus solet morum difcipli- næque immemor, matrimonia ex victis affumere, paulatimque externos mores trahere, ac mox profano ritu idolis sacri- ficare occœpit. Adeo cuncta cum exter- nis societas perniciosa est, quæ Deus lon- ge ante prospiciens, salubri Hebræos res- pōso instruxerat, devictas gentes ut inter- necioni darent. Sed plebs cupida dominā- di imperare victis cum pernicie malebat. Igitur cum relicto Deo idola colerent, de- stituti divino auxilio, a rege Mefopotamię evicti & subacti, vii. annis captivitatē pe- penderunt : donec Gothoniel duce in li- bertate restituti, per quinquaginta annos rerū potiti sunt. Rursumq; corrupti lon- gæ pacis malo, idolis litaverunt, moxq; a- derat pœna peccantibus : ab Eglon. rege Moabitarum devicti, duo de viginti annis servieservierunt,donec instinctu Dei Adō re-gem hostium dolo interemit contractoq; tumultuario exercitu libertate armis vi-dicavit.Idem per lxxx.annos in pace He-braeis praefuit.Huic Semigar successit:hic-que adversus Allophylos congressus se cundo evētu praelium fecit. Rursumque Hebraeos sectates idola rex Chananaeorum Iabin nomine subjugavit, gravissimamque in eos per xx. annos dominationem exercuit: donec pristinum Debbora mulier statu reddidit. Adeo nihil spei in co- rum ducibus erat,ut muliebri auxilio defenderentur. Quamquam haec in typum Ecclesiae forma praemissa fit,cujus auxilio captivitas est depulsa. Sub hac duce vel judice,xl. annis Hebraei fuerunt. Rursumque ob peccata Madianitis traditi duro imperio habebatur, afflictique malo servitutis divinum auxilium imploraverunt. Ita semper in secundis rebus immemores caelestium beneficiorum idolis supplicabant: in adversis Deo. Vnde cum reputare in animo soleo populum tot beneficiis Dei obligatum,tot cladibus cum peccaret coercitum, expertumq; & misericordiam & severitatem Dei, nequaquam emedatum:& cum semper veniam erroris ac- ciperet,semper peccasse post veniam,nihil mirum videri potest Christū ab his non esse receptum,cum jam inde ab initio to- ties in Dominum rebelles deprehendan- tur:magisq; mirum est,illis seper[?] peccan- tibus, nunquam Dei, si quando eum im- ploraverunt,defuisse clementiam. Igitur- cum eis, ut supra retulimus, Madianitæ dominarentur,cōversi ad Dominū,mise- ricordiam solitam flagitantes impetrave- runt. Erat in Hebræis Gedeon quidam no- mine vir justus & carus Domino accep- tusq;.huic Angelus de campo messis do- mum revertenti astitit, Dominus,inquit, tecum potens in virtute. At ille voce hu- mili,non esse in se Dominum ingemisce- bat,si quidem populum captivitas preme- ret:virtutumq; Domini, qui eos de terra Aegypti eduxerat, ªflens recordabatur. Tum Angelus: Vade,inquit,in hoc spiri- tu,quo locutus es,& populū de captivita- re eripe. Ille vero abnuere se infractis suo- rū viribus,cum ipse minimus esset,tātum onus suscipere: perstare cōtra angelu, ne dubitaret posse fieri queDominus loqué- batur. Perfecto igitur sacrificio dirutaq; ara, quam Baalis idolo Madianitæ sacraverant, ad suos profectus, castra castris hostiū contulit: sed Madianitis etiam gens Ama-lech se conjunxerat. Gedeo vero non amplius quam ad triginta & ii. millia exer-citum paraverat. Sed, priusquam conslige-ret, Deus ad eum locutus est, nimiam esse hanc multitudinē, quam in prælium vellet educere. Hebræos pro solita perfidia e ventu pugnæ non Deo, sed virtuti suæ daturos. Itaq; daret volentibus discedēdi potestate, quod ubi populo diuulgatū, xx. & ii. M. a castris recesserūt. Sed ex x. millib., quæ reliederat, admonitus a Domino non amplius quam trecentos tenuit: reliquos ab armis dimisit. Ita media vigilia castra hostium ingressus, jussis omnibus tuba canere, magnum terrore injecit: neq; cuiquam resistendi animus fuit, turpi fuga quo quisque potuit dilapsis. Sed occurrē-tibus omni ex parte Hebræis, passim fugientes cadunt. Reges Gedeo persecutus ultra Iordanem comprehensos neci dedit.
units.tr: XLI After Moses' death, the chief authority passed to Joshua, the son of Nun, for Moses had appointed him as his successor, a man very like himself in his virtues. At the start of his rule, he sent messengers through the camp and warned the people to prepare provisions, announcing that they would march in three days. But the Jordan, a very strong river, blocked the crossing, since at that time there was no supply of boats, and the river, flowing in full flood, could not be forded. He therefore ordered the ark to be carried forward by the priests and told them to stand in the river against the current. When this was done, the Jordan is said to have been cut off, and so the army crossed over on dry ground. In these parts there was a town called Jericho, fortified with very strong walls, not easily taken by assault or by siege. But Joshua, trusting in the Lord, did not attack the city with arms or force; he ordered the ark of God to be carried around the walls, with the priests going before the ark and sounding trumpets. And when the ark had been carried around seven times, the walls and towers fell down; the town was plundered and burned. Then Joshua is reported to have prayed to the Lord. Next the army was led against Ai, and after an ambush had been placed behind the city, Joshua feigned fear and turned his back on the enemy. Seeing this, those in the town opened the gates and came out in pursuit. So those in ambush took the empty city, and all the men were slain without any escape. The king was captured and put to the most severe punishment. When this became known to the kings of the neighbouring peoples, they conspired to drive the Hebrews away by arms. But the Gibeonites, a powerful people with a wealthy city, surrendered themselves to the Hebrews of their own accord, promising to do whatever was commanded; once received into the covenant, they were ordered to carry wood and water. But their surrender had stirred up the kings of the nearby cities, and so they gathered forces and laid siege to their town, called Gibeon. Then the townspeople, hard pressed, sent messengers to Joshua asking him to come to their aid while they were besieged. He therefore hurried on his march and came upon the enemy unawares, and after many thousands of the enemy had been cut down to the last man, when the daylight was failing and the night seemed likely to help the defeated, the Hebrew leader, rightly trusting in God, made the sun stand still so that the day continued; thus the enemy had no way of escape. Five kings were captured and put to death. With the same onslaught the neighbouring cities were also brought under his rule, and their kings were destroyed. But since it was not my purpose to pursue all these things in order, while I aim at brevity, I have taken care to note only this: twenty-nine kingdoms were made subject to the rule of the Hebrews, and their land was distributed by lot among the eleven tribes. For the Levites, who had been taken into the priesthood, were given no portion, so that they might serve God more freely. Indeed, I would not pass over this example in silence, and I would gladly press it upon the ministers of the churches to read. For those who are supposed to be ministers seem to me not only forgetful of this precept but even ignorant of it. In this age such a great desire of possessing has seized their minds like a plague: they gasp after estates, they cultivate farms, they brood over gold, they buy and sell, and they strive for profit in every way. And if some seem to have a better purpose, neither possessing nor trading, which is much more shameful, they sit waiting for gifts, and they regard all the honour of their life as corrupted by a price, while they offer themselves as if for sale. But I have gone further than I intended, as I am troubled and wearied by our times. I return to my subject. Therefore, as I said above, once the captured land had been divided among the tribes, the Hebrews enjoyed the greatest peace: their neighbours were terrified by war, they were famous for so many victories, and no one dared to take up arms against them. In this same course of events Joshua died in the hundred and tenth year of his life; I define little about the length of his rule. Yet it is a common opinion that he ruled the Hebrews for twenty-seven years. If this is so, from the beginning of the world to the year of his death there are M. DCCC. LXXX, and 1111. After Joshua's death the people went on without a leader. But when they had to fight against the Canaanites, Judah was taken up as leader of the war. Under his command affairs went well: at home and in war they enjoyed the greatest quiet, and the people ruled over the nations either subdued or received by surrender. Then, as usually happens with success, they became forgetful of morals and of discipline; they began to take wives from the defeated peoples, gradually to adopt foreign customs, and soon to sacrifice to idols with profane rites. So fatal is fellowship of every kind with foreigners, which God, looking far ahead, had warned the Hebrews against in a wholesome command, that they should put the conquered nations to destruction. But the common people, eager to dominate, preferred to rule over the conquered to their own ruin. So, when they abandoned God and worshipped idols, deprived of divine help, they were conquered and subdued by the king of Mesopotamia and paid the penalty of captivity for seven years; until, restored to freedom under the leadership of Othniel, they held power for fifty years. Again, corrupted by the evil of long peace, they sacrificed to idols, and soon punishment came upon the sinners: they were conquered by Eglon, king of the Moabites, and served him for eighteen years, until at God's prompting Ehud killed the enemy king by a trick, and, gathering a makeshift army, vindicated their freedom by arms. The same man ruled the Hebrews in peace for eighty years. Shamgar succeeded him, and he fought against the Philistines and won a battle with a successful outcome. Again the Hebrews followed idols, and Jabin, king of the Canaanites, subdued them and exercised a most severe rule over them for twenty years, until the woman Deborah restored them to their former state. So little hope was there in their leaders that they were defended by the help of a woman. Although this form was put forward as a type of the Church, by whose help captivity was driven away. Under this leader or judge the Hebrews were for forty years. Again, because of their sins they were handed over to the Midianites and held under a harsh rule, and, afflicted by the evil of servitude, they begged for divine help. So always, in prosperity, they forgot the heavenly benefits and prayed to idols; in adversity, they prayed to God. Hence, when I often reflect in my mind that a people bound to God by so many benefits, and restrained by so many disasters whenever they sinned, having experienced both the mercy and the severity of God, were by no means reformed, and that though they always obtained pardon for their error they always sinned again after pardon, it can seem no wonder that Christ was not received by them, since from the very beginning they are found so often rebellious against the Lord. It is even more wonderful that, though they always sinned, God's mercy never failed them whenever they called upon him. Therefore, when the Midianites ruled over them, as we have related above, they turned to the Lord, begged for his accustomed mercy, and obtained it. There was among the Hebrews a certain man named Gideon, a just man, dear and acceptable to the Lord. An angel from the threshing floor stood by him as he was returning home, saying, "The Lord is with you, mighty in valour." But he, in a humble voice, lamented that the Lord was not with him, since captivity oppressed the people; and, weeping, he recalled the mighty deeds of the Lord who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. Then the angel said: "Go in this spirit with which you have spoken, and snatch the people from captivity." But he refused, saying that with his strength broken, since he was the least of them, he could not undertake so great a burden; he persisted against the angel, saying that he doubted that what the Lord was speaking could be done. Therefore, when the sacrifice had been completed and the altar of Baal, which the Midianites had consecrated to their idol, had been torn down, he set out for his own people and brought his camp against the camp of the enemy; but the Amalekites had also joined the Midianites. Yet Gideon had prepared an army of no more than thirty-two thousand. But before he could engage, God spoke to him, saying that this multitude was too great for him to lead into battle. The Hebrews, according to their usual treachery, would attribute the outcome of the fight not to God but to their own strength. So he should let those who wished depart at liberty. When this was announced to the people, twenty-two thousand withdrew from the camp. But of the ten thousand who were left, admonished by the Lord, he kept no more than three hundred and dismissed the rest from arms. Thus, entering the enemy camp in the middle watch, he ordered all of them to sound their trumpets, and he struck great terror into them; no one had any mind to resist, and with shameful flight each scattered wherever he could. But the Hebrews met them from every side, and the fugitives fell everywhere. Gideon pursued the kings across the Jordan, captured them, and put them to death.

units.la: Ea pugna centum & xxm. ex hostibus casa, xv capta traduntur. Tunc consensu omniū Gedeoni, ut princeps populi esset, delatū. Quod ille aspernatus, cōmuni ju-re cum re cum civibus vivere quam præesse suis, maluit. Depulsa igitur captivitate, quæ septem annos populum continuerat, pax per xl. annos fuit. Sed defuncto Gedeoni, filius ejus Abimelech, ex concubina ortus, fratribus interemptis, pēsimis quibusq; consentientibus, & maxime Sichimorum principibus operā ei navantibus, regnum occupavit. Ifq; discordiis civilibus exercitus, cum suos bello premeret turrim quandā, in quam fe amisso ᵃopido fugientes receperat, expugnare aggressus, dum incautius subit, faxo a muliere ictus periit, cum triennio imperium tenuisset.
units.tr: In that battle, a hundred and twenty thousand of the enemy are reported slain and fifteen thousand taken. Then, by the consent of all, the leadership of the people was offered to Gideon, to be their prince. He refused it, preferring to live with his fellow citizens under common law rather than to rule over his own people. So, with the captivity that had held the people for seven years thrown off, there was peace for forty years. But after Gideon died, his son Abimelech, born of a concubine, killed his brothers, with the worst men agreeing and especially the princes of Shechem lending him their help, and seized the kingdom. Harried by civil discord, he attacked a certain tower into which the fugitives had withdrawn after the town was lost. He approached it too carelessly, and a woman struck him with a stone and he died, after he had held power for three years.

units.la: Huic succesfsit Thola, qui duobus & xx, annis regno potitus est. Post hunc Iair fuit, qui cum æque viginti & duos annos principatum obtinuisset, populus, relicto Domino, idolis se mancipavit. Obq; id Israelitæ subacti sunt ab Allophylis & Ammonitis, duoq; de xx. annis sub eorum imperio fuerunt. Quo tempore eis, Dominū invocatibus, divinum scilicet responsum redditum est: Simulacra potius invocarent, se non ultra misericordiam ingratis præstiturum. At illi flentes culpam fateri, & precari veniam, abjectisq; idolis Deū implorarn. plorantes, negatam licet misericordiā im-petraverunt. Igitur Iepta{a} duce ad libertatem armis vindicandam frequentes conveniunt, misis prius ad Amon regem legatis, ut finibus suis contentus bello abstineret. At ille prælium non abnuens aciem instruxit. Tum Iepta, priusquam signum pugnæ daretur, vovisse dicitur, si prospere pugnasset, eum qui sibi primus revertenti obvius fuisset, hostiam Deo dandum. Ita victis hostibus, cum domum rediret, filia ei obviam fit,quæ patrem exceptura victoré cum tympanis & choris læta processerat. Tum Iepta consternatus, dolore conscisis vestibus, indicat filiæ voti necessitatem. At illa{b} non fœmina constantia, mori non recusans, duos tantum tamen menses vitæ spatium petit, ut æquales suas priusvideret. Quibus actis, ultro ad patrem rediit, votumq; Domino reddidit. Iepta princi-patum sex annis tenuit. huic{c} Efebon suc-cessit,& tranquillis rebus exacto imperio anno septimo decessit. Postq; illum{d} Al-lon Zabulonites ānis x. itemq; Abdon an-nis viii. rerum potiti, pacis tempore nihil quod historia loqueretur ediderunt. Rursum Israelitæ ad idola coversi,divino destituti præsidio, subjecti Asilophylis [?] per XL. captivitatis annos pœnas perfidiæ pe-penderunt. Ea rempestate Samson natus traditur. Hujus mater, diu sterilis, angeli[?] vidit, diȼumque ci est, vino & sicera atq; immundis abstineret, fore uti puerum e- deceret libertatis vindicē & hostium ultos Ita mulier enixa puerum Sãson no- mē ci indidit, Is intonto capite mitæ vir- tutis suisse traditur adeo ut leonem in via obvium manu discerperet uxorem ex Al- lophylis habuit, quæ cum absente viro in alterius matrimonium convenisset, dolo- re ereptæ coniugis pernicieni genti mo- litus est fretus Domino & viribus, palam vi&tores clade afficiebat. CCC. siquidem vulpibus captis, ardentes lampades ea- rum illigavit caudis, atq; eas agris hosti- um immisit. At tum forte maturis messis bus facile incendium tuit, vinearq; & olive- varum arbores exustæ. Grandi Allopylo- rum exitio abreptæ uxoris injuriam ultus videbatur. Quo dolore Alloph[?]ylis permo- ti mulierem, tanti mali causam cum do- mo & patre incendio consumpserunt. Sed Samson parum se vindicatum ratus, urgere omnibus incommodis profanam gentem non desinebat. Tum cōpulsi Iudæi vinctum eum Allophylis tradiderūt; sed traditus, ruptis vinculis arrepto {a}osse asini, quod calus telum dederat, mille ex hostibus prostravit. Ingravescente autem æstu, cum siti affectus esset, invocato Domino, {b}ex osse quod manu tenebat, aqua fluxit. Ea tempestate Samsō Hebræis præ-rat, Allophylis unius virtute domitis. Igi-tur inlidiantes vitę ejus, nec palam eum [?]ter-tare audentes, {c}uxore ejus, quam ille pe-stea[?] acceperat, pecunia corrumpūt, virtutem viri uti proderet. Illa eum blandimento mulicbri aggressa, diu eludentem & multum cūctatum perpulit, ut indicaret, in crinibus capitis virtutem suam subsistere. Mox dormienti insidiata, crinem ejus abstulit atq; ita eum Allophylis tradidit. Nam sæpe prius traditum coprehendere nequiverat. Tum illi effossis oculis vinctum compedibus in carcere conjecerunt. Sed spatio temporis accisus crinis crescere, & cū eis virtus redire occeperat. Iaq; Samson cōscius recepti roboris, tempus modo justæ ultionis {d}opperiebatur. Erat Allophylis moris, cum dies festos ageret, Samson quasi in pompam publicam producere, ducere,capto insultantes.Ita die quodam, cum publicum epulum in honorem idoli dedicarent, Samson exhiberi jubent. Templum autem, in quo omnis populus, omnefq; Allophylorum principes epulabantur, duabus subnixu columnis miræ magnitudinis erat. Productus Samson, inter columnas statuitur. Tum ille tempore arrepto, invocato prius Domino, columnas disjecit: turbaq; omnis ruina domus obruta, ipse cum hostibus non inultus occubuit, cum xx. ānis Hebreis praefuisset. Huic Simmichat successit, de quo nihil aliud Scriptura prodidit. Nam neq; finem imperii ejus reperi, & fuisse populo fine duce invento. Ideo, cum adversus Benjamin tribu civile bellum fuit, Iudas tempora. rius dux belli afsuptus est. Sed plerique; qui de temporibus scripserunt, annum unum imperio ejus . Plerique; ita eum praeterierunt ut post Samsō Heli sacerdotem subjunxerint: nos eam rem, ut parum compertam, in medio relinquemus. Per hæc tempora civile, ut diximus, bellum exarserat. Causa autem motus hæc fuit; Levites quidam cum concubina iter faciens, urgente nocte compulsus, in opido Gabaa, quod ab Benjamitis incolebatur, lecelserat[?]. Cum eum senex quidam hof-pitio benigne recepisset, juvenes ex opi-do hospitem circumsistunt, stupro eum subdere parates. Multum a fene increpiti, aegreque exhortati, vicario demum con-cubinae ejus corpore in ludibrium acce-pto, advenae pepercerunt: illufamq; noĉte tota, postero die reddiderunt. Sed illa, ftu-pri injuria, an verecundia, parum definio, viso viro, animam efflavit. Tum Levita in testimonium diri facinoris membra ejus in duodecim diffcifa partes, per duodecim tribus misit, quo promptius omnes facti invidia commoveret. Quod ubi omnibus compertum, undecim reliquae tribus adversum Benjamin in bellum conspirant. Huic bello b Iudas, ut diximus, dux fuit. Sed duobus praeliis male pugnatum: tertio demum Benjamitę vi[?]i caesique ad internecionem. Ita paucorum scelus publico exitio punitum. Haec quoq; Iudicum volumine continentur. Regum libri fe-quentur: sed mihi annorum ordinem & feriem temporum persequenti patrum continuata videtur historia. Nam quum post Samfon judicem Semigar fuerit, pauloq; post historia consignet pos-pulum fine ludicibus egifle, Heli etiam fa-cerdos libris regnorū fuisse referatur: sed quum quot anni inter Heli & Samson sus-erint minime Scriptura prodiderit: video medii quiddam fuisse temporis, quod la-boret ambiguo, Caeterum adie mortis los-fue, usque in id tempus quo Samson des- funćtus est, numerantur anni * CCCC.& xix. A mundi autem exordio anni 1111 ccc.& 111. Quanquā ab hac suppura-tione nostra cæteros discordare non ne-sciam. Sed mihi conscius sum, menon in-curiose latentem annorum ordine m pro-tulifle, donec in hæc temporaincidi, de quibus dubitare me fateor: nunc reliqua exequar.Igitur, ut, supra retuli, Hebrei fi-ne iudice aut duce ullo, preprio arbitrio agebantur. Heli sacerdos erat: sub hoc Sa-muel natus est. Huic pater Elchana, mater Anna. hæc dia sterilis, cum conceptum a Deo peteret, vovisse traditur, fi puer na-fceretur, sacrandum Domino. Ita enixum puerum Heli sacerdoti tradidit. Mox, cum adoleviffer, Dominus ad eum locutus est. Heli sacerdoti iram [?] denunciat ob vi- tam filiorum, qui sacerdotium patris in quæstum verterant, munera a sacrificantibus exigentes, quanquam plerunq; eos pater increpasse referatur. Sed levior objurgatio non satisfecerat disciplinæ. Igitur Allophylis in Iudæam irruentibus obviam itum. Sed victi Hebræi, parant aci-em restituere: arca Domini secum in pugnam efferunt, & cum ea filii sacerdotis prodeunt: quia ipse annis gravior, luminibus obductis, satisfacere officio nequiverat. Sed ubi arca in conspectum hostium deducta est, majestate quadam præsentis{*} Domini territi, fuga parabant. Assumpta que rursum constantia, & non sine Domino mutatis animis, totis viribus concurrunt. Victi Hebræi, arca capitur, filij sacerdotis cadunt. Heli, delato ad se mali nuncio, consternatus, animam expiravit, cum{b} per annos viginti sacerdotium administrasset. Victores secundo prælio Allophyli, arcam DEI, quæ in potestatem venerat, eorum opido Azoto in templum Dagon intulerunt. Sed simulachrum dæmoni dicatum, ubi arca illata est, corruit. Gumq; idolum loco restituissent, nocte insecuta discerptum est. Inde mures per omnem regionem exorti, noxijs morbis multa
units.tr: Tola succeeded him and held power for twenty-three years. After him came Jair, who likewise held the leadership for twenty-two years. Then the people, forsaking the Lord, gave themselves over to idols. For this the Israelites were subdued by the Philistines and the Ammonites, and they were under their rule for eighteen years. At that time, when they called upon the Lord, a divine answer was given: they should rather call upon the images they had chosen, since he would no longer show mercy to such ungrateful people. But they, weeping, confessed their fault and begged pardon, and casting away their idols they implored God; and although mercy had been refused, they obtained it. Therefore, with Jephthah as their leader, they gathered in numbers to win their liberty by arms, having first sent envoys to the king of Ammon to ask that he be content with his own borders and refrain from war. He did not refuse battle and drew up his line. Then Jephthah, before the signal for battle was given, is said to have vowed that if he fought successfully, whoever first met him on his return would be offered to God as a sacrifice. So the enemy were defeated, and as he was returning home, his daughter came to meet him, having gone out joyfully with timbrels and dancing choirs to receive her father the victor. Then Jephthah, dismayed, tore his garments in grief and told his daughter the necessity of the vow. But she, with a constancy beyond a woman's, not refusing to die, asked only two months of life, that she might see her companions first. When this was done, she returned of her own accord to her father, and he fulfilled his vow to the Lord. Jephthah held the leadership for six years. Ibzan succeeded him, and his rule, with affairs quiet, ended with his death in the seventh year. After him Elon the Zebulunite held power for ten years, and likewise Abdon for eight years; in these times of peace they produced nothing that history might record. Again the Israelites turned to idols, abandoned by divine protection and subject to the Philistines, and for forty years of captivity they paid the penalty of their faithlessness. At this time Samson is said to have been born. His mother, long barren, saw an angel, and she was told that she should abstain from wine, strong drink and all unclean things, and that she would bear a son who would be an avenger of liberty and a punisher of the enemies. So the woman bore a boy and gave him the name Samson. He is said to have been of wondrous strength while his head remained unshorn, so much so that he tore a lion apart with his bare hands when it met him on the road. He had a wife from among the Philistines, who, while he was away, went over into another man's marriage. Grieving at the loss of his wife, he planned ruin for that nation, trusting in the Lord and his own strength, and openly struck the victors with calamity. Indeed, having caught three hundred foxes, he tied burning torches to their tails and let them loose in the enemy's fields. Since the harvest was ripe, the fire spread easily, and the vineyards and olive trees were burned. With great slaughter of the Philistines he seemed to have avenged the wrong done to his wife. Stirred by this grief, the Philistines burned the woman, the cause of so great an evil, together with her house and her father. But Samson, thinking himself insufficiently avenged, did not cease to press the profane nation with every kind of harm. Then the Jews, under pressure, handed him over to the Philistines bound; but once delivered, he broke his bonds, seized the jawbone of an ass, which chance had given him as a weapon, and struck down a thousand of the enemy. As the heat grew and he was afflicted with thirst, he called upon the Lord, and water flowed from the bone he held in his hand. At that time Samson ruled the Hebrews, the Philistines having been subdued by his valour alone. Therefore they plotted against his life, not daring to attack him openly, and bribed with money his wife, whom he had afterwards taken, to betray the secret of her husband's strength. She approached him with womanly flattery, and when he had long evaded her and hesitated, she persuaded him to reveal that his strength lay in the hair of his head. Soon, lying in wait while he slept, she cut off his hair and so handed him over to the Philistines; for they had often before failed to seize him when he was delivered up. Then they gouged out his eyes, bound him in fetters, and threw him into prison. But in the course of time the cut hair began to grow, and with it his strength began to return. Samson, aware of his restored vigour, was now waiting for the moment of just vengeance. It was the custom of the Philistines, when they kept their festival days, to bring Samson out as if for a public show, to lead him about and mock him as a captive. So on a certain day, when they were holding a public feast in honour of their idol, they ordered Samson to be brought out. The temple, in which all the people and all the leaders of the Philistines were feasting, rested on two pillars of wondrous size. Samson was brought out and stationed between the pillars. Then he, seizing the moment and first calling upon the Lord, pushed the pillars apart; the whole house collapsed and buried the crowd, and he himself perished with his enemies, not unavenged, after having led the Hebrews for twenty years. Shamgar succeeded him, of whom Scripture has handed down nothing else. For neither is the end of his rule recorded, nor is it stated that the people had been found without a leader. Therefore, when civil war broke out against the tribe of Benjamin, Judah was taken on as a temporary leader for the war. Yet most of those who wrote about the chronology assign him only one year of rule, and many passed him over so as to place Eli the priest directly after Samson; we shall leave that matter open, as little ascertained. During these times, as we have said, civil war had broken out. The cause of the uprising was this: a certain Levite, travelling with his concubine and pressed by the approaching night, had turned aside into the town of Gibeah, which was inhabited by Benjamites. When an old man had received him kindly as a guest, the young men of the town surrounded the house, intending to subject the guest to abuse. Rebuked severely by the old man and only with difficulty persuaded, they at last accepted the Levite's concubine as a substitute to be mocked, and spared the stranger; they abused her throughout the night and gave her back the next day. But she, whether from the outrage of defilement or from shame, I cannot clearly say, breathed her last when she saw her husband. Then the Levite, as a witness of the dreadful crime, cut her body into twelve pieces and sent them through the twelve tribes, so that he might the more readily stir all men to hatred of the deed. When this became known to all, the other eleven tribes conspired to make war on Benjamin. Judah, as we have said, was the leader in this war. But in two battles they fought badly; at the third the Benjamites were at last defeated and cut down to utter destruction. Thus the crime of a few was punished by public ruin. These events too are contained in the book of Judges. The books of Kings follow; but to me, pursuing the order of years and the sequence of times, the history seems to run on without a break. For after Samson there was the judge Shamgar, and shortly afterwards the history records that the people lived without judges; Eli the priest is also said to appear in the books of Kings. Yet since Scripture nowhere gives how many years there were between Eli and Samson, I see that there was some intervening time, and this is uncertain. Moreover, from the death of Joshua to the time when Samson died, four hundred and nineteen years are counted; from the beginning of the world, the years are reckoned as 1111 and 303. Although I am not unaware that others disagree with this reckoning of ours, I am conscious that I have not carelessly set out the order of years, until I came to these times, about which I confess I am in doubt. Now I shall go on with what remains. Therefore, as I related above, the Hebrews were governed without any judge or leader, each by his own will. Eli was priest; under him Samuel was born. His father was Elkanah and his mother Hannah. She, long barren, when she asked God for a child, is said to have vowed that if a boy were born, he would be consecrated to the Lord. So, when she had borne the boy, she gave him to Eli the priest. Soon, when he had grown up, the Lord spoke to him. He announced wrath to Eli the priest on account of the conduct of his sons, who had turned their father's priesthood into a source of profit, extorting gifts from those who offered sacrifices, although the father is often reported to have rebuked them. But a milder rebuke had not satisfied the demands of discipline. Therefore, when the Philistines burst into Judea, the Hebrews went out to meet them. But the defeated Hebrews, preparing to restore their battle line, carried the ark of the Lord with them into the fight, and the priest's sons went out with it, because the priest himself, heavy with years and his eyes dimmed, had been unable to perform his office. But when the ark was brought into the sight of the enemy, they were struck with fear by a certain majesty of the Lord present, and prepared to flee. Then, regaining their courage, and their minds changed not without the Lord, they charged with all their strength. The Hebrews were defeated, the ark was captured, and the priest's sons fell. Eli, when news of the disaster was brought to him, was dismayed and breathed his last, after he had administered the priesthood for twenty years. The Philistines, victorious in the second battle, carried the ark of God, which had come into their power, into the temple of Dagon in their town of Ashdod. But the image dedicated to the god fell down when the ark was brought in. And when they had set the idol back in its place, on the following night it was broken to pieces. Then mice appeared throughout the whole region, and with pestilential diseases began to carry off many

units.la: {b} b quadra-ginta annos ju-dicavit [?] hominum millia letho dabant. Quo malo compulsi Azotii, ad declinadam calamitatem, arcam Dei ad Gethæos transtule-runt. Qui cum simili clade afficerentur, in opidum Ascalonensium arcam trans-vexerunt. His vero, advocatis gentis ejus primoribus, consilium fuit arcam Domi-ni Hebræis reddere. Ita ex sententia prin-cipum augurumque & sacerdotum, im-posita vehiculo, multis cum muneribus remittitur. Illud mirabile, quod cum one-ri boves fœminas subjecissent, vitulosque earum domi retinuissent, iter nullo duce in Iudæam pecudes direxerunt, non re-vocante affectu fœtus relicti. Cujus rei miraculo reguli Allophylorum, usque in fines Hebræorum arcam secuti, religiosum officium præstiterunt. Iudæi autem, ubi referri arcam viderunt, certatim ex opido Bethsamis cum gaudio obviam ruere, fes-tinare, exultare, grates Domino referre. Mox Levitæ, quorum hoc negocii erat, sacrificium Deo celebrant: bovesque eas, quæ arcam adduxerant, immolant. Sed in opido, quod supra diximus, teneri arca non potuit. Itaque passim Dei nutu per totam urbem sævitum. Arca in Cariath-jarim jarim opidum translata est, ibiq; per vigin-ti annos fuit. Ea tempestate Samuel a sa-cerdos Hebraeis praerat, quietis a bello re-bus populus in ocio degebat. Pax deinde Allophylorum irruptione turbata, trepi-dantibus cunctis ob conscietiam peccati. Samuel, cæsa prius hostia, Domino fretus, suos in prælium deduxit: primoque impetu fusis hostibus, victoria penes Hebræ-os stetit. Sed hostili metu remoto, secun-dis tranquillisque rebus, corruptis consi-liis, more vulgi, cui præsentia fastidio, in-sueta desiderio sunt, regium nomē, (cun-ctis fere liberis gentibus semper invisum) populus desiderabat, planeque non fine exemplo amentiæ præoptabat libertatem servitio mutare. Igitur frequetes Samue-lem circumsistunt, ut quia jam ipse senu-isset, regem eis constitueret. At ille placi-de salubri oratione ab insana voluntate detorquere plebem, dominationem regi-am & superba imperia exponere, libertatem extollere, servitutem detestari: po-stremo, divinam eis iram denunciare, si-quidem homines mente corrupti, Deum regem habentes, regem sibi ex hominibus flagitarent. His atque aliis istiusmodi frustra dictis, cum populus in sententia perseveraret, Dominum consulit. Qui permotus vecordia insanæ gentis, nihil adversum se perentibus[?] negandum respondit.
units.tr: For forty years he judged. Thousands of men were given over to death. Driven to avert this calamity, the Ashdodites carried the ark of God over to the Gittites. When they too were struck by a similar disaster, they moved the ark to the town of the Ashkelonites. But these men, summoning the leading men of their nation, resolved to return the ark of the Lord to the Hebrews. So by the judgment of the princes, augurs and priests, it was loaded on a cart and sent back with many gifts. The marvel was this: they yoked milch cows to the cart and kept their calves at home, and with no driver the cows took the road into Judea, not turning back, though their calves were left behind. Struck by this miracle, the petty kings of the Philistines followed the ark as far as the borders of the Hebrews and performed a dutiful office. The Jews, when they saw the ark being brought back, rushed eagerly from the town of Beth-shemesh to meet it, hurrying, exulting and giving thanks to the Lord. Soon the Levites, whose task this was, celebrated a sacrifice to God and slaughtered the cows which had brought the ark. But the ark could not be kept in the town mentioned above, so by God's will punishment raged throughout the whole city. The ark was then transferred to the town of Kiriath-jearim and remained there for twenty years. At that time Samuel, a priest, presided over the Hebrews, and the people, free from war, lived in leisure. Then the peace was broken by an invasion of the Philistines, and everyone trembled, conscious of their sin. Samuel, having first offered a victim and trusting in the Lord, led the people into battle; the enemy was routed by the first onslaught, and victory stood with the Hebrews. But with the fear of the enemy removed and their affairs prosperous and tranquil, their counsels were corrupted. Following the way of the crowd, for whom the present is tedious and the unaccustomed is desired, the people longed for a royal name, which almost all free nations have always hated, and they plainly preferred, not without precedent of folly, to exchange liberty for servitude. So they crowded round Samuel, asking that, since he was now old, he appoint a king for them. But he, with a calm and wholesome speech, tried to turn the people from their mad wish, setting out the domination of kings and their proud commands, extolling liberty and detesting servitude. Finally he announced God's wrath upon them, since men corrupted in mind, having God as their king, were demanding a king for themselves from among men. When, after these and similar words spoken in vain, the people persisted in their opinion, he consulted the Lord. Moved by the madness of this insane nation, the Lord answered that nothing should be denied to those who demanded it against him.

units.la: Igitur Saul sacerdotali prius a Samue-le unguento perfusus rex constitutus est. Hic ex tribu Benjanuin[?], Cis patre ortus, modestus animi, forma excellenti erat: ut merito dignitas corporis dignitati re-gia conveniret. Sed principio regni hu-jus aliquanta ab eo pars populi defcive-rat, parere imperio abnuēs, seque Ammo-nitis conjunxerat. Verum hos Saul impi-gre ultus est, victique hostes & venia He-braeis data. Tum Saul iterato a Samuele unctus traditur. Inde Allophylorum ir-ruptione atrox bellum exortum, locum exercitui ad conveniendum Saul in Galga-lis constituerat. Et cum per septem dies Samuelem opperitus esset, ut sacrificium Domino fieret; tardante illo, cum populus dilaberetur, illicita præsumpti-one rex ad vicem sacerdotis holocau-stum obtulit: multumque a Samuele in-crepitus, fera peccatum poenitentia fa-tebatur. Igitur ex peccato regis metus omnem exercitum pervaserat, castra hostium haud longe sita praesens periculum ostendebant: neque cuiquam exeundi in praelium animus, plures lachrimas & late bras petiverant. Nam praeter imbecillitate animorum, qui alienum a se Dominum delicto regis arbitrabantur, in maxima ferramentorum inopia exercitus erat: adeo ut, praeter Saul & Ionathan filium ejus, nemo gladium aut lanceam habuisse [?]rrada-tur. Nam Allophyli superiore bello victo-res usum Hebraeis ademerant, neque cuiusquam conficiendi teli bellici, aut rustici ferramenti potestas fuerat. Igitur Iona{c}than audaci consilio, solo armigero suo comite, castra hostium ingressus, viginti fere ex hostibus interemptis, universum exercitu terrore perculerat. Tum vero nutu Dei in fugam versi, non imperia exequi, non ordines observare, omne praesidium in pedibus habere. Quod ubi Saul animadvertit, suis propere eductis, fugientes persecutus, victoria potitus est. Eo die rex edixisse traditur, ne quis, nisi confectis hostibus, cibu caperet. Sed Ionathae interdictionis eius inscius, favo reperto, tincto spiculo, mel degustaverat. Sed ubi regi exDo, mini ira compertum est, morte affici filiū jussit. Sed populi auxilio ab exitio vindicatus est. Ea tempestate Samuel a Domino monitus, regem adiit verbis Domini nuncians, uti géti Amalech, quæ olim Hebræos ex Aegypto venientes transitu prohibuerat, bellum inferret: addito interdicto, ne quid ex spoliis devictorū concupisceret. Ita in fines hostiū ductus exercitus, rex capt[?], gēs subacta. Saul victus prædæ magnitudine, præcepti divini immemor, capta servari & ferri jubet. Quo facto offensus Dominus, Samuelē alloquitur: pœnitere se, quod Saul regē constituerit. Dictū sacerdos regi refert. Mox a Domino monitus, David regali unguēto per-[?]init, parvum etiamnum puerum, sub patre agentem, pastorem ovium, assuetū sæpius cithara canere: ob quod posteā a Saule assumptus, inter ministros regios habebatur. Qua tēpestate, Allophylis atq; Hebræis bello flagrātibus, cum ex adverso acies constitissent, Goliath quidā ex Allophylis, vir mirae magnitudinis & roboris, suorū ordines prætergressus, ferocibus verbis probra in hostes jaciēs, {a}singulare pugnā ciebat. Tum rex magna præmia & filiae nuptias despondit, si quis provocantis spolia retulisset. Sed nemo ex tanto agmine aggredi audebat. Igitur David, etiamnū pu-er, pugnæ se obtulit: reiectisq; armis, quibus infirma ætas gravabatur, virga tantum & quinque lapidibus sumptis, in prælium processit: primoq; ictu, misso funda lapide, Allophylum percussit: caput victi & spolia abstulit, gladium postea in tem-plum posuit. Allophyli autem omnes in fugam versi victoriam concesserunt. Sed e prælio reversis, multus circa David favor, invidiam regis accenderat. Timens autem tam charum omnibus cum invidia & pernicie necare, sub specie honoris objectare eum periculis statuit. Ac primum tribunum eum fecerat, ut rem bellicam curaret. Inde, cum ei filiam spopondisset, fidem fregit eamque alteri tradidit. Mox filia regis natu minor, Melchol nomine, amore David flagrare occœperat. Igitur nuptiarum ejus istiusmodi conditione propo-nit: si centum præputia David ex hostibus retulisset, regiam virginē matrimonio illius cessuram. Sperabat enim juvenem periculosa audentem facile perituram. Sed longe aliter, ac ratus erat, evenit. Nam ut proposuerat, impigre David centum præputia ex Allophylis retulit: atque ita regis filiam in matrimoniū accepit, cebatin [?] dies in eum regis odium, stimu-lante invidia: quia bonos semper mali in-sectantur, igitur ministris & Ionathæ filio imperavit vitæ ejus ut insidias pararent. Sed Ionathæ charus acceptusq; jam inde a principio David fuerat. Itaque rex increpitus [?] a filio, cruentum imperium repres-sit. Sed non diu mali boni sunt. Nam cum spiritu erroris Saul affligeretur, eique David asisteret, cithara laborantem deli-niens, lancea eum ferire conatus est, nisi ille lethalem ictum propere declinasset. Ex-inde jam non occulte, sed palam ei necem parabat: nec ultra se David regi credidit. Ac primum fugiens ad Samuelem se contulit: inde ad Abimelech, postremo ad regem Moab confugit. Mox per Gad prophetam monitus in terram {b}Iudæ re-gressus, vitæ periculum adiit. Eatempe-state Saul Abimelech sacerdotem intere-mit, quod David recepisset: & cum ex mi-nistris regiis nemo in sacerdotem manus inferre auderet, Doeg {c} Syruscruen-tum ministerium executus est. Post id David{a} deiertum petiit: illic quoq; eum Saul persecutus est, sed inani opera ejus exitium moliebatur, quem Dominus protegebat. Erat in deserto Ipelunca vasto recessu patens. In hujus interiora David fe conjecerat. Saul nesciens, in primo spe-lunceaditu [?] reficiendi corporis gratia luc. ccflera:{b}tibique somno captus requiesce-bat. Quod ubi David animadvertit, hor-tantibus cunctis, ut opportunitate utere-tur, abstinuit regis exitio: {c}diploidem ra-men ejus abstulit. Mox egreflus, ruto emi-nus loco a tergo regem allocutus est, sua in illum commemoras beneficia, ut saepe, pro regno ejus caput periculis objectaf-set: utque postremo, praefenti tempore a Domino sibi traditu, interimere noluif-set. Ad haec, culpam Saul fateri, veniam precari, lachrymas fundere, pietatem David extollere, malitiam suam incusare, regem eum & filium appellans. Tatum ex feroci illo animo mutatu: crederes nihil ultra adversum generum ausurum. Sed David qui {d}penitius ingenium mali fpectatu habe-ret & cognitum, nihil regi credendum ratus, intra eremu fe cotinebat. Saul vecors ani-mi, quia comprehendendi generu potestas non
units.tr: So Saul, first anointed with oil by Samuel, was made king. Born of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Kish, he was modest in spirit and of excellent appearance, so that the dignity of his body fitted royal dignity. But at the beginning of his reign a considerable part of the people had revolted from him, refusing to obey and joining the Ammonites. Saul promptly avenged this; the enemies were defeated, and pardon was granted to the Hebrews. Then Saul was anointed a second time by Samuel. Soon a fierce war broke out with the Philistine invasion, and Saul had appointed a place in Gilgal for the army to assemble. When he had waited seven days for Samuel, so that a sacrifice might be offered to the Lord, and Samuel delayed while the people were dispersing, the king, by a presumptuous and unlawful act, offered the burnt offering in place of the priest. Rebuked severely by Samuel, he confessed his sin with repentance. Then fear from the king's sin spread through the whole army; the enemy camp, lying not far off, showed the danger at hand, and no one had the spirit to go out to battle; they preferred to seek tears and lamentations. For besides the weakness of their spirits, since they thought the Lord was estranged from them because of the king's offence, the army was in great want of iron. So that, except Saul and his son Jonathan, no one, it is reported, had a sword or spear. For the Philistines, victors in the previous war, had taken away the use of arms from the Hebrews, and there was no means of making any weapon of war or even a farm tool. So Jonathan, with a bold plan, taking only his armour-bearer as companion, entered the enemy camp, killed about twenty of the enemy, and struck the whole army with terror. Then, by God's will, they turned to flight, not obeying orders, not keeping ranks, relying only on their feet. When Saul noticed this, he quickly led out his men, pursued the fleeing, and gained the victory. That day, it is said, the king had decreed that no one should eat until the enemy was finished off. But Jonathan, ignorant of this prohibition, found some honeycomb, dipped the tip of his spear in it, and tasted the honey. When the king learned of this in his anger, he ordered his son put to death; but the people saved him from destruction by their help. At that time Samuel, warned by the Lord, approached the king and declared the Lord's words: that he should make war on the nation of Amalek, which had long ago barred the Hebrews' passage when they came out of Egypt, adding the prohibition that he should covet nothing from the spoils of the conquered. So the army was led into the enemy's territory, the king captured the people, and the nation was subdued. But Saul, overcome by the size of the booty and forgetful of the divine command, ordered the captives and the cattle to be spared and brought back. Offended by this, the Lord addressed Samuel, saying that he repented of having made Saul king. The priest reported this to the king. Soon, warned by the Lord, Samuel anointed David with royal oil. David was still a little boy, tending his father's sheep, and often used to sing to the cithara; because of this he was afterwards taken up by Saul and counted among the royal attendants. At that time, when the Philistines and Hebrews were blazing with war and the battle lines faced each other, a certain Goliath of the Philistines, a man of wonderful size and strength, went forward beyond the ranks of his men, hurled insults at the enemy with fierce words, and challenged them to single combat. Then the king promised great rewards and his daughter in marriage to anyone who would bring back the spoils of the challenger. But no one from so great an army dared to engage him. So David, still a boy, offered himself for the fight. Rejecting the arms that his tender age found burdensome, taking only a staff and five stones, he advanced into battle; with the first throw, slinging a stone, he struck the Philistine, took the head of the vanquished and his spoils, and afterwards placed the sword in the temple. All the Philistines turned to flight and gave up the victory. But when the men returned from battle, the great favour surrounding David kindled the king's envy. Fearing, however, to destroy one so dear to everyone with envy and ruin, he resolved to expose him to dangers under the pretext of honour. First he made him a tribune, to attend to military affairs. Then, having promised him his daughter, he broke his word and gave her to another. Soon the king's younger daughter, named Michal, began to burn with love for David. So he set this condition for her marriage: if David brought back a hundred foreskins from the enemies, the royal maiden would pass to his marriage. For he hoped that the youth, daring such perilous things, would easily perish. But things turned out far otherwise than he had reckoned. As he had proposed, David promptly brought back a hundred foreskins from the Philistines, and so took the king's daughter in marriage. Then the king's hatred of him grew, stimulated by envy; since the wicked always pursue the good, he ordered his servants and Jonathan's son to lay snares for David's life. But Jonathan had been dear and welcome to David from the beginning, and so the king, rebuked by his son, restrained his bloody command. But the wicked do not remain good for long. For when Saul was afflicted by an evil spirit, and David attended him, soothing him with the cithara as he laboured, Saul tried to strike him with a spear, unless David promptly avoided the deadly blow. From then on he prepared David's death openly rather than in secret, and David no longer trusted the king. First he fled to Samuel; then he went to Ahimelech; finally he fled to the king of Moab. Soon, warned through the prophet Gad, he returned to the land of Judah and faced danger to his life. At that time Saul slew the priest Ahimelech because he had received David; and since none of the royal servants dared to lay hands on the priest, Doeg the Syrian carried out the bloody service. After this David sought the desert, where Saul pursued him too, but in vain did he plot the destruction of the one whom the Lord protected. In the desert there was a cave, a vast recess, deep inside which David had thrown himself. Saul, unaware, entered the first part of the cave to refresh his body, and overcome by sleep, lay down to rest. When David noticed this, with everyone urging him to use the opportunity, he refrained from the king's destruction, but he took away a part of his garment. Soon, coming out, he addressed the king from a place a little behind him, recalling his own benefits, how often he had exposed his life to dangers for the king's kingdom, and how, when the Lord had delivered the king into his hands at this time, he had not wished to kill him. To this Saul confessed his fault, begged pardon, shed tears, extolled David's piety, accused his own malice, and called David his son and himself the king's enemy. You would have believed that his fierce spirit had wholly changed and that he would dare nothing more against his son-in-law. But David, who had observed and understood more deeply the nature of such evil, judging that nothing should be trusted to the king, kept himself within the wilderness. Saul, mad in mind, since the power of seizing his son-in-law was not...
