units.la: {d} penitus Col. non erat, filiam suam Melchol David, ut supra retulimus, nuptam, Faitim cuidam in matrimonium dedit. David ad Allophylos confugit. Ea tempestate Samuel diem functus est. Saul, Allophylis bellum inferentibus, Dominum consulit, nullumque est ei responsum redditum. Tum per mulierem, cujus viscera spiritus erro-risimpleverat, Samuelem evocatū{a} con-fulit. Dictum ei ab eo est, postero illum die cum{b} filio victum ab Allophylis in praelio casurum. Igitur Allophyli castris in hostili salo positis, postero die aciem instruunt: David tamen ex castris remisso, quia parum crediderant sibi illum adversum suos fidum fore. Sed conferto praelio, Hebraei fusi, filii regis cadunt: Saul equo delapsus, ne vivus in potestatem hostium veniret, gladio suo incubuit. De aetate imperii ejus parum certa comperimus, nisi quod in Actibus apostolorum xl.annos regnasse dictus est. Quamquam ego arbitror, tum a Paulo, cujus illa praedicatio refertur, etiam Samuelis annos sub regis istius aetate numeratos. Plerique tamē qui de temporibus scripserunt, xxx. eum annos regnasse annotaverunt: cui
units.tr: Saul had by no means been using a Col.; he had given his daughter Michal, whom, as we related above, David had married, to a certain Phalti in marriage. David fled to the Philistines. About that time Samuel died. Saul, when the Philistines made war on him, consulted the Lord, but no answer was given him. Then, through a woman whose belly was filled with a spirit of divination, he consulted Samuel, who was summoned. He was told by Samuel that on the next day he and his son would fall in battle, defeated by the Philistines. So the Philistines pitched their camp on hostile ground and drew up their line of battle the next day. David, however, was sent back from the camp, because they had not trusted that he would be faithful to them against his own people. But when battle was joined, the Hebrews were routed and the king's sons fell. Saul, having fallen from his horse, fell upon his own sword so that he would not come alive into the power of the enemy. We have no very certain information about the length of his reign, except that in the Acts of the Apostles he is said to have reigned forty years. Yet I think that the years of Samuel are also counted under the age of that king, since that teaching is attributed to Paul. Most of those who have written about the chronology, however, have noted that he reigned thirty years; we do not at all agree with that opinion.

units.la: opinioni nequaquam accedimus. nam ea tempestate, qua Domini arca in Cariath-jarim opidû translata est, necdum regnare Saul coeperat: refertur autem per David regem ex illo opido arcam sublatam, cum per xx. annos ibi constitisset. Ergo, cum intra id tempus Saul regnaverit atque decesserit, parvo admodum spatio tenuit imperium. Eadem nobis de temporibus Samuelis caligo, ut qui cū Heli sacerdote natus, admodum senex sacerdotio fungus referatur. A nonnullis tamen qui de temporibus scripsere, (quia vere nihil de ejus annis sacra historia signavit) Lxx. annis praefuisse populo refertur. Sed unde hæc authoritas fuerit assumpta, non repeti. Nos in tanta erroris copia, Chronicorum annotationem secuti, quia eam ex Apostolorum actibus (sicut superius memoravimus) profectam arbitramur, Samuelē & Saulem xl. annos principatum egisse referimus. SAVL perempto, David in terra Allophylorum perlato ad se mortis ejus nuncio, miro pietatis exemplo flevisse traditur. Tum Chebron Judæ opidum petiit. Ibi rursum regali unguento illitus rex appellatus est. Sed Abner, qui iterum unctus
units.tr: For at the time when the ark of the Lord was carried to the town of Kiriath-jearim, Saul had not yet begun to reign; it is related, moreover, that King David later carried the ark away from that town, after it had stood there twenty years. Therefore, since Saul reigned and died within that period, he held the kingdom for a very short space. The same darkness surrounds for us the times of Samuel, who, born along with Eli the priest, is reported to have performed the priesthood as a very old man. Yet some who have written about the chronology (since sacred history has recorded nothing certain about his years) report that he ruled the people for seventy years. But where this authority came from is not known. Amid so great a abundance of error, we, following the chronological notes, because we judge that they derive from the Acts of the Apostles (as we mentioned above), report that Samuel and Saul together held the leadership for forty years. When Saul had perished, and news of his death had been brought to David in the land of the Philistines, he is said to have mourned with a remarkable example of piety. Then he went to Hebron, a town of Judah. There, again anointed with royal oil, he was called king. But Abner, who had been commander of Saul's army and had been anointed too, rejected David and set up Ish-bosheth, son of his king, as king.

units.la: magister militiæ Saul regis fuerat, spreto David, Iibaal [?] regis sui filium regem con-stituit. Crebris deinde præliis inter duces regum concursum: pulsus Abner sæpius: {*}fratrem tamen Ioab, qui ex parte David exercitui præcerat, fugiens peremit. Quo dolore postea Ioab, cum se Abner David regi dedisset, jugulari cum præcepit non fine dolore regis, cujus fide cruentaverat. Per idem tempus omnes fere natu majo-res Hebræorum publico consensu regnū ei totius gentis detulerunt. nam per septē annos{b} in Chebron tantum regnaverat, ita tertio rex ungitur, annorum circiter xxx. Allophylos in regnum irruentes, se-cundis præliis repulit. Ea tempestate ar-cam Domini, quæ in Cariathiarim opido, ut supra retulimus, erat, in Sion transtulit. Cumque ædificare Domino templum in animo haberet, divinum ei responsum redditum, feminí illius id{*} reservari. Bel-lo deinde Allophylos domuit, Moabi-tas subjugavit, Syriam subegit,{4} stipendi-umq; ei imposuit, Auri atque æris ex pre-daimmenfum [?] modum retulit. Bellum deinde adversum{4} Ammonitas ex inju-ria Chanun regis corum exortum, Syris denuo rebellatibus, qui cum Ammonitis in bellum conjuraverat. David summam rerum Ioab principi militiae permiserat: ipse a bello remotus, intra Hierusalem commorabatur. Qua tepestate Beriaben quandam, mirae foeminam pulchritudinis, stupro compertam habuit. Haec viri cujusdam uxor, qui tum in castris erat, su isse traditur. Hunc David, iniquo pugnae loco objectum hostibus interficiendum curavit. Ita mulierem in matrimonio viduam, sed jam ex stupro gravida, numero uxorem aggregavit. Tum per Nathan prophetam graviter increpitus, licet agnito errore, castigationem Domini non effugit. Namque filium ex furtivo illo concubitu editum, paucos post dies amisit, multaque in domum familiamque ejusExcranda acciderunt. Ad extremum Absalon filius ejus arma impia adversus patrem sustulit, regno eum depellere cupiens. Adversus hunc Ioab acie conflixit, admonitus a rege ut victo parceret. Sed ille spreto imperio parricidiales conatus ferro ultus est. Flebilis ea victoria fuisse regi traditur. Tanta in eo pietas erat, ut etiam parricidae filio ignosci voluerit. Vix hoc bellum extinctum. cum ali extinctum videbatur, *aliud rursum ex-ortum, Sabæa {b}quodam duce, qui pefsi-mum quemq; ad arma incitaverat. Sed propere mot omnis morte ducis repre-sus. Crebra deinde adversus Allophylos David prælia tecundo eventu habuit:cum ctifq; bello domitis, & tam exteris quam domesticis motibus compressis, floren-tifsimum regnum in pace habebat. Tum cum subita cupido incessit ad metic ndas imperii vires populum censere. Ita a Ioab militiæ magistro decies centena & trecen-ta civium millia dinumerata. Hujus eum facti mox piguit pœnitu itq;, veniä a Do-mino petens, {c}cur in id animos extulit-set,ut regni fui potentiam ex suorum po-tius multitudine, quam ex favore divino æstimaret. Itaque missus ad eum angelus, trinam ci pœnam denunciat, datque arbi-trium unam eligendi. Sed propolitatrien-ni fame, trium mensium fuga, morte tri-dui, fugam & famem detestatus, {e}mortem elegit. momentoque temporis Lxx. mil-lia virorum interiere. Tum David vi-dens angelum, cujus dextra populus pro-ternebatur, veniam precari, feque {f} vi-vum pro omnibus pœnæ obijcere:fe di-gnum gnum exitio,quia ipse peccasset. Ita aver-sum plebis supplicium; David in loco,in quo angelum viderat, aram Domino sta-tuit. Mox annis & morbo intractior,Salo-mone filium ex Bersabee Uriæ uxore suf-ceptum, successorem regni constituit. is regali unguento per Sadoc sacerdote un-ctus,patre adhuc incolumi,rex appellatus. David,cum regnasset annos xl,defunctus est. Salomon initio regni urbem muro circundedit. Huic per soporem astare Do-minus visus est, petendi quæ vellet tribu-ens optione. Sed ille non aliud sibi quam sapientiam dari poposcit, reliqua omnia parvi æstimans. Ita somno excitatus,cum ante *sacrarium Domini constitisset, in-{a}dultæ sibi a Domino sapientiæ documen-tum dedit. Namque duæ{b} mulieres una in domo diversantes,cum eodem tempo-re pueros edidissent, atque ex his alter post diem tertium noste obiisset,mater de-functi somno alterius insidiata,mortuum suum suppositi,viventem abstulit. Inde inter eas de{c} puero altercatio, postremo res ad regem delata: difficilis iudicii absolutio inter negates,ubi testis deerat. Tum Salomon divinæ sapientiæ munere perimi puerum, corpusque ejus dividi inter ambigentes jubet, Cumq; una earum jus dicio acquievisset, alia vero cedere potius puero quam discerpi eum mallet, Salo-mon ex affectu fœmina hanc vere mas trem esse conjectans, puerum illi adjudi-cavit, non fine circumstantium admirati-one: siquidem latentem veritatem pru-dentia protulisset. Ita in admirationem ingenii prudentiæq; ejus reges vicinarum gentium amicitiam ab eo fœdusq; petis[?] re, parati imperata facere, Queis opibus confisus, templum Domino immensito-peris facere aggressus, paratis per triennia um impendiis, quarto fere imperii anno primum fundamentum jecit: a professio-ne Hebræorum ex Ægypto anno fere oc-tavo & octogesimo & quingētefimo. Li-cet libro Regnorum tertio, CCCC. ²xL. etiam in fuisse referantur: quod nequaquam con-venit. Siquidem per seriem superius com-prehensa facilius fuerit, ut minus fortasis annorum, quam amplius annotarim. Sed non dubito, librariorum potius negligen-tia, præsertim tot jam seculis intercedenti-bus, veritate fuisse corrupta, quam ut pro-pheta erraverit. Ficut in hoc ipso nostro opusculo futurum credimus, ut descri-bentium incuria, quæ non incuriose à nobis sunt digesta, vitientur. Igitur Salomon coeptum templi opus vigesimo anno exsplicuit. Celebrato deinde ibidem sacrificio dictaque oratione, quā populum tem-plumque benedixit, Dominus ad eum locutus est, denuncians fore, si quando peccassent, ac Dominum reliquissent, templum illud solo æquādum[?]. Quod jampridem impletum videmus, & mox connexum rerum ordine exponemus. Interea Salomon florens opibus, omnium, qui unquam fuerant regum ditissimus; quisque semper ordo rerum est, ab opibus in luxū & vitia[?] delapsus, cum adversum interdictum Dei ex alienigenis {a}coniugia sumpsisset, etiā septingentas uxores & trecentas concubinas haberet, idola eis ritu gentium suarum, quibus litarent {b}, constituit. Quibus rebus aversus Dominus, graviter increpito pœnā denunciavit, fore ut regnum ex parte maiore adēptū filio, servo illius traderetur. Idque ita accidit. Defuncto Salomone anno imperii quadragesimo, cum Roboā filius anno ætatis {c}sexto & decimo regnū {d}patriū tenere coepisset.
units.tr: Then there were frequent battles between the leaders of the kings; Abner was often beaten; yet in flight he killed his brother Joab, who was commanding the army on David's side. Later Joab, out of grief for this, when Abner had surrendered himself to King David, commanded that he be cut down, not without grief to the king, whose trust Abner had betrayed with blood. At about the same time almost all the eldest of the Hebrews, by common consent of the people, offered him the kingdom of the whole nation. For he had reigned only in Hebron for seven years; so, in the third year, the king was anointed, at about thirty years of age. The Philistines, attacking his kingdom, he repulsed in successive battles. At that time he transferred to Zion the ark of the Lord, which, as we related above, had been in the town of Kiriath-jearim. And when he intended to build a temple to the Lord, a divine answer was given him that this was to be reserved for his offspring. Then he subdued the Philistines, conquered the Moabites, subdued Syria, and imposed tribute on it; he brought back from the spoil an immense quantity of gold and bronze. Next a war arose against the Ammonites, begun by the injury done by their king Hanun, while the Syrians, who had conspired with the Ammonites for war, rebelled again. David had entrusted the chief command of affairs to Joab, the commander of the army; he himself, withdrawn from the war, stayed in Jerusalem. At that time he had a certain Bathsheba, a woman of remarkable beauty, seduced; she is said to have been the wife of a man who was then in the camp. David had this man placed in an unfavourable position in the battle, exposed to the enemy to be killed. So he added to the number of his wives a woman who had been a widow in marriage but was by now pregnant from her illicit union. Then, though he acknowledged his error, he was severely rebuked through the prophet Nathan, and he did not escape the chastisement of the Lord. For the son born from that secret union he lost a few days later, and many dreadful things befell the house and family. At last his son Absalom raised impious arms against his father, desiring to drive him from the kingdom. Against him Joab fought in battle, after being warned by the king to spare the defeated man. But Absalom, scorning this command, avenged his parricidal attempt by the sword. That victory is said to have been mournful for the king. So great was his piety that he wished even the parricide's son to be pardoned. Scarcely was this war ended when, as it seemed to be over, another rose up, stirred by a certain leader, Sheba, who had incited the worst men to arms. But the whole matter was quickly suppressed by the death of the leader. Then David had frequent battles against the Philistines with success; once they were subdued and both foreign and domestic disturbances were quelled, he held a most flourishing kingdom in peace. Then a sudden desire seized him to number the strength of his kingdom by a census of the people. So ten hundred and thirty thousand citizens were counted by Joab, the commander of the army. Soon after this deed he repented and grieved, seeking pardon from the Lord for having raised his spirits to it, so that he valued the power of his kingdom more by the multitude of his subjects than by the favour of God. And so an angel was sent to him, who announced a threefold punishment and gave him the choice of one. But three years of famine, three months of flight, three days of death were set before him; he rejected flight and famine and chose death. In an instant seventy thousand men perished. Then David, seeing the angel, by whose right hand the people were being struck down, prayed for pardon and offered himself, alive, to bear all the punishment, declaring that he himself deserved destruction, since he had sinned. So the punishment of the people was turned aside; David set up an altar to the Lord in the place where he had seen the angel. Soon, weakened by age and sickness, he appointed as successor to the kingdom Solomon, the son he had received from Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah. Anointed with royal oil by the priest Zadok while his father was still alive, he was called king. David, having reigned forty years, died. At the beginning of his reign Solomon walled the city around. The Lord seemed to stand by him in a dream, offering him the choice of whatever he wished. But he asked for nothing else for himself than wisdom, esteeming all other things as of little worth. So, roused from sleep, when he had taken his stand before the sanctuary of the Lord, he gave proof of the wisdom granted him by the Lord. For two women living together in one house had borne sons at the same time, and one of these had died in the night after the third day; the mother of the dead child, lying in wait for the other, secretly substituted her dead child and carried off the living one. Then a dispute arose between them about the child, and finally the matter was carried to the king: the judgment was difficult to settle between the two, since there was no witness. Then Solomon, by the gift of divine wisdom, ordered the child to be killed and its body divided between the two who disputed it. When one of them acquiesced in this judgment, while the other preferred rather to yield the child than to see it torn apart, Solomon, conjecturing from her feeling that this woman was truly the mother, adjudged the child to her, not without the admiration of those standing by; for by his prudence he had brought the hidden truth to light. So, because of the admiration for his talent and prudence, the kings of neighbouring nations sought from him friendship and a covenant, ready to do whatever he commanded. Trusting in these resources, he undertook to build a temple of immense size to the Lord, after preparing the expenses over three years; in the fourth year of his reign, about the 480th year from the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt, he laid the first foundation. Although in the third book of Kings it is reported as 440 years, which by no means agrees: for by the sequence comprehended above it would be easier that I should have noted fewer years rather than more. But I do not doubt that the truth was corrupted by the carelessness of copyists rather than that the prophet erred, especially since so many centuries have intervened. Just as we believe will happen in this little work of ours, that it may be spoiled by the carelessness of those who copy what we have set in order with care. So Solomon completed the work of the temple, begun, in the twentieth year. Then, after a sacrifice had been celebrated there and a prayer spoken, in which he blessed the people and the temple, the Lord spoke to him, declaring that if they should ever sin and abandon the Lord, that temple would be levelled with the ground. This we see has long since been fulfilled, and we shall set it out in the order of events that follows. Meanwhile Solomon, flourishing in wealth, was the richest of all the kings who had ever been; as is always the order of things, from wealth he slid into luxury and vices, and when, against the prohibition of God, he had taken marriages with foreign women, and had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, he established for them idols, after the rites of their nations, to which they might offer sacrifice. Angered by these things, the Lord, after a severe rebuke, announced punishment: that the kingdom would be taken from his son and handed over to his servant for the greater part. And so it happened. When Solomon died in the fortieth year of his reign, Rehoboam, his son, at the age of sixteen, began to hold his ancestral kingdom.

units.la: {b} sacrificarent a pars populi ab eo offensa discedit. Ete-nim cum laxari sibi stipendium popoficit, quod Salomon gravissimum impofu-erat, repudiatis precibus fapplicum, fa-vorem universæ plebis averterat. Itaque consensu omnium, imperium ad Hiero-boam defertur. Is medio genere ortus, ali-quandiu Salomoni servitute pependerat. Sed cum ci refpofo Achiæ prophetæ reg-num{b} Hebreorum annunciatu comperif-set, necare eum clam destinaverat. Quo metu in Aegyptum confugit:ibiq; uxore accepta ex stirpe regia, cognita demum Salomonis morte, in solum patrium regref-sus, voluntate populi, ut supra retulimus, sumpsit imperium. Penes Roboam tamen duæ tribus, Iudæ & Benjamin, resederant: ex his ad trecenta millia paravit exercitum. Quumq; acies promoverentur, verbis Dei populus admonetur, prælio abstineret, ex suo nutu Ieroboam regnum accepisse. Ita spreto regis imperio exercitus dilapsus, Hieroboam imperiū invaluerat. Sed cum Hierosolymam Roboam obtineret, ubi templo a Salomone facto populus sacrificare Domino consueverat: veritus Hieroboam, ne ab eo plebe religio a-verteret. verteret,statuit animos ejus superstitione occupare. Itaq;* vaccam auream in Beth-el, alteram apud Dan constituit, quibus populus litaret: sacerdotesque, omissa Levi tribu, ex plebe instituit. Invisum Domino flagitium, expostulatio consecuta. Crebra adeinde inter reges praelia dubio eventu regnum obtinebant. Roboam septimo & decimo imperii anno exacto vita functus est. In hujus locum Abiud filius ejus regnum Hierosolymae sex annos tenuit: quamvis in Chronicis trienio regnasse referatur. Huic Asab filius successit, a David quintus fere, quippe abnepos ejus: fuit religiosus Domini cultor. Namq; deletis aris lucisque idolorum vestigia paternae perfidiae sustulit. Foedus cum rege Syriae firmavit: ejus auxilio Hieroboae reg. num, quod tum a filio tenebatur, multa clade affecit: ac saepe victis hostibus praedam ex victoria retulit. Post unum & quadragesimum annum, aeger pedibus decessit. Huic triplex peccatum adscribitur: unum, quod societate regis Syriae nimium confisus sit: alterum, quod prophetam Domini, hoc ipsum increpantem, in vincula conjecit: tertium quia in pedum do-
units.tr: {b} to sacrifice. A part of the people, offended by him, broke away. For when the people asked that the burden which Solomon had imposed most heavily be lightened, he rejected their prayers and so lost the goodwill of the whole populace. Therefore, by the consent of all, the rule was offered to Jeroboam. Being of humble birth, he had for some time been in Solomon's service. But when he learned from a response of the prophet Ahijah that the kingdom of the Hebrews had been promised to him, Solomon resolved to kill him secretly. Fleeing in fear to Egypt, he took a wife there from the royal line. Then, when Solomon's death was at last known, he returned to his native land and, by the people's will, as we related above, took up the rule. Yet two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, remained with Rehoboam, and from these he raised an army of about three hundred thousand. As the battle lines were advancing, the people were warned by the word of God not to fight, since Jeroboam had received the kingdom by God's own will. So the king's command was disregarded, the army scattered, and Jeroboam's rule grew strong. But since Rehoboam held Jerusalem, where the people had been accustomed to sacrifice to the Lord in the temple built by Solomon, Jeroboam, fearing that the people's religion would turn them away from him, resolved to win their minds by superstition. So he set up a golden calf at Bethel and another at Dan, for the people to sacrifice to, and he appointed priests from the common people, leaving out the tribe of Levi. The crime was hateful to the Lord, and a rebuke followed. Thereafter frequent wars between the kings were fought with doubtful outcomes. Rehoboam died in the seventeenth year of his reign. In his place his son Abijah held the kingdom of Jerusalem for six years, although in Chronicles he is said to have reigned only three. His son Asa succeeded him, roughly the fifth from David, being his great-grandson. He was a devout worshipper of the Lord: he destroyed the altars and groves of the idols and removed the traces of his father's faithlessness. He made a covenant with the king of Syria, and with his help he inflicted heavy losses on the kingdom of Jeroboam, which was then held by Jeroboam's son; and often, after defeating the enemy, he brought back spoil from his victory. After forty-one years he died, diseased in his feet. Three sins are charged against him: first, that he trusted too much in his alliance with the king of Syria; second, that he cast the prophet of the Lord into prison for rebuking him for this; third, that in the pain of his feet he sought a remedy

units.la: {a} aviulnm aureum [?] lore remedium nona Domino, sed ame[?]. dicis speraverit. Sed initio regni hujus, Hieroboam rex decem tribuum defun-ctus est, regnū Nadab filio reliquit. Is mas-a patre- lis operibus, & tam suis quam * maternis meritis invisus Domino, non ultra bien-nium regno potitus est, privataq; imperio. indigna progeniēs b Banachiæ filium fuc-cessoré habuit, æque a Domino alienissi- mum.c[fq; sexto & vigesimo imperii āno defunctus est: regnum ad Helam filium devolutum,nec ultra biennium retētum; namque eum Zambri princeps equitum epulantem interfecit, regnumque occu-pavit: vir perinde in Dominum atque ho-mines impius. Ab hoc pars populi fecef-fit, Thamni cuidam regium nomen dela-tum. Sed Iambri ante hunc septem annos, & cum eodem duodecim regnavit. At in parte tribus Iudæ Asab mortuo, Iofa. phat filius ejus regnare coepit, vir religi- osis virtutibus merito clarus. Is cum lam-bri pacem habuit. Defunctus est autem cum regnasset annos v. & xx. Hujus im-perii tempore Achab Iambri filius rex decem tribuum fuit, ultra omnes in Do-minum impius. Namque Iezabel filia Basæ regis ex Sidone in matrimonio ac cepta, Baali idolo aram lucosq; constituit, & prophetas Domini interemit. Quo tempore Helias propheta oratione cœ-lum cōclusit, ne pluviam terræ daret: idq; regi denunciavit, ut se impius causam malı esse cognosceret. Igitur sulpensis cœlo aquis, cum loca omnia adusta solis ardo-ribus non victum hominibus, non pabulum iumentis darent, ipse se intra periculum famis propheta concluderat. Ea tempestate cum eremum petisset, corvis cibum ministrantibus, vixit. Aquam {a}torrens proximus, donec aruit, dedit. Inde admonitus a Domino,{b} Sareptæ oppidum petiit: ad mulierem viduam divertit. Cumq; ab ea esuriens cibum peteret, illa causari, non esse sibi nisi pusillum farris & pusillum olei: quo absumpto, una cum{c} filiis morte expectaret. Sed cum Helias verbis Dei polliceretur, nec hydriam farre, nec vas oleo esse minuendum, mulier poscēti fidem non cunctata prophetæ credere promissorum fidem consecuta est. Siquidem divinis incrementis tantum accresce-ret, quantum quotidie detrahebat. Eodem tempore, ejusdē viduæ filium mor-
units.tr: {a} a golden calf [?] not from the Lord but from physicians, he hoped. But at the beginning of this reign, Jeroboam, king of the ten tribes, died and left the kingdom to his son Nadab. He, hateful to the Lord both for his father's deeds and for his own and his mother's, held the kingdom for no more than two years, and his unworthy line was deprived of power. He was succeeded by Baasha, son of Ahijah, equally most alien to the Lord. He died in the twenty-sixth year of his reign, and the kingdom passed to his son Elah, who did not keep it beyond two years; for Zimri, commander of the chariots, killed him while he was feasting and seized the kingdom, a man as impious toward the Lord as toward men. From him a part of the people revolted, and the royal title was conferred on a certain Tibni. But Zimri had reigned seven years before this, and Omri twelve years alongside him. In the part of the tribe of Judah, after Asa died, his son Jehoshaphat began to reign, a man rightly famed for his devout virtues. He kept peace with Omri. He died after reigning twenty-five years. In the time of Jehoshaphat, Ahab, son of Omri, was king of the ten tribes, more impious toward the Lord than all the others. For he took as his wife Jezebel, daughter of King Ethbaal of Sidon, set up an altar and grove for the idol Baal, and killed the prophets of the Lord. At that time the prophet Elijah, by prayer, shut up heaven so that it gave no rain to the earth, and he announced this to the king, so that the impious man might know that he was the cause of the evil. So, with the waters of heaven withheld, and all places scorched by the sun's heat yielding neither food for men nor fodder for beasts, the prophet himself had shut himself up within the peril of famine. In that time, having gone into the wilderness, he lived, with ravens bringing him food. The nearby torrent gave him water until it dried up. Then, admonished by the Lord, he went to the town of Sarepta and lodged with a widow. When he, hungry, asked her for food, she excused herself, saying that she had only a little meal and a little oil, and once these were used up she and her sons would await death. But when Elijah promised in God's words that neither the jar of meal nor the jug of oil would be diminished, the woman, without hesitation, believed the prophet's promise and saw it fulfilled. For by divine increase it grew as much as she drew from it each day. At the same time Elijah brought the dead son of this widow back to life. Then, at the Lord's command, he went to the king, reproached him for his sacrilege, and demanded that all the people be gathered before him. When they had assembled quickly, and about four hundred and fifty priests of the idols and groves had been summoned, a dispute arose among them: Elijah proclaimed the Lord, while they defended their superstitions. Finally it was agreed to make a trial: whichever sacrificed victim fire sent from heaven consumed, that religion would be counted true which had shown its power. So the priests, having slain a calf, began to call upon the idol Baal; and when their invocations had been spent in vain, they tacitly confessed the weakness of their lord. Then Elijah, mocking them, said: "Perhaps he is asleep; shout louder, so that he may wake from the sleep in which he is held." Indeed the wretches, trembling, fell silent, and yet waited to see what Elijah would do. But he laid the slain calf on the altar, after first filling the trench around it with water. Then, calling upon the Lord while all waited, fire fell from heaven and consumed the water along with the victim. Then the people, prostrate on the ground, confessed the Lord and cursed the idols. Finally, at Elijah's command, the profane priests were seized

units.la: {a} Carith.
units.tr: {a} Cherith.

units.la: {b} vel Sarepta.
units.tr: or Zarephath.

units.la: {c} τοῖς τέκνοις, υἱοῖς LXX. tuum Helias in vitam reduxit. Tum jussu Domini regem adiit, exprobratoque ei sacrilegio, poposcit ad se omnem populum congregari. Qui cum propere conveniisset, accitis idolorum ac lucorū sacerdotibus CCCC.{a} fere & L. inter eos inde orta est altercatio, Helia Dominum prædicante, illi superstitiones suas asserebant. Postremo, placuit fieri periculum, ut si cujus cæsam hostiam missus cœlo ignis absumeret, rata esset religio, quæ virtutem edidisset. Ita sacerdotes occiso vitulo Baal idolum invocare cœperunt: frustraque consumptis invocationibus imbecillitatem domini sui tacite fatebantur. Tum forte Helias irridens eos: Ne{b} forte, inquit, dormiat, clamate vehementius, ut somno, quo tenetur, evigilet. Enimvero miseri trepidantes mussare, & tamē quid nam Helias facturus esset, exspectare. At ille, cæsum vitulum imposuit, quum primus sacrarium aqua opplesset: invocatoque Domino, exspectantibus cunctis, ig-nis cœlo delapsus, aquam cum hostia absumpsit. Tum vero populus solo stratus Dominum fateri, idola execrari: postremo, Heliæ jussu prophani sacerdotes comprehensi.
units.tr: [τοῖς τέκνοις, υἱοῖς] LXX. "Elijah brought your son back to life." Then, at the Lord's command, he went to the king, rebuked him for his sacrilege, and demanded that the whole people be gathered together. When they had hurried together and the priests of the idols and groves, about 450 men, had been summoned, a dispute arose among them: Elijah proclaimed the Lord, while they defended their superstitions. At last it was agreed to make a trial: whichever god sent fire from heaven to consume the sacrifice that was offered would be judged the true religion, since it had shown its power. So the priests killed a calf and began to call upon the idol Baal, but when their invocations were spent to no effect, they tacitly admitted their lord's weakness. Then Elijah, mocking them, said: "Perhaps he is asleep; shout louder, so that he may wake from the sleep that holds him." The wretched men, trembling, fell silent but waited to see what Elijah would do. He laid the slaughtered calf on the altar after first filling the altar with water; then, calling upon the Lord while everyone watched, fire fell from heaven and consumed the water along with the victim. At this the people, prostrate on the ground, confessed the Lord and cursed the idols; finally, at Elijah's command, the profane priests were seized.

units.la: {b} reddidit [?]. Vide Sig. prehensi deductique ad *torrentem neca-{a}ti iunt. Redeuntem inde regem propheta prosecutus est. Sed cum ei Iezabel regis uxor vitae periculum pararet, {b}ad remo-tiora secessit, ibi eum Dominus allocutus est, septem millia virorum esse adhuc pronuncians, qui se idolis non dedissent. Mirum id Heliae fuit, qui solu se a{c} sacrilegio immunem esse crediderat. Ea tempestate Achab rex Samariae vineam Nabuthaei, adhaerentem {d}sibi concupivit. Quam cum ille ei vendere noluisset, dolis leza-bel interfectus est. Ita Achab vinea potitus est, cum tamen Nabuthaei mortem doluisse referatur. Mox per Heliam verbo Domini increpitus, agnitoque crimine, cilicio indutus, egisse poenitentiam traditur. Quo facto, imminentem poenam avertit. Namque rex Syriae magno cum exercitu, duobus & triginta regibus in so-cietatem belli alcitis, fines Samariae ingressus, cum rege urbem obsidere coepit.
units.tr: rendered [?]. See Sig. They were seized and led down to the brook and put to death. As the king returned from there, the prophet followed him. But when Jezebel, the king's wife, plotted to take his life, he withdrew to a more remote place, where the Lord spoke to him, declaring that there were still seven thousand men who had not given themselves to idols. This was a marvel to Elijah, who had believed that he alone was free from sacrilege. At that time Ahab, king of Samaria, desired the vineyard of Naboth, which adjoined his own. When Naboth refused to sell it to him, he was put to death by Jezebel's treachery. So Ahab obtained the vineyard, although he is said to have grieved over Naboth's death. Later, rebuked by Elijah with the word of the Lord and acknowledging his crime, he is said to have put on sackcloth and performed repentance. By this act he averted the punishment that was hanging over him. For the king of Syria, with a great army, having enlisted thirty-two kings as allies in the war, entered the borders of Samaria and began to besiege the city together with the king.

units.la: *Actis deinde obsessorum rebus, dat belli conditiones, si aurum & argentum & foeminas tradidissent, fore uti vitae eorum parceret. Sed tam injustis conditionibus extrema perpeti satius visum. Et cum jam omnium desperata effet salus, pro-pheta a Domino mislus, regem adit, hor-tatur ut in prelium exeat: cunctante mul-tis confirmat, ita eruptione facta fusi hostes copiosaque præda reperta. Sed post an-num reparatis viribus, Syrus in Samariam regressus, acceptam cladem ultum ire cu-piens, rursum victus est. Eo prælio cxx. millia Syrorum interiere. Regi venia da-ta, regnum ei & pristinus status concessus. Tum Achab verbis Dei a propheta increpitus, cur abusus divino munere, hosti fi-bi tradito pepercisset. Igitur Syrus post triennium bellum Hebræis intulit. Ad-versum hunc Achab, pseudopropheta-rum impulsu, in prælium descendit: spre-to Michæa propheta & in vincula conjec-to, quod ei exitiabilem fore pugnam de-nunciasset. Ita eo prælio Achab interfe-ctus Ochoziæ filio imperium reliquit.
units.tr: *Then, after the situation of the besieged was made known, he offered terms of war: if they handed over gold, silver and women, he would spare their lives. But it seemed better to endure the worst than to accept such unjust terms. And when all hope of safety had been abandoned, a prophet sent by the Lord came to the king and urged him to go out to battle. When the king hesitated, the prophet assured him, and so, a sortie having been made, the enemy were routed and abundant spoil was found. But a year later, the Syrian, having restored his strength, returned to Samaria, desiring to avenge the defeat he had suffered, and was again defeated. In that battle 120,000 Syrians perished. The king was granted pardon, and his kingdom and former status were restored to him. Then Ahab, rebuked by the prophet with God's words, was reprimanded for having misused the divine gift and spared the enemy delivered into his hand. So the Syrian, after three years, made war on the Hebrews. Against him Ahab went into battle, at the urging of false prophets, having scorned the prophet Micaiah and cast him into prison, because he had foretold that the battle would be fatal for him. So in that battle Ahab was killed and left the kingdom to his son Ahaziah.

units.la: Is æger corpore, cum ex ministris, qui idolum pro salute ejus consulerent, mi-sset: Helias a Deo monitus, obviam se eis obtulit, increpitosq; renunciare re-gi jubet, mortem ejus confequuturam.
units.tr: He, sick in body, had sent some of his ministers to consult the idol about his health. Elijah, warned by God, met them on their way, rebuked them, and ordered them to tell the king that he would die.

units.la: Tum rex comprehendi eum ac deduci ad se jubet: sed missi, cœlesti igne absumpti. Rex, ut propheta prædixerat, obiit. Successit autem Ioram ei, frater ejus: isque duodecim annis imperio potitus est. At in parte duarum tribuum Iosaphat rege defuncto, Ioram filius regnum tenuit annos duodeviginti. Is Achab filiam uxorem habuit, socero quam patri propior. Post hunc Ochozias filius imperium adeptus est. Hoc regnante Helias translatus fertur. Eodem tempore Helisaeus discipulus ejus multis signis potens extitit: quæ omnia notiora sunt, quam ut nostro stylo egeant. Abeo est viduæ filius resuscitatus, Syrus lepra purgatus. Famis tempore, omnium rerum copia fugatis hostibus invecta, in usum trium exercituum aquæ præbitæ: de exiguo olei immodicis incrementis solutum mulieris debitum, & ipsi sufficiens vivendi substantia data. Hujus temporibus, ut diximus, Ochozias duarum tribuum erat rex: decem vero Ioram, ut supra retulimus, imperabat. Interque eos fœdus ictum. Nam & adversus Syros junctis viribus bella-tum: & adversum Iehu, qui per prophetam in regem decem tribuum unctus fuerat, pariter in prælium egressi, eadem pugna interiere. Sed regnum Ioram Iehu tenuit, positò Ochozia in Iudæa regè. Quì uno anno regnavit: mater ejus Gotholia imperium occupavit, adempto nepotiimperio, etiam tum parvo puero, cui Ioas nomen fuit. Sed huic ab avia prærceptum imperium, post octo fere annos per sacerdotem & populum depulsa avia redditum.
units.tr: Then the king ordered that Elijah be seized and brought before him, but the men he sent were consumed by fire from heaven. The king died, as the prophet had foretold. His brother Joram succeeded him and held the rule for twelve years. Meanwhile, in the part made up of two tribes, Jehoshaphat died and his son Joram held the kingdom for eighteen years. He had married Ahab's daughter, and so was closer to his father-in-law than to his own father. After him his son Ahaziah obtained the rule. In his reign Elijah is said to have been taken up. At the same time his disciple Elisha became powerful through many signs, all of which are too well known to need our style to describe them. Through him the son of the widow was raised to life, and the Syrian was cleansed of leprosy. In a time of famine, when the enemy had been put to flight, an abundance of all things was brought in, and water was supplied for the use of three armies. A debt owed by a widow was paid from a little oil, which multiplied beyond measure, and she was given enough means to live on. In his time, as we have said, Ahaziah was king of the two tribes, while Joram, as we related above, ruled the ten. Between them a covenant was made: they fought together against the Syrians with united forces, and when they went out together against Jehu, who had been anointed by a prophet as king of the ten tribes, both perished in the same battle. But Jehu held the kingdom of Joram, and Ahaziah was set aside as king in Judah. He reigned for one year. His mother Athaliah seized the rule, depriving her grandson, who was still a small boy named Joash. But after about eight years the rule was restored to him from his grandmother, who was driven out by the priest and the people.

units.la: Hic initio regni observantissimus divini cultus fuit, magnisque sumptibus templum exornavit: post adulatione principum depravatus, adoratusque ab eis, DEI iram meruit. Namque ei Azael rex Syriæ bellum intulit: inclinatisque rebus suis, auro templi pacem redemit. Nec tamen ea potitus est, facti invidia a suis interfectus, anno imperii quadragesimo. Huic Amasias filius successit.
units.tr: At the beginning of his reign he was most devoted to the worship of God and adorned the temple at great expense. Afterwards, corrupted by the flattery of the princes, and worshipped by them, he incurred the wrath of God. For Hazael, king of Syria, made war on him; when his affairs were weakened, he bought peace with the gold of the temple. Yet he did not long enjoy it, for, through the resentment caused by this deed, he was killed by his own people in the fortieth year of his reign. Amaziah his son succeeded him.

units.la: At in parte decem tribuum defuncto Iehu, Ioachas filius ejus regnavit, invisus DEO, malis operibus, ob quæ regnum ejus Syris prædæ fuit, donec Dei misericordia depulsis hostibus, pristinum habere statu coeperunt.
units.tr: In the part made up of the ten tribes, after Jehu died, his son Jehoahaz reigned, hateful to God for his evil deeds, on account of which his kingdom became plunder for the Syrians, until, by the mercy of God, the enemies were driven off and they began to have their former state again.

units.la: Ioachas diem functus, Ioæ filio reliquit regnum. Is Amasiæ regi duarum tribuum civile bellum intulit, victoriaq; potitus, multam prædã in regnum suum convertit.
units.tr: Jehoahaz died and left the kingdom to his son Joash. He made war on Amaziah, king of the two tribes, in a civil war; having gained the victory, he carried much booty into his own kingdom.

units.la: {a} Amasias 4.Reg.13. (note referring to Ochozia) ; {c} Amasiæ Paris. vertit. Idque ob Amasiæ deliĉtum acci-disse traditur. Siquidem Idumæorum fi-nes victor ingressus, idola gentis ejus asfumpserat. Hic * novem annos regnasse{a} scribitur, quantum in libris Regnorum re-peri. Sed in Paralipomenis, atque etiam in Chronicis, novem & viginti annos imperium tenuisse annotatū *est. Ea nimirum id persuadente ratione, quæ in his Regnorum libris facile perspici poterat. Ioram enim rex decem tribuum {b}octavo anno imperii Amasiæ traditur regnare cœpisse, unumq;[?] & quadraginta annos imperium tenuisse, regnante demum Ozia Amasiæ filio, quarto imperii ejus anno defunctus est. Qua ratione{c}viginti & novem annos regi Amasiæ effecit. Itaque nos hoc ipsum secuti, quia rationem temporum persequi placet, Chronicorum authoritati accessimus. Igitur Amasiæ, Ozia filius successit, nam in parte decem tribuum Ioas diem functus, Ioram filio locum fecerat: postea[?] hunc Zacharias ejus filius regnavit. Horum nos regum, omniumque qui in parte decem tribuum Samariæ præ-fuerunt, annotanda esse tempora non putavimus: quia brevitati studentes, superflua omisimus,& ad cognitionem temporum a duarū ejus potissimum {a}partis annos credimus persequendos, quæ in captivitatem post-erius abducta, prolixius tempus in regno habuit. Igitur Ozias regnum Iudæ adep-tus, præcipuam curā Domini cognoscen-di habuit, Zacharia propheta plurimum usus. Esaias etiam sub hoc primum pro-phetasse traditur, quo merito prosperis eventibus adversus finitimos bella gesit. Arabas etiam devicit. Iamque Aegyptū terrore nominis sui concusserat,elatusq; secundis rebus,illicita præsumens,incen-sum Deo obtulit: quod solis facere sacer-dotibus fas erat.Itaque cum per Azariam sacerdotem increpitus eo loco decedere cogeretur, atque in iram exarsiset, lepra {e}templo oppletus,{b} decessit.Quo morbo affectus, vita functus est,quū regnasset annos duos & quinquaginta. Regnū inde loathę filio datum : isque admodum sanctus fuisse traditur,prospereque imperium admini-stravit: gentem Ammonitarum bello vi-ctam,stipendium præstare coegit. regna-vit autem annis xvi. eidemque Achaz fi-lius successit.Celebris circa hæc tempora Ninivitarum fides traditur. Id opidum olim
units.tr: {a} Amasias 4.Reg.13.; {c} The Paris translation renders this as Amasiae. This is said to have happened because of a sin of Amasias: having entered as victor into the territory of the Edomites, he had taken up the idols of that people. He is written as having reigned nine years, as I find in the books of Kings. But in the Chronicles, and indeed in the Paralipomena, it is noted that he held the rule for twenty-nine years. Doubtless it was the reasoning that could easily be seen in these books of Kings that led to this: for King Joram of the ten tribes is said to have begun to reign in the eighth year of Amaziah's rule, and to have held the rule for forty-one years, and he died in the fourth year of the reign of Uzziah, son of Amaziah. By this reckoning he makes twenty-nine years for Amaziah. And so we, following this very view, because we wish to pursue the order of the times, have adopted the authority of the Chronicles. Therefore Uzziah, son of Amaziah, succeeded; for in the part of the ten tribes Joash had died and had made room for his son Joram; afterwards Zechariah, his son, reigned after him. We did not think that the times of these kings, and of all who presided over the part of the ten tribes of Samaria, needed to be noted, because, aiming at brevity, we have left out what was superfluous, and we believe that the years should be followed chiefly in the part of the two tribes, which later was led away into captivity and had a longer time in the kingdom. So Uzziah, having obtained the kingdom of Judah, had a particular care to know the Lord, making much use of the prophet Zechariah. Isaiah too is said to have first prophesied under him, and by his merit he waged wars successfully against his neighbours. He also conquered the Arabs. And already he had shaken Egypt with terror at his name, and, puffed up by his successes and presuming on what was unlawful, he offered incense to God, which only the priests were permitted to do. So when he was rebuked by the priest Azariah and compelled to withdraw from that place, and flared up in anger, he was struck by leprosy on his forehead in the temple, and he died. Afflicted by this disease, he died after reigning fifty-two years. The kingdom then passed to his son Jotham, who is said to have been very holy and governed the realm prosperously: he forced the Ammonite nation, defeated in war, to pay tribute. He reigned sixteen years, and Ahaz his son succeeded him. The faith of the Ninevites is said to have been celebrated around this time. That town, founded long ago by Asshur, son of Seon, was the capital of the kingdom of the Assyrians,

units.la: {a} tribum. olim ab Afsur, * Seon filio conditum,ca-{a} put regni Assyriorum fuit: frequens tum incolétium multitudine, alens {b}virorum millia c. & xx. atque, ut in magno populo, abundans vitiis. Queis Deus motus, Ionam prophetam ex Iudæa ire præcepit, ac denunciare urbi excidium,{c} sicut olim Sodoma & Gomorrha divinis ignibus conflagrasent. Verum propheta prædicationis istius ministerium detrectans, non contumacia, sed præscientia,{d} qua videbat Dominum pœnitentia populi placandum, navim, quæ longe diversa regione{e} Tharsos petebat, conscendit. Sed ubi in altum processu, nautæ lævitia maris compulsi, quis nam esset mali causa forte exploravere. Cum super Ionam fors decidisset, tanquam piaculum tempestatis in profundum projectus est: exceptusque à ceto, marino monstro, ac devoratus, post triduum fere Ninivitarum littoribus ejectus, jussa prædicat, urbem scilicet ob peccata populi triduo perituram. Igitur non dissimulanter, ut olim Sodomis, audita est vox prophetæ: ac statim jussu regis exemploque, populus universus, quin & recens nati, cibo potuq; abstinere iubentur:iumenta itidem & diuersi gene-ris animalia compulsa fame ac siti,lamen-tantium speciem cum hominibus præbe-bant. Ita imminens malum auersum. longe [?] apud Deum conquerenti, quod fides di-ctis non affuisset, responsum:pœnitenti-bus veniā negari non posse. At in Sama-ria Zachariam regem admodum impium, quem superius regnasse memoravimus, {a}Sella quidam interemit,regnumque oc-cupavit:idemque Manæ insidiis, exemplo facti fui, periit. Mane {b}ereptum Sellæ im-perium tenuit, filioque {c}Pache reliquit. Eundem vero {d}Pache quidam ejusdē no-minis interemit, regnumque occupavit. Mox ab Ofee peremptus, eodem scelere, quo assumpserat, imperium amisit. Hic ultra omnes reges superiores impius, poenam sibi perpetuamq; genti captivita-tem a Deo meruit. Namq; ei Salmanasar rex Asyriorum intulit bellum, victumq; tributarium sibi effecit. Sed cum occul-tis consiliis rebellionem pararet, regem-que Aethiopum, qui tum Aegyptum obtinebat, in auxilium accerseret, idque Salmanasar comperisset, perpetuis eum vinculis in carcerem conjecit,urbemq; ex-cidit, {a}cidit, populum universum in regnum suum abduxit, Assyrius in hostili iolo[?] ad custodiam positis. Exinde ea pars Samaria appellata: quod lingua Assyriorum custodes Samaritas vocant. ex quibus plerique divinas ceremonias receperunt, reliquis in errore gentilitatis perseverantibus. Hoc bello Tobias in captivitatem ductus est. At in parte duarum tribuum rex Achas ob impietatem invisus D E O, cum finitimorum bellis saepe premeretur, deos gentium colere decrevit, nimirum quia eorum illę auxilio victores {b}frequē-tibus praeliis exstitissent. Ita in hoc nefarie metis[?] piaculo diem functus est, cum x v i. annis in regno fuisset. Huic Ezechias filius successit, multum paterni dissimilis ingenii. Namque initio regni, populum sacerdotesq; ad Dei cultum cohortatus, multis disseruit[?], ut frequenter castigati a Domino, sæpius essent misericordia consequuti, ut postremum decem tribus in captivitate nuper abductæ, sacrilegii pœnas dissolverent: curandum eis sedulo, ne eadem pati mereantur. Ita conversis ad religionem omnium animis, levitas sacerdotesque omnes ad celebranda fecundum legem sacrificia ordinavit: cele-brariq; Pascha instituit, quod jampridem fuerat omissum. Cumque dies festus ad-esse[?] dimissis per omnem terram nunciis, conventus diem edixit: ut si qui post ab-ductionem decem tribuum in Samaria re-sedissent, ad solenne sacrum convenirent. Ita frequentissimo conventu dies sacer publica laetitia exactus, longo post intervallo religione legitima per Ezechiam re-stituta. Pari deinde industria, qua divina curaverat, rem bellicam administravit, Allophiloque frequentibus praeliis con-tudit: donec ei Sennacherib rex Assyrio-rum bellum intulit, magno cum exercitu fines ejus ingressus: lateque agris vastatis, nullo obsistente, urbis obsidionem urge-bat. Ezechias enim multitudine inferior, non aulus manum conferre[?], muris se tu-ebatur. Rex Assyrius portis alsultans, mi-nitari excidium, deditionem imperare, Ezechiam frustra Deo confidere, se Dei nutu potius arma {b}supprelsisse: victorem omnium gentium, eversorem Samariae, effugi non posse, ni matura deditione si-bimet consuluissent. In hoc rerum sta-tu Ezechias Deo fretus, Esaiam prophetam consulit: ejusque responso edocetur, nihil ex hoste periculi fore, divinû autem auxilium non defuturum. Nec multo post * Tirchac rex Aethiopum reg num Aflyriorum invadit. Quo nuncio Sennacherib ad luatuenda converl us,fre- mens & clamitans, victori sibi victoriam eripi,bellum omisit:missis ad Ezechiali- teris,cum verborum contumeliis denun- cians,se paulo post rebus domi composi- tis,ad excidium ludeae-maiure rediturum. Sed nihil his Ezechias motus, orasse Do- minum traditur, ne hanc tantam hominis insolentiam inultam sineret. Ita eadem nocte angelus castra Assyriorum aggref- sus,multa hominum millia letho dedit. Rex trepidus in opidum Niniven consu- git, ibique a filiis interfectus, dignum se exitium tulit. Per idem tempus Ezechias, æger corpore,morbo incubuerat. Cum- que Esaias ei verbum Domini annunci- asset, vitæ ejus finem adesse, flesle rex tra- ditur. ita xv. annos prorogari sibi ad vi- tam meruit. Quibus peractis,nono & vi- gefimo imperii anno decessit: regnum Manasse filio reliquit. Is a patre multu de- generas, relicto Domino,culturas impia exercuit: ob quod in potestatem Assyriorum traditus, malo coactus agnovit errorem: populumque adhortatus est, uti relictis idolis Dominum colerent. Nihil sane dignum memoria gessit, regnavit annos v. & l. Amō deinde filius ejus regnum adeptus est, nec ultra biennū eo potitus est: paternæ impietatis hæres, Domini negligens, suorum insidiis circum-vētus periit. Ad Iosiam filium imperium devolutū. Is admodum religiosus fuisse traditur, summaque cura divina admini-stra[?]sse[?] Helchia sacerdote usus bene. Is cum in tēplo {b}verbi Dei scriptum, repertum a sacerdote, legisser[?]quo cōtine-batur, Hebræam[?] gente ob crebras impietates & sacrilegia delēdam, piis ad Deū precibus fletuque jugi imminentem cladem avertit. Quod ubi indultum sibi per ᶜ Olam prophetissam comperit, majore cura, utpote obligatus divinis beneficiis, cultum Dei exercuit. Igitur vasa omnia, anteriorum regum superstitionibus idolis consecrata, cremavit. Namque eō prophani ritus invaluerant, ut soli ac lunæ divinos honores darent, eisdemque etiam ex metallis sacratia ædificarent. Quibus Iofias in pulverem redactis, sacerdotes quoque prophanarum aedium interfecit. Sed ne sepulchris quidem impiorum pepercit: quod olim praedictum a propheta, impletum animadversum est. Huius octa-vo & decimo imperii anno Pascha celebratum. Post triennium fere, adversus Nechao regem Aegypti, qui bellum Assyriis inferebat, in praelium egressus, priusquam inter se acies concurrerent, sagitta ictus est. Exq; eo vulnere in urbem relatus decessit, cum regnasset annos 1.& *xx. Ioachas inde filius eius regnum adeptus tribus mensibus tenuit, captivitati ob impietatem destinatus. Namque eum Nechao rex Aegypti vinctum captumque duxit. Nec multo post in vinculis diem functus est. Iudaeis stipendium annuum impera-tum. Rex eis Eliachim arbitrio victoris datus, qui postea immutato nomine Ioachis vocitatus est. Hic Ioachae fratris Iosiae F. fuit, fratri quam patri propior, sacrilegio invisus Deo. Igitur cum regi Aegyptio pareret, quippe cui tributum penderet, Nabuchodonosor rex Babylonius Iudaeam terram occupavit armis, & per triennium iure belli victor possedit. Etenim cedentes jam rege AEgypti, determinatisque inter eos imperii finibus, convenerat Iudaeos ad Babylonem pertinere. Ira cum Ioachis, exactis in regno annis undecim, * filioe-iusdem nominis locum fecisset, ifq; regis Babylonii in se iram concitasset, Deo nimirum agente, cui constitutum erat Iudę[?] gentem captivitati & internecioni da-re, Nabuchodonosor Hierosolymam cum exercitu ingressus, urbem murosque ac templum solo stravit: auri immensū modum & sacra ornamenta vel publica vel privata, puberesq; omnes virilis ac muliebris sexus transtulit: relictis, quorum imbecillitas aut ætas fastidio victoribus fuit. Quæ turba inutilis servitio, exercendis colendisque agris, ne incultum esset solum, deputata. Eisdemque rex Sedechias præpositus, ademptis viribus inani tantum umbra regii nominis concessa. Sed Ioachis tribus mensibus tempus imperii habuit. Is cum populo Babylonem translatus, & in carcerem conjectus est: trigesimum post annum emissus, atque a rege in amicitiam receptus, mensaque & consiliis participatus, non sine solatio depulsae calamitatis decessit. Interea Sedechias rex turbæ inutilis, quanquam fine viribus, infido ingenio & Dei immemor, qui non intelligeret captivitatem ob delicta gen-tis illatam: postremis denique malis de-bitus, regis animum offendit. Ita ei post novem annos Nabuchodonosor bellum intulit: compulsumque intra muros con-fugere triennio obsedit. Qua tempestate Ieremiam prophetam, qui jam sæpius im-minere urbi captivitatem pronunciave-rat, consulit, si quid spei forsitan superesset. Sed ille, cœlestis iræ non ignarus, eadem sæpius interrogatus, respondit, ipsi regi specialem pœnam denuncians. Tum vero Sedechias in iram excitatus, trudi prophetam in carcerem jubet: moxque eum crudelis facti piguit. Sed obstinatis Iudæorum principibus, quibus jam inde a principio moris fuerat bonos præmere, absolvere innocentem non est ausus. Iisdem cogentibus, in lacum immensi profundi, cœno, ac sordibus, atque ex eo exitiabili factore horridum, demissus est, ut ne simplici quidem morte expiraret. Sed rex, licet impius, aliquanto tamen sacerdotibus mitior, educi prophetam de la-cu,& carceris custodiæ reddi jubet. Interea obsessos vis hostium & penuria urgebat: consumptisque omnibus quae mandi poterant, fames invaluerat. Ita defessis intus inedia defensoribus opidum captum incensumque. Rex, ut propheta dixerat, effosis oculis, Babyloniam translatus: Hieremias misericordia hostili carcere exemptus. Cum eum Nabuzardan princeps regius, captivum cum caeteris duceret, delata sibi optione ab eo, utrum in solo patrio deferto desolatoque subsistere, an secum abire in summis honoribus vellet, residere in patria maluit. Nabuchodonosor abducto populo, reliquis, quos belli conditio vel praedae fastidium reliquos a victoribus fecerat, Godolian ejusdem gentis praeposuit, absque ullo insigni regio, aut imperii nomine: quia praeesse paucis & calamitosis, nulla dignitas erat.
units.tr: Nineveh, once founded by Asshur, son of Seon, was the capital of the kingdom of the Assyrians. It was then populous, with a large number of inhabitants, about 120,000 men, and, as is usual in a great population, it abounded in vices. God, moved by these, ordered the prophet Jonah to go from Judea and announce the destruction of the city, just as Sodom and Gomorrah had once been consumed by divine fire. But the prophet, refusing this ministry, not out of obstinacy but from foreknowledge that the Lord could be appeased by the repentance of the people, boarded a ship bound for Tarshish, in a region far away. When the ship had gone out to sea, the sailors, driven by the fury of the waves, asked by lot who was the cause of the evil. When the lot fell on Jonah, he was thrown into the deep as the expiation of the storm; he was swallowed by a whale, a sea monster, and after nearly three days was cast up on the shores of Nineveh, and he preached what he had been commanded: that the city would perish within three days on account of the people's sins. Therefore the voice of the prophet was not disregarded, as once at Sodom; at once, by the king's command and example, the whole people, even infants, were ordered to abstain from food and drink. The cattle and animals of every kind, likewise driven by hunger and thirst, lowed and bellowed along with the men. So the impending evil was averted. When Jonah complained to God that his word had not come true, he received the answer that penitent people could not be refused pardon. But in Samaria, Zechariah, a very wicked king whom we mentioned above as having reigned, was slain by a certain Shallum, who seized the kingdom; and this same man, by the treachery of Menahem, perished in the manner of his own deed. Menahem, having seized the kingdom taken from Shallum, held it and left it to his son Pekahiah. But a certain Pekah, of the same name, killed this Pekahiah and seized the kingdom. Soon afterward he was slain by Hoshea, and, by the same crime by which he had gained it, lost the kingdom. This king, more impious than all the kings before him, deserved from God a punishment and perpetual captivity for his people. For Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, made war on him and reduced him to the status of a tributary. But when he was preparing a rebellion by secret plans, and was summoning to his aid the king of the Ethiopians, who then held Egypt, Shalmaneser, learning of this, cast him into prison in lasting chains, destroyed the city, and led the whole people off into his own kingdom, placing Assyrian guards in the conquered territory. From this, that part of Samaria was called Samaritan, because in the Assyrian language they call the guards Samaritans. Of these, many accepted the divine rites, while the rest persisted in the error of paganism. In this war Tobias was led into captivity. But in the part of the two tribes, King Ahaz, hated by God for his impiety and often hard pressed by wars with neighboring peoples, resolved to worship the gods of the nations, no doubt because those gods, by their help, had made the victors in frequent battles. Thus he died in this impious sin, after having reigned sixteen years. His son Hezekiah succeeded him, very unlike his father in character. For at the beginning of his reign he exhorted the people and the priests to the worship of God, and he argued at length that those whom the Lord had often chastened had more often obtained mercy, and that the ten tribes lately carried off into captivity had paid the penalty for sacrilege; the people must take care that they not deserve to suffer the same. So, with the minds of all turned to religion, he ordained the Levites and all the priests to celebrate the sacrifices according to the law, and he restored the Passover, which had long been neglected. When the feast day was near, he sent messengers through all the land and proclaimed an assembly, so that whoever, after the carrying away of the ten tribes, had remained in Samaria should come to the solemn sacred feast. Thus, with a very full assembly, the holy day was spent in public joy, the lawful worship having been restored after a long interval by Hezekiah. Then with the same diligence with which he had ordered divine worship, he managed the military affairs, and he crushed the Philistines in frequent battles. Until Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, made war on him, entering his territory with a great army, and, the fields being laid waste far and wide with no one opposing him, he pressed the siege of the city. Hezekiah, being inferior in numbers and unwilling to join battle, defended himself behind the walls. The Assyrian king, insulting the gates, threatened destruction, demanded surrender, and said that Hezekiah trusted in God in vain, and that God had rather by his will taken away his arms; he, the conqueror of all nations, the overthrower of Samaria, could not be escaped, unless they consulted their own interests by timely surrender. In this state of affairs Hezekiah, relying on God, consulted the prophet Isaiah, and by his answer was taught that there would be no danger from the enemy, and that divine help would not be lacking. Not long after, Tirhakah, king of the Ethiopians, invaded the kingdom of the Assyrians. On hearing this news Sennacherib turned back to deal with it, raging and crying out that a victory already his was being snatched from him; he gave up the war. He sent letters to Hezekiah, threatening him with insulting words, that soon after settling affairs at home he would return to destroy Judea more fiercely. But Hezekiah, unmoved by these, is said to have prayed the Lord not to allow such great human arrogance to go unpunished. So that same night an angel attacked the camp of the Assyrians and gave many thousands of men to death. The king, in panic, fled to the city of Nineveh, and there, slain by his sons, received the death he deserved. At the same time Hezekiah, sick in body, had fallen into a disease. When Isaiah announced to him the word of the Lord that the end of his life was at hand, the king is said to have wept, and so he earned fifteen more years of life. When these were over, in the twenty-ninth year of his reign he died, leaving the kingdom to his son Manasseh. He, greatly degenerate from his father, abandoned the Lord and practised impious worship. For this he was handed over into the power of the Assyrians, and, compelled by suffering, acknowledged his error; and he urged the people that, abandoning idols, they should worship the Lord. Indeed he did nothing worthy of memory, and reigned fifty-five years. Then his son Amon obtained the kingdom, and held it no more than two years; the heir of his father's impiety, neglectful of the Lord, he perished, ensnared by the plots of his own people. The kingdom passed to his son Josiah. He is said to have been very devout, and to have managed divine affairs with the greatest care, using Hilkiah the priest well. When he had read in the temple the writing of God's word, found by the priest, in which it was contained that the Hebrew nation was to be destroyed for its frequent impieties and sacrileges, he averted the impending ruin by pious prayers to God and continual weeping. When he learned that this had been granted to him through the prophetess Olam (Huldah), with greater care, as one bound by divine benefits, he exercised the worship of God. Therefore he burned all the vessels consecrated to idols by the superstitions of earlier kings. For these profane rites had so prevailed that they gave divine honours to the sun and moon, and had even built sacred shrines of metals for them. When Josiah had reduced these to powder, he also slew the priests of the profane shrines. But he did not spare even the tombs of the impious: what had once been foretold by a prophet was fulfilled and noticed. In the eighteenth year of his reign the Passover was celebrated. About three years later, he marched out to battle against Necho, king of Egypt, who was making war on the Assyrians, and before the battle lines met, he was struck by an arrow. Carried from there into the city with this wound, he died, having reigned thirty-one years. Jehoahaz, his son, obtained the kingdom after him and held it for three months, destined for captivity on account of his impiety. For Necho, king of Egypt, took him, bound, and led him away. Not long after he died in chains. A yearly tribute was imposed on the Jews. A king, Eliakim, was given to them at the victor's discretion, who afterward, his name being changed, was called Jehoiakim. He was the brother of Jehoahaz, son of Josiah, nearer to his brother than to his father, and hated by God for sacrilege. So, while he obeyed the Egyptian king, to whom he paid tribute, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, seized the land of Judea by arms, and for three years held it as victor by the law of war. For when the king of Egypt had already withdrawn, and the boundaries of the kingdoms had been fixed between them, it had been agreed that the Jews should belong to Babylon. So when Jehoiakim, after eleven years in his kingdom, had given place to his son of the same name, and he had provoked the anger of the king of Babylon against himself, God indeed acting, for it had been determined that the nation of Judea should be given over to captivity and destruction, Nebuchadnezzar entered Jerusalem with an army and levelled the city, its walls, and the temple to the ground. He carried off an immense quantity of gold and sacred ornaments, both public and private, and all the young people of both sexes, male and female, leaving behind those whose weakness or age made them contemptible to the victors. This useless crowd, unfit for service, was assigned to cultivate and work the fields, so that the land might not lie untilled. Over these Zedekiah was set as king, stripped of power and granted only the empty shadow of the royal name. But Jehoiachin had held the kingdom for three months. He, carried off with the people to Babylon, was cast into prison; after thirty years he was released, received by the king into friendship, admitted to his table and counsels, and died not without some consolation for the calamity that had befallen him. Meanwhile King Zedekiah, a useless crowd's king, though without strength, of faithless character and forgetful of God, who did not understand that captivity had been brought upon the nation on account of its sins, at last, owing the final evils, offended the king's mind. So Nebuchadnezzar made war on him after nine years, and, having forced him to flee within the walls, besieged him for three years. In this crisis Zedekiah consulted the prophet Jeremiah, who had often announced that captivity was impending on the city, asking whether perhaps some hope still remained. But Jeremiah, not ignorant of heavenly wrath, answered the same thing when asked repeatedly, announcing a special punishment for the king himself. Then Zedekiah, roused to anger, ordered the prophet to be thrust into prison; and soon he regretted the cruel deed. But being unable to acquit the innocent man, he did not dare, because the obstinate leaders of the Jews, who from the beginning had been accustomed to oppress the good, compelled him. At their urging, Jeremiah was lowered into a pit of immense depth, foul with mire and filth, and horrid with its deadly stench, so that he would not even die a simple death. But the king, though impious, somewhat milder than the priests, ordered the prophet to be brought up from the pit and returned to the custody of the prison. Meanwhile the force of the enemy and want pressed the besieged; all that could be eaten being used up, famine had grown severe. So the defenders, exhausted by hunger within, saw the city taken and burned. The king, as the prophet had said, had his eyes put out and was carried to Babylon; Jeremiah, through the compassion of the enemy, was freed from prison. When Nebuzaradan, the king's chief officer, was leading him captive with the others, and gave him the choice whether he would remain in his native land, now deserted and desolate, or go with him and be in the highest honours, he preferred to stay in his homeland. When Nebuchadnezzar had led the people away, he set over the remainder, whom the conditions of war or scorn of plunder had left behind by the victors, Gedaliah, of the same nation, without any royal badge or title of rule, because to preside over a few wretched people brought no dignity.

units.la: SVLPICII SEVERI SACRÆ HISTORIÆ LIBER II.
units.tr: Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, Book II.

units.la: C[?]APTIVITATIS tempora prophetarum vaticiniis atque actibus illustrata sunt.
units.tr: The times of the captivity were made illustrious by the prophecies and deeds of the prophets.

units.la: Maxime itaque Danielis egregiam ad conservandam legem perseve-rantiam, & in absolutionem Susannæ divino consilio, cæteraque ab eo gesta ordine persequemur. Hic sub rege Ioachim captus deductusque Babyloniam, parvus admodum puer: postea ob elegantiam vultus inter ministros regios assum-ptus, unaque cum eo Ananias, Mifael & Azarias. Sed cum eos rex delicatioribus cibis curari præcepisset, idque Asphanæ eunucho negotii dedisset, Daniel patrium traditionum memor, ne ex mensa regis gentilium cibis participaret, poposcit ab eunucho, ut leguminibus tantum uterentur. Causante Asphane, ne dissimulatum imperium regis consecutura macies proderet: Daniel Domino fretus pollicetur maioris decoris sibi vultus ex leguminibus, quam ex cibis regiis fore: Fidesque distis affuit,ita ut minimè eorum vultus comparabiles haberentur, qui imperialibus impendiis procurabantur. Igitur a rege in honore & gratia adhi-biti, prudentia & disciplina brevi omni-bus regis proximis antelati. Peridem tem-pus Sufanna quaedam loachim nupta, spectatae foemina pulchritudinis, a duo-bus presbyteris appetita, cum impudicis non acquievisset,fallo crimine incessitur, iisdē presbyteris deferentibus,in remotis locis adolescētem cum ea deprehensum, sed illum juvenili alacritate senu manus effugisse. Ita presbyteris fides habita, judicio populi Sufana damnatur. Quae cum secundum legem ad supplicium ducere-tur, Daniel tum annos natus xii. increpi-tis Iudaeis, quod innocentem mortí dedis-sent, reducere eam in judicium, caufamq; denuo audiri postulat. Enimvero multi-tudo Iudaeorum, quae tum aderat, non sine Domino existimans puerum contemptae aetatulae in hanc constantiâ prorupisse, fa-vore accommodato, in cöfilium reverti-tur. Initur denuo judicio. Danieli, ut inter majores natu residèret, delatum. Igitur separari accusatores jubet: bununquæ ex eis interrogat, sub cuius generis arbore adulteram deprehendisset: ex varietate responsi, falsitas deprehensa. Susanna absoluta: presbyteri, qui innocenti periculum creaverant, capite damnati. Ea tempestate Nabuchodonosor somnium vidit, mysterio futurorum mirabile. Cuius interpretationem quū per se non posset evolvere, acitis ad interpretandū Chaldaeis, qui magicis artibus, extisq; hostiarum scire occulta & futura praecinere videbantur: mox veritus ne more hominum non vera, sed placita regi ex somnio conjectarent, visa supprimit, poposcitq; ab eis, ut si vera in his divinatio esset, somnii ipsum sibi divini cerent: tum demum interpretationi eorum crediturū, si prius enunciando somnium, artis periculum fecissent. Illi vero tantam molem abnuentes, non esse id humanę opis confitebātur. Rex motus, quod falsa divinandi professione homines erroribus illuderent, cum astricti praesenti negocio nihil scire se confiterentur: ita edicto regis in eos animadversum, palamque omnes huius artis interficiebantur.
units.tr: Above all, we shall follow the outstanding perseverance of Daniel in keeping the law, his deliverance of Susanna by divine counsel, and the other things he did, in order. Taken captive under King Jehoiakim and carried off to Babylon, he was still a very small boy. Later, because of his fine appearance, he was chosen among the royal attendants, together with Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. The king ordered them to be fed with richer foods and entrusted this to the eunuch Ashpenaz. Daniel, mindful of his ancestral traditions, did not want to eat from the king's table, since the food was that of the Gentiles, and so asked the eunuch that they might use only vegetables. Ashpenaz objected that the wasting of their bodies would reveal that they had disobeyed the king's command. Daniel, trusting in the Lord, promised that their appearance would be finer on vegetables than on the royal food. His word was borne out, so that their looks could not be compared with those who were fed at the imperial expense. Therefore the king received them with honour and favour, and in a short time they surpassed all the king's closest advisers in wisdom and discipline. At about this time a certain Susanna, wife of Joakim, a woman of notable beauty, was desired by two elders. When she would not yield to their lust, they falsely accused her, and the same elders alleged that they had found a young man with her in a secluded place, but that he had escaped their hands with youthful agility. The elders were believed, and Susanna was condemned by the judgment of the people. As she was being led to execution according to the law, Daniel, then twelve years old, rebuked the Jews for putting an innocent woman to death, and demanded that she be brought back to judgment and the case heard again. The crowd of Jews who were present, thinking that this boy of tender age had not spoken with such firmness without the Lord, favoured his request and returned to the court. The trial began again, and Daniel was given a seat among the older men. He ordered the accusers to be separated, and questioned each of them as to under what kind of tree they had caught the adulteress. From the variance of their answers the falsehood was exposed. Susanna was acquitted, and the elders, who had brought danger upon an innocent woman, were condemned to death. In those days Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream, wonderful for its mystery of things to come. Since he could not himself unravel its meaning, he summoned the Chaldeans to interpret it, men who seemed to know hidden and future things by magic arts and by the entrails of victims. But he soon feared that, as men do, they would conjecture not what was true but what pleased the king, so he kept the dream to himself and demanded that they tell him the dream itself, if their divination was real; only then would he believe their interpretation, if first, by declaring the dream, they had tested the reliability of their art. They refused so great a task, declaring that it was beyond human power. The king, moved because men deceived others with errors under the false profession of divination, and since they admitted they knew nothing of the matter before them, ordered them punished by an edict; and so all who practised this art were put to death openly.

units.la: Quod ubi Danieli compertum, regis proximū appellat: enunciationem somnii interpreterpretationemque ejus pollicetur. Res ad regem defertur: Daniel accersitur. jam revelato sibi per Dominum mysterio, visio regis refertur solutioque. Sed res postu-lat, ut regis somnium & interpretationem prophetae, & consequentium fidem expo-namus. Viderat rex per soporem {a}statu-am capite aureo, {b}brachiisque argenteis, ventre & femoribus aereis, cruribus fer-reis, quae in pedes partim ferreos, partim fictiles desinebat. Sed ferrum atque te-stum {c}inter confusum coire non poterat. ad extremum, statuam lapis sine manibus abscisus proterebat: redactaq; omnia in pulverem, vento ablata. Igitur secundum prophetae interpretationem statua visa fi-guram mundi gerit. Caput aureum, Chal-daeorum imperium est: siquidem id pri-mum & opulentissimum fuisse accepi-mus. Pectus & brachia argentea, secun-dum regnum annunciant. Cyrus enim, vi-dis Chaldaeis atque Medis, imperium ad Persas contulit. In ventre aereo, tertium regnum portendi pronunciatur: idque impletum videmus. Siquidem Alexan-der ereptum Persis imperium, Macedo-niae vindicavit. Crura ferrea, imperium quartum: idq; Romanū intelligitur, {a}a o- nibus ante regnis validissimum. Pedes vero partim ferrei, partim fictiles, dividē- dum esse Romanum regnum, ita ut nūn. quam inter se coeat, praefigurant: quod æ- que impleta est. Siquidem jam non ab u- no imperatore, sed etiam a pluribus, sem- perq; inter se armis aut studiis disentien- tibus, res Romana administratur. Deniq; commisceri testum atq; ferrum nunquam inter se coeuntem materiam; commissiones humani generis futurae, a se invicem disidentes, significantur. Siquidem Romanum solum ab exteris gentibus aut re- bellibus occupatu, aut dedentibus {b}b fem- per pacis specie traditum constat: exerciti. busque nostris, urbibus atque provinciis permissas barbaras nationes, & praecipue Iudaeos inter nos degere, nec tamen in mores nostros transfire {b}b videamus. Atque haec esse postrema tempora prophetae annunciant. In lapide vero fine manibus abicisso, qui aurum, argentum & ferrum testumq; comminuit, Christi figurā esse. Is enim non conditione humana editus(siquidem non ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo natus est) mundum istum, in quo sunt regna terrarum, in nihilum redigit, regnumq; aliud incorruptum atque perpetuū, id est, futurum seculum, quod sanctis paratum est, confirmabit. De quo uno adhuc quorundam fides in ambiguo est, non credendum de futuris, cum de praeteritis convincantur. Igitur Daniel multis a rege muneribus donatur, praefectus Babyloniae, atque omni imperio, in summis honoribus habebatur. Ejus suffragio Ananias, Azarias & Misael ad summam aeque dignitatem & potestatem provecti.
units.tr: When this came to Daniel's knowledge, he approached the king's officer and promised to declare the dream and its interpretation. The matter was reported to the king, and Daniel was summoned. Now that the mystery had been revealed to him by the Lord, he related the king's vision and its interpretation. But the matter requires that we set out the king's dream and the prophet's interpretation, and the fulfilment of what followed. In his sleep the king had seen a statue with a golden head, arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, and legs of iron, which ended in feet partly of iron and partly of clay. But the iron and the clay could not cohere. At last a stone, cut without hands, struck the statue and crushed it; and everything was reduced to dust and carried away by the wind.
