Now, according to the prophet's interpretation, the statue represents the figure of the world. The golden head is the empire of the Chaldeans, for we have learned that it was the first and the most wealthy. The chest and arms of silver announce the second kingdom: for Cyrus, having overthrown the Chaldeans and the Medes, transferred the empire to the Persians. The bronze belly signifies the third kingdom, and we see that this was fulfilled: for Alexander, taking the empire from the Persians, claimed it for Macedonia. The iron legs signify a fourth empire, which is understood to be the Roman, the strongest of all the kingdoms before it. The feet, partly iron and partly clay, foreshadow that the Roman kingdom would be divided and would never cohere, and this too has been fulfilled. For now the Roman state is governed not by one emperor but by many, who are always at odds with one another in arms or in aims. Finally, the mixing of clay and iron, which never unite, signifies the future mingling of the human race, disagreeing with one another. For it is well known that the Roman land has been occupied or handed over by foreign and rebellious peoples, always under the appearance of peace; and we see that barbarian nations, and especially the Jews, have been permitted to live among us, in our armies, cities and provinces, yet do not pass over into our customs. The prophet announces that these are the last times. But the stone cut without hands, which crushed gold, silver, iron and clay, signifies Christ. For he, not born in the human way (since he was born not of the will of man but of God), reduces this world, in which the kingdoms of the earth lie, to nothing, and establishes another kingdom that is incorruptible and everlasting, that is, the age to come, which is prepared for the saints. Some still hesitate in belief about this one point, but it is not to be doubted concerning the future when the past has proved true. Therefore Daniel was richly rewarded by the king, made governor of Babylon and over the whole empire, and held in the highest honour. Through his support, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael were likewise raised to equal dignity and power.

units.la: Eodem fere tempore, praeclara Ezechielis prophetia exstitit, revelato ei futurorum & resurrectionum mysterio. Extat liber magni operis & cum cura legendus. At in Iudaea, cui post excidium Ierosolymæ[?] Go-doliam praepositum supra memoravimus, aegre ferentes Iudaei {a} principem sibi ex arbitrio victoris datum: Ismael quodam duce & concitatore nefandæ conjurationis, dispositis eum in convivio insidiis peremerunt. At hi{c} qui extra noxiam fuerant, ultum ire facinus cupientes, propere adversum Ismael arma capiunt. Sed ille quia cognovit exitium sibi imminere, relicto exercitu, quem cō[?]-traxerat,
units.tr: At about the same time the remarkable prophecy of Ezekiel appeared, the mystery of things to come and of the resurrections being revealed to him. There is a book of great work, which is to be read with care. But in Judaea, where, after the destruction of Jerusalem, we have mentioned that Gedaliah was set over them, the Jews, resenting a ruler given to them at the will of the victor, were slain by Ishmael, a leader and instigator of a wicked conspiracy, who laid an ambush for him at a banquet. Those who had not been part of the crime, wishing to avenge the deed, quickly took up arms against Ishmael. But he, knowing that destruction threatened him, abandoned the army which he had gathered,

units.la: {a} quidam traxerat, non amplius quam octo comitantibus ad Ammonitas confugit. Igitur populum universum metus pervaserat, ne paucorum scelus omnium exitio rex Babylonius ultimum iret. nam praeter Godoliam, multos ex Chaldeis cum eo interfecerant. Iraq; consilium ineunt fugiendi in Aegyptum. Sed prius Ieremiam frequentes adeunt, sciscitantes divinum responsum. At ille verbis Dei universos hortari, in solo patrio manerent: si id fecissent, Dei praesidio tuendos nullumque a Babyloniis periculum fore. Sin Aegyptum petierent, omnes ibi ferro ac fame diversoque mortis genere perituros. Sed plebs assueto malo in-solens parēdi salubribus consiliis, & divi-no imperio, profecta est in Aegyptum. Quid de ea postea actū sacris litteris [illegible, ~8 letters]: nobis nihil compertum. Hoc tractu temporū Nabuchodonosor, elatus rebus secundis, statuam sibi auream immensae magnitudinis posuit, adorarique eam ut sacram effigie praecepit. Quod cum certatim ab omnibus depravatis adulatione omnium animis fieret, Ananias, Azarias & Misael prophano officio abstinuerunt, non ignorantes honorem hunc soli Deo debitum. igitur rei ex edicto regis constituuntur: propositaq; eis conditio poenarum ardes caminus, ut praesenti metu adorare statuā cogerentur. Verum illi devorari ignibus, quam piaculum committere, maluerunt. Itaque vincti pedibus in medias flammas coniiciuntur. Sed ministros infandi operis, dum promptius damnatos in ignem propellunt, flamma absorbuit: Hebræos (mirum dictu & incredibile non visenti- bus) ignis non attigit, quum aspectanti- bus deambulantes in camino psalmum Deo dicere cernerentur. Visusque cum his inter ignem quartus specie {a}angeli, quem Nabuchodonosor propius intui- tus, {b}filiū Dei se vidisse confessus est. Tū rex haud dubius divinā in re praesenti su- ipse[?] virtutem, missis per omne regnum suum edictis, facti miraculum provulga- vit: confessus, soli Deo honorem defe- rendum. Nec multo post, rex objecto sibi somnio, mox voce etiam coelo emissa, admonitus, potestate regia abjecta, atq; ab omni conversatione humana remotus, herbis tantum vitam sustinens, egisse poenitentiam traditur. Servatum ei nutu Dei imperium, donec impleto temporc,agnito demum Deo, post septem annos regno & statui pristino restitutus est. Hic post devictum, ut supra diximus, Sedechiam, quem captivum Babylone transtulit, regnasse traditur annos VI. & XX. quanquam id non in Sacra historia scriptum invenerim. Sed forte accidit, ut dum multa evolverem, annotationem hanc jam interpolato per aetatem libello, sine authoris nomine, reperirem, in quo regum Babyloniorum tempora continebantur: quam praeterea non putavi. Siquidem & Chronicis consentirent, & ita illius ratio quadraret, ut per ordinem regum, quorum tempora continebat, usque in primum Cyri regis annum, LXX annos (tot enim per sacram historiam a captivitate usque ad Cyrum fuisse referuntur) impleret. Post Nabuchodonosor filius ejus regnum est adeptus, quem in Chronicis Evilmarodac fuisse vocatum reperi. Hic duodecimo imperii anno diem functus, fratri minori, qui Balthasar dictus est, locu fecit. Is cum quarto & decimo anno publicu epulu principibus ac praefectis suis daret, sacra vasa quae per Nabuchodonosor de templo Hiero-
units.tr: which some men had gathered, and fled to the Ammonites with no more than eight companions. Then fear seized the whole people, lest the crime of a few should bring the Babylonian king's final vengeance upon them all; for besides Gedaliah, they had killed many Chaldeans with him. So they resolved to flee into Egypt. But first they approached Jeremiah in large numbers, asking for a divine answer. He, in the words of God, exhorted them all to remain in their native land: if they did so, they would be protected by the help of God, and there would be no danger from the Babylonians; but if they sought Egypt, they would all perish there by the sword, by famine, and by various kinds of death. But the common people, unaccustomed to obeying wholesome counsel and the divine command, because of their habitual wickedness, set out for Egypt. What was afterwards done with them is [illegible in the text], and nothing certain is known to us from the sacred letters. In the course of this time Nebuchadnezzar, elated by his prosperity, set up a golden statue of immense size for himself, and ordered that it be worshipped as a sacred image. While all the corrupt men, in flattery of the king, were eagerly doing this, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael abstained from the profane observance, not ignorant that this honour is owed to God alone. Therefore they were brought before the king under his edict, and the penalty proposed to them was a blazing furnace, so that by present fear they might be compelled to worship the statue. But they preferred to be consumed by the fires rather than commit a sacrilege. So they were bound and cast, feet first, into the midst of the flames. But the flame devoured the ministers of this wicked deed while they hurried to push the condemned men into the fire more eagerly; yet the fire did not touch the Hebrews (a wonderful and incredible thing, unseen by the onlookers), for they were seen walking about in the furnace and singing a psalm to God. And with them, within the fire, a fourth figure appeared, in the form of an angel, whom Nebuchadnezzar, looking at him more closely, confessed to be like the Son of God. Then the king, no longer doubting the divine power in the present matter, sent edicts throughout his whole realm and proclaimed the miracle that had happened, confessing that honour must be paid to God alone. Not long after, when a dream was set before him, and then a voice sent from heaven admonished him, he is said to have laid aside his royal power, withdrawn from all human company, sustained his life only on herbs, and done penance. By the will of God his empire was kept for him until the appointed time was fulfilled; then, having at last acknowledged God, he was restored to his former kingdom and position after seven years. After he had defeated Zedekiah, whom, as we said above, he carried off captive to Babylon, he is said to have reigned for twenty-six years, though I have not found this written in the Sacred History. But by chance, while I was turning over many sources, I came upon this note in a little book, long since worn with age and without the author's name, which contained the times of the Babylonian kings. I did not think it should be passed over, since it agrees with the Chronicles, and its reckoning fits so well that, through the succession of kings whose times it records, it reaches down to the first year of King Cyrus and fills out the seventy years (for so many years, according to the sacred history, are reckoned from the captivity to Cyrus). After Nebuchadnezzar his son took the kingdom, whom I found called Evil-merodach in the Chronicles. He died in the twelfth year of his reign and gave place to his younger brother, who was called Belshazzar. In the fourteenth year of his reign, when he gave a public banquet for his nobles and officers, he ordered the sacred vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple of Jerusalem and put to royal use, but which were kept in the treasuries, to be brought out. With these, in the luxury and licence of the royal feast, all the men and women of his household, his wives and concubines, drank; and suddenly the king…

units.la: {b} Evilmarodac vocatur etiam Regum 25.27. & Dan. 5. folymae ablata,ac in regales ulus usurpata, sed recondita in thelauris habebantur, proferri imperavit. Cum his per luxu ac licentiam regalis convivii promiscue {a}o-mnis virilis ac muliebris sexus,uxores concubinaeq; ejus uterentur,subito rex in pa-riete conspicit digitos scribentes: cerne-[?]bantur; {b}inversum ductae literae. Sed qui posseт scripta legere,non reperiebatur. Igitur rex perterritus, magos & Chaldaeos advocat. Quibus mussitantibus,nec quic-quā respondentibus,{c}regina regę admo-net, esse quendā Hebraeum Daniel nomine, qui olim Nabuchodonosor occulti mysterii somnium revelasset,jam tum ob illustrem sapientiam summis honoribus donatum. Itaq; accitus Daniel,perlegit interpretatusq; ob delictum regis, qui sacra Deo vasa temerasset, ipsi exitium immi-nere, regnumque ejus Medis ac Persis da-tum: quod mox consecutum est. nam eadem nocte Balthasar interiit,regnumque ejus Darius natione Medus occupavit: qui Danielem illustri opinione compertum, universo impetio praepoluit, secundus superiorum regum judicium. Nam & Nabuchodonosor cum regno praefe-cerat, cerat, & Balthalar veste purpurea & tor-que aureo donatū, tertium regni principe constituerat. Igitur hi qui una cum eo rerum potetes erant, exagitati invidia, quod eis alienigena captivæ gentis fuisset æqua-tus, regem depravatum adulatione compellunt, ut sibi diebus proximis triginta divini honores darentur, neque cuiquam liceret {a}Dominū, nisi regem precari. Fa-cile id Dario persuasum, stultitia regum omnium, qui sibi divina vindicant. Igitur Daniel non rudis neque inscius Deo preces, non hominii[?] deferendas, reus constituitur, edicto regis non paruisse. Multiq; abnuente Dario, cui charus acceptusque semper fuerat, principes pervicere, ut in {b}lacum demitteretur. Sed objecto be-stiis, nullum periculum fuit. Quod quum rex comperisset[?], accusatores {c}de-putari leonibus præcepit: qui non simili exemplo perfuncti sunt, nam continuo devorati, ferarum famem expleverunt. Daniel clarus ante, clarior haberi coepit. Rex antiquato edicto suo, novum proposuit: religionis erroribus ac superstitionibus, Deum Danielis colendum. Exstant etiam visiones ejus quibus consequentium seculorum ordinem revelavit: annorum etiam numerum complexus, intra quem Christum, sicut factum est, descensurum ad terras pronunciavit, venturumque Antichristum manifeste exposuit. Quod si quis studiosior erit, rectius ibi quaesitum repe-riet: nobis propositum est, rerum tantum ordinem contexere. {a}Darius duodevigin. ti annos regnasse traditur. Qua tempesta-te Astiages Medis imperabat. Hunc Cy-rus ex filia nepos ejus, regno expulit, Per-sarum usus armis: unde summa imperii ad Persas translata est. Babylonii quoque in potestatem ditionemque eius concessere. Igitur initio regni, propositis publice edictis, dat potestatem Iudaeis, in solum patrium redeundi: sacra etiam vasa, quae Nabuchodonosor de templo Hierosolymae abstulerat, reddidit. Itaque pauci tum in Iudaeam regressi: caeteris redeundi animus, an facultas defuerit, parum comperi-mus. Erat ea tempestate apud Babylonios Beli antiquissimi regis, cuius etiam Virgilii meminit, ex aere simulachrum, quod superstitione hominum consecratum, Cyrus quoq; adorare erat solitus, antistitu[?] ejus dolo illusus, qui veluti[?] effigiem illam atq; potare affirmabant: cum diurnam pensi- tationem, quæ idolo inferebatur, clam ip-si abluimerent. Igitur Cyrus cum Danie-le familiariter uteretur, quæsiit ab eo, cur simulachrum non adoraret, cum manifestum viventis Dei esset indicium, abstu-mentis ea quæ inferebantur? Daniel ridens hominis errorem, negare id posse fieri, ut æs illud, id est, bruta materies, cibo uteretur, aut potu. Accersi ergo rex iacer-dotes jubet. nam fere ad septuaginta erat. adhibitoq; eos terrorem increpitat, quis im-pensa consumeret? cum Daniel, vir pru-dentia insignis, minime id ab insensibili si-mulachro posse fieri contenderet. Tum illi cofi fi parato dolo, inferre & obsignari a rege templum deposcunt, uti nisi omnia postero die absumpta deprehenderentur, morte poenas persolverent: dum eadem conditio Danieli maneret. Itaque signo regis templum obsignatur, cum priusDa-niel, sacerdotibus insciis, pavimentum ci-nere aspersisset, ut introeuntiū occultos aditus vestigia proderent. Igitur postero die rex templum ingressus, animadver-tit absumpta quæ idolo apponi jusserat. Tum Daniel occultam fraudem vestigiis[?] prodentibus referat: sacerdotes cum uxoribus & filiis, subfosso foramine ingressos, ea, quæ idolo apposita fuerant, devorasse. Ita omnes iussu regis interfecti, tem-plum ac simulacrum Danicli in potestate datum, atq; arbitrio ejus dirutum. Interea ludæi, quos ex permissu Cyri in patriam regressos supra memoravimus, urbem ac templum restituere aggressi, ut pauci atq; inopes, parum proficiebant: donec centre-simo fere anno, Artaxerxe rege Persis a im-peritante, per eos qui b locis præerant, ab ædificando sunt deterriti. Etenim tum Sy-ria atq; omnis ludæa sub Persarum impe-rio per magistratus ac præsides regebatur. Igitur his consilium fuit, regi Artaxerxi scribere, non oportere ludæis restituendæ urbis suæ copiam dari, ne pro contumaci ingenio, relumptis viribus, aliis gentibus imperare soliti, non paterentur sub alieno imperio degere. Ita comprobato a rege præsidum consilio, prohibita urbis ædifi-catio, ufq; in secundum b Darii regis an-num dilata est. Sed hoc tractu temporum qui reges Persis imperaverint inferemus, quo facilius annorum series in ordinem contexta prodatur. Post Darium Medum, quem duodeviginti annos regnasse significavimus, Cyrus uno & triginta annis rerum potitus est. Scythis bellum inferes, in praelio cecidit: secundo anno postquam Tarquinius superbus Romae regnare coepit. Cyro Cambyses filius ejus successit, regnavitq; annos novem. Hic cum AE. gyptum atq; Aethiopiam bello premeret & subegisset, victorq; in Persas revertere. tur casu scipsum vulneravit, ex eo q; ictu[?] periit. Post hujus mortem magi duo fratres, natione Medi, menses septem Persarum regnum obtinuerunt. Ad hos interficiendos septem nobilissimi Persae conjuraverunt; quorum princeps fuit Darius Hystaspis filius, natus ex fratre patruele Cyri, omniumq; consensu regnum ei delatum: regnavit annos sex & xxx. Hic ante quadriennium quam decederet, apud Marathonem pugnavit, celeberrimo Graecis Romanisque historiis praelio. Id gestum post Romam conditam anno fere ducentesimo & sexagesimo, Mache- rino & Augurino consulibus: abhinc annos, si tamen investigatio Romanorum consulum non fefellit, DCCC LXXX. & VIII. Omne enim tempus in Stiliconem consulem direxi. Post Darium Xerxes fuit, ifq; uno & viginti annis re-gnasse traditur: quanquam in plerifq; exemplaribus viginti & quinq; annos impe-rii ejus fuisse reperi. Huic successit Artaxerxes, cujus supra mentionem feci. Hic cum inhiberi ædificationem ur-bis ludæ, templique jussisset, suspensum opus usque in secundum Darii regis annum pependit. Sed ut usque ad eum tem-porum ordo connexus fit, Artaxerxes re-gnavit annos unum & quadraginta, Xerxes duobus mensibus. Postq; eum Sucdi-anus septem mensibus fuit. Darius deinde, sub quo templum est restitutum, re-gnum adeptus est, cui Ochus tum nomen erat. Hic cum ex Hebraeis tres adolescentes spectatæ fidei, corporis custodes haberet, unumq; ex his prudentiæ documento ad-mirationem regis in se convertisset, delato sibi optione petendi si quid animo coce-pisset, ingemiscens patriæ ruinis, copiam restituendæ urbis poposcit meruitq; a re-ge, ut subregulis ac præsidibus imperaret, ut ædificationem sacræ ædis præbitis im-pendiis maturarent. Ita templum quadri-ennio consummatum, sexto post anno, quam Darius regnare coeperat, idq; Iudeis latis visum: & quia magnæ molis erat urbem restituere, dissili viribus, opus multi laboris incipere nō ausi, templo continebantur. Per idem tempus Esdras scriba legis post viginti fere annos quam templum fuerat consummatum, defuncto jam Dario, qui unum de viginti annis rerum fuerat potitus, permissu Artaxerxis{*} secundi,{a} non illius qui inter duos Xerxes fuit: sed hujus qui Dario Ocho successerat, Baby[?] Ionia profectus: multiq; eum sequuti Hierosolymā pervenere. Vasa quoq; diversi operis, & dona, quæ rex templo Dei miserat, cum duodecim Levitis. Vix enim hic numerus ex illa tribu repertus traditur. Is cum deprehendisset Iudæos gentili-um connubiis permissos, multis increpitos, renunciare istiusmodi matrimoniis, ac filios ex his susceptos extrudi jubet o-mnesq; dicto paruere. Purgatus populus, veteris legis ritum habebat. Ceterum El-dram nihil super reficienda urbe egisse comperio. credo potiorem curam ratus, plebem corruptis moribus reformare. erat ea tempestate apud Babyloniam Ne.[?]emias{b}, minister regius, gente Iudæus, Ar-
units.tr: Evilmarodac is also so called at 2 Kings 25:27 and Dan. 5. He ordered the vessels taken from Jerusalem, which had been put to royal use but were kept in the treasuries, to be brought out. While he and his wives and concubines, with every man and woman of his court, were drinking at the royal banquet in wanton license, the king suddenly saw fingers writing on the wall. The letters were traced backwards. But no one could be found who could read the writing. So the king, terrified, summoned the magi and Chaldeans. While they muttered and gave no answer, the queen reminded the king that there was a Hebrew named Daniel, who had once disclosed to Nebuchadnezzar the meaning of a hidden mystery in a dream and who, for his outstanding wisdom, had already been given the highest honours. Daniel was therefore sent for. He read the writing and interpreted it: because the king had profaned the sacred vessels of God, destruction was hanging over him, and his kingdom was to be given to the Medes and Persians. This came to pass soon after. For that very night Belshazzar died, and his kingdom was seized by Darius, a Mede by birth. Darius, who had found Daniel to be of outstanding reputation, set him over the whole empire, placing him second to himself, as Nebuchadnezzar had once placed him over the kingdom and as Belshazzar, who had clothed him in purple and given him a gold chain, had made him third ruler of the realm. Those who were in power with Daniel, stung with envy because a foreigner from a captive nation had been raised to equal rank with them, pressed the king, who had been corrupted by flattery, to grant him divine honours for thirty days, and that no one should be allowed to pray to anyone but the king. This was easily persuaded to Darius, through the folly of all kings who claim divine honours for themselves. So Daniel, who was neither ignorant nor unskilled in offering prayers to God, and not to men, was charged as guilty of not obeying the king's edict. When Darius, who had always held him dear and favoured, was reluctant, the leaders prevailed upon him to have Daniel thrown into a den. But when he was thrown among the beasts, there was no danger. When the king learned of this, he ordered the accusers to be thrown to the lions. They did not meet with a similar outcome: at once they were devoured, and satisfied the hunger of the wild beasts. Daniel, who had been famous before, began to be held in even greater renown. The king, abolishing his former edict, issued a new one: that the God of Daniel should be worshipped, in place of the errors and superstitions of religion. His visions also survive, in which he revealed the order of the ages to come; he embraced the number of years within which he foretold that Christ would come down to the earth, as indeed happened, and he plainly set out that Antichrist would come. Whoever is more eager to know will find these things treated more accurately there; my purpose here is only to set out the order of events. Darius is said to have reigned eighteen years. At that time Astyages ruled the Medes. Cyrus, his grandson through his daughter, drove him from the kingdom, using Persian arms; and so the supreme power passed to the Persians. The Babylonians also came under his power and authority. Therefore, at the beginning of his reign, by public edicts he gave the Jews permission to return to their native land, and he restored the sacred vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from the temple at Jerusalem. Few then returned to Judea; whether the rest lacked the will or the means to return, I find it hard to determine. At that time, among the Babylonians, there was a bronze image of Bel, the most ancient king, whom Virgil also mentions. Consecrated by the superstition of men, Cyrus too used to worship it; but he was deceived by its priests, who insisted that the image itself actually ate and drank, while they secretly washed away the daily allowance of food which was brought to the idol. So Cyrus, who was on familiar terms with Daniel, asked him why he did not worship the image, since its eating what was brought to it was a clear sign of a living God. Daniel, laughing at the man's error, replied that it could not happen that that bronze, that is, lifeless matter, should eat or drink. So the king ordered the priests, who were about seventy in number, to be summoned. When they came, he rebuked them with a threat: who was consuming the offerings? But Daniel, a man of remarkable prudence, insisted that this could in no way be done by an insensible image. Then the priests, with a plot already prepared, demanded that the temple be entered and sealed by the king, on the condition that, if everything had not been consumed by the next day, they would pay the penalty with their lives, while the same condition still held for Daniel. So the temple was sealed with the king's seal; but before this, Daniel, without the priests knowing, had strewn ashes over the pavement, so that the footprints of those entering would reveal the hidden passages. So on the next day the king entered the temple and saw that the things he had ordered to be set before the idol had been consumed. Then Daniel, pointing out the footprints which revealed the hidden fraud, showed that the priests had entered with their wives and sons through a passage dug under the floor, and had devoured the offerings set before the idol. Thus, by the king's command, they were all put to death, and the temple and the image were given over to Daniel, to be pulled down at his discretion. Meanwhile the Jews, whom we have mentioned as having returned to their country by the permission of Cyrus, undertook to restore the city and the temple; but being few and poor, they made little progress, until about the twentieth year, when Artaxerxes was reigning over the Persians, they were deterred from building by those who presided over the districts. For at that time Syria and all Judea were governed under Persian rule by magistrates and governors. So these men resolved to write to King Artaxerxes that the Jews should not be given the opportunity to restore their city, lest, being of a stubborn disposition and, once their strength was recovered, being accustomed to rule other nations, they should not endure living under foreign rule. Thus, the governors' plan being approved by the king, the building of the city was forbidden, and was postponed until the second year of King Darius. But in this course of time I shall set out which kings reigned over the Persians, so that the sequence of years may be presented more easily in order. After Darius the Mede, whom we have said reigned eighteen years, Cyrus held power for thirty-one years. He waged war on the Scythians and fell in battle, in the second year after Tarquin the Proud began to reign at Rome. Cyrus was succeeded by his son Cambyses, who reigned nine years. While he was waging war on Egypt and Ethiopia and had subdued them, returning victorious to Persia, he accidentally wounded himself, and died from that blow. After his death, two Magi, brothers, of Median birth, held the Persian kingdom for seven months. To kill these, seven most noble Persians conspired; their leader was Darius, son of Hystaspes, born of a paternal cousin of Cyrus, and by the agreement of all the kingdom was offered to him; he reigned thirty-six years. Four years before he died, he fought at Marathon, a battle most famous in Greek and Roman histories. This was done about the two hundred and sixtieth year after the founding of Rome, in the consulship of Macherinus and Augurinus; from that time, if the reckoning of the Roman consuls has not deceived us, there are 880 years to the present, for I have referred all the time to the consulship of Stilicho. After Darius came Xerxes, who is said to have reigned twenty-one years, although in most copies I have found that his reign lasted twenty-five years. He was succeeded by Artaxerxes, whom I mentioned above. When he had ordered the building of the city of Judah and of the temple to be halted, the work was suspended until the second year of King Darius. But so that the order of the times may be linked up to that period: Artaxerxes reigned forty-one years, Xerxes two months. After him Sogdianus was for seven months. Then Darius, under whom the temple was restored, obtained the kingdom; at that time he was called Ochus. When he had three young Hebrews of proven fidelity as his bodyguards, and one of them had won the king's admiration by a display of wisdom, he was offered the choice of asking for whatever he wished. Lamenting the ruin of his country, he asked for the opportunity to restore the city, and he obtained from the king the right to order the subordinate kings and governors to hasten the building of the sacred house by supplying funds. Thus the temple was completed in four years, in the sixth year after Darius had begun to reign; and this seemed right to the Jews. But because it was a great undertaking to restore the city, and they had too few strength for so great a labour, they did not dare to begin, and kept to the temple. About the same time Ezra, a scribe of the law, after about twenty years from when the temple had been completed, Darius, who had held power for only one of those twenty years, now being dead, set out from Babylon by the permission of Artaxerxes the Second, not the one who came between the two Xerxes, but the one who had succeeded Darius Ochus; and many who followed him came to Jerusalem. They also brought vessels of various workmanship and gifts which the king had sent to the temple of God, together with twelve Levites, for it is said that scarcely this number could be found in that tribe. When he discovered that the Jews had been allowed to marry foreign women, he rebuked many of them and ordered them to renounce such marriages and to cast out the sons born of them; and all obeyed his command. The people, having been purified, observed the rite of the ancient law. But I find that Ezra did nothing about rebuilding the city, thinking, I believe, that the more pressing concern was to reform the people whose morals had been corrupted. At that time at Babylon there was Nehemiah, a royal officer, a Jew by race, very dear to Artaxerxes for his good service. When he inquired of the Jews how the city of his fathers stood, he learned that their homeland lay in the same ruins; he was utterly distressed, and is said to have prayed to God with groaning and many tears, reflecting on the sins of his people and begging for divine mercy.

units.la: taxerxi merito obfequiorū charissimus. Is ludæos percotatus,quis paterne urbis status esset, ubi comperit in iisdem ruinis. iacere patriam, totis sensibus coturbatus, cum gemitu multisq; lachrymis orafle ad Deum traditur,delictagentis suę reputās, mifericordiamq;divinam efflagitans. Igi- tur quum eum rex inter epulas moestum extra solitum animadvertisset,poposcit ab eo caussam dolorum, ut exponeret. Tum ille adversa gentis suæ, & ruinam civitatis deflere, quæ jam per annos fere ducentos & quinquaginta solo strata, malorum testimonium, ipectaculum ini- micis præberet; daret sibi eundi, & resti- tuenda ejus potestatem. Paruit rex piis precibus: statimque cum pnesidio equitum, quo tutius iter ageret, dimisit: datis ad prætores epistolis, ut necessaria præberent. Is quum Hierosolymā perve- nisset,viritim populo opus urbis distribu- it, & certatim jussa omnes curabant: jam- que ad medium machinæ processerant, quum flagrante invidia gentium vicinæ urbes conspirant opera interrumpere,Iu- dæos ab ædificando deterrere. Sed Nee- mias dispositis adversum incursantes prefidiis,nihil territus,coepta explicuit: conf summatoq; & valvis portarū perfectis, per familias construendis interius domibus urbem dimensus est.Censuitq;po-pulum minime urbi parem. Neque enim amplius quam ad quinquaginta millia promiscui sexus atque ordinis reperta.
units.tr: Dear to Artaxerxes for his well-deserved services, he questioned the Jews about the state of their fathers' city. When he learned that the homeland lay in the same ruins, he was utterly disturbed in every sense. It is said that he prayed to God with groaning and many tears, reflecting on the sins of his people and begging for divine mercy. So when the king noticed him sad during a banquet, out of his usual manner, he asked him the cause of his grief and told him to explain it. Then he lamented the misfortunes of his nation and the ruin of the city, which for nearly two hundred and fifty years had lain flat on the ground, a testimony of evils and a spectacle for its enemies. He asked to be allowed to go and be given the authority to restore it. The king granted his pious request and at once sent him off with a guard of horsemen, so that he might travel more safely. He also gave letters to the governors ordering them to supply whatever was needed. When Nehemiah reached Jerusalem, he distributed the work on the city among the people, man by man, and everyone eagerly carried out his orders. The building had already risen to the middle of its height when the neighbouring cities, their envy blazing, conspired to interrupt the work and frighten the Jews from building. But Nehemiah posted guards against those who attacked and, undaunted, carried on with what he had begun. When the upper parts were finished and the gate-doors fitted, he measured the city, with the houses inside to be built by families. He judged the population to be by no means equal to the city, for no more than about fifty thousand people of both sexes and every rank were found.

units.la: Tantum ex illo quondam immani nu-mero frequentibus bellis absumptum, aut captivitate detentum. Nam olim hæ duæ tribus, quarum hoc residuum fuit, quum ab his decem tribus separatæ sunt, CCC. & xx. millia virorum armaverant. Adeo ob peccatum internecioni & captivitati datæ, ad hanc usque paucitatem devenerant. Sed hæc, ut dixi, plebs duarum tribuum fuit: decem vero prius duƈtæ, per Parthos, Medos, Indos, atq; Æthiopas dispersæ, nunquam in solum patrium sunt regressæ, hodieq; barbarārum gentium imperiis continentur. Sed consummatio restitutæ urbis, xxx. & ii. Imperii Artaxerxis anno refertur. A quo tempore re usque ad Christi crucem, id est, Fusi-um Geminum & Rubellium consules, anni CCCXC. & viii. Ceterum, a restitutione templi usque in eversionem, quæ sub Vespasiano, consule Augusto, per Titum Cæsarem consummata est, anni CCCCLxxx. & iii. Prædictum id olim est à Daniele, qui ab instauratione templi usque in eversionem Lx. & ix. hebdomadas{a} futuras pronuntiaverat. A die autem captivitatis ludæorum, usque in tempus restitutæ civitatis, fuerunt anni c'c Lx. Hoc temporum tractu, Hefter atq; ludith fuisse arbitramur. Quarum quidem actus, quibus potissimum regibus connectam, non facile perspexerim. Nam cum Hefter sub Artaxerxe{b} rege referatur, porro du- os hujus nominis Persarum reges fuisse reperi, multa cunctatio est, cujus hæc tem- poribus applicetur. Mihi tamen visum est, huic Artaxerxi,{c} sub quo Hierosolyma est restituta, Hefter historiam conectere, quæ dante fuit verisimilis: ut si sub priore Artaxerxe fuisset, cujus{e} tempora complexus est, nullam tam illustris fœminæ mentionem nem{f} reruliset, maxime cum ab illo Artaxerxe inhibitam templi ædificationem, sicut supra memoravimus, constet: neque Hefter-palsura fuerit tu, si in illius matrimonio monio tum fuisset. Nunc gesta edifierā. E- rat ea tepestate regi in matrimonio Vastis quædam,
units.tr: So great a number had once been consumed by frequent wars or held in captivity. For formerly these two tribes, of which this remnant was, when they had been separated from the ten tribes, had armed three hundred and twenty thousand men. So greatly, because of their sin, had they been given over to slaughter and captivity that they had dwindled to this small number. But this people, as I said, was of the two tribes. The ten tribes, which had been carried off earlier, were scattered among the Parthians, Medes, Indians and Ethiopians; they never returned to their native soil and to this day are held under the rule of barbarian nations. The completion of the restored city is dated to the thirty-second year of the reign of Artaxerxes. From that time to the cross of Christ, that is, to the consulship of Fusius Geminus and Rubellius, there were three hundred and ninety-eight years. Moreover, from the restoration of the temple to its overthrow, which was completed under Vespasian, with Augustus as consul, by Titus Caesar, there were four hundred and eighty-three years. This was foretold long ago by Daniel, who had declared that there would be sixty-nine weeks from the rebuilding of the temple to its destruction. From the day of the captivity of the Jews to the time of the restoration of the city there were two hundred and sixty years. We think that Esther and Judith lived during this period. Under which kings their deeds are best linked I cannot easily see. For although Esther is said to have lived under King Artaxerxes, I find that there were two Persian kings of that name, so there is much doubt as to which of these times her story belongs to. Yet it seemed to me best to connect Esther's history with this Artaxerxes, under whom Jerusalem was restored, since that is more plausible. For if it had been under the earlier Artaxerxes, whose times he covered, he would never have left out mention of so illustrious a woman, especially since it is agreed that the building of the temple was forbidden by that Artaxerxes, as we have mentioned above. Nor would Esther have remained unknown if she had been in his marriage at that time. Now I shall recount the deeds. At that time the king had in marriage one Vashti,

units.la: {a} Dan. 9. quaedam, mirae foemina pulchritudinis.
units.tr: {a} Dan. 9. a certain woman of remarkable beauty.

units.la: Cujus cum forma omnibus praedicaret, die quodam, cum publicum convivium dabat, adeo ut reginam demonstrandae pulchritudinis gratia iuber[?]. Illa vero stultiore geconsultior, pudēs virorum oculis spectaculum corporis praebere, jussa abnuit.
units.tr: Her beauty was praised by everyone. One day, when he was giving a public banquet, he ordered the queen to be summoned so that her beauty might be displayed. But she, more prudent than foolish, refused the command out of modesty, unwilling to show her body to the eyes of men.

units.la: Qua contumelia barbarus animus permotus, uxorem matrimonio ac regia depellit. Igitur quum in locū ejus puella regis conjugio quaereretur, reperta est Hester caeteras specie vincere. Haec Iudaea, ex tribu Benjamin, utroque parente orba, a Mardochaeo patruele fratre educta. Quum ad {*}regales nuptias duceretur, mandante ducatore, genus ac patriā occultavit: ad monita, ne {b}paternarum traditionum immemor, & si in matrimonium alienigenae captiva succederet, gentilium cibis participaret. Igitur iuncta Regi, brevi (ut fit) vi pulchritudinis totum eius animum facile coepit: adeo ut eam aequatam imperio, insignī Regio vestē purpurea donaret. Qua tempestate Mardochaeus inter proximos regis erat, pro virili portione negotiorum familiarium curator. Is compositas a duobus spadonibus regi insidias prodiderat: diderat: atq; ex eo charior, summisq; honoribus donatus. Erat ea tempestate regi Haman quidam perfamiliaris, quem æ-quatum sibi, adorari more regum præce-perat. Id Mardochæus unus ex omnibus facere fastidiens, odia Persæ in se gravi-ter accenderat. Igitur Haman ad perniciem {b}Hebraei animum intendens, regem adiit: affirmatq; se in regno ejus hominū genus pravis superstitionibus, Deo homi-nibusq; invitum, externis legibus vi-vens, dignum exitio. Rectum esse omnes huius gentis internecioni dare: exque eorum bonis immensas opes pollicetur. Facile id barbaro persuasum. Edictū emitti-tur, Iudæos necandos. Misiq; continuo, qui per omne regnum ab India usq; Aethiopiam edictum promulgarent. Id ubi Mardochæo compertum, con-scissis ve-stibus sacco obvolvitur: conspersusque cinere pergit ad reginam, ibique eiulatu multo, cuncta questibus replet: Facinus indignum, immeritam gentem perire, neq; ullam pereundi causam dari. Hester lamentantis voce excita, rem, ut erat, co-gnoscit. Tum vero anceps consilii, quia adeundi regem potestas non erat (etenim more Persarum,{a} reginæ introire ad regè, nisi accersitæ, non licet: nec tamen,{b} quū fuerit regi libitum, sed statuto tempore admittitur) & forte tum ita evenerat, ut diebus triginta proximis separata a con-spectu regis Hester haberetur. Igitur audendum aliquid pro civibus rata, etsi certa pestis adesset, pulchro in negocio occumbere parat: invocato prius Domino, {c} auiam[?] regis ingreditur. At barbarus re-insolita perculsus, paulatim blandimento muliebri delinitus: postremo ad coenam reginæ perducitur: unaque cum illo Haman ille regi charus, & ludæ{d} gentis in-festus. Igitur quum jam post epulas multis poculis convivium calere coepisset, Hester genibus regis advolvitur, getis[?] suæ perniciem deprecatur. Rex vero nihil{e} a se petenti, si quid ultra peteret, negatum pollicetur. Tum Hester arrepto tempore,{f} Hamanis mortem flagitat, in ultionem gentis, quam perditam cupie-rat. Sed rex amici memor, paulisper cunctatur: deliberandiqué gratia modicum secessit. Deinde regressus, vidit Haman reginæ genua complexum: succen-sus ira, & s[?] appetitam reginam clamitans, morte eum affici iubet. Et tum regi com- pertum erat, poenam crucis per Haman Mardochaeo paratam. ItaHaman eidécru- ci affigitur, Omniaque bona ejus Mardo- chaeo data, Iudaeique sunt absoluti. Artax- erxes regnavit annos duos & sexaginta, eidemq; Ochus successit. Huic rerum or- dini recte Iudith actus conferam. Tradi- tur enim, post captivitatem fuisse sed quis eo tempore Persis regnaverit, histo- ria divina non edidit, regem tamen, sub quo illa gesta sint, Nabuchodonosor nū- cupat, non utiq; eum qui Hierosolymam ceperit. Sed nullum hoc nomine post captivitatem apud Persas regnasse repe- rio, nisi si ob impatientiam & pariles co- natus quicum ille rex Nabuchodonosor aludaeis vocitatus est. Pleriq; tamen Cam- bysen, Cyri regis filium, putant esse: quod victor Aegyptum atque Aethio- piam penetraverit. Sed huic opinioni ea- dem Sacra historia repugnat, nam duode- cimo regis illius annoludith fuisse signas- tur. Porro, Cambyses non ultra novem annos rerum potitus est. Unde si in hi- storia opinari licet, sub Ocho rege, qui post Artaxerxem secundū fuit, hæc gesta crediderim: idq; vel ex hoc conjicio, quod idem Ochus (ut in fecularibus quibusdam scriptis legi) natura immitis, cupidusque bellorum traditur. Nam & arma finitimis intulit, & AEgyptum, quae ante multos annos desciverat, bello recuperavit. Quo tempore etiam sacra eorum, & Apim in Deum receptum, irrisisse traditur: quod postea Baguas, spado ejus, natione AEgyptius, indignatus, contumeliam gentis morte regis ultus est. Meminit autem hujus Baguae historia divina. nam cum Holofernes jussu regis adversus Iudaeos duxerat exercitum, Baguam in iisdem castris fuisse memoravit. Unde non immerito in argumentum nostrae opinionis adduxerim, ut rex ille Nabuchodonosor nuncupatus, Ochus fuerit, sub quo Baguam fuisse {a}mundiales historici prodiderunt. Ceterum illud nemini mirum esse oportebit, quod scriptores saecularium litera- rum, nihil ex his quae sacris voluminibus scripta sunt, attigerunt: Dei Spiritu praevalente, ut intanimata ab ore corrupto, & falsis vera miscente, intra sua tantum mysteria contineretur historia, quae separata a mundi negociis, & sacris tantum
units.tr: Her insolence stirred the barbarian's spirit, and he cast his wife out of the marriage and out of the royal house. So when a girl was sought for the king's bed in her place, Esther was found to surpass the others in beauty. She was a Jewess of the tribe of Benjamin, orphaned of both parents, and had been raised by her cousin Mordecai. When she was led to the royal wedding, at the guide's instruction she concealed her race and country. She was warned not to forget her fathers' traditions, and that, even as a captive, if she succeeded to a foreigner's marriage she should not eat the food of the Gentiles. So, joined to the king, she soon, as happens, by the power of her beauty easily won his whole heart, so that he raised her to a share in his rule and clothed her in the royal purple robe. At that time Mordecai was among the king's closest attendants, looking after the household business as far as his share went. He had revealed a plot against the king made by two eunuchs, and from this he was held dearer and was given high honours. At that time the king had a certain Haman, very close to him, whom he had ordered to be honoured as his equal, to be worshipped in the manner of kings. Mordecai alone of all refused to do this, and so he had kindled the Persian's hatred against himself fiercely. Therefore Haman, intent on the destruction of the Hebrews, went to the king and declared that in his kingdom there was a race of men, living by foreign laws, hostile to God and to men, bound up in wicked superstitions, and deserving of death. It was right, he said, to give all of this nation over to slaughter, and he promised immense wealth from their goods. This was easily persuaded to the barbarian. An edict was issued that the Jews were to be put to death, and messengers were sent at once to publish the edict throughout the whole kingdom, from India to Ethiopia. When Mordecai learned of this, he tore his clothes, wrapped himself in sackcloth, sprinkled himself with ash, and went to the queen, and there with much wailing he filled everything with lamentation: an outrageous deed, that an innocent nation should perish with no cause for its destruction. Esther, roused by the voice of the mourner, learned the matter as it was. Then indeed she was uncertain what to do, because she had no power to approach the king. (For by Persian custom it is not lawful for a queen to go in to the king unless she is summoned, and even then she is admitted not whenever the king pleases, but at an appointed time.) And it so happened at that time that Esther had been kept apart from the king's sight for the previous thirty days. So she judged that something must be risked for her people, and though a sure destruction was at hand, she prepared to perish in a noble cause. Having first invoked the Lord, she entered the king's hall. The barbarian, struck by this unaccustomed sight, was gradually softened by a woman's flattery. At last he was brought to the queen's banquet, and with him Haman, dear to the king and hostile to the Jewish people. So when, after the feast, the party had begun to grow warm with many cups, Esther threw herself at the king's knees and begged that the destruction of her people be spared. The king promised that he would deny her nothing she asked of him, even if she asked for more. Then Esther, seizing the moment, demanded the death of Haman, in revenge for the nation she had wished to be destroyed. But the king, mindful of his friend, hesitated for a while and withdrew briefly to deliberate. When he returned, he saw Haman clinging to the queen's knees; flaring with anger, and crying out that he had tried to force the queen, he ordered him to be put to death. And at that time it became known to the king that the punishment of the cross had been prepared by Haman for Mordecai. So Haman was fastened to that same cross, all his goods were given to Mordecai, and the Jews were set free. Artaxerxes reigned for sixty-two years, and Ochus succeeded him. I shall rightly compare the story of Judith with this sequence of events. For it is related that she lived after the captivity, but in what period she reigned over the Persians the divine history does not state. Yet the king under whom those deeds took place is called Nebuchadnezzar, not of course the one who took Jerusalem. However, I find that no king of this name reigned among the Persians after the captivity, unless perhaps because of his restlessness and similar attempts that king was called by the Jews by the name Nebuchadnezzar. Still, most think that he was Cambyses, son of King Cyrus, because as a conqueror he penetrated Egypt and Ethiopia. But this opinion is contradicted by the same sacred history, for in the twelfth year of that king Judith is marked as having lived. Moreover, Cambyses held power for no more than nine years. Hence, if it is permitted to conjecture in history, I would believe that these events happened under King Ochus, who was the second after Artaxerxes. I infer this also from the fact that the same Ochus, as I have read in certain secular writings, is described as savage in nature and eager for wars. For he both attacked his neighbours with arms and recovered by war Egypt, which had revolted many years before. At that same time he is also said to have mocked their sacred rites and the Apis, which had been accepted as a god. Because of this, Bagoas, his eunuch, who was an Egyptian by birth, was indignant, and later avenged the insult to his nation by the death of the king. Sacred history also mentions this Bagoas. For when Holofernes had led an army against the Jews by the king's command, it records that Bagoas was in the same camp. Hence I would not unreasonably adduce as an argument for my opinion that the king called Nebuchadnezzar was Ochus, under whom the secular historians report that Bagoas was. Yet no one should be surprised that the writers of secular literature have touched on none of the things written in the sacred volumes. The Spirit of God prevailed, so that history, which was to be proclaimed only with holy words and kept separate from worldly affairs, should be contained within its own mysteries, and not be mixed, like lifeless things from a corrupt mouth that blends truth with falsehood, with others as if on equal terms by chance. For it would have been most unseemly that, while others were doing other things or seeking other things, these matters too should be mixed in with the rest. But I shall go on to the remaining matters, and through...

units.la: vocibus proferenda, permisceri cum aliis velut æquali forte nô debuit. Etenim erat indignissimum, ut alia aguntibus, aut alia quærerētibus, hæc quoq; cum reliquis mis- cerentur. Sed pergam ad cætera, ac per
units.tr: ...should not have been mixed with other matters as if they were of equal weight. For it would have been most unworthy for these things to be jumbled together with the rest, when others were treating other subjects or seeking other things. But I will proceed to the remaining matters, and through them...

units.la: Igitur reversis, ut supra memoravimus, in solum patrium ludæis, nec dum com- posito rerum aut urbis statu, rex rum Medis bellum infert, atque adversus regem eorum Arsaxat nomine, acie con- fligit, secundo eventu. Perempto rege, ge- tem imperio adjungit. Idem reliquis naș tionibus facit, præmissoHolofernę, quem principem militiæ delegerat, cum milli- bus peditum centum & viginti, equitum duodecim. Is Cilicia & Arabia bello va- statis, multas urbes aut vi capit, aut metu in deditionem compellit. Iamq; Damas- cum admotus exercitus, magno Iudæos terrore perculerat. Sed impares ad resi- stendum, neque ad deditionem acquies- centibus animis, expertis quippe usque ante captivitatis mala, ad c templum fre- quentes concurrunt. sbi communi gemi- tu, permistoque ululatu, divinum auxili- um implorant: satis se Domino ob peccata vel crimina dedisse poenarum: reliquis saltem servitio nuper exemptis, parceret. Interea Holofernes Moabitis{a} in deditionem acceptis, atq; adversum Iudæos in so-cieratem belli assumptis, quum ab eorum principibus inquireret, quibusnam viribus freti Hebræi, deditioni animos nō de- dissent. Accitor quidam comperta edisserit, Iudæos Dei cultores, pio a patribus [?]tu institutos, olim in Ægypto pependisse servitium: inde divino munere eductos, ac siccatum{b} mare pedibus emensos: postremo, omnibus gentibus devictis, habitatas{c} majoribus terras recepisse. Exin, vario rerum statu floruisse, aut concidisse atque iterum malis emersisse: secundum merita, iratum ac placatum Deum vicissitudine expertos, dum peccantes incursionibus hostium aut captivitatibus coercentur, propitio numine semper invicti.
units.tr: So, when they had returned, as we noted above, to their native land, the Jews, whose affairs and city were not yet settled, were attacked by the king in a war against the Medes. He fought against their king, named Arsaxat, in battle, with success. When the king had been killed, he added the people to his empire. He did the same with the other nations, sending ahead Holofernes, whom he had appointed commander of the army, with 120,000 foot soldiers and 12,000 horsemen. Holofernes laid waste Cilicia and Arabia, took many cities by force, and compelled others to surrender through fear. Then the army, having been moved up to Damascus, struck great terror into the Jews. But they were not equal to resisting, and their spirits would not submit to surrender, since they had already experienced the evils of captivity. They gathered in great numbers at the Temple, and with common groaning and mingled wailing they implored divine help. They said that they had already given the Lord enough punishment for their sins and crimes; he should at least spare the rest, who had only recently been freed from slavery. Meanwhile Holofernes, having received the Moabites into surrender and taken them into alliance against the Jews, asked their leaders by what strength the Hebrews trusted that they had not inclined their minds to surrender. A certain man, Achior, was summoned, and he set out what he had learned: the Jews were worshippers of God, instituted in piety by their fathers, who long ago in Egypt had endured slavery; then, led out by divine favour, they had crossed the dry sea on foot; lastly, after all the nations had been conquered, they had received the lands once inhabited by their ancestors. After this, through changing fortunes, they had flourished, or fallen and again risen from their troubles; according to their merits, they had experienced God angry and reconciled in turn, and while they were restrained by the attacks of enemies or by captivities for their sins, they were always unconquered by the favour of the divine will.

units.la: Ceterum, si præsenti tempore absque peccato sint, nullo modo eos posse superari: sin aliter se habeant, facile vincendos. Ad hæc Holofernes ferox multis victoriis, nihil sibi invictum ratus, ira accensus, cur ex peccato potissimum Iudæorum pede re illius victoria putaretur, propelli Accitor in castra Hebræorum jubet, ut cum his periret, quos vinci non posse affirmaverat. At tum Iudæi montes petiverant, ita quibus id negotii datum, ima montiū successere, ibiq; vinctum Accitor reliquerunt. Quod ubi Iudæi animadverterūt, ex-emptum vinculis in {a}collem perducunt. Causas rei quærentibus, gesta exponit, receptusq; parem exitum operiebatur. Is post victoriam circumcisus, {b}Iudæus factus est. Igitur Holofernes difficultate locorum comperta, quia adiri præcelsa non poterant, montes militibus circundat, & summa cura Hebræos aquationibus prohibet: eoque maturius obsidionem sense-re, Itaque victi penuria aquæ, ad Oziam principem concurrunt, proni omnes ad deditionem. Ille vero opperiendum paulisper, & divinum auxilium exspectandum respondens, {c}quintodecimo die deditionis tempus constituit. Quod ubi Iudith compertum, quæ viro vidua, prædiues opibus, insignis specie, sed moribus quam vultu illustrior, tum in castris erat, arctis suorum rebus, etiam certo sibi exitio audendum aliquid & tentandum rata, caput comit, vultu expolitur, comite ancilla castra
units.tr: Moreover, if at the present time they are without sin, they cannot be overcome in any way; but if they are otherwise, they will be easily conquered. To this, Holofernes, fierce from many victories, thinking nothing could be invincible to him, was inflamed with anger. Because the Jews' victory was to be attributed above all to their sin, he ordered Achior to be driven to the camp of the Hebrews, so that he might perish with those whom he had declared could not be conquered. But by then the Jews had made for the mountains. Those to whom this task had been assigned came to the foot of the mountains and there left Achior, bound. When the Jews saw this, they freed him from his chains and led him up to the hill. When they asked the reason, he explained what had happened, and once received, he awaited an equal end. After the victory he was circumcised and became a Jew. Then Holofernes, having learned that the places could not be approached because they were lofty, surrounded the mountains with soldiers and with great care kept the Hebrews from water. They felt the siege all the sooner, and so, worn down by lack of water, they ran together to the leader Ozias, all of them ready to surrender. But he replied that they must wait a little longer and expect divine help, and he fixed a time of five days for the surrender. When Judith learned this, a widow, rich in wealth and notable in beauty but more illustrious in character than in appearance, who was then in the camp, she judged that, since her people's affairs were cramped and certain ruin awaited them, she must dare and attempt something. She arranged her hair, adorned her face, and went into the enemy's camp with a maidservant.

units.la: {a} Bethulia, collem.
units.tr: Bethulia, the hill.

units.la: {b} Achior sacra In-deorum suscipit.
units.tr: Achior receives the sacred rites of the Jews.

units.la: {c} quinto est Iud. 7.23 intexta Graeco. castra hostiū ingreditur. Statimq; ad Ho-[?]lofernem deducta, perditas res suorum memorat, se transfugio vitæ consuluisse. Deinde a duce poscit liberum extra castra nocturno tempore egressum, orandi gratia. mandatum id vigilibus, portarumque custodibus. Sed ubi per triduum egredien-di ac redeundi consuetudinem sibi {a}bar baris fidem fecit, Holofernem cupido in-cesit, dediticiæ corpore {b}abuti. Etenim forma excellenti, Persam facile permove-rat. Ita ad ducis tentorium per Baguam eunuchum {c}deducunt, initioque convivii, barbarus multo se vino obruit. Tum re-motis ministris, priusquam vim mulieri inferret, somno captus est. Judith tempo-rearrepto, caput hostis desecat, secumque aufert. Et cum secundum consuetudinem castris egredi crederetur, incolumis ad suos regressa est. Postero die {d}Hebræi, caput Holofernis de superioribus ostentantes, eruptione facta, ad castra hostium pergunt. Tum vero barbari signum pugnæ poscentes, tabernaculum ducis frequentes assistunt. Ubi truncum corpus repertum, foeda formidine in fugam versi, terga hostibus præbuerunt. Judæi fugientes persecuti,cæsisq;multis millibus,castrisac praeda potiti. Iudith summis laudibus celebrata, centum & quinq; annos vixisse traditur. Hæc, Ocho rege,ut opinamur, gesta sunt, anno imperii ejus * duodeci-mo. A tempore Hierosolymæ restitutæ, usq; in id bellum,fuerunt anni duo & viginti. Ceterum Ochus viginti & tres annos regnavit. Fuit autem ultra omnes cruentus,& plusquâ barbaro animo. Hûc Bagua spado ægrotantem venenis sustulit. Post cum Arxes, filius ejus, triennio imperium tenuit. Darius annos quatuor. Adversum hunc Alexander Macedo acie conflixit. Eo victo,Persis imperium ademptum: quod ab initio Cyri steterat annos ducetos & quinquaginta. Alexander victor fere omnium gentium, adiisse Hierosolymæ templum dicitur, ac dona intulisse: edixitque per omne imperium, quod sui juris effecerat, ut Iudæis ibidem degentibus liberum esset in patriam reverti. Exacto duodecimo imperii anno, septimo postquam Darium devicerat, apud Babyloniam defunctus est. Re-gnum amici ejus, qui simul cum illo maxima illa bella gesserant, partiti sunt.
units.tr: {c} The fifth (day): Judith 7.23, woven into the Greek. She went into the enemy's camp. Immediately she was brought before Holofernes, and she recounted the ruin of her people and said that she had sought refuge by desertion. Then she asked the commander for permission to go out of the camp at night to pray. This was granted to the sentries and the gate-guards. But when, over three days, she had given the barbarians proof of her custom of going out and coming back, desire for her body seized Holofernes, who wished to abuse the surrendered woman. For he had been easily moved by her excellent beauty. So through Bagoas the eunuch they brought her to the commander's tent, and at the beginning of the banquet the barbarian drowned himself in much wine. Then, with the attendants removed, he fell asleep before he could force himself on the woman. Judith, seizing the moment, cut off the enemy's head and carried it away with her. And since it was believed that she was going out of the camp as was her custom, she returned safe to her people. On the next day the Hebrews, displaying the head of Holofernes from the heights, made a sortie and advanced against the enemy's camp. Then indeed the barbarians, calling for the signal of battle, crowded round the commander's tent. When the headless body was found, they turned in fear of a dreadful kind and offered their backs to the enemies. The Jews pursued the fugitives, slew many thousands, and gained possession of the camp and the booty. Judith was celebrated with the highest praise, and is said to have lived one hundred and five years. These things, as we suppose, were done in the reign of Ochus, in the twelfth year of his rule. From the time Jerusalem was restored until that war there were twenty-two years. Ochus reigned twenty-three years; he was more cruel than all others and more than barbarous in spirit. Bagoas the eunuch killed him with poison while he was sick. After him Arses, his son, held the empire for three years, and Darius for four. Alexander the Macedonian fought in battle against him. When Darius was defeated, the empire was taken from the Persians, which had stood from the beginning of Cyrus for 550 years. Alexander, victor over almost all the nations, is said to have gone to the Temple at Jerusalem and offered gifts, and he issued an edict throughout the whole empire that he had brought under his rule, that the Jews living there should be free to return to their homeland. When the twelfth year of his rule was complete, seven years after he had conquered Darius, he died at Babylon. His friends, who had waged those great wars with him, divided the kingdom.

units.la: [Notes are marginal references and are placed beside their lines above; the margin readings are doubtful, see notes.] Inde aliquanto tempore finc usurpatione regali susceptas partes procuraverunt, {a} Arrideo[?] quodam Philippo Alexandri fratre regnate, cui perimbecillo verbo datum imperium videbatur: res autè penes eos erat, qui sibi exercitum & provincias distribuerant. Nec vero hic rerum status diu mansit, omne[?]q; se reges appellari malu- erunt. Primus in Syria post Alexandrū Seleucus rex fuit, subjecta eidem Perside ac Babylone. Qua tempestate Iudæi annuum stipendium trecenta argenti talenta regi dabant: nec tamen per {b}ternos magistratus; sed per sacerdotes suos regebantur, patrioque ritu vivebant. Donec ple-rique eorum longa rursum pace corru-pti, miscere omnia seditionibus & turbare coeperunt, affectantes summum sacerdotium libidine, avaritia & dominan-di cupidine. Namque primum sub rege Seleuco, Antiochi magni filio, Oniam sacerdotem, virum sanctum atque inte-grum, Simon quidam falsis apud regem criminibus insimulatum, {c}exquirere ne quiverat. Interiecto deinde tempore, la-son frater Oniae,{d} Antiochum regem, qui Seleuco fratri successerat, adiit, augmen-
units.tr: [Notes are marginal references and are placed beside their lines above; the margin readings are doubtful, see notes.] After that, for some time, without a royal title, they pursued the parts they had taken up, with Arrhidaeus(?), a certain brother of Philip the son of Alexander, reigning, to whom the empire seemed to have been given by a very weak title; but the real power was in the hands of those who had distributed the army and the provinces among themselves. Nor did this state of affairs last long, and they all preferred to be called kings. The first king in Syria after Alexander was Seleucus, to whom Persia and Babylon were also subject. In that period the Jews paid the king an annual tribute of three hundred talents of silver, yet they were not governed by triumvirs but by their own priests, and lived according to their ancestral custom. Until many of them, corrupted by a long peace again, began to stir up everything with seditions and to disturb it, desiring the high priesthood out of lust, greed, and a desire for domination. For first, under King Seleucus, son of Antiochus the Great, Simon, a certain man, accused Onias the high priest, a holy and upright man, before the king with false charges, and was unable to prevail against him. After some time had passed, Jason, brother of Onias, approached King Antiochus, who had succeeded his brother Seleucus, promising an increase of tribute if the high priesthood were handed over to him. And although it was unusual, and had never before been permitted to anyone, to hold the priesthood for life, nevertheless the king's mind, eager and sick with greed, was easily overcome...

units.la: {a} Arideo: the marginal note above, as printed beside line 2. tum stipendii pollicens, si sibi {a}summum sacerdotium traderetur. Et quamquam insolitum, neq; ante permissum cuiquam erat perpetuo sacerdotio {b}perfungi: foli- citus tamen regis animus atq; æger avari-tia, facile superatus est. Ita depulso Onia, Iasoni sacerdotium est mandatum. Is soe- de admodum cives, patriamque laceravit. Dein quum per Menelaum quendam, Si- monis illius fratrem, promissam regi pe- cuniam misisset, patefacta semel ambitio- ni via, iisdem artibus quibus Iason prius, Menelaus quoq; sacerdotium {c}obtinue-rat. Nec multo post, quum is promissum argenti modum non reddidisset, loco pel-litur, Lysimachus substituitur. Inde inter Iasonem & Menelaum foeda fuere certa-mina, donec Iason profugus patria excef-sit. His initiis corruptis moribus, eo us-que processum, ut plerique popularium ab Antiocho poscerent, permitti {d}sibi more gentilium vivere. Quod quum rex petentibus annuisset, certatim pessi-mus quisque delubra extruere, idolis supplicare, legem profanare occœperat. Interea Antiochus rediens ab Alexandria (namq; tum bellū {e}regi Aegyptio intule-rat, rat, quod juslu senatus & populi Romani deposuit, Paulo & Craso consulibus) Hi-erosolymam adiit, cum discordantem su-perstitionibus suscep-tis populum reperiset, legem Dei destruens & his fauens, qui impia sequebantur, omnia templi orna-menta detraxit, ac multa cæde vastavit. Id gestum ab excessu Alexandri anno ce-tesimo uno & quinquagesimo, Paulo (ut diximus) Craisoque consulibus, post quinquennium fere quam Antiochus regnare coeperat. Sed ut temporum ordo confertus sit, ac liqueat evidentius, quis hic fuerit Antiochus, regum qui post A-LEXANDRUM in Syria fuerunt, & nomina & tempora enumerabimus. De-functo[?], ut supra retulimus, rege Alexandro, ab amicis ejus regnum omne divi-sum, ac regio nomine aliquamdiu administratum est. {b}Seleucus post novem annos in Syria rex est appellatus, regnavitq; annos duos & triginta. Post eum Antiochus filius ejus, annos unum de viginti. Inde Antiochus Antiochi filius, qui & Theus cognominatus est, annos quinde-cim.post hunc Seleucus{c} filius, cognomi-ne Callinicus, annos unum & viginti. Ita Seleucus {a}filius Callinici, annos tres. Hoc {b}defuncto, {c}Antiochus frater Callinici A-tiam & Syriam tenuit, annos (septē & tri-ginta. Hic est Antiochus, adversus quem Scipio Africani frater bellavit: quo bello victus, & imperii parte multatus est. Hic duos filios habuit, Selcucū & Antiochū, quem obsidem Romanis dederat. Ita An-tiocho magno mortuo, {d}Seleucus ejus filius natu minor regnum adeptus est: sub quo Oniam sacerdotem a Simone insi-mulatum diximus. Tum Antiochus a Romanis dimissus, datusque in locum ejus obses Demetrius Seleuci regis, qui eo tempore regnabat, filius. Seleuco mortuo, anno imperii duodecimo, rex frater Antiochus, qui Romae obses fuerat, occupavit. Is post quinquennium, quam regnare coeperat, ut supra docui-mus, Hierosolymam depopulatus est. Ete-nim grave Romanis stipendium pensi-tans, ipse immensis sumptibus pene necessa-rio cogebatur pecunias rapto quaerere, neque ullam praedandi occasionem o-mittere. Post biennium deinde, pari rursum clade affectis Iudaeis, ne forte fre-quentibus malis compulsi bellum fume-rent, rent, praesidium arci imposuit. Inde sacra legem evertere aggressus, misit edictum, ut omnes reliquis majorum suorum traditionibus {a}gentilium ritu viverent. Nec defuere, qui profano imperio volentes parerent. Tum vero fœdum spectaculum, per universam urbe palam in plateis Diis litabatur: sacra etiam legis & prophetarum volumina igni cremata. Ea tempestate Mathathias, Iohannis filius, sacerdos erat. hic quum a regiis cogeretur edicto parere, egregia constantia prophana contemnens, Hebræum publice {b}profanan-temin[?] ore omnium iugulavit. Tum demum reperto duce facta secessio est. Mathathias opido egressus {c}, multis ad eum confluentibus, speciem justi exercitus effecerat: queis omnibus destinatum erat adversus profanum imperium se armis tueri, & in bello potius occubere, quam impias ceremonias exercere. Interea Antiochus per Græcas quoq; urbes, quæ in illius imperio erant, repertos Iudæos sacrificare cogebat, inauditisque cruciatibus relu-stantes afficiebat. Qua tempestate illa passio {d}septem fratrum, matrisq; trisq; fuit: qui omnes, cum legem Dei & instituta maiorū violare suppliciis coge-rentur,mori maluerunt. Ad extremū poe-nas mortefq; eorum comitata mater est. Interea Mathathias moritur : vicarium exercitui,quem paraverat,ducem {a}Iudam filium substituit. Hujus duƈtu adversus regios frequentibus praeliis prospere pu-gnatum. Nam primum {b}Apollonium ducem hostium, qui magnis copiis in conflictum descenderat, cum omni exer-citu delevit. Quod cum Seron quidam, qui tum Syriae praerat, comperiflet,mul-tiplicatis legionibus Iudam aggreflus, fe-rox, quia numero praestabat, ubi in certa-men descensum,fusus ac fugatus,octingē-tis ferme amisis, in Syriam regressus est. Id ubi compertum est Antiocho, ira & dolore succensus ( quippe angebatur du-ces suos cum magnis exercitib. devictos) auxilium per omne regnū contrahit, do-nativum militibus exhaustis penitus the-fauris largitur. Etenim tum praecipue gra-viter pecuniae inopia affectus erat. Nam deficientibus Iudaeis ab eo,qui ei ultra trecenta argenti talenta annua penfitaves-rant,praeterea Graecis urbibus multisq;re-gionibus persecutionis malo turbatis (ne {a}gentilibus quidem pepercerat: quos de-ferere inveteratas superstitiones,&ad unum ritu deducere tentaverat){b}illis quidem,{c} ubi nihil sancti erat, facile relinquētibus: sed tamen omnibus metu ac clade affectis, vectigalia cessaverant. Quibus rebus æstuans (etenim ipse olim omnibus regibus opulentior, suomet ícelere inopiam perferat) copias cum Lysia partitur, eiq; Syriam & bellum adversus Iudæos committit, ipse in Persas ad cogēda vectigalia profectus. Igitur Lysias duces belli delegit, Ptolemæum, Gorgiam, {d}Doronem, & Nicanorem: his quadraginta millia pedi-tum, septem equitum data. Ac primo impetu magnum Iudæis terrorem intulerūt. Tum Iudas cūctis desperantibus suos ad-hortatus, forti animo descēderent in præ-lium: Deo fretis, nihil invictum fore. Sæpe antea a paucioribus adversum plures{e} be-ne pugnatum. Iejunio indicto, celebratoque sacrificio, in aciem descensum, fusæ hostium copiæ: Iudas castris potitus, mul-tumque ibi auri & Tyriarum opum repertum. Namque ex Syria negociatores nihil de victoria dubitantes, regium exercitum sequuti, spe captivos mercandi, prædæ præda fuere. Hæc ubi Lysiæ ex nunciis comperta, majore cura copias parat, an-noq; post immani exercitu Iudæos aggre-ditur: victus denuo Antiochiam se rece-pit. Iudas pulsis hostibus Hierosolymam regressus, purgare templum & restituere animum intendit: quod eversum ab An-tiocho, prophanatum q; a gentibus, fœdā sui speciem præbebat. Sed Syris arcem tenentibus, quæ continua templo, & loci natura superior, atq; inexpugnabilis erat, adiri c subjecta non poterant, crebris eru-ptionibus prohibentibus. Adversum hos Iudas validissimam suorum aciem obje-cit. Ita opus sacræ sedis curatum, tem-plumque muro circumdatum, constituti-que qui perpetuum præsidium armati a-gitarent. At Lysias multiplicato exercitu in Iudæam regressus rursum vincitur, magnaclade exercitus & auxiliorum, quæ ei a civitatibus missa in bellum conspira-verant. Interea Antiochus, quem in-Persidem profectum [?] supra memoravi-mus, opidum Elymum d, regionis illius opulentissimum, fanumque ibi situm multo auro refertum, diripere conatus, confluente undique ad defensionem lo-ci multi. ci multitudine, fugatus: insuper nuncium accepit, res a Lysia improspere gestas. Ita ex moerore animi corporis morbo incubuit. Sed cum internis doloribus angeretur, reminiscens malorum, quibus populum Dei vexaverat, merito sibi illa accidisse confitebatur. Deinde post pau- cos dies moritur, cum regnasset annos undecim. Antiocho filio regnum reliquit, cui Eupator nomen erat. Eatenus [?] pestate Iudas Syros in arce positos obsidebat. Qui cum fame atque inopia afficerentur, misisset ad regem nuncios, praesidium implorant. Ita Eupator cum centum millibus, & equitum viginti millibus, suis subsidio venit: praeeuntibus aciem cum ingenti terrore elephantis. Tum Iudas laxata obsidione, regi obviam tendit, primo praelio Syros fundit. Rex petit pacem, quia infido ingenio male usus, per fidem consecuta ultio. Nam Demetrius Seleuci filius, quem Romanis obsidem datum supra memoravimus, ut audivit Antiochum decessisse, petivit ut se in regnum remitterent. Quod cum ei negatum fuisset, clam Roma profugit: in Syriam venit, regnumque occupavit. Antiocho filio, qui annum unum &men.[?]ses lex regnaverat, interfecto. Hoc regnante, primum Judaei a populo Romano amicitiam foedusq; petiere: benigneq; excepta legatio, decreto Senatus socii atque amici appellati. Interim Demetrius adver-sus Judam per duces suos bellum gerebat.
units.tr: Jason, the brother of Onias, approached King Antiochus, who had succeeded his brother Seleucus, and promised a large sum of money if the high priesthood were handed over to him. Although it was unusual, and no one had previously been permitted to hold the priesthood for life, the king's mind, eager and sick with greed, was easily won over. So Onias was driven out and the priesthood was entrusted to Jason. He harassed the citizens with sedition and tore the fatherland apart. Then, when he had sent the promised money to the king through a certain Menelaus, the brother of that Simon, the way to ambition was opened once, and Menelaus obtained the priesthood by the same tricks Jason had used before. Not long afterwards, when Menelaus did not pay the promised amount of silver, he was removed from his post and Lysimachus was put in his place. After this, shameful contests broke out between Jason and Menelaus, until Jason, a fugitive, left his country. With morals corrupted by these beginnings, matters went so far that many of the people asked Antiochus to allow them to live in the manner of the Gentiles. When the king granted this to those who asked, every worst man rushed to build shrines, to offer supplication to idols, and began to profane the law. Meanwhile Antiochus, returning from Alexandria (for he had then made war on the king of Egypt, which he gave up at the command of the Senate and people of Rome, in the consulship of Paulus and Crassus), came to Jerusalem. Finding the people divided by their adopted superstitions, and destroying the law of God and favouring those who followed impious practices, he stripped the temple of all its ornaments and laid waste the city with great slaughter. This was done in the one hundred and fifty-first year from the death of Alexander, in the consulship of Paulus and Crassus (as we have said), about five years after Antiochus had begun to reign. But so that the order of the times may be clear and set out more plainly, who this Antiochus was, and the names and dates of the kings who reigned in Syria after Alexander, we shall enumerate them. Alexander having died, as we related above, his friends divided the whole kingdom, and for some time it was administered in the name of the kingdom. Seleucus was called king in Syria after nine years, and reigned thirty-two years. After him, his son Antiochus, for nineteen years. Then Antiochus, the son of Antiochus, who was also surnamed Theos, for fifteen years. After him his son Seleucus, surnamed Callinicus, for twenty-one years. Then Seleucus, the son of Callinicus, for three years. When he died, Antiochus, brother of Callinicus, held Asia and Syria for thirty-seven years. This is the Antiochus against whom the brother of Scipio Africanus waged war; defeated in that war, he was stripped of part of his realm. He had two sons, Seleucus and Antiochus, whom he had given as a hostage to the Romans. So, when Antiochus the Great died, his son Seleucus, the younger, obtained the kingdom; under him, as we have said, Onias the priest was slandered by Simon. Then Antiochus, released by the Romans, was replaced as hostage by Demetrius, the son of King Seleucus, who was then reigning. When Seleucus died, in the twelfth year of his reign, his brother Antiochus, who had been a hostage at Rome, seized the throne. Five years after he had begun to reign, as we showed above, he laid waste Jerusalem. For, bearing the heavy tribute owed to the Romans, he was himself almost forced by his enormous expenses to seek money by plunder, and he let no opportunity for looting pass. Two years later, when the Jews were again struck by a similar disaster, he set a garrison in the citadel, lest the Jews, driven by repeated misfortunes, should take up war. Then he undertook to overthrow the sacred law and sent out an edict that all should abandon the traditions of their ancestors and live in the manner of the Gentiles. Nor were there lacking those who, willing to obey the profane command, complied. Then indeed a shameful spectacle appeared: throughout the whole city sacrifices were offered to the gods openly in the squares, and the sacred books of the law and the prophets were burned in the fire. In those times Mattathias, son of John, was a priest. When he was ordered by the royal edict to obey, despising the profane command with remarkable steadfastness, he slew in public, before everyone's eyes, a Jew who was about to offer profane sacrifice. Then at last, a leader having been found, a secession was made. Mattathias left the town, and many gathered to him, and he formed the appearance of a righteous army; all of them had resolved to defend themselves with arms against the profane rule, and to fall in battle rather than perform impious ceremonies. Meanwhile Antiochus, through the Greek cities also which were under his rule, compelled the Jews he found to sacrifice, and punished those who resisted with unheard-of tortures. In that time occurred the suffering of the seven brothers and their mother, who, when they were compelled by punishments to violate the law of God and the customs of their ancestors, chose to die. At last their mother accompanied their punishments and deaths. Meanwhile Mattathias died, and he appointed as leader of the army he had raised his son Judas as his deputy. Under his leadership, many battles were fought successfully against the royal forces. For first he destroyed with his whole army Apollonius, the leader of the enemy, who had come down to battle with large forces. When a certain Seron, who was then governing Syria, learned of this, he attacked Judas with multiplied legions, proud because he excelled in numbers; but when he came down to the contest, he was routed and put to flight, and returned to Syria having lost about eight hundred men. When this was reported to Antiochus, he was inflamed with anger and grief (for he was tormented that his leaders had been defeated with great armies), and he gathered auxiliaries throughout the whole kingdom and gave the soldiers a bonus from his treasuries, which were now quite exhausted. For at that time he was especially oppressed by a serious lack of money.
