For the Jews, who had paid him more than three hundred talents of silver a year, had now defaulted, and besides, the Greek cities and many regions were troubled by the evil of persecution (he had not even spared the Gentiles, whom he had tried to turn away from their long-established superstitions and bring all to one custom); these, where nothing was sacred to them, readily abandoned their rites, but nevertheless, all being struck with fear and devastation, they had stopped paying tribute. Troubled by these things (for he himself, though once richer than all the kings, was now suffering want through his own wickedness), he divided his forces with Lysias, and committed to him Syria and the war against the Jews, while he himself set out against the Persians to collect tributes. So Lysias chose leaders of the war: Ptolemy, Gorgias, Doron and Nicanor; to these were given forty thousand foot soldiers and seven thousand horsemen. At the first onslaught they struck great terror into the Jews. Then Judas, when all were despairing, exhorted his men to go down into battle with brave spirits: trusting in God, nothing would be unconquerable. Often before, fewer men had fought well against more. A fast was proclaimed and a sacrifice celebrated, and they went down into battle; the enemy forces were routed. Judas took the camp, and much gold and Tyrian wealth was found there. For merchants from Syria, not doubting the victory, had followed the royal army, hoping to buy captives, and became the spoil of the spoil. When Lysias learned this from messengers, he prepared his forces with greater care, and a year later attacked the Jews with a huge army; defeated again, he withdrew to Antioch. Judas, having driven off the enemy, returned to Jerusalem and set his mind on cleansing the temple and restoring worship, which, overthrown by Antiochus and profaned by the Gentiles, presented a foul appearance. But the Syrians held the citadel, which adjoined the temple and was higher by the nature of its site and impregnable, so that it could not be approached below, the garrison hindering them with frequent sorties. Against these Judas set his strongest line of his men. Thus the work of the sacred place was attended to, the temple was walled round, and men were stationed to keep a perpetual armed guard. But Lysias, having gathered a multiplied army, returned into Judea and was again defeated, with great slaughter of his army and of the auxiliaries which the cities had sent him to join the war. Meanwhile Antiochus, whom I have mentioned as having set out against Persia, tried to plunder the town of Elymais, the richest of that region, and a temple situated there filled with much gold; but the many men who gathered from everywhere to defend the place put him to flight. Moreover, he received news that Lysias' affairs had gone badly. So, from grief of mind, he fell ill in body. But while he was tormented by internal pains, remembering the evils with which he had afflicted the people of God, he confessed that these things had justly befallen him. Then, after a few days, he died, having reigned eleven years. He left the kingdom to his son Antiochus, who was called Eupator. Meanwhile at that time Judas was besieging the Syrians stationed in the citadel. When these were pressed by famine and want, they sent messengers to the king and implored help. So Eupator came to their aid with one hundred thousand men and twenty thousand horsemen, with elephants going before the battle line to cause great terror. Then Judas, lifting the siege, moved to meet the king and in the first battle routed the Syrians. The king sought peace, but, having misused his faithless nature, he was overtaken by a vengeance deserved through faith broken. For Demetrius, the son of Seleucus, whom we mentioned above as given to the Romans as a hostage, when he heard that Antiochus had died, asked that they send him back to his kingdom. When this was refused him, he secretly fled from Rome, came into Syria, and seized the kingdom, Antiochus the son having been put to death, who had reigned only one year and some months. Under this king, the Jews for the first time sought friendship and alliance with the Roman people; the embassy was kindly received, and by a decree of the Senate they were called allies and friends. Meanwhile Demetrius was waging war against Judas through his commanders.

units.la: Ac primum per Bacchidem quendam & {a}Alchimū ludęum ductus exercitus: post Nicanor bello praepositus in praelio occu-buit. Tum Bacchides & Alchimus re-sumptis viribus, auctisque copiis, adver-sum Judam confligunt. In ea pugna vi-ctores Syri, cruente admodum victoria sunt usi. Hebraei in locum Judae Ionathan fratrem ejus deligunt. Interea Alchi-mus cum foede Hierosolymam vastasset, moritur. Bacchides socio destitutus, ad regem redit. Dein post biennium rursus Bacchides bellum Judæis intulit, victus pacem petit. Quæ propositis conditioni-bus data, si perfugas captivosque & o-mnia bello rapta redderet. Dum hæc intra Judaeam geruntur, adolescens quidam Rhodi educatus, nomine Alexander, An-tiochi se esse filium dictitans, (quod sal-sum erat) adjutus opibus Ptolemaei regis AlexanAlexandrini, in Syriam cum exercitu venit: Demetrium bello superatum occidit, cum regnasset annos xii. Hic{a} Alexander, priusquam adversus Demetrium coflige-ret, foedus cum Ionatha fecerat, eumque{b} veste purpurea & c insignibus regiis donaverat, ob quod eum Ionathas auxiliis juverat: victoque Demetrio, primus omnium congratulatum occurrerat. Neque postea Alexander datam fidem violavit. Itaque quennio[?], quo rerum potitus est, res Iudaeorum tranquillae fuerunt. Igitur{d} Demetrii filius, qui post mortem patris Cretam confugerat, hortante Lasthene Cretensium duce, regnum patrium bello repetens, impar viribus, Ptolemaeum{e} Philometorem regem Aegypti, Alexandri socerum, jam tum genero infestum, ut sibi fit auxilio implorat. Ille vero non tam supplicis precibus, quam spe Syriae occupandae illectus, copias cum eo jungit: ac{f} filiam, Alexandro nuptam, dat Demetrio. Adversus hos Alexander acie confligit. eo prelio vincitur Ptolemaeus, cadit Alexander. {g}Vincitur Ptolemaeus, & paulo post interficitur, cum regnasset annos v. vel, ut in plerisque authoribus
units.tr: At first the army was led by a certain Bacchides and Alchimus, a Jew. Afterwards Nicanor, who had been put in charge of the war, fell in battle. Then Bacchides and Alchimus, recovering their strength and increasing their forces, engaged Judas. In that battle the victorious Syrians used their victory most bloodily. The Hebrews chose Jonathan, Judas's brother, in his place. Meanwhile Alchimus, after he had cruelly laid waste Jerusalem, died. Bacchides, deserted by his ally, returned to the king. Then, two years later, Bacchides again made war on the Jews, but being defeated he sought peace. It was granted on the condition that the Jews should hand back the deserters, the captives and all the goods seized in the war. While these things were happening within Judea, a young man brought up at Rhodes, named Alexander, who kept claiming to be a son of Antiochus (which was false), was aided by the resources of Ptolemy, king of the Alexandrians, and came into Syria with an army. He defeated Demetrius in battle and killed him, after Demetrius had reigned twelve years. Before he had gathered his forces against Demetrius, this Alexander had made a covenant with Jonathan and had presented him with a purple robe and royal insignia, for which reason Jonathan had helped him. When Demetrius was defeated, Jonathan was the first of all to run to congratulate him. Nor did Alexander afterwards break the pledge he had given. Thus, during the five years in which he held power, the affairs of the Jews were peaceful. Then the son of Demetrius, who after his father's death had fled to Crete, at the urging of Lasthenes, leader of the Cretans, sought to recover his father's kingdom by war. Being unequal in strength, he implored Ptolemy Philometor, king of Egypt, Alexander's father-in-law, who was already hostile to his son-in-law, to help him. Ptolemy, drawn less by the suppliant's entreaties than by the hope of seizing Syria, joined forces with him and gave his daughter, who had been married to Alexander, to Demetrius. Alexander engaged these men in battle. In that fight Ptolemy was defeated and Alexander fell. Ptolemy was defeated, and a little later was killed, after he had reigned five years; or, as in most authors...

units.la: {d} ddeest[?] De-metrius.
units.tr: {d} Demetrius is wanting.

units.la: {e} Propter insidias quas ei struxerat per Ammonium quendam † Cleopatram. reperi, novem. Demetrius regnum {a}ade-ptus, Ionathan benigne habuit, foedus cū eo fecit, Iudæos legibus suis reddidit. In-terea {b}Tryphon, qui partium Alexandri fuerat, præfectus Syriæ regno. eum[?] bello prohibiturus, contra Ionathā in prælium descendit, terribilis x l.[?] millium exercitu. Tryphōn, ubi se imparem cernit, pacem simulat: receptumq; in amicitiam, invita-tumq; Ptolemaidam, interfecit. Post Io-nathan, summa rerum ad Simonem fra-trem defertur. Is funus fratris magnifice curavit: septemque illas pyramidas nobi-lissimi operis exstruxit, in quibus & fra-trum & patris ossa condidit. Tum Deme-trius, refecto cum Iudæis fœdere, con-templatione cladis a Tryphone illatæ (nam post Ionathæ necem urbes eorum atque agros bello vastaverat) annua {b}ejus vectigalia in perpetuum remittit. Etenim usq; ad id tempus, regibus Syriæ, nisi cum armis resisterent, stipendium pensitave-rant. Id gestum Demetrii regis anno {c}se-cundo. quod ideo signavimus, quia us-que in hunc annum per tempora Asia-norum regum cucurrimus, ut ratio tem-porum digesta luceret. Nunc autem per tempora eorum qui Iudæis vel pontifices vel reges fuerunt, utq;ad Christi nativita-tem rerum ordinem digeremus. Igitur post Ionathan, Simon frater ejus, ut supra dictum est, Hebræis præfuit jure pontifi-cis. id enim ei tum a suis, tum & a{a} po-pulo Romano honoris delatum. Hic cum fecundo Demetrii regis anno civibus præesse coepisset, post octo annos infidus{b} Ptolemæi circumventus occubuit. Huic Iohannes filius successus qui cum adversus Hyrcanos, gentem validissimam, egregie pugnasset, Hyrcani cognomen accepit. Mortuus est, annos vi. & xx. rerum post titus. Post hunc Aristobulus pontifex substitutus, primus omnium post captivi-tatem regium nomen assumpsit, capitiq; diadema imposuit. Exacto anno diem functus est. Alexander deinde, filius ejus, rex pariter & pontifex fuit: regnavit annos vii. & viginti. in cuius d actibus nihil, præter crudelitatem, memoriā dignum reperi. Hic, cum Aristobulum & Hyrcanum parvos filios reliquisset, e Sofilina sive Alexandra uxor ejus regnum per novem annos tenuit. Post hujus obi tum, fœda inter fratres de regno certamina. Ac primum Hyrcanus imperium ob-tinebat: mox ab Aristobulo fratre pullus confugit ad Pompeium: qui tum Mithri-datico bello confecto, pacataq; Armenia & Ponto, victor omnium gentium, quas adierat, ultrorsum pergere, & vicina quae-que Romano imperio adjungere cupi-ens, causas belli & materiam incendii quaerebat. Igitur Hyrcanum libens excepit, ductuque ejus Judaeos aggreditur: urbe capta atque arce, templo pepercit, Aristobulum {a}victum Romam mittit, Hyrcano jus pontificatus restituit: impo-sitoque Judaeis stipendio, procuratorem eis Antipatrum quendam Ascalonitem praepoluit. Hyrcanus quatuor & {b}tri-ginta annos rerum potitus, dum adver-sum Parthos bella gerit, capitur. Tum Herodes alienigena, Antipatri Ascaloni-tae filius, regnum Judaeae a Senatu & po-pulo Romano petiit accepitque. Hunc primum Judaei externum regem coepe-runt habere. Etenim jam adventante Christo necesse erat, secundum vaticinia prophetarum, suis eos ducibus privari, ne quid ultra Christum exspectarent. Sub hoc Herode,anno imperii ejus ter-tio & tio & xxx. Christus natus est, Sabino & Rufino consulib. VIII Kalend. Ianuarias. Verum hæc quæ Euangeliis ac deinceps Apostolorum actibus continentur, attingere nō aulus[?], ne quid forma præcisi operis rerum dignitatib. diminueret, reliqua exsequar. Herodes post nativitatē Domini regnavit annos iiii. Nam omne imperii ejus tempus, vii & xxx anni fuerunt. Post quem Archelaus tetrarcha annis ix. Herodes ann.{b}xx & iiii. Hoc regnante, anno regni octavo & decimo. DOMINUS crucifixus est, Fusio Gemino & Rubellio Gemino consulibus. A quo tempore usque in Stiliconem consulem, sunt anni *CCCXVII. Apostolorum actus Lucas edidit, usque in tempus quo Paulus Romam deductus est, Nerone imperante: qui non dicam regum, sed omnium hominum, & vel immanium bestiarum sordidissimus, dignus exstitit, qui persecutionem in Christianos primus inciperet: nescio an & postremus{b} explerit. Siquidem opinione multorum receptum sit, ipsum Antichristum venturum, hujus vitia, ut plenius exponerem, res admonebat, nisi non esset hu-
units.tr: {e} On account of the plots which he had laid against him through a certain Ammonius, Cleopatra... I found nine. Demetrius, having obtained the kingdom, treated Jonathan kindly, made a covenant with him, and restored the Jews to their own laws. Meanwhile Tryphon, who had been on Alexander's side, having been placed in charge of Syria, intending to prevent the king from taking the throne, went down to battle against Jonathan with an army of forty thousand men, a terrifying force. When Tryphon saw that he was the weaker, he pretended to seek peace; having received Jonathan into friendship and invited him to Ptolemais, he killed him. After Jonathan, the chief command passed to his brother Simon. He gave his brother's funeral a magnificent honour and erected seven pyramids of most noble workmanship, in which he laid the bones of his brothers and his father. Then Demetrius, renewing the covenant with the Jews, and moved by consideration of the disaster inflicted by Tryphon (for after Jonathan's death Tryphon had laid waste their cities and fields in war), remitted their annual tribute for ever. For up to that time they had paid tribute to the kings of Syria, unless they resisted with arms. This was done in the second year of King Demetrius. We have marked it because up to this year we have followed the times of the Asian kings, so that the order of the times might be clear. But now we shall follow the times of those who were high priests or kings of the Jews, and so arrange the sequence of events down to the birth of Christ. So after Jonathan, his brother Simon, as has been said above, presided over the Hebrews with the right of high priest; for this honour had been conferred on him both by his own people and by the Roman people. When he had begun to govern the citizens in the second year of King Demetrius, after eight years he was betrayed by Ptolemy's treachery and died. His son John succeeded him; he fought brilliantly against the Hyrcanians, a most powerful people, and received the surname Hyrcanus. He died, having lived twenty-six years and having ruled... After him Aristobulus was appointed high priest; he was the first of all, after the captivity, to take the royal title and to place a diadem on his head. When a year had passed he died. Then his son Alexander was both king and high priest in like manner; he reigned twenty-seven years. I have found nothing worthy of memory in his deeds except cruelty. He left two small sons, Aristobulus and Hyrcanus, and his wife Sofilina, or Alexandra, held the kingdom for nine years. After her death there were foul struggles between the brothers over the kingdom. At first Hyrcanus held the power; soon the younger brother Aristobulus drove him out and fled to Pompey. Pompey, having finished the Mithridatic war and pacified Armenia and Pontus, was victor over all the peoples he had visited, and, eager to push further onward and to join the neighbouring lands to the Roman empire, sought causes of war and a pretext for fire. So he gladly received Hyrcanus and attacked the Jews under his guidance. He took the city and the citadel, but spared the temple; he sent Aristobulus as a captive to Rome, and restored to Hyrcanus the right of the high priesthood; he imposed a tribute on the Jews and set over them as procurator a certain Antipater of Ascalon. Hyrcanus, having held power for thirty-four years, was captured while waging war against the Parthians. Then Herod, a foreigner, son of Antipater of Ascalon, sought the kingdom of Judea from the Senate and the Roman people, and received it. The Jews began to have him as their first foreign king. For, since Christ was now at hand, it was necessary, according to the prophecies of the prophets, that they be deprived of their own leaders, lest they expect anything further beyond Christ. Under this Herod, in the thirty-third year of his reign, Christ was born, in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. But I will not touch on the things contained in the Gospels and afterwards in the Acts of the Apostles, lest I diminish by a brief treatment the dignity of matters that deserve more; I shall pursue the rest. Herod reigned four years after the Lord's nativity; for the whole period of his rule was thirty-seven years. After him Archelaus, tetrarch, for nine years; Herod [Antipas] for twenty-four years. In the eighteenth year of this reign of his, the Lord was crucified, in the consulship of Fusius Geminus and Rubellius Geminus. From that time until the consul Stilicho there are 317 years. The Acts of the Apostles Luke published, down to the time when Paul was brought to Rome, under the reign of Nero, who, I will not say of kings, but of all men, and even of savage beasts, proved the most foul and worthy to be the first to begin persecution against the Christians; I do not know whether he was also the last to finish it. For it is the opinion of many that Antichrist himself is to come, and the matter itself would have prompted me to set out his vices more fully, had not this work been unsuited to such a vast field...

units.la: {b} expletus fit. jus operistam vasta ingredi:id tantum an-notasse contentus fuit, hunc per omnia foedissima & crudelissima eo processisse, ut matrem interficeret: post etiam Pythagorae{a} cuidam in modum solemnium cōjugiorum nuberet, inditumq; imperatori flammeum, dos & genialis thorus & faces nuptiales: cuncta denique quae vel in foeminis non sine verecundia cōspiciuntur, spectata. Reliqua vero ejus, incertum pigeat an pudeat magis differre. Hic primus Christianum nomen tollere aggressus est: quippe semper inimica virtutibus vitia sunt, & optimi quique ab improbis, quasi exprobrantes, aspiciuntur.
units.tr: {b} is completed. Nor would I enter upon the vast scope of this work; I was content merely to have noted this: that he went to every most foul and cruel length, to the point of killing his mother; afterwards he even married a certain Pythagoras in the manner of solemn weddings, the bridal veil was put on the emperor, and a dowry, a marriage bed and wedding torches were displayed; in short, all those things which in women are not seen without shame were exhibited. As for the rest of his conduct, it is uncertain whether one should be more reluctant or more ashamed to relate it. He was the first to set about destroying the Christian name; for vices are always hostile to virtues, and the best men are looked at by the wicked as if they were reproaching them.

units.la: Namque eo tempore divina apud urbem religio invaluerat, Petro ibi episcopatum gerente: & Paulo, postea quam ab iniusto praesulis{b} iudicio Caesarem appellaverat, Romam deducto ad quem tum audien-dum plures conveniebant, qui veritate intellecta, virtutibusque apostolorum, quas tum crebro ediderant, permoti, ad cultum Dei sese conferebant. Etenim tum illustris illa adversus Simonem Petri ac Pauli congressio fuit. Qui cum magicis artibus, ut se Deum probaret, duobus suffultus{a} dæmonibus evolasset, orationibus apostolorum fugatis dæmo-nibus, delapsus in terram, populo inspe-ctate, diruptus est. Interea abundate jam Christianorum multitudine, accidit ut Roma incendio conflagraret, Neronea-pud Antiu constituto. Sed opinio omni-um invidiam incedii in principem retor-quebat, credebaturq; imperator gloriam innovandæ urbis quæsisse. Neque ulla re Nero efficiebat, quin ab eo jussum incen-dium putaretur. Igitur vertit invidiam in Christianos, actaeque in innoxios crude-lissimæ quæstiones: quin & novæ mortes excogitatæ, ut ferarum tergis contecti, la-niatu canum interirent. Multi crucibus affixi, aut flamma usti. Pleriq; in id reser-ati, ut cum defecifler dies, in usum no-curni luminis urerentur. Hoc initio in Christianos sæviri coeptum. Posteriam {b}datis legibus religio vetabatur: palamq; edistis propositis, Christianum esse non licebat. Tum Paulus ac Petrus capitis damnati: quorum uni cervix gladio de-secta, Petrus in crucem sublatus est. Dum hæc Romæ geruntur, Iudæi, præsidis sui {c}Festi Flori injurias non ferentes, rebellare coeperunt. Adversus eos Vespasianus proconsulari imperio a Nerone missus multis gravibusq; praeliis devictos, coegit intra muros Hierosolymæ confugere. In-terim vero iam etiam sibi pro conscientia scelerū invisus, humanis rebus eximitur: incertum an ipse sibi mortem conscive-rit: certe corpus illius interemptum. Unde creditur, etiam si se gladio ipse transfixerit, curato vulnere ejus servatus, fecū-dum illud quod de eo scriptū est: Et plaga mortis ejus curata est, sub seculi fine mitredus, ut mysterium iniquitatis exerceat. Igitur post excessum Neronis, Galba imperium rapuit: mox Otho, Galba interfecto, occupavit. Tunc Vitellius {a}in Gallias, fretus exercitibus, quibus præerat, urbem ingressus, Othone interfecto, summam rerum usurpavit: quæ postea quam ad Ves-pasianum delata, licet malo exemplo, bono tamen affectu Reip. ab improbis vindicandæ, cum Hierosolymam obsideret, sumit imperium: &, ut mos est, diademate capiti impositō, ab exercitu Imperator consalutatus, Titum filium Cæsarem fecit. Eidem pars copiarum, & obsidendæ Hierosolymæ negotium datum. Vespa-
units.tr: For at that time the divine religion had flourished in the city, with Peter serving as bishop there; and Paul, after he had appealed to Caesar from the unjust judgment of the governor, had been brought to Rome, where many gathered to hear him at that time. Moved by the truth they understood and by the virtues of the apostles, which they had often displayed then, they turned to the worship of God. Indeed, that famous contest between Simon and Peter and Paul took place at that time. When Simon, relying on magic arts, tried to prove that he was God, and had flown up supported by two demons, the demons were put to flight by the prayers of the apostles; he fell to the ground and was shattered, in the sight of the people. Meanwhile, since the multitude of Christians had now greatly increased, it happened that Rome was destroyed by fire, a fire that broke out in Nero's gardens at Antium. But the general opinion turned the odium of the fire onto the emperor, and it was believed that the emperor had sought the glory of rebuilding the city. Nor did Nero do anything to prevent it from being thought that the fire had been ordered by him. So he turned the odium onto the Christians, and most cruel tortures were inflicted on innocent people; indeed new kinds of death were devised, so that they perished covered in the hides of wild beasts, torn by dogs. Many were fastened to crosses or burned with fire. Many were set aside so that, when the daylight had failed, they might be burned to serve as nocturnal lamps. From this beginning the persecution of the Christians was started. Afterwards the religion was forbidden by published laws, and when edicts were posted openly, it was not lawful to be a Christian. Then Paul and Peter were condemned to death: Paul's neck was cut with a sword, and Peter was raised upon a cross. While these things were happening at Rome, the Jews, not bearing the wrongs of their governor Festus and of Florus, began to rebel. Against them Vespasian, sent by Nero with proconsular power, defeated them in many severe battles and forced them to take refuge within the walls of Jerusalem. Meanwhile Nero, already hated by his own conscience for his crimes, was removed from human affairs; it is uncertain whether he himself procured his death, though his body was certainly found slain. Hence it is believed that, even though he had stabbed himself with a sword, he was kept alive after his wound was healed, in accordance with what is written of him: "and his deadly wound was healed," and that he is to be sent back at the end of the age to carry out the mystery of iniquity. So after Nero's death, Galba seized the empire; soon afterwards Otho, having killed Galba, took possession of it. Then Vitellius, relying on the armies he commanded in Gaul, entered the city, killed Otho and seized supreme power. When this was reported to Vespasian, though it was set by a bad example, yet with good intent for the public good, to punish the wicked, he assumed the empire while he was besieging Jerusalem; and, as is the custom, a diadem being placed on his head, he was saluted as emperor by the army, and he made his son Titus Caesar. A part of the forces and the task of besieging Jerusalem were also given to him. Vespasian...

units.la: {a} a ex Gallis Sig. sianus[?] Romam profectus summo favore senatus & populi receptus, cum se Vitelli-us interfecisset, imperium confirmavit. In terea[?] Iudæi obsidione clausi, quia nulla neq; pacis neq; deditionis copia dabatur, ad extremum fame interibat, passimq; viæ oppleri cadaveribus coepere, victo jam officio humanditi[?] quin omnia nefanda in- super ausi, ne humanis quidem corporibus pepercerunt, nisi quæ ejusmodi alimentis tabes præripuerat. Igitur defesis defensoribus irrupere Romani. Actum forte in die Paschæ omnis ex agris aliisq; Iudææ opidis multitudo convenerat, nisi & Orosi- mirum ita Deo placitum, ut eo tempore, qu[illegible, ~6 letters]um cruci affixerat, gens impia in[illegible, ~6 letters]ni daretur. Pharisæi aliquanti-ꝓ templo acerrime restiterunt: do-nec obstinatis ad mortem animis, ultro se subjectis ignibus intulerunt. Numerus peremptorum ad undecies centena millia refertur: capta vero C millia ac venunda-ta. Fertur Titus adhibito consilio prius deliberasse, an templum tanti operis everteret. Etenim nonnullis videbatur, ædem sacratam, ultra omnia mortalia illustrem, non debere deleri: quæ servata modestiæ Romanæ testimonium, diruta per- ennem crudelitatis notam præberet. At contra alii & Titus ipse, evertendu tem-plum inprimis censebant, quo plenius Iudæorum & Christianorum religio tollere-tur. Quippe has religiones, licet contra-rias sibi, iisdem tamen auctoribus prose- stas. Christianos ex Iudæis exstitisse radice sublata, stirpem facile perituram. Ita Dei nutu, accensis omnium animis, templum dirutum, abhinc annos trecentos triginta & unum. Atque hæc ultima templi eversio, & postrema Iudæorum captivitas, qua extorres patria, per orbem terrarum dis-persi cernuntur: quotidie mundo testi-monio sunt non ob aliud eos, quam ob illatas Christo impias manus, fusse puni-tos. nam sæpe alias cum propter peccata captivitatibus traderentur, nunquam ta-me ultra septuaginta annos servitutis poe-nam pependerunt. Interiecto deinde tem-pore, Domitianus, Vespasiani filius, perse-cutus est Christianos. Quo tempore lo-annem apostolum atq; euangelistam, in Pathmum insulam relegavit: ubi ille ar-canis sibi mysteriis revelatis, librum sacræ Apocalypsis (qui quidem plerisque aut stulte aut impie non recipitur) conscriptū edidit. Non multo deinde intervallo, tertia persecutio per Traianum fuit, qui cum tormentis & quaestionibus nihil in Christianis morte aut poena dignum reperiset, saeviri in eos ultra vetuit. Sub HADRIANO deinde Iudaei rebellare a voluerunt, Syriam ac Palaestinam diripere conati: missoq; exercitu subacti sunt. Qua tempestate Hadrianus existimans se Christianam fidem loci injuria perempturum, in templo ac loco Dominicae passionis daemonum simulacra constituit. Et quia Christiani ex Iudaeis potissimum putabantur (namque tum Hierosolymae non nisi ex circumcisione habebat ecclesia sacerdotem) militum cohortem custodias in perpetuum agitare jussit, quae Iudaeos omnes Hierosolymae aditu arceret. Quod quidem Christianae fidei proficiebat: quia tum pene omnes Christum De-um, sub legis observatione credebant. Nimirum id Domino ordinante dispositum, ut legis servitus a libertate fidei atq; ecclesiae tolleretur. Ita tum primum Marcus ex gentibus, apud Hierosolymam episcopus fuit. Quarta sub Hadriano persecutio numeratur, quam tamen po-ftea exerceri prohibuit: injustum esse pro-nūcians, ut quisquā sine crimine reus cō-stituerētur. Post Adrianum Antonino Pio imperante pax Ecclesiis fuit. Sub Aurelio deinde Antonini filio, persecutio quinta agitata. Ac tum primū intra Gallias mar-tyria visa[?], serius trans Alpes Dei religione suscepta. Sexta deinde, Severo imperante, Christianorum vexatio fuit. Quo tem-pore Leonidas, Origenis pater, sacrum in martyrio sanguinem fudit. Interjectis deinde annis viii & {b}xxx. pax Christia-nis fuit: nisi quod medio tempore, Ma-ximinus nonnullarum Ecclesiarum cleri-cos vexavit. Mox, Decio imperante, jam septima persecutione sævitum in Christianos. Inde Valerianus octavus sanctorum hostis fuit. Post eum, interje-ctis annis fere quinquaginta, Diocletiano & Maximiano imperantibus, acerbissima persecutio exorta, quæ per x. continuos annos plebem Dei depopulata est. qua tempestate omnis fere sacro martyrum cruore orbis infectus est: quippe certatim gloriosa in certamina ruebatur, multo-que avidius martyria gloriosis mortibus quæres quærebatur, quam nunc episcopatus pra-visambitionibus appetuntur. Nullis unquam magis bellis mundus exustus[?] est: neq; majore unquam triumpho vicimus, quam cum decem annorum flagibus vin-ci non potuimus. Exstant etiam mandatæ literis præclaræ ejus temporis martyrum passiones: quas connectendas non putavi, ne modum operis excederem. Sed finis persecutionis illius fuit, abhinc annos ix & Lxxx. a quo tempore Christiani imperatores esse coeperunt. Namque tum CONSTANTINUS rerum potiebatur, qui primus omnium Romanorum principum Christianus fuit. Sane tum 307. LICINIUS, quia adversus CONSTANTINUM de imperio certavit, milites suos litare præceperat: abnuentes, militia rejiciebat. Sed id inter persecutiones non computatur: adeo res levioris negotii fuit, quam ut ad Ecclesiarum vulnera perveniret. Exinde tranquillis rebus pace perfruimur, neque ulterius persecutione fore credimus, nisi cum quam sub fine jam se-culi Antichristus exercebit. Etenim sacris vocibus, decem plagis mundum afficien-dum pronunciatum est: ita cum jam ix fuerint, quæ luperest,ultima erit.Hoc te- porum tractu mirum est quantum inva- luerit religio Christiana. Tum siquidem Hierosolyma horrens ruinis, frequentis- simis ac magnificentissimis ecclesiis est adornata. Namq; Helena,mater principis Constantini,quæ Augusta cum filio con- regnabat, cum Hierosolymam agnoscere concupisceret, reperta ibi idola ac tem- pla protrivit: mox usa regni viribus, ba- silicam in loco Dominicæ passionis & re- surrectionis & ascensionis constituit, illud mirū, quod locus ille,in quo postre- mum initiierant divina vestigia, cum in cœlum Dominus nube sublatus est, con- tinuari pavimeto cum reliqua stratorum parte non potuit. Siquidem quæcunque applicabantur, insolens humana suscipe- re terra respueret, excusis in ora appo- nentium sæpe marmoribus: quinetiam calcati Deo pulveris adeo perenne docu- mentum est, ut vestigia impressa cernan- cerratim Domino calcata diripiat, dam- num tamen arena non sentiat: & eadem adhuc sui speciem, velut impressis signa- ta vestigiis,terra custodit. Ejusdem reginæ beneficio crux Domini tum reperta: quæ neq; in principio obstitentibus ludę-is potuerat consecrari, & poltea dirutæ civitatis opprella ruderibus, non nisi tam fideliter requirenti meruit ostendi. Igitur Helena primum de loco passionis certior facta, admota militari manu, atq; omnium provincialium multitudine in studia re-ginæ certantium, effodi terram, & conti- gua quæq; ac vastissima ruinarum purgari jubet: mox pretium fidei & laboris tres pariter cruces, sic ut olim Domino ac la- tronibus duobus fixæ fuerant, reperiun-tur. Hic vero major dignoscendi patibuli, in quo Dominus pependerat, difficultas omnium animos mentesque turbaverat, ne errore mortalium forsitan pro cruce Domini latronis patibulum consecra-rent. Capiunt deinde consilium, ut ali-quem recens mortuum crucibus admo-verent. Nec mora, quasi Dei nutu{a} funeris extincti solemnibus exequiis deferebatur concursuq; omnium ferretro corpus eripitur. Duabus prius frustra crucibus admotis, ubi Christi patibulo attactum est, dictu mirabile, trepidantibus cunctis {b}funus excussum, & inter spectatores
units.tr: {a} From the Gauls he set out for Rome, where he was received with the highest favour of the senate and people. When Vitellius had killed himself, he confirmed his power. Meanwhile the Jews, shut in by the siege, since no hope of peace or surrender was offered, were perishing at last from famine. Corpses began to lie scattered along the roads, and once all sense of humanity was gone they dared every unspeakable deed and spared not even human bodies, except those which the wasting disease had snatched away from such food. So, the defenders being worn out, the Romans broke in. It happened by chance on the day of the Passover that a vast crowd had gathered from the fields and the other towns of Judaea, unless it was God's will, a marvellous thing, that at the very time when they had nailed Jesus to the cross, that impious nation should be given up to destruction. Some Pharisees resisted most fiercely in the temple, until, with their minds set on death, they threw themselves into the flames of their own accord. The number of those destroyed is reported as eleven hundred thousand, and seventy thousand were taken captive and sold. It is said that Titus, having taken counsel, first deliberated whether he should overthrow a temple of such great workmanship. For some thought that a sacred shrine, renowned beyond all mortal things, ought not to be destroyed, since if it were preserved it would bear witness to Roman moderation, but if overthrown it would bring a lasting mark of cruelty. But others, and Titus himself, held that the temple above all should be overthrown, so that the religion of the Jews and of the Christians might be abolished more completely. For these religions, though opposed to each other, nonetheless had sprung from the same authors: the Christians had come forth from the Jews, and once the root was cut away the stock would easily perish. So by God's will, with the minds of all inflamed, the temple was thrown down three hundred and thirty-one years ago. And this final overthrow of the temple and the last captivity of the Jews, by which they were driven from their homeland and are seen scattered throughout the earth, are daily a witness to the world that they were punished for no other reason than the impious hands laid upon Christ. For often before, when on account of their sins they were handed over to captivities, they never endured the penalty of slavery for more than seventy years. Then, after an interval of time, Domitian, son of Vespasian, persecuted the Christians. In his time he banished the apostle and evangelist John to the island of Patmos, where he, with mysteries revealed to him, wrote the book of the sacred Apocalypse (which indeed is by many either foolishly or impiously not received). Not long after, a third persecution occurred under Trajan, who, when he had found nothing deserving death or punishment in the Christians, even after torments and interrogations, forbade that they be harassed further. Under Hadrian the Jews then wished to rebel, attempting to plunder Syria and Palestine, but an army was sent and they were subdued. At that time Hadrian, supposing that he would destroy the Christian faith by disgracing the place, set up images of demons in the temple and in the place of the Lord's passion. And because the Christians were chiefly thought to be drawn from the Jews (for at that time the congregation at Jerusalem had no bishop except from the circumcision), he ordered a cohort of soldiers to keep watch perpetually, to keep all the Jews from access to Jerusalem. This indeed served the Christian faith, since at that time almost all believed that Christ was God, under observance of the law. Surely the Lord ordained this, so that the bondage of the law might be taken away from the liberty of faith and of the Church. Thus at that time Mark, from the Gentiles, became the first bishop at Jerusalem. The fourth persecution under Hadrian is counted, which nevertheless he afterwards forbade to be carried on, declaring it unjust that anyone be made a defendant who was without crime. After Hadrian, under Antoninus Pius, there was peace for the Churches. Then under Aurelius, son of Antoninus, a fifth persecution was stirred up; and then for the first time martyrdoms were seen within the Gauls, and later beyond the Alps the religion of God was received. Next, under Severus, there was a sixth persecution of the Christians. In that time Leonidas, the father of Origen, shed his holy blood in martyrdom. Then after an interval of thirty-eight years there was peace for the Christians, except that in the meantime Maximinus harassed the clergy of some Churches. Soon after, under Decius, the seventh persecution raged against the Christians. Then Valerian was the eighth enemy of the saints. After him, after an interval of about fifty years, under Diocletian and Maximian, a most bitter persecution arose, which for ten continuous years laid waste the people of God. In that season almost the whole world was stained with the holy blood of the martyrs; for men rushed eagerly into glorious contests, and martyrdoms were sought with greater zeal through glorious deaths than bishoprics are now sought through the ambitions of the proud. Never was the world burned by more wars, nor did we ever win a greater triumph than when we could not be conquered by ten years of scourges. There also survive excellent accounts, committed to writing, of the martyrs of that time, which I have not thought fit to connect, lest I exceed the bounds of my work. But the end of that persecution came eighty-nine years ago, from which time Christian emperors began to reign. For then Constantine held power, who was the first of all the Roman princes to be a Christian. Indeed at that time, in the year 307, Licinius, because he contended for the empire against Constantine, had commanded his soldiers to offer sacrifice; those who refused were dismissed from the army. But this is not counted among the persecutions, so trivial a matter was it, not reaching the wounds of the Churches. From then on we enjoy tranquil times in peace, and we believe there will be no further persecution, except that which Antichrist will wage near the end of the age. For by sacred words it has been declared that the world will be struck with ten plagues; since nine have already come, the one that remains will be the last. In the course of these times it is remarkable how greatly the Christian religion has grown. For then Jerusalem, once bristling with ruins, was adorned with very many magnificent churches. For Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine, who reigned as Augusta together with her son, when she desired to visit Jerusalem, found there idols and temples and trampled them down. Soon, using the resources of the kingdom, she set up a basilica at the place of the Lord's passion, resurrection and ascension. It is a marvel that the place where the divine footprints were last imprinted, when the Lord was taken up into heaven in a cloud, could not be paved over with the rest of the paved area. For whatever stones were laid there, the unyielding earth rejected them, the marble slabs often being thrust out at the edges of those laying them. Indeed the dust trodden by the Lord has become so lasting a witness that the imprinted footprints can still be seen, and the earth, as if sealed with the impressed marks, still keeps the image of his feet, though it is trodden by many, without the sand feeling any loss. Through the kindness of this queen the cross of the Lord was also found at that time; it could not be consecrated at the beginning because of the opposition of the Jews, and afterwards, buried under the rubble of the destroyed city, it was revealed only to one who sought it so faithfully. So Helena, first informed about the place of the passion, with a military force brought up and a crowd of all the provincials vying with one another in zeal for the queen, ordered the earth to be dug up, and the adjoining and most vast heaps of ruins to be cleared. Soon, as the reward of her faith and labour, three crosses alike were found, just as they had once been fixed, one for the Lord and two for the robbers. But here a greater difficulty in distinguishing the gibbet on which the Lord had hung troubled all minds and hearts, lest by the mistake of mortals they might perhaps consecrate the robber's gibbet instead of the Lord's cross. Then they took counsel to bring a recently dead man near the crosses. Without delay, as if by God's will, the body of a man who had just died was carried out with the solemn rites of the funeral, and the corpse was snatched from the bier by the crowd of all. Two crosses having first been applied to it in vain, when it was touched to the cross of Christ, wonderful to say, the corpse, all trembling, was shaken off and among its spectators

units.la: {a} a funus. suos aflitit: crux reperta, dignoque am-bitu consecrata.
units.tr: {a} The funeral. It struck down its own spectators; the cross was found and consecrated with a worthy circuit.

units.la: His per Helenam gestis, principe Christiano libertatem atque exemplum fidei mundus acceperat: sed longe atrocius periculum cunctis Ecclesiis illa pace genera-tum, namq; tum hæresis Arrii proru-pit, totumq; orbem invecto errore turba-verat. Etenim duobus Arriis, acerrimis perfidiæ hujus auctoribus, Imperator etiam depravatur: dūq; sibi religionis officium videtur implere, vim persecutionis exercuit: atque in exilium episcopi, servitum in clericos, animadversum in laicos, qui fe ab Arrianorum communione secreverant. Quæ autem Arriani prædicabant, erant hujusmodi: patrem Domini instituendi orbis causa genuisse filium: a eo pro potestate sui ex nihilo, in substantiam novam atque alteram, factum Dominum novum alterumque: fuisse autem tempus, quo filius non fuisset. Igitur hujus mali causa synodus apud Nicæam ex toto orbe contrahitur. CCC fi-quidē & duo de viginti episcopis cōgregatis, fides plena conscribitur: hæresis Arriana damnatur, Imperator decretū epi-scopale fcopale complectitur. Arriani nihil cōtra sanam fidem retractare ausi,fe quoq; tan- quam acquiescentes, nec aliud sentientes, Ecclesiis miscuerunt: manebat tamen in pectoribus eorum insitum in catholicos viros odiū: & adversus quos de fide disce- ptare non poterant, eos subornatis accu- satoribus, fictisq; criminibus appetebant. Itaque primum Athanasium Alexandriæ episcopum, juriscons[?]ultum, qui apud Nicænam synodum Diaconus adtuerat, aggrediuntur, absentemq; condemnant. Ɇtenim[?] ad crimina, quæ falsi testes congesserant, aggregabant, quod Marcellum atque Photinum, hæreticos sacerdotes, Synodi judicio condemnatos, pravo studio recepisset. Sed de Photino dubium non erat, merito fuisse damnatum: in Marcello nihil tum damnatione dignum repertum videbatur, maximeque ei studium partium innocentium accesserat, quod eosdem illos judices, a quibus fuerat condemnatus, hæreticos esse nemo dubitabat. Ceterum Arriani non hos potius, quam Athanasium, removere cupiebant. Itaque Imperatorem eo usque compellerunt, ut Athanasius exulatum ad Gallias mitteretur. Mox in Aegypto octogin-ta epilcopi congregati, Athanafiu injufte condemnatum efle pronunciant. Res ad Conftantinum refertur, jubet ex toto or-be apud Sardicam epilcopos congregari: atque omne judicium, quo Athanafius damnatus fuerat,retractari. Inter hæc Co-ftantinus moritur: fynodus congregata jā, Coftantino imperatore, Athanafiū ablo[?] uit[?]: Marcellus quoq; epilcopatui reddi-tur. Nam de Photino epilcopo Sirmienfi non eft refcifla fententia, quia etiam no-ftrorum judicio hæreticus probabatur. Et tamē hoc ipfum Marcellum gravabat, quia Photinus auditor ejus fuifle in ado-lescentia videbatur. Verumtamen ad Athanafii ablolutionem etiam illud accef-ferat, quod Ursatius & Valens, principes Arrianorum, cum poft fynodum Sardi-cenfem viderentur a communione fecre-ti, coram pofiti, a Iulio Romanæ urbis episcopo veniam popoícerunt, quod innoxium condemnaffent: meritoque cum fententia concilii Sardicenfis ablolutum profefsi funt. Interiecto deinde tempore Athanafius, cum Marcellum parum fanæ fidei effe penitus comperiflet, a communione suspendit[?].habuitq; ille hanc vere-cundiam, ut tanti viri judicio notatus, sponte concederet. Ceterum antea inno-cens, postea depravatus, videri poterat jam tum nocens fuisse, cum de eo fuerat judicatum. Nacti ergo Arriani istiusmodi occasionem, conspirant penitus, Sardi-censis synodi decreta subvertere. Etenim eis color quidam suppetere videbatur, quod tam iniuste fuisset pro Athanasio judicatum, quam Marcellus fuerat absolutus, qui nunc etiam Athanasii judicio haereticus esse probaretur. Namque Marcellus Sabellianæ haeresis assertor exstitit, Photinus vero novam haeresim jam ante protulerat, a Sabellio quidem in unione dissentiens, sed initium Christi ex Maria praedicabat. Igitur Arriani astuto consilio miscent innoxium criminosis, damnationemque Photini & Marcelli & Athanasii eadem sententia comprehenduntur: illud nimirum apud Imperatorum animos praestruentes, ut non putarentur de Athanasio perperam judicasse, qui de Marcello atque Photino vera sensissent. Verumtamen ea tempestate Arriani perfidiam suam occultabant, non ausi palam erroris sui dogmata prædicare, catholicos se gere-bant, nihil sibi prius agendum rati, quā ut Athanasium ecclesia submoverent, qui semper eis velut murus obstiterat: quo remoto, reliquos in libidinem suam cessuros sperabant. Sed pars episcoporum quæ Arrium sequebatur, damnationem Athanasii cupitam accepit: pars coacti metu & factione, in studia partium concesserant, pauci, quibus fides chara, & veritas potior erat, injustum judicium non receperunt: inter quos Paulinus, episcopus Treverorum, oblata sibi epistola ita subscripsisse traditur, se in Photini atque Marcelli damnationem præbere consensum, de Athanasio non probare. Tum vero Arriani, ubi doli mali processerant, vi agere decernunt. Nam quodlibet audere atque agere facile erat, regis amicitia subnixis, quæ sibi pravis adulationibus devinxerat. Quinetiam ex consensione multorum inexpugnabiles erant: nam omnes fere duarum Pannoniarum episcopi, multique Orientalium, ac tota Asia in perfidia eorum conjuraverant. Sed principes mali istius habebantur, a Sinciduno Vrsatius, Valens a Murscia, ab Heraclia Theodorus, Stephanus Antiochenus, Acatius a Caesarea, Meno-phanes Epheso, Georgius Laodicea, Nar-cissus {a}Neapoli. Hi ita Palatium occupa-verant, ut nihil fine eorum nutu ageret Imperator: obnoxius quidem omnibus, sed praecipue Valenti deditus. Nam eo tem-pore, quo apud {b}Morsam cotra Magnen-tium armis certatum, Constantius desce-dere in conspectum pugnae non ausus, in basilica martyrum extra opidum lita, Va-lente tum ejus loci episcopo in solatium assumpto, diversatus est. Ceterum Valens callide per suos disposuerat, ut quis prelii fuisset eventus, primus cognosceret: vel gratiam regis captans, si prior bonum nun-cium detulisset: vel vitae consulens, ante capturus fugiendi spacium, si quid con-tra accidisset. Itaque paucis, qui circa re-gem erant, metu trepidis, Imperatore an-xio, primus nunciat hostes fugere. Cum ille indicem ipsum intromisti posceret, Valens, ut reverentiam sui adderet, angelum sibi suisse nuncium respondit. Facilis ad credendum Imperator, palam postea dicere est solitus, le Valentis meritis, non virtute exercitus vicisse. Ab hoc initio illecti principis, extulere animos Arriani potestate regis usuri, ubi authoritate sua parũ valuissent. Igitur cum sententiam eorum, quam de Athanalio dederant, nostri non reciperent, edictum ab Imperatore propositur, ut qui in damnationem Athanasii non subscriberent, in exilium pellerentur. Ceterum a nostris tum apud relatem ac Buteras opida Galliarum, episcoporum concilia fuere. Petebatur, ut priusquam in Athanasium subscribere cogerentur, de fide potius disceptarent: nec tum demum de re cognoscendum, cum de persona judicium constitisset. Sed Valens sociiique ejus prius Athanasii damnationem extorquere cupiebant, de fide certare non ausi. Ab hoc partium conflictu agitur in exilium Paulinus. Interea Mediolanum convenitur, ubi tum adest Imperator, eadem illa contentio nihil invicem relaxabat. Tum Eusebius a Vercellensium, & Lucifer a Caralis Sardiniæ episcopi relegati, Cetera Dionysius Mediolanensium sacerdos, in Athanasii damnationem se consentire subscripsit, dummodo de fide inter episcopos quæreretur. Sed Valens & Vrsatius, ceterique, metu plebis, quæ Cathocatholicam fidem egregio studio conser-vabat, non aut piacula profiteri, intra palatium congregantur. Illinc epistolam sub Imperatoris nomine emittunt, omni pravitate refertam: eo nimirum consilio, ut si ea aequis auribus populus recepisset, publica authoritate cupita proferrent. Sin aliter fuisset excepta, omnis invidia esset in rege, & ipsa venialis: quia etiam tum catechumenus, sacramentum fidei meri to videretur potuisse nescire. Igitur le-ctam in Ecclesia epistolam, populus aver-satur. Dionysius, quia non esset alsenlus, urbe pellitur: statimque ejus in locum episcopus subrogatur. Liberius quoque urbis Romae, & Hilarius Pictavorum episcopus, dantur exilio. Rhodanium quoque, & Dofanum antistitem (qui natura lenior, non tam suis viribus, quam Hilarii societate non cesserat[?]). Arrianis eadem conditio implicuit: cum tamen homines parati eisent Athanasium a communione suspendere, modo ut de fide inter episcopos quaereretur. Sed Arrianis optimum visum, praestantissimos viros a certamine submovere. Ita pulsi in exilium, quos supra memoravimus, abhinc annos quinque & quadrin-ginta, Arbitrone & Lolliano consuli-bus, Sed Liberius paulo post urbi reddi-tur, ob ieditiones[?] Romanas. Ceterumexules latis cōstat totius orbis studiis ce-lebratos, pecuniaq; eis insumptum af-fatim congestas, legationibus quoq; cosplebis catholicae, ex omnibus fere pro-vinciis frequetatos. Interea Arriani nonocculte, ut antea, sed palam ac publice haeresis piacula praedicabant: quin etiam synodum Nicenam pro se interpretates, quam unius litera adjectione corrupe-rant, caliginem quandam injecerant ve-ritati. Nam ubi ὁμοούσιον[?] erat scriptū, quodunius est substantiae: illi ὁμοιούσιον[?], quod estsimilis substantiae, scriptum esse dicebat: coccedentes similitudinem, dum adime-rent unitatem: quia multum ab unitate similitudo distaret. ut, verbi gratia, pictu-ra humani corporis esset homini similis, nec tamen haberet hominis {b}veritatem. Sed quidam ex his ultra processerant, A-nomoeousiam, id est, dissimilem substantiam confirmantes. Eoque his certamini-bus processum, ut istiusmodi piaculis orbis terrarum implicaretur. nam Italiam, IllyriIllyricum, atque Orientem Valens & Vr-satius, caeterique quorum nomina edidimus, infecerant. Gallias nostras Saturni-nus Arelatensium episcopus, homo importunus potes & factiosus, premebat. Osium quoque ab Hispania in eandem perfidiam cō. cessisse opinio fuit: quod eo mirum atq; incredibile videtur, quia omni fere aetatis suae tempore constantissimus nostrarum partium, & Nicęna synodus aurore illo confecta habebatur: nisi fatiscente aevo (etenim major centenario fuit, ut sanctus Hilarius in epistolis refert) deliraverit. quibus rebus perturbato orbe terrarum, & morbo quodam Ecclesiis languentibus, segnior quidem, sed non minus gravis cura principem exercebat: quod licet Arriani, quibus favebat, superiores videntur, necdum tamen de fide inter Episcopos conveniret. Igitur apud Ariminum, urbem Italiae, synodum congregari jubet, idque Tauro praefecto imperat, ut collectos in unum non ante dimitteret, quam in unam fidem consentirent: promisso eidem consulatu, si rem effectui tradidisset. Ita missis per Illyricum, Italiam, Africa, Hispanias, Galliasq; magi[?]Afris officialibus, acciti{*} numerative qua{*} aut attingenti[?] & aliquanto amplius Occidens tales episcopi; Ariminum convenere: qui bus omnib. annonas & cellaria {b}dare Imperator praecoperat, (ed id nostris {c}, id est, Aquitanis, Gallis, ac Britannis, indecens vilium repudiatis fiscalibus, propriis item-[?]ptibus vivere maluerunt. Tres tantum ex Britania, inopia proprii, publico usi sunt, cum oblatam a ceteris collationem re-spuiscent sanctius putantes fiscum grava-re, quam singulos. Hoc ego Gavidium episcopum nostrum, quasi obtrectantem referre solitum audivi. sed longe aliter senserim laudiq; attribuo episcopis, tam-pauperes fuisse, ut nihil proprium habe-rent, neque ab aliis potius quam fisco fume-rent, ubi neminem gravabant,{d} ita in utri-que egregium exemplum. De reliquis nihil memoria dignum traditur. Sed re-deo ad ordinem. Postquam omneis, ut supra dictum, in unum collecti sunt, fit partium secessio. Ecclesiam nostri obtinent, Arriani{e} Edentum de industria va-catem[?], orationis loco capiunt; sed hi non amplius quam octoginta. Reliqui nostra-rum partium erant. Igitur frequentibus
units.tr: When these events had taken place through Helena, the world had received liberty and an example of faith from a Christian prince. But a far more dangerous peril, born of that peace, fell upon all the Churches, for then the heresy of Arius broke out and had thrown the whole world into confusion with its imported error. The Emperor himself was corrupted by two Arians, the most fierce authors of this treachery. While he thought he was discharging a duty of religion, he unleashed the violence of persecution: bishops were sent into exile, clergy were enslaved, and laymen who had separated themselves from the communion of the Arians were punished. The teachings the Arians proclaimed were of this kind: the Father begot the Son for the purpose of establishing the world; by his power he made a new and different Lord out of nothing, in a new and different substance; and there was a time when the Son did not exist. Therefore, to deal with this evil, a synod was called from the whole world at Nicaea. Three hundred and eighteen bishops came together, and a full statement of faith was drawn up. The Arian heresy was condemned, and the Emperor embraced the episcopal decree. The Arians, not daring to retract anything against sound faith, pretended to acquiesce and to hold no other view, and mixed themselves with the Churches. Yet the hatred they had planted in their hearts against the orthodox remained. Against those whom they could not contest on the matter of faith, they went after them with suborned accusers and invented charges. So first they attacked Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, a man learned in law, who had attended the Nicene synod as a deacon, and they condemned him in his absence. They added to the charges which false witnesses had gathered the accusation that he had, with a corrupt purpose, received Marcellus and Photinus, heretical bishops who had been condemned by the judgment of a synod. But concerning Photinus there was no doubt that he had been rightly condemned. In the case of Marcellus, nothing worthy of condemnation was then found, and he had gained much sympathy from the cause of the innocent, since no one doubted that those same judges by whom he had been condemned were heretics. Yet the Arians wished to remove not these men but Athanasius. So they drove the Emperor so far that Athanasius was sent into exile in Gaul. Soon afterwards, in Egypt, eighty bishops gathered and declared that Athanasius had been condemned unjustly. The matter was referred to Constantine, who ordered that bishops be assembled from the whole world at Sardica, and that the whole judgment by which Athanasius had been condemned be reviewed. In the meantime Constantine died. The synod, which had already been gathered under the Emperor Constantine, absolved Athanasius; Marcellus too was restored to his bishopric. For the sentence against Photinus, bishop of Sirmium, was not rescinded, since even by the judgment of our own people he was held to be a heretic. Yet this very fact weighed against Marcellus, because Photinus was thought to have been his pupil in youth. Nevertheless, to the absolution of Athanasius there was also added this circumstance: Ursacius and Valens, leaders of the Arians, who after the Sardican synod seemed to have separated themselves from communion, were brought before the bishop of Rome, Julius, and asked for pardon for having condemned an innocent man; and they rightly professed that he was absolved along with the sentence of the Sardican council. Then, after some time had passed, Athanasius, having discovered that Marcellus was of doubtful soundness in faith, suspended him from communion. Marcellus, however, showed such modesty that, once censured by the judgment of so great a man, he willingly yielded. But he who had been innocent before and was later corrupted could be seen to have been already guilty at the time he was judged. The Arians, therefore, seizing this kind of opportunity, conspired wholly to overturn the decrees of the Sardican synod. For a certain pretext seemed to be available to them: it had been as unjust to judge Athanasius as it had been to absolve Marcellus, who, even by the judgment of Athanasius, was held to be a heretic. For Marcellus was an advocate of the Sabellian heresy, while Photinus had already earlier put forward a new heresy: he differed from Sabellius on the union, but he taught that Christ began from Mary. So the Arians, by a crafty plan, mixed the innocent with the guilty, and the condemnation of Photinus, Marcellus and Athanasius was comprised under one sentence. Their aim, clearly, was to prepare the minds of the Emperors so that they would not think they had judged Athanasius wrongly, since he had held true views about Marcellus and Photinus. Yet in that period the Arians concealed their treachery. Not daring to proclaim the doctrines of their error openly, they called themselves Catholics, and they thought nothing should be done first except to remove Athanasius from the Church, who had always stood against them like a wall. With him removed, they hoped the rest would yield to their will. But the part of the bishops who followed Arius received the condemnation of Athanasius with delight; part, compelled by fear and faction, went over to the side of the parties; a few, to whom faith was dear and truth more precious, did not accept the unjust judgment. Among these Paulinus, bishop of Trier, is said to have subscribed, when a letter was put before him, to the condemnation of Photinus and Marcellus, but not to the condemnation of Athanasius. Then indeed the Arians, now that their wicked deceit had gone forward, resolved to act by force. For it was easy to dare and to do anything, supported by the friendship of the king, whom they had bound to themselves by wicked flattery. Moreover, through the agreement of many, they were invincible: almost all the bishops of the two Pannonias, many of the Eastern bishops, and the whole of Asia had conspired in their treachery. But the leaders of this evil were held to be: from Singidunum, Ursacius; from Mursa, Valens; from Heraclea, Theodorus; Stephen of Antioch; Acacius of Caesarea; Menophantus of Ephesus; Georgius of Laodicea; and Narcissus of Neapolis. These men so occupied the court that the Emperor did nothing without their nod. He was indeed compliant to all, but especially devoted to Valens. For at the time when the battle against Magnentius was fought at Mursa with arms, Constantius, not daring to go down into sight of the battle, stayed in the basilica of the martyrs outside the town, taking as his comfort Valens, then bishop of that place. Valens, meanwhile, had cleverly arranged through his own people that he would learn first of the outcome of the battle, so that either he might win the king's favour if he brought the good news first, or, if the opposite happened, he might look after his own life, since he would have time to flee before anyone else. So when a few men around the king, trembling with fear, and the Emperor, anxious, had been left in suspense, Valens first announced that the enemy were fleeing. When the Emperor demanded that the messenger himself be brought in, Valens, to add to his own authority, replied that an angel had been his messenger. The Emperor, easy to believe, afterwards used to say openly that he had conquered not by the courage of his army but by the merits of Valens. From the start of this flattery of the prince, the Arians, having been enticed, lifted up their spirits, intending to use the king's power, since their authority had counted for little on its own. Therefore, when our people did not accept the sentence they had passed concerning Athanasius, an edict was published by the Emperor that those who would not subscribe to the condemnation of Athanasius should be driven into exile. Meanwhile, among our people, councils of bishops were held at Reims and at Béziers, cities of Gaul. They asked that, before they were compelled to subscribe concerning Athanasius, they should first dispute about the faith, and that the matter of the person should not be taken up until a judgment on the faith had been settled. But Valens and his companions wished first to extort the condemnation of Athanasius, not daring to contend about the faith. From this conflict of parties Paulinus was driven into exile. Meanwhile, the bishops came together at Milan, where the Emperor was then present, and the same dispute yielded nothing on either side. Then Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, and Lucifer, bishop of Caralis in Sardinia, were relegated; Dionysius, bishop of Milan, subscribed, consenting to the condemnation of Athanasius, provided that the question of faith be investigated among the bishops. But Valens and Ursacius and the others, fearing the common people, who were preserving the Catholic faith with remarkable zeal, did not dare to profess their impieties openly, and they gathered within the palace. From there they sent out a letter under the Emperor's name, filled with every wickedness, plainly intending that, if the people received it with fair ears, they might bring forward what they desired with public authority; but if it were received otherwise, the whole odium would fall on the king, and even that would be pardonable, since the Emperor, still a catechumen, could rightly be thought not to know the sacrament of faith. So when the letter was read in the Church, the people turned away from it. Dionysius, because he did not assent, was driven out of the city, and at once another bishop was put in his place. Liberius of the city of Rome and Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, were also given over to exile; and Rhodanius, and Dosanus the bishop (who, gentler by nature, had yielded not so much from his own strength as from his association with Hilary). The same condition entangled the Arians, although these men were ready to suspend Athanasius from communion, provided only that the question of faith be investigated among the bishops. But it seemed best to the Arians to remove the most outstanding men from the struggle. Thus those whom we have mentioned were driven into exile, forty-five years ago, in the consulship of Arbitio and Lollianus. But Liberius was restored to the city shortly afterwards, on account of the Roman petitions. Moreover, it is established that the exiles were honoured with the zeal of the whole world, that money was heaped up for them in abundance, and that they were visited by embassies from almost every province of the Catholic people. Meanwhile the Arians no longer taught their heresy secretly, as before, but openly and publicly; and not only that, but by interpreting the Nicene synod in their own favour, they had corrupted it by adding a single letter, and so cast a certain darkness over the truth. For where the word homoousion [ὁμοούσιον] had been written, meaning of one substance, they said that homoiousion [ὁμοιούσιον] had been written, meaning of like substance; granting likeness while taking away unity, since likeness is far removed from unity. It is as if a painting of a human body were like a man but did not have the reality of a man. Some of them went further still, asserting anomoeousia, that is, unlike substance. Matters went so far in these contests that the whole world was entangled in such impieties. For Valens and Ursacius and the others whose names we have given had infected Italy, Illyricum and the East. Our Gallic provinces were pressed by Saturninus, bishop of Arles, a restless and factious man. It was also widely believed that Osius, from Spain, had gone over to the same treachery; this seems strange and incredible, since for almost the whole of his life he was the most steadfast of our party, and the Nicene synod was held to have been largely his work, unless, with his age failing (for he was more than a hundred years old, as St. Hilary reports in his letters), he had lost his wits. While the world was thrown into disorder by these things, and the Churches were languishing with a kind of sickness, the prince was troubled by a care that was slower, but no less serious. Although the Arians, whom he favoured, seemed to be on top, still the bishops had not come to agreement on the faith. Therefore he ordered a synod to be gathered at Ariminum, a city of Italy, and commanded the praetorian prefect Taurus that he should not dismiss those gathered together until they agreed on one faith, with the consulship promised to him if he brought the matter to a conclusion. So, with officials sent through Illyricum, Italy, Africa, the Spains and the Gauls, bishops were summoned to Ariminum, and from the West came as many as about four hundred, or somewhat more. The Emperor had arranged to give all of them provisions and allowances; but our men, that is, the Aquitanians, Gauls and Britons, rejecting the shameful gifts of the treasury, preferred to live on their own resources. Only three from Britain, being poor and having nothing of their own, made use of public support, since they rejected the contribution offered by the others, thinking it more honourable to burden the treasury than individuals. I have heard that our bishop Gavidius used to report this, as if he were disparaging them; but I think quite otherwise, and I attribute praise to those bishops who were so poor that they had nothing of their own, and took from others rather than from the treasury, where they burdened no one; thus in both cases there was an outstanding example. Nothing worthy of memory is handed down about the rest. But I return to the order of events. After all, as said above, had been gathered together into one place, a division of parties took place. Our men took possession of the church, while the Arians, having deliberately emptied a place, took up a position for prayer; but these were no more than eighty. The rest were of our party. Therefore, with many gatherings...

units.la: {b} Ariminum/Ariminensis: the printed word is dare, not dari. [?] conciliis nihil actum, nostris in fide ma-nentibus, illis de perfidia non cedentibus.
units.tr: {b} Ariminum/Ariminensis: the printed word is dare, not dari. [?] Nothing was accomplished at the councils: our side stood firm in the faith, while they would not give up their perfidy.

units.la: Ad postremum placuit, decem legatos mit-ti ad Imperatorem, ut quae eflet partium fides & sententia cognosceret, Iciretque pacem cum haereticis esse non posse. Idem Arriani faciunt, mittuntque numero pa-ri legatos, qui adversum nostros coram Imperatore confligerent. Ied[?] ex parte no-ftrorum leguntur homines adolescentes, parum docti & parum cauti: ab Arrianis autem missi, senes, callidi & ingenio va-lentes, veterno perfidiae imbuti, qui apud regem facile superiores exstiterunt. Sed nostris mandatum, ne quo modo cum Ar-rianis communionem inirent, omnia que integra Synodo reservarent. Interim in Oriente exemplo Occidentalium im-perator jubet cunctos fere episcopos a-pud Seleuciam Isauriae opidum cogrega-ri. Qua tempeftare Hilarius, quartum jam exilii annum in Phrygia agens, inter re-liquos episcopos, per vicarium ac praefi-dem data evectionis copia, adesse con-pellitur: cum tamen nihil de eo fpecia-liter mandaset imperator, judices tan-tum generalem jussionem fequuti, qua omomnes episcopos ad concilium cogere iubebantur, hunc quoq; inter reliquos{*} volentes{b} miscere, ut ego conjicio, Dei nutu ita gestum, ut vir divinarum rerum instructissimus, cum de fide dilceptadum erat, intereflet. Is ubi Seleucia venit, magno cum favore exceptus, omnium in fe animos & studia converterat, ac primum quaesitum ab eo, quae effet Gallorum fides; quiatum Arrianis prava de nobis vulgantibus, suspecti ab Orientalibus habeba-mur, trionymam solitarii Dei unionem fecundum Sabellium credidisse. Sed posita fide sua, juxta ea quae Niceae erant a patribus conscripta, Occidentalibus perhibuit testimonium. Itaque absolutis omnium animis, intra conscientiam commu-nionis, nec non etiam in societatem recce-ptus, concilioque ascitus est. Agi deinde coeptum: repertique pravae haeresis auctoꝛes, atque ab Ecclesiae corpore avulsi. In eo numero fuere, Georgius ab Alexan- dria, Acatius, Eudoxius, Vranius, Le- ontius, Theodosius, Evagrius, Theodo- lus. Sed confessa Synodo, decreta ad Im- peratorem legatio, quae gesta insinuaret. damnati quoque ad regem profecti, fa-tis tis freti sociorum viribus,& Principis fo-cietate. Interea legatos Ariminensis con- cilii ex parte nostrorum compellit Impe-rator, uniri hæreticorum communioni: eisdemque conscriptam ab improbis fidem tradit, verbis fallentibus involutam; quæ Catholicam disciplinam, perfidia latente, loqueretur. Namque Vsiæ verbum tanquam ambiguum & temere a patribus usurpatum, neq; ex authoritate Scripturarum profectum, sub specie falsæ rationis abolebat, ne unius cum patre substantiæ filius crederetur. Eadem fides similem patri filium fatebatur: sed interius aderat fraus parata, ut elset similis, non esset æqualis. Ita dimissis legatis, Præfecto mandatum, ut Synodum non ante laxaret, quàm conscriptæ fidei confetire se omnes subscriptionibus profitentur. Ac, si qui pertinacius obsisterent, dummodo is numerus intra quindecim elset, in exilium pellerentur. Sed regressis legatis, licet vim regiam deprecantibus, negata communio. Enimvero compertis quæ decreta erant, major rerum & consiliorum perturbatio: dein paulatim plerique nostrorum, partim imbecillitate tate ingenii,partim tædio peregrinationis evicti,dedere le adversarius, iam post redi-tum legatoru superioribus: & ecclesiam noltris inde detrusis obtinentibus.factaq; semel inclinatione animorum,catervatim in partem alteram concelsum : donec ad viginti ufq; nostrorum numerus immi-nutus est. Sed hi quanto pauciores,tanto validiores erant. conftantifsimulq; inter eos habebatur noster Fægadius & Ser-vatio Tungrorum episcopus. hos, quia minis & terriculis non celserant, Taurus precibus aggreditur,ac lachrymans obte-ratur, mitiora uti consulerent. Claulos intra unam urbem episcopos jam lepti-mum mensem agere: injuria hyemis & inopia confectis, nullam spem reversio-nis dari: quis tandem elset finis? feque. rentur plurium exemplum,auctoritatem saltem ex numero sumerent. Etenim ve-to Fægadius paratum fe exilio atque ad omne supplicium,in quod deposceretur, profiteri:fe ab Arrianis conceptam fidem non recepturum. Ita in hoc certamine aliquot dies tracti, ubi parum ad pacem{b} proficiebant, paulatim & ipse infractior, ad extremum propositá conditione evin-citur.
units.tr: At last it was agreed to send ten envoys to the Emperor, to learn what the faith and opinion of our side was, and to tell him that peace with heretics was not possible. The Arians did the same and sent an equal number of envoys to contend against ours before the Emperor. But on our side the envoys were young men, little learned and little cautious; the Arians' envoys were old, shrewd, strong in ability, and steeped in the dullness of perfidy, and they easily proved the superior before the king. Our men, however, had been ordered in no way to enter into communion with the Arians, and to keep everything whole and reserved for the Synod. Meanwhile in the East, following the example of the Western emperor, the emperor ordered almost all the bishops to be gathered at Seleucia, a town in Isauria. At that time Hilary, already in the fourth year of his exile in Phrygia, was compelled to attend among the other bishops, since the vicar and governor had been given the means of transport. The emperor had given no specific order about him; the judges followed only the general command, by which all bishops were to be summoned to the council, and they wished to mix him in with the rest too. I think that by God's will this was so arranged, so that the man most learned in divine things should be present when the faith was to be disputed. When he came to Seleucia he was received with great favour, and he turned the minds and eagerness of all towards himself. First they asked him what the faith of the Gauls was, since, because the Arians were spreading false reports about us, we were suspected by the Easterners, who believed that we held the threefold unity of a solitary God according to Sabellius. But, having set out his own faith in accordance with what the Fathers had written at Nicaea, he bore witness to the Westerners. So, with the minds of all set at rest, he was received into communion in conscience, and even into fellowship, and admitted to the council. Then they began to act, and the authors of the perverse heresy were found and torn from the body of the Church. Among them were George of Alexandria, Acacius, Eudoxius, Uranius, Leontius, Theodosius, Evagrius and Theodulus. The Synod having given its confession, a legation was sent to the Emperor to report what had been done. The condemned also went off to the king, trusting in the strength of their allies and the support of the Prince. Meanwhile the Emperor pressed the envoys of the Council of Ariminum, on the part of our side, to unite in communion with the heretics, and handed them a creed drawn up by wicked men, wrapped in deceptive words, which spoke the Catholic discipline while the perfidy lay hidden. For it did away, under the pretence of false reasoning, with the word *Usia*, as ambiguous and rashly used by the Fathers and not drawn from the authority of Scripture, lest the Son be believed to be of one substance with the Father. The same creed confessed the Son to be like the Father, but inwardly there was a prepared trick: that he should be like, not equal. So, the envoys having been dismissed, the governor was ordered not to dissolve the Synod until all had agreed by signature to the written faith, and if any resisted too stubbornly, they were to be driven into exile, provided that their number was within fifteen. But when the envoys returned, although they pleaded against the royal force, communion was refused. Indeed, once the decrees were known, there was a greater disturbance of affairs and counsels. Then gradually most of our men, partly overcome by weakness of mind, partly by weariness of their travels, yielded to the adversary, now that the envoys had returned to their former position, and the Arians, our men having been thrust out, held the church. Once the minds had been inclined, they went over in troops to the other side, until our number was reduced to about twenty. But these, the fewer they were, the stronger they were. The most steadfast among them was our Faegadius, and Servatius, bishop of the Tungri. Because these had not yielded to threats and frights, Taurus approached them with entreaties, and, weeping, begged them to consider milder courses. The bishops had now spent a seventh month shut up in one city, worn down by the hardship of winter and want, with no hope of return being given; what end would there be? They should follow the example of the many, and at least take authority from the numbers. Faegadius, however, replied that he was prepared for exile and for any punishment to which he might be condemned, but that he would not accept the faith drawn up by the Arians. So, dragged through several days in this struggle, when they made little progress toward peace, Faegadius himself, gradually weakened, was at last overcome by the condition proposed.
