units.la: {b} proficicitur. Namque Valens & Vrsatius affir-mantes praesentem fidem Catholica ratione conceptam, ab Orientalibus, Imperatore auctore, prolatam, cum piaculo repu-diari,{a} ut quis dissidiarum finis foret, si quae Orientalibus placuisset[?], Occidentalibus displicerer? oltremo[?] si quid minus plene praesenti fide editum videretur, ipsi adderent, quae addenda putarent praebituros(e[?], in his quae essent adiecta, confessum. Favorabilis professio pronis omnium animis excepta: nec ultra nostri repugna-re ausi, jam quoque modo finem rebus imponere cupientes.
units.tr: {b} ... For Valens and Ursacius, asserting that the present faith, framed on Catholic reasoning, had been put forward by the Easterners on the Emperor's authority, said that it was sacrilege to reject it. What end of disputes would there be, they asked, if what pleased the Easterners was displeasing to the Westerners? Finally, if anything seemed less than fully expressed in the present faith, they themselves would add whatever they thought should be added, and they would consent to whatever was added.

units.la: Dein conceptae a Faegadio & Servatione professiones, edi[?] coepere: in quis primum damnatur Arri-us, totaq; ejus perfidia: ceterum[?] non etiam patri aequalis,{b} & sine initio, sine tempore Dei filius pronunciatur. Tum Va-lens tanquam[?] nostros adjuvans, subjecit sententiam, cui inerat occultus dolus: filium Dei non esse creaturam sicut ceteras creaturas, fefellitque audientes fraus professionis. Etenim his verbis, quibus similis esse ceteris creaturis filius negaba-tur, creatura tamen, potior tantum ceteris, pronunciabatur. Ita neutra pars vi-cisse cisse fe penitus, aut vi&am putare poterat: quia fides ipsa pro Arrianis, profesiones vero postea adje&ç pro nostris erant: prae-ter illam quam Valens subjunxerat, quae-rum non intellecta, sero demum animad-versa est. Hoc vero modo concilium di-missum, bono initio, foedo exitu est con-summatum. Igitur Arriani rebus nimium prospere & secundum vota fluentibus, Constantinopolim ad Imperatorem con-currunt: ibi repertos Seleucienis synodi legatos, vi regia compellunt, exemplo Occidentalium, pravam illam fidem reci-pere. Pleriq; abnuentes injuriola custodia ac fame vexati, captivam conscientiam de-dere. Multi constantius renitentes, adem-pto episcoparu, in exilium detrusi, atque in eorum locum alii dati. Ita optimis sa-cerdotibus aut metu territis, aut exilio deductis, perfidiae paucorum cunc̈ti con-cesserant. Aderat ibi tum Hilarius, a Se-leucia legatos secutus, nullis certis de se mandatis operiens Imperatoris voluntā-tem, si forsitā redire ad exilium juberetur. Is ubi extremum si lei[?] periculum animad-vertit, Occidentalibus deceptis, Orienta-les per scelus vinci tribus libellis publice datis audientia[?] in regis poposcit,ut de fide coram adversariis dilceptaret. Id vero Arriani maximopere abnuere. Postremo quasi discordiæ feminariù & perturbator Orientis, redire ad Gallias iubetur, abíq; exilii indulgentia. Verum ubi permensus est orbem pene terrarum malo perfidiæ infectum, dubius animi & magna curarum molæstuans, cum plerisque videretur non incundam cum his communionem, qui Ariminensem synodum receperunt, optimum factu arbitratus revocare cunctos ad emendationem & pœnitentiam frequentibus intra Gallias conci-liis,atque omnibus fere episcopis de errore profitentibus, apud Ariminum gesta condemnant, & in statum pristinum Ecclesiarum fidem reformant. Resistebat sanis consiliis Saturninus Arelatensium episcopus, vir sane pefsimus, & ingenio malo pravoq;. Verum etiam præter hæresis infamiam, multis atq;infandis criminibus convictus, Ecclesia ejectus est. Ita partium vires amisso duce infractæ. Paternus etiam a Petrocoris æque vecors, nec detrectans perfidiam profiteri, sacerdotio pulsus: ceteris venia data. Illud apud omnes constitit,unius Hilarii bene-ficio Gallias nostras piaculo hæresis libe-ratas. Ceterum Lucifer tum Antiochiæ longe diversa sententia fuit. Nam intantū eos qui Arimini fuerant condemnavit,ut se etiam ab eorum communione secreve-rit,qui eos sub satisfactione,vel pœniten-tia recepissent.Id recte, an perperā consti-tuerit,dicere non ausi[?]m. Paulinus & Rho-danius in Phrygia defuncti. Hilarius sexto anno postquam redierat in patria obiit.
units.tr: Then the professions drawn up by Faegadius and Servatius began to be published. In these, first Arius is condemned, with his whole perfidy; and the Son of God is pronounced equal to the Father, without beginning and without time. Then Valens, as if helping our side, appended a sentence in which lay a hidden trick: that the Son of God is not a creature as the other creatures are. The trick in the profession deceived the hearers, for by these words, by which the Son was denied to be like the other creatures, he was nonetheless pronounced a creature, only more excellent than the rest. So neither side could think that it had wholly won or been defeated: the faith itself was on the Arians' side, while the professions added afterwards were on ours, except for that which Valens had appended, whose meaning was not understood and was noticed only late. In this way the council was dismissed with a good beginning and concluded with a shameful end. Therefore the Arians, with their affairs flowing too prosperously and according to their wishes, ran together to the Emperor at Constantinople. There they found the envoys of the Synod of Seleucia and, by royal force, compelled them to accept that perverse faith after the example of the Westerners. Many refused, and, harassed by unjust imprisonment and hunger, surrendered their captive conscience. Many who resisted firmly were deprived of their bishoprics, thrust into exile, and others were put in their place. Thus the best priests, either terrified by fear or led away into exile, had all yielded to the perfidy of a few. Hilary was there at that time, having followed the envoys from Seleucia, awaiting the Emperor's will without any definite instructions about himself, in case he might perhaps be ordered back into exile. When he saw the final danger, since the Westerners had been deceived and the Easterners were being beaten by wickedness, he presented three pamphlets publicly and asked for a hearing before the king, so that he might dispute about the faith in the presence of his adversaries. But the Arians strongly refused this. At last, as a sower of discord and a disturber of the East, he was ordered back to Gaul, without any indulgence of exile. But when he had travelled through almost the whole world infected by the evil of perfidy, anxious in mind and troubled by great cares, and since most people seemed to think communion with those who had accepted the Synod of Ariminum unwelcome, he judged it best to recall all to amendment and repentance by frequent councils within Gaul. With almost all the bishops confessing their error, they condemned at Arles what had been done at Ariminum and restored the faith of the Churches to its former state. Saturninus, bishop of the Arelatenses, resisted these sound counsels; he was a truly wicked man, of a malign and perverse nature. But, convicted of many unspeakable crimes besides the infamy of heresy, he was cast out of the Church. Thus the strength of their party, its leader lost, was broken. Paternus also, from Périgueux, equally mad and not refusing to profess perfidy, was driven from his priesthood, while pardon was granted to the rest. It was agreed by all that our Gaul was freed from the stain of heresy by the good offices of Hilary alone. Lucifer, however, at Antioch then held a quite different opinion. For he condemned those who had been at Ariminum so far that he even separated himself from the communion of those who had received them under satisfaction or repentance. Whether he settled this rightly or wrongly I dare not say. Paulinus and Rhodanius died in Phrygia. Hilary died in the sixth year after he had returned to his homeland.

units.la: Sequuntur tempora ætatis nostræ gra-via & periculosa, quibus non usitato malo pollutæ ecclesiæ, & perturbata om-nia. Namque tum primum illa Gnosti-corum hæresis intra Hispanias deprehen-sa,superstitio exitiabilis arcanis occultata secretis. Origo istius mali oriens ab Ae-gyptiis. Sed quibus ibi initiis coaluerit, haud facile est disserere. Primus eam in-tra Hispanias Marcus intulit, Aegypto profectus, {a}Memphis orrus, hujus au-ditores fuere, Agape quædam non igno-bilis mulier, & rhetor Helpidius. Ab his Priscilliaonus[?] est institutus, familia nobilis, prædives opibus, acer, inquies, facundus, multa lectione eruditus, dis-ferendi
units.tr: Now come the times of our own age, grave and dangerous, when the Church has been defiled by an unusual plague and everything thrown into confusion. For then, for the first time, that heresy of the Gnostics was discovered within Spain, a deadly superstition concealed in secret mysteries. The origin of this evil lies in Egypt. By what beginnings it took hold there is not easy to explain. Marcus was the first to bring it into Spain. He had come from Egypt, a native of Memphis, and his hearers were a certain not undistinguished woman, Agape, and the rhetorician Helpidius. From these Priscillian was instructed. He came of a noble family, was very rich, keen, restless, eloquent, learned through wide reading, and most ready in speaking and disputing.

units.la: {a} aMemphi. ferendi ac disputandi promptissimus: felix profecto, si non pravo studio corrumpisset optimum ingenium, prorsus multa in eo animi & corporis bona cernere. vigilare multum, famem, sitim ferre poterat, habendi minime cupidus, utendi parcissimus. Sed idem vanissimus, & plus justo inflatior profanarum rerum scientia: quin & magicas artes ab adolescentia eum excercuisse creditum est. Is ubi doctrinam exitiabilem aggressus est, multos nobilium, plurosque populares authoritate persuadendi & arte blandiendi allicuit in societatem. Ad hoc mulieres novarum rerum cupidae, fluxa fide, & ad omnia curioso ingenio, catervatim ad eum confluebant. Quippe humilitatis speciem ore & habitu praetendens, honorem sui & reverentiam cunctis iniecerat. Iamque paulatim perfidiae illius tabes, pleraque Hispaniae pervaserat: quin & nonnulli episcoporum depravati, inter quos Instanti-us & Salvianus, Priscillianum non solum consensione, sed sub quadam etiam conjuratione susceperant. Quo a A-dyginus episcopus Cordubensis ex vici-no agens comperto, ad Idacium b emeritae…
units.tr: (Memphis, as corrected.) ...ready in speaking and disputing. He would have been fortunate indeed, had he not corrupted his excellent talent by a wicked zeal, for one could see in him many gifts of mind and body. He could keep vigil for long, and bear hunger and thirst. He had no desire for wealth and was most sparing in his use of it. But he was also very vain, and too puffed up with his knowledge of secular learning. Indeed, it is believed that from his youth he had practised magic arts. When he set about this deadly teaching, he drew into his fellowship many of the nobles and more of the common people, by his authority in persuading and his skill in flattering. Women eager for novelties, of fickle faith and curious minds for everything, flocked to him in crowds. For, putting on a show of humility in his face and dress, he had won the respect and reverence of all. And now the rot of that treachery had gradually spread through most of Spain. Indeed, some of the bishops had been corrupted, among them Instantius and Salvianus, who had received Priscillian not only with agreement but with a kind of conspiracy. When Hyginus, bishop of Cordoba, who lived nearby, learned of this, he reported it to Idacius, an elderly priest of...

units.la: b Emer. ... {a}ætatis sacerdote refert. Is vero sine mo-do, & ultra quam oportuit Instantiu foci, ofq; ejus lacessens, facem quandam nascē-[?]ti incendio subdidit: ut exasperaverit ma-los potius, quam compresserit. Igitur post multa inter eos, & digna memoratu cer-tamina, apud Cæsaraugustam synodus congregatur: cui tum etiam Aquitani e-piscopi interfuere. Verum hæretici com-mittere se judicio non ausi, in absentes tum lata sententia, damnatique Instantius {b}episcopus Salvianus, Helpidius & Prif-cillianus laici. Additum etiam, ut si quis damnatos in communionem recepisset, sciret in se eandem sententiam promendam. Atq; id Ithacio Soffubenfi episcopo negotium datum, ut decretum episcoporum in omnium notitiam deferret, maxi-me{c}que Iginum extra communionem faceret: qui cum primum omnium insectari palam hæreticos coepisset, postea turpiter depravatus, in communionem eos recepisset. Interim Instantius & Salvianus damnati judicio sacerdotum, Prifcillianum etiam laicum, sed principem malorum omnium, una cum Cæsaraugustana synodo notatum, ad
units.tr: b Emeritae... of advanced age, a priest, reports it. He, however, acted without moderation, and beyond what was proper, attacking Instantius and his supporters, and so he added a spark to a fire just beginning, and exasperated the evils rather than checking them. So after many contests between them, worthy of record, a synod was assembled at Caesaraugusta, to which the bishops of Aquitaine also came. But the heretics did not dare to submit themselves to judgment, and sentence was passed in their absence: Instantius, bishop, and Salvianus, Helpidius and Priscillian, laymen, were condemned. It was added that if anyone had received the condemned into communion, he should know that the same sentence would be pronounced against himself. This task was given to Ithacius, bishop of Sossuba, to bring the decree of the bishops to everyone's notice, and above all to put Hyginus outside communion. He, who had first begun to attack the heretics openly, was afterwards shamefully corrupted and had received them into communion. Meanwhile Instantius and Salvianus, condemned by the judgment of the priests, together with Priscillian, a layman but the leader of all the evils, who was also noted by the synod of Caesaraugusta, ...

units.la: {c} Hygin. [?] ad confirmandas vires suas episcopum in Labilensi opido constituunt: rati nimi-{a}rum, si hominem acrem & callidū sacer-dotali auctoritate armassent, tutiores fore sese. Tum vero Idacius atq; Ithacius acrius instare, arbitrantes posse inter initia malū comprimi: sed parum sanis consiliis, secu-lares judices adeunt, ut eorum decretis atq; executionibus hæretici urbibus pel-lerentur. Igitur post multa & fœda, Idacio supplicante, elicitur a Gratiano tum imperatore rescriptum, quo universi hæretici excedere non ecclesiis tantum aut urbibus, sed extra omnes terras propelli ju-bebantur. Quo comperto, Gnostici diffisi rebus suis, non ausi judicio certare, spon-te cessere, qui episcopi videbantur: cæte-ros metus dispersit. At tum Instantius, Salvianus & Priscillianus Romā profecti, ut apud Damasum urbis ea tempestate episcopum objecta purgarent. Sed iter eis præter interiorem Aquitaniam fuit: ubi tum ab imperitis magnifice suscepti, sparsere perfidiæ semina{b}, maximeq; Elufanam[?] plebem, sane tum bonam & religi-oni studentem, pravis prædicationib. per-vertere. a Burdigala per Delphinum res pulsi, tamen in agro Euchrociæ aliquantisper morati, infecere nonnullos suis erroribus. Inde iter coeptum ingressi, turpi sane pudibundoq; comitatu, cum uxoribus atq; alienis etiam fœminis, in quis erat{a} Eu-chrocia, ac filia ejus Procula: de qua fuit in sermone hominum, Priscilliani stupro gravidam, partum sibi graminibus abegisse. Hi ubi Romam pervenere, Damaso le purgare cupientes, ne in conspectum quidem ejus admissi sunt. Regressi Mediolanum, æque aversantem sibi Ambrosiū repererunt. Tum vertere consilia, ut quia duobus episcopis, quorum ea tempestate summa authoritas erat, non illuserant, largiendo & ambiendo ab imperatore cupita extorquerent. ita corrupto Macedo-nio, {b}cum magistro officiorum, referi-ptum eliciunt, quo calcaris quæ prius decreta erant, restitui ecclesiis jubebantur. Hoc freti Iustantius & Priscillianus, repetivere Hispanias. Nam Salvianus in urbe obierat: ac tum sine ullo certamine ecclesias, quibus præfuerant, recepere. Ve-rū{c} Trachio ad resistendum non animus, sed facultas defuit: quia hæretici corrupto Volventio proconsule, vires suas confir-maverant, maverat.Quin etiam Ithacius,ab his quasi perturbator ecclesiarum reus postulatus, juflufq; per atrocem executionem dedu- ci, trepidus profugit ad Gallias: ibi Gre- gorium praefectum adiit. Qui compertis quae gesta erant, rapi ad se turbarum au[?]thores jubet,ac de omnibus ad imperato- re refert ut haereticis viam ambiendi prae- cluderet. Sed id frustra fuit:quia per libi- dinem & potentiam paucorum, cuncta ibi venalia erant. Igitur haeretici suis artibus grandi pecunia Macedonio data,obtinuer, ut imperiali auctoritate praefecto erepta cognitio,Hispaniarum vicario. Nam jam proconsulem habere desierant: misiq; a Magistro officiales, qui Ithacium tum in Treveris agentem ad Hispanias retrahe- rent. Quos ille callide frustratur: ac po- stea per Pritannium episcopum defensus illusit. Iam rumor incesserat Clemen-tem Maximum intra Britannias sumpsisse imperium, ac brevi in Gallias eruptu-rum. Ita tum Ithacius statuit, licet rebus dubiis,novi imperatoris adventum expe- ctare: interim sibi nihil agitandum. Igi- tur ubi Maximus opidum Treverorum victor ingressus est, ingerit preces plenas in Priscillianū ac socios ejus invidiæ atq; criminum. Quibus permotus Imperator datis ad prætectum Galliarum atq; ad vicariū Hispaniarum literis, omnes omnino, quos labes illa involverat, deduci ad synodum Burdegalensem jubet. Itadeducti Instantius & Priscillianus: quorum Instantius prior jussus causam dicere, post quam se parum expurgabat, indignus esse episcopatu pronunciatus est. Priscillianus vero, ne ab episcopis audiretur, ad Principem provocavit, permissumq; id nostrorum inconstantia, quia aut sententiam in refragantem ferre debuerant, aut si hi ipsi suspecti habebantur, aliis episcopis audientiam reservare, non causam Imperatori de tam manifestis criminibus permittere.
units.tr: c Hyginus [?]. ...set up a bishop in the town of Labilis to strengthen their power, thinking that if they armed a keen and cunning man with priestly authority they would be safer. Then indeed Idacius and Ithacius pressed harder, believing that the evil could be checked at its beginnings. But with ill-judged counsels they went to the secular judges, so that by their decrees and enforcement the heretics might be driven from the cities. So after much foul dealing, at Idacius's entreaty, a rescript was obtained from Gratian, then emperor, by which all heretics were ordered to be expelled, not only from churches or cities, but from all lands. When this became known, the Gnostics, distrustful of their own position and not daring to contend in judgment, gave way of their own accord, those who were the bishops; fear scattered the rest. But then Instantius, Salvianus and Priscillian set out for Rome to clear themselves before Damasus, bishop of the city at that time. Their road lay past inner Aquitaine, where they were received with great honour by the unlearned, and scattered the seeds of treachery, and corrupted especially the people of Elusa, then truly good and devoted to religion, with their wicked preaching. Driven out of Burdigala by Delphinus, yet they lingered for a while on the estate of Euchrocia and infected several people with their errors. Then, setting out again, they went with a shameful and shameless company, with their wives and other women too, among whom was Euchrocia, and her daughter Procula, about whom there was talk that she was pregnant by Priscillian's debauchery and had procured abortion by herbs. When they reached Rome, wishing to clear themselves before Damasus, they were not even admitted to his presence. Returning to Milan, they found Ambrose equally opposed to them. Then they changed their plans: since they had not gained favour with the two bishops, who then held the highest authority, they would extract by largesse and canvassing what they wanted from the emperor. So, having bribed Macedonius, the master of offices, they obtained a rescript by which the decrees that had been passed against them were revoked, and the churches were ordered to be restored to them. Relying on this, Instantius and Priscillian made their way back to Spain, for Salvianus had died in the city, and then without any struggle they recovered the churches over which they had presided. But Thrasius had no will to resist, but lacked the means, because the heretics, having corrupted Volventius the proconsul, had strengthened their forces. Moreover, Ithacius, accused by them as a disturber of the churches, was summoned and ordered to be brought under violent escort, and fled in alarm to Gaul. There he approached the prefect Gregorius. He, having learned what had been done, ordered the instigators of the disturbances to be brought before him, and reported everything to the emperor, so as to cut off the heretics' means of canvassing. But this was in vain, because through the greed and power of a few, everything there was for sale. So the heretics, by their own arts and a large sum of money given to Macedonius, obtained that by imperial authority the case was taken from the prefect and given to the vicar of Spain. For by now they had ceased to have a proconsul. And they sent officials from the master to bring Ithacius back to Spain, who was then staying at Trier. He cleverly evaded them, and afterwards, defended by Pritannius, the bishop, he mocked them. Now a rumour had spread that Clement Maximus had taken up the empire within Britain, and would soon break into Gaul. So at that time Ithacius decided, though affairs were uncertain, to await the arrival of the new emperor, and meanwhile to do nothing himself. So when Maximus entered Trier as victor, Ithacius poured out petitions full of hatred and charges against Priscillian and his associates. Moved by these, the emperor sent letters to the prefect of Gaul and to the vicar of Spain, and ordered that absolutely all whom that plague had involved be brought to the synod at Bordeaux. So Instantius and Priscillian were brought there. Instantius, being ordered to plead first, after he had cleared himself poorly, was pronounced unworthy of the episcopate. But Priscillian, so as not to be heard by the bishops, appealed to the prince. This was allowed through the inconsistency of our side, because they ought either to have pronounced sentence against one who objected, or, if these very men were suspected, to have reserved the hearing for other bishops, and not to have left to the emperor a case about such manifest crimes.

units.la: Ita omnes, quos causa involverat, ad re-gem deducti. Secuti etiam accusatores, Idacius & Ithacius episcopi: quorum studium in expugnandis hæreticis non reprehenderem, si non studio vincendi plus quam oportuit certassent. Ac mea quidem sententia est, mihi tam reos quam accusatores displicere. Certe Ithacium nihil pensi, nihil sancti habuisse definio. Fuit enim audax, loquax, impudens, lum-ptuofus, ptuofus, ventri & gulæ plurimum impertiens. Hic stultitiæ eo utq; processerat,ut omnes etiam sanctos viros, quibus aut ftudiū inerat lectionis, aut propofitū erat certare jejuniis, tanquā Pritcilliani socios aut discipulos,in crime arcesseret. Ausus etiam miler est, ea tempestate Martino episcopo a,viro plane Apostolis conferen-do, palam objectare hæresis infamiam. Namq; tum Martinus apud Treveros con- stitutus, non desinebat increpare Ithacium, ut ab accusatione desisteret: Maximum orare, ut sanguine infelicium abstineret: satis superque sufficere, ut episcopali sententia hæretici judicati ecclesiis pellerentur: novum esse & inauditum nefas, ut causam ecclesiæ judex sæculi judicaret.
units.tr: Thus all whom the case had involved were brought before the ruler. Their accusers followed too, the bishops Idacius and Ithacius. I would not blame their zeal in attacking the heretics, if they had not contended with more eagerness for victory than was right. My own opinion is that I dislike both the accused and the accusers. Certainly I judge that Ithacius had no sense of what was proper, nothing sacred about him. He was bold, talkative, shameless, extravagant, and gave himself very much to his belly and gullet. He had gone so far in folly that he accused of crime all the holy men who either had a love of reading or had resolved to outdo one another in fasting, as if they were companions or disciples of Priscillian. The wretch even dared, at that time, to bring the charge of heresy openly against Martin, a bishop truly comparable to the Apostles. For Martin, who was then at Trier, did not cease to rebuke Ithacius, urging him to desist from the accusation, and begging Maximus to abstain from the blood of the unhappy: it was enough and more than enough that the heretics, judged by episcopal sentence, should be driven from the churches; it was a new and unheard-of wickedness for a secular judge to judge a cause of the Church.

units.la: Denique quoad usque Martinus Treveris fuit, dilata cognitio est: & mox discessurus egregia authoritate a Maximo exlicuit sponsionem, nihil cruentum in reos constituendum. Sed postea Imperator per Magnum & Rufum episcopos depravatus, & a mitioribus consiliis deflexus, caussam præfecto Evodio permisit, viro acri & severo. Qui Priscillianum gemino judicio auditum convictumque maleficii, nec diffitetem obscoenis sestu-duisse doctrinis, nocturnos etiam turpiu foeminarum egisse conventus, nuduMq; orare solitum, nocentem pronunciavit, redegitq; in custodiam donec ad principe referret. Gestis ad palatium delatis, censuit imperator, Priscillianum iocisq; ejus capitis damnari oportere. Ceterum Ithacius videns, quam invidiosum sibi apud episcopos foret, si accusato, etiam postremis rerum capitalium judiciis astitisset (etenim iterari judicium necesse erat) subtrahit se cognitioni frustra calido jam sece lere perfecto[?]. At tum per Maximum accusator apponitur Patricius quidam, fisci patronus. Ita eo insistente, Priscillianus capitis damnatus est, unaq; cum eo Felicisimus & Armenius, qui nuper a catholicis, clerici Priscillianum secuti, desciverant. Latronianus quoq; & Euchro-cia gladio perempti. Instantius, quem superius ab episcopis damnatum diximus, in Sylinam infulam, quæ ultra Britanniam sita est, deportatus. Itum deinde in reliquos sequentibus judiciis, damnatiquè Asurinus & Aurelius diaconus gladio. Tyberianus, ademptis bonis, in Sy-
units.tr: At last, for as long as Martin was at Trier, the hearing was put off. When he was about to leave, he obtained from Maximus, by his outstanding authority, a promise that nothing bloody would be decreed against the accused. But afterwards the Emperor, corrupted by the bishops Magnus and Rufus and turned away from milder counsels, entrusted the case to the prefect Evodius, a man sharp and severe. Having heard Priscillian in a double trial, Evodius found him convicted of sorcery, and of having not denied his devotion to obscene doctrines; he had also held nocturnal gatherings of shameless women and was accustomed to pray naked. Evodius pronounced him guilty and committed him to custody until he could refer the matter to the Emperor. When the records had been sent to the palace, the Emperor judged that Priscillian and his followers ought to be condemned to death. But Ithacius, seeing how hateful it would be for him among the bishops if, having brought the charge, he stood by at the final judgments in capital cases (for the trial had to be repeated), withdrew from the hearing, his effort having already been made in vain. Instead, through Maximus, a certain Patricius, advocate of the treasury, was appointed as accuser. With him pressing the case, Priscillian was condemned to death, together with Felicissimus and Armenius, who had recently deserted from the Catholics after following Priscillian as clerics. Latronianus and Euchrocia were also put to death by the sword. Instantius, whom we said above had been condemned by the bishops, was deported to the Scilly Isles, which lie beyond Britain. Proceedings then went on against the rest by successive judgments: Asurinus and Aurelius, a deacon, were condemned to the sword. Tyberianus, stripped of his goods, was sent into exile on the Scilly Isles. Tertullus, Potamius and Johannes, as less important persons, deserving of pity, who had betrayed the investigation and their associates, were relegated to temporary exile within Gaul. Men most worthy of light were in this way put to death or fined with exile, in a most evil precedent. This had been defended at the outset by the law of the courts and by public good order, but afterwards Ithacius, accustomed to the law courts, was at last himself convicted and turned it back against those on whose mandate and advice he had brought it about. Yet of all the bishops he alone was thrust out of his see. Nardacius, though less guilty, had voluntarily given up his episcopate; he did this wisely and modestly, unless he afterwards tried to recover the place he had lost. But once Priscillian was killed, the heresy that had broken out under his leadership was not only not suppressed but was strengthened and spread more widely. For his followers, who had earlier honoured him as a saint, then began to worship him as a martyr. The bodies of those put to death were carried back to Spain, and their funerals were celebrated with great ceremony. Indeed, swearing by Priscillian was thought to be a matter of supreme religion, and among our own people a perpetual monster of discord had flared up; although for fifteen years it had been stirred by foul dissensions, it could in no way be quieted. And now, when everything was seen to be thrown into confusion or mixed up by the discords of the bishops, and all affairs were corrupted through them by hatred or favour, fear, fickleness, envy, faction, lust, greed, arrogance and sloth, in the end many were fighting with mad counsels and obstinate zeal against a few who advised well. Meanwhile the people of God and every upright man were held in disgrace and mockery.

units.la: {e} ero.devi. vs illu- fr. Ath. Chri- fi 3'7 [marginal notes, partly illegible] linam infulam datus. Tertullus, Potamius & Johannes, tanquam viliores personæ & digni misericordia, quiane quæstionem se ac locios prodidissent, temporario exilio intra Gallias relegati. Hoc fere modo homines luce indignißimi, pessimo exemplo necati, aut exiliis multati: quod initio jure judiciorum & {a}egregio publico defensum, postea Ithacius in jure solitus, ad postremum convictus, in eos retorquebat, quorum id mandato & consiliis effecerat. Solus tamen omnium episcopatu detrusus. Nardacius, licet minus nocens, sponte se episcopatu abdicaverat. Sapienter id & verecunde, nisi postea amissum locum repetere tentaret. Ceterum Priscilliano occiso, non solum non repressa est hæresis, quæ illo authore proruperat, sed confirmata, latius propagata est. Namque sectatores ejus, qui eum prius ut sanctum honorave-rant, postea ut martyrem colere coeperunt. Peremptorum corpora ad Hispanias relata, magnisque obsequiis celebrata eorum funera. Quin & jurare per Priscillianum summa religio putabatur, ac inter nostros perpetuum discordiarum bolbelluȩ exarserat: quod iam per quinde-cim annos foedis dissentionibus agitatum nullo modo sopiri poterat. Et nunc, cum maxime discordiis episcoporum turbari aut miiceri omnia cernerentur, cunctaq; per eos odio, aut gratia, metu, inconstan-tia, invidia, factione, libidine, avaritia, ar-rogantia, {*}desidia essent depravata: postremo plures adversum paucos bene consulentes insanis consiliis & pertinacibus studiis certabant: inter haec plebs Dei & optimus quisque probro atq; ludibrio habebatur.

units.la: Scire te volo, Lector, nomina Ebraica, quae in hoc libro, pleraque omnia corrupta esse. Quod accidit incuria, ne dicam inscitia[?], describentium: tum etiam quia Sulpitius secutus fuit editionem Graecam vulgatam, ubi pariter haec nomina corrupta sunt. Ea nunc ordine alphabetico digesta & e regione, ad priscam consuetudinem, quam a Hieronymo didicimus, emendata, in medium conferimus, vacaturas alioqui paginas, ex consilio typographi, hoc modo explicantes. Habe & boni consule. Aaron, Aharon. Abel, Habel. Abimelech, Achimelech. Abiron, Abirom, vel Abiram. Abiud, pag. 69. Abiam vel Abia. Abiud, pag. 31. Abihu.
units.tr: I want you to know, reader, that most of the Hebrew names in this book are corrupted. This happened through the carelessness, not to say ignorance, of the copyists, and also because Sulpicius followed the common Greek edition, where these names are corrupted in the same way. I have now arranged them in alphabetical order, each set opposite its correction, restored to the old usage we learned from Jerome, and I set them out here, since otherwise the pages would be left blank, as the printer proposed. Take them in good part. Aaron, Aharon. Abel, Habel. Abimelech, Achimelech. Abiron, Abirom or Abiram. Abiud, p. 69. Abiam or Abia. Abiud, p. 31. Abihu.

units.la: Abraham recte quidem dicitur, sed in hoc libro aliquoties occurrit pro Abram. Quod antiquum huius patriarchae nomen, qui postea unius litterae additione Abraham dictus fuit. Absalon, Absalom. Accitor, Achior. Achas. Achaz. Sed A-chas se tuetur consuetudine Graeca, quam notavi Observat. lib. 9. cap. 9. Sic Ioachas. Adon. c/Ahod. Alchimus, Alcimus. Allon, Ailon vel Elon. Amalech, c/Amalec. Amalechitae, Amalecitae. Amasias, c/Amasias. Amon, pag. 45, Ammon. Ananias, Hananias. Anna, Hanna. Appollinius, Appollonium. mendum chalcographi. Arphaxat, c/Arphaxad. Asab, pag. 69. c/Asa. Asphane, c/Asphanez.
units.tr: Abraham is indeed the correct form, but in this book it sometimes occurs for Abram. Abram was the old name of this patriarch, who was later called Abraham after the addition of one letter. Absalon, Absalom. Accitor, Achior. Achas, Achaz. But Achas is defended by Greek usage, which I noted in Observ. book 9, chapter 9. So Ioachas. Adon, for Ahod. Alchimus, Alcimus. Allon, Ailon or Elon. Amalech, for Amalec. Amalechitae, Amalecitae. Amasias, for Amasias. Amon, p. 45, Ammon. Ananias, Hananias. Anna, Hanna. Appollinius, Appollonium: a printer's error. Arphaxat, for Arphaxad. Asab, p. 69, for Asa. Asphane, for Asphanez.

units.la: NOTAE AD SVLPICII SEVERI Historiae Sacrae, Lib. I.
units.tr: NOTES ON SULPICIUS SEVERUS' SACRED HISTORY, BOOK I.

units.la: Pag. 1. Sulpicii Severi historia facta] ita libri omnes quos vidi. Est tamen qui appellet, Sulp. Severi chronicon. Gennadius quoque hanc historiam significat, cum ait, composuit & chronica, id est, τὰ χρονικά. Foxius de historiae institutione, Chronica a Graeco verbo χρόνῳ [?], id est, tempus, ita appellatae dicuntur narrationes per temporum ordinem distinctae, cujus generis sunt illa quae per aetates singulas omnia describunt, ut quid ante diluvium, quid postea, quid unoquoque demum tempore gestum sit. Nisi legendum, composuit & chronicam. Nam ea aetas inflectebat Chronica, Chronicae; ut Biblia, Bibliae; pascua, pascuae. Quod postremum invenies in versione Niero [?]. Psal. 74. 2, oves pascuae tuae. Isidorus, Chronica Graece dicitur, quae Latine temporum series appellatur. Autor is qui disput, Athanasij cum Arrio in Latinum convertit: Sed si illud recolat, quod in Chronica sua b. m. Sulpitius Severus posuit dicens, duo Arrij tanquam duo serpentes ex uno ore sibilabant, &c. Porro aut praecedentium nominum prius praenomen esse videtur, & posterius nomen proprium. Sic enim certe dicitur Sulpicius Severus, ut Septimius Tertullianus, Aurelius Prudentius, Decimus Ausonius, Sulpicius Pius, Aurelius Augustinus. Quanquam in Gennadio, Severus cognomento Sulpicius.
units.tr: Page 1. The Sacred History of Sulpicius Severus] All the books I have seen read so. Some do call it the Chronicle of Sulpicius Severus. Gennadius also refers to this history when he says, "he also composed chronicles," that is, τὰ χρονικά [ta chronika]. Foxius, on the institution of history: chronicles are so called from the Greek word χρόνος [chronos], that is, time. Narratives arranged in the order of times are called by this name, and of this kind are those that describe everything by individual ages, such as what happened before the Flood, what afterwards, and what happened at each period. Unless one should read "he composed also a chronicle," for that age inflected Chronica, Chronicae, as Biblia, Bibliae; pascua, pascuae. You will find the last in Niero's version [?]. Ps. 74.2: "the sheep of your pasture." Isidore: "What is called in Greek chronica is called in Latin the succession of times." The author of the disputation translated the Athanasius against Arius into Latin. But if one recalls what Sulpicius Severus, of blessed memory, put in his Chronicle, saying that the two Arii hissed like two serpents from one mouth, etc. Moreover, either the first of the preceding names seems to be the praenomen and the later one the proper name. For thus Sulpicius Severus is certainly named, as Septimius Tertullianus, Aurelius Prudentius, Decimus Ausonius, Sulpicius Pius, Aurelius Augustinus. Although in Gennadius, Severus is given Sulpicius as a cognomen.

units.la: Pag. 3, A mundi exordio] A mundi origine. Moses princi-pium appellat, cum ait, In principio creavit Deus caelum ac terram. Sensu est, in principio temporis, vel certe creationis. Nam tempus est spatium quod mensuratur motu caeli solisque, secundum Physicos. Sol autem tunc nondum erat, ergo nec tempus. Nos qui Mosen sequimur, scimus tempus ante solem fuisse, imo simul cum ipso mundo coepisse. Quod sic probatur. In principio, quum Deus creavit mundum, hoc est caelum ac terram [?]. tenebræ erant in superficie abyssi. Has tenebras Deus nobilem appellavit. Idem lucem, quæ primo extitit, diem nominavit. Nox & dies partes sunt temporis. Tempus ergo ante solem. Nam sol quarto demum die fuit. Proinde non peccaret, meo judicio, si quis, a mundi exordio, exponeret, ab eo tempore quo Deus creavit cælum ac terram.
units.tr: Page 3, From the beginning of the world] From the origin of the world. Moses calls it the beginning when he says, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The sense is: in the beginning of time, or at least of creation. For time is the interval measured by the motion of the heavens and the sun, according to the Physicists. But the sun did not yet exist then, so neither did time. We who follow Moses know that time existed before the sun, indeed began together with the world itself. This is proved thus. In the beginning, when God created the world, that is, heaven and earth [?], "darkness was upon the face of the deep." This darkness God called night. He also named the light which first appeared day. Night and day are parts of time. Time therefore existed before the sun, for the sun came only on the fourth day. Accordingly, in my judgement, one would not be wrong to explain "from the beginning of the world" as "from the time when God created heaven and earth."

units.la: tam Apocryphis, quam Canonicis. Apocryphas voco, qui antiquitus & Ecclesiastici dicebantur, quos Ecclesia recepit non ad dogmatum veritatem, sed ad morum institutionem historiaque fidem. Siquidem absque primo Machabæorum, qui liber Hasamonæorum dicitur, gesta regum templi se[?]cundi magna ex parte hodie ignorarentur.
units.tr: Both the Apocryphal and the Canonical books. I call Apocryphal those which were anciently also called ecclesiastical, which the Church received not for the truth of doctrines but for the instruction of morals and for the credibility of history. For without the first book of the Maccabees, which is called the book of the Hasmoneans, the deeds of the kings of the second temple would for the most part be unknown today.

units.la: edere est foras dare, quod Græci dicunt ἐκδοῦναι. Id non solum autor scriptor vel facit, sed etiam interpres. Apostolorum actus Lucas edidit, utque in id tempus quo Paulus Romam deductus est. Nepos Iesu Sirach, qui avi librum Græce convertit, πρὸς τὰ ἴδια ἀγοράζειν τὰ βιβλία, ut ad finem perductus liber ederetur. Hinc ἔκδοσις, editio.
units.tr: To "edere" is to give forth, which the Greeks call ἐκδοῦναι [ekdounai]. This is done not only by the author or writer but also by the translator. Luke published the Acts of the Apostles, carrying it down to the time when Paul was taken to Rome. Jesus Sirach's grandson, who translated his grandfather's book into Greek, bought the books πρὸς τὰ ἴδια [pros ta idia] so that the book might be published when finished. Hence ἔκδοσις [ekdosis], edition.

units.la: nos eam breviter perstringimus, id uno verbo dicunt breviare. Quintilianus de paraphrasi, qua & breviare quædam & exornare, salvo modo poetæ sensu, permittitur. Noster post paullo, quæ de sacris voluminibus breviata digessimus. Atque hinc sane breviarium. Epitomam alij vocant.
units.tr: I briefly sum up these matters. They express this in one word, "to abridge." Quintilian, on paraphrase, by which certain things are both abridged and embellished, the poet's sense being preserved, is permitted. Our author a little later: "what we have abridged and arranged from the sacred volumes." And hence, certainly, breviary. Others call it an epitome.

units.la: recte. Siquidem historiæ lumen est distinctio sive dispositio temporum.
units.tr: Rightly. For the light of history is the distinction or arrangement of times.

units.la: ad annum Christi CCCC. quo Fl. Stilico & Fl. Aurelianus consules erant. In hunc sane annum perduxit historiam suam Severus. omne tempus in Stilliconem consulem direxi.
units.tr: To the year of Christ 400, when Fl. Stilicho and Fl. Aurelianus were consuls. Severus certainly brought his history down to this year. "I have directed the whole period toward the consul Stilicho."

units.la: Hinc inde carpendo, ut videbitur. Sallustius in Catilin. statuit res gestas P.R. carptim, ut quæque memoria digna videbuntur, perscribere. Adverbium est a carpo. Cicero, in multorum peccata carpi paucos ad supplicium non oportet.
units.tr: Gathering here and there, as will be seen. Sallust in the Catiline stated that he would write about the deeds of the Roman people piecemeal, as each seemed worthy of memory. It is an adverb from carpo. Cicero: "It is not right that a few be punished for the faults of many, which are picked at here and there."

units.la: misericordiamque divinam efflagitans. In uno edito inveni, flagitantibus.
units.tr: and imploring the divine mercy. In one edition I found "imploring" in the plural.

units.la: libris historicis V.T., qui sunt ex lege
units.tr: the historical books of the Old Testament, which are from the Law

units.la: lege Genesis, Exodus, Numeri, Deuteronomium: e Prophetis, Ia-fue, Iudices, duo Samuelis & totidem Regum ex Hagiographis, duo Paralip. Daniel, Ezras, Nehemias, Esther: ex Apocryphis Iu-dith, duo Machabaeorum cum historia Susannae Belique.
units.tr: From the Law: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy; from the Prophets: Joshua, Judges, the two books of Samuel and as many of Kings; from the Hagiographa: the two books of Chronicles, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther; from the Apocrypha: Judith, the two books of the Maccabees, with the story of Susanna and Bel.

units.la: Viq; ad Christi crucem] lib.2. A quo tempore ad Christi crucem, id est, Fusium Geminum & Rubellium consules. Alij dicerent, ad Christum crucifixu, sive ad Christum passum.
units.tr: Up to the cross of Christ] book 2. From which time to the cross of Christ, that is, the consuls Fusius Geminus and Rubellius. Others would say "to the crucifixion of Christ," or "to the passion of Christ."

units.la: Apoitolorumq; actus] [?]. Sic lib.2. Apostolorum actus Lucas edidit. Alij malunt, acta: & ita est in editione vulgata. Sed in libris veteribus habetur, actus Apostolorum. Vsi sunt hoc vocabulo Suetonius, Plinius & Lucanus. Budaeus utrumque recte dici tradit. Noster infra, quarum quidem actus, quibus potissimum regibus connectam, non facile perspexerim. Intelligit acta Iudith & Esther.
units.tr: The Acts of the Apostles] [?]. So in book 2: "Luke published the Acts of the Apostles." Others prefer acta, and so it stands in the common edition. But in the old manuscripts it reads actus Apostolorum. Suetonius, Pliny and Lucan used this word. Budé states that both forms are correctly used. Our author below: "I could not easily see by which kings in particular I might connect the deeds of these women." He means the Acts of Judith and Esther.

units.la: Post gesta] aemulatus est Sallustium in oratione Lepidi, supplicia in post futuros composuit.
units.tr: After the deeds] He imitated Sallust in the speech of Lepidus, composing "punishments" for those who would come afterwards.

units.la: Convertere] non displicet coniectura Victoris Gifelini, qui Sulpicium scripsisse putat, connectere: quo verbo usus est non semel, ut pag.67. connexum rerum ordinem: & pag.108. quibus potissimum regibus connectam: & dial.2, segm.6. Licet diversis in palatio temporibus gesta connectam. Proclivis sane lapsus de connectere in convertere. Minus placet quod alij reponunt, ad post gesta convertere.
units.tr: Convertere] The conjecture of Victor Gifelinus does not displease me, who thinks Sulpicius wrote connectere, a word he used more than once, as on p. 67, "the connected order of things," and p. 108, "by which kings in particular I might connect," and Dialogue 2, section 6, "although the deeds of different times in the palace I might connect." It is certainly an easy slip from connectere to convertere. Less pleasing is what others propose, to read "ad post gesta convertere."

units.la: Pag.4. Historicis ethnicis] ethnicos, gentiles & paganos olim vocabant omnes eos, qui neque Iudaei neque Christiani erant.
units.tr: Page 4. Pagan historians] Formerly all those who were neither Jews nor Christians were called ethnic, gentile and pagan.

units.la: Imperitos] temporum.
units.tr: Inexperienced] in matters of time.

units.la: Litteratos] peritos quidem, sed aliter tempora digerentes.
units.tr: Learned] skilled indeed, but arranging the times differently.

units.la: Vniversa divinarum rerum mysteria] qualia sunt de resurrectione, de vita aeterna, de lapsu hominis, de redemptione generis humani, & alia.
units.tr: All the mysteries of divine things] such as those concerning the resurrection, eternal life, the fall of man, the redemption of mankind, and others.

units.la: Ex ipsis fontibus] ex sacris litteris, unde haec derivata sunt tanquam e fonte. Sic pag.28. fontem ipsum adeat, id est, sacros codices. Lastantius lib.7. cap.25. Qui autem haec diligentius voluerit scire, ex ipso fonte hauriat. Alibi fontes appellantur eadem litterae lingua originali conscriptae; quarum comparatione versiones omnes rivuli sunt & lacunae: e quibus parum feliciter hauriunt qui fontes linguarum ignoran[?]
units.tr: From the very fountains] from the sacred letters, from which these things are derived as from a spring. So on page 28: "let him go to the fountain itself," that is, the sacred codices. Lactantius, book 7, chapter 25: "But whoever wishes to know these things more carefully, let him draw from the very fountain." Elsewhere the same writings, composed in the original language, are called fountains; in comparison with them all versions are streams and pools, from which those who do not know the languages draw with little success.

units.la: Mundus a Domino constitutus] Cœlum & quicquid ejus complexu continetur, hoc est totum istud universum, quod mundum vocitamus, Deus absolvit sex dierum spatio. Primo die creavit cœlum & terram, quæ initio rudis erat indigestaque moles, quam tenebræ vestiebant, e quibus lucem eduxit. Secundo soluit, vel potius jussit, ut esset expansum, quod firmamentum vocant, in medio duarum aquarum; quarum aliæ superiores, aliæ dicuntur inferiores. Sunt autem superiores aquæ pluviæ, quæ in media regione aëris. Tertio produxit terra herbas & arbores omnis generis. Quarto extiterunt duo luminaria & stellæ. Quinto pisces & aves. Sexto terrestres animantes. Quibus omnibus perfectis.
units.tr: The world constituted by the Lord] God completed heaven and whatever is contained in its embrace, that is, the whole universe which we call the world, in a space of six days. On the first day he created heaven and earth, which at the beginning was a rough and undigested mass, clothed in darkness, from which he drew forth light. On the second he ordered, or rather commanded, that there be an expanse, which they call the firmament, in the middle of two waters, of which some are called upper and others lower. The upper waters are the rains, which are in the middle region of the air. On the third he brought forth from the earth herbs and trees of every kind. On the fourth there came into being the two lights and the stars. On the fifth fishes and birds. On the sixth land animals. When all these had been perfected.

units.la: Sanctius his animal, mentisque capacius altæ Deerat adhuc, & quod dominari in cetera posset, Natus homo est.
units.tr: A more holy animal, and one more capable of a lofty mind, was still lacking, one who could rule over the rest: man was born.

units.la: A Domino] hic Severum minus proprie locutum annotat Sigonius. Nam cum de creatione agatur dicendum fuisse, a Deo constitutus. Deus enim, inquit, creationem respicit, Dominus imperium in res creatas & legem. Cum bona venia tanti viri a Domino, i. יהוה, Quod non minus creationem respicit quam illud a Deo. Iesa.45.18. Sic dicit Dominus creans cœlum, ipse Deus est faciens terram.
units.tr: By the Lord] Sigonius notes that Severus has spoken here less properly. For when creation is the subject, he should have said "constituted by God." For God, he says, regards creation; the Lord regards dominion over created things and law. With due respect to so great a man: "by the Lord," i.e. יהוה [YHWH]. This regards creation no less than "by God." Isaiah 45:18: "Thus says the Lord who creates the heavens, he is God who makes the earth."

units.la: Constitutus] conditus, creatus, factus. Creandi verbo usus est Moses. Id significat ex eo quod non est, facere aliquid ut sit, sive, ut Scholastici loquuntur, ex non ente facere ens. Nec refert ex nihilo id fiat an ex materia. Sane quidem ex humo creatus fuit homo, & ex aqua pisces, quos Thanninim Ebræi vocant.
units.tr: Constituted] founded, created, made. Moses used the verb "create." It signifies making something to be from what was not, or, as the Schoolmen say, making a being out of non-being. Nor does it matter whether this is done out of nothing or out of matter. Indeed man was created from the earth, and fishes from the water, which the Hebrews call Thanninim [תנינים].

units.la: Abhinc annos pœne sex millia] fuerunt siue cuiq; seculo ut verba sua sic vitia orationis. Cujus generis est anni sex millia pro annorum. Orofius lib.1,cap.1. anni tria millia; & colligunt anni duo millia. Idem lib.2. cap. 10 onerarias tria millia. Vetus interpres 4, Reg.19.33. decem millia cororum; vel, coros decies mille.
units.tr: Almost six thousand years ago: every age has its own turns of speech, just as it has its own faults of style. Of this kind is "six thousand years" for "years." Orosius, book 1, chapter 1, has "three thousand years," and he makes it "two thousand years." The same author, book 2, chapter 10, has "three thousand transport ships." The Old Translator, 4 Reg. 19.33, has "ten thousand cors," or "a cor ten thousand times."

units.la: Pœne] decrant anni 171. Nam ex supputatione ipsius colliguntur usque ad consulatum primum Stiliconis, hoc est, usque ad annum Christi quadringentesimum, 5819.
units.tr: Almost: there are lacking 171 years. For by his reckoning they run up to the first consulship of Stilicho, that is, to the year of Christ 400, which gives 5819.

units.la: Digeremus] sic Livius dixit, digerere tempora: & digerere acta. Cicero quoque digerere rempublicam dixit, pro disponere. disponere & ordinare. Supra, quae de sacris voluminibus breviata digesimus.
units.tr: We shall arrange: so Livy spoke of arranging the times and arranging the deeds. Cicero also spoke of arranging the commonwealth, meaning to set in order, to dispose and arrange. Above, what we have briefly digested concerning the sacred volumes.

units.la: Quam inter se parum consentiant] maxima dissensio est inter Graecos & Ebraeos. Nam uti alia omittam, ab exordio mundi adusque diluvium Graeci annos computant bis mille ducentos quadraginta duos: Ebraei vero mille sexcentos quinquaginta sex tantum. Haec est prima aetas. In secunda Graeci ponunt annos 942. Ebraei 292. Hos fere sequuntur Hieronymus, Beda & chronologi hujus aevi: illos Eusebius Pamphyli, Nicephorus, Cedrenus, Zonoras, Nicetas, Isidorus, autor Fasciculi temporum & alij. Qui etiam inter se parum consentiunt. Quod ex hac tabula V. Gisellini perspicuum fiet. A mundo condito ad Christi natalem numerant annos, R. Nabasson in libro de cyclo Paschatis | 3740 Rabbini recentiores | 3760 men.4 Thalmudici | 3784 Biblia Regia | 3919 Hiero. in quaest. Ebraicu[?] | 3941 Iohan. Carion in chron. | 3944 Beda cap. 21. de rat. temp. | 3952 Iohan. Picus Mirandulae comes | 3958 Philo Iudaeus | 3960 Abbas Vrspergensis, Funccius, Gerardus Mercator & plerique Germani | 3962 Moses Gerundensis | 4058 men.5 Gilb. Genebrardus | 4121 Iosephus | 4192 men.6 Odiaton sive Educon astrolo. | 4320 Cassiodorus | 4697 Metheodorus[?] | 5000 Epiphan. cont. Manichaeos | 5029 Paulus Orosius | 5049 Eusebius | 5190 Isidorus in 5. Etymolog. | 5210 Albumasar & alij astronomi | 5328 Augustinus | 5311 Sulpicius Severus | 5414 Theophilus Antiochenus | 5476 Suidas sive Sudas | 5600 Philastrius de Haeresibus 801 Alphonsus rex 984 Onuphrius Panuinius in Chron. eccl. 6309
units.tr: How little they agree among themselves: the greatest disagreement is between the Greeks and the Hebrews. To omit other points, from the beginning of the world to the flood the Greeks count 2,242 years, but the Hebrews only 1,656. This is the first age. In the second age the Greeks put 942 years, the Hebrews 292. These mostly follow Jerome, Bede and the chronologers of this period; the others follow Eusebius of Pamphilus, Nicephorus, Cedrenus, Zonaras, Nicetas, Isidore, the author of the Fasciculus temporum and others. These too disagree among themselves, as will be clear from this table of V. Gisellinus. From the created world to Christ's birth they count the years: R. Nabasson, in his book on the Passover cycle, 3740; recent rabbis 3760; the Talmudists 3784; the Biblia Regia 3919; Jerome, in the Hebrew Questions 3941; John Carion, in his Chronicle 3944; Bede, chapter 21 of De ratione temporum 3952; John Pico, count of Mirandola 3958; Philo the Jew 3960; Abbot of Ursperg, Funccius, Gerard Mercator and most Germans 3962; Moses of Gerona 4058; Gilbert Genebrard 4121; Josephus 4192; Odiaton or Educon the astrologer 4320; Cassiodorus 4697; Metheodorus 5000; Epiphanius against the Manichaeans 5029; Paulus Orosius 5049; Eusebius 5190; Isidore in the fifth book of the Etymologies 5210; Albumasar and other astronomers 5328; Augustine 5311; Sulpicius Severus 5414; Theophilus of Antioch 5476; Suidas or Sudas 5600; Philastrius, On Heresies 801; King Alphonsus 984; Onuphrius Panvinius, in the Chronicle of the Church 6309.

units.la: Nutu Dei] omnia fiunt Dei nutu, si nutum accipias pro voluntate simpliciter. Sed est voluntas quaedam cum approbatione. Hoc sensu quae prava sunt Deus non vult, dicitur. Quae pertinent numeri, qui in libris Graecis & Latinis. Nam dicere nutu Dei eos corruptos esse infame impium est. Potius igitur ut dicamus id accidisse vitio vetustatis, aut errore chronologorum.
units.tr: By the nod of God: all things happen by the nod of God, if you take nod simply as will. But there is a certain will that carries approval, and in this sense God does not will what is perverse. Those things pertain to the numbers, which are in the Greek and Latin books. For to say that these were corrupted by the nod of God is an infamous impiety. Rather, then, let us say that this happened through the fault of antiquity, or the error of the chronologers.

units.la: Quanquam, ut Augustinus ait, errores illi, si errores sunt, quandam videntur habere constantiam; nec casum redolent, sed industriam. Forsan per hanc varietatem exercere voluit ingenia hominum Deus, quemadmodum vir quidam doctus & pius de iis quae obscura extant in sacris litteris, ait ipsum posuisse cruces Theologis, quo ad sobrietatem sapere discerent.
units.tr: Yet, as Augustine says, those errors, if they are errors, seem to have a certain consistency; they do not smell of chance but of diligence. Perhaps God wished through this variety to exercise the minds of men, just as a certain learned and pious man, speaking of the obscure passages in the sacred letters, said that God had set crosses for theologians, so that they might learn to be wise with sobriety.

units.la: Mundo autem condito] homo fuit ultimus conditorum, in quo mundi fabrica expleta. Improprie igitur loquitur. Aut mundum dicit caelum ac terram. Sic Lactantius lib. 2. c. 9. Sed ne perspiceret homo Dei opera, noluit eum inducere in hunc mundum, nisi perfectis omnibus: sed ne induci quidem poterat. Quomodo enim subsisteret cum fabricaretur desuper caelum, terra subter funderetur, &c.
units.tr: Man was the last of the things created, and with him the making of the world was completed; so the phrase "the world was created" is used improperly. Or by "world" he means heaven and earth. So Lactantius, book 2, chapter 9: "But lest man should perceive God's works, He was unwilling to bring him into this world until all things were finished; nor indeed could he have been brought in. For how could he have endured while the heaven was being built above and the earth was being laid beneath, and so on?"

units.la: Homo factus est] Gen. 1.16. faciamus hominem, & 2.7. formavit Deus hominem. Rursum 1.17. creavit Deus hominem. Quae labefactant discrimen illud quod interpretes ponunt inter haec verba. Saltem ostendunt non esse perpetuum.
units.tr: Man was made: Gen. 1.16, "let us make man," and 2.7, "God formed man." Again, 1.17, "God created man." These undermine the distinction that the interpreters draw between these words. At the least they show that it is not a constant one.

units.la: Homo] hominis appellatione tam feminam quam masculum contineri ait Cajus lib. 10. Hieronymus quoque, hominis nomen, inquit, tam viro quam foeminae convenit. Manahem Ricinensis sol. 13. col. 2. Homo denotat utrumque sexum. Nam est nomen amborum. Id firmabis auctoritate sacrarum litterarum. Vide Gen. 1.27. & 5.2. Hinc est quod dicant in tractatu Iebamoth, omnis homo qui non habet uxorem non est homo. Sub. perfectus & consummatus. Nam est tantum dimidiatus. Interdum de primo homine dicitur, etiam cum articulo. Quae de re scripsi ad Baudartium, quae de libro Belgico huc translata, cum auctario supplementoque nunc iterum divulgo.
units.tr: Man: Cajus, book 10, says that the name of man includes both woman and man. Jerome too says that the name man applies to woman as well as to man. Menahem of Recanati, sol. 13, col. 2: "Man denotes both sexes, for it is the name of both." You will confirm this by the authority of the sacred letters; see Gen. 1.27 and 5.2. Hence they say in the tractate Yebamoth: "Every man who does not have a wife is not a man" (understand: perfect and complete), for he is only half. Sometimes it is said of the first man, even with the article. What I wrote on this subject to Baudartius, and what has been translated here from the Belgian book, I now publish again, with an addition and supplement.

units.la: I. DRVSIVS
units.tr: I. Drusius

units.la: Guilielmo Baudartio suo.
units.tr: To his friend Guilielmus Baudartius.

units.la: Fœminam non esse hominem probare quidam conantur ex versione nostra, Santisque Pagnini & aliorum, qui Gen.2,25. legunt homo & uxor ejus. Quæris an recte. Et sciendum in antiqua Hieronymi esse, Adam & uxor ejus. Quomodo sane vertendum ego putarem; nisi obstaret articulus, qui propriis nominibus in hac lingua præponi non solet. Quum enim in fonte sit Haadam, ut si Græce dicas ὁ ἀνθρωπος [?], videtur potius appellativè sumendum vertendumque homo & uxor ejus. Hic no-tabis non eandem esse per omnia rationem linguæ sanctæ & aliarum. In lingua sancta, quæ & lingua Mosis, Adam & commune omnium hominum est & proprium primi parentis, qui sexu mas erat. Omitto alias linguas. In Latina homo est nomen commune, & Adam proprium dumtaxat. Id credo movit Hieronymum ut verteret, Adam & uxor ejus. Quam versionem non solicito. Nam licet Haadam constructione appellativum sit, sensu tamen proprium est, cum usurpetur de uno individuo, ut si quis dicat ὁ ποιητὴς [?] de Homero, aut Hannabi, ὁ προφήτης [?] de Mose, aut Apostolus de Paulo. Quæ Grammatici per excellentiam ita dici tradunt. Per excellentiam, id est. κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν. Iam vero ut demus veram interpretationem esse homo & uxor ejus, non tamen inde sequitur quod illi volunt. Siquidem vocabulum hominis, quod in lata significatione utrumq; sexum comprehendit Gen.1,27.& 5.2. quando stricte & anguste sumitur, usurpatur de viro sæpius, interdum de fœmina tantum, ut Ies.44.13, secundum decus hominis, id est, fœminæ aut mulieris, ut recte Ionathan [illegible, ~8 letters]. Quem locum adducens autor libri, qui Pesitha Zutartha vocatur, sol.62. col.4. Vir, inquit, est mas & homo foemina. Quorsum hæc? nempe ut robur adimant argumento, Solus vir aliquando vocatur homo, ergo fœmina non est homo: cum similiter argumentari liceat, fœmina sola vocatur homo, ergo vir non est homo. Ceterum homo de solis fœminis usurpatur etiam Num. 31. 35. ubi vetus interpres, animæ hominum sexus fœminei, quæ non cognoverant viros. De viro tantũ sumitur, cum alibi passim, tum Matth. 19.10 si talis caussa hominis cum uxore, non expedit nubere. Contra vir hominem denotat utriusque sexus. Autor More, sæpe vocant genus humanum vir. Interdum Adam significat virum sapientem ac bonum. Quo sensu olim Diogenes accensa lucerna hominum quærivisse perhibetur. Cohel. 7. 29. hominem unum de mille inveni & mulierem in his omnibus non inveni. Vbi etiam mulier pro muliere bona vel strenua qualem describit Salomo Proverb. 31. Mulierem strenuam quis inveniat? ac si diceret, difficulter inveniri potest. Revera difficilis inventu & cervo rarior albo. Vnde μισόγυνος- poeta,
units.tr: Some people try to prove that woman is not a human being from our version, and from the version of Santes Pagninus and others, which at Gen. 2:25 reads "the man and his wife." You ask whether this is right. It should be noted that the ancient Latin of Jerome reads "Adam and his wife." I would certainly translate it that way myself, were it not for the article, which is not usually placed before proper names in this language. Since the source has Haadam, which if you said ho anthrōpos [ὁ ἀνθρωπος] in Greek, it seems better taken and translated as a common noun: "the man and his wife." Here you will notice that the reasoning of the holy language and that of other languages is not the same in every respect. In the holy language, which is also the language of Moses, Adam is both the common name of all human beings and the proper name of the first parent, who was male. I leave aside other languages. In Latin, homo is a common noun, and Adam is only a proper name. I think this moved Jerome to translate "Adam and his wife." I do not worry about that version. For although Haadam is a common noun in its construction, it is a proper noun in meaning, since it is used of one individual, just as one might say ho poiētēs [ὁ ποιητὴς] of Homer, or of Hannibal, ho prophētēs [ὁ προφήτης] of Moses, or "the Apostle" of Paul. Grammarians say that such words are used in this way "by excellence," that is, kat' exochēn [κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν]. Now even if we grant that "man and his wife" is the true translation, it does not follow what they want. For the word man, which in its wide sense includes both sexes (Gen. 1:27 and 5:2), when taken strictly and narrowly, is used of the male more often, and sometimes of the female only, as at Isa. 44:13, "according to the beauty of a man," that is, of a woman or wife, as Jonathan rightly renders it [illegible]. The author of the book called Pesitha Zutartha, citing this passage at fol. 62, col. 4, says: "Man is a male, and a human being is a female." Why say this? Clearly to take the force from the argument: since the man alone is sometimes called "human being," therefore woman is not a human being; whereas one could argue in the same way: woman alone is called "human being," therefore man is not a human being. Moreover, "human being" is used of women alone also at Num. 31:35, where the old translator has "the souls of human beings of the female sex, who had not known men." It is used of the male only, as elsewhere often, and at Matt. 19:10, "if such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry." On the other hand, "man" denotes a human being of either sex. The author of More often calls the human race "man." Sometimes Adam means a wise and good man. In this sense, it is said, Diogenes once looked for men with a lit lamp. Eccl. 7:29: "one man among a thousand I have found, and a woman among all these I have not found." Here also "woman" stands for a good or capable woman, such as Solomon describes in Prov. 31: "Who can find a capable woman?" as if he said, she can be found only with difficulty. Indeed she is hard to find, rarer than a white stag. Hence the misogynist [μισόγυνος] poet:

units.la: Fœmina nulla bona est: vel si bona contigit ulla,
units.tr: No woman is good; or if any good one happens to exist,

units.la: Nescio quo satores mala facta bon'est.
units.tr: I know not by what cause, a good deed is made bad for her.

units.la: Cui assensum præbet Philosophus ille qui fœminam dixit esse ἀναγκαῖον κακὸν, hoc est, malum necessarium. Non laudo. Nam si nulla bona, quærsum illud sapientis nostri, mulier prudens à Domino: & Qui invenit uxorem, invenit bonum, & excipit favorem a Domino. Vbi bonam uxorem absolute vocat uxorem, ac si mala quæ sit, uxor dici non meretur.
units.tr: The philosopher who said that woman is [ἀναγκαῖον κακὸν] , that is, a necessary evil, agrees with this. I do not praise it. For if none is good, what of that saying of our sage: "a prudent wife is from the Lord," and "whoever finds a wife finds a good thing, and obtains favour from the Lord"? Here he calls a good wife simply "wife," as if one who is bad does not deserve to be called a wife.

units.la: Ex his liquet quid respondendum sit quærenti, an fœmina sit homo. Nam homo vocatur.
units.tr: From these points it is clear what should be answered to the one who asks whether woman is a human being. For "human being" is applied:

units.la: 1. Adam, id est primus homo κατ' ἐξοχήν.
units.tr: 1. to Adam, that is, the first man, by excellence.

units.la: 2. Vir tantum.
units.tr: 2. to the man only.

units.la: 3. Mulier tantum.
units.tr: 3. to the woman only.

units.la: 4. Tam vir quam mulier.
units.tr: 4. to man and woman alike.

units.la: Ergo, Fœmina est homo, falsum in prima et secunda acceptione, & in tertia & quarta verum.
units.tr: Therefore, "woman is a human being" is false in the first and second senses, and true in the third and fourth.

units.la: Viro Adam dictus Adam a terra, unde formatus fuit, quam Adama vocant. Sic Homo ab humo. Quid rides Quintiliane? Nam licet omnium animalium eadem origo, homo peculiariter appellatus fuit ab humo: unde ei nomen. Adama proprie humus, quæ colitur, a colore sic appellata, quem exhibet, teste Iosepho Orig. Iudaic. lib. 1. cap. 2. ν πυρρόν, cum alia sit pulla, vel cinericea, &c. In Procopio Iesa. 15. habetur γαῖα Σιων: unde forsitan Hesychius, Adamus, γαῖα Σιων. Terra virgo, id est, incorrupta, & rufus id est Adom. Quæritur fueritne Adam creatus in paradiso, an extra paradisum? Quidam illud, alij hoc censent. Pro his facit locus qui habetur Gen. 2, 15. Et collocavit eum (Deus) in horto Eden, nempe translatum ex eo loco, in quo conditus fuerat, hoc est, ut quidem traditio habet, ex monte Moria. Ionathan diserte, Et traduxit Dominus Deus hominem e monte cultus, loco ubi ubi creatus fuerat, & collocavit eum in monte Eden. Salmanticensis Iudæus in libro Iobasin, Ibi homo primus obtulit oblationem, & inde creatus fuit. Loquitur de illo monte, in quo Davidis ævo fuit area Ornan Iebusæi. Idem ait traditionem esse, quæ in omnium manu versetur.
units.tr: Adam was named from the earth from which he was formed, which they call Adama. So "man" comes from humus, ground. Why do you laugh, Quintilian? For although all animals have the same origin, man was called by a special name from the earth, and from that comes his name. Adama is properly the ground that is tilled, so called from its colour, which, as Josephus witnesses in Antiquities book 1, chapter 2, is red [πυρρόν], though other soil is dark or ashen, etc. In Procopius on Isaiah 15 we find "the land of Zion" [γαῖα Σιων], whence perhaps Hesychius says: Adamus, "the land of Zion." A virgin earth, that is, uncorrupted, and red, that is, Adom. It is asked whether Adam was created in paradise or outside it. Some hold the one view, others the other. The passage at Gen. 2:15 supports this: "And God placed him in the garden of Eden," namely, moved from the place where he had been formed, that is, as tradition indeed has it, from Mount Moriah. Jonathan plainly says: "And the Lord God brought the man down from the mountain of worship, the place where he had been created, and placed him on the mountain of Eden." The Jew of Salamanca in the book Iobasin says: "There the first man offered a sacrifice, and from there he was created." He speaks of that mountain on which, in David's time, was the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. He says that this is a tradition that is in everyone's hands.

units.la: Mulieri Eva nomen fuit [scribendum Heva cum aspiratione]. Adhibui sicilicum ex Isidoro. Is indicat litteram, cui superimponitur, geminandam esse, cuius locoesl dages in scriptura Ebraica. Critici Ebræorum elegerunt Hava. Forte quia Heva in sermone Syrorum serpens fœmina. Eusebius in libris [illegible, ~12 letters] pag. 40. [illegible, ~20 letters] Heva aspiratum est serpens fœmina. Conjectura huic firmanda est Epiphanius, lib. 3. contra hæreses, tom. 2. Eva citra aspirationem Ebræis mulierem, cum aspiratione serpentem significat. Miseret me patrum quando talia lego. Heva, id est, חוה. id adhuc quæro חוה & חוה mihi lecta observataque apud Thargumistas. In Clementis quoq; Protreptico habetur Hevia, pag. 8 edit. lat. Verba sunt, Si accurate spectetur vox Ebraica, nomè Hevia adspiratu exponitur serpens fœmina. חוה Hevja. prisci, est ut חלל Hellel. Nunc esset Hivia. Ab hac origine in lingua Arabica חיה serpens, et in Hispaniola regione Indiæ serpentes sunt, quæ Hyvana vocantur. Quod etymon attinet, est in Heva significatio vitæ. Nam, חוה Hava vivo: unde Have, id est vive, & in Plauti Poenulo Havo donni, salve domine, quod perperam in libris Hano. Hinc intelliges quid sit in editione Græca, τὸ ὄνομα τῆς γυναικὸς αὐτῆς Ζωή. Quæ pleniora & auctiora leguntur in Chrysostomo, τὸ ὄνομα τῆς γυναικὸς αὐτοῦ Εὔα, ὅτις ἐστὶ ζωή. Puto interpretes ita edidisse. Liber nominum Ebraicorum, Eva, vita. Nam mater erat omnium viventium, ubi hominum subintelligitur: aut viventium, id est, hominum; quia sic a vita vocantur peculiariter, ut a morte mortales dicuntur. Id Ebraice sonat חיה cum schewa sub mem. In Ebræo est ad verbum, omnis viventis. Gen 3. 20. Sic creaturæ nomen generale ad solos homines restringitur. Idem dicendum de carnis vocabulo. Iosephus Ant. hist. lib 1. cap. 2. Nomen ejus Eva erat, quod significat omnium viventium matrem. Barcepha Syrus, pag. 163. De paradiso. Sciendum est vi quadam fatidica, atque divino instinctu, Adamum appellasse uxorem suam Evam: & ea verba quæ subjiciuntur, eo quod ipsa esset mater omnis viventis, non Adami, sed Mosis esse, Evæ vocabulum ea interpretatione explicantis. Et ante, viventium vocabulo hic soli homines, non etiā bruta animalia significantur; sicut illic quoq;, Effundam spiritum meum super omnem carnem, de hominibus solis, non de pecudibus loquitur Scriptura. Vide sequentia. Nam ibi disputat cur dicta sit Mater viventium potius quam Adam Pater viventium: subtilius tamen quam verius.
units.tr: The woman's name was Eve [to be written Heva with aspiration]. I have used the sicilicus from Isidore. He indicates that the letter over which it is placed must be doubled, whose place in Hebrew writing is taken by the dagesh. The critics of the Hebrews have chosen Hava. Perhaps because Heva in the speech of the Syrians means a female serpent. Eusebius in his books [illegible] p. 40 [illegible] Heva with aspiration means a female serpent. This conjecture is to be confirmed by Epiphanius, book 3 against heresies, vol. 2: Eva without aspiration means woman to the Hebrews, with aspiration it means serpent. I pity the Fathers when I read such things. Heva, that is, חוה. I still ask about חוה and חוה, which I have read and noted among the Targumists. In Clement's Protrepticus also we find Hevia, p. 8 of the Latin edition. The words are: "If the Hebrew word is examined closely, the name Hevia is explained with aspiration as a female serpent." Hevja [חוה] of the ancients is like Hellel [חלל]. Now it would be Hivia. From this origin in the Arabic language [חיה] means serpent, and on the island of Hispaniola in India there are serpents called Hyvana. As to the etymology, Heva has the meaning of life. For [חוה] Hava means I live, whence Have, that is, live, and in Plautus's Poenulus "Havo donni," that is, "hail, master," which in the books is wrongly given as Hano. From this you will understand what is meant in the Greek edition: "the name of his wife was Zoē" [τὸ ὄνομα τῆς γυναικὸς αὐτῆς Ζωή]. The fuller and enlarged reading is found in Chrysostom: "the name of his wife was Eua, which is life" [τὸ ὄνομα τῆς γυναικὸς αὐτοῦ Εὔα, ὅτις ἐστὶ ζωή]. I think the translators published it thus. The book of Hebrew names: Eva, life. For she was the mother of all living, where "of human beings" is understood, or "of the living," that is, of human beings; because they are called specially from life, as mortals are named from death. In Hebrew this sounds like חיה with a schwa under the mem. In Hebrew it is literally "of every living thing." Gen. 3:20. In this way the general name of creature is restricted to human beings alone. The same must be said of the word "flesh." Josephus, Antiquities book 1, chapter 2: "Her name was Eve, which means mother of all living." Barhebraeus the Syrian, p. 163, on Paradise: It must be known that by a certain prophetic power and divine impulse Adam called his wife Eve, and that the words which follow, because she was the mother of every living*, belong not to Adam but to Moses, who explains the name Eve by this interpretation. And earlier, by the word "living" only human beings are meant here, not also brute animals; just as there too, "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh," Scripture speaks of human beings only, not of cattle. See what follows. For there it disputes why she was called "mother of the living" rather than Adam "father of the living": more subtly, however, than truly.

units.la: Mulieri] Vbi quædam editiones habent, vocabitur mulier quia de viro sumpta est: malim, vocabitur vira quia de viro sumpta est. Quod olim notavi ante annos 24. plus minus. Nam virago, quod in antiqua Hieronymi, aliud est. Vox Ebræa etiam uxorem denotat. Sic γυνὴ[?] apud Græcos tam uxor quam mulier. In Genesi magno lestum[?], Qui caret uxore, caret bono, auxilio, gaudio, benedictione, expiatione. R. Iosua, nomine. R. Levi addit, etiam vita. R. Hija filius Gamri dicit, non est homo perfectus. In Capitulis R. Iofe: est absque muro, absque gloria, divitiis, corona, favore. Quæ firmata invenies testimoniis divinarum litterarum in Manabemo, comment. super Mosen, sol.20.col 2.
units.tr: To the woman: Some editions read "she will be called woman because she was taken out of man." I would prefer "she will be called vira because she was taken out of vir." I noted this about twenty-four years ago, more or less. Virago, which appears in Jerome's old text, is a different word. The Hebrew word also denotes a wife, and the Greek [γυνὴ] likewise means both wife and woman. In the great Genesis commentary (Bereshit Rabbah) it is said: "He who lacks a wife lacks good, help, joy, blessing and atonement." Rabbi Joshua, in the name of another, says this. Rabbi Levi adds "and life." Rabbi Hija, son of Gamri, says "he is not a complete man." In the Capitula of Rabbi Jose it is said: "He is without a wall, without glory, riches, crown or favour." You will find these sayings confirmed by testimonies from the divine letters in Menahem, Commentary on Moses, p. 20, col. 2.

units.la: Sed constituti in Paradiso] a Deo collocati fuerunt in Paradiso, translati eo e terra, unde formati fuerant. Quod probo his locis. Gen. 2.8. Et plantaverat Dominus Deus hortum in Eden ab oriente, & posuerat ibi hominem quem formaverat, & vers.15. Et accepit sive tulit Dominus Deus hominem & collocavit eum in horto Eden ad colendum eum & ad custodiendum eum. 3,23. Et emisit eum Dominus Deus ex horto Eden, ad colendum humum, unde sumptus fuerat.
units.tr: But placed in Paradise: God set them in Paradise, having transferred them there from the earth from which they had been formed. I prove this from these places. Genesis 2:8: "And the Lord God had planted a garden in Eden eastward, and there he put the man whom he had formed." Verse 15: "And the Lord God took the man and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it." Genesis 3:23: "And the Lord God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he had been taken."

units.la: De hac humo traditio est apud Ebræos, cujus supra meminimus: quam roborat Ionathan Uzielides[?] verba Mosis, pulverem e terra, interpretans, pulverem e domo sanctuarii. Meminit & autor Iohasiu[?], sol. 9. ubi de Ifahaco[?].
units.tr: There is a Hebrew tradition about this ground, which I mentioned above. Jonathan ben Uziel confirms it, interpreting the words of Moses, "dust from the earth," as "dust from the house of the sanctuary." The author Johasiu also mentions it, p. 9, where he speaks of Ifahacus.

units.la: In Paradiso] terrestri, qui in nostra terra, Erat alius cœlestis, de quo Christus, hodie mecum eris in Paradiso. Hunc Ebræorum sapientes ajunt receptaculum animarum esse post hanc vitam. Unde dicitur, Quies ejus Eden, id est, Paradisus. Nam breviter dictum pro hortus Eden. Qua de re alias. Porro terrestrem Adami Paradisum fuisse cum fluvii, qui ex eo manant, attestantur, tum illud imprimis quod legatur plantatus in Eden ad orien-tem. tem. Eden locus erat in Babylonia, quæ ad orientem Iudææ. Scio Sulpicium aliter sensisse, sed ego nunc verum, non Severi sequor.
units.tr: In Paradise: the earthly Paradise, which is in our world. There was another, heavenly Paradise, of which Christ said, "Today you will be with me in Paradise." The wise men of the Hebrews say that this is the receptacle of souls after this life. Hence it is said, "Her rest is Eden, that is, Paradise," for "Paradise" is used briefly for the garden of Eden. I will treat this matter elsewhere. Moreover, that Adam's Paradise was earthly is attested both by the rivers that flow from it, and above all by the fact that it is said to have been planted in Eden to the east. Eden was a place in Babylonia, which lies east of Judea. I know that Sulpicius thought otherwise, but I follow the truth here, not Severus.

units.la: Cum interdictam sibi arborem degustassent] præceptum homini erat ne vescerentur de arbore scientiæ boni ac mali, quæ in medio Paradisi, idque sub hac pœna, Quocumq; die comederis ex ea, moriendo morieris.
