Gen. 2.17. Id explicant, mortalis eris. Sed extendi debet. Nam in omnia genera mortium hoc facto incurrit. Harum prima & gravissima est mors animæ, quæ & mors secunda dicitur. Proxima est mors peccatorum. Peccatores enim pro mortuis habentur, & sic etiam vocantur, ut ibi, Sine ut mortui sepeliant mortuos suos. Tertia est mors corporis sive naturalis: & quarta mors calamitatum, quæ ærumnis plena. Sane misera vita mors est, non vita.
units.tr: When they had eaten of the tree forbidden to them: the command given to the man was not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which stood in the middle of Paradise, under this penalty: "In whatever day you eat of it, dying you shall die" (Genesis 2:17). Commentators explain this as "you shall be mortal." But it ought to be extended, for by this act he incurred every kind of death. The first and gravest of these is the death of the soul, which is also called the second death. The next is the death of sinners, for sinners are regarded as dead, and are so called, as in "Let the dead bury their dead." The third is the death of the body, or natural death; and the fourth is the death of calamities, which are full of woes. Indeed, a wretched life is death, not life.

units.la: Interdictam arborem ]arborem dixit cum ejus fructum significaret. Hanc arborem vulgus malum fuisse putat; sed vulgus & ideo errat. Nam neque ratio est quæ hoc doceat, neque autoritas ulla. Unde igitur nata illa opinio? Si conjecturæ locus, existimo ex pomi vocabulo, quo usi sunt plerique omnes veteres, nam esse. Pomum aliud Gallice sonat, aliud Latine. Galli dicunt vne pomme, & pro malo usurpant, quod Belgis <bl>esseen appel</bl>. Sed in Latio pomi vox latius patet. Nam etiam ficum comprehendit. Ficum autem fuisse hanc arborem multi patrum opinantur. Pomum ergo vetitum erat, ficus, si credendum Theologis veteribus. Testantur idem ex Ebræis R. Salomo & alii nonnulli. Sunt tamen qui citrum, plures vitem, aliqui frumentum fuisse autumant. Nec obstat arboris nomen, quum vox Ebraica etiam de culmo dicatur. Sed operæpretium est audire rationes, quas adferunt, qui de ficu suspicantur. Hugo de sancto Victore, Confuerunt folia ficus, & fecerunt sibi perizomata. Per hoc quidam existimat ficum fuisse lignum scientiæ boni & mali, & quia Dominus dixit ad Nathanaelem, priusquam te Philippus vocaret, cum esses sub ficu, novi te. Theodoretus, sive Theodoritus, Arborem fici puto fuisse, ex qua præceptum fuerit Adam ne comederet, cujusque ex foliis confutis tegumenta sibi pudendorum confecerint. Idem scribit Gennadius. Quin traditio hac de re apud majores erat, cujus meminit Isidorus Pelusiota per hæc verba, Quædam secreta ratio hanc quoque rem comitatur, quæ a senioribus atque majoribus nostris nobis tradita est, arborem scilicet transgressionis Adam ficum fuisse, ex cujus etiam Foliis scitexerit. Moses Barcepha Syrus de Parad. parte prima, capite decimonono, Censent quidam frumentum fuisse hanc arborem, atq; ideo Christum quoque suum corpus in pane dedisse, ut qua re contractum esset debitum, eadem & exsolveretur. Rursus alii vitem fuisse contendunt, & idcirco sanguinem suum dedisse Christum in vino pro expiāda primorum parentum noxa.
units.tr: The forbidden tree: he said "tree" when he meant its fruit. The common people think this tree was an apple tree, but the common people err here too. For there is no reason that teaches this, nor any authority. Whence, then, did that opinion arise? If there is room for conjecture, I think it arose from the word pomum, which nearly all the ancients used. Pomum sounds one thing in French and another in Latin. The French say une pomme and use it for apple, which the Belgians call esseen. But in Latin the word pomum has a wider range, for it also includes the fig. Many of the Fathers think this tree was a fig tree. So the forbidden fruit was a fig, if we are to trust the ancient theologians. Rabbi Solomon and some others among the Hebrews testify to the same. Yet some say it was the citron, many the vine, and some think it was grain. Nor does the name of the tree stand in the way, since the Hebrew word is also used of a stalk. But it is worth hearing the reasons which those give who suspect a fig. Hugh of Saint Victor: "They sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths." From this some conclude that the fig was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and because the Lord said to Nathanael, "before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I knew you." Theodoret, or Theodoritus, says: "I think it was a fig tree from which Adam was commanded not to eat, and from whose leaves, when sewn together, they made coverings for their private parts." Gennadius writes the same. Indeed, there was a tradition on this matter among our forefathers, which Isidore of Pelusium mentions in these words: "A certain hidden reason also accompanies this matter, which was handed down to us by our elders and ancestors: that the tree of transgression was the fig tree of Adam, from whose leaves they also sewed." Moses Bar-Cepha the Syrian, On Paradise, part one, chapter nineteen, says: "Some judge that this tree was grain, and that for this reason Christ also gave his body in bread, so that the debt incurred by the same means might be paid by the same means. Again, others contend that it was the vine, and for this reason Christ gave his blood in wine, to expiate the offence of our first parents."

units.la: Sed nos hæc vera non esse putamus: frumentum enim seges non arbor dicitur, ut neque vitis. Igitur Philoxenus Mabugensis oratione de arbore vitę, & multi alii existimant ficum fuisse eam arborem, qua, cum esset Adamo interdictum, non abstinuit. Huic sententiæ nos quoque ut verisimiliori subscribimus. Credibile enim est simul atque de ea arbore edessent, pudore correptos ex eo quod proxime ad manum erat, subligaculä sibi comparavisse, quibus sua obvelarent pudenda. Ea vero ex sculptéis fuisse foliis facta testatur ipsa Scriptura. Nequeenim simile veri potest existimari, ipsos prætermissa ea arbore, quæ proxima erat, ad aliam longiuscule dissitam festinasse, ex cujus foliis concinnatis subligaculis suam contegerent nuditatem. Erat ergo ficus arbor illa scientiæ boni & mali, qua non vesci cum essent jussi, non paruerunt edicto. Hæc homo Syrus, Quid Ebræi? Iam diximus. Manahem Rakinenfis in Mosen, Quæ-nam erat illa arbor, de qua comedit homo primus? R. Juda filius. R. Elai dicit uvas fuisse, Et mox, dixerunt arborem illam, de qua comedit primus noster parens, vitem fuisse. Et aliquanto post, R. Meir ait arborem illam, de qua comedit primus homo, vitis erat. Quanquam partim doctorum dicunt frumentum fuisse, ut R. Abba citrum. Hucusque Manahem ille. Pirke R. Eliezer, invenit Noe vitem, quæ ejecta fuerat e paradiso. Vide Manahemum 24. & 40, 4. In tractatu Sanhedrin, cap. 8.
units.tr: But we do not think these things are true. For grain is called a crop, not a tree, and neither is the vine. Therefore Philoxenus of Mabbug, in his discourse on the tree of life, and many others think that the fig was the tree which Adam did not refrain from eating, although it had been forbidden. We too subscribe to this view as the more probable. For it is credible that, as soon as they had eaten of that tree, struck with shame, they made loincloths for themselves from what lay nearest to hand, with which they might cover their private parts. Scripture itself testifies that these were made of fig leaves. For it cannot reasonably be thought that they, passing over that tree which was nearest, hastened to another a fair distance away, from whose leaves they might fashion loincloths to cover their nakedness. That fig tree, then, was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which, though they were commanded not to eat of it, they did not obey. [Thus the Syrian man. What do the Hebrews say? We have already said. Menahem of Recanati on Moses: "What was that tree of which the first man ate?"] Rabbi Judah, son of... Rabbi Elai says it was grapes. And soon after: "They said that tree of which our first parent ate was the vine." And a little later, Rabbi Meir says that the tree of which the first man ate was the vine. Yet some of the learned say it was grain, as Rabbi Abba says the citron. Thus far Menahem. Pirke Rabbi Eliezer says Noah found the vine, which had been cast out of Paradise. See Menahem, p. 24 and 40, 4. In the tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 8.

units.la: R. Meir dicit, arbor illa, de qua comedit homo primus, vitis erat: nulla enim res adducit hominem ad ejulatum præter vinum. R. Juda dicit, Frumentum erat, quia puer non potest vocare patrem aut matrem nisi gustato frumento. R. Nehemia dicit, ficus erat. Nam quare corrupti, eadem correcti sunt, sicut dicitur, & confuerunt sibi folia ficus. Ceterum in ficum plures consentiunt: unde vulgo ficum appellant [illegible, ~3 letters], id est, filias fovet, eo quod ruine cælusme causam dederint primis parentibus. Gerundensis tamen ad citrum magis inclinat, quem Ebraice Hadar dici scribit, & Syriace Ethrog, a desiderio sive cupiditate quod est Ragag. Cui firmando quod in Breseth rabba, dicit R. Abba, Citrus erat. Hoc est quod habetur Gen.3.6. Et vidit mulier bonam esse arborem. Dicit Rabba, Exi & vide num arbor sit cujus lignum edatur sicut fructus ejus, & non invenies nisi citrum. Vide sis dictum Manahemum sol.24. col.4. Videatur quoque Nicetas in Gregorium, pag.446. ubi scribit quosdam in ea sententia esse ut putent arborem scientiae boni & mali ficum fuisse. Temporarius ficum Indicam fuisse probat ex eo quod habetur apud Mosen, Gen.3.8. Abscondit se homo & uxor ejus, a facie Domini Dei, in medio arboris horti. Nam id sub ficu Indica commode fieri certum est. Quasi vero non possit exponi in medio arborum horti. Mihi nullum dubium quin haec expositio melior sit. Nicolaus de Lyra Gen.3.7. ad locum consuerunt folia ficus, Ebraeorum opinionem de ficu adstruit his verbis, ex hoc dicunt Ebraei quod ficus erat arbor de cujus fructu comederunt.
units.tr: Rabbi Meir says: that tree of which the first man ate was the vine, for nothing brings a man to lamentation except wine. Rabbi Judah says: it was grain, because a child cannot call his father or mother until he has tasted grain. Rabbi Nehemiah says: it was a fig. For by what they sinned, by the same they were corrected, as it is said, "and they sewed fig leaves together." Moreover, most agree on the fig; hence the common people call it [illegible, about three letters], that is, "it cherishes daughters," because it gave the first parents the occasion of their fall. The Gerundensis, however, leans more towards the citron, which he writes is called in Hebrew Hadar, and in Syriac Ethrog, from desire or lust, which is Ragag. To confirm this, Rabbi Abba says in Bereshit Rabbah that the citron was the tree. This is what is found at Genesis 3:6: "And the woman saw that the tree was good." Rabbah says: "Go out and see whether there is a tree whose wood is eaten as its fruit is, and you will find none except the citron." Let Menahem be consulted, p. 24, col. 4. Nicetas on Gregory, p. 446, may also be consulted, where he writes that some hold the view that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was the fig. Temarius proves that it was the Indian fig from what is found in Moses, Genesis 3:8: "The man and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord God in the midst of the trees of the garden." For it is certain that this could conveniently happen under an Indian fig. As if it could not be explained as "in the midst of the trees of the garden." To me there is no doubt that this explanation is the better. Nicholas of Lyra, on Genesis 3:7, at the words "they sewed fig leaves together," supports the opinion of the Hebrews about the fig in these words: "From this the Hebrews say that the fig was the tree from whose fruit they ate."

units.la: In nostram velut exsules terram ejecti sunt] sentit cum iis qui paradisum extra nostrum orbem constituunt: de quo in hunc modum B. Augustinus ad Orosium, Paradisus in oriente situs est, interjecto oceano, & a nostro orbe longe remotus, in altissimo loco constitutus, pertingens usque ad lunarem circulum. Et venerabilis Beda, Quod dicimus a principio, antiqua traslatio dicit, ad orientem. Unde volunt in orientali parte esse paradisum, longo interjacente spatio vel maris vel terrae, a regionibus, quas incolunt homines, secretum: unde nec aquae diluvij illuc pervenerunt. Et Strabus, Quidam codices habent Eden ad ortum: ex quo posumus conjicere paradisum in oriente situm. Vbicunque autem sit[?], scimus eum terrenum esse, & interjecto oceano montibusque oppositis remotissimum a nostro orbe, in alto situm, pertingente ad lunare circulum. Barcepha Syrus, pag.35. Quidam ultra mare paradisum constituunt, & mare ibi navigabile esse ajunt. Alii inter mare positum tradunt, verum ob montes invios nemine illuc accessisse. Sic fere omnes alij patres. Quos falli ac decipi tam certum mihi, quam certum orientem paradisi Mosaici Judææ orientem, non solis dici. Nec obstat quod ex hac falsa opinione veterum orta sit consuetudo precandi orientem versus, apud omnes Christianos usitata: qui etiam templa sua sic extruunt ut ea pars, in quo sacerdotes versantur, quem chorum indigitant, semper orientem respiciat, quasi hoc modo declaremus nos expetere et desiderare locum, unde parentes nostri sua culpa ejecti fuerunt. Nihil verius. Ceterum ejecti sunt ne vescerentur de arbore vitae cujus fructum si semel degustassent, vixissent in sempiternum, cum poena gustatae arboris interdictae esset mors. Nam si non peccassent, immortales fuissent. Manahemus in Mosen sol. 10, col. 1. Dicunt sapientes nostri, nisi homo peccasset, non fuisset unquam moriturus. Nam anima, quae ipsi adflata divinitus, dedisset ei vitam in aeternum.
units.tr: They were driven out into our land, as if exiles. He agrees with those who place Paradise outside our world. On this, Saint Augustine writes to Orosius: Paradise lies in the east, beyond the ocean, far removed from our world, set in a very high place, reaching up to the circle of the moon. And the venerable Bede: "What we say from the beginning, the ancient translation says, 'to the east.' So they hold that Paradise is in the eastern part, set apart from the regions inhabited by men by a long stretch of either sea or land; for this reason the waters of the Flood never reached it." And Strabus: "Some codices have Eden at the east, from which we may conjecture that Paradise lies in the east. Wherever it is, we know that it is earthly, and, with the ocean between and mountains opposed, most remote from our world, set high, reaching up to the circle of the moon." Barcepha the Syrian, p. 35: "Some place Paradise beyond the sea, and say that the sea there is navigable. Others say it lies within the sea, but that because of impassable mountains no one has reached it." Almost all the other Fathers say much the same. I am as certain that these men are mistaken and deceived as I am certain that the east of Moses' Paradise is the east of Judea, not the east of the sun. Nor is it an objection that this false opinion of the ancients gave rise to the custom of praying toward the east, common among all Christians. They also build their churches so that the part where the priests stand, which they call the choir, always faces east, as if by this we declared that we long for and desire the place from which our parents were cast out through their own fault. Nothing could be truer. Moreover, they were cast out so that they would not eat of the tree of life; had they once tasted its fruit, they would have lived for ever, whereas the penalty for tasting the forbidden tree was death. For if they had not sinned, they would have been immortal. Manahem on Moses, sol. 10, col. 1: "Our wise men say: if man had not sinned, he would never have been destined to die, for the soul breathed into him by God would have given him life for ever."

units.la: Velut exules] ut loquitur circumspecte. non dicit exsules; sed, velut exsules. Nam exul est proprie, quia solo patrio exulat. Illi tantum exulabant e paradiso, traducti eo e terra nostra, de qua sumpti erant. Quae illis terra patria, non paradisus. In Basilij tamen anaphora, quam ex Syrorum lingua transtulit Andreas Masius Bruxellensis, legimus, Tu vero in exilium quidem misisti aequissimis judiciis tuis extra paradisum deliciarum in hunc mundum, atque ad eam ipsam terram denuo redire coegisti eum, ex qua desumptus fuerat.
units.tr: Velut exules] He speaks cautiously. He does not say "exiles" but "as if exiles." For an exile is properly one who is banished from his native soil. They were removed from Paradise, having been brought there from our land, from which they had been taken; that land was their native land, not Paradise. Yet in Basil's anaphora, which Andreas Masius of Brussels translated from the Syriac language, we read, "You indeed sent them into exile, by your most just judgments, out of the paradise of delights into this world, and compelled them to return again to that very earth from which they had been taken."

units.la: Cain] κτᾶμαι τὸ קָנִיתִי [?] possideo, acquiro. Etymologia haec vera est, quamquam dura. Mater enim, quum eum peperet, dicebat, Acquisivi virum cum Domino. Sensus est, Domini ope atque auxilio, sive quod idem, Domino auxiliante: et virum sexu hoc est masculam prolem. Gaudebant enim de tali prole veteres. Quin hodieque mares feminis anteferuntur. Ridicule quidam, acquisivi virum Dominum. Quod Ebraice diceretur אֶת־יְהוָה [?] repetito articulo.
units.tr: Cain] Ktāmai (κτᾶμαι), "I possess, I acquire," corresponds to qanithi (קָנִיתִי). This etymology is true, though harsh. For when his mother bore him, she said, "I have acquired a man with the Lord." The sense is "with the help and aid of the Lord," or, what is the same, "the Lord helping"; and "man" here means in the male sex, that is, a male offspring. For the ancients rejoiced in such offspring, and even today males are preferred to females. Some ridiculously read "I have acquired the Lord as a man." In Hebrew this would have been et-YHWH, with the article repeated.

units.la: Abel] Antea monui scribendum esse Habel, cum aspiratione: quod nunc legunt Hebel extra pausam. Pausam voco accentum majorem distinguentem. Hebel, id est, vanitas. Recepta scriptura impositu Josepho et aliis, qui Abel, [illegible, ~6 letters] interpretantur. Id enim significat Ebel sive Abel, ultima correpta. Nam Abel ultima producta, id est, lugens.
units.tr: Abel] I have already noted that it should be written Habel, with the aspirate, which they now read as Hebel outside a pause. I call a pause the major accent that marks a division. Hebel means vanity. The received spelling follows Josephus and others, who interpret Abel as [illegible]. For Ebel or Abel with the last syllable short means that, whereas Abel with the last syllable long means mourning.

units.la: Cain impius] רָשָׁע [?] improbus aut impius proprie. Dicebat enim, teste Ierosolymitano, non est judex, neque judicium, neque praemium, neque poena, neque futurum seculum, etc,
units.tr: Cain the impious] Rasha (רָשָׁע) properly means "wicked" or "impious." For he said, according to the Jerusalem Targum, "There is no judge, nor judgment, nor reward, nor punishment, nor world to come," etc.

units.la: Pag.5. A quo primum civitas condita erat. Non enim a filio condita fuit, sed a patre, qui eam de filij nomine Henoch sive Henochiam appellavit. Res nimis clara. Tamen in eundem lapidem impegit Cajetanus, ita scribens: Alter Henoch primus inter malos primum locum obtinet a Cain, in terra condit ciuitatem, radicem spei sue ponit in terra. Hujus urbis inquit Nauclerus; hodie maxima & ingentis molis fundamenta visuntur juxta montem Libanum, & vocatur ab incolis, Civitas Cain, ut nostri mercatores & peregrini referunt, qui in Damasco & Libano sunt assueti, secundum Ioh. Viterbiensem. Fides horum penes Viterbiensem esto. Ispatrum memoria nobis obtrusit Berosum, & multis imposuit. Unde apud me non est plane [?]. Sed quare Cain urbem condidit? An ut in ea tutus esset? Sunt qui scribant eum in perpetuo metu fuisse, verentem ne homines, qui tunc omnes fratres aut fratrum filii erant, eadem Habeli consanguinei sui vindicarent. Atque hoc initium fuit, ut putatur, condendarum urbium.
units.tr: P. 5. "By whom the city was first founded." For it was not founded by the son but by the father, who named it after his son, Henoch or Henochia. This is a very plain matter. Yet Cajetan stumbled over the same stone, writing thus: "The other Henoch, first among the wicked, holds the first place after Cain; he founds a city in the land and places the root of his hope in the earth. Of this city, says Nauclerus, the greatest and huge foundations are seen today near Mount Lebanon, and the inhabitants call it the City of Cain, as our merchants and foreigners report, who are accustomed to be in Damascus and Lebanon, according to John of Viterbo." Let the trust in these men rest with John of Viterbo. In our fathers' memory Berosus has been thrust upon us and has deceived many; so with me it is not plainly [?]. But why did Cain found a city? So that he might be safe in it? Some write that he lived in constant fear, dreading that men, who were then all brothers or sons of brothers, would avenge Abel, their kinsman, upon him. And this, it is thought, was the beginning of founding cities.

units.la: Autoris nomine vocitata] hic autor conditorem significat. Nam qui aliquod opus condidit, autor dicitur. Cicero, praeclarus ille autor suae civitatis.
units.tr: "Called after the name of the author": here "author" means the founder. For whoever founded some work is called its author. Cicero: "that famous author of his state."

units.la: Vocitata] pro vocata. Cicero, Demetrius qui Phalereus vocitatus est. Plautus, Pegminum vocitatus est. Rursum Cicero, Quas nostri septem toliti vocitare triones. Infra 97. Quem in Chronicis Evilmerodach fuisse vocitatum reperi: & pag. 112. Rex Nabuchodonosor a Iudaeis vocitatus est. Sic pag. 102. Artaxerxe rege Persis imperante, pro imperante.
units.tr: "Vocitata" for "vocata." Cicero: "Demetrius who was called [vocitatus] Phalereus." Plautus: "Pegminum was called." Again Cicero: "which our people call [vocitare] the seven plough-oxen." Below, p. 97: "whom I found to have been called Evilmerodach in the Chronicles," and p. 112: "King Nebuchadnezzar was called by the Jews." So on p. 102: "Artaxerxes being king of Persia," where "imperante" is used in place of "vocitante."

units.la: Irad] miror, si hoc ita scripsit Severus, si non transcripsit ex novella Hieronymi. Nam in libris omnibus Graecis est γαιδάδ[?] (ita scribendum, non γαιδὰδ cum diaeresi) Gen. 4.18 ut & apud Augustinum de civitate Dei lib. 15. cap. 20. Gaidad. In qua Scriptura primum ain per γ expressa, ut in [illegible, ~2 letters] Gaza, & similibus: deinde Daleth lectum praesens, qui error frequens est in illis libris. Nam affinitas magna inter has litteras, quae, tenuë apice distinguuntur. Postremo chirec longum per αι expressum, ut sferi in En-regel, Asyeayλ: Engaddi, Assyaddi[?] etc.
units.tr: Irad] I am surprised if Severus wrote this so, unless he copied it from Jerome's new translation. For in all the Greek books it is [gaidad] (so it should be written, not with a diaeresis on the second alpha), Gen. 4.18, as also in Augustine, City of God, book 15, chapter 20: Gaidad. In this name the aleph is first expressed by gamma, as in Gaza and similar words; then the daleth is read as a resh, an error frequent in those books, for there is a great affinity between these letters, which are distinguished only by a thin stroke. Lastly, the long chireq is expressed by ai, as in En-regel, Asyeayl, Engaddi, Assyaddi, etc.

units.la: Maviael] ita Hiero. Quem forte Severus nunc secutus est. Nam in Graecis μαλελεήλ[?], perspicuo errore, cum Maleleel alius fuerit. Vide Gen. 5.13, Editio ad exemplar Complutense [illegible, ~6 letters]. Forte legi μαυιὰλ[?], vel certe μαυϊὰλ[?], id est, מְחוּיָאֵל[?]. Nunc legunt alij apicibus מַחוּיָאֵל[?] Mehujael vel Mahujael. In Augustini loco citato Mavichel (alias Mavibel) ut apud Eusebium Mevia & Maviael. Hoc posterius correctum videtur ex Hiero, editione. Debet autem legi per u vocalem et j consonam. Vulgo Maviabel, inserta aspiratione, quæ hic consistere nequit, non magis sane quam in Iohel & similibus. Quæ ita scribuntur contra consuetudinem utriusque linguæ. Nam & aleph lenis est apud Ebræos, & Græci dictiones in medio raro aut nunquam aspirant.
units.tr: Maviael] So Jerome, whom perhaps Severus now follows. For in the Greek, by an obvious error, it is [Maleleel] though Maleleel was another person; see Gen. 5.13, the Complutensian edition [illegible, about six letters]. Perhaps I read [Mauiel], or certainly [Mauiel], that is, Mehuiael. Others now read, with vowel points, Mehuiael or Mahuiael. In Augustine's passage cited, it is Mavichel (otherwise Mavibel), as in Eusebius Mevia and Maviael; this latter seems corrected from Jerome's edition. It ought to be read with u as a vowel and j as a consonant. Commonly it is Maviabel, with an aspiration inserted, which cannot stand here, no more truly than in Iohel and similar names. These are written so against the custom of both languages: for aleph is soft among the Hebrews, and the Greeks rarely or never aspirate a word in the middle.

units.la: Mathusalam alibi est Mathusalem, ut etiam apud Eusebium. Sed in codicibus Græcis μαθουσάλα. Nec aliter Iosephus. Quanquam in versione antiqua, quæ Rufini esse creditur, Mathusael, Scholia Græca admonent mendum librarii esse in μαθουσάλα, rescribendum; μαθουσάλα, cum accentu in ultima. Nam alium ex posteris Seth μαθουσάλα dici, accentu in penultima. Ebræi hunc nominant מְתוּשֶׁלַח Mathusale vel Methusala: illum vero, qui ex posteris Cain, מְתוּשָׁאֵל Methusael sive Mathusael.
units.tr: Mathusala is elsewhere Mathusalem, as also in Eusebius. But in the Greek codices it is [methousala], and Josephus is no different. Although in the old version, believed to be Rufinus's, it is Mathusael. The Greek scholia warn that [methousala], with the accent on the last syllable, is a scribal error to be corrected. For another of Seth's descendants is called [methousala], with the accent on the penultimate. The Hebrews name the first Methushelach (מְתוּשֶׁלַח), that is, Mathusale or Methusala; but the other, who was among the descendants of Cain, is Methushael (מְתוּשָׁאֵל), Methusael or Mathusael.

units.la: Lamech λάμεχ[?] primum duas uxores duxisse legitur, quarum uni nomen Ada & alteri Sella. Et his tres filios genuit, videlicet ex Ada, Iabal & Iubal, & ex Sella, Thubalcain. Moses Gerundensis ait hunc Lamechum fuisse virum sapientem, qui docuerit maximum natu artem pastoritiam, & proximum ab eo musicam, tertium vero artem poliendi ferrum & æs. Vide Gen. Ibi in verbis illis, pater habitantium in tentoriis, etc. Et pater canentium cithara & organo, vocabulum pater significat primum autorem inventoremque. Quod si verum, profecto Lamech non invenit illas artes, sed ipsius filij.
units.tr: Lamech [λάμεχ] is first read to have taken two wives, one named Ada and the other Sella. By them he had three sons: namely, by Ada, Jabal and Jubal, and by Sella, Tubal-cain. Moses of Gerona says that this Lamech was a wise man who taught the eldest the art of herding, the next the art of music, and the third the art of working iron and bronze. See Gen. In those words, "father of those who dwell in tents," etc., and "father of those who play the harp and organ," the word "father" signifies the first author and inventor. But if this is true, Lamech certainly did not invent those arts; his sons did.

units.la: A quo juvenis quidam νεανίσκος[?] adolescentulus. Sic Hiero, & LXX. verba sunt, Occidi virum & juvenem, id est, virum juvenem. Nam unum duntaxat occisum fuisse, præter Severum nostrum, Theodoretus & Augustinus prodiderunt. Alij duos occisos volunt: sunt etiam qui referunt, non occidi virum. Quidam, occidam, id est, occidere possem si vellem, tantum in me roboris. Qui vertunt (Oncelos in his est) non occidi virum, &c. Verba Mosis legunt cum interrogatione, occidi virum? quasi diceat minime. Multi fabulantur occisum fuisse ab eo Cainum, & deinde alium juvenem ductorem ejus. Hunc Thubalcain fuisse conjiciunt. Fabula refertur a Salomone Iario Ebræo, & in Fasciculo temporum, & apud Rabanum Strabumque & alios. Loens autem est Gen.4.17. Quem sic ex Ebraeo non male conuertas, occidi virum pro vulnere meo, & juvenem pro livore meo. נַעַר[?] tuer[?], adolescens, juvenis, a nascendi conditione. Sæpius ætatis est. Aliquando natum denotat, ut quidem sumitur ea vox in illo Plauti, natus nemo in ædibus.
units.tr: From him came a certain young man (Greek neaniskos [νεανίσκος]), a little youth. So Jerome and the Seventy have it: "I have slain a man and a youth," that is, a young man. Theodoret and Augustine report that only one man was killed, besides our Severus. Others hold that two were killed, and some report that no man was killed at all. Some read "occidam" ("I could kill," that is, "I have strength enough to kill if I wished"). Those who translate otherwise, Onkelos among them, render "I have not killed a man," and so on. Others read Moses' words as a question, "Have I killed a man?", as if he meant "by no means." Many tell the tale that Cain was killed by him, and then by another young man, his guide, whom they conjecture to have been Tubal-cain. The story is told by Solomon Jarchi the Hebrew, in the Fasciculus temporum, and by Rabanus, Strabo and others. The passage is Gen. 4.17. It may fairly well be rendered from the Hebrew thus: "I have slain a man for my wound, and a youth for my bruise." The Hebrew word naar (youth, young man) comes from the condition of being born. It more often denotes age. Sometimes it means a son, as the word is used in Plautus: "no son in the house."

units.la: Nec tamen nomen refertur occisi] in textu sacro. Ceterum interpretes nonnulli eum nominant Thubal-cain, ut diximus. Quod non videtur mihi verisimile, cum dicat puerum vel juvenem: vel, si malis, adolescentulum. Dixisset enim tenerè[?] natum meum aut filium meum. Nam unus ex filiis ipsius erat. Iam vero quod de Caino commīniscuntur, æque vanum videtur. Siquidem Caino nota apposita fuit, ne, si quis in eum incidisset, occideretur. Gen.4. 15. posuitque Dominus in Cain signum, &c.
units.tr: The name of the slain man is not given in the sacred text. Moreover, some interpreters call him Tubal-cain, as I said. This does not seem likely to me, since the text says "a boy" or "a youth," or, if you prefer, "a little young man." For he would have said "my tender son" or "my son," since he was one of his own sons. As for what they invent about Cain, it seems equally empty. For a mark was set upon Cain so that, if anyone came upon him, he would not be killed. Gen. 4.15: "The Lord set a mark upon Cain..."

units.la: Quod quidem futuro mysterio fuisse præmissum a prudentibus æstimatur] mysterium hoc aperit Hieronymus, cujus hæc verba sunt in Glos. Ordin. Ajunt ab Adam usq; ad Christum generationes esse LXXVII. secundum Lucam. Sicut ergo septima generatione peccatum Cain solutum est (non enim judicabit Deus bis in idipsum: & qui semel receperit in vita sua, non eosdem cruciatus patietur in morte, quos passus est in vita sua) ita & Lamech, id est, totius mundi peccatum, Christi solvetur adventu. Et Alcuinus sive Al-binus Caroli magni præceptor, Peccatum Lamech, qui interpretatur humiliatus, significat dejectionem humani generis, quod præuaricante Adam corruit: nec per legem vel per circumcisionem, nec per suam justitiam surgere potuit, donec post septuaginta septem generationes, secundum Lucam, Christus in mundum veniens effusione sanguinis peccatum delevit. Unde Matth. 18.c. Non dico tibi septies, sed usq; septuagies septies, hoc est Judæum recipiendum esse post LXXVII. vindicas, si resipuerit, & Christi indul-gentiam quæsierit.
units.tr: Which the wise judge to have been sent beforehand as a sign of a future mystery. Jerome unfolds this mystery, and his words are these, in the Glossa Ordinaria. They say there are seventy-seven generations from Adam to Christ, according to Luke. Just as the sin of Cain was loosed in the seventh generation (for God does not judge twice for the same thing, and one who has once received punishment in his life does not suffer the same torments in death that he suffered in life), so too Lamech, that is, the sin of the whole world, will be loosed at the coming of Christ. And Alcuin, or Albinus, tutor of Charlemagne, writes: "The sin of Lamech, who is interpreted 'brought low,' signifies the fall of the human race, which collapsed when Adam transgressed. It could not rise again either through the law or through circumcision, nor through its own righteousness, until, after seventy-seven generations according to Luke, Christ came into the world and by the shedding of his blood blotted out the sin." Hence Matt. 18: "I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven." That is, a Jew is to be received after the seventy-seventh, if he has repented and sought the indulgence of Christ.

units.la: Seth filium procreavit] præter hunc & alios duos, qui præterea in sacris memorantur. putatur genuisse filios triginta. Quæ in sententia fuit B. Augustinus, ut patet ex libris de civit. Dei. Sed Methodus centum filios edidisse tradit (mirum unde habeat) Filias quoque aliasque dubio multas procreavit. Samuel Solem in Iohasiu[?] sol. 134. pag. 2. Postquam genuisset Seth, genuit filios & filias, secundum opinionem gentium (Christianorum-
units.tr: Seth begot a son, besides this one and two others who are also mentioned in the sacred books. He is thought to have begotten thirty sons. This was the opinion of St Augustine, as is clear from the books De civitate Dei. But Methodius records that he produced a hundred sons (where he got this, it is a wonder). He also begot daughters, and many others, no doubt. Samuel Solem, in Iohasiu, sol. 134, p. 2. After he had begotten Seth, he begot sons and daughters, according to the opinion of the Gentiles (Christians-

units.la: sexaginta. Phile in libro Antiquitatum, Initio mund Adam genuit tres filios & unam filiam. Vixitque postquam genuit Seth annos DCC. & genuit filios 12. & filias 8. Vide Gen.5.4. Hem,pœne excideræt. In Medras Ruth, Adam primus creatorum, Cain primus occidentium, Habel primus oc- ciforum, Noe primus eorum qui evaserunt, Abraham pri- mus circumcisorum, &c.
units.tr: sixty. Philo, in the book of Antiquities: At the beginning of the world Adam begot three sons and one daughter. He lived after he begot Seth 700 years, and begot twelve sons and eight daughters. See Gen. 5.4. "Hem, I had almost left it out." In the Midrash Ruth: Adam was the first of created beings, Cain the first of slayers, Abel the first of the slain, Noah the first of those who escaped, Abraham the first of the circumcised, and so on.

units.la: Seth] diftus. ωαχὰ τὸ Sath, posuit. Mater enim imposuit ei hoc nomen, dicens, Quia posuit mihi Deus semen aliud pro Habel, quem occidit Cain. Gen. 4.25. Id pro eo babendum ac si dixisset, dedit mihi semen aliud. Nam dare & ponere se mutuo explicant, Quod ita notum ut nihil magis.
units.tr: Seth: so called from the Hebrew verb sath, "he placed." For his mother gave him this name, saying, "Because God has appointed me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain slew." Gen. 4.25. This is to be taken as if she had said, "has given me another seed." For giving and placing are explained by each other, which is so well known that nothing is better known.

units.la: Cum jam tricesimum & ducentesimum annum ætatis impleficet] consentit Iosephus. Ebraei codices habent, tricesimum & centesimum. Sed paulo post, ubi Adam dicitur vixisse post genitum Seth, annos septingentos, idem referunt ofingentos ita conveniunt in numero annorum, quibus vixit Adam. Vide Gen. 5.2.
units.tr: When he had now completed his two hundred and thirtieth year. Josephus agrees. The Hebrew manuscripts have "the thirtieth and the hundredth." But shortly after, where Adam is said to have lived seven hundred years after begetting Seth, the same manuscripts give eight hundred. So they agree on the number of years Adam lived. See Gen. 5.2.

units.la: Enos] ἰνὸς. Hujus ævo cœptum est invocari nomen Domini. Gen. 4. 26. hoc est, instituti fuerunt certi ritus colendi Dominum, Verba Mosis alij reddunt, pollutum fuit invocando nomen Domini. Nam tunc, inquiunt, homines cœperunt colere Deos falsos. Prior expositio verior, meo judicio. In libro nominum Enos, homo. rete. Appellatio a dolore. Nam Anas, doluit. Nomen cum re convenit. Est enim animal ærumnis plenum. Imo ipsa ærumna & calamitas, ut est apud Herodotum. Minus rete Eusebius Enos, ἀλλʼ ἀνθρωπος. Non enim magis denotat verum homi- nem, quam Adam. In eodem, Enos, ἐπιλανθάνομαι, tanquam a 7 oblitus fuit. Quo accommodabis illud Davidis, Quid mortalis ut ejus memor sis? Nam Enos in fonte,
units.tr: Enos: [Greek Enōs]. In his age men began to call upon the name of the Lord (Gen. 4.26), that is, certain fixed rites of worshipping the Lord were instituted. Others render Moses' words: the name of the Lord was profaned by invoking it, for then, they say, men began to worship false gods. The former explanation is truer, in my judgment. In the book of names: Enos, man, mortal. The name derives from grief, for anash means "he grieved." The name agrees with the thing, for he is a creature full of troubles, indeed calamity and misery itself, as in Herodotus. Less correctly, Eusebius [says] Enos is "but man" [allʼ anthrōpos]. For it denotes the true man no more than Adam does. In the same book, Enos, [epilanthanomai], "to forget," as if he was forgotten. To what will you adapt that saying of David: "What is mortal man that you should be mindful of him?" For Enos, in the spring,

units.la: Cainan] ita refituit Gelasius, cum prius esset Nainan, per- spicuo errore scribarum. Nam in LXX. Κωνὰν sive Καινὰν, sed perperam Καϊνὰν in ed. Ro. Hieronymus quoque Cainan habet, idest, ʃʃʃ Quod nunc legunt ʃʃʃ Kenan. Sæpe hoc modo et & permutantur. Mortuus est, teste Iudæo Salmanticensi, animo mundi 1135. Idem ejus mentionem usurpari ait in epistola Alexandri ad Aristotelem scripta quæ extat in historia Ebraica lib. 2. [cap. 11.] Verba sunt, Quum veni ad terram Pharliacon dictam, quæ est regio Indiæ, in insula quadam maris offendi homines non dissimiles fœminis, qui piscibus vescebantur, lingua Græca utentes. Hi narrarunt sepultum ibi esse regem antiquum, cui nomen Cainan, filium Enos: qui ante diluvium regnabat super totum mundum. Erat autem vir sapiens & multarum artium callens, dominabaturque in spiritus & dæmones, eosque quos Mazicim appellant, id est, [illegible, ~5 letters], propterea quod noxam inferant hominibus. Is cognovit per sapientiam suam Deum inducturum diluvium super terram. Itaque scripsit in tabulis lapideis id quod futurum erat, usus scriptura Ebraica. Idem scripsit in tabulis illis tempore suo oceanum inundasse tertia parte orbis, ut etiam in diebus Enos filij Seth, filii Ada, etc. stus est, transferam eum. ex Brefith rabba, cap.25.
units.tr: Cainan: Gelasius restored it thus, when before it had been Nainan, through an obvious error of the scribes. For in the Seventy it is Kōnan or Kainan, but wrongly Kaïnan in the Roman edition. Jerome also has Cainan, which is [Hebrew qenan]; what they now read is Kenan. These letters are often interchanged in this way. He died, according to the Jew of Salamanca, in the year of the world 1135. The same author says his mention is used in Alexander's letter to Aristotle, which is found in the Hebrew history, book 2, [chapter 11]. The words are: "When I came to the land called Pharliacon, which is a region of India, on a certain island in the sea I met men not unlike women, who ate fish and used the Greek language. They related that an ancient king was buried there, named Cainan, son of Enos, who reigned over the whole world before the flood. He was a wise man, skilled in many arts, and he ruled over spirits and demons, and over those whom they call Mazicim, that is, [illegible], because they inflict harm on men. Through his wisdom he knew that God would bring a flood upon the earth. So he wrote on stone tablets what was to come, using Hebrew writing. In those tablets he also wrote that in his time the ocean had flooded a third part of the world, as also in the days of Enos, son of Seth, son of Adam, etc." He was taken, I will transfer him (Gen. 5.24). From Bereshit Rabba, ch. 25.

units.la: Translatus ]μετετέθη[illegible, ~3 letters] Usi sunt hoc verbo praeter Apostolum, Iesus Syrach Eccles. 44.18. & autor sapientiae, loco citato: qui etiam usurpat verbum ἁρπαγὴν[?], id est, raptus fuit, ut Sirachides Eccles. 49.19. verbum ἀντιληφθὴν[?] sublatus vel assumptus fuit.
units.tr: Translated [metetethē]. Besides the Apostle, Jesus son of Sirach (Ecclus. 44.18) and the author of Wisdom, in the passage cited, used this word. He also uses the word [harpagēn], that is, "was caught up," as the son of Sirach does (Ecclus. 49.19) with the word [antilēphtheis], "was taken up or assumed."

units.la: In Mose habetur וַיִּקַּח[?] accepit, tulit: & in Genesi magno, לְהַעֲלוֹת[?] ascendere faciam eum, id est, auferā ex medio vel tollam in altum. Sed quo translatus fuit in coelum an in paradisum? Hoc ille novit qui translulit. Nostrum non est, in ea, quae nos celata voluit, anxie inquirere. Porro translatus est anno mundi 987. qui erat post obitum Adae 7. Vixit igitur cum eo annos 308. autor Salmanticensis.
units.tr: In Moses it is found as [vayyiqqach], "he took, he carried." In the great Genesis it is found as [leha'alot], "I will make him ascend," that is, "I will take him out of the midst or lift him up on high." But to what place was he translated, to heaven or to paradise? He knows who translated him. It is not for us to inquire anxiously into those things which he chose to keep hidden from us. Moreover, he was translated in the year of the world 987, which was seven years after Adam's death. He therefore lived with Adam 308 years, according to the author of Salamanca.

units.la: Mathusala] μαθουσαλᾶ[?], qui & Mathusale; unde Mathusalem. Critici Ebraeorum legunt Mathusela. Vixit usque ad annum diluvij, ut Hiero. tradit. Nam quod LXX. interpretes post diluvium annos xiiij ei tribuunt, error est in numeris, cum octo tantum animae post diluvium conservatae sint, videlicet Noe cum uxore, tribus filiis & totidem nuribus. Hieronymi sententiam roborat Salmanticensis per haec verba, Annus diluvij erat 1656. eo implevit Mathusala iustus annos suos, & mortuus est paullo ante diluvium. Et mox, Deus expectavit adhuc septem dies, quibus durabat luctus Mathusalae: post adduxit super eos aquas diluvij. Quae habentur & in Brefith rabba sectione Noach ad locum. Ettuit[?] post septem dies, his verbis concepta: docet hic locus Deum suspendisse septem dies luctus ipsius Mathusale iusti, ut facerent poenitentiam & non fecerunt. Mortuus est 7. diebus ante diluvium. Samuel Solem in Iobasin[?] sol 134. p.2.
units.tr: Methuselah: [Greek Mathousalā], who is also called Mathusale, whence Mathusalem. The critics of the Hebrews read Mathusela. He lived until the year of the flood, as Jerome records. For the Seventy, who assign him fourteen years after the flood, are in error about the numbers, since only eight souls were preserved after the flood, namely Noah with his wife, his three sons and as many daughters-in-law. The Salamanca author supports Jerome's view in these words: "The year of the flood was 1656. In that year the righteous Methuselah completed his years and died a little before the flood." And soon after: "God waited yet seven days, during which the mourning for Methuselah lasted; afterwards he brought the waters of the flood upon them." These things are also found in Bereshit Rabba, in the section on Noah, at that place, and so, after seven days, in these words: this passage teaches that God suspended for seven days the mourning for Methuselah the righteous, so that they might repent, and they did not. He died seven days before the flood. Samuel Solem, in Iobasin, sol. 134, p. 2.

units.la: Lamech] Sepultus fuit an. mundi 1554. ut est apud Salmanticensem. Quod aliis examinandum relinquo. Nam in codice, Mathusale sepeliit filium suum quinquennio ante diluvium. Quae si vera, sepultus fuit an. mundi 1651. Quod autem in codicibus Ebraeis Lemech, simile est ut Hebel, Habel: lered, Iared.
units.tr: Lamech: He was buried in the year of the world 1554, according to the Salamanca text. I leave this for others to examine. In a manuscript, however, it says that Methuselah buried his son five years before the flood. If that is true, Lamech was buried in the year of the world 1651. As for the Hebrew manuscripts having Lemech, this is like Hebel for Habel, and Lered for Iared.

units.la: Noe] Noe an Noa dicas parum refert. Illud antiquum est: hoc recenti consuetudine scriptum. Recentem voco quae a temporibus Massoritarum inoleviit, quando primum coepta sunt Biblia legi cum adscriptis punctis vel apicibus. Qui Noach scribunt, perperam ex eo declinant Noachus, cum dicendum sit Nochus; sicut a Ruach dicimus Ruchoth, non Ruachoth. Noe, decimus ab Adam, natus est anno mundi 1056. anno sexcentesimo post exitit diluvium. Ab Adam ergo usque ad diluvium anni sunt, secundum Ebraeos, 1656. Quod ex hac tabula planum fiet, Adam genuit Seth an. ætatis | 130 Seth genuit Enos an. | 105 Enos genuit Cainan an. | 90 Cainan genuit Malaleel an. | 70 Malaleel genuit Iared an. | 65 Iared genuit Henoch an. | 162 Henoch genuit Mathusale an. | 65 Mathusale genuit Lamech an. | 187 Lamech genuit Noe an. | 182 Summa annorum | 1656 Vixit Noe post diluvium annos | 350 Summa igitur annorum vitæ ipsius | 950
units.tr: Noe: It matters little whether you say Noe or Noa. The first is ancient; the second was written by recent custom. I call recent what has grown up since the time of the Masoretes, when the Bibles first began to be read with points or accents attached. Those who write Noach wrongly form the oblique case Noachus, when it should be Nochus, just as from Ruach we say Ruchoth, not Ruachoth. Noah, the tenth from Adam, was born in the year of the world 1056, in the six hundredth year of which the flood came. From Adam to the flood there are therefore, according to the Hebrews, 1656 years. This will be plain from the following table: Adam begat Seth at the age of 130; Seth begat Enos at 105; Enos begat Cainan at 90; Cainan begat Malaleel at 70; Malaleel begat Jared at 65; Jared begat Enoch at 162; Enoch begat Methuselah at 65; Methuselah begat Lamech at 187; Lamech begat Noah at 182. Sum of years: 1656. Noah lived 350 years after the flood. Sum total of his life: 950.

units.la: Unde & illud sequitur mortuum esse anno mundi 2006. Nomen inditum ei a patre, qui dicebat, Iste consolabitur nos, &c. Genes. 5.29. Quocirca R. Salomo arbitratur decurtatum esse ex נחם[?] consolatio. Sed in libro nominum, Noe, requies; & Hiero. in Quæst. Ebra. dictus Noe quia sub illo omnia retro opera per diluvium quieverunt. Hinc solatium. Habetur ergo ratio sensus, non vocis.
units.tr: From this it also follows that he died in the year of the world 2006. His father gave him the name, saying, "This one will comfort us," etc. (Gen. 5.29). For this reason Rabbi Solomon thinks the name is shortened from נחם [nacham], consolation. But in the book of names, Noah means rest; and Jerome, in the Hebrew Questions, says Noah was so called because under him all the works of the earlier times ceased through the flood, and hence came the solace. So the reason is found in the meaning, not in the word.

units.la: Iustitia egregius] Gen. 6.9. Noe vir iustus integer erat in ætatibus suis.
units.tr: Outstandingly righteous: Gen. 6.9. Noah was a righteous man and blameless in his generations.

units.la: Et præ ceteris mortalibus Domino charus] Ibidem, cum Deo ambulavit Noe. Id valet, ex Dei præscripto vixit; aut, ad Dei voluntatem vitam egit. Tales quin Deo præ ceteris chari & accepti sint, non dubitabit qui rerum divinarum vel mediocrem peritiam habet.
units.tr: And dear to the Lord beyond other mortals: Ibid., Noah walked with God. This means that he lived according to God's commandment, or that he conducted his life according to the will of God. That such men are dear and acceptable to God above others, no one will doubt who has even a modest knowledge of divine things.

units.la: Qua tem-pestate] Sallustianum est. Bello Iugurthino, ea tem-pestate in exercitu nostro complures fuere. Idem ibid. so-lertissimus omnium in paucis tempestatibus factus est.
units.tr: In what season: This is Sallustian. In the Jugurthine War: "at that time there were many of us in our army." The same author also says: "he became the most skilful of all in a few campaigns."

units.la: Abundaret] abundare sive abunde copiosum esse inciperet. Gen. 6. 1.
units.tr: Abundaret: to abound, or to begin to be abundantly numerous. Gen. 6.1.

units.la: Angeli quibus cœlum sedes erat, &c.] Hujus sententiæ fuerunt ex Ebraeis Iosephus & Philo: ex Græcis, Iustinus, Tatia-nus, Proclus, Athanagoras: ex Latinis, Tertullianus, Lactantius, hic noster. Contra eam quinq; argumenta proferuntur, quæ nunc, ut potero, refutabo; non quod ita sentiam, sed ut offendam in tu[?]um argumentis, si rite expendantur, parum soliditatis esse.
units.tr: Angels, for whom heaven was a seat, etc.: Among the Hebrews, Josephus and Philo held this view; among the Greeks, Justin, Tatian, Proclus and Athenagoras; among the Latins, Tertullian, Lactantius and our author here. Five arguments are brought against it, which I will now refute as best I can. I do not hold this view myself, but I wish to show that, if they are rightly weighed, the arguments against it have little solidity.

units.la: Primum argumentum est Chrysostomi hom. 22. in Genesin, Homines filii Dei dicuntur, angeli nunquam. Hoc perspicue falsum est. Nam angeli sic dicuntur, Iob 1. 6. Vide Mifcel. cent.
units.tr: The first argument is Chrysostom's, in Homily 22 on Genesis: men are called sons of God, but angels never are. This is plainly false, for angels are so called in Job 1.6. See the Miscellanea, cent.

units.la: Secundum exstat apud Nicolaum de Lyra, qui ait diluvium hominum causa immissum fuisse, non angelorum. Id verum est, sed ex eo non sequitur quod vult Nicolaus ille. Nam angeli, cum se matrimoniis mortalibus miscuissent, paulatim mores noxios conferentes, ut cum Severo nostro loquar, humanam corrupere progeniem. Ea corrupta, diluvium secutum est, Deo humanum genus delente ob propriam malitiam, quae ultra modum excæ[?]-verat. Non ergo propter angelos, sed propter homines, licet an-geli hominibus peccandi occasionem dederint.
units.tr: The second is found in Nicolas of Lyra, who says the flood was sent because of men, not because of angels. That is true, but it does not follow what Nicolas wants. For the angels, having mingled with mortal marriages and gradually introducing harmful morals, corrupted the human race, to use the words of our Severus. When that race was corrupted, the flood followed, God destroying mankind on account of its own wickedness, which had grown beyond measure. The flood was therefore not on account of the angels but on account of men, although the angels gave men the occasion to sin.

units.la: Tertium, daemones cum sint spiritus corporis expertes venereo congressu uti non posse. Contra censent Ebræi, qui scribunt eos liberis operam dare. Augustinus quoque quaedam hac de re lib. XV. de civit. Dei. Vide sis etiam Eodinum[?] adversus Vierum, pag. 44. Quanquam sermo hic non est de filiis diaboli, sed de filiis Dei, hoc est angelis, qui ad haec inferiora detrusi humanam induere natu-ram. Vnde in Medras Ruth, facti sunt sicut homines. Nam in specie humana versati sunt cum hominibus, corpora terrena gestantes, ex quatuor elementis composita. Itaque legimus in eodem libro, Inter eos angelos qui mixti fuerunt hominibus, non fuerunt sicut illi qui בני האלהים[?], id est, viri vocantur, nec sicut illi qui filii Dei vocantur. Nam postquam a Deo deiecti fuerunt, involuti elementis humanis vestierunt se eis. Reliqui angeli cum descenderent parati fuerunt ad re-deundum in locum suum, aerea corpora habentes. Haec fere ibi. Quae produxi ut ostenderem argumentum a natura daemonum hoc loco nullius ponderis esse. Sane quidem Aza et Azael, qui hos angelos inter numerantur, nusquam daemones dicuntur, licet parentes daemonum quidam eos fuisse putent. Nam relatum in libro pervetusto Hazohar, dictos angelos, quos filios Dei autor libri vocat, consuetudine usos Naamae sororis Thubalcain, ex ea genuisse daemones, quos Sedim appellant, et spiritus malos, qui nunc in mundo.
units.tr: The third argument is that demons, being spirits without bodies, cannot engage in sexual intercourse. The Hebrews, who write that they beget children, think otherwise, and Augustine has some things to say on this matter in book 15 of The City of God. See also Eudinus against Vierus, p. 44. Yet this discussion is not about the sons of the devil but about the sons of God, that is, the angels, who, having been thrust down to these lower regions, put on human nature. Hence in Midrash Ruth they became like men: they dwelt among men in human form, bearing earthly bodies composed of the four elements. So we read in the same book: "Among those angels who mingled with men, not all were like those who are called בני האלהים [bene ha-elohim], that is, men, nor like those who are called sons of God. For after they were cast down by God, they clothed themselves in human elements and were enveloped in them. The other angels, when they descended, were ready to return to their place, having aerial bodies." That is roughly what is said there. I have brought these things forward to show that the argument from the nature of demons has no weight here. Indeed, Aza and Azael, who are counted among these angels, are nowhere called demons, although some think they were the parents of demons. For it is related in the very ancient book Zohar that the angels whom the author of that book calls sons of God used Naamah, sister of Tubal-cain, and from her begat the demons whom they call Shedim, and the evil spirits that are now in the world.

units.la: Quartum argumentum. Matth. 22, 30. habetur, In refurre-ctione neque uxores ducunt, neque nuptum dantur: sed erunt ut angeli in coelo. Respon. Fatemur angelos non celebrare nuptias in coelo: sed hic agitur de angelis, qui vel e coelo deciderant, vel certe missi erant ad haec inferiora ut humanum genus custodi-rent. Scribunt Platonici subtilia daemonum corpora, cum ad nos feruntur, erasiora[?] effici. Quod Augustinus approbare videtur. Ebraei quoq; ita de hac re opinantur. Manahemus Riciuenfis commentario in Genesin, Iosua filius Corcha dicit, angeli sunt ignis flammans: sed ea ipsa hora qua ceciderunt e loco sanctificationis suae e coelo facta est substantia eorum similis substantiae hominum, & induerunt corpus terrenum.
units.tr: The fourth argument is Matt. 22.30: "In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels in heaven." Reply: we grant that angels do not celebrate marriages in heaven, but here we are speaking of angels who either had fallen from heaven or were certainly sent to these lower regions to guard the human race. The Platonists write that the subtle bodies of demons, when they are brought to us, become thicker. Augustine seems to approve this. The Hebrews also think so about this matter. Menahem of Recanati, in his commentary on Genesis, says that Joshua son of Korcha states: "Angels are a flaming fire; but in the very hour in which they fell from the place of their holiness, from heaven, their substance was made like the substance of men, and they put on an earthly body."

units.la: Quintum argumentum. Daemones non vocantur uspiam filii Dei. Sic est profecto, nec angeli hi, dum in terris versarentur, daemones erant; sed postea tales effecti sunt, cum ob peccatum in terris admissum a Deo exclusi essent, nec in supera illa alta redire possent. Quanquam ipse quoque Satan in coelo fuisse legitur. Testis mihi autor libri Iob, qui inter filios Dei, id-est angelos Satanam ponit. Iob.1.[?] Redeamus unde digressi sumus. Dixi hujus sententiae fuisse Lactantium. Vide sodes[?] illum lib.2. de origine errorum.
units.tr: The fifth argument is that demons are nowhere called sons of God. That is indeed so, and these angels, while they were on earth, were not demons; but afterwards they became such, when, having been excluded from God because of sin committed on earth, they could not return to those heights above. Yet Satan too is read to have been in heaven. The author of the book of Job is my witness, for he places Satan among the sons of God, that is, the angels (Job 1.6). But let us return to where we digressed. I said that Lactantius held this opinion. See him in book 2 of On the Origin of Errors.

units.la: Hilarius vero scribens in Pfal. 132.[?] ait ea de recujusdam libri extitisse, in quo refertur angelos concupiscentes filias hominum, cum de coelo primum descenderent, in Phoenicia maxime celsum montem Hermon convenisse, montemque illum, si quis interpretetur, anathema sonare. Liber est Ebraeus, qui vocatur [illegible, ~4 letters] [illegible, ~7 letters], quem Serarius cum [illegible, ~6 letters] confundit.
units.tr: Hilary, however, writing on Psalm 132, says that this view arose from a certain book, in which it is related that the angels, when they first came down from heaven and desired the daughters of men, gathered in Phoenicia on the very high mountain Hermon, and that this mountain, if one interprets it, sounds like "anathema." It is a Hebrew book, which is called [illegible, ~4 letters] [illegible, ~7 letters], and which Serarius confuses with [illegible, ~6 letters].

units.la: In eo memoria usurpatur horum angelorum per haec verba, Angeli delapsi e coelo viderunt filias Cain, quae illo tempore nudae incedebant, oculos stibio pingentes, more meretricum.
units.tr: In it the memory of these angels is preserved in these words: "Angels who had fallen from heaven saw the daughters of Cain, who at that time walked about naked, painting their eyes with antimony, in the manner of harlots."

units.la: In Medrafoth R. Hanina, Viderunt filii Dei Aza & Azael, qui duo angeli fuerunt, filias hominum. Hi dominum suum accusarunt; propterea dejecti fuerunt e coelo. Quum in aerem nostrum descendissent, facti sunt similes hominib.
units.tr: In the Midrashim, Rabbi Hanina says: "The sons of God, Aza and Azael, who were two angels, saw the daughters of men. They accused their Lord, and therefore they were cast down from heaven. When they had descended into our air, they became like men."

units.la: Quae omnia fabulosa & commentitia esse prudentiores censent, nec immerito. Nam locus Geneseos, unde haec hauriunt, aliter accipi potest, imo debet. Vide quae scripsimus Miscel.cent.1.cap.25. Et in Habdala R. Aquibae, Aza & Azael secreta domini sui patefecerunt, qui pertoratis naribus eorum suspendit eos in montibus tenebricosis, ubi solem non viderunt, nec ventus flavit super facies eorum ullo tempore aut ulla hora. Nominatur etiam in libro Iobafin Ma-bafael five Machafael[?] ex filiis Dei, qui sub diluvij tempus rem habuerit cum uxore Chami, unde natus sit Sthon. Ceterum exiis[?] qui descenderunt e coelo, alij redierunt ad locum suum, alij mi-nime, ut Aza & Azael, de quibus in monumentis doctorum, dixit anima Mosis, Mundipotens domine, a latere tuo de-scenderunt duo angeli Aza & Azael, qui concupiverunt fi-lias terrae, & corruperunt viam suam in terra, donec suf-pendisti eos inter terram & coelum. Propemodum excidérat. Apud Origenem libro quinto contra Celsum ex libro Henoch re-censentur angeli e coelo delapsi sexaginta vel septuaginta. Quod an vere abs eo relatum sit, nescio. Nam filij Dei diversi sunt ab iis qui Nephilim vocantur. Gen.6.4. Hi sexaginta fuisse perhibentur. Nam scriptum ibidem, hi sunt potentes: & alibi, sex-aginta potentes circum eam[?]. Quot in terra, totidem erant in coelo. Videndus Manahen[?] in Genesin sol.17.col.1. Ne quid celem, Ionathan is qui legem interpretatum est, gigantes etiam angelos fuisse opinatur, qui a cadendo Nephilim dicti sint, quod viderunt e coelo deciderunt. Verba ejus habentur Gen.6.4. ad locum, & gigantes erant in terra: quem sic interpretatur, referente Ma-nahemo[?], Samhazai & Azael (in textu Ionathae est Oziel sive Vziel) ceciderunt e coelis & erant in terra in diebus illis. Idem, quos Moses filios Dei nominat, non angelos, sed cum Oncelo filios principum five magnatum, id est, [illegible, ~4 letters], interpretatur. Quæ commemoro ut discas in fabulis Iudaicis omnia incerta esse, nec autores earum inter se convenire.
units.tr: Those more judicious scholars think all of these things are fabulous and invented, and not without reason. The passage of Genesis from which they draw them can be, and indeed should be, understood otherwise. See what I wrote in Miscellanea, century 1, chapter 25. In the Habdala of R. Akiba, Azah and Azael revealed the secrets of their lord, and he hanged them by their nostrils on dark mountains, where they never saw the sun, and no wind ever blew on their faces at any time or hour. In the book of Iobafin, Ma-bafael or Machafael [?] is also named among the sons of God, who had relations with the wife of Ham at the time of the flood, from whom Sthon was born. Moreover, of those who came down from heaven, some returned to their place and others did not, such as Azah and Azael. Concerning them, in the records of the teachers, the soul of Moses said: "Lord, almighty, two angels, Azah and Azael, came down from your side; they lusted after the daughters of the earth and corrupted their way on the earth, until you hanged them between earth and heaven." I had almost forgotten this. In Origen, book 5 against Celsus, from the book of Enoch, angels fallen from heaven are listed as sixty or seventy. I do not know whether this is truly reported by him. For the sons of God are different from those who are called Nephilim, Gen. 6.4. These are said to have been sixty. For it is written in the same place, "these are the mighty"; and elsewhere, "sixty mighty men around her." As many were on earth as were in heaven. Manahem [?] on Genesis, see sol. 17, col. 1. Lest I conceal anything: Jonathan, who translated the Law, also thinks the giants were angels, who were called Nephilim from falling, because they fell down from heaven when they saw. His words are found at Gen. 6.4 on the passage "and there were giants in the earth"; he interprets it thus, as reported by Manahem: Samhazai and Azael (in the text of Jonathan it is Oziel or Uziel) fell from the heavens and were on the earth in those days. The same Jonathan, whom Moses calls "sons of God," not angels, interprets with Onkelos as "sons of princes or magnates," that is, [illegible, about four letters]. I mention these things so that you may learn that everything in the Jewish fables is uncertain, and that their authors do not agree among themselves.

units.la: Superioribus] comparat, pro absoluto. Supera enim dicunt pro ipsis coelis. Quod etiam substantive usurpant, ut supera alta tenentes. Talia sunt inferior, plures, iemor[?]. Quod postremum Linacer omisit.
units.tr: "Superioribus" is a comparative used for the absolute. For they say "supera" for the heavens themselves, and they also use it as a noun, as in "holding the high places above." Such are "inferior," "plures," "iemor" [?]. Linacer omitted this last one.

units.la: Matrimoniis se mortalibus miscuerunt[?]] duxerunt uxores feminas mortales. Notum ut matrimonia ponantur pro uxoribus ipsis. Sic infra p.40. matrimonia ex victis assumere. Similiter pag.67. cum adversum interdictum Dei ex alienigenis conjugia sumpsisset, id est, conjuges.
units.tr: "Matrimoniis se mortalibus miscuerunt": they took mortal women as wives. It is well known that "matrimonia" is put for the wives themselves. So below, p. 40: "to take wives from the conquered." Similarly p. 67: when he had taken marriages from foreigners against the forbidden command of God, that is, spouses.

units.la: Ex quorum coitu gigantes editi esse dicuntur] Sic quoque Iosephus, & cum Ambrosius, cuius haec verba sunt. Non
units.tr: "From whose union giants are said to have been born": so also Josephus, and Ambrose, whose words these are. Not

units.la: poetarum more terrae filios vult videri divinae scripturae conditor : sed ex angelis & mulieribus generatos asserit, quos hoc appellat vocabulo, volens eorum exprimere cor-poris magnitudinem. Haec opinio jam olim communi consensu doctorum explosa est: qui melius sentientes tradunt gigantes, quorum ibi mentio fit, procreatos fuisse ex generis nostri ejusdemq; naturae parentibus. Quod mirum non esse docet Augustinus in quaest. super Genesin ita scribens, de gigantibus, id est, nimium grandibus atque fortibus, puto non esse mirandum quod ex hominibus nasci potuerint, quia & post diluvium quidam tales fuisse reperiuntur, non solum virorum, sed etiam foeminarum. Fidem dictis adstruit aetas posterior, quae gigantes dedit etiam ex mediocris statura hominibus. Idem Augustinus de civit. Dei lib. 15. cap. 23. Ante paucos annos cum Romae urbis, quod a Gothis factum est, appropinquaret excidium, Romae fuit foemina cum suo patre & sua matre, quae corpore quodammodo giganteo longe ceteris praeminceret. Ad quam visendam mirabilis fiebat usquequaque concursus. Et hoc erat maxime admirationi, quod ambo parentes ejus nec saltem tam longi homines erant, quam longissimos videre consuevimus.
units.tr: the author of Scripture wants them to be seen as sons of the earth in the manner of the poets, but he asserts that they were born of angels and women, whom he calls by this word, wishing to express the size of their bodies. This opinion was long ago rejected by the common consent of the learned, who, judging better, teach that the giants mentioned there were born of parents of our own kind and nature. Augustine teaches that this is not surprising, in his Questions on Genesis, writing thus about giants, that is, very large and strong men: "I think it is not to be wondered at that they could be born of men, because even after the flood some such are found, not only men but also women. Later times confirm what is said, which have produced giants even from men of middling stature." The same Augustine, De civitate Dei, book 15, chapter 23: "A few years ago, when the destruction of the city of Rome by the Goths was approaching, there was a woman in Rome with her father and her mother, who in her body was in some way a giant, far surpassing the others. A wonderful crowd came from everywhere to see her. And what was especially astonishing was that her parents themselves were not even as tall as we usually see the very tallest men to be."

units.la: Gigantes] vocantur hic a Mose Nephilim, ut alij existimant, a cadendo: ut ego, ab irruendo. Naphal enim & irruere significat, ut apud Davidem, irruit validis suis in turbam attritorum. Etymo huic firmando est interpretamentum Aquilae Pontici, ἐπιπίπτοντες[?], irruentes, quod male Hiero. exponit, cadentes. Alibi gigantes vocantur Emim, a terrendo, ut Gibbarim, a robore, & Enacim, a torque, ut quidam volunt, quasi torquatos dicas: item Raphaim & Zomzommim. Quod postremum linguae Ammonitice est. Deut. 2. 20. Gigantes Raphaim habitarunt in ea, quos Ammonitae vocant Zomzommim. alias Zamzummim.
units.tr: Giants] are called here by Moses Nephilim, as others think, from falling; as I think, from rushing upon. For naphal also means to rush upon, as in David: "he rushed upon a crowd of the crushed with his strong ones." To confirm this etymology is the rendering of Aquila of Pontus, ἐπιπίπτοντες [epipiptontes], "rushing upon," which Jerome wrongly explains as "falling." Elsewhere giants are called Emim, from terrifying; Gibbarim, from strength; and Enacim, from a neck-chain, as some want, as if you should say "those with neck-chains"; likewise Raphaim and Zomzommim. The last is in the Ammonite language. Deut. 2.20: "The giants Raphaim dwelt in it, whom the Ammonites call Zomzommim," otherwise Zamzummim.

units.la: Hoc loco notabis in fontibus esse non, ex his nati sunt gigantes: sed gigantes autem erant in terra diebus illis. Unde qui colligunt eos ex filiis Dei, id est, angelis, & matrimoniis mortalibus editos esse, meo judicio, vehementer balucinantur. Sunt etiam qui hos gigantes angelos fuisse putant, in quos Ionathan Vzieli- des, cujus supra mentionem fecimus. Cave sequaris. Nugae sunt nugacissimae. Quibus annumerabis & illud quod Simphorianus Camperius Prax. lib. 2 cap. 5 scriptum reliquit, multos videlicet affirmare dæmones in succubi forma, virili femine accepto, eadem-que sub imagine incubi in sulcos muliebres ejaculata, gigantes ipsos genuisse. Vide Iosephum Ant. hist. l. 1, c. 4. Porro multa quae de gigantum proceritate & magnitudine prodita sunt vera esse probat Hieronymus Magius Miscellaneorum lib. 1. c. 4.
units.tr: In this place you will note that in the sources it is not that "from these were born the giants," but "there were giants in the earth in those days." Hence those who gather that they were born from the sons of God, that is, angels, and from mortal marriages, in my judgment greatly rave. There are also those who think these giants were angels, and Jonathan Uzzielis, whom I mentioned above, is cited for this. Beware of following him. They are the most idle trifles. Among these you may also count what Symphorianus Campererius wrote in his Praxis, book 2, chapter 5: that many affirm that demons, in the form of succubi, having received male seed, and then in the form of incubi, ejaculated into female furrows, themselves begot the giants. See Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, chapter 4. Moreover, Hieronymus Magius, Miscellanea, book 1, chapter 4, proves that many things handed down about the height and size of giants are true.

units.la: Pag. 6, Monstra gigneret] Gigantes monstra vocat ob permixtionem duarum naturarum, angelicae scilicet & humanae. Alio sensu Horatius cecinit l. 3. od. 4. Injecta monstris terra dolet suis, Moeretque partus fulmine lividum Missos ad Orcum.
units.tr: Page 6, "would bring forth monsters": he calls the giants monsters because of the mixing of two natures, namely angelic and human. In another sense Horace sang, book 3, ode 4: "The earth, struck by monsters, grieves for its own, and mourns its offspring, sent down to Orcus, livid with the thunderbolt."

units.la: Quum enim staturam hominis longissimi excedant, recte monstra eos appellat. Monstrum enim, autore Donato, est omne id quod praeter naturam deficit aut excedit.
units.tr: For since they exceed the stature of the very tallest man, he rightly calls them monsters. For a monster, according to Donatus, is whatever departs or deviates from nature.

units.la: Malitia] κακία, vitiositate.
units.tr: Malice] kakia [κακία], wickedness of character.

units.la: Ultra modum] ultra usurpat pro supra, ut in vita B. Martini, ultra humanum modum. Sic histo. Sacrae lib. 2, aedem sacratam, ultra omnia mortalia illustrem.
units.tr: "Beyond measure": ultra is used for supra, as in the Life of St. Martin, "beyond human measure." So in the Historia sacra, book 2: "a temple consecrated, renowned beyond all mortal things."

units.la: Vita innocens distinctae exemit sententiae] imo Deus eum exemit, non innocentia. Na innocentia nihil agit, cum sit accidens. Sed est genus loquendi, vita innoces eum exemit pro Deus eum exemit ob vitae innocentiam. Simile, iustitia liberat a morte, pro Deus liberat hominem a morte propter iustitiam, sive, quod idem, pro-pter virtutem. Nam iustitia eo in loco virtute denotat, nisi opes justitias intelligas. Praecedit enim exce. nō prosunt thesauri impro-bitatis, id est, improbe parti. Sunt qui iustitiae vocabulo eleemosynam innui putet. Vt ut sit, eleemosyna non liberat a morte, sed ipse De-us propter eleemosynam. Geminum est, integritas rectorum custodit eos. Nam Deus tales custodit proprie loquendo.
units.tr: "Innocent life freed him from the sentence set down": rather God freed him, not innocence. For innocence does nothing, since it is an accident. But it is a manner of speaking: "innocent life freed him" stands for "God freed him because of the innocence of his life." Similar is "righteousness delivers from death," for "God delivers a man from death on account of righteousness," or, what is the same, on account of virtue. For in that place "righteousness" denotes virtue, unless you understand "righteous wealth." For the preceding words, "treasures of wickedness do not profit," mean wealth gained wickedly. Some think that by the word "righteousness" alms-giving is hinted at. However that may be, alms do not deliver from death, but God himself on account of alms. The rest is double: "the integrity of the upright preserves them." For God preserves such people, properly speaking.

units.la: Noe] Noë, qui & Noa & Noach. Sed Noe antiquum est. Graeci enim & Latini veteres aliter non scribunt. Iudicium Augustini Steuchi Eugubini de hac scriptura tale est, Mirum cur hæc vox apud Graecos & Latinos sacris litteris corrupte legatur, apud Berosum tamen legitur ut legenda est. Appellat itaque eum Noach, ut Ebraice quoque profertur. Quem locum adduxi propter iuventutem nostram. Nam hæc legens putaret Noe corruptum esse. Non est magis corruptum quam Thare, quam Sue, quam Laree, aliaque sexcenta. Noach legitur quidem in Berosō Annii, sed an etiam in vero Berosō? hoc probandum erat. Annius quo tempore vixerit, non est obscurum. Mirarer si uspiam in antiquis Noach extaret. Neque tamen improbo. Sed ab eo non recte dicitur Noachus, cum Nochus dici debeat. Siquidem a furtivum, quale in Noach, quum aliquid addi-tur, penitus perit. Sane a ruach, quod spiritum & ventum denotat, pluralis est ruchoth, non ruachoth. Intelligens intelligit quid velim.
units.tr: Noe] Noë, who is also Noa and Noach. But "Noe" is the old form, for the Greeks and the old Latins write it no other way. The judgment of Augustinus Steuchus of Gubbio on this spelling is as follows: "It is strange that this word is read corruptly in the sacred letters among Greeks and Latins, yet in Berosus it is read as it should be read. He therefore calls him Noach, as it is also pronounced in Hebrew." I have cited this place because of our young students, for reading this they might think Noe was a corruption. It is no more corrupt than Thare, Sue, Laree, and six hundred other names. "Noach" is indeed read in the Berosus of Annius, but is it also in the true Berosus? That had to be proved. When Annius lived is not obscure. I would be surprised if "Noach" were found anywhere in the ancient authors. Yet I do not condemn it. But it is not rightly said "Noachus," since it ought to be "Nochus." For when a letter is added to a word, as in Noach from the letter "a," it is utterly lost. Indeed, from ruach, which denotes spirit and wind, the plural is ruchoth, not ruachoth. The one who understands will understand what I mean.

units.la: Iustum] probum, virtute praeditum.
units.tr: Just: upright, endowed with virtue.

units.la: Arcam] [illegible, ~3 letters] navigij genus absque remis & velis, arca in modum constructa tectumq; LXX. κιβωτὸν[?] vocant: Iosephus λάρ-νακα: Chaldaei [illegible, ~4 letters], unde βιβλά[?] in Clemente Stromat. l. 5. Hujusmodi navigia vel ex ligno fiebant, ut arca Noe, vel ex pa-pyro, ut scirpea illa rates, quae Mosen infantulum vexit. Hanc LXX. interpretes βίβλῳ[?] appellat, haud obscuro vestigio vocabuli Ebraici. Videndus Suidas. Lexicon Hesychij, Θίβα[?], πόλις Βοιωτίας[?] καὶ κιβωτὸς, recte. proprie κιβωτὸς: ab eo Thebae dictae fuit[?]. Cadmus n. Thebarum conditor a navicula, qua vectus in Europam trajecit, nomen urbi imposuit. Vt Iosephus arcam λάρνακα, ita etiam Lucianus appellat, quam proluvij tempore Deucalion conscendit. Glossae veteres, λάρναξ, arca, riscus. Pro Θιβᾶ Cyprij dicunt Θιβαν[?]. De arca forma Albinus in Genesin, Vt videtur, inquit, habuit quatuor angulos ex imo ad surgentes, & eisdem paulatim usque ad summum in angustum attractis in spatium unius cubiti fuit collecta, &c. Vide quaestiones ipsius in Genesin.
units.tr: Ark: a kind of vessel without oars or sails, built in the shape of a chest and roofed over. The Seventy call it [κιβωτὸν]; Josephus calls it [λάρνακα]; the Chaldeans call it [illegible], whence [βιβλά] in Clement, Stromata book 5. Vessels of this sort were made either of wood, like Noah's ark, or of papyrus, like the bulrush raft that carried the infant Moses. The Seventy call this one [βίβλῳ], a clear trace of the Hebrew word. See Suidas. Hesychius' lexicon has [Θίβα], a city of Boeotia, and [κιβωτὸς], rightly. Properly, κιβωτός: Thebes was named after it, since Cadmus, the founder of Thebes, gave the city its name from the little boat in which he crossed into Europe. As Josephus calls the ark [λάρνακα], so Lucian calls it, the chest which Deucalion boarded at the time of the flood. Old glosses: [λάρναξ], ark, chest. For [Θιβᾶ] the Cyprians say [Θιβαν]. On the form of the ark, Albinus on Genesis says: "It seems to have had four corners, from the bottom rising upward, and these, gradually drawn in to a narrow point at the top, were gathered into the space of one cubit," and so on. See his Questions on Genesis.

units.la: Immensae magnitudinis] longitudinis trecentorum cubitorum, latitudinis quinquaginta, altitudinis vere triginta.
units.tr: Of immense size: three hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth, and truly thirty in height.

units.la: Per cubitum autem Origenes ex traditione Iudaeorum ait Mosen intelligere cubitum Geometricum, quem alij Mathematicum vocitant, qui sex nostros cubitos continet. Qua de re scripsimus in examine versionum supra Genesin, quae nunc inde describemus. Quum varij cubiti sint, merito quaeritur de quo cubito hic locus accipiendus sit. Nam est cubitus regius major eo quo pro mensura utimur, inquit Herodotus, tribus digitis: & cubitus virilis, Deut.3.11. quem Oncelos eundem facit cum cubito regio. Est & cubitus geometricus, & vulgaris sive communis. Geometricus tantum valet quantum sex alij. De hoc loqui Mosen censet Origenes, cujus haec de re verba sunt in Catena patrum. Sed haec nos quae a prudentibus viris & Ebraicarum traditionum gnaris, atque a veteribus magistris didicimus, ad auditorum notinotitiam deferemus, Ajebant ergo majores, quod Moses, qui (ut Scriptura testatur de eo) omni sapientia Ægyptiorum fuerat eruditus, secundum artem geometricam, quam præcipue Ægyptii callent, cubitorum numerum hoc in loco posuit. Apud Geometras enim secundum eam rationem, quæ apud eos virtus vocatur, ex solido & quadrato vel in sex cubitos unus deputatur, fi generaliter, vel trecentos, fi minutatim deducatur. Quæ utique ratio fi observetur in hujus arcæ mensura, invenientur & longitudinis & latitudinis tanta spatia, quæ vere totius mundi reparan-da germina, & universorum animantium capere redivivâ seminaria potuerunt. Hanc opinionem approbat Augustinus de civit. Dei lib. 15 cap. 27. Quam & ego probarem, nisi scirem Mosen ubique se accommodare ad captum vulgi. Quocirca non est credibile eum nunc locutum esse de cubito geometrico, cujus mensura eruditis tantum nota erat. Neque causa est cur eo confusi-giamus, cum simpliciter numerus horum cubitorum, ut a Mose positus est, sufficiat ad omnes animantium species capiendas, & eorum in annum alimoniam, & spatium etiam reliquum superfit, ut docte Buteo rationibus geometricis & mathematicis ostendit. Buteo ille scripsit de Fabrica arcæ, quem nondum mihi videre contigit. Mercerus, qui vidit, valde commendat. Idem cubitos intelligit vulgares sive communes, quales erant hominum illius ævi. A quo non longe abest Gerundensis, qui Mosen loqui censet de cubito ipsius Noe.
