Sed tamen, inquit, cum ejusdem magnitudinis elephantorum, & multa essent animalia, arcâ capere sine miraculo non potuisse. Vide illum, ut vacas, Noe certe præstitit quod potuit, reliquum Deus supplevit. Hucusque,
units.tr: Origen, following the tradition of the Jews, says that by the cubit Moses means the geometric cubit, which others call the mathematical cubit, and which contains six of our cubits. We have written about this matter in our examination of the versions on Genesis, and we shall now set it out from there, for the benefit of the hearers. Since there are various cubits, it is rightly asked which cubit this passage is to be taken as meaning. For there is the royal cubit, longer than the one we use as a measure by three fingers, says Herodotus; and the common man's cubit, Deut. 3.11, which Onkelos makes the same as the royal cubit. There is also the geometric cubit, and the ordinary or common cubit. The geometric cubit is worth as much as six of the others. Origen thinks Moses speaks of this one, and his words on the matter are in the Catena of the Fathers. But these things, which we have learned from prudent men, who know the Hebrew traditions, and from old teachers, we shall pass on to the knowledge of our hearers. The elders therefore said that Moses, who (as Scripture testifies of him) had been educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, put the number of cubits in this place according to the geometric art, which the Egyptians especially understand. For among geometers, according to that reckoning which they call virtue, one unit of a solid and a square is reckoned as six cubits, if taken generally, or three hundred if worked out in detail. If this reckoning is applied to the measure of this ark, the lengths and breadths found will be such spaces as could indeed hold the seeds to restore the whole world and the living seed-stock of all the animals brought back to life. Augustine approves this opinion, City of God book 15 chapter 27. I too would approve it, were I not aware that Moses everywhere adapts himself to the grasp of the common people. Therefore it is not credible that he is speaking now of the geometric cubit, whose measure was known only to the learned. Nor is there any need to take refuge in it, since the simple number of these cubits, as Moses set it down, is enough to hold all kinds of animals and their food for a year, and space also remains over, as the learned Buteo shows by geometric and mathematical arguments. That Buteo wrote on the construction of the ark, which I have not yet had the chance to see. Mercerus, who has seen it, commends it highly. The same writer understands the ordinary or common cubits, such as were used by men of that age. Not far from this is the Gerundensis, who thinks Moses speaks of the cubit of Noah himself. Yet, he says, since the elephants were of the same size and there were many animals, they could not be held in the ark without a miracle. See him, as you have time. Noah certainly did what he could; God supplied the rest. So far.

units.la: Ex lignis [?] ex lignis gopher, id est, lævigatis, ut nostra tran-slatio habet; aut quadratis, ut LXX. quod Græce dicitur ἐκ ξύλων τετραγώνων, quæ insolubilia sunt. Qua ratione cavit ne aqua ventorum vi aut aquarum inundatione solveretur, ait Albinus. Sed Gopher alij aliter interpretantur. Ebrei dicunt esse genus arboris. Chaldæi cedrum exponunt. Cedrum autem appellant, quod legunt Cadros, cum legi possit cedros, id est, cedrus. Græcum scholion est, ex antiquis editionibus, ut puto, desumptum ἐκ ξύλων ἀσήπτων, ex lignis imputribilibus: ἢ πεύκινον, aut buxeus, Hiero, in quæstio. pro quadratis lignis, bituminatis legimus in Ebræo. Confundit [illegible, ~3 letters] cum כֹּפֶר. Siquidem Chopher bitumen. Gopher putatur esse cedri spe-cies, cariem non sentiens. Sed haec omnia incerta sunt. Praestat ἀρτίζειν, quam temere aliquid affirmare. Vox Ebraea non reperitur alibi. R. Levi scribit esse lignum quod longo tempore durat & est, inquit, species cedri, quemadmodum doctores nostri felicis memoriae. R. Abraham Hispanus, nomen est ligni levissimi. Eadem scribit R. David, Quod notat propter interpretem nostrum, in quo, de lignis laevigatis ut diximus. In Genesi magno (liber est ejus nominis, quem Bresith rabba vocant) ligna Gopher sunt ligna cedrina. In gopher significatio sulphuris, quod גָּפְרִית gophrith dicitur. Unde quidam innui putant sulphure perdendos esse. Cui firmando Hisceni adhuc modum scribens, Gopher, unde sulphur exit, non confunditur in aqua. Praecepit autem ut uteretur ligno isto ad ostendendum quo supplicio digni essent.
units.tr: Of planed wood: of gopher wood, that is, smoothed, as our translation has it; or squared, as the Seventy have it, [ἐκ ξύλων τετραγώνων], which are not to be dissolved. By this means, says Albinus, he took care that the ark should not be loosened by the force of winds or the inundation of waters. But others interpret gopher differently. The Hebrews say it is a kind of tree. The Chaldeans explain it as cedar, and they call it cadros, which is read as cedros, that is, cedar. There is a Greek scholion, taken, I think, from the old editions: [ἐκ ξύλων ἀσήπτων], of imperishable wood; or [πεύκινον], of pine, or boxwood, Jerome, in the Questions. For "squared timbers" we read "bituminous" in the Hebrew. [illegible] confuses it with [כֹּפֶר]. For kopher is bitumen. Gopher is thought to be a kind of cedar which does not feel decay. But all this is uncertain. It is better to [ἀρτίζειν] than to assert something rashly. The Hebrew word is found nowhere else. R. Levi writes that it is a wood which lasts a long time, and is, he says, a kind of cedar, as our teachers of blessed memory have it. R. Abraham the Spaniard says it is the name of a very light wood. R. David writes the same, which refers to our translator, who has, as we said, "planed wood." In the great Genesis (that is the title of the book which they call Bereshit Rabba), the gopher woods are cedar woods. Gopher carries the sense of sulphur, which is called [גָּפְרִית gophrith]. Hence some think it is hinted that they were to be destroyed by sulphur. To confirm this, Hisceni, writing again on the subject, says: gopher, from which sulphur comes, is not dissolved in water. He ordered them, however, to use this wood to show by what punishment they deserved to die.

units.la: Bitumine illitam] Gen.6.14. illines eam bitumine. Biblia Graeca ἀσφαλτώσεις ἀσφάλτῳ, bituminabis eam bitumine. Apud Ambrosium cap.6. illinies legitur, & in vulgata nostra, bitumine liniet. Ebraice חֵמָר limus est seu terra lenta, pici persimilis. Eo utebantur veteres pici loco: sed & calcis vice. Hocgenus חֵמָר, illud חֵמָר vocant Ebraei. Euchenius in Genesin, Bitumen est fervidissimum & violentissimum gluten, cujus est haec virtus ut ligna, quae ex eo fuerint lita, nec vermibus exedi, nec solis ardore vel vento-rum flatibus aut aquarum posint assiduitate dissolvi. Sic etiam Rabanus & Albinus, Plinius lib. 35. cap. 15. Bitumen alibi limus, alibi terra, limus e Iudaeae lacu emergens: terra in Syria circa Sidonem opidum maritimum. Abenezra. Sunt qui dicunt חֵמָר simile pici esse, & sunt qui dicunt esse lutum in terra e pulvere quod adhaeret & consistit, ut pix, & sunt qui dicunt esse quod in lingua Ismaelitica sive Arabica חֵמָר appellatur, Chaphin Cophverfa.
units.tr: Smeared with pitch: Gen. 6.14, "you shall smear it with bitumen." The Greek Bibles have [ἀσφαλτώσεις ἀσφάλτῳ], you shall pitch it with pitch. In Ambrose, chapter 6, we read "you shall smear" (illinies), and in our Vulgate, "he shall smear it with bitumen." In Hebrew, [חֵמָר] is slime, or sticky earth, very like pitch. The ancients used it in place of pitch, and also in place of lime. The Hebrews call this kind [חֵמָר], and that one [חֵמָר]. Euchenius on Genesis: bitumen is a very hot and very strong glue, and its virtue is that wood smeared with it is neither eaten by worms, nor dissolved by the heat of the sun, the blasts of winds, or the constant action of waters. Rabanus and Albinus say the same. Pliny, book 35, chapter 15: bitumen is sometimes slime, sometimes earth; slime rising from the lake of Judaea; earth found in Syria, near the seaport town of Sidon. Abenezra. Some say that [חֵמָר] is like pitch; some say it is mud from the earth, which clings to dust and hardens like pitch; and some say that what is called [חֵמָר] in the Ishmaelite or Arabic tongue is [Chaphin Cophverfa].

units.la: Totidem nuribus] nomina harum in iis quae sub Berosi nomine circumferuntur, Pandora, Noela & Noegla. Vxor autem Noe ibidem vocatur Tytea, quam & Vestam dici ajunt. Sed Vesta est חֲשׁוּקָה, id est ignis. Ovidius,
units.tr: Wives in equal number: the names of these, in those writings which circulate under the name of Berosus, are Pandora, Noela and Noegla. The wife of Noah is called there Tytea, whom they also say is Vesta. But Vesta is [חֲשׁוּקָה], that is, fire. Ovid:

units.la: Nec tu aliud vestam quam vivam intellige flammam.
units.tr: "Nor understand Vesta as anything but the living flame."

units.la: Eftha, Vesta, ut is Vesta, Vestis. Pandora Graecum vocabulum est. Quanquam in Aruch חָמָר. Id invenies in voce חָמָר.
units.tr: Eftha, Vesta, as is Vesta, Vestis. Pandora is a Greek word. Although in the Aruch [חָמָר]. You will find it under the word [חָמָר].

units.la: In salo] in mari: quod ita dictum vel a sale; vel, ut alij volunt, a σαλίω[?].
units.tr: In the sea: in the open sea; so called either from salt, or, as others prefer, from [σαλίω].

units.la: Ratus id quod erat aquas decedere] Iosephus Originum Iudaicarum lib.1. c.4. Quum arca distituta esset in vertice cujusdam montis in Armenia, id sentiens Noe aperuit eam: deinde post aliquot dies, magis recedente aqua, emisit columbam.
units.tr: Thinking that the waters were receding: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities book 1, chapter 4. When the ark had come to rest on the top of a certain mountain in Armenia, Noah, perceiving this, opened it; then, some days later, when the water had gone down further, he sent out a dove.

units.la: Eoque non revertente] Vide Proverbia mtt[?] sacra in adagio Corvus nuncius: item Miscella. cent. 1. cap. 3. ubi disputo utrum corvus a Noche[?] emissus redierit, nec ne.
units.tr: And since it did not return: see the Proverbs, the sacred ones, under the adage "The raven, a messenger." Also my Miscellanea, century 1, chapter 3, where I discuss whether the raven sent out by Noah returned or not.

units.la: Vt ego conjicio, cadaveribus detento] conjectura haec sumpta est a natura animantis, quae cadaveribus vescitur. Intelligit autem cadaverasubmersorum, qui fere septimo aut nono die emergunt in superficie aquae fluitantes. Quod quare fiat, docet Levinus[?] Lemnius de miraculis naturae lib 2.cap.6.
units.tr: As I conjecture, held fast by the corpses: this conjecture is drawn from the nature of the bird, which feeds on carcasses. He means the bodies of those drowned, which commonly rise to the surface and float about on the seventh or ninth day. Why this happens, Lemnius explains in On the Miracles of Nature, book 2, chapter 6.

units.la: Vt ego conjicio] Idem alij quoque conjecerunt. Augustinus, Quaeritur utrum corvus mortuus fuerit, an aliquo modo vivere potuerit? Si enim fuit terra ubi requiesceret, similiter columba requiem invenisset. Unde conjicitur quod cadaveri potuit corvus insidere, quod naturaliter refugit columbā. Albinus sive Alcuinus, Quaeritur ubi corvus qui-everit si columba non invenit ubi requiescere? Resp. po-tuit corvus cadaveri cujuslibet animantis insidere, quod columba naturaliter fugit. Isidorus, post XL. dies corvus non rediit aut aquis interceptus, aut cadavere natante illectus. Nicolaus de Lyra, Secundum communem expositio-nem non est intelligendum quod corvus reversus sit ad Noe aquis desiccatis, sed remansit apud cadavera, ut communiter dicitur.
units.tr: As I conjecture: others too have conjectured the same. Augustine: "It is asked whether the raven was dead or could in some way have remained alive. For if there was land where it could rest, the dove would likewise have found rest. Hence it is conjectured that the raven could settle on a corpse, which the dove naturally shuns." Albinus, or Alcuin: "It is asked where the raven went if the dove found no place to rest? Answer: the raven could settle on the carcass of any animal, which the dove naturally avoids." Isidore: "After forty days the raven did not return, either hindered by the waters or enticed by a floating corpse." Nicholas of Lyra: "According to the common exposition, it is not to be understood that the raven returned to Noah once the waters had dried up, but that it stayed among the carcasses, as is commonly said."

units.la: Cum consistendi locum non reperiisset] mirum hoc, quum jamdiu detecta essent cacumina montium. An terra limo erat op-pleta, quem aqua recedens[?] reliquerat? videtur. Limo enim columbae, ut & aliae aves, non possunt consistere. Nam cænum mollius, cujusmodi est limus, corpori etiam levissimo cedit, nec consistendi locum et præbet.
units.tr: When it had not found a place to alight: this is strange, since the tops of the mountains had long been uncovered. Or was the earth covered with mud, which the receding water had left behind? That seems so. For doves, like other birds, cannot settle on mud. Soft mire, such as mud is, gives way even to the lightest body, and does not offer a place to stand.

units.la: Rursum remissa] rectum puto, emissa. quod placuit etiam Sigonio. Antea nos monuerat quoque de eo Victor Gifelinus.
units.tr: Again, sent out: I think the correct reading is "sent out," which Sigonius also approved. Victor Giselinus had already warned us of this.

units.la: Folium olivae] Augustinus de doctrina Christiana l.2 cap 16. Oleae ramusculo, quem rediens ad aream columba pertu-lit, lit, significatur pax perpetua. Nam novimus & olei lenem contactum non facile alieno humore corrumpi, & arbo- rem ipsam frondere perennitèr. Quod postremum ita esse docet nos Theophrastus, dum oleam recenset inter eas arbores quæ perpetuo virent, nec unquam folia amittunt. Huc refer Prudentij tetrastichon.
units.tr: A leaf of an olive: Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 16: "By the little olive branch which the dove brought back to the ark, perpetual peace is signified. For we know that olive oil, touched lightly, is not easily spoiled by another moisture, and that the tree itself keeps its leaves forever green. Theophrastus teaches us the last point as well, when he lists the olive among those trees which are always green and never lose their leaves." Refer here also Prudentius' tetrastich.

units.la: Nuntia diluvii jam decrescentis ad arcam: C[?]re columba refert jamum viridantis olivae: Corvus enim ingluvie per foeda cadavera captus Haeserat, illa datae revehit nova gaudia pacis.
units.tr: The messenger of the flood now receding to the ark: the dove brings back the fresh green olive. For the raven, caught by its greed among the foul corpses, had stayed there; the dove brings back the new joys of the peace given.

units.la: Ita Noe arcam egressus est, arca quievit in uno aliquo mo-tium Ararat, id est, Armeniae. Inde igitur descendit Noe. Loco nomen Armeni fecerunt ἀποβατήριον[?], id est, egressorium. Hujus diluvij & arcae meminerunt Berosus Babylonius, Hieronymus Aegyptius, qui antiquitates Phoenicum conscripsit, Mnaseas, Nicolaus Damascenus & alij plures. Autor Iosephus Orig. Iudaic. lib. 1 cap 4. Meminit & Sybilla Cumæa, cujus verba reperies apud Lactantium de ira Dei, cap. 13.
units.tr: So Noah went out of the ark, and the ark rested on one of the mountains of Ararat, that is, of Armenia. From there, therefore, Noah came down. The Armenians named the place apobaterion [ἀποβατήριον], that is, the place of disembarking. Of this flood and the ark have made mention Berosus the Babylonian, Hieronymus the Egyptian, who wrote the antiquities of the Phoenicians, Mnaseas, Nicolaus of Damascus, and many others. The author is Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, book 1, chapter 4. The Cumaean Sibyl also mentions it, whose words you will find in Lactantius, On the Anger of God, chapter 13.

units.la: Pag.7. CC.[?] : duos & quadraginta ] Sigonius numerat CCC, duos & quadraginta: perspicuo errore, quia Seth genitum scribit anno Adami 330. cum natus sit 230. Ceterum Ebraei ad diluvium annos putant 1656. Quod ex hac tabula clarum fiet.
units.tr: Page 7. CC.: forty-two. Sigonius counts 300 and forty-two, through an obvious error, since he writes that Seth was born in the year 330 of Adam, whereas he was born in the year 230. Moreover, the Hebrews reckon 1656 years up to the flood. This will become clear from the following table.

units.la: Series annorum a mundi exordio usque ad diluvium.
units.tr: Series of years from the beginning of the world up to the flood.

units.la: Ebraei. | Graeci. Adam genuit Seth an. | 130 | 230 Seth Enos | 105 | 205 Enos Cainan | 90 | 190 Cainan Malaleel | 70 | 170 Malaleel Iared | 65 | 165 Iared Henoch | 162 | 162 Henoch Mathusalem | 65 | 165 Mathusalem Lamech | 187 | 187 Lamech Noe an. | 182 | 188
units.tr: Hebrews | Greeks. Adam begat Seth in the year | 130 | 230. Seth begat Enos | 105 | 205. Enos begat Cainan | 90 | 190. Cainan begat Malaleel | 70 | 170. Malaleel begat Jared | 65 | 165. Jared begat Enoch | 162 | 162. Enoch begat Methuselah | 65 | 165. Methuselah begat Lamech | 187 | 187. Lamech begat Noah in the year | 182 | 188.

units.la: Hic anno ætatis sexcentesimo arcam inivit propter diluvium. Duos & quadraginta adde mensem unum & dies viginti septem. Ceterum Noe arcam egressus est anno ætatis 601. Mense secundo, die mensis 27. Gen.8.14. Ingressus autem fuerat, ut dixi-mus, anno 600. ejusdem mensis die septimo supra decimum.
units.tr: In this year, in his six hundredth year of life, he entered the ark on account of the flood. Add forty-two, one month, and twenty-seven days. Moreover, Noah went out of the ark in the six hundred and first year of his life, in the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month (Gen. 8:14). He had entered, as I have said, in the six hundredth year, on the seventeenth day of the same month.

units.la: Gen. 7. 11. Hinc liquet ipsum in arca fuisse annum integrum lunarem & dies undecim. Qui efficiunt justum annum solarem. Sic dico, quo die ingressus est, anno evoluto & ad solis cursum putato, eodem egressus est, ut Strabus memoriae prodidit. Quem vide, si placet, in glossa ordinaria, sol.145. Vide quoque Nicolaum de Lyra.
units.tr: Gen. 7:11. From this it is clear that he was in the ark for a full lunar year and eleven days, which make a full solar year. So I say: on the day he entered, when the year has run its course and is reckoned by the course of the sun, on that same day he went out, as Strabo has handed down to memory. See him, if you wish, in the ordinary gloss, at the word "sol" (sun), p. 145. See also Nicholas of Lyra.

units.la: Aram] altare, θυσιαστήριον. Gen. 8.20.
units.tr: Altar [θυσιαστήριον]. Gen. 8:20.

units.la: Hostiasque immolavit] holocaustaque obtulit, quae & holocaustomata dicuntur. Erant autem integra hostiarum corpora, quae tota comburebantur: unde nomen acceperunt. Invenitur & holo-carpos hoc sensu.
units.tr: And he offered sacrifices: he presented whole burnt offerings, which are also called holocausts. Now these were whole bodies of the victims, which were burned entirely; hence they received their name. The word holocarpos is also found in this sense.

units.la: Ex volucribus] ex omnibus avibus mundis. Omisit pecudes mundas: quare nescio. Nam in LXX, ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν πτηνῶν [?] τῶν καθαρῶν, quod reddunt, ab omnibus pecoribus mundis.
units.tr: Of the birds: of all clean birds. He omitted clean cattle, and I do not know why. For in the LXX, the Greek reads "of all clean birds" [ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν πτηνῶν τῶν καθαρῶν], which they render as "of all clean cattle."

units.la: Mox a Domino benedicitur] paullo post, aut deinde Dominus ei filiisque benedixit. Fons hujus benedictionis est favor divinus, effectus autem rerum omnium prosperitas ac felix successus, sed imprimis propagatio generis. Ideo sequitur in Mose Fructificate, &c.
units.tr: Soon he is blessed by the Lord: shortly afterwards, or then, the Lord blessed him and his sons. The source of this blessing is divine favour; its effect, however, is the prosperity of all things and a happy success, but above all the propagation of the race. Therefore in Moses there follows, "Be fruitful," and so on.

units.la: Ne sanguine vescerentur] Moses Aegyptius in lib. perplexorum, quem More nebuchim appellat, scribit Chaldaeos adversari sanguinem, eumque habere pro re immunda. Magi tamen, inquit, eum edebant cum aut daemonibus conjurgerentur, aut ex illis futura praedicerent. Sed quare Deus prohibuit vescisanguine? An quia magi eo vescebantur? aut quia sanguinis cursus, ut ait Seneca, vitalis continetur calor? Scire licet in fontibus esse Gen.9.4. carnem in anima eius, in sanguine ejus non comedetis: quod explicant, cum anima, hoc est cum sanguine, vel certe cum anima quae est sanguis ejus. Per animam autem intelligunt vitam, quae in sanguine per operationem & virtutem. Nam anima sine sanguine impes [?] est actionum vitalium. Quin sanguine omni effuso vita hominis extinguitur. Sic dico, sanguis est in anima ut in instrumento proprio ipsius. Cum enim sint duplices motus in animante, quidam dicuntur esse corporis, ut ambulare; quidam animi per se, ut irasci, gaudere, timere, erubescere. Horum est sanguis cum spiritu fluens instrumentum proprium. Psal. 30. 10. Quae utilitas in sanguine meo? Ad haec verba R. David, in sanguine meo, hoc est, inquit, in anima mea. Nam sanguis est anima, hoc est vita qua vivimus. est profecto: sanguis metonymice pro anima i. vita sumitur: ut quo Virgilius, purpuream vovit ille animam. Quod ab Euri-pide sumpsit, qui animam dicebat esse sanguinem. Cicero in I. Tuscul. Empedocles animum esse censet cordi circumfusum sanguinem. Ejus verba, quibus hoc significat, habentur in Etymologico,
units.tr: That they should not eat blood: Moses the Egyptian, in his book of the Perplexed, which he calls Moreh Nevukhim, writes that the Chaldeans opposed blood and held it to be an unclean thing. The magi, however, he says, ate it when they were conjuring demons, or foretelling the future from them. But why did God forbid eating blood? Was it because the magi ate it? Or because, as Seneca says, the vital warmth is contained in the course of the blood? We know that in the sources there is the flesh in its soul; you shall not eat its blood in the blood (Gen. 9:4), which they explain as: with the soul, that is, with the blood, or certainly with the soul which is its blood. By the soul they understand life, which is in the blood through its operation and power. For without blood the soul is powerless for vital actions. Indeed, when all the blood has been poured out, the life of a man is extinguished. So I say: the blood is in the soul as in its own instrument. For since there are two kinds of movement in a living creature, some are said to belong to the body, such as walking; others to the mind by itself, such as being angry, rejoicing, fearing, blushing. The blood, flowing together with the spirit, is the proper instrument of these. Psalm 30:10: What profit is there in my blood? On these words Rabbi David says: "in my blood," that is, he says, "in my soul." For the blood is the soul, that is, the life by which we live. Indeed, blood is taken metonymically for soul, that is, life, as when Virgil says, "he vowed his purple soul." He took this from Euripides, who said that the soul is blood. Cicero, in Tusculan Disputations I Empedocles holds that the mind is the blood poured around the heart. His words by which he signifies this are found in the Etymologicum,

units.la: Αἷμα γὰρ ἀνθρώποις πνεῦμα ἐστὶ νόημα [?]
units.tr: For to men blood is the spirit of thought [Αἷμα γὰρ ἀνθρώποις πνεῦμα ἐστὶ νόημα].

units.la: Hinc lucem accipit locus qui habetur Levit. 17. 14. Quoniam anima omnis carnis sanguis ejus in anima ejus est. Et dixit filijs Israel sanguinem omnis carnis non comedetis, quia anima omnis carnis sanguis ejus est. Hoc est sanguine retinetur in corpore, ut sanguis sit ejus quasi vehiculum & retinaculum. Nam vigente sanguine viget animalium vita, & eo deficiente deficit. Anima ergo sanguis esse dicitur quia extincta sanguine, anima, qua vivimus, simul una extinguitur.
units.tr: Hence light is received by the passage which is found at Lev. 17:14: "For the soul of all flesh is its blood in its soul." And he said to the sons of Israel, you shall not eat the blood of all flesh, because the soul of all flesh is its blood. That is, by the blood it is retained in the body, so that the blood is as it were its vehicle and holder. For while the blood is vigorous, the life of the animal is vigorous, and when it fails, life fails. The soul is therefore said to be blood, because when the blood is extinguished, the soul by which we live is at the same time extinguished together with it.

units.la: Aut sanguinem hominum effunderet] aut homicidium committeret vel eadem patraret. Lex haec habetur Gen. 9. 6. sanguinem autem effundere dicitur non solum qui ferro hominem occidit, sed etiam qui veneno eum e medio tollit, aut quovis alio modo interficit.
units.tr: Or should shed the blood of men: or should commit murder or perpetrate the same. This law is found at Gen. 9:6. To shed blood is said not only of one who kills a man with the sword, but also of one who removes him by poison, or kills him in any other way.

units.la: Mandati istius liber] nam lex nulla, quae eadem prohiberet, tum extabat.
units.tr: Book of this command] for at that time no law existed forbidding the same.

units.la: - Primordia] origines, exordia, principia.
units.tr: Beginnings] origins, first beginnings, principles.

units.la: Ex filiis Noe Sem fuit] hunc Noe genuit anno mundi 1658, cum ageret annum alterum supra quingentesimum qui fuit ante diluvium annus 98. Biennio post diluvium genuit Arphaxad anno aetatis 500. Creditur obiisse anno decimo post connubium Ifabaci, cum explesset annum sexcentesimum. Nomen hoc Gre-ce declinatur σῆμος [?], id est, Semus: quod obvium in Athenaeo, lib. 3. & est ibi nomen autoris cujusdam, pag. 109 edit. Lugd.
units.tr: Shem was one of the sons of Noah] Noah begot him in the year of the world 1658, when he was in his 502nd year; the year before the flood was the 98th. Two years after the flood he begot Arphaxad, in the 500th year of his own age. He is believed to have died in the tenth year after the marriage at Ifabaci, when he had completed his 600th year. The name is declined in Greek as Semus [σῆμος ?], which occurs in Athenaeus, book 3, where it is the name of a certain author, p. 109 of the Lyon edition.

units.la: Tres enim habuit Sem, Cham, Iapheth] opinio quorundam est maximum natu fuisse Iapheth, minimum autem Cham, & inter hos medium Sem: qui tamen Gen. § 32. & 10. 1. primo loco recensetur. Respondent hoc fieri propter dignitatem eorum qui ab ipso descenderunt. Haec opinio firmatur tribus locis Scripturae. Primus est Genes. 10. 21. qui tamen aliquid ambiguitatis habet. Quippe tam potest reddi, fratre Iapheth majore: quam fratre Iapheth majoris, id est, maximi natu. Alter est Gen. 9. 24. & cognovit quae sibi fecisset filius minor. Sive minimus natu,
units.tr: For Shem, Ham and Japheth were the three sons he had] The opinion of some is that Japheth was the eldest and Ham the youngest, with Shem in the middle; yet Shem is listed first at Gen. 10.1 and 10.32. They reply that this is done because of the dignity of those who descended from him. This opinion is supported by three passages of Scripture. The first is Gen. 10.21, which however has some ambiguity. For it can be rendered "with his brother Japheth the elder", or "the brother of Japheth the elder, that is, the eldest". The second is Gen. 9.24, "and he knew what his younger son had done to him", whether the youngest,

units.la: Nam loquitur de Cham. Sed potius ut sermo fit de Chanaan, in quem maledictio stricta. Sequitur enim ecce, maledictus Cha- naan. Tertius est Gen. 11.10. Sem erat centum annorum quando genuit Arphaxad, biennio post diluvium. Ecce ait Sem biennio post diluvium egisse annum 100 Noe autem coepit gignere anno ætatis 500. Igitur non Sem maximus natu, sed la- phetb. Nam Cham minimus erat, ut diximus. Audiamus nunc Salmanticenses Iudaeum hac de re. In libro Iobafin ait, Noe a- gebat annum quingentesimum cum gigneret Sem, Cham & Iapheth. Vixit autem annos 950. Iepultusque est anno mundi texto & bis millesimo. Iapheth maximus natu ge- nitus fuit anno mundi 1556. Cham fecundo genitus natus est anno mundi 1557. Sem tertius filiorum Noe natus fuit anno mundi 1558. Nam legimus Sem erat filius centum annorum & genuit Arphaxad biennio post diluvium. Testus autem eum præposuit propter justitiam & æstimationem ejus tum etiam quia natus est circumcisus, & quia ex- it ex eo Abraham. Hucusque Salmanticenses.
units.tr: For it speaks of Ham. But the discourse rather concerns Canaan, against whom the curse is directed; for it follows: "Behold, cursed is Canaan." The third is Gen. 11.10: "Shem was a hundred years old when he begot Arphaxad, two years after the flood." Behold, he says, Shem in the second year after the flood had lived 100 years; but Noah began to beget at the age of 500. So Shem was not the eldest, but Japheth; for Ham was the youngest, as we have said. Let us now hear the Salmanticenses, a Jew, on this matter. In the book Jobafin he says: Noah was in his 500th year when he begot Shem, Ham and Japheth. He lived 950 years and was buried in the year of the world 2006. Japheth, the eldest, was born in the year of the world 1556. Ham was born second, in the year 1557. Shem, the third son of Noah, was born in the year 1558. For we read that Shem was a son of a hundred years and begot Arphaxad two years after the flood. But the text placed him first on account of his righteousness and esteem, and also because he was born circumcised, and because Abraham came from him. Thus far the Salmanticenses.

units.la: Cham] vel Ham. Nam est Hethin scriptura Ebraica. Hiero- nymus, Septuaginta pro Ham, χάμ scribunt, exprimentes duplicem affirmationem litteræ Heth per χ: a quo & Æ- gyptus usque hodie Ægyptiorum lingua Ham dicitur. Communiter Ægyptus vocatur Mefraim, a filio Chami, qui Mef- raim nominatur. Dicitur etiam terra Cham sive Ham Pfalm. 106.22.
units.tr: Ham] or Ham. For in the Hebrew Scripture it is written with a different consonant, but the sense is the same. Jerome notes that the Seventy write Ham as χάμ [χάμ], expressing the double aspiration of the letter heth by χ; from this, even today, Egypt is called Ham in the Egyptian language. Commonly Egypt is called Mizraim, from Ham's son, who is named Mizraim. The land is also called the land of Ham, Ps. 106.22.

units.la: Iapheth] qui Græcis Iapetus in quo afflirat attenuantur, Sic ex Iosephi idem fecerunt Ἰάφεθ.
units.tr: Japheth] who among the Greeks is Iapetus, in which the aspiration is weakened. So, likewise, from Japheth they made [Ἰάφεθ].

units.la: Quod sopitum vino patrem riserit] hoc non habetur. di- ferte in textu sacro. Tamen ex iis, quæ ibi habentur, doctores col- ligunt eum derisisse patrem, Chryfostomus, Animad verte quo- modo intus in domo, visa patris turpitudine, quod debe- bat obtegere, egressus evulgavit, & risui ac fubiannatioñi, quantum in ipso erat, exposuit, fratresque pravæ suæ vo- luntatis socios fieri voluit, cum deberet, fi omnino pro- diturus erat, illos intra domum vocare & sic nuditatem effari. Idem, Fortasse autem & irrisit ac subsannavit pa- trem, turpitudinem illius nuncupando. Quidam existimant non ipsum risisse, sed filium ejus Chanaan. Qua de re traditio fuit apud veteres, cujus meminit doctissimus Theodoritus in Genesin scribens. seribus, quaest.57. ἰφιζειν δὲ ὁ Ἐβραῖος ὁ ταῦτα [?] τοῖς τοιαύτην [?] ἐπιγνωκὼς ἀπὸ ἠδεξ ἡ τὴν παρα[?]δόσι. ὡς ἀρχὴ ὁ χαναὰν πρότερον ἐθεὶν τὸν ἀρχηγὸν [?] τῆ πατρὶ ὁμ[?]άτου [?] ἀρ[?] ἀπ[?]γγέλλει αὐτῷ πρὸς τοῦτο ἀμεταλλαξ[?] ἀρτίως ὁ [?]γεγὶ εἶ [?]. R. Salomo, Sunt ex doctoribus nostris qui dicunt Chanaan primum vidisse, patrisque suo indicasse. Abeneẓr, Cham vidit, nec texit patrem. Quod cum audisset Chanaan fecit aliquid quod in historia reticetur. Nam de illo capiendum, Quæ fecisset sibi, &c.
units.tr: That he mocked his drunken father] this is not stated plainly in the sacred text. Yet from what is there, the teachers gather that he mocked his father. Chrysostom: Observe how he, having seen his father's shame inside the house, went out and made it known, and exposed it, as far as lay in him, to laughter and derision; and he wished his brothers to become partners in his wicked will, when he ought, if he was going to reveal it at all, to have called them inside the house and spoken of the nakedness there. The same author: Perhaps he also laughed at and mocked his father by naming his shame. Some think that it was not he himself who laughed, but his son Canaan. There was a tradition about this among the ancients, which the most learned Theodoret mentions in his writing on Genesis, Questions 57. R. Solomon: Some of our teachers say that Canaan first saw it and told his father. Abenezra: Ham saw and did not cover his father. When Canaan heard this, he did something which is passed over in the history. For that must be understood of him: "what he had done to him", and so on.

units.la: Sopitum vino] nam vite fata, cum ex ea vinum bibisset & inebriatus fuisset, in tabernaculo suo dormiens virilitatem nudatam habuit. Ejus natura visa Chamus ad fratres suos retulit: vel certe Chanaan vidit, patriqué nuntiavit, qui deinde fratribus suis id indicavit. Vt ut sit, non temere ita maledictum conceptum fuit, maledictus Chanaan, servus servorum erit fratribus suis. Ceterum non assentioriis qui ex hoc loco colligunt vitis primum repertorem fuisse Noam. Quin fabulam esse reor quam hoc loco in Chronico suo refert Ioh. Nauclerus, videlicet hircum quendam, cum eum in Coricum Ciliciæ montem emisset, invenistas labruscas gustasse, exeoque ebrium factum reliqua animantia cornibus petiisse. Quo animadverso Noam conjectantem quod erat vino vim aliquam singularem inesse, labruscam sanguine leonis, porci, agnis jimiaque inseruisse, exeoque vitem enatam: unde postea vinum expresserit, quo gustato inebriatus sit, ut Scriptura testatur.
units.tr: Drunk with wine: for when he had drunk wine from the vine and was intoxicated, sleeping in his tent, he had his nakedness exposed. Ham, seeing his condition, reported it to his brothers; or certainly Canaan saw and told his father, who then made it known to his brothers. However it may be, the curse was not uttered rashly: "Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers." Moreover, I do not agree with those who gather from this passage that Noah was the first discoverer of the vine. Indeed, I think the fable which John Naucler relates in this place in his Chronicle is false: namely, that a certain goat, having been let out on Mount Corycus in Cilicia, found wild grapes and tasted them, and having become drunk, attacked the other animals with its horns. Noah, observing this and conjecturing that some singular power lay in the wine, mixed the wild grapes with the blood of a lion, a pig, a lamb and an ape, and from this a vine sprang up; from which he afterwards pressed wine, which, once tasted, made him drunk, as Scripture testifies.

units.la: Maledictum a patre meruit] in filio Chanaan. Quidam sensent ipsum filio maledixisse, quod pater ante a Deo benedictus fuisset. Sic enim certe legimus, Gen.9.1, benedixit Noacho & filiis ejus.
units.tr: Deserved to be cursed by his father] in the son Canaan. Some think that he cursed the son because the father had previously been blessed by God. For so we read, Gen. 9.1: "he blessed Noah and his sons."

units.la: Chus] pater Æthiopum, qui Chusæi nuncupantur, id est, χυσαῖοι; quorum regio Arabia. Thargum Ionathæ, Filii Cham, Chus & Mefraim : nomina vero regionum quas inhabitaverunt, Arabia & Ægyptus. Non me fugit aliam Æthiopiam esse supra Ægyptum, qua Ptolemæo dicitur ἀιθιοπία ἡ ὑπὲρ Αἰγύπτου. Hæc hodie continet regnum Abyssinorum, quod Benjamin Tudelensis Habas & Alhabas appellat .i, ⵄⵃ.
units.tr: Cush] the father of the Ethiopians, who are called Cushites, that is, Χυσαῖοι [χυσαῖοι]; their region is Arabia. Targum of Jonathan: "The sons of Ham: Cush and Mizraim; but the names of the regions they inhabited are Arabia and Egypt." I am not unaware that there is another Ethiopia beyond Egypt, which Ptolemy calls Ethiopia above Egypt [ἀιθιοπία ἡ ὑπὲρ Αἰγύπτου]. Today this contains the kingdom of the Abyssinians, which Benjamin of Tudela calls Habas and Alhabas, [Ethiopic: ʿḤ].

units.la: Nebrod] τὸν Νεβρωδ Gen.10.8 in LXX. licet in fonte fit Nimrod, quod antiquitus legebant Nemrod, vel Namrod: unde in Iosepho Ναβρωδ. Dubito sitne mendum ex antiquo characterē Græco, quale in σπερματικῷ & similibus? an culpa manus errantis scriptum Nebrod pro Nembrod, cui simile Mambres in antiquitate.
units.tr: Nimrod] Νεβρωδ in Gen. 10.8 in the Septuagint, although in the source it is Nimrod, which the ancients read as Nemrod or Namrod; whence in Josephus it is Ναβρωδ. I doubt whether this is an error from the old Greek letter forms, as in σπερματικῷ and similar words, or the fault of a copyist writing Nebrod for Nembrod, like Mambres in antiquity.

units.la: Gigantem] sic eum appellat quoque Ambrosius, Chus Nemrod gigantem genuit, qui fuit venator coram Domino. Sed & Augustinus de civit. Dei lib. 16. cap. 4. & cap. 3. Opinio hæc manavit ex verbis Gen. 10. 8. ἤρξατο εἶναι γίγας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς: ubi tamen γίγας non significat gigantem. Quid igitur putavim vertendum, cœpit esse potens in terra. Certum enim est antea gigantes fuisse. Lexicon Hesychii: γίγας, δυνάστης, ἰσχυρός: potens, robustus. Aliter Pamllo Chrysostomus, γίγας, τοῦ τις τύπων. Minus hoc se probat mihi. Nam in fonte ꞌ גִּבּוֹר potens. Scire licet in Chaldaico gigantes גִּבּוֹרִים dici, cujus prima origo גִּבּוֹר. Non est dubitandum quin LXX. eo reppexerint. Sic γίγας ἰσχυρὸς, potens venator. Quis non animadvertit γίγας hic adjectivum esse? non ergo magis gigantem significat quam גִּבּוֹר, quod robustum ac potentem interpretantur; ninguam gigantem denotat, quod sciam.
units.tr: Giant] So Ambrose also calls him: "Cush begot Nimrod the giant, who was a hunter before the Lord." But Augustine too, in De civitate Dei, book 16, chapters 3 and 4, says the same. This opinion arose from the words of Gen. 10.8, ἤρξατο εἶναι γίγας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς [ἤρξατο εἶναι γίγας ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς], where, however, γίγας does not mean "giant". What, then, do I think should be rendered? "He began to be powerful on the earth." For it is certain that giants existed before. Hesychius' lexicon: γίγας = δυνάστης, ἰσχυρός: powerful, strong. Chrysostom explains it otherwise, as a certain kind of type [γίγας, τοῦ τις τύπων]. This seems less probable to me. For in the Hebrew source the word is גִּבּוֹר [gibbor], "powerful". It is well known that in Chaldean the giants are called גִּבּוֹרִים [gibborim], whose first origin is גִּבּוֹר [gibbor]. There is no doubt that the Seventy had regard to this. So γίγας ἰσχυρὸς [γίγας ἰσχυρὸς] means a powerful hunter. Who does not notice that γίγας here is an adjective? Therefore it signifies no more a giant than גִּבּוֹר [gibbor] does, which they interpret as strong and mighty; so far as I know, it denotes a giant nowhere.

units.la: A quo Babylon civitas constructa traditur] Augustinus loco citato, Babylon quippe interpretatur confusio. Unde colligitur gigantem illum Nemrod fuisse, illius conditorem, quod superius breviter fuerat intimatum. Quidam Babylonis conditorem Ninum faciunt, quem cum Nemrodo condiderunt. Sed repugnant tempora. Vixit enim certe Ninus diu post Nemrodum. Iohannes Sarefbervienfis de nugis Curialium lib. 8 cap. 20. Primum ergo tyrannum nobis objecit divina pagina Nemrod robustum contra Dominum (sic interpretatur cum Augustino ἐναντίος Κυρίῳ, quod alij melius reddunt, coram Domino) venatorem, quem & Ninum dici non nullæ tellantur historiæ, etsi ratio temporis non acquiescat. Forte conditam a Nemrodo Ninus postea reparavit. Orosius lib. 2. cap. 7. Babyloniam a Nemrod gigante fundatam, a Ninno vel Semiramide reparatam multi prodidere. Mosi verba, unde id colligunt, habentur Gen. 10. 10. Fuitque principium regni ejus Babel, Orech, &c. id est, urbes regni sive imperij ejus præcipuæ. Loquitur autem de Nemrodo.
units.tr: From whom the city of Babylon is said to have been built] Augustine, in the place cited, interprets Babylon as "confusion". Hence it is gathered that this giant Nimrod was its founder, which had been briefly hinted at above. Some make Ninus the founder of Babylon, whom they set alongside Nimrod; but the times contradict this, for Ninus certainly lived long after Nimrod. John of Salisbury, in On the Trifles of Courtiers, book 8, chapter 20: "The divine page first set before us a tyrant, Nimrod, a mighty hunter against the Lord" (so he renders it with Augustine, ἐναντίος Κυρίῳ, which others render better as "before the Lord"), "whom some histories also name Ninus, although the reckoning of time does not agree. Perhaps Ninus later restored what Nimrod had founded." Orosius, book 2, chapter 7: Many have handed down that Babylon was founded by the giant Nimrod and later restored by Ninus or Semiramis. The words of Moses from which they gather this are in Gen. 10.10: "And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, and so on", that is, the chief cities of his kingdom or empire. But he is speaking of Nimrod.

units.la: Babylon civitas] nam turris erat hoc nomine, & regio quæque, Turris proprie Babel vocatur, urbs Babylon & regio Babylonia. lonia. Sed confundi scias. Nam & urbs quandoque Babylonia dicitur, & ipsa turris Babylon. A turri,ut credo,civitas appellata, aut simul nomen acceperunt a confusione linguarum. Babel, quasi Balbel, id est,σύγχυσις confusio,ταραχὴ τὸ בלל[?] confundo. Hi-storia nota est.
units.tr: Babylon city] For there was a tower of this name, and also a region. The tower is properly called Babel, the city Babylon, and the region Babylonia. But you should know these are confused: the city is sometimes called Babylonia, and the tower itself Babylon. The city was named, I believe, from the tower, or they received the name together from the confusion of tongues. Babel, as if Balbel, that is, confusion [σύγχυσις], to confuse [בלל]. The story is well known.

units.la: Constructa] anno diluvij 1 cı[?]. aut, ut Græci putant. 5 3 1.
units.tr: Built] In the year of the flood 1 [illegible], or, as the Greeks think, 5 3 1.

units.la: Quo tempore & linguarum confusio facta est, & dispersio mortalium accidit per orbem terrarum.
units.tr: At the time both the confusion of tongues took place and the scattering of mortals occurred over the earth.

units.la: Pleraque etiam opida ea tempestate condita memorantur] in queis Arach sive Orech, Achad & Chalanne : item Nini-ve, Roboboth civitas, Chale & Refen. Quæ nominatim recensentur Gen 10 10.& 11.
units.tr: Many towns also are recorded as founded in that age] Among them Arach or Orech, Achad and Chalanne; likewise Nineveh, the city Rehoboth, Calah and Resen. These are named individually at Gen. 10:10 and 11.

units.la: Ita turrim facere aggressi] id gestum anno Eberi trigesimo quarto, qui fuit natalis Phalegi: unde & nomen accepit.
units.tr: Thus they set about building the tower] This was done in the thirty-fourth year of Eber, who was the father of Phaleg, from whom he also received his name.

units.la: Turrim] & urbem Gen. 1 1.4. Utriusque meminit Hieronymus in libro locorum per hæc verba, Babylon metropolis regni Chaldæorum, ubi eorum, qui ædificabant turrim, linguæ divisæ sunt: a quo & regio circumposita Babylonia vocatur. Hanc fuisse potentissimam, & in campestribus per quadrum sitam, ab angulo usque ad angulum muri sedecim millia passuum tenuisse, hoc est simul per circuitum sexaginta quatuor millia, refert Herodotus & multi alii, qui Græcas historias conscripserunt. Arx autem, id est, capitolium illius urbis, est turris, quæ post diluvium ædificata quatuor millia passuum tenere dicitur: cujus post ruinam muri tantum fictiles remansisse, & ob bestias, quæ illic abundant, captandas recuperati esse traduntur. Memi-nit hujus turris & Sybilla. Vide sis Josephum, Eusb.[?] & alios.
units.tr: The tower and the city, Gen. 11:1, 4. Jerome mentions both in his book on places, in these words: "Babylon, the metropolis of the kingdom of the Chaldeans, where the tongues of those who were building the tower were divided, from which the surrounding region is also called Babylonia." Herodotus and many others who wrote Greek histories report that it was very powerful, lying in a square on the plain, and that from corner to corner of its wall it measured sixteen thousand paces, that is, sixty-four thousand around in all. The citadel, that is, the capitol of that city, is the tower, which is said to have been built after the flood and to cover four thousand paces. After its wall fell, only the brick remains are said to have survived, and they were recovered to catch the beasts which abound there. The Sibyl also remembers this tower. See Josephus, Eusebius and others.

units.la: Vna tantum omnes lingua utebantur] lingua sancta. R. Salomo, Abenmelech, alij: in qua conditus fuit mundus, Ionathan, autor Ierofolymitanæ. Hi assentiuntur omnes patres, imo universa antiquitas. Hiero.epist. 142. Initium oris & communis eloquii, & hoc omne quod loquimur, Ebræam esse linguam, qua vetus testamentum scriptum est, universa tradidit antiquitas. Cui firmando sunt nomina propria Heva, Cain, Seth, Noe, Phaleg, Babel & appellativa אָדָם[?] homo, אִישׁ[?] vir, אִשָּׁה[?] vira & alia, quæ alia commemorabo. Vide Augustin. de civitat. Dei lib. 16. cap. 11.
units.tr: They all used one language] The holy tongue: Rabbi Solomon, Abenmelech and others, the tongue in which the world was created; Jonathan, the author of the Jerusalem paraphrase. All the Fathers agree with these, indeed all antiquity. Jerome, letter 142. Universal antiquity has handed down that the beginning of speech and common discourse, and all that we say, is the Hebrew language, in which the Old Testament was written. To confirm this there are the proper names Eve, Cain, Seth, Noah, Peleg and Babel, and the common words 'adam' man [אָדָם], 'ish' man [אִישׁ], 'ishah' woman [אִשָּׁה] and others, which I shall mention elsewhere. See Augustine, City of God, book 16, chapter 11.

units.la: Pag. 8. Velut alicnigenam] imo velut barbarum. barbarus qui non intelligitur. Sic Latini Græcis olim barbari erant. Unde lingua barbara, id est, Latina, & Marcus vortit barbare, id est, Latine. Hinc etiam Ovidius cecinit, Barbarus hic ego sum quia non intelligor ulli,
units.tr: Page 8. As if a foreigner] indeed as if a barbarian: one who is not understood. Thus the Latins were once barbarians to the Greeks. Hence the barbarian tongue, that is, Latin, and Mark translates "barbare", that is, "Latine". Hence also Ovid sang: "I am a barbarian here, because I am understood by no one."

units.la: Sed hīs Noe ita diuisus orbis fuit] casu hoc accidit, non deliberato. Nam cum alius alium non intelligeret, qui potuissent de orbis diuisione inter se deliberare? Verba i ofephi hac de re clara & perspicua, Quo quemque fors & Deus tulit, eam terram cum suis occupavit, ut tam maritima quam mediterranea cultoribus replerentur. Nec defuerunt qui conscensis navibus ad insulas habitandas trajicerent.
units.tr: But in this way the world was divided by Noah's sons] This happened by chance, not by deliberate plan. For since one did not understand another, how could they have deliberated among themselves about dividing the world? Josephus's words on this matter are clear and plain: "Each man occupied with his people whatever land chance and God brought him to, so that both the coastal and the inland lands were filled with inhabitants. Nor were there lacking those who, boarding ships, crossed over to inhabit the islands."

units.la: Ita ut Sem intra orientem, &c.] Alcuinus, Sem, ut æstimant, Asiam, Cham Africam, Japheth Europam sortitus est.
units.tr: So that Shem within the east, etc.] Alcuin: Shem, as they reckon, received Asia by lot, Ham Africa, Japheth Europe.

units.la: Orientem] Asiam. Hiero. quæst. in Genesin, Filij Sem ab Euphrate fluvio usque ad Indicum oceanum tenent.
units.tr: East] Asia. Jerome, Questions on Genesis: the sons of Shem hold the land from the river Euphrates to the Indian Ocean.

units.la: Occidentem] Europam & Asiæ partem quæ vergit ad occidentem. Hiero. ibid. Iapheth filio Noe nati sunt septem filij, qui possederunt terram in Asia ab Amano Tauroque, Syriæ coeles & Ciliciæ montibus usque ad fluvium Tanaim: in Europa vero usque ad Gadira, nomina locis & gentibus relinquentes, e quibus postea immutata sunt plurima, cetera permanent ut fuerunt
units.tr: West] Europe and that part of Asia which tends toward the west. Jerome, ibid.: Seven sons were born to Japheth, son of Noah. They possessed the land in Asia from the Amanus and Taurus mountains, the mountains of Coele-Syria and Cilicia, as far as the river Tanais; and in Europe as far as Gades, leaving their names to places and peoples. Many of these names were later changed, while the rest remain as they were.

units.la: Cham mediis continetur] mediis regionibus inter orientem & occidentem, ut sunt Arabia, Syria, Ægyptus, totaque adeo Africa, quæ Austrum respicit: quam & Lybiam appellant. Sed Lybiæ nomen hodie angustius. Hieronymus quæst. in Genesin. Quare autem in una tantum climatis parte antiquum Lybiæ nomen resederit, & reliqua terra vocata sit Africa, differere non hujus loci nec temporis est.
units.tr: Ham is contained in the middle] in the central regions between east and west, such as Arabia, Syria, Egypt, and indeed all Africa, which faces the south; this is also called Libya. But the name Libya is narrower today. Jerome, Questions on Genesis. Why the ancient name Libya remained in only one part of the climate, while the rest of the land was called Africa, is not a matter for this place or time to discuss.

units.la: Vsque Abram] usque ad Abram, edit. Paris
units.tr: As far as Abram] "as far as Abram", Paris edition.

units.la: Abram] sic emendavimus. prius erat in omnibus libris, quos vidi, Abraham. Egone ut credam Severum ita scripsisse? nunquam factum. Scripsit enim certe initio Abram: postea, cum additione unius litteræ nomen immutatum esset, Abraam, videlicet ex Græco ἀβραὰμ. Græci enim dissiones in media raro adspirant.
units.tr: Abram] We have emended it thus; in all the books I have seen, it was previously Abraham. Am I to believe that Severus wrote it so? Never. For he certainly wrote Abram at first; later, with the addition of one letter, the name was altered to Abraam, namely from the Greek ἀβραὰμ. For the Greeks rarely aspirate in the middle of words.

units.la: Patre Thara natus] natus fuit anno Thare 70. an 130? Priùs habetur Gen. 11. 26. posterius colligitur ex narratione Stephani protoprotomartyris Act.7. Nam Thare mortuus est apud Carras post quam vixisset annos quinque supra ducentos Gen. 11. 32. Post ejus obitum Abram inde discessit, Act.7.4. Discessit autem annos natus septuaginta quinque. Diserte Moses, septuaginta quinq; annorum erat Abram cum egrederetur ex Haran. Gen.12. 4. Demehos 75[?]. annos ex annis Thare, supersunt 130. Res est; non conjectura: nihil tamen audeo statuere. Nam in narratione illa quadam habentur, qua[?] cum historia Geneseos non usque-quaque conveniunt; imo, si libere licet, quibus jure merito con-tradici potest. Quod cum lapsu memoriæ vel culpa librariorum acciderit, calumnia carere debet.
units.tr: Born of father Terah] He was born in the year 70 of Terah, or in the year 130? The former is in Gen. 11:26; the latter is inferred from the speech of Stephen, the first martyr, Acts 7. For Terah died at Haran after he had lived two hundred and five years, Gen. 11:32. After his death Abram departed from there, Acts 7:4. He departed at the age of seventy-five. Moses says plainly that Abram was seventy-five years old when he went out of Haran, Gen. 12:4. Subtract 75 from Terah's years, and 130 remain. This is a matter of fact, not conjecture; yet I dare not settle anything. For in that narrative there are some things which do not agree in every respect with the history of Genesis; indeed, if I may speak freely, there are things which can rightly be contradicted. Since this may have happened through a lapse of memory or the fault of copyists, it ought to be free from calumny.

units.la: Anno millesimo & septuagesimo] omisit duos annos Semi, quos vixit post diluvium antequam Arphaxad procrearet, ut sit, anno millesimo & septuagesimo secundo. Nam ea summa est annorum secundum Græcos. Dico secundum LXX. interpretes, quos Græci chronologi sequuntur. Nam Ebræi pauciores annos numerant, videlicet 292[?] tantum. Quod ex hac tabula perspicuum fiet.
units.tr: In the thousand and seventieth year] He has omitted the two years of Shem which he lived after the flood before he begot Arphaxad, so that it falls in the year 1072. For that is the sum of years according to the Greeks. I mean according to the Seventy translators, whom the Greek chronologers follow. For the Hebrews count fewer years, namely only 292. This will become clear from the following table.

units.la: Sem anno post diluvium altero, sive secundo, genuit Arphaxad | 2 Arphaxad Sale an. ætatis | 35 Sale Eber, | 30 Eber Phaleg, | 34 Phaleg Reu, | 30 Reu Sarug, | 32 Sarug Nachor sive Nahor, | 30 Nachor Thare, | 29 Thare Abram, | 70 Summa, | 292
units.tr: Shem begot Arphaxad in the second year after the flood | Arphaxad at the age of 35 begot Salah | Salah begot Eber at 30 | Eber begot Phaleg at 34 | Phaleg begot Reu at 30 | Reu begot Serug at 32 | Serug begot Nahor at 30 | Nahor begot Terah at 29 | Terah begot Abram at 70 | Total 292

units.la: Aut sequendo eos qui genitum Abram contendunt anno Thare centesimo trigesimo. | 352
units.tr: Or following those who maintain that Abram was begotten in Terah's 130th year | 352

units.la: Quod autem Sigonius putat annos 353. error est manifestus in Phaleg, cui tribuit annos triginta & unum. Vide Gen.11,18.
units.tr: That Sigonius thinks 353 years is a manifest error in Phaleg, to whom he assigns thirty-one years. See Gen. 11:18.

units.la: Series annorum secundum Græcos.
units.tr: The series of years according to the Greeks.

units.la: Sem genuit Arphaxad post diluvium an. | 2 Arphaxad Cainan an. ætat. | 135[?] Cainan Sale | 130 Sale Eber, | 130 Eber Phaleg, | 134 Phaleg Reu Serug vel Sarug. | 132 Sarug Nachor, | 130 Nachor Thare. | 79
units.tr: Shem begot Arphaxad in the year 2 after the flood; Arphaxad (begot) Cainan at the age of 135[?]; Cainan (begot) Shelah, 130; Shelah (begot) Eber, 130; Eber (begot) Phaleg, 134; Phaleg (begot) Reu, Serug or Sarug, 132; Serug (begot) Nahor, 130; Nahor (begot) Terah, 79.

units.la: Sic editio quæ ad exemplar Venetum edita Basileæ in octavo folium complicat. Romana & Complutensis habent, | 179 Thare Abram | 70
units.tr: So the edition that was printed at Basel in octavo from the Venetian exemplar. The Roman and Complutensian editions have: Terah (begot) Abram, 179 (?); 70.

units.la: Summa 1072. de quibus Augustinus de civit. Dei lib.16. cap. 10. Ceterum Isidorus, omisso Cainan, qui in fonte Ebræo non habetur, supputat annos 942. Epiphanius 1040. Nicephorus vero 1081.
units.tr: The sum is 1072, which Augustine gives in De civitate Dei, book 16, chapter 10. Moreover, Isidore, omitting Cainan, who is not found in the Hebrew source, reckons 942 years. Epiphanius gives 1040, and Nicephorus 1081.

units.la: Sara] codices Ebræi Sarai. Sed nostrer secutus est τὰς ἑβδομή-κοντα χρονολογία, qui ὀρθῶς scribunt, non [?]. Hanc traditio doctorum cum lectio eandem facit, quæ fuit filia Haranis fratris Abrahæ. Nata est, ut Salmanticensis prodidit, anno creationis 1958. Sed aetum dentibus meis quod in eodem sequitur, Haran genuit eam anno ætatis septimo. Forte mendum est pro decimo septimo. Libet integrum locum ex Ebræo Latinum facere. Quid enim vetat? nam facit ad lucem huius historiæ, & liber ille, in quo hæc habentur, Christianus fere ignotus est. Anno mundi conditi 1658. hoc est biennio post diluvium, natus fuit Arphaxad Semo filio Noe, &c. Anno 1693. natus est Sale Arphaxado. Anno 1727. natus fuit Eber, qui primus instituit gymnasium & scholam, & ipse est pater omnium filiorum Eber. Anno 1727. natus est Phaleg, cujus pater Eber prophetavit de illo fore ut in fine dierum ejus divideretur terra in varias linguas. Vixit autem Phaleg annos 239. obiitque anno conditus 1996. quo anno divisa fuit terra.
units.tr: Sarah: the Hebrew manuscripts have Sarai. But our text followed the Seventy's chronology [τὰς ἑβδομήκοντα χρονολογία], who write correctly [ὀρθῶς], not [?]. The tradition of the teachers and the reading make her the same person, who was the daughter of Haran, Abraham's brother. She was born, as the Salamanca writer reported, in the year of creation 1958. But the sentence that follows in the same text, that Haran begot her in his seventh year, I have gnawed over with my teeth. Perhaps there is an error for seventeenth. I would like to make a whole passage from the Hebrew into Latin, for what prevents it? For it sheds light on this history, and that book in which these things are found is almost unknown to Christians. In the year of the world's creation 1658, that is, two years after the flood, Arphaxad, son of Shem, son of Noah, etc., was born. In 1693 Shelah was born to Arphaxad. In 1727 Eber was born, who first established the gymnasium and the school, and he is the father of all the sons of Eber. In 1727 Phaleg was born, whose father Eber prophesied that the earth would be divided into various languages in his days. Phaleg lived 239 years and died in the year 1996, in which year the earth was divided.

units.la: Anno 1787. natus fuit Reu. Anno 1819. natus fuit Sarug. Anno 1849. Nahor. Anno 1879. Thare pater Abrahami, Anno 1948. natus est Abram, deinde Nahor, & postea Haran. Diluvium accidit anno mundi 1656. A diluvio ad Abram anni sunt 292. Anno 1958. creationis nata est Sara, de qua traditio est apud magistros, Sara est Iescha filia Haran fratris Abrahami, qui genuit eam, cum ageret annum septimum. Nam ecce Haran est tertius post Abraham. Anno mundi 1996. fuit divisio linguarum, qui est annus 340. post diluvium, ut habetur in Brefith rabba,
units.tr: In 1787 Reu was born. In 1819 Serug was born. In 1849 Nahor. In 1879 Terah, father of Abraham. In 1948 Abram was born, then Nahor, and afterwards Haran. The flood happened in the year of the world 1656. From the flood to Abram there are 292 years. In the year of creation 1958 Sarah was born, of whom there is a tradition among the masters that Sarah is Iscah, the daughter of Haran, Abraham's brother, who begot her when he was in his seventh year. For behold, Haran is the third after Abraham. In the year of the world 1996 there was the division of tongues, which is the year 340 after the flood, as is found in Bereshit Rabbah,

units.la: cap. 26. Series horum annorum, Adam 130. Seth 105. Enos 90. Cainan 70. Malaleel 65. Iared 162. Henoch 65, Mathusale 187. Lamech 182. Noe 600. annum agebat diluvii tempore. Ecce anni 1656. usque ad diluvium. A diluvio autem usque ad divisionem 340. Series horum. Altero anno post diluvium natus est Arphaxad. Arphaxad 35. Sale 30. Eber 34. Phaleg 239. in cujus fine divisa fuit terra. Ecce 340. anni a diluvio usque ad divisionem, quae fuit anno mundi 1996. Ceterum omnes anni Noe 950. qui vitam cum morte commutavit anno mundi bis millesimo sexto, qui est decimus a divisione. Abraham autem tempore divisionis agebat annum 48. Vnde sequitur anno ipsius 58. mortuum fuisse Noe. Et aliquanto post. A diluvio usque ad natum Abrahamum, qui est caput generis, pater multitudinis gentium, anni sunt 292. Quum ageret annum 48 decennio ante obitum Noe fuit divisio linguarum in fine dierum Phalegi, ut habetur capite primo in tractatu de Sabbatho, & in Seder Olam. Vocatur autem Phaleg, non solum quia ejus tempore divisae sunt linguae, sed etiam quia tum divisio facta est annorum hominis, qui non produxit vitam nisi ad dimidium priorum. Quin ipse quoque mortuus est in medio dierum patris sui Eber. Verum Sem filius Noe vixit 1[?]. aetates usque ad annum 50. Iacobi. Eber autem filius nepotis ipsius Sem vixit usque ad annum 79, Iacobi Patriarchae. Haflenus Salmanticensis
units.tr: chapter 26. The series of these years: Adam 130, Seth 105, Enosh 90, Kenan 70, Mahalalel 65, Jared 162, Enoch 65, Methuselah 187, Lamech 182, Noah 600, the age at which he was at the time of the flood. Behold, 1656 years up to the flood. From the flood, however, up to the division, 340. The series of these: Arphaxad was born in the second year after the flood. Arphaxad 35, Shelah 30, Eber 34, Phaleg 239, at whose end the earth was divided. Behold, 340 years from the flood up to the division, which was in the year of the world 1996. Moreover, all the years of Noah were 950, and he exchanged life for death in the year of the world 2006, which is the tenth after the division. Abraham, however, was 48 years old at the time of the division. Whence it follows that Noah died in his fifty-eighth year of Abraham's life. And a little after. From the flood up to the birth of Abraham, who is the head of the race, the father of a multitude of nations, there are 292 years. When he was 48 years old, ten years before Noah's death, there was the division of tongues at the end of the days of Phaleg, as is found in chapter one of the treatise on the Sabbath and in the Seder Olam. Phaleg is so called not only because the tongues were divided in his time, but also because at that time the lifespan of men was divided, since men did not live beyond half of the earlier years. Indeed he himself also died in the middle of the days of his father Eber. Yet Shem, son of Noah, lived [?] generations until the 50th year of Jacob. Eber, moreover, son of Shem's grandson, lived until the 79th year of Jacob the Patriarch. Haflenus the Salamanca writer.

units.la: In regione Chaldaeorum] ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ τῶν Χαλδαίων ἐστὶ[?] in editione Graeca Gen. 11. 28. ubi vulgata nostra, in Vr Chaldaeorum. Pro Graecis fecit Manahem homo Iudaeus, qui Vr interpretatur, אור[?] id est, campum, planitiem, vallem: quod aliis nomen urbis, Ovpλω & Ovgίαν vocant. Meminit Eupolemus. Eusebius autor lib. ix. Πεοταγ etiam Camarinam dici. Forte quod ibi Chamarim, id est, sacerdotes gentis, qui peculiariter Chaldaei vocantur, habitarent. Sane Καμαρίνα eodem teste, dicebatur χαλδαικὴ πόλις, id est, civitas Chaldaeorum. Iuvat nos judicium Josephi Scaligeri viri eminentissimi, qui scribit nomine Chaldaeorum hoc loco philosophos & sacerdotes intelligi: quo sensu Abrahamus τῷ χαλδαικῷ invenisse perhibetur. Fabula est, quam tamen autores magni graveseque prodiderunt, de igne Chaldaeorum, in quem conjectus Abraham, postea mirabiliter, inde evaserit. Legimus certe in vulgata nostra 2. Reg.[?] 9.7. da igne Chaldæorum: & in libro quæstionum Ebraicarum, de incendio Chaldæorum. [illegible, ~3 letters] ignis, & ab eo Germanicum bper[?] five buer. Referunt hæc fabula in Medras Haggada. Citatur autem a Salomone Gallo, a Mose Hispano quem Gerundensem vocant, & ab aliis.
units.tr: "In the land of the Chaldeans": in the Greek edition of Genesis 11:28, [ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ τῶν Χαλδαίων ἐστὶ[?]], where our Vulgate has "in Ur of the Chaldeans." Manahem, a Jewish man, following the Greek, interprets Ur as [אור], that is, a plain, a level field, a valley. Others call it the name of a city, Ovpλω and Ovgίαν. Eupolemus mentions it. Eusebius, in book 9, says that it was also called Pēotag [Πεοταγ], and Camarina. Perhaps because the Chamarim, that is, the priests of the people, who are called Chaldeans in particular, lived there. Indeed Camarina, by the same witness, was called [Καμαρίνα] a Chaldean city, that is, a city of the Chaldeans. The judgment of Joseph Scaliger, a most eminent man, helps us, who writes that under the name of Chaldeans in this place philosophers and priests are to be understood; in this sense Abraham is said to have discovered [τῷ χαλδαικῷ] by Chaldean learning. There is a fable, which nevertheless great and serious authors have handed down, about the fire of the Chaldeans, into which Abraham was cast and afterwards wonderfully escaped. We certainly read in our Vulgate, 2 Kings [?] 9:7, "from the fire of the Chaldeans," and in the book of Hebrew questions, about the burning of the Chaldeans [illegible, about three letters] fire, and from it the German bper or buer. These fables are recounted in the Midrash Haggadah. They are cited by Solomon the Frenchman, by Moses the Spaniard whom they call the Gerundian, and by others.

units.la: [illegible, ~7 letters] malim, apud Carras. [illegible, ~6 letters] cuiusmodi le Chermel, Carmelus. Græci enim nomina Ebraica quandoque ita declinant ut aspiratam in tenuem mutent. Sic ex Phasē, declinarunt Pasc̃ha. Carræ urbs est Mesopotamiæ Crassi clade nobilitata. Apud interpretes Haran legitur, Haran, Charan, ut Ham, Cham. Sic Hebron & Chebron, Hermon & Chermon, id accidit iis nominibus, quæ abH, Heth iuncipiunt: quæ Græci propterea per χ exprimunt ut doceant aspiranda esse, inquit Hieronymus. Male igitur faciunt, qui talia exiliter scribunt, nihil interesse putantes Hasidæus dicas an Asidæus, Haceldama an Aceldama. Vide setlas nostras.
units.tr: [illegible, about seven letters] I would prefer "at Carrhae" [apud Carras]. [illegible, about six letters], of the kind "le Chermel," Carmel. For the Greeks sometimes decline Hebrew names so that the aspirate changes to the smooth. Thus from Phase they declined Pascha. Carrhae is a city of Mesopotamia, made famous by the defeat of Crassus. In the translators it is read Haran, Haran, Charan, as Ham, Cham. So Hebron and Chebron, Hermon and Chermon; this happens with those names that begin with H, Heth. The Greeks therefore express these with χ, so that they may teach that they are to be aspirated, says Jerome. Those therefore do wrong who write such things carelessly, thinking it makes no difference whether you say Hasidaeus or Asidaeus, Haceldama or Aceldama. See our notes.

units.la: paternam.
units.tr: paternal.

units.la: Mesopotamiam, in qua Carræ, ubi commorabatur cum Deus eum admoneret de relinquenda patria his verbis, Exi e terra tua, &c. Nam patria, in qua quis habitat. Sic Haran vocatur civitas Nachor, & Sion urbs Davidis. Aut dic Syriam interamnem fuisse partem Chaldææ. Sane ipsam Chaldæam Stephanus Mesopotamiam appellat, Actō. 7. 2.
units.tr: Mesopotamia, in which Carrhae is, where he was staying when God admonished him to leave his homeland with these words, "Go out from your land," etc. For the homeland is the place in which one dwells. Thus Haran is called the city of Nahor, and Zion the city of David. Or say that Syria between the rivers was a part of Chaldea. Indeed Stephen calls Chaldea itself Mesopotamia, Acts 7:2.

units.la: Sigonius emendat, ac fratrem relinquens. Nam pater ante discessum obierat. Reliquit ergo non patrem, sed fratrem Nachor. Quid si, domum, id est, familiam, cognationem: & patrem, id est, domum paternam? Gen. 12.1. Egredere e terra tua, & e cognatione tua, & e domo patris tui. Sic dicimus, ivit ad Pompeium pro ad domum Pompei. Aut patrem relinquens ibi sepultum.
units.tr: Sigonius emends it to "and leaving his brother." For the father had died before the departure. He therefore left not his father but his brother Nahor. What if it means "house," that is, family, kindred; and "father," that is, the paternal house? Genesis 12:1, "Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father's house." Thus we say he went to Pompey, meaning to the house of Pompey. Or "leaving his father," buried there.

units.la: fratris Haran, qui vrē Chaldæorum decesserat, relicto filio Lot. Obiter noto, Haran quum est proprium viri scribi cum aspiratione simplici, quam vocant he. Sed quum est nomen urbis, tum scribitur cum aspiratione geminata, quam vocant Heth. Hanc ambiguitatem tollit Charan: unde Carræ. Vide quæ supra nota vimus.
units.tr: of his brother Haran, who had died in Ur of the Chaldeans, leaving a son Lot. I note in passing that when Haran is a man's name it is written with the single aspirate, which they call he. But when it is the name of a city, it is written with the doubled aspirate, which they call heth. The spelling Charan removes this ambiguity, whence Carrhae. See what I have noted above.

units.la: locum pro urbe posuit, ut Gen. 12.6. usque ad locum Sichem. Quod Gerundensis Iudæus expo-nit ponit, usque ad urbem Sichem. Sic Amos 4.6. in omnibus urbibus veitris, & mox, in omnibus locis veltris. idem aliter Editio Coloniensis, in locum, cui Sichem nomen. minus probo.
units.tr: he put the place for the city, as in Genesis 12:6, "as far as the place of Shechem." Which the Gerundian Jew explains as "as far as the city of Shechem." So Amos 4:6, "in all your cities," and soon after, "in all your places." The Cologne edition has it differently, "to the place which is called Shechem." I do not approve this much.

units.la: Sichem] hæc est Sicima, quam posterior ætas Sechythopolim appellavit. Nomen habuit a Sichem filio Hemor, qui Dinam Iacobi filiam stupravit. Nota figura quam anticipationem, alij prolepsin vocant. Ea utuntur frequenter sacri scriptores. Quanquam sunt qui potius filium Hemor ab urbe ejusdem nominis appellatu censent. Quod mihi non videtur.
units.tr: Sichem] This is Sicima, which a later age called Sechythopolis. It took its name from Shechem son of Hamor, who violated Dinah the daughter of Jacob. This is a notable figure, which some call anticipation and others prolepsis. The sacred writers use it often. Yet there are those who think rather that the son of Hamor was named after the city of the same name. This does not seem so to me.

units.la: Ac rursum reversus Lot] Sigonio magis placet, ac rursum reversus. Lot, &c. mihi quoque hoc vehementer placet.
units.tr: And again Lot returned] Sigonius prefers "and again returned Lot, etc." I also very much like this reading.

units.la: Vacuæ tum regionis] quomodo vacuæ cum in ea tunc habitarent Chananæi & Pherezæi Gen. 13.7? An vacua erat pecoribus & armentis? nam Chananæi mercatores magis erant quam pastores. Contendebant autem utriusque pastores de finibus agri pascui. Vide Gen. 13. Iosephum Orig. Iudaic. lib. 1 cap. 16.
units.tr: Of an empty region] How was it "empty" when the Canaanites and Perizzites then lived in it (Gen. 13.7)? Was it empty of flocks and herds? For the Canaanites were merchants more than shepherds. Moreover, the shepherds of both sides were quarrelling over the boundaries of the pasture land. See Gen. 13, and Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 1, chapter 16.

units.la: In Sodomis consedit] Gen. 14. 12. Sed in Ebræo, tetendit Sodomam usque, ut exponi posset Σοδόμοις, in regione, vel p mavis[?], in territorio Sodomorum. Nam τὰ Σοδόμα & de ipsa urbe usurpatur & de territorio ejus, aut circumjacente regione. Porro non dubitandum quin in ipsa urbe quoque habitaverit.
units.tr: They settled among the Sodomites] Gen. 14.12. But in Hebrew it reads "pitched his tent as far as Sodom", which could be explained as the Greek [Σοδόμοις], in the region, or, if you prefer, in the territory of the Sodomites. For [τὰ Σοδόμα] is used both of the city itself and of its territory or surrounding region. Nor is there any doubt that he also lived in the city itself.

units.la: Infame incolis] propter mores incolarum, qui in proverbium abierunt, ut mores Mafsiliensium. Plautus, Vbi tu es qui colere mores Mafsilienses postulas? Sic mores Sodomitani. Vide Adagia nostra. Dicunt etiam [illegible, ~4 letters] ingenium habet Sodomitarum, vel, colit mores Sodomitanos. Minus recte alii & nos olim, conditio ei Sodomitana. Nam conditio de fortunis dicitur, non de qualitate mentis.
units.tr: Infamous to its inhabitants] On account of the morals of the inhabitants, which have passed into a proverb, as the morals of the Massilians. Plautus: "Where are you, you who want to cultivate Massilian morals?" So also "Sodomite morals". See our Adages. They also say [...] "he has a Sodomite character", or "he cultivates Sodomite morals". Others, and I myself formerly, less correctly said "a Sodomite condition" for him. For condition is said of fortunes, not of the quality of the mind.

units.la: Viris in viros irruentibus, masculis in masculos operantibus turpitudinem. Hoc crimen Sodomiæ nomine hodie innotuit. Vt a Simone mago Simonia, sic a Sodoma urbe Sodomia dicitur.
units.tr: Men rushing upon men, males committing shameful acts upon males. This crime has become known today by the name of sodomy. As simony is named from Simon the magician, so sodomy is named from the city of Sodom.

units.la: Reges vicinarum gentium] Amraphel rex Sennaar, Arioch rex Ellafar, Chodorlaomor rex Elamitarum, & Thadal rex Goijm sive gentium. Hos Diodorus Persas finxisse scribit. Iosephus vero Assyrios; penes quos Asiæ imperium tunc fuerit.
units.tr: Kings of the neighbouring nations] Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of the Elamites, and Tidal king of Goiim or of the nations. Diodorus writes that these were invented as Persians. Josephus, however, says Assyrians, in whose hands the rule of Asia then was.

units.la: Gentium] nomen hic est generale, quod ad certam speciem restringitur Gen. 14.1. βασιλεὺς ἐθνῶν, rex gentium: nisi mens, reliquarum gentium. Nam plures fuisse, quam ibi commemorantur. rentur, probabile est. R. Salomo ex Genesi magno (liber est eo nomine, qui Ebraice vocatur Brefith rabba) Goijm locus est ejus nominis, ubi convenerunt ex plurimis locis & nationibus, & regem crearunt quendam Thadal nomine. Ma-nahemus Ricineufis, Rex gentium constitutus fuit super diversos populos, qui eum sibi ducem elegerunt. Abeneẓra, nomen est provinciæ ut Ilam[?], aut significat regem aliarum gentium, præter eas quas ibi memoravit, Genef. 14. 9. [illegible, ~3 letters] Sym. συνδῶν, & in scholio παμφυλίας[?] Pamphilia, an omnium gentium? Nam Φυλὴ aliquando gens.
units.tr: Of the nations] Here the name is general, though it is restricted to a certain kind (Gen. 14.1). [basileus ethnōn], king of nations; unless the meaning is "of the remaining nations". For there were more of them than are mentioned there. It is probable, as the rabbis think. R. Solomon, from the Great Genesis (a book which in Hebrew is called Bereshit Rabba), says that Goiim is a place of that name, where people gathered from very many places and nations and made a king named Tidal. Manahem of Ricineus: the king of the nations was set over diverse peoples, who chose him as their leader. Abenezra: it is either the name of a province, or it means a king of other nations besides those he mentioned (Gen. 14.9). Symmachus [synDōn], and in a scholium [pamphylias], Pamphylia, or of all nations? For [phylē] sometimes means nation.

units.la: Cum antea nullum inter mortales certamen fuisset[?] idem habetur in Thanbuma[?], qui et Ilmedenu. sol. 7. col 1. Hactenus non fuerat bellum in mundo. Aliter Iosephus Orig. lib. 1. cap. 10. A Iofepho stat ipsa veritas. Nam hoc potius alterum bellum fuit, natum ex defectione harum gentium, quæ servierunt Chodorlaomor Elamitarum regi annos duodecim, ut habetur Gen. 14. 4. Aut sensus est, nullum certamen, quod quidem in sacris litteris memoretur. Nam credibile plura ante certamina fuisse. Nemrod enim absque certamine regnum sibi parare qui potuit? Siclamech primus bigamus fuit. Nam ante illum nemo simul duas uxores habuisse legitur.
units.tr: Since there had been no war among mortals before] The same is found in the ... Hitherto there had been no war in the world. Otherwise Josephus, Antiquities, book 1, chapter 10. Josephus's view is the very truth. For this was rather a second war, arising from the revolt of those nations which had served Chedorlaomer king of the Elamites for twelve years, as is found in Gen. 14.4. Or the sense is: no contest that is recorded in the sacred letters. For it is credible that there were many contests before. For how could Nimrod have won a kingdom for himself without a contest? Lamech was the first bigamist. For before him no one is read to have had two wives at once.

units.la: Sodomorum] Σοδομῶν. In Ebraeo est [illegible, ~5 letters] Sodoma, ubi vulgata nostra Sodomorum. Nam Graeci τὰ Σόδομα dicebant, ut τὰ ἱεροσόλυμα[?]. Hoc nomen aliquando late sumitur[?] pro tota regione Pentapolitana. Hieronymus, Gomorra una de quinq; civitatibus Sodomorum, quæ cum reliquis divina ultione subversa est.
units.tr: Of Sodom] [Σοδομῶν]. In Hebrew it is the singular Sodom, where our Vulgate has "of Sodom". For the Greeks said [ta Sodoma], as [ta Hierosolyma]. This name is sometimes taken broadly for the whole Pentapolitan region. Jerome: Gomorrah is one of the five cities of the Sodomites, which was overthrown by divine vengeance along with the rest.

units.la: Gomorrhæorum] Sic Orosius lib. 1. cap. 6. quos saltem de hoc exitu Sodomorum & Gomorrhæorum monco: & veteris interpres. Gen. 18. 11. tulerunt autem omnem subsistentiam Sodomorum & Gomorrhæorum. Esset autem potius, Gomorrhae. Quomodo Græci [illegible, ~6 letters] & analogia postulat. Eorum reges dicit quos alij regulos appellant, vicinarumque regionum] præferrim, vicinarumq; ut videlicet Adamæ, Seboim & Segor. Pentapolin confinem Arabiae regionem vocat Orosius lib. 1. cap. 5. Aut regiones appellat urbium singularum territoria, ut regio Adamæ sit territorium Adamæ, & sic deinceps,
units.tr: Of the Gomorrhaeans] So Orosius, book 1, chapter 6, whom I warn at least about this departure of the Sodomites and Gomorrhaeans; and the old translator (Gen. 18.11): "they took away all the substance of Sodom and Gomorrah." It ought rather to be "of Gomorrah". As the Greeks [...] and analogy requires. He calls their kings what others call petty kings, and the regions of the neighbouring lands, especially and neighbouring, namely Adama, Seboim and Segor. Orosius, book 1, chapter 5, calls the Pentapolis a region bordering on Arabia. Or he calls the regions the territories of the individual cities, so that the region of Adama is the territory of Adama, and so on.

units.la: Sodoma direpta] utrum τὰ σόδομα, an magis ut fit nomen singulare Sodoma, &c. Sic infra, pag. 10. Sodoma divinis ignibus conflagravit.
units.tr: Sodom plundered] Whether [ta sodoma], or rather, as is the usual form, the singular noun "Sodom, etc." So below, p. 10. Sodom was burned with divine fires.

units.la: Praedae hostibus fuit, &c.] Lot captus & substantia ipsius praedae fuit: aut, Sodoma directa praedae hostibus fuit. Pahl-lo post, reges victoria feroces, exutos praeda armisque in fugam compulit.
units.tr: Was prey to the enemies, etc.] Lot was taken captive, and his property itself became the prey. Or: "Sodom was laid waste and was prey to the enemies." Later, the kings, fierce in victory, drove them into flight, stripped of booty and arms.

units.la: Servis suis] verus sive vernaculis: quibus se junxerant federati Abra, Aner, Eschol & Mamre.
units.tr: His servants] Home-born or native slaves, with whom Abram, Aner, Eshcol and Mamre had joined themselves in alliance.

units.la: Numero trecentis decem & octo] Hinc lux Prudentij bisce versibus, Nos esse largæ vernularum divites Si quid trecenti bis novenis additis, Possint, figura noverimus mystica.
units.tr: Numbering three hundred and eighteen] Hence the light of Prudentius in these verses: "We know that the rich number of home-born slaves, if three hundred is added to twice nine, could be made by a mystical figure."
