units.la: Figura mystica est Thau littera, crucis figuram habens, cum supra scriptis duabus primis litteris nominis Ιησ[?], hoc modo ΙΗ[?] Hae litterae simul efficiunt 318. Vide quae scripsimus lib. 2. quaest. 21.
units.tr: The mystical figure is the letter Tau, which has the form of a cross, with the first two letters of the name Jesus written above it, thus [ΙΗ]. These letters together make 318. See what we wrote in book 2, question 21.

units.la: Melchisedec] hoc nomen interpretantur alii, βασιλεὺς δικαιοσύνης, rex justitiae: & alii, βασιλεὺς δίκαιος, rex justus, perinde est. Nam rex justitiae ex idiotismo linguae idem quod rex justus. Sed & Sedec antiqua declaratione δίκαιος. Sic reddunt LXX. Cohel 3,16. Aquila & Hiero. Psal. 17,1. צֶדֶק[?] justus, ut צָדוֹק[?] longus, צַדִּיק[?] gravis. In historia Ebraica Sedec est nomen urbis, quae & Salem, quam posterior aetas Ierosolymam dixit. Cui firmando Abenezrain commentatur ad hunc locum. Vocatur Malchi-sedec, quia erat rex super locum Sedec. Sedec ergo nomen loci, cujus rex proprio nomine Ieboram sive Ioram dicebatur. Abben-Gorion, nomen tuum Sedec, & de nomine tuo vocatus fuit rex tuus[?] Malchi-sedec. Dubito an verum sit. Dubitandi causa ex ipso textu, Melchisedec, rex Salem. Nam si Sedec idem cum Salem, quorsum illa repetitio? An exegetica est? Plerisque Melchisedec est Sem filius Noe. Sic fere doctores Ebraei. Quod notatum a Hieronymo, Primasio, Mose Gerundensi & aliis. Nec aliter interpretes Chaldaei Jonathan & Ierosolymitanus. Sed quomodo sine patre, sine matre, sine genere, si filius Noe? locus Apostoli clarus est Ebraeo 7,3. An quia sub nomine Melchisedec nusquam ejus genus memoratur? Nam patrem et matrem habuisse certum est. Nec omnino sine genere fuit, hoc est, ut Apostoli verbo utar, ἀγενεαλόγητος. Quid igitur? ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, &c. quia ejus parentes nusquam recensentur aut describuntur. Non ergo Sem, cujus genealogia ex Mose notissima est, magis errant, meo judicio, qui eum angelum aut filium Dei, non hominem fuisse asserunt, in quibus Origenes. Vide nunc, si placet, historiam vel fabulam de Melchisedeco, quae apud Athanasium tom. 2. pag. 8.
units.tr: Melchisedec] Others interpret this name as βασιλεὺς δικαιοσύνης [basileus dikaiosynes], king of righteousness, and others as βασιλεὺς δίκαιος [basileus dikaios], a righteous king; it comes to the same thing. For "king of righteousness," by an idiom of the language, means the same as "righteous king." But also in the old explanation Sedec means δίκαιος [dikaios], righteous. So the Seventy render it, Cohel 3,16. Aquila and Jerome, Psal. 17,1. righteous, as צֶדֶק [tsedeq] means righteous, as צָדוֹק [tsadoq] means long, צַדִּיק [tsaddiq] means weighty. In Hebrew history Sedec is the name of a city, which is also Salem, and which a later age called Jerusalem. To confirm this, Abenezra comments on this passage: he is called Melchisedec because he was king over the place Sedec. Sedec, then, is the name of the place, whose king was called by his proper name Jeboram or Joram. Ben-Gorion: your name is Sedec, and your king was called Melchisedec from your name. I doubt whether this is true. The reason for doubt lies in the text itself: Melchisedec, king of Salem. For if Sedec is the same as Salem, why that repetition? Is it explanatory? To most people Melchisedec is Shem, the son of Noah, and so mostly the Hebrew teachers say. This was noted by Jerome, Primasius, Moses of Gerona and others, and the Chaldee interpreters Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum agree. But how could he be without father, without mother, without genealogy, if he was the son of Noah? The passage of the Apostle in Hebrews 7,3 is clear. Is it because under the name Melchisedec his family is nowhere recorded? For it is certain that he had a father and a mother. Nor was he altogether without lineage, that is, to use the Apostle's word, ἀγενεαλόγητος [agenealogētos]. What then? ἀπάτωρ [apatōr], ἀμήτωρ [amētōr], and so on, because his parents are nowhere enumerated or described. Therefore, in my judgment, those are in greater error who assert that he was not Shem, whose genealogy is very well known from Moses, but an angel or the Son of God and not a man; among them is Origen. Now see, if you please, the history or fable about Melchisedec that is found in Athanasius, vol. 2, p. 8.

units.la: Sacerdote] simul & rex erat & sacerdos. Quod minime novum aut insolens in illis locis. Notant Ebraei ante legem omnes primogenitos sacerdotes fuisse: nec est dubitandum, quin iidem parentibus in regno successerint. Porro sacerdos erat non deorum falsorum; sed Dei Elion, id est, excelsi vel supremi aut altissimi, quem Ὑψιστον Graeci vocant.
units.tr: Priest] He was at once both king and priest. This is by no means new or unusual in those places. The Hebrews note that before the law all firstborn sons were priests; nor is it to be doubted that these succeeded their parents in the kingdom too. Moreover, he was priest not of false gods, but of God Elion, that is, of the high, or supreme, or most high, whom the Greeks call [Hypsistos].

units.la: Reliqua his, quibus ereptae erant reddidit] praeter vitium duntaxat juvenum & partem eorum qui ipsum comitati fuerant. Nam hi partem suam auferebant. Gen. 14.24.
units.tr: He restored the rest to those from whom they had been taken, except for the young men and some of those who had accompanied him, since these kept their own share. Gen. 14.24.

units.la: In hostili solo] potius, in peregrino solo. Nam intelligit Chananaeam & Aegyptum. Chananaei autem eo tempore non bo-fles [?] ipsorum erant, sed hospites.
units.tr: In a hostile land: better, in a foreign land. He means Canaan and Egypt. At that time the Canaanites were not their enemies but their guests.

units.la: Per quadringentos annos] tempus istud incipit a nato Isaaco, qui anno aetatis sexagesimo genuit Iacobum. Iacob autem, cum Aegyptum intraret, agebat annum centesimum & trigesimum. His adde annos ducentos decem, quibus fuerunt in Aegypto; en numerum, quem hic Severus posuit, & qui habetur, Gen. 15 13.
units.tr: For four hundred years: this period begins from the birth of Isaac, who begot Jacob in his sixtieth year. When Jacob entered Egypt he was a hundred and thirty years old. Add to these the two hundred and ten years they spent in Egypt, and you have the number that Severus gives here, which is also found in Gen. 15.13.

units.la: Ex Abram, Abraam] ita correximus. Nam & in editione Graeca Ἀβραάμ & in Abraham, quod in antea vulgatis, adjectio est duarum litterarum, non unius. Correctionem nostram firmat Hiero, ita scribens, nec mirandum quare non apud Graecos & nos a littera videatur addita, nos he litteram Ebraeam additam dixerimus. Idioma enim linguae illius est per he quidem scribere, sed per a legere: sicut e contra a litteram saepe per he pronuntiant. Vide quoque Iustinum disputatione cum Tryphone Iudaeo, pag. 109.
units.tr: Abram, Abraham: we have corrected it so. In the Greek edition it is Abraam, and in the Abraham printed in earlier editions there is an addition of two letters, not one. Jerome confirms our correction, writing: "Nor is it surprising that the letter seems to have been added not only among the Greeks but also among us; we would say that the Hebrew letter he was added." For it is a feature of that language to write with he but read with a, just as, conversely, they often pronounce a letter for he. See also Justin in his dialogue with the Jew Trypho, p. 109.

units.la: Ex Sara, Sarra dicitur] prius erat ex Sarai Sara: ubi non adjecta littera, sed ablata. In Ebraeis codicibus littera cum littera commutatur, videlicet שָׂרַי [?] in שָׂרָה [?] cum he quod in שָׂרַי [?]. Sed nostr absque dubio Graecos secutus est, in quorum libris Gen. 17, 15. σαρὰ ἡ γυνή σου οὐ καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆς· Σάρα, σάρα ἔ-[?] τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆς: Sara uxor tua non vocabitur nomen ejus Sara, Sarra erit nomen ejus. Adhibe nunc Quaesita mea, epist. vij.
units.tr: Sarai, Sarah is called: formerly it was Sarai, Sara, where the letter was not added but removed. In the Hebrew manuscripts one letter is exchanged for another, namely the letter in Sarai for the letter in Sarah, with he in place of the other. But our author has undoubtedly followed the Greeks, in whose books at Gen. 17.15 we read: "Sarah your wife shall not be called by this name; Sara, Sarra shall be her name," which is Sara uxor tua non vocabitur nomen eius Sara, Sarra erit nomen eius. Now consult my Quaesita, epistle vii.

units.la: Non inane mysterium] inane mysterium dicit quod caret ratione. Ea peti debet e scriptura Ebraica. Quanquam sunt qui alterum πῶ[?] adjectum existimant in [illegible, ~5 letters], ad significandum annum Abrahæ centesimum, quo filium genuit ex Sara uxore vetula, nempe nonagenaria. Sed, ut dixi, nullum est ζ in Ebraismo. Quocirca alia ratio quærenda est. Hieronymus quæstion. in Genesin, Errant qui putant primum Sara per unum R. scriptum fuisse, & postea ei alterum R. additum, & quia R. apud Græcos centenarius numerus est, multas super hoc nomine suspicantur ineptias: cum utique, utcumque volunt ei vocabulum commutatum, non Græcam, sed Ebræam debent habere rationem: Ebræum enim est. Nemo autem in altera lingua quempiam vocans, etymologiam vocabuli sumit ex altera. Sarai igitur primum vocata est per Sin, R es, Iod. Sublato igitur Iod, id est, I element o, addita est He littera, quæ per a legitur & vocata est Sara. Caussa autem ita nominis immutati hæc est, quod antea dicebatur princeps mea, unius tantum domus materfamilias: postea vero dicitur absolute princeps, id est, αὐτοκράτωρ. Sequitur enim, dabo tibi ex ea filium, & benedicam ei, eritque in gentes & reges populorum erunt ex eo. Signanterque * in Ebræo habetur, non vocabis nomen ejus Sarai, id est, non dices ei, princeps mea es: omnium quippe gentium futura jam princeps est. Quidam pessime suspicantur ante eam lepram fuisse vocitatam, & postea principem: cum lepra Saraath dicatur, quæ in nostra quidem lingua videntur habere aliquam similitudinem, in Ebræo autem penitus diversa sunt. Scribitur enim per Sadic, Res, Ein & Thau: quod multum a superioribus litteris, quibus Sara scribitur, discrepare manifestum est.
units.tr: An empty mystery: he says "an empty mystery" for what lacks reason. This must be sought from the Hebrew Scripture. Yet there are some who think that another letter has been added, to signify the hundredth year of Abraham, when he begot a son by his aged wife Sarah, who was ninety years old. But, as I said, there is no such letter in Hebrew. Therefore another explanation must be sought. Jerome, Questions on Genesis: They are wrong who think that Sara was first written with one R and that a second R was later added, and because R among the Greeks stands for the number one hundred, they suspect many absurdities about this name. Whatever change they want to make to the word, they must consider not Greek but Hebrew, for the name is Hebrew. No one who calls someone in another language takes the etymology of the name from that other language. So Sarai was first called by Sin, Resh, Yod. Removing the Yod, that is, the letter I, he was given the letter He, which is read as a and she was called Sarah. The reason for the change of name is this: she was previously called "my princess," mistress of one household only, but later she is called simply "princess," that is, sovereign. For it follows: "I will give you a son by her, and I will bless him, and he shall be a mother of nations, and kings of peoples shall come from him." And in the Hebrew it is significant that it reads, "you shall not call her name Sarai," that is, you shall not say to her, "you are my princess," for she was now to be princess of all nations. Some wickedly suspect that she was formerly called by the name of leprosy and later princess, since the leprosy is called Saraath, which in our language seems to have some resemblance, but in Hebrew is completely different. For it is written with Sadhe, Resh, Ayin and Taw, which is clearly far from the letters above, with which Sara is written.

units.la: Videndus & Albinus quæstionibus in Genesin.
units.tr: Albinus also should be consulted, in his Questions on Genesis.

units.la: Pag.10. Filius Ismael] tredecim annorum, unde Ismaelitæ ante decimum tertium annum neminem circumcidunt. Consulendus hac de re Iosephus.
units.tr: Page 10. Son of Ishmael: thirteen years old, which is why the Ishmaelites circumcise no one before their thirteenth year. On this matter Josephus should be consulted.

units.la: Annorum centum] nonaginta novem. Gen. 17. 24. & mox pro nonaginta octoginta novem. Nam tunc promissio facta est.
units.tr: A hundred years old: ninety-nine. Gen. 17.24; and soon after, for ninety, eighty and nine. For the promise was then made.

units.la: Quamobrem cum hæc scriberet Sulpicius, aut memoria lapsus fuit, aut in mente habuit dicereque voluit futurum eis filium cum ipse esset annorum centum & uxor ejus nonaginta. Anno enim post promissio completa fuit.
units.tr: Therefore, when Sulpicius wrote these things, he either slipped in memory or had in mind and wished to say that a son would be born to them when he was a hundred years old and his wife ninety. For the promise was fulfilled a year later.

units.la: Futurum ei filium Isaac] locus est Gen. 18.10. Quid hic sibi velit Sigonius nescio. Nam cum apparuit in convalle Mamre, cum comites habuit duos angelos. Eodem tempore hæc promissio facta Gen. 17.16. & 21.
units.tr: That a son Isaac would be born to her: the passage is Gen. 18.10. I do not know what Sigonius means here. For when he appeared in the valley of Mamre, he had two angels as companions. At the same time this promise was made, Gen. 17.16 and 21.

units.la: Inde Sodomam misi angeli] duo: quorum unus Sodomam delevit; alter Lotum eduxit cum uxore ac filiabus. Tertius enim legatione sua functus evanuerat. Dicunt autem Ebrei unum angelum non obire duas legationes. Quod verum an falsum sit, alii discutiendum relinquo.
units.tr: Then I sent angels to Sodom: two, of whom one destroyed Sodom, and the other led Lot out with his wife and daughters. The third, having performed his mission, had vanished. The Hebrews say that one angel does not perform two missions. Whether that is true or false, I leave for others to examine.

units.la: Cœnatos] cœna excepit. Gen. 19.3. fecit illis convivium, id est, συμπόσιον[?], quod LXX. hic πότον dixerunt. Sic Athenæus lib.4. ὅτι[?] ὁ βασιλεὺς πότον ποιῶν[?]. Mox sequitur, & coxit azyma, id est, panes azymos sive infermentatos. Nam hi panes paratu faciles sunt. Consuluit ergo hospitibus ex via fessis, ut tanto maturius cubitum irent & se quieti darent. Cœnatus, qui cœnavit; ut pransus, qui prandit.
units.tr: Were fed: he received them at supper. Gen. 19.3. He made them a feast, that is, a drinking party, which the Seventy here call a drinking. So Athenaeus in book 4: "the king, making a drinking." Next follows "and he baked unleavened bread," that is, unleavened loaves. For such loaves are easy to prepare. So he was looking after guests who were tired from the road, so that they might go to bed the sooner and give themselves to rest. "Cenatus" means one who has supped, as "pransus" means one who has dined.

units.la: Iuventus improba] tam senes quam juvenes, id est, mariti, ut est in edit. τὰ LXX.
units.tr: Wicked youth: both old and young, that is, husbands, as is in the Septuagint edition.

units.la: Ab injuria vindicantes] semper verissimum est illud Comici, In bono hospite atque amico quæstus est quod sumitur.
units.tr: Defending them from injury: that saying of the comic poet is always very true: "Profit is made from a good host and friend when something is taken."

units.la: Cæcitatem] ἀόρασίαν[?], ut sit evidentiam dicas, inquit Augustinus quæst. 43. quando non videmus quod opus est aut quod quærimus. Talis cæcitas, teste Nicolao, ἀμβλυωπία[?] etiam dicitur. Impedit enim visum, quo minus res objectas discernere possit. Sed forte legendum ἀορασία[?], quam vocem Ambrosius & alii cæcitatem interpretantur. Vide, si vis, editionem Romanam.
units.tr: Blindness: aorasia, so that you may call it lack of sight, says Augustine in Question 43, when we do not see what we need or what we seek. Such blindness, according to Nicolaus, is also called amblyopia. For it hinders sight so that it cannot distinguish the objects before it. But perhaps we should read aorasia, which Ambrose and others render as blindness. See, if you wish, the Roman edition.

units.la: Humano malo quo ægrius vetitis abstinetur] supra, quibus illicita potius desiderio erant. Seneca Oetheo, Illicita amantur, excidit quicquid licet. Ovidius, Nitimur in vetitum semper cupimusque negata, & Cui peccare licet peccat minus.
units.tr: Human evil, by which what is forbidden is abstained from with more difficulty: above, the things that were unlawful rather tempted desire. Seneca in the Oedipus: "What is forbidden is loved; whatever is allowed is cast aside." Ovid: "We strive for what is forbidden, and always desire what is refused," and "one who may sin sins less."

units.la: Mulier] ἡ γυνὴ, id est, uxor Lothi.
units.tr: The woman: he wife, that is, the wife of Lot.

units.la: Reflexit oculos] ἐνέβλεψεν εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω[?], respexit retrorsum. Veritas Hebraica respexit post eum, Lotum. [illegible, ~20 letters] & fuit statua salis. Graece est σήλη ἁλὸς[?]. Ebraice autem [illegible, ~3 letters], unde Nisibis, quae & Nesebis & Nasebis. Sic interpretatur hoc nomen Philo Byblius, ut est apud Stephanum de urbibus. Statuam autem alii cumulum, alii columnam vocant. Distat a mari Sodomeno duabus leucis: constatque adhuc cumulus ille, ait Benjamin in Itinerario, qui a gregibus aliquando lambendo imminutus denuo ad pristinam crescit molem. Targum Ierosolymitanum, Quia uxor Lot erat ex filiabus Sodomae, respexit post se, ut videret quid tandem eventurum esset domui patris sui: & ecce ipsa stetit (id est, manhit) columna salis, duratura usque ad tempus illud quo reviviscent mortui.
units.tr: She looked back: she looked backward, she turned round to look behind. The Hebrew truth is that she looked behind him, Lot. [illegible] and there was a pillar of salt. In Greek it is pillar of salt. In Hebrew [illegible], whence Nisibis, which is also Nesebis and Nasebis. Philo of Byblos so interprets this name, as cited in Stephanus, On Cities. Some call that statue a heap, others a column. It lies two leagues from the Dead Sea, and that heap still stands, says Benjamin in his Itinerary, which, though diminished at times by flocks licking it, grows back again to its former size. The Jerusalem Targum: Because Lot's wife was one of the daughters of Sodom, she looked behind her to see what would finally happen to the house of her father; and behold, she stood (that is, remained) a pillar of salt, to endure until the time when the dead shall revive.

units.la: Siquidem opidulo Segor parcitum fuit ad preces Loti, Gen.19.21. Quanquam video esse qui credant postea eversam fuisse, cum videlicet Lot, ea relicta (non enim audebat ibi manere) in montem quendam vicinum se recepisset, sed hoc quoque in dubio est. Nam inter eas urbes, quae una cum Sodoma perierunt, non recensetur Segor Deut.29 23.[?] Adhaec legimus apud Iosephum Orig. lib.5. cap.5. Longitudo lacus 150. stadiis patet, qui ad Zoar usque Arabiae tenditur. Quum circumcideretur Abraham agebat annum 99. tunc fuit eversio Sodomae, qui erat 51. annus a diluvio, proximus 52. anno. Verum Soar sive Segor anno uno habitata fuit post habitatam Sodomam. Et hoc est quod in Genesi dicitur, Evadam nunc, id est [?], quod in numeris valet 51. prout est capite primo in tractatu de Sabbatho.
units.tr: For the little town of Zoar was spared at Lot's prayer, Gen. 19.21. Although I see that some believe it was afterwards overthrown, namely when Lot, having left it (for he did not dare to remain there), withdrew to a certain nearby mountain; but this too is doubtful. For Zoar is not counted among the cities which perished together with Sodom, Deut. 29.23. Moreover, we read in Josephus, Origen book 5 chapter 5: the length of the lake extends 150 stadia, reaching as far as Zoar in Arabia. When Abraham was circumcised he was ninety-nine years old; then came the overthrow of Sodom, in the fifty-first year after the flood, or the next, the fifty-second year. But Soar or Segor was inhabited for one year after Sodom had been inhabited. And this is what is said in Genesis: "Let me escape now," that is, which in numbers is worth fifty-one, as is stated in the first chapter of the treatise on the Sabbath.

units.la: Quare sal? An ad sterilitatem terrae conciliandum? videtur. Sulphur autem ignem, qui natura levis est & sursum fertur, gravitate sua in terram deprimebat.
units.tr: Why salt? Is it to make the land barren? It seems so. But sulphur, which is light by nature and tends upward, pressed the fire down to the earth by its weight.

units.la: maxima enim natu dicebat alteri, Vir non est in terra qui congrediatur nobilcum Unde colligitur verum esse quod de Segor quidam suspicantur. Nam si non conflagaverat, utique scient ibi homines esse quibuscum congredi possent. Omnino exiHimabant[?] (verone an falsse novit ille qui omnia) humanum genus in illis locis interiisse.
units.tr: For the eldest said to the other: "There is no man on earth who may come in to us" (Gen. 19:31). From this it is gathered that what some suspect about Zoar is true. For if it had not been burned, people would surely have known there were men there with whom they could have intercourse. In any case, (whether truly or falsely, he knows who knows all things) the human race perished in those regions.

units.la: Moab] unde genus ducunt Moabitæ. Dictus Moab, ut vulgo exi-stimant, quia e patre natus, quod est מאב[?] Meab: nisi verior interpretatio, Moab, aqua patris. Mo enim in lingua Ægyptiorum aquam significat: quæ vox usurpatur quandoque in re venerea, ut ubi legimus, ab aqua aliena abstine. Quo pertinet & illud, Aqua furtiva dulcior.
units.tr: Moab: from him the Moabites trace their descent. Moab is so called, as the common view holds, because he was born of his father, which is מאב [Meab]; unless the truer interpretation is "Moab, water of the father." For mo in the language of the Egyptians means water. The word is sometimes used of sexual matters, as where we read, "Abstain from another's water" (Prov. 5:15 and following). To this belongs also the saying, "Stolen water is sweeter."

units.la: Ammon] Gen.19.38. Græci codices variant. Nam in uno est Ἀμμὼν & in aliis Ἀμμάν, ut paullo post Ἀμμανῖται, qui & Ammonitæ dicuntur. Hieronymus, Ammon ipse est pater Ammonitarum. Quæ omnia fusius reddit veritas Ebraica, in qua Ben-ammi, id est filius populi mei (ὁ υἱὸς τῆς λαοῦ μου[?] LXX.) & pater filiorum Ammon. Ab his Ammonitæ, id est, בְּנֵי־עַמּוֹן[?] distinguuntur. Quæ de re dicemus alias, si Deus voluerit.
units.tr: Ammon: Gen. 19:38. The Greek manuscripts vary. In one it is Ammōn [Ἀμμὼν], and in others Ammán [Ἀμμάν], as a little later Ammanītai [Ἀμμανῖται], who are also called Ammonites. Jerome says Ammon himself is the father of the Ammonites. The Hebrew text expounds all this more fully: there is Ben-ammi, that is, "son of my people" (ὁ υἱὸς τῆς λαοῦ μου in the LXX), and he is the father of the sons of Ammon. The Ammonites, that is, bnei-Ammon [בְּנֵי־עַמּוֹן], are distinguished from these. We shall speak of this matter elsewhere, if God wills.

units.la: Pag. 11. Cum Abraham effet etiam centum annorum] Si in ea sententia fuit ut existimarit Isaacum natum eo anno quo promissio facta est Abrahamo, fallitur. Nam promissio facta est cum annum ageret nonagesimum nonum, ut diximus. Isaac autem natus fuit cum esset annorum centum. Græca editio nihil ju-vat Sulpicium, quem ita sensisse colligo ex particula etiam.
units.tr: Page 11. "When Abraham was also a hundred years old": If he was of the opinion that Isaac was born in the year the promise was made to Abraham, he is mistaken. For the promise was made when Abraham was in his ninety-ninth year, as we have said. Isaac, however, was born when Abraham was a hundred. The Greek edition does nothing to help Sulpicius, whom I gather to have thought so from the particle "also."

units.la: Tum ancillam] Hagar: unde Hagareni, qui & Ismaelitæ & Arabes, & Saraceni: non a Sara, ut quidam arbitrantur, sed a verbo שָׁרָה[?], quod perspicuum ex scriptura [?], quæ in Thargum Ierosolymitano: pro quo [?] in Genesi magno, Tabernacula Saracenorum qui vagantur five vagi sunt, & e loco suo transferuntur. Recte Jane. Est enim genus hominum vagum νομαδικῶν[?] & latrociniis etiamnum hodie, viventes. Porro Hagareni Ebraice הַגְּרִים[?] dicuntur, quorum memoria usurpatur in odis Davidis.
units.tr: "Then the maidservant": Hagar, whence the Hagarenes, who are also Ishmaelites, Arabs and Saracens. They are named not from Sarah, as some think, but from the verb שָׁרָה, as is clear from Scripture. In the Jerusalem Targum, in place of this, in the large Genesis, we find "the tents of the Saracens, who wander or are nomads and are moved from their place." Rightly so. For they are a wandering race of nomads, living by brigandage even today. Moreover the Hagarenes are called in Hebrew הַגְּרִים [hagrim], and their memory is recalled in the Psalms of David.

units.la: Quæ habitasse in deserto] primum erravit in deserto Berfabee: post habitavit cum filio in deserto Pharan, ubi uxorem Ægyptiam filio dedit Gen. 21.21, ex qua is duodecim filios procreavit: unde fere gentes Arabum.
units.tr: "Who dwelt in the desert": First she wandered in the desert of Beersheba; afterwards she lived with her son in the desert of Paran, where Abraham gave his son an Egyptian wife (Gen. 21:21), by whom he begot twelve sons. Whence come nearly the tribes of the Arabs.

units.la: Præsidio Domini defensa traditur] nam indicabat ei puteum aquæ, cum extrema siti afficeretur in deserto.
units.tr: "Is said to have been defended by the Lord's protection": for he showed her a well of water when she was in the extremity of thirst in the desert.

units.la: Non multum post] Cicero dixisset patiùs, non multo post. Sic, multo ante, multo aliter, paullo post.
units.tr: "Not long after": Cicero would have said more correctly non multo post. So also multo ante, multo aliter, paullo post.

units.la: Immolandum sibi a patre Isaac filium poscit] agebat tunc Isaac annum 37, qui erat annus mundi conditi 208 r. natus enim est anno 2048. ut Salmanticensis annotavit: quibus, si addas 37. emergit numerus, quem dixi.
units.tr: "He demands that Isaac be offered to him as a sacrifice by his father": Isaac was then thirty-seven years old, in the year 208? of the created world; for he was born in the year 2048, as the Salamanca annotator noted. If you add 37 to this, the number I mentioned emerges.

units.la: Cum ara puerum superposuisset] ara haec extructa fuisse traditur in monte Moria, ubi postea templum aedificatum fuit. Salmanticensis, Ligatus fuit Isaac pater noster in monte Moria: traditio autem est in manu omnium locum hunc esse aream Areunae Iebusaei, in quo David & Salomon aedificarunt. In eodem loco Abraham extruxit altare, in quo filium suum ligavit. (Ebraice עקידת יצחק. Hinc עקידת יצחק[?] li-gatio Isaaci, de qua liber est apud Ebraeos peculiaris, quem nondum videre mihi contigit) in eodem loco Noe ex arca egressus aram erexit, ibique tam Cain quam Habel obtulerunt. Similiter obtulit in eo primus homo oblationem, cum creatus esset. Quin inde creatus fuit. Autor Moses Aegyptius capite secundo, in iis quae de domo electa composuit. Hucusque Iudaeus ille.
units.tr: "When he had laid the boy on the altar": this altar is said to have been built on Mount Moriah, where the temple was later built. The Salamanca annotator: "Our father Isaac was bound on Mount Moriah. It is the tradition of all that this place is the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, on which David and Solomon built. In the same place Abraham built the altar on which he bound his son. (In Hebrew, akedat Yitzchak [עקידת יצחק], the binding of Isaac, about which there is a special book among the Hebrews, which I have not yet had the chance to see.) In the same place Noah, coming out of the ark, erected an altar, and there both Cain and Abel offered. Likewise the first man offered a sacrifice there when he had been created; indeed he was created from there. The author is Moses the Egyptian, in chapter two, in what he wrote about the chosen house." Thus far that Jew.

units.la: In Hebron Chananaeorum opido] mortua est in opido Ar-be, quod a Graecis πόλις Ἀρβίξ[?] vocatur, & alio nomine Hebron sive Chebron dicitur: sepulta vero in spelunca Machphela, quam Abraham emerat ab Ephrone Hetthaeo. Historia refertur Gen. 23. Haec urbs Metropolis erat Iudaeae, condita septem annis ante ur-bem Aegypti, quae Tanis nuncupatur. Dicitur & Cariath-arbez a viro quodam Arbe dicto, non a quatuor patriarchis ibi sepultis, ut Hiero. opinatur. Distat ab Aegypto, teste Gerundensi, itinere septem dierum.
units.tr: "In Hebron, a city of the Canaanites": Sarah died in the town of Arba, which the Greeks call Arbix [Ἀρβίξ], and which is also called by another name Hebron or Chebron. She was buried in the cave of Machpelah, which Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite. The story is related in Gen. 23. This city was the metropolis of Judea, founded seven years before the city of Egypt called Tanis. It is also called Kiriath-arba, from a man named Arba, not from the four patriarchs buried there, as Jerome thinks. According to Gerundensis, it is a seven days' journey from Egypt.

units.la: Chananaeorum opido] Gen. 23. 1. ipsa est Chebron in terra Chanaan. Moses Gerundensis ait esse vicinam Chananaeae. Virumque simul verum esse potest. Nam angustè sumptum hoc nomen usurpatur de una e septem gentibus, cum late acceptum omnes septem comprehendat. Sane Chananaea etiam terra septem gentium appellatur.
units.tr: "A city of the Canaanites": Gen. 23:1. It is Hebron in the land of Canaan. Moses of Gerona says it is near Canaan. Both can be true at once. For in a narrow sense the name is used of one of the seven nations, while in a broad sense it covers all seven. Indeed the land of Canaan is also called the land of the seven nations.

units.la: Quadragesimum annum aetatis agebat] Scriptum hoc diserte Gen. 25. 20. Duxit ergo uxorem tertio anno a matris obitu, quae decesserat anno aetatis ipsius 37. Apud Iosephum lib. 1. cap. 16. [illegible, ~12 letters] Sed περὶ redundat, ut alibi saepe, & aliquando in hac historia (ad).
units.tr: "He was in his fortieth year of age": This is stated plainly in Gen. 25:20. So he took a wife in the third year after his mother's death, who had died in the thirty-seventh year of his own age. In Josephus, book 1, chapter 16, [illegible, about twelve letters]. But περὶ [peri] is redundant, as often elsewhere, and sometimes in this history.

units.la: Servo suo] quem domi seniorem tum habebat, nomine ElieIer. ut Lyra & Ionathan annotarunt.
units.tr: "His servant": whom he then had at home as his senior, named Eliezer, as Lyra and Jonathan noted.

units.la: De qua ipse oriundus videbatur] e Mesopotamia, ubi commoratus fuerat, & fratrem reliquerat, patre ibidem sepulto. Et bene dicit videbatur, quia revera oriundus erat e terra Chaldæorum.
units.tr: "From whom he himself seemed to be descended": from Mesopotamia, where he had lived and had left his brother, his father having been buried there. He rightly says "seemed," because in fact he was descended from the land of the Chaldeans.

units.la: Infolum patrium] Carras in patriam Abrahami, qua ei patria erat commigrationis, non ortus. Sic Christus tres patrias habuit, Bethlehem, in qua natus: Nazareth, in qua educatus: & Capharnaum, ubi aliquot annos versatus fuerat. Consule libellos meos, si habes.
units.tr: "His native land": Haran was Abraham's country, which was his homeland by migration, not by birth. So Christ had three homelands: Bethlehem, where he was born; Nazareth, where he was brought up; and Capernaum, where he had lived for some years. Consult my little books, if you have them.

units.la: Exea tamen tribu] In Græco codice Φυλὴ legitur, quod secutus est Sulpicius, sed in Hebræo, מִשְׁפָּחָה[?] ex cognatione mea. Tribus שֵׁבֶט dicitur. Id per מִשְׁפָּחָה exponit Abenezra Ief. 19. 13. Interpretes familiam reddunt. Φυλὴ etiam pro natione seu gente ponitur Esth.13.4[?]: in omnibus per orbem tribubus. Legitur ex eadem tribu; id est, ex eadem gente. Sed melius, ex eadem cognatione.
units.tr: "Yet from the same tribe": The Greek manuscript reads phylē [Φυλὴ], which Sulpicius followed, but the Hebrew has mishpachah [מִשְׁפָּחָה], "from my kindred." The word for tribe is shebet [שֵׁבֶט]. Abenezra explains it by mishpachah, and the interpreters render it "family." Phylē is also used for a nation or people, as in "in all the tribes throughout the world" (Esth. 13:4). It is read "from the same tribe," that is, from the same people. But better, "from the same kindred."

units.la: Pag.12. Contacto domini fœmine] femore alii, ut Græci μηρὸν[?]. Hic mos antiquus admodum, ut iurantes manum femori supponerent ejus cui jurabant. Notatum ab Aloysio Lippomano Indos hodieque isto ritu uti in jurando. Quod an verum sit aliis disquirendum relinquo.
units.tr: Page 12. "Having touched the thigh of the woman": others read "femur," as the Greeks have μηρόν [meron]. This custom was very ancient: those swearing placed their hand under the thigh of the one to whom they swore. Aloysius Lippomanus has noted that the Indians still use this rite in swearing. Whether this is true I leave for others to inquire.

units.la: Sacramentum dedit] id est, juravit solenniter. Cicero ita dixit, jusjurandum dare. Est autem sacramentum solenne jusjurandum, sive, ut ait Festus, quod jusjurandi sacratione interposita geritur.
units.tr: "He gave an oath": that is, he swore solemnly. Cicero spoke thus, "to give an oath." A solemn oath is a sacrament, or, as Festus says, it is what is done when an oath is sworn with a sacred act interposed.

units.la: Ad opidum Nachor] Carras, ubi Nachor cum patre habitaverat. Ita Sion vocatur civitas David. Sed cur non potius dicitur, opidum Thare? An quia Nachor ibi sedem fixam habebat. Nam pater ante abiisse Abraham obierat.
units.tr: "To the town of Nahor": Haran, where Nahor had lived with his father. So Zion is called the city of David. But why is it not rather called the town of Terah? Perhaps because Nahor had his fixed seat there, for the father had died before Abraham departed.

units.la: Nachor] vel Nabor, Sic Rachab et Ruhab. Hujus filius Bathuel, nepos Laban, qui tamen filius Nachor appellatur Gen. 29.5. Sed novum non est ut filius pro nepote ponatur. Gerundensis annotat hunc Nachorem, patre in Chaldæam concedente, mansisse in Haran, hoc est Carris, ubi etiam natus creditur: vel e Chutha inde translatus, quæ inde abest itinere sex dierum duntaxat. Hæc ille Gen. 11. in fine.
units.tr: "Nahor": or Nabor, as Rachab and Ruhab. His son was Bethuel, grandson of Laban, who is nonetheless called son of Nahor (Gen. 29:5). But it is not unusual for a son to be put for a grandson. Gerundensis notes that this Nahor, when his father left for Chaldea, stayed in Haran, that is Carrhae, where he is also believed to have been born; or he was transferred from Chutha, which is only a six days' journey from there. So he writes on Gen. 11, at the end.

units.la: Bathuelis Syri] Sic Laban Syrus. Quod autem in Græcis codicibus, Doeg[?] Syrus, error est legentium Res pro Daleth, hoc est. ארמי[?] Syrus, pro אדומי[?] Idumæus.
units.tr: Bathuel the Syrian Likewise Laban the Syrian. But the reading "Doeg the Syrian" in the Greek manuscripts is an error of readers, who took Resh for Daleth, so that the Syrian [ארמי] appears in place of the Edomite [אדומי].

units.la: Rebeccam] ex Græco ῥιβίκκα[?], quod hodie legunt Ribca. Sonat autem σιτιστήριον[?], id est, faginarium, locum in quo vituli saginantur. Sic uxor quædam Davidis nominatur Egla, id est, vitula. Cujusmodi nomina mulierum sunt Rachel, ovis: Sebia, caprea (unde Tabitha in actis Apostolorum. Nam Syri S, Sade cum Teth permutant) Iaala, ibex, rupicapra, aut, ut Davidi Camio placet, hyrcus sylvestris.
units.tr: Rebecca] from the Greek [ῥιβίκκα], which they now read as Ribca. It means, however, [σιτιστήριον], that is, a fattening-place, the place where calves are fattened. So a certain wife of David is called Eglah, that is, heifer. Of this kind are the women's names Rachel, ewe; Sebia, roe-deer (whence Tabitha in the Acts of the Apostles, for the Syrians exchange S and Sade with Teth); Iaala, ibex, mountain goat, or, as David Camio prefers, wild goat.

units.la: Popscit] pleuum esset, popscit in matrimonio, ut infra pag.14. eamque sibi in matrimonio a patre postulans.
units.tr: Popscit] If it were the plural, "popscit" would mean took in marriage, as below, p. 14, asking her for himself in marriage from her father.

units.la: Ceturam] Sic emendavimus. Prius erat Cethura. Nam est Teth in scriptura Ebraica. Id Hieronymus expressit semper per t, simplex. Nam aspirato Thau respondet potius. In editione Græca κιτλούρα[?], & apud Iosephum χιτούρα[?]. Malim, κιτλούρα[?]. Cetura, Cettura, ut Mesias, Mesias, Habacuc, Habbacuc, Debora, Debbora.
units.tr: Ceturam] We have emended this. It was previously Cethura. For the Hebrew text has Teth. Jerome always rendered this with a simple t, and the aspirated Thau corresponds rather to another letter. In the Greek edition it is [κιτλούρα], and in Josephus [χιτούρα]. I would prefer [κιτλούρα]. Cetura or Cettura, as Messias or Mesias, Habacuc or Habbacuc, Debora or Debbora.

units.la: In Paralipomenis] 1.Paralip.3.1.
units.tr: In Paralipomenis] 1 Paralip. 3.1.

units.la: Concubina[?] dicitur] recte. Nam uxor erat illegitima, quoniam cum viro convenerat absque scripto & cæremonijs legitimis: unde filij ejus hæreditatem patris non adibant, tantum accipiebant munera.
units.tr: Concubina dicitur] Rightly. For she was an illegitimate wife, since she had joined with the man without a written contract and without legitimate ceremonies. Hence his sons did not take up their father's inheritance but received only gifts.

units.la: Filios] sex Gen.25.2[?].
units.tr: Filios] Six, Gen. 25.2.

units.la: Sarra edito] hoc participium tam de fœminis quam de maritis dicitur. Tacitus, ubi Agrippina novissimo partu Iuliam ediderit. Cicero, editus Iovi satu. Plerique scribunt editus cum diphthongo, nempe quia prima in hoc verbo, quando extra seu foras dare significat, longa est. Quod etiam fecerunt in sæculum. Quanquam a sequendo dictum concedant. Sæpius occurrit, edere in lucem. Cicero, qui nascitur in lucem edi dicitur.
units.tr: Sarra edito] This participle is used of women as well as of men. Tacitus speaks of where Agrippina, after her last delivery, bore Julia. Cicero has "born of Jupiter's seed." Most write editus with a diphthong, namely because the first syllable of this verb, when it means to give out or bring forth, is long. They did the same with "in saeculum," though they concede that the word is derived from following. It often occurs in the phrase edere in lucem, to bring into the light. Cicero says that one who is born is said to be brought forth into the light.

units.la: Substantiam] bona, facultates. Substantia Græce οὐσία, ὑπαρξις[?]. Quintilianus, ut plus substantiæ filio relinquerem. Lexicon Græco-Latinum vetus, Οὐσία, patrimonium, sub-stantia, res familiaris. ὑπαρξις[?], substantia, opes.
units.tr: Substantiam] goods, means. Substance in Greek is [οὐσία], [ὑπαρξις]. Quintilian: "that I might leave more substance to the son." The old Greek-Latin lexicon gives for [οὐσία]: patrimony, substance, family property; for [ὑπαρξις]: substance, wealth.

units.la: Ex concubinis] Hagar & Cetura.
units.tr: Ex concubinis] Hagar and Keturah.

units.la: Separati] amandati orientem versus.
units.tr: Separati] dismissed towards the east.

units.la: Diem functus est] diem obiit cum complevisset annos 175. Dicunt Ebrei Abrahamum cœpisse anno ætatis tertio, complevisse autem scientiam suam anno 48. cum vidisset divisionem linguarum. Nam eo anno Abrahami divisio facta est. Dicunt tiam, Anno quinquagesimo secundo coepit inquirere in legem: anno autem ieptuagesimo venit in foedus inter segmenta, & rediit in Haran: anno vero septuagesimo quinto dictum ei est, Exi e terra tua, &c. Salmanticensis, erat modestus, minimeque invidus, spiritu depresso, animoque humili & munificus admodum. Beatusi[?] ipse & beati filij ejus post eum.
units.tr: Diem functus est] He died, having completed 175 years. The Hebrews say that Abraham began to know God in his third year of age, and completed his knowledge in his forty-eighth year, when he had seen the division of tongues, for in that year the division was made. They also say that in his fifty-second year he began to inquire into the law; in his seventieth year he entered into covenant between the pieces and returned to Haran; and in his seventy-fifth year it was said to him, "Go out from your land," etc. Salmanticensis: he was modest and very far from envious, of humble spirit and lowly heart, and very generous. Blessed was he, and blessed were his sons after him.

units.la: , Vigesimo fere anno] Isaac quadragenarius duxit uxorem, Gen. 25.20. Sexagenarius ex ea suscepit geminos. ibid. Abundat igitur ad verbium fere. Sunt qui post annum a die matrimonij vi-gesimum Rebeccam peperisse scribunt, in quibus Lyra & Sigonius. Verba Lyrae, fuit cum Rebecca uxore sua viginti annis an-tequam pareret. Sigonij, Post vigesimum annum Rebecca, precibus Isaac ad Deum, geminos peperit. Notatum in Iobafin ex Siphri (liber est ejus nominis) nisi fallor, Rebeccam cum Isaaco nuberet, egisse annum decimum quartum. Unde sequitur, cum gemines[?] ederet, fuisse annorum 34. Sed hac in re autores variant.
units.tr: Vigesimo fere anno] Isaac, forty years old, took a wife, Gen. 25.20. At sixty years old he had twins by her, ibid. The text is therefore almost redundant as to the word. There are those who write that Rebecca bore children after the twentieth year from the day of marriage, among them Lyra and Sigonius. The words of Lyra: she was with Rebecca his wife twenty years before she gave birth. Of Sigonius: after the twentieth year Rebecca, at Isaac's prayers to God, bore twins. It is noted in Iobafin, from the Siphri (a book of that name), unless I am mistaken, that Rebecca was fourteen years old when she married Isaac. Hence it follows that when she bore the twins she was thirty-four years old. But the authorities differ on this point.

units.la: Geminos edidit] Id accidit anno Abrahami centesimo septu-agesimo, videlicet quinque annis ante mortem ipsius: aut, ut Cajetanus putat, decem & quinque.
units.tr: Geminos edidit] This happened in the 170th year of Abraham, that is, five years before his death; or, as Cajetan thinks, fifteen.

units.la: Geminos] duos uno partu.
units.tr: Geminos] Two at one birth.

units.la: Exsultasse saepius] ἰοχίζων[?] exponit, exsultabant saepius. Locus est Gen. 25.22. In editione Romana est, exultabant. Quo verbo usus est Ambrosius in libro de Isaac, cap.4. & interpres vulgatus Psalm. 113. Augustinus praetulit, gestiebant. Hiero. in Tradit. Ebraicis, & movebantur filii ejus in ea. Pro motione LXX. interpretes posuerunt ἰοχίζων, id est, ludebant sive calcitrabant, quod Aquila transtulit constringebantur, Symmachus vero ἀλλάσσων[?], id est, in similitudinem navis in superficie ferebantur. Pro constringebantur, in fragmentis a me collectis invenio, confringebantur, quod genuinum esse puto. Nam יצחק[?] quasso, concutio, & est apud Graecos verbum ἰοχίζω, quod eodem modo exponitur. Cui affine quod apud Scholiasten ex Symmacho ἀλλάσσων, collustrabantur. Unde in fragmentis meis.
units.tr: Exsultasse saepius] The Greek [ἰοχίζων] is explained as "they leaped more often." The passage is Gen. 25.22. In the Roman edition it reads "they leaped." Ambrose used this word in his book on Isaac, ch. 4, and the Vulgate translator in Psalm 113. Augustine preferred "were eager." Jerome, in the Hebrew Traditions: "and his sons moved within her." For "moved," the Septuagint put [ἰοχίζων], that is, they played or kicked; Aquila rendered it "were pressed together," and Symmachus [ἀλλάσσων], that is, were carried on the surface like a ship. For "were pressed together," I find in the fragments I have collected "were broken together," which I think is genuine. For the Hebrew [יצחק], meaning to crush or shake, and the Greek verb [ἰοχίζω] is explained in the same way. Close to this is what the scholiast gives from Symmachus, [ἀλλάσσων], "were tossed about." Whence in my fragments.

units.la: יצחק[?] Sym. ἀλλάσσων.
units.tr: Hebrew [יצחק], Symmachus [ἀλλάσσων].

units.la: Redeamus eo unde degressi sumus, Lexicon Graeco-Latinum vetus, ἰοχίζω, exulto. Sic Luc. 1. ἰοχίζησεν ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει τὸ[?] βιφ[?]@·, exultavit lætitia fœtus. Nos ex Hebræo olim Vertimus, collidebant sese.
units.tr: Let us return to where we digressed. The old Greek-Latin lexicon: [ἰοχίζω], I exult. So Luke 1: [ἰοχίζησεν ἐν ἀγαλλιάσει τὸ βρέφος], the babe leaped for joy. We once translated from the Hebrew: they struck against one another.

units.la: Dictumque responso Domini est] Rebecca enim super ea re Dominum consuluit, qui respondit duas gentes esse in utero ejus, duos populos diversos inde oriturus.
units.tr: And it was said to her by the Lord's answer] For Rebecca consulted the Lord about this matter, and he answered that there were two nations in her womb, two different peoples who would arise from her.

units.la: Subdendum principio] cur adjecit, principio? nam si adverbialiter accepit, falsum est quod hic dicit. Non enim principio subditus fuit major minori: sed tunc primum cum David Idumæos tributarios fecisset. Quod accidit multis annis post hæc tempora. Forte principio posuit pro principatu, ut dicat majorem futurum aliquando sub minoris dominio. Sic principium sumitur, Psal. 109.3. tecum principium in die virtutis. Nam in Græco est ἀρχή. Lexicon Vetus, ἀρχή, imperium, magistratus, magisterium, præsidatus, principium.
units.tr: Subdendum principio] Why did he add "principio"? For if he took it adverbially, what he says here is false. The greater was not subject to the lesser from the beginning, but only then, when David had made the Idumaeans tributary, which happened many years after these times. Perhaps he used "principio" for principality, so that he means the greater would at some time be under the lordship of the lesser. Principium is taken in this sense in Ps. 109.3, "with you is the principality in the day of your power." In Greek it is [ἀρχή]. The old lexicon: [ἀρχή], rule, magistracy, mastery, presidency, principium.

units.la: Aspersetis[?] ] שעיר[?] est in edit. τριχῶδ[?]. Lexicon Vetus, s[?] hirsutus, pilosus. Veritas Ebraica, sicut pallium villosum. Siquidem שעיר[?] pallium, quod s[?] interpretantur, vocis affinitate decepti. Nam pellis שעיר[?] dicitur. Porro sera est pilus crassior rigidiorque aut erectus, qualem sues habent.
units.tr: Aspersetis] In the edition the Hebrew [שעיר] is rendered [τριχῶδες], hairy. The old lexicon: hirsute, shaggy. The Hebrew text has "like a shaggy cloak." For [שעיר] means a cloak, which they interpret, deceived by the similarity of the word; for the skin is called [שעיר]. Moreover, the hair of swine is a coarser and stiffer bristle, or one that stands erect.

units.la: Esau] dictus ita παρὰ τὸ עשה facio, perficio. Nam perfectior erat quam pueri solent, utpote pilis instructus. R. Salomo, Omnes vocabant eum Esau eo quod esset factus & absolutus pilis suis, ut qui multos annos habent. Aben-Ezra, Qui videbant, vocabant eum Esau: id sonat opus per se, live factus per se. Erat autem partus iste mirabilis, quia omnis homo prodit in lucem cum secunda, quæ ipsum tegit: & ecce duæ istæ secundæ fractæ sunt momento uno.
units.tr: Esau] He was so named from the Greek parallel [παρὰ τὸ עשה], to make, to perfect. For he was more perfect than boys usually are, being furnished with hair. R. Solomon: "All called him Esau because he was made and complete with his hair, like those who have many years." Aben Ezra: "Those who saw him called him Esau; that sounds like a work by itself, or made by itself." The birth was remarkable, because every man comes forth into the light with the afterbirth covering him, and behold, those two afterbirths were broken in one moment.

units.la: Iacob] παρὰ τὸ עקב calce teneo seu prehendo, non supplanto. Nam supplantat proprie qui pede suppositio aliquem in terra dejicit, quod Græci dicunt ὑποσκελίζειν. Utraque significat decipio. Quo significatu & ἐπιπνίζω usurpatur. Sed ἐπιπνίζω etiam supplanto. Huc respexit Esau frater Gen. 27.38[?]. cum ait, recte vocatum est nomen ejus Iacob, decepit enim jam me secundo. Ebraice est יעקב quod a propria significatione contumeliose detorquet ad translatam. Non enim certe a decipiendo sic appellatus est, sed ab eo quod calcaneum ejus manu apprehenderit. Res clara ex textu Mosis. Quocirca miror eos qui Iacob supplantorem interpretantur. Nam ἀντιγενὴς [?] non tam supplantator, quam qui calce. serit aut contingit aliquem. Sed quia etiam supplantatorem de-notat, veteres plerique omnes, verae etymologiae ignari, ita alii exposuerunt. Irenaeus lib.4. cap.38. adversus haereses. Origenes hom.12. in Genesin, & hom.11. in Exodum. Hieronymus in nom. de Matthaeo, & epist. ad Hebraeos: Augustinus, sermo.40. de verbis Domini: Arnobius in Psal.92[?]. & alij. Sunt interpretes viri docti, qui nomen Iacob compositum esse putant ex Iad nomi-ne manum significante, & ex verbo Acab calcem prehendere: sed, meo judicio, falluntur. Nam Iod in principio adhibetur ad confi-cienda nomina propria. Quale est in Isaac, & in Tetragrammato, quod vocant Iod, He, Vau, He: & in Israel. Hoc nomen vel ex Grammatica jam ipsis pueris.
units.tr: Iacob] From [παρὰ τὸ עקב], to hold or seize the heel, not to supplant. For to supplant properly means to throw someone to the ground by putting a foot under him, which the Greeks call [ὑποσκελίζειν]. Both mean to deceive, and in that sense [ἐπιπνίζω] is also used, though [ἐπιπνίζω] also means to supplant. Esau his brother looked to this when he said, "Rightly was he named Jacob, for he has now deceived me twice," Gen. 27.36. The Hebrew is יעקב, which from its proper meaning is turned contemptuously to a figurative one. He was surely not named from deceiving, but from having grasped his heel with his hand. The matter is clear from the text of Moses. Therefore I wonder at those who interpret Jacob as "supplanter." For [ἀντιγενής] is not so much "supplanter" as one who seizes or touches someone's heel. But because it also denotes a supplanter, nearly all the ancients, ignorant of the true etymology, explained it so: Irenaeus, Against Heresies, book 4, ch. 38; Origen, homily 12 on Genesis and homily 11 on Exodus; Jerome, in the book of Hebrew names and in his letter to the Hebrews; Augustine, sermon 40 on the words of the Lord; Arnobius on Ps. 92, and others. There are learned interpreters who think the name Jacob is compounded of Iad, meaning hand, and the verb Acab, to seize the heel; but, in my judgment, they are mistaken. For Iod is placed at the beginning to form proper names, as in Isaac, in the Tetragrammaton, which they call Iod, He, Vau, He, and in Israel. This is known even to boys from grammar.

units.la: Terras incesserat] malim, terram incesserat. Nam innuit regionem illam, in qua habitabat, hoc est Chanaan tam, non re-giones alias Gen.26.1. Fuit autem fames in terra, ἐν τῇ γῇ[?]: sive, ut LXX. ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς[?].
units.tr: I would prefer "the land" (terram) to "the land" as printed: the author means the region in which he lived, that is Canaan, and not other regions. Gen. 26.1: There was a famine in the land [ἐν τῇ γῇ]; or, as the LXX have it, [ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς].

units.la: Pag.13. In Gerarisl[?] Sigonius corrigit, in Gerara. Quomodo locutus est interpres noster Gen.26.1. Idem tamen 20.1. pere-grinatus est Abraham in Geraris. Scire licet veteres promiscue usos hac praepositione, Cicero in primo de Oratore, ut se ab-jiceret in herba. Caesar de bello Gallico, lib.6. aut se in Mena-piis abderet. Terentius Eunucho, deinde illam in lecto illae collocant. Haec omnia pugnant contra canones Grammaticorum. Cessit] concessit, profectus est.
units.tr: Page 13. Sigonius corrects "in Gerarisl" to "in Gerara." This is how our translator has put it, Gen. 26.1. Yet at 20.1 the same translator has: "Abraham sojourned in Gerar." It must be recognised that the ancients used this preposition interchangeably. Cicero, in the first book of De Oratore: "to throw himself down on the grass." Caesar, De Bello Gallico, book 6: "or hide himself among the Menapii." Terence, Eunuchus: "then they lay her on the bed." All these contradict the rules of the grammarians. Went] that is, set out, departed.

units.la: Ad regem Abimelech] ad Abimelech regem Palaestinorum, sive Philistheorum, quem Graeci vocant βασιλέα Φυλιστιείμ, οἳ[?] & rex Gerarae dicitur. Hos Palaestinos iidem Graeci appellant etiam ἀλλοφύλως[?]: quorum rex communi nomine Abimelech dicebatur, si credendum Davidi Camio homini Ebraeo ad Psal.34. ita scribenti, Abimelech nomen fuit olim commune regibus Palaestinorum, ut Agag Amalecitarum. Vide sis Ba-silium hom.59. in Psalmos: Hieronymum Ezec.29[?]. Procopium in Genesin pag.158. Glossam Graecam & Lippomanum Catena in Gen. sol.280.
units.tr: To Abimelech the king] to Abimelech, king of the Palestines, or Philistines, whom the Greeks call the king of the Philistines [βασιλέα Φυλιστιείμ], and he is also called king of Gerar. These Palestines are also called by the same Greeks [ἀλλοφύλως], "foreigners"; their king was commonly called Abimelech, if we may believe David Kimchi, a Hebrew, who writes thus on Ps. 34: "Abimelech was formerly a common name for the kings of the Palestines, as Agag was for the Amalekites." See Basil, homily 59 on the Psalms; Jerome on Ezekiel 29; Procopius on Genesis, p. 158; the Greek Gloss; and Lippomano's Catena on Genesis, p. 280.

units.la: Agente invidia] hoc alibi dixit, impellente invidia, & alio loco, stimulante invidia.
units.tr: Driven by envy] He says this elsewhere as "impelled by envy," and in another place as "prompted by envy."

units.la: Apud Puteum juramenti] ita scribendum cum majuscula P. Nam est loci nomen. Locus ipse ab Ebraeis Bersabee nuncupa-tur. Id Graeci reddunt Φρέαρ τοῦ ὅρκου[?], Gen.26.13. Verba fun[?] [illegible, ~8 letters] ἐπὶ Φρέαρ τοῦ ὅρκου[?]. ubi Latinus interpres, quem vulgatum appellitant, ascendit autem ex illo loco in Bersabee. Quanquam censent eam urbem sic appellatam non a juramento, quod Sebua dicitur, sed a septem agnis, quorum ibi memoria usurpatur. Septem enim Ebraei Sabee dicunt, id est, שְׁבַע[?] quod nunc legunt Seba.
units.tr: At the well of the oath] It should be written with a capital P, for it is the name of a place. The place itself is called Beersheba by the Hebrews. The Greeks render this [Φρέαρ τοῦ ὅρκου], Gen. 26.13. The words [...] [ἐπὶ Φρέαρ τοῦ ὅρκου] where the Latin translator, whom they call the Vulgate, has: "he went up from that place to Beersheba." Although they think the city was so called not from the oath, which is called Sheba, but from the seven lambs, whose memory is kept there. For the Hebrews say Sabee for "seven," that is [שְׁבַע], which they now read as Seba.

units.la: Luminibus obductis] cum tenebrae obduxissent lumina, id est, oculos; sive, cum luminibus tenebrae obductae essent. Significat autem caliginem & hebetem visum; vel, si placet, caecutientiam. Nam prae senio caecutiebat. Erat enim annis gravior, hoc est aetate provectior. Sic dicimus natu gravior, aetate gravis, etc.
units.tr: With his eyes dimmed] when darkness had covered his eyes, that is, his sight; or, when darkness had been spread over his eyes. It signifies dimness and dull sight, or, if you prefer, failing sight, for he was growing blind from old age. For he was heavier in years, that is, advanced in age. So we say "heavier by birth," "heavy with age," etc.

units.la: Cum Esau filium benedicere pararet] cum ei bene precari vellet. Benedicit Latino sermone qui bona exoptat, & ut bona eveniant precatur, Cicero, cui benedixit unquam bono? Benedicere filium, ut benedicere Deum. Nam sic Graeci loquuntur εὐλογῆν τὸν Θεὸν[?]. Graecos imitati sunt interpretes antiqui, veteresque theologi Latini, qui vix aliter loquuntur. Apuleius in Asclepio editione Aldina, si modo interpres Asclepij est Apuleius, de quo ego sane dubito. Restat hoc solum nobis, ut benedicentes Deum orantesque ad curam corporis redeamus.
units.tr: When he was about to bless his son Esau] when he wished to bless him, that is, to pray well for him. In Latin, one who wishes good things and prays that they may come to pass "blesses" (benedicit), as in Cicero: "to whom did he ever bless with good?" To bless a son is like blessing God, for so the Greeks speak [εὐλογῆν τὸν Θεὸν]. The old interpreters imitated the Greeks, and the older Latin theologians, who hardly speak otherwise, as did Apuleius in the Aldine edition of the Asclepius, if indeed Apuleius is the translator of the Asclepius, about which I am quite doubtful. There remains for us only this: that, blessing God and praying, we return to the care of the body.

units.la: Adorandus principibus] Gen. 27, 29. προσκυνησάτωσάν σοι ἄρχοντες, adorent te principes: ubi tamen in Hiero, adorent te tribus, & in fonte sacro, לְאֻמִּים[?] nationes, populi.
units.tr: To be worshipped by princes] Gen. 27.29: [προσκυνησάτωσάν σοι ἄρχοντες], "let princes bow down to you." Yet in Jerome: "let tribes bow down to you," and in the sacred fountain [לְאֻמִּים], "nations, peoples."

units.la: Ex domo Laban] ex familia Laban, qui erat filius Bathuel, nepos Nachor fratris Abrahae, & frater Rebeccae matris Esau & Iacobi. Quod autem Gen. 29, 5. vocatur filius Nachor, eo in loco filius nepotem denotat, ut alibi saepe. Nam juxta proverbium Ebraeorum, Filij filiorum tanquam filii sunt. Notior enim erat Nachor, inquit Gerundensis: ideoque pro Bathuele nominatur, qui minus notus erat.
units.tr: From the house of Laban] from the family of Laban, who was the son of Bethuel, grandson of Nahor, brother of Abraham, and brother of Rebekah, mother of Esau and Jacob. But where Gen. 29.5 calls him the son of Nahor, in that place "son" denotes a grandson, as often elsewhere. For according to the Hebrew proverb, "the sons of sons are as sons." Nahor was better known, says the Gerundensis; therefore he is named instead of Bethuel, who was less known.

units.la: Genus tamen intra familiam suam ducere] quo impolluta sanguinis sinceritas servaretur in Christo, qui ex femine Iuda oriturus erat. Vide caput ultimum in Numeris.
units.tr: Yet to keep the race within his own family] so that the unpolluted purity of the blood might be preserved in Christ, who was to come from the seed of Judah. See the last chapter of Numbers.

units.la: Locum somnij sacratum habens] In hoc loco putant quidam templum postea extructum fuisse: sed falluntur, meo judicio. Nam templum extructum fuit in area Ornan Iebusæi, in monte Moria. Locus autem hic, qui prius Luza dicebatur, vicus erat in duodecimo ab Aelia, id est, Ierosolyma lapide, ut Eusebius autor est. Lapidem unum ex lapidibus illius loci, quo usus fuerat pro cervicali.
units.tr: Having a stone consecrated to the dream] Some think that a temple was built afterwards in this place, but in my judgment they are mistaken. For the temple was built on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, on Mount Moriah. This place, which was earlier called Luz, was a village twelve miles from Aelia, that is, Jerusalem, as Eusebius reports. One stone from the stones of that place, which he had used as a pillow.

units.la: cippum, statuam, stelen.
units.tr: A pillar, a statue, a stele.

units.la: Est cur malim domus Dei: Dei, inquam, non Domini. Nam sic utique legimus Gen.28, 22. Lapis iste quem in cippum sive titulum erexi, domus Dei erit. Hic est Elohim in Ebraeo, licet locus ille Ebraice Bethel nominetur. Est autem Bethel, domus sive locus Dei. Nam El Deus, idem videlicet quod Elohim, etymon tamen diversum. Nam El a robore quasi Deus fortis: Elohim autem quasi vindex & judex. Vide libellum meum de hoc nomine. Porro novum non est ut Deus pro Dominus & contra Dominus pro Deus ponatur. Amant enim interpretes ista confundere.
units.tr: I would prefer "house of God": God, I say, not Lord. For so indeed we read at Gen. 28.22: "This stone which I have set up as a pillar or monument shall be the house of God." Here in Hebrew it is Elohim, although that place is called Bethel in Hebrew. Bethel is the house or place of God. For El is God, the same as Elohim, but the etymology is different: El from strength, as it were "God the strong," but Elohim as avenger and judge. See my little book on this name. Moreover, it is nothing new for God to be put for Lord and Lord for God, for interpreters love to confuse these.

units.la: id est, avunculum.
units.tr: that is, the maternal uncle.

units.la: vel, Lea. Assa, Lea vel Lia, ut Αχεῖ & Daeus vel Darius. Sic Augia stabulum, quod & Augeae dicitur. Critici Ebraeorum, cum apices adderent, scripserunt ꞑ7, id est, Assa, Lea. Videtur ita dicta, inquit Mercerus, quod esset debilis nec bene habita, quasi lassa ex debilitate constitutionis. Unde nihil mirum si oculos quoque debiles habuit.
units.tr: or, Leah. Assa, Leah or Lia, as Αχεῖ and Daeus or Darius; so Augia for the stable, also called Augeae. When the Hebrew critics added the vowel points, they wrote it as Assa, Leah. It seems so named, says Mercerus, because she was weak and not well kept, as if worn out by a feeble constitution. Hence it is no wonder if she had weak eyes too.

units.la: scribi posset Rahel, sed in antiquis tantum Rachel: ideo nihil innovandum. Sonat autem ovis foemina. Quanquam in LXX. ἀμνὸς & in Hiero agnus Ief. 43.7.
units.tr: Rahel could be written, but only Rachel in the old texts, so nothing should be changed. It means a female sheep, though in the LXX [ἀμνός], and in Jerome "lamb," Jer. 43.7.

units.la: deformes oculos Liae molles sive teneros Moses dicit: Hieronymus lippos. Graeci ἀσθενεῖς, id est, debiles, infirmos. Ex tribus Chaldaicis editionibus una, videlicet Onceli, habet pulchros: altera, quae Ierosolymitana vocatur, molles: tertia vocem usurpat, quam Iustus Nathanus in Lexico suo Thalmudico exponit de iis qui finum oculorum rotundum habent. Hic tamen aliud significare videtur.
units.tr: Moses calls Leah's eyes weak or tender; Jerome calls them bleary. The Greek is [ἀσθενεῖς], that is, weak, infirm. Of the three Chaldee editions, one, namely Onkelos, has "beautiful"; another, called the Jerusalem, has "soft"; the third uses a word which Justus Nathan in his Talmudic lexicon explains of those who have a round socket of the eye. Here, however, it seems to mean something else.

units.la: Cujus specie Iacob captus] pulchritudo enim corporis, ut Cicero ait, apta compositione membrorum, movet oculos & delectat hoc ipso, quod inter se omnes partes quodam lepore consentiunt.
units.tr: By whose beauty Jacob was captured: for bodily beauty, as Cicero says, arising from a fitting arrangement of the limbs, moves the eyes and delights by this very fact, that all the parts agree among themselves with a certain charm.

units.la: post septem dies nuptiarum, non post septennium alterum, ut quidam volunt.
units.tr: after seven days of the wedding feast, not after another seven years, as some want.

units.la: quae mater eis imposuit, ut mos erat vet« terum. Aliquando pater nomen imponebat, rarius affines aut vicini vicinaeve.
units.tr: which the mother gave them, as was the custom of old. Sometimes the father gave the name, and more rarely relatives or neighbours, men or women.

units.la: Ruben] Hiero interpretatur, filius visionis. male. Sonat ut si dicas, videte filium. q. d. ecce filium peperi, non filiam. Notum ut הִנֵּה[?] vide pro adverbio ecce ponatur.
units.tr: Reuben] Jerome translates it "son of vision," wrongly. It sounds as if you said "see, a son," that is, "behold, I have borne a son, not a daughter." It is known that [הִנֵּה] is used as the adverb "behold."

units.la: Simeon] libri Graeci συμεών, quod non ita se probat mihi Contractum est Simon, quod scribunt שִׁמְעוֹן[?] Sin in Samech versa: aut est Graecum Σιμὼν, ut dici possit Latine Simo. Sic Πλάτων, Plato. Appellatio ab eo quod mater exaudita fuerit a Deo cum eum parceret, quem assiduis precibus abs eo petierat.
units.tr: Simeon] The Greek books have Συμεών, which does not commend itself to me so well. It is a contraction of Simon, which they write [שִׁמְעוֹן], with Sin changed into Samech; or it is the Greek Σιμὼν, so that it can be said in Latin Simo, as Πλάτων becomes Plato. The name derives from the fact that his mother was heard by God when she bore him, whom she had asked of him with constant prayers.

units.la: Levi] Etymon habetur Gen 29.34. in verbis illis, nunc vice hac vir meus mihi copulabitur, id est, לֵוִי[?] quod alius vertit, adjungetur: Aquila, applicabitur. In libro nominum Levi, additus. Quid si, additamentum? Sed additamentum לְוִי[?] dicitur. Verbum Ebraeum significat etiam deducere & prosequi aliquem honoris causa. Hieronymus, Vbi nos legimus, apud me erit vir meus (sic Graeci πρὸς ἐμὲ ὁ ἀνὴρ μου) quod Ebraice dicitur illave, Aquila interpretatus est applicabitur mihi, & a doctoribus Ebraeorum aliter transfertur, ut dicant, prosequetur me vir meus, &c.
units.tr: Levi] The etymology is found at Gen. 29.34, in those words: "now this time my husband will be joined to me," that is [לֵוִי], which another renders "will be joined"; Aquila, "will be applied." In the book of names, Levi is "added." What if it is "an addition"? But an addition is called [לְוִי]. The Hebrew verb also means to escort and accompany someone as a mark of honour. Jerome: where we read "my husband will be with me" (so the Greeks, [πρὸς ἐμὲ ὁ ἀνὴρ μου]), which in Hebrew is said "illave," Aquila translated "will be applied to me," and the Hebrew teachers render it otherwise, so that they say "my husband will escort me," etc.

units.la: Iudas] mater enim dicebat, hac vice confitebor Domino. In libro nominum, Iuda, confessio, laudatio. Confessio, ἐξομολόγησις: laudatio, αἴνεσις. Significat etiam ἐξομολογῶ, gratias ago, ut ibi, confiteor tibi pater Deus coeli ac terrae. Certe a Iosepho Iudas exponitur εὐχαριστία, i. gratiarum actio. Hiero. Confessio hic pro gratiarum actione seu pro laude accipitur, ut frequenter in Psalmis & Euangelio. In textu Biblico semper scriptum יְהוּדָה Iehuda, quod interpretes contraxerunt, Iuda scribentes, abiecta littera He, id est, יְהוּ[?]. Id repertum mihi in more Nebuchim cum Aleph in fine, dicit Samuel filius Iudae, יְהוּדָא[?].
units.tr: Judah: For my mother said, "This time I will confess to the Lord." In the book of names, Judah means confession or praise. Confession [ἐξομολόγησις]; praise [αἴνεσις]. It also signifies [ἐξομολογῶ], I give thanks, as in "I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth." Certainly Josephus explains Judah as [εὐχαριστία], that is, the giving of thanks. Jerome: Here "confession" is taken for thanksgiving or praise, as often in the Psalms and the Gospel. In the biblical text it is always written יְהוּדָה Yehudah, which the translators shortened to Iuda, dropping the letter He, that is, יְהוּ. I have found this in the More Nebuchim with an Aleph at the end, where Samuel son of Judah says יְהוּדָא.

units.la: Iflachar] nomen ex mercede factum, quod Iosephus dixit, ἐκ μισθοῦ γινόμενον. Nam Sachar, merces, Gen. 30. 18. Ἰσσαχάρ, ὁ ἐστι μισθός. Deest aliquid ut sit, ὁ ἐστι μισθός, quod est i. significat, est merces. שָׂכָר est, שָׂכָר merces. In libro nominum, Issachar, est merces.
units.tr: Issachar: a name made from wages, as Josephus says, [ἐκ μισθοῦ γινόμενον]. For Sachar means wages, Gen. 30.18, [Ἰσσαχάρ], which is [μισθός]. Something is missing so that it reads [ὁ ἐστι μισθός], that is, it signifies: it is wages. [שָׂכָר] is wages. In the book of names, Issachar is wages.

units.la: Zabulon] ζαβουλὼν: τὸ Zabal, habita vit, quod mater diceret, hac vice habitabit mecum vir meus. Gen.30.20. Hiero. in tradit. Ebra. Vbi nos posuimus habitabit mecum (nota vulgatum interpretem habere, mecum erit: quod in Latio significat, rem habebit, Plautus, hac nocte mecum fuit jussu hospitis.) &c. LXX. interpretati sunt, deliget me, in Ebraeo habetur Iz-beleni: & est sensus, quia sex filios genuit Iacob, propterea jam secura sum, habitabit enim mecum vir meus. Unde & filius meus vocatur habitaculum. Cum venia Hieronyme, Zebul est habitaculum, non Zabulon quod scribunt זבול vel זבולון Zebulun. Sed Graeci legerunt Σαβυλών[?].
units.tr: Zebulun: [ζαβουλών]. From zabal, to dwell, because the mother said, "This time my husband will dwell with me," Gen. 30.20. Jerome, in his Hebrew Questions: "Where we have put 'will dwell with me' (note that the Vulgate translator has 'will be with me,' which in Latin means 'will have the thing,' as Plautus has, 'last night he was with me by the host's order'), etc." The Seventy translated it "will join me to himself." In the Hebrew it is Zebul; the sense is that, since she had borne six sons to Jacob, she now feels secure, for her husband will dwell with her. Hence her son is also called a dwelling. With respect to Jerome, Zebul is "dwelling," not Zabulon; they write זבול or זבולון, Zebulun. But the Greeks read Σαβυλών.

units.la: Dina] דינה vel Δίνα[?] vel Δεῖνα[?]. Nam libri variant. Hiero. Haec transfertur in caussam, quam significatius Graeci Δεινὼ vocant. Iurgii enim in Sicimis caussa extitit. Fabulam redolet quod in antiquitatibus Philonis, Iobum, occiso Sichem priore ipsius marito, Dinam in matrimonio habuisse, ex eaque liberos multos procreasse. Si libere licet, antiquitates illae mihi nimium suspectae sunt: quas ideo rarius in his notis cito aut laudo.
units.tr: Dinah: דינה, or Δίνα, or Δεῖνα; the books vary. Jerome: this is turned into a cause, which the Greeks more expressively call Δεινώ, for it was the cause of the quarrel at Shechem. It smacks of fable what Philo says in the Antiquities, that Dinah, after her first husband Shechem was killed, had been married to Jobus and had borne him many children. If I may speak freely, those Antiquities seem to me too suspect; therefore I rarely cite them quickly in these notes.

units.la: Ex ancilla Liae] Zelpha.
units.tr: From Leah's maidservant: Zilpah.

units.la: Gad] Iosephus τύχαιον interpretatur, id est, fortuitum. Potius fortunam denotat, hoc est τύχη. In libro nominum Gad, fortuna. Dicebat enim Lia גד quod scribunt גד, & legunt גד venit fortuna. Thargum Ierosolymitanum, fortuna bona. Ionathan, fydus bonum, quod idem cum ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ. Nos dicere mus, affulsit benignius astrum & fortunae influentis donum. Sic fere Iudaei, Graeci & Latini veteres, cum apices abessent, legerunt גד ἐν τύχῃ, in fortuna. id est ἐντυχὼς, fortunate, feliciter. Quod postremum invenies in Hieronymo. Apud Theodoretum in Genesin, quaest. 36 ἐντυχῶν, bona fortuna ufalum[?].
units.tr: Gad: Josephus interprets it as τύχαιον, that is, fortuitous. It rather denotes fortune, that is, [τύχη]. In the book of names, Gad is fortune. For Leah said, "Gad has come," which they write גד and read as "fortune has come." The Jerusalem Targum: good fortune. Jonathan: a good star, which is the same as [ἀγαθὴ τύχη]. We say that a more kindly star has shone upon her and fortune has granted its gift. So, roughly, the Jews, the Greeks and the old Latins, when the vowel points were lacking, read גד as ἐν τύχῃ, "in fortune," that is, ἐντυχὼς, fortunately, happily. You will find this last reading in Jerome. In Theodoret on Genesis, question 36, ἐντυχῶν, with good fortune.

units.la: Afer] In hoc nomine significatio est beatitudinis. Vide Gen. 30. 13. male igitur in antiquis codicibus edit. LXX. Ἀσὴρ, ὁ [illegible, ~8 letters]. Nam divitiae Ofer dicuntur, quod scribunt עשר prima Ain. Discrimen est primum in vocalibus, deinde in litteris consonantibus. Nam Afer scribitur cum Aleph in principio אשר.
units.tr: Asher: this name signifies blessedness. See Gen. 30.13. Therefore the Seventy in the old codices wrongly give Ἀσήρ, ὁ [illegible]. For riches are called Ofer, which they write עשר with an initial Ayin. The difference lies first in the vowels and then in the consonants, for Asher is written with an initial Aleph, אשר.

units.la: Hieronymi verba haec dere sunt, Afer ergo non divitiae sed beatus dicitur, duntaxat in praesenti loco. Nam in aliis secundum ambignitatem verbi possunt & divitiae sic vocari. Nescio quid velit. Nam in ה W nulla est ambiguitas, nisi cum Latine scribitur Afer vel Ofer. Nec Afer est ambiguum, sed Ofer. Nam si prima fuerit Ain, significat divitias: si vero Aleph, significat beatitudinem aut felicitatem. Nihil verius.
units.tr: These are Jerome's words: "Asher, therefore, is called not rich but blessed, at least in the present place; for elsewhere, according to the ambiguity of the word, riches too can be so called." I do not know what he means. For in the letter Waw there is no ambiguity, except when it is written in Latin as Asher or Ofer. Nor is Asher ambiguous, but Ofer is. For if the first letter is Ayin, it means riches; but if it is Aleph, it means blessedness or happiness. Nothing could be truer.

units.la: Ex ancilla Rachel] Balha sive Bala.
units.tr: From Rachel's maidservant: Bilhah, or Bala.

units.la: Dan] a iudicando, unde & Daniel. Iosephus, Δὰν [illegible, ~10 letters] ἀλλήλων γλώσσαν. Hoc est a Deo iudicatum, vel Dei iudicio electum Θεόκτιστος[?] ut Θεόκτιστος[?], a Deo conditus. In libro nominum, Dan, iudicium vel iudicans. Iudicium id est, [?] Iudicans [?], quod rectum puto. Rachel enim, cum eum Bala peperisset, dixisse traditur, iudicavit me Deus. Id Ebraice dicitur Dathanni, propterea nominavit eum Dan,
units.tr: Dan: from judging, whence also Daniel. Josephus: Δάν [...] the language of each other. That is, judged by God, or chosen by God's judgment, [Θεόκτιστος], as if [Θεόκτιστος], created by God. In the book of names, Dan is judgment or judging. Judgment, that is [...], judging, which I think is right. For Rachel, when Bilhah had borne him, is said to have said, "God has judged me." In Hebrew this is dathanni, therefore she named him Dan.

units.la: Nephthalim] Νεφθαλὶμ sive Νεφθαλί. Huic scripturae adversatur consuetudo Ebraea, sed et Graeca. Nam ut Ausonius canit, Vocibus in Graiis nunquam ultima conspicitur M. Quocirca in libris melioribus est Νεφθαλὶμ sive Νεφθαλί, quod hodie Naphthali. Similis varietas in Nephtha et Naphtha: Melchi-sedec et Malchi sedec.
units.tr: Naphtali: [Νεφθαλὶμ] or [Νεφθαλί]. Hebrew usage opposes this spelling, but so does Greek usage. For, as Ausonius sings, "Among Greek words the final M is never seen." Hence in the better books it is [Νεφθαλὶμ] or [Νεφθαλί], which today is Naphtali. There is similar variation in Nephtha and Naphtha, Melchi-sedec and Malchi-sedec.

units.la: Desperato iam partu] cum iam partum non amplius speraret.
units.tr: Her labour now despaired of: when she no longer hoped to bear more children.

units.la: Ioseph edidit] nomen ex futuro quale Iareb, Graece Ἰωσὴφ. Qui exponunt Iosephi, addens, arbitrati sunt esse nomen ex Beniamin, quos refellit plenior scriptura יֹסֵף Iehosephi, Psal.81.6. In libro nominum, Iosephi, augmentum. Veritas interpretationis, Iosephi addet. Nam dicebat, addet mihi Dominus filium alterum. Dictum ergo non quod ipse esset additus, sed quod speraret alium addendum, aut quod ad eum addi optaret alterum. Nicolaus de Lyra, ex desiderio habendi secundum nominavit primum. Natus fuit Ioseph Iacobo annum agente nonagesimum primum, cum iam finiti essent anni quatuordecim, quibus servierat pro Rachele et Lia. De ceteris filiis Iacobi nihil constat. Qua de re Salmanticensis in Iohafin, Iacob pater noster natus est anno sexagesimo Isaaci, qui erat anus mundi conditi bis millesimus centesimus octavus. Et mox, Quod filios ejus attinet, nisi scimus quando nati fuerint, Iosephi excepto, qui, patre Aegyptum ingresso, agebat annum trigesimum nonum. Constat autem ex testimonio veritatis minime dubio, Iacobum tunc habuisse annos centum triginta. Proinde Iosephum genuit anno nonagesimo primo aetatis suae. Porro tum finiti fuerunt anni quatuordecim, quibus servierat pro Rachel et Lea. Conjicimus autem Levi natum fuisse quum Iacob ageret annum 86, quinque videlicet annis ante Iosephum, et hoc apparet ex verbis sapientum, quorum fausta sit memoria. A tempore quo editus fuit Ioseph, Iacob pavit oves Labani sex annos; ecce 97. Idem cum Sichem versus tenderet hælit in Sochoth annum cum dimidio, ut R. Salomo scribit. Quod si verum est, anno 99 Iacob venit in urbem Sichem, ac tum Levi filius erat annorum tredecim. Quo concesso natus est anno Iacobi 86, qui est mundi 2194, obiit autem anno 2331. Nam vixit 130 annos. Caath vixit 133 annos. Amram 130, ut avus ipsius Levi. Hucusque Salmanticensis.
units.tr: Joseph: a name from the future, like Jareb; in Greek [Ἰωσήφ]. Those who explain it as "of Joseph" add "and" and think the name derives from Benjamin, which the fuller text refutes: יֹסֵף [Yehosef], Ps. 81.6. In the book of names, Joseph means increase. The truth of the interpretation is "he will add." For she said, "The Lord will add to me another son." So it was said not because he himself was added, but because she hoped for another to be added, or wished that another be added to him. Nicholas of Lyra says that out of desire to have a second she named the first. Joseph was born to Jacob when he was ninety-one years old, when the fourteen years for which he had served for Rachel and Leah had now ended. Nothing is known about the other sons of Jacob. On this matter the Salmanticensis writes on Joachin: "Our father Jacob was born in the sixtieth year of Isaac, which was the two thousand one hundred and eighth year of the created world. And soon after: As for his sons, unless we know when they were born, apart from Joseph, who was thirty-nine years old when his father entered Egypt. It is established, however, from the testimony of truth, which is beyond doubt, that Jacob then was one hundred and thirty years old. Therefore he begot Joseph in the ninety-first year of his life. Moreover, the fourteen years for which he had served for Rachel and Leah had then ended. We conjecture that Levi was born when Jacob was eighty-six years old, five years, that is, before Joseph; and this appears from the words of the sages, whose memory is blessed. From the time that Joseph was born, Jacob pastured the flocks of Laban for six years; behold ninety-seven. The same, when he set out for Shechem, stayed in Succoth a year and a half, as R. Solomon writes. If this is true, in the ninety-ninth year Jacob came to the city of Shechem, and then Levi was thirteen years old. Granting this, Levi was born in Jacob's eighty-sixth year, which is the year 2194 of the world; he died in the year 2331, for he lived one hundred and thirty-seven years. Kohath lived one hundred and thirty-three years, Amram one hundred and thirty-six, as Levi's own grandfather." Thus far the Salmanticensis.

units.la: Partem pecorum] Græci τὰ ἐπίσημα, quibus signum vel nota impressa erat. Chaldæi [illegible, ~6 letters] pecudes primores vel primi temporis, ut vertit Hieronymus. Alij, compactas. & contrario τὰ ἄσημα [?] cedebant Labano, quas alij seriores pecudes, alij aliter interpretantur.
units.tr: A portion of the flocks: the Greeks have τὰ ἐπίσημα, those marked with a sign or brand. The Chaldeans [...] the chief or first-born beasts of the flock, as Jerome translates. Others, compact ones. And on the contrary, [τὰ ἄσημα] were left to Laban; some interpret these as later-born flocks, others otherwise.
