units.la: Dolum ab eo suspectans] nam quia dolo eum circumvenerat, verebatur ne par pari referret: tum etiam ne uxores sibi eriperet. Ergo etiam vim suspectabat.
units.tr: Suspecting deceit from him: for since Laban had cheated him, he feared he would repay like with like; also lest he snatch his wives from him. So he also suspected force.

units.la: Clam profectus] inscio socero, qui tum domo aberat ad tonsuram ovium profectus.
units.tr: Departed secretly: without the knowledge of his father-in-law, who at that time was away from home, having gone to shear the sheep.

units.la: Vigesimo primo fere anno] usus est adverbio fere, ut supra, pag. 12. Vigesimo fere anno gemmos edidit. Nam utrobique redundare videtur. Vide Gen. 31. 41.
units.tr: In about his twenty-first year: he uses the adverb "about," as above, p. 12. "In about his twentieth year he produced gems." For in both places it seems to be superfluous. See Gen. 31.41.

units.la: Patris idola] τὰ εἴδωλα LXX. Alii aliter. Aquila [illegible, ~6 letters]. Symmachus [?] quæ terminatio Chaldaica est pro Θεραφὶμ. Sunt qui opinantur fuisse Deos penates ipsius, cui opinioni favet Iosephus Orig. Iudaic. lib. 1. c. 19. appellando τὰς τῶν θεῶν, ὡς ... ὄντας ... [?] id est, sigilla deorum patriæ religionis, ut interpretatur Gelenius. Ut ut sit, vocat Deos suos, infra vers. 30. Quocirca melius redditur idola, quam imagines aut simulachra. Nam licet εἴδωλα Græce sonet, si interpretari velis Latine, simulachra: tamen ecclesiastici scriptores usurpant peculiariter de iis simulachris, quæ numē aliquod repræsentant, aut quæ pro diis habentur. Notatū autē has imagines figurā humanā habuisse, quod colligunt ex historia David. Vide sodes 1 Sam. 19.13. R. David, Theraphim sunt imagines in quibus futura vident. Abenezra, Sunt qui dicunt esse instrumentum æneum factum ad cognoscendum partes horarum, hoc est horologium: alii dicunt astrologos ea vi pollere ut possint facere certis horis imaginem quæ loquatur: cui probando citant, & Theraphim locuta sunt vari. vanitatem: sed aliter is locus exponi debet. Ceterum opinio mea est quod imagines istae fuerint forma humana, factae ad recipiendam vim sive virtutem superiorum, quam non valeo enarrare. Vide sequentia. Verbis hīs facem allucet Marsilius Ficinus, de vita coelitus producenda, cap. 20. ita scribens, Arabes & Ægyptii tantum statuis & imaginibus attribuunt arte astronomica & magica fabricatis, ut spiritus stellarum in eis includi putent. Spiritus autem stellarum intelligunt alii quidem mirabiles coelestium vires, alii vero daemones etiam stellae huius illiusve pedisequas. Spiritus igitur stellarum qualescunque sint, inseri statuis & imaginibus arbitrantur, non aliter ac daemones solent humana nonnunquam corpora nuncupare, perque illa loqui. Similia quaedam per imagines facere stellarum spiritus arbitrantur.
units.tr: His father's idols: [τὰ εἴδωλα] in the Seventy; others otherwise. Aquila [...]. Symmachus [...], which is a Chaldean ending for Teraphim. Some think they were his household gods, and Josephus favours this opinion in Antiquities, book 1, chapter 19, calling them the images of the gods, as Gelenius translates, the figures of the gods of the ancestral religion. However that may be, he calls them his gods, below, verse 30. Therefore "idols" is better rendered than "images" or "likenesses." For although [εἴδωλα] in Greek sounds like "images," if you wish to translate it into Latin as "simulacra," ecclesiastical writers nonetheless use it particularly of those images which represent some divinity or which are regarded as gods. It is noted that these images had human form, which they gather from the story of David. See, I pray, 1 Sam. 19.13. Rabbi David: the teraphim are images by which they see future things. Ibn Ezra: some say it is a bronze instrument made for knowing the parts of the hours, that is, a clock; others say that astrologers have such power that they can make an image which speaks at certain hours. To prove this they cite also that "the teraphim have spoken vanity," but that passage must be explained otherwise. My own opinion, however, is that these images were of human form, made to receive the power or virtue of the higher beings, which I cannot explain. See what follows. In these words Marsilio Ficino sheds light, in On Bringing Life down from Heaven, chapter 20, writing thus: "The Arabs and Egyptians attribute to statues and images made by astronomical and magical art such power that they think the spirits of the stars are enclosed in them. Some understand by the spirits of the stars the wonderful powers of the heavenly bodies, while others understand demons, even attendants of this or that star. Whatever the spirits of the stars may be, they believe they are inserted into statues and images, just as demons are accustomed sometimes to take on human bodies and speak through them. They think the spirits of the stars make similar things through images."

units.la: Furto abstulit] ut patrem ab idololatria revocaret, Theodoretus, nepe ea cognosceret qua via Iacob fugisset, Abenezra. ob pretium materiae unde facta erant, vel quod illa marito deberi putaret, alij. Vtcumque fit, hoc factum Rachelis excusari non potest. Qui furtum committit, quocunque praetextu hoc faciat, peccat in legem illam, Non furaberis. Quae tam late patet, ut etiam alienationem qualemcunque rei alienae per eam vetari perhibeant.
units.tr: Took it away by theft] so that he might call his father back from idolatry, says Theodoret; or that he might learn by what route Jacob had fled, says Abenezra; or on account of the value of the material the images were made of, or because he thought they were owed to her husband, say others. However that may be, Rachel's deed cannot be excused. Whoever commits theft, whatever pretext he uses, sins against that law, "You shall not steal." This law extends so widely that they maintain it forbids every kind of alienation of another's property.

units.la: Laban generum prosecutus] Quum Iacob discederet, abierat domo Laban, ut diximus. Triduo post nuntiatum ei fuit quod accideraẗ[?]. Tum ad vocatis amicis, generum, quem Deos suos[?] furto abstulisse sibi persuadebat, persecutus est septem dierum viam, eumque assecutus est in monte Galaad, ubi & foedus cum eo pepigit. Hinc eruimus Carras inter & Galaad montem, in quo generum comprehendit, intervallum esse septem dierum.
units.tr: Laban pursued his son-in-law] When Jacob was leaving, he had gone away from Laban's house, as we said. Three days later he was told what had happened. Then, having called together his friends, Laban pursued the son-in-law, whom he was convinced had stolen his gods, along a seven days' journey, and overtook him on Mount Gilead, where he also made a covenant with him. From this we gather that the interval between Haran and Mount Gilead, where he overtook his son-in-law, was seven days.

units.la: Ne uxores filiabus suis superinduceret] item, ne filias suas durius haberet.
units.tr: Lest he bring other wives upon his daughters] likewise, lest he treat his daughters more harshly.

units.la: Pag. 15. Angelos & castra Domini] vidit castra Dei, & occurrerunt illi angeli Dei. Sic Graeci. Occurrerunt ei angeli Dei: & dixit, Castra Dei haec sunt. Ebraei, Chaldaei. fuerunt ei obviam angeli Dei. Quos cum vidisset, ait, castra Dei sunt haec. Hieronymus. Unde locum illum appellavit Mahanaim, id est, Castra. Id Graeci reddiderunt παρεμβολήν[?], licet in usu majore sit παρεμβολή.
units.tr: Page 15. The angels and the camp of the Lord] "He saw the camp of God, and the angels of God met him." So the Greeks. "The angels of God met him, and he said, This is the camp of God." The Hebrews and Chaldeans: "The angels of God came to meet him; and when he saw them he said, This is the camp of God." Jerome. Hence he called that place Mahanaim, that is, Camps. The Greeks rendered this [παρεμβολήν], although [παρεμβολή] is in more common use.

units.la: Prætter regionem Edom] infra 14. Sed cum obinterje-ctum sinum rubri maris præter terram Philistijm via duceret.
units.tr: Past the region of Edom] see below, on chapter 14. But the way led past the land of the Philistines, with the gulf of the Red Sea lying between.

units.la: Muneribus] munera erant capræ & oves ducenæ, hirci & arietes viceni, cameli lactantes cum suis pullis triginta, vaccæ quadraginta, juvenci decem, asini viginti & pulli asinorum decem Gen. 32.14. & 15. Hæc munera missa placandi animum fratris, quem iratum sibi putabat.
units.tr: Gifts] The gifts were two hundred she-goats and ewes, twenty he-goats and rams, thirty milch camels with their young, forty cows, ten bulls, twenty she-asses and ten foals of asses (Gen. 32.14–15). These gifts were sent to appease the mind of his brother, whom he thought was angry with him.

units.la: Dominus humana specie assumpta] Deum fuisse, qui colluctatus est cum Iacobo nullum omnino dubium est. Humana autem specie apparuisse vel ex eo patet quod Moses eum virum appellet. Iosephus φάντασμα [?], id est, ἄγγελον [?], forsan vocare maluit, & post ἄγγελον [?] ex ambiguo nominis Elohim, quod & Deum & angelos denotat: imo etiam angelum. Nam si de solo Mose dicitur & de uno idolo, cur non etiam accipi possit de uno angelo? Ceterum quem Dei angelum vocat Iosephus, eum possumus intelligere qui angelus fœderis aut magni consilij angelus vocatur. Neque novum in libris ritualibus Ebræorum ut idem & Deus vocetur & angelus. Deus, inquam Elohim, & interdum Adonai vel Iave. Ne longe abeam, ecce locus insignis, Hos. 12.3. & 4. De principatu contendit cum Deo: de principatu, inquam, contendit cum angelo & prævaluit. Vbi hunc ipsum virum qui Iacobo apparuit, & Deum vocat & angelum. In nomine Israel vocatur etiam Deus, sed Deus El, non Elohim. Observant Cabbalistæ præceptorem Iacobi fuisse Raphaelem, ut Iosephi Gabrielem, & Abrahami Sadkielem: gentis autem Israelitice angelum perhibent fuisse Michaelem, de quo alias.
units.tr: The Lord, having assumed human form] That it was God who wrestled with Jacob is beyond any doubt. That he appeared in human form is clear from the fact that Moses calls him a man. Josephus preferred, perhaps, to call him a [phantasma], that is, an [angelos], and afterwards an angel, from the ambiguous name Elohim, which denotes both God and angels, and indeed even a single angel. For if it is said of Moses alone and of one idol, why could it not also be understood of one angel? Moreover, the angel of God whom Josephus means we may understand to be the one called the angel of the covenant or the angel of great counsel. Nor is it new in the ritual books of the Hebrews for the same being to be called both God and angel: God, I say, Elohim, and sometimes Adonai or Jave. Not to go far afield, here is a notable passage, Hos. 12.3–4: he contended with God over the princedom; he contended, I say, with the angel and prevailed. There the very man who appeared to Jacob is called both God and angel. In the name Israel he is also called God, but God El, not Elohim. The Cabbalists observe that Jacob's teacher was Raphael, as Joseph's was Gabriel and Abraham's Sadkiel; they say the angel of the Israelite people was Michael, of whom more elsewhere.

units.la: Adversus Dominum] id est, Deum. Nam est Elohim in sensu. Sed familiare huic scriptori Dominus usurpare pro Deus, ut pag. 4 & pag. 13. Sic interpretes aliquando Κύριος [?] cum Θεὸς [?] confundunt, & contra Θεὸς cum Κυρίως [?].
units.tr: Against the Lord] that is, against God. For the sense is Elohim. But this writer habitually uses Lord for God, as on pages 4 and 13. Thus the translators sometimes confuse [Kyrios] with [Theos], and conversely [Theos] with [Kyrios].

units.la: Non esse mortalem non ignoravit] pro eo habendum ac si dixisset, scivit esse immortalem, hoc est Deum aut angelum, ideo sibi abs eo benedici voluit.
units.tr: He did not fail to know that he was not mortal] This is to be taken as if he had said: he knew that he was immortal, that is, God or an angel, and therefore wished to be blessed by him.

units.la: Israel diceretur] compositio nominis ex Sara, de principatu contendit, & El Deus. Eo respexit prophetes Hoseas cum ait, de principatu contendit cum Deo & prævaluit. Nugantur patres cum Israel exponunt vir videns Deum: aut rectus Dei. Nam ut significet virum, & ISAAR [?] rectum, tamen in hoc nomine Iod formai [?] nomen proprium, quale in Iacob, in Isaac & similibus.
units.tr: Israel was to be called] The name is compounded from sarah, "to strive," and El, "God." The prophet Hosea had this in view when he said, "he strove with God over the princedom and prevailed." The Fathers talk nonsense when they explain Israel as "a man seeing God" or "upright of God." For although ISAAR means "upright" and it signifies a man, nevertheless in this name the Iod forms a proper name, like that in Jacob, in Isaac and similar names.

units.la: A Domino nomen Domini quaereret] nomen loco pronominis. Nos diceremus, a Domino nomen ipsius quaereret. Talia sunt, pluit Dominus a Domino; dixit Moses socero Mosis: dixit Dominus ascende ad Dominum, Adhibe libellos meos.
units.tr: "He would ask the name of the Lord from the Lord": the name is used in place of a pronoun. We would say, he would ask his name from the Lord. Such are: "the Lord rained from the Lord"; "Moses said to Moses' father-in-law"; "the Lord said, Go up to the Lord"; "Apply my little books."

units.la: Quia admirabile esset] hæc parenthesi circumcludenda. Non enim habentur in codicibus Ebraeorum, nec etiam in Græcis emendatioribus. Nihil dico, si non absunt in Hispanico & Romano. Olim etiam aberant in Exaplo, ut Græca scholia notant. Sumpta vel potius transcripta videntur ex Iesa. 9.6 aut magis ex Iud 13.18. Ceterum exemplaria, unde hæc hausit Sulpicius, non per omnia consentiunt. Nam in Aldino & Basileensi, ὁ ἐν Σαυμασὶν. Vidi etiam ubi scriptum esset, ἡ τοῦτο ἐν Σαυμασὶν: & hoc est mirabile.
units.tr: "Because it would be wonderful": this clause should be enclosed in parentheses. For it is not found in the Hebrew manuscripts, nor in the more accurate Greek ones. I say nothing if it is absent from the Spanish and Roman texts. In the past it was also missing from the Hexapla, as the Greek scholia note. It seems to have been taken, or rather copied, from Isaiah 9.6 or more probably from Judges 13.18. Moreover, the copies from which Sulpicius drew this do not agree in every respect. For in the Aldine and Basel editions it reads [ho en Saumasin]. I have also seen where it was written [hē touto en Saumasin], and this is the wonderful part.

units.la: Latitudo femoris] latum os coxæ, quod ex contactu angeli loco suo motum claudicandi occasionem præbuit. Latitudo femoris, τὸ πλατὺ τῆς μηρῆς. Sic Oncelos & Ionathan. Apud Iosephum est τὸ νεῦρον τὸ πλατύ. Qui latum nervum videtur dixisse τὸ νεῦρον τὸ συνεχὲς τῷ κοτυλῷ πρὸς τὸν μηρόν. A Græcis ἰσχίον appellatur, id est, coxa vel coxendix.
units.tr: Breadth of the thigh: the broad bone of the hip, which, moved from its place by the touch of the angel, gave occasion for limping. "Breadth of the thigh" is [to platy tēs mērēs]. So Onkelos and Jonathan. In Josephus it is [to neuron to platy], which seems to be the broad sinew, though he appears to mean [to neuron to syneches tō kotylō pros ton mēron], the sinew joined to the socket at the thigh. By the Greeks it is called [ischion], that is, the hip or haunch.

units.la: Fratris domum] montem Seir aut Idumaeam.
units.tr: His brother's house: Mount Seir or Idumaea.

units.la: In Salem Sicimorum opidum] sic Græci εἰς Σαλὴμ πόλιν Σικιμῶν. Hieronymus quoque, in Salem urbem Sicimorum. Sicima nomen est urbis. Quomodo igitur Salem Sicimorum urbs? An urbs Sicimorum ita dicitur, ut urbs Romæ, herba Lapathi, & quæ præterea Grammatici annotarunt? videtur. Nam Salem eadem cum Sicima, si modo Salem est nomen urbis hoc in loco, de quo dubitari video. Nam potest esse nomen appellativum, ut dicat Iacobum salvum & incolumen pervenisse ad urbem Sichem, εἰς Σικιμῶν χωρίον ἡ πόλις, inquit Iosephus. Hanc sententiam expresserunt interpretes Chaldaei Oncelos & Ionathan, quam & R. Salomo approbare videtur. Priorem sequuntur fere Christiani. Unde legimus apud Eusebium, Salem civitas Sicimorum, quæ est Sichem. Scribunt eadem Hieronymus epist. CXXVI, Primasius epist. ad Ebræos, Eucherius in Gen. pag. 145. Eucherij verba sunt: Salem quæ nunc pro Sichem nominatur, sonat consummatam atque perfectam: illa vero quæ postea Ierusalem dicta est pacificam. Utrumque enim accentu paullulum declinato hoc vocabulum sonat. Nos intelligo quod ait, accentu paullulum declinato. Nam idem accentus in Salem quando est nomen urbis, & quando appellative significat perfectum, incolumen, salvum. Nam pacificum nunquam significat, quod sciam, nisi forte Salem legerunt pro שָׁלֵם[?] Selem, ut Habel pro Hebel; quod sacrificium pacificum designat שְׁלָמִים[?] Amos 5.22. cuius pluralis in frequentiusu שְׁלָמִים[?] pacifica. Hæc forma nominis accentum gerit in penultima. Puto Euche-rium hoc voluisse.
units.tr: Salem, a town of the Shechemites: so the Greeks [eis Salēm polin Sikimōn], and Jerome likewise, "to the city of Salem of the Shechemites." Sichem is the name of the city. How then is Salem a city of the Shechemites? Or is "city of the Shechemites" used in the way that "city of Rome" or "herb of the sorrel" is, and as the grammarians have noted in other cases? It seems so. For Salem would be the same as Shechem, if indeed Salem is the name of a city in this place, which I see is open to doubt. For it may be a common noun, so that the sense is that Jacob came safe and sound to the city of Shechem, [eis Sikimōn chōrion hē polis], as Josephus says. The Chaldean translators Onkelos and Jonathan expressed this meaning, which R. Solomon also seems to approve. The Christians mostly follow the former view. Hence we read in Eusebius, "Salem, a city of the Shechemites, which is Shechem." Jerome writes the same in Epistle 126, Primasius in his epistle to the Hebrews, and Eucherius on Genesis, page 145. These are Eucherius's words: "Salem, which is now called Shechem, means consummate and perfect; but that which was afterwards called Jerusalem means peaceable. For the word means both, with the accent slightly shifted." I understand what he says about the accent slightly shifted. For the same accent falls on Salem when it is the name of a city and when it signifies, as an appellative, perfect, unhurt, safe. It never signifies peaceable, so far as I know, unless perhaps they read [Selem], the Hebrew [שָׁלֵם], as Habel for Hebel; this designates the peace-offering [שְׁלָמִים], Amos 5.22, whose plural, in more frequent use, is [shelamim], peace-offerings. This form of the noun bears the accent on the penultimate. I think Eucherius meant this.

units.la: Pretio accepto] quem pretio emerat. Quod intelligentiam habet ex illo, qui eum pretio acceperat, id est, emerat. Nam qui emit, accipit ab alio quod emit. Contra tradere, idem quod vendere. Nam qui vendit, tradit emptori quod vendidit. Emisse autem centum agnis Moses ait, sive numum agni effigie signatum intellexerit, sive ex antiqua consuetudine permutabatur locus ille cum centum agnis, quos pro eo Iacob tradebat. Vide quæ scripsimus Miscell. cent. 1. cap. 7. Quibus addo ea[?] primum signatum fuisse ovium boumque effigie. Quod de Servio rege Plinius asserit, hist. nat. lib. 18. cap. 3.
units.tr: For a price received] which he had bought for a price. The phrase "received for a price" means "bought for a price": for he who buys receives from another what he buys. On the other hand, "to deliver" means the same as "to sell," for he who sells delivers to the buyer what he has sold. Moses says he bought with a hundred lambs, whether he understood a coin stamped with the image of a lamb, or whether, by ancient custom, that place was exchanged for a hundred lambs, which Jacob delivered in its place. See what I have written in Miscellanea, century 1, chapter 7. To these I add that such coins were first stamped with the image of sheep and oxen, as Pliny asserts of King Servius, Natural History, book 18, chapter 3.

units.la: Emor, Chemoreus princeps] locus corruptus. Suspicor legendum, Hemor, Chorræus princeps, vel certe, Hemor Hevæus. Sed Χοββ[?] vocatur, Gen. 34.2. in editione quam Aldus impressit, & post eum Basileenses typographi. Forte alterum horum nominum superest a glossemate. Nihil adfirmo; tamen fieri potest ut Severus initio scripserit Hemor princeps.
units.tr: Emor, Chemoreus princeps] The text is corrupt. I suspect it should read "Hemor, prince of the Chorraeans," or certainly "Hemor the Hivite." But in Gen. 34.2 the name is written Χοββ[?] [Chobb?] in the edition Aldus printed, and after him the Basel printers. Perhaps one of these two names is left over from a gloss. I affirm nothing, but it is possible that Severus originally wrote "Hemor the prince."

units.la: Sane Hemor dicimus & Chemor, ut Horeb & Choreb. Ab Hemor Iosephus declinavit Hemorus. Sic Chemorus. Quod ex eo nomen natum (ita conjicio) in margine, ut fit, inde postea in contextum irrepsit, depravatum in Chemoreus. Iudicent qui has res intelligunt.
units.tr: Indeed we say both Hemor and Chemor, as Horeb and Choreb. Josephus made the declined form Hemorus from Hemor, and so Chemorus. I conjecture that the name arose from this: a marginal note, as often happens, crept later into the text and was corrupted into Chemoreus. Let those who understand these matters judge.

units.la: Emor] aspirandum est ut fit Hemor. Hoc nomen Græci & Iosephus cum duplici μ scribunt Εμμὼρ. Cui simile Debo-bora. Sic Habbacuc, Messias, & alia non pauca.
units.tr: Emor] It should be aspirated, as in Hemor. Greeks and Josephus write this name with a double mu, Εμμὼρ [Emmōr]. Similar is Debo-bora. So also Habbacuc, Messias, and not a few other words.

units.la: Princeps] rex Iosepho. perinde est. Nam rex in Ebraismo princeps, dux, comes: quos regulos Latini autores appellant.
units.tr: Prince] Josephus has "king," which comes to the same thing. For in Hebrew usage a king is a prince, leader, or lord: the petty rulers whom Latin authors call reguli.

units.la: Sichem] minus recte alij Sychem ex Græco συχέμ: quod & συχέμ[?] scribunt, unde Σίχεμα[?] civitas: ab hoc Sichem appellata, si credimus Eusebio, cuius hæc de re verba clara sunt in libro loco-rum [?]um. Sed & filius Hemor appellabatur Sichem, a quo & locus nomen accepit. Alij putant Sichem ab urbe sua nominatum. Gerundensis, Sichem filius Hemor de nomine urbis suae vocatus fuit. Prius verius videtur.
units.tr: Sichem] Others less correctly write Sychem, from the Greek συχέμ [sychem]; they also write συχέμ[?], whence the city Σίχεμα [Sichema]. If we believe Eusebius, the city was named after this Sichem, and his words on the matter are clear in his book on places. But also a son of Hemor was called Sichem, from whom the place took its name. Others think Sichem was named after his city. Jerome (?) says: Sichem, son of Hemor, was called after the name of his city. The former seems more correct.

units.la: Dinae fratres] uterini, quos ideo ὁμομητρίους τῆς κόρης Iosephus appellat. Vide, si [?]ium est, & si vis.
units.tr: Dinah's brothers] Uterine brothers, whom Josephus therefore calls ὁμομητρίους τῆς κόρης [homomētrious tēs korēs], "of the same mother as the girl." See, if it is useful to you, and if you wish.

units.la: Addenda
units.tr: Additions

units.la: In hac pagina omissum quod jam notabo. Sicimorum oppidum est Sichem. In libro nominum, Sicimorum, humeri: ipsa est quae & Sichem. eam posterior aetas Neapolin dixit. Hieronymus de locis ex Actis Apostolorum, Sichem civitas Iacob, nunc Neapolis dicta, juxta sepulchrum Iosephi, quae a filio Hemor sui regis vocabulum sumpsit. Tbanchuma, qui & Ilmenu, Sichem haec est Napoli, id est, Neapolis. Ne quid celem, in Ebraeo codice scriptum Napolin, cum Nun in fine. Eusebius in locis, Sichem & Salem, quae Latine & Graece Sicima vocata est, civitas Iacob, nunc deserta est. Ostenditur autem locus in suburbanis Neapoleos (Naplosa hodie) juxta Sepulchrum Iosephi, quam subvertit Abimelech, & seminavit in ea salem, sicut in libro Iudicum scriptum est. Postea vero instaurata est a Ieroboam, ut Regnorum narrat historia, & sita est in finibus tribus Ephraim. Et mox, fuit autem & altera Sichem in monte Ephraim, civitas fugitivorum. In Evangelio Iohannis vocatur Sichar, ubi nunc ecclesia fabricata est, inquit Hieronymus, in latere montis Garizin. Locus est Iohan. 4. §. Iosephus autor Alexandri Macedonis tempore Samaritas metropolim babuisse Sicimam, [illegible, ~20 letters] Mafius in Iosuam, Ruinae Sichem nunc Ist-hac vocantur. Nam Neapolis non eodem solo substructa nunc visitur. Haec addenda erant: pergamus nunc ad alia.
units.tr: On this page I will now point out something that was omitted. The town of Sicimorum is Sichem. In the Book of Names, "Sicimorum, shoulders": this is the same as Sichem. Later ages called it Neapolis. Jerome, on the places from the Acts of the Apostles: "Sichem, city of Jacob, now called Neapolis, near the tomb of Joseph, which took its name from Hemor, the son of its king." Tanchuma, who is also Ilmenu: "This Sichem is Napoli, that is, Neapolis." Lest I conceal anything: in the Hebrew codex it is written Napolin, with a Nun at the end. Eusebius, in his Places: "Sichem and Salem, which is called Sicima in Latin and Greek, city of Jacob, is now deserted. The site is shown in the suburbs of Neapolis (today Naplosa), near the tomb of Joseph, which Abimelech destroyed, sowing salt in it, as is written in the Book of Judges. Afterwards, however, it was restored by Jeroboam, as the history of the Kings relates, and it lies within the borders of the tribe of Ephraim." And soon after, there was also another Sichem on the mountain of Ephraim, a city of refuge. In John's Gospel it is called Sychar, where now a church has been built, says Jerome, on the side of Mount Garizim. The place is in John 4. Josephus, the author, says that in the time of Alexander the Macedonian the Samaritans had Sicima as their metropolis. [illegible] Mafius on Joshua: the ruins of Sichem are now called Ist-hac. For Neapolis, built on a different site, is now seen. These additions were needed; let us now proceed to other matters.

units.la: Pag. 16. Beth-leem petit ] sequentia docent legendum, Bethel petit. Nam ibi altare Domino statuit, non in Beth-leem.
units.tr: Page 16. "He went to Beth-lehem"] The following sentences show that it should read "He went to Bethel," for there he set up an altar to the Lord, not in Beth-lehem.

units.la: In parte turris] Sensus est, in tractu illo ubi turris Gader erat. Male Viator, in parte aliqua turris, & fustra Sigonius Sed verum hic reprehendit, quem non intellexit. Graeca versio, [illegible, ~12 letters] trans aut ultra turrim.
units.tr: "In the part of the tower"] The sense is: in the district where the tower of Eder was. The Viator is wrong to render it "in some part of the tower," and Sigonius in vain. He rightly censures this, though he did not understand it. The Greek version has [illegible] "beyond or across the tower."

units.la: Gader] vel Ader. Ea vox gregem sonat, unde apud Hieronymum, trans turrim gregis. Eusebius de locis Ebraicis, Gader turris;ubi, habitante Iacob, Ruben patris violavit to-rum: quae absque g littera in Ebraeo Ader scribitur. In parte turis Gader Ebraei dicerent [illegible, ~3 letters]. Sic alibi, civitas in parte Iuda. Nam pars in ea lingua pro agro sumitur. Syri [illegible, ~3 letters] dicunt inversis litteris, unde Haceldama, ager sanguinis.
units.tr: Gader] or Ader. This word means "flock," whence in Jerome "across the tower of the flock." Eusebius, on Hebrew places: "Gader, a tower, where, while Jacob was dwelling there, Reuben violated his father's concubine." In Hebrew it is written Ader without the letter g. Hebrews would say "in the part of the tower Gader" [illegible]. So elsewhere: "a city in the part of Judah." For in that language "part" is taken for "field." The Syrians [illegible] say it with the letters inverted, whence Haceldama, the field of blood.

units.la: Benjamin vocatus, elt] id sonat filius dexterae. Ita pater cum vocavit, ut appareret, boni eminii causa, cum prius a matre Benoni nominatus fuisset, quod Graece interpretantur [illegible, ~6 letters] id est, filius doloris mei.
units.tr: Benjamin, as he was called] This means "son of the right hand." Thus the father named him, so that it might appear to be for the sake of a good omen, since earlier his mother had named him Benoni, which the Greeks interpret [illegible] that is, "son of my sorrow."

units.la: Benjamin] compositum ex nomine Ben filius, & Iamin dextera. Quidam filius austri. Nam auster dextera vocatur, id est, [illegible, ~4 letters] quia qui respicit orientem austrum habet ad dexteram. Sed quare filius austri? An quia natus in terra Chanaan, quae australis est respectu Mesopotamiae; unde profectus fuerat, & ubi reliquos filios genuerat?
units.tr: Benjamin] Compounded of the name Ben, "son," and Iamin, "right hand." Some (say he was called) "son of the south." For the south is called the right hand, because one who faces east has the south on his right. But why "son of the south"? Was it because he was born in the land of Canaan, which lies south of Mesopotamia, whence he had set out, and where he had begotten his other sons?

units.la: Vxoribus] Ada & Oholibama,
units.tr: To wives] Adah and Oholibamah,

units.la: E Chananaeorum gente] Hetthaeorum & Hevaeorum.
units.tr: Of the race of the Canaanites] of the Hittites and the Hivites.

units.la: In hoc tam praecilo opere] in hac epitoma, sive in hoc breviario. Vocat historiam suam praecisum opus, ut pag.3 i. Quae ego, quia prolixa admodum videbantur, inferenda huic tam praecise operi non putavi.
units.tr: In this so concise a work] in this epitome, or in this summary. He calls his history a concise work, as on page 3. Since these things seemed very lengthy, I did not think they should be included in so concise a work.

units.la: Ad origines revertatur] supra fontes dixit in eodem sensu, videlicet pag.4. Sed potius ut per Origines ipsam Genesin innui dicamus.
units.tr: Let him return to the origins] Above he said "sources" in the same sense, namely on page 4. But it is better to say that Genesis itself is meant by "Origines."

units.la: Post excessum patris] excessum pro morte posuit, ut Cicero, post excessum suum Romulus Iulio Proculo dixit se Deum esse. Idem alibi, & excessum e vita, & in vita mansionem.
units.tr: After the departure of the father] He used "departure" for "death," as Cicero did when Romulus, after his departure, told Julius Proculus that he was a god. Elsewhere too he uses both "departure from life" and "remaining in life."

units.la: In solo eo, in quo pater vixerat] in terra Chanaan, Gene.
units.tr: In the very soil in which the father had lived] in the land of Canaan, Gen.

units.la: Aliquantum ab eo] in Sichem, & inde in Dothan, ubi Iosephos invenit.
units.tr: Some distance from him] at Shechem, and from there at Dothan, where he found Joseph.

units.la: Parvus] minimus filiorum.
units.tr: Youngest] the least of the sons.

units.la: Carus admodum Iosephi patri] cum quia e Rachele nata erat, quam tenerrime amabat: tum etiam quia senex eum genuerat.
units.tr: Very dear to Joseph's father] both because he had been born of Rachel, whom he loved most tenderly, and also because he had begotten him in old age.

units.la: Frequentibus ejus somniis] duo tantum commemorantur apud Mosen.
units.tr: By his frequent dreams] Only two are recorded in Moses.

units.la: A patre missus] e valle Hebron. Gen. 37. 14. Hinc potest colligi patrem habitasse tum in ea valle.
units.tr: Sent by the father] from the valley of Hebron, Gen. 37.14. From this it may be gathered that the father was then living in that valley.

units.la: In lacum demissus] lacum vocat, quem Græci λάκκον [?], & Ebrei בור [?], id est, cisternam aut puteum, siue in aquam continent siue non. Sic sæpe interpres vetus, quem vulgatum nuncupamus. Fuit aliquando tempus cum putarem scribendum, in lacum demissus, cum duplici C, quomodo scriptum hoc nomen in Lexico veteri. Nunc dubito. Dubitandi causa ex Hieronymo, in quo etiam lacus unico C. Videtur ea ætas aliter non scripsisse hoc vocabulum. Quanquam lacus in Latio aliud est. Vsurpatur in sacris & pro sepulchro.
units.tr: Let down into a pit] He calls it a lacus, which the Greeks call λάκκον [lakkon], and the Hebrews בור [bor], that is, a cistern or well, whether it holds water or not. The old interpreter, whom we call the Vulgate, often does so. At one time I thought it should be written lacus with a double c, as this word is written in the old Lexicon. Now I doubt it. The reason for doubt is Jerome, who also writes lacus with a single c. That age seems not to have written the word otherwise. Although lacus in Latin is something else. It is also used in sacred writings for a tomb.

units.la: Pag. 17. Negotiatoribus] mercatoribus Ismaelitis e Galaad venientibus. Hi a Ionatha interprete Chaldæo vocantur Arabes, & a Ierosolymitano Saraceni, & infra in textu Mosis, Madianitæ. Forte inter eos erant Madianitæ: aut Madianitæ generali vocabulo ita nominantur. Quorundam opinio est Iosephum ab Ismaelitis, qui cum emerant a fratribus, venditum postea fuisse Madianitis, a quibus deinde eunucho Pharaonis traditus fuerit. Nihil temere statuendum.
units.tr: Page 17. Merchants] Ismaelite merchants coming from Gilead. These are called Arabs by Jonathan the Chaldee interpreter, and Saracens by the Jerusalem paraphrast, and further on in Moses' text Midianites. Perhaps Midianites were among them, or the Midianites are called by that general term. Some hold that Joseph, sold by his brothers to the Ismaelites, was afterwards sold to the Midianites, by whom he was then handed over to Pharaoh's eunuch. Nothing should be asserted rashly.

units.la: Vendiderunt] viginti argenteis. Tradunt autem Ebrei, quotiescunque mentio fit argenteorum in lege, siclos intelligi debere: quibus ego assentior potius quam Ionathæ vertenti hoc loco, viginti obolis argenteis. Nam pretium hoc nimis vile fuisset. Siquidem viginti oboli efficiunt dumtaxat unum siclum, ut habetur, Leuit. 27.5.
units.tr: They sold him] for twenty pieces of silver. The Hebrews, however, maintain that wherever silver is mentioned in the law, shekels must be understood. I agree with this rather than with Jonathan's rendering here, "twenty obols of silver." For that price would have been too low. Indeed twenty obols make only one shekel, as is found in Lev. 27.5.

units.la: Ab his] negotiatoribus Madanæis, Gen. 37.36. quos supra Madianitas dixi, haud ignorans esse qui Madanæos inter & Madianitas distinguant. Mihi religio hic discedere a veteribus, præsertim cum appellative dicamus מדנים [?] & מדינים [?] eodem significatu. Si aliam sententiam sequi mavelis, non repugno, cum fieri posset ut in communem societatem coiverint hi tres populi Madianitæ, Ismaelitæ & Madanæi, simulque Iosephum & emerint & vendiderint.
units.tr: By these] merchants, Midianites, Gen. 37.36, whom above I called Midianites, though I am not unaware that some distinguish the Madanites from the Midianites. For my part I scruple to depart here from the older authorities, especially since we say מדנים [madanim] and מדינים [madinim] with the same meaning. If you prefer to follow another opinion, I do not object, since these three peoples, Midianites, Ismaelites and Madanites, may have joined in a common partnership and both bought and sold Joseph together.

units.la: Potifari] est cur malim Photiphari. Nam P. Latino carebant olim Ebrei. In Aquila & Symmacho Φωτιφάρ [?] & in Hieronymo Phutiphari. Prius LXX. habebant Φιτιφὲν [?] vel Φιτιφὲ [?] variantibus libris. Sic etiam Demetrius apud Eusebium Περὶ τῶν Ἑβραϊκῶν [?] lib. 9. In libro nominum Phethefre vel Fetefre reperio & Φιτιφὲς [?]. Hiero Quæst. in Gen. Venditus est igitur Iosephi principi exercitus & bellatorum, non Petephre, ut in Latino scriptum est: sed Phutiphar eunucho. Hinc forte quod in editione Parisiensi, Phutiphari præpositο Pharaonis.
units.tr: Potifari] I would rather read Photiphari, since the Hebrews formerly had no letter P. In Aquila and Symmachus it is Φωτιφάρ, and in Jerome Phutiphari. The Seventy earlier had Φιτιφέν or Φιτιφέ, the manuscripts varying. So too Demetrius in Eusebius, On the Hebrew Names, book 9. In the book of names I find Phethefre or Fetefre, and Φιτιφές. Jerome, Questions on Genesis. Joseph was therefore sold to the captain of the king's army and of his fighting men, not to Petephre, as the Latin has it, but to the eunuch Phutiphar. Perhaps this is why the Parisian edition has Phutiphari chief officer of Pharaoh.

units.la: Præpositο] LXX. [illegible, ~8 letters] id est, spadoni vel eunuchο. Sic etiam Ebræi. E Chaldæorum paraphrastis duo reddunt, principi: unus, videlicet autor Ierosolymitanæ; dominatori, vel, dynastæ; quod in idem ferme recidit. Hic Phutifar princeps erat satellitum, vel magis carnificum sive spiculatorum Pharaonis, quos Hieronymus in milites transfert, dum ab eo magister militum vocatur. Quanquam in LXX. ἀρχιμαγείρος[?]: quod Augustinus, quaest. 127. & Ambrosius in libro de Iosepho, cap. 4. reddunt, præpositο coquorum.
units.tr: Præpositο] The Seventy have [illegible], that is, a eunuch or chamberlain. So too the Hebrews. Of the Chaldee paraphrasts, two render it "prince": one, namely the author of the Jerusalem Targum, and "ruler" or "dynast", which comes to nearly the same thing. Here Phutiphar was the prince of the guards, or rather of the executioners and spearmen of Pharaoh, whom Jerome turns into soldiers when he calls him master of the soldiers. Yet the Seventy have ἀρχιμάγειρος [archimageiros], which Augustine, Questions 127, and Ambrose, in his book on Joseph, chapter 4, render "chief of the cooks".

units.la: Pharaonis] Amosin vocat Orosius lib. 1. cap. 8. Scilicet Pharao commune nomen esse regum Ægypti, aut potius apud eos regem significare. In qua opinione videtur fuisse Iosephus, Ant.bisto[?].lib. 8. cap. 2. cum ita scriberet, Pharao nomen secundum Ægyptios significat regem. Vocatos autem eo nomine ait a Minoe, qui Abrahamum præcesserit, usque ad tempora Salomonis, hoc est per annos mille trecentos & amplius. Testimonium perhibet hujus rei & Manetho, quem Eusebius in Chronico laudat, inquiens, Ægyptiorum reges omnes tunc Pharaones dicebantur, non hoc proprium habentes nomen, sed pro dignitate reges tunc utebantur hoc nomine, sicut & apud nos imperatores Augusti appellantur. Hoc nos ex libris Manethonis, Ægyptii lectum posuimus. Ab eo sumpsit Ambrosius in epist. ad Romanos, cap. ix. Pharao nomen regum erat apud Ægyptios, sicut & apud Romanos reges Augusti appellantur: & Hiero. Iesa 30. Pharao apud Ægyptios nomen est regiæ potestatis, & unusquisque speciali appellatur vocabulo, ut Pharao Nechao, Pharao Vafre, &c.
units.tr: Pharaonis] Orosius, book 1, chapter 8, calls him Amosis. Clearly Pharaoh was a common name of the kings of Egypt, or rather meant "king" among them. Josephus seems to have held this view, Antiquities, book 8, chapter 2, when he wrote: "Pharaoh, according to the Egyptians, means king." He says that the kings were called by this name from Minoes, who came before Abraham, down to the time of Solomon, that is, through more than thirteen hundred years. Manetho, whom Eusebius quotes in his Chronicle, also bears witness to this, saying that all the kings of Egypt were then called Pharaohs, not having a name of their own, but using this name according to their dignity, just as among us the emperors are called Augusti. We have set this down from the books of Manetho, an Egyptian, as he read them. Ambrose took it from him in his epistle to the Romans, chapter 9: "Pharaoh was the name of the kings among the Egyptians, just as the Romans call their kings Augusti." And Jerome on Isaiah 30: "Pharaoh is a name of royal power among the Egyptians, and each one is given a special appellation, such as Pharaoh Necho, Pharaoh Hophra," and so on.

units.la: Suam Chananæam] ita Græci LXX. Gen. 38. 2. [illegible, ~40 letters] Σαυὰ, καὶ εἰσῆλθε πρὸς αὐτήν[?]. Unde non dubito, quin Sulpicius initio scripserit, Savam Chananæam. Sava, Sua, ut Aux[?], Vx[?]: Lauz, Luz. Ceterum in Ebræo est שוע[?] quod Græci convertunt. Sane viri nomen esse Sua, & non mulieris paret ex 1. Paralip. 2.3. Hieronymus ambigue transstulit, viditque ibi filiam hominis Chananæi, vocabulo Sua. Dicitur & Sue: quod in antiquis codicibus. Aliquot Græca exemplaria σαβὰ habent, in quo β pro υ. Sic promiscue Δαυὶδ & Δαβὶδ scribebant, Λαυὶ & Λαβὶ. Quod in his nominibus defendi potest, in σαβὰ non item. item. Non enim Vau ibi consonans est, sed vocalis quam modo per u, modo per au exprimebant.
units.tr: Suam Chananæam] So the Greeks, the Seventy, Genesis 38:2: "Σαυά, and he went in to her." Hence I have no doubt that Sulpicius at the start wrote "Savam the Canaanitess." Sava, Sua, as Aux, Vx; Lauz, Luz. Moreover the Hebrew is שוע, which the Greeks render. Indeed that Sua was a man's name, and not a woman's, appears from 1 Chronicles 2:3. Jerome translated it ambiguously and took it to be the daughter of a Canaanite named Sua. It is also called Sue, which is found in old codices. Some Greek copies have σαβά, where β stands for υ. So they wrote Δαυίδ and Δαβίδ indiscriminately, Λαυί and Λαβί. This can be defended in these names, but not in σαβά, for the Vav there is not a consonant but a vowel, which they expressed now by u, now by au.

units.la: In matrimonium assumpsit] alibi hoc dixit, in matrimonio accepit.
units.tr: In matrimonium assumpsit] elsewhere he says, took in marriage.

units.la: Her] Sic emendavimus ex editione Parisiensi, cum in aliis esset Heth: veritas scriptura Er. Nam sic est in Ebraeo [illegible, ~3 letters] & in Graecis codicibus [illegible, ~2 letters] : quod tamen Severus noster cum aspiratione legisse videtur. Novum non est ut quae leniter scribenda sunt aspirentur, et contra. Quae corrigenda viro docto, non imitanda sunt, meo judicio.
units.tr: Her] I have emended this from the Parisian edition, where the others have Heth. The true reading of Scripture is Er, for so it is in the Hebrew [illegible] and in the Greek codices [illegible]; yet our Severus seems to have read it with an aspiration. It is not new for letters that should be written softly to be aspirated, and the reverse. Things that are to be corrected by a learned man are not to be imitated, in my judgment.

units.la: Onan] vel Aunan: quod in libris Graecorum Αὐναν[?]. Onan, Aunan, ut Hofe, Haufe: vulgo Ause.
units.tr: Onan] or Aunan, which in the books of the Greeks is Αὐναν. Onan, Aunan, as Hofe, Haufe; commonly Ause.

units.la: Selam] potest esse quartus casus ex Sela. Si secus est, tum in mendo cubat, ut σηλὰμ[?], quod in editione Romana, Selam, Selom, ut Adam, Odom. Prius erat σηλὰ[?]. Sela, Selo, ut Lecha, Lecho, Attha, Attho. Dialectus enim Syriaca a cum o permutat. Inde Selam & Selom. Hujusmodi errores libentius scribis imputave-rim quam interpretibus, Ebr. שלם[?]
units.tr: Selam] may be the fourth case of Sela. If not, then it lies in an error, such as σηλάμ, which in the Roman edition is Selam, Selom, as Adam, Odom. Earlier it was σηλά, Sela, Selo, as Lecha, Lecho, Attha, Attho. For the Syriac dialect changes a into o. Hence Selam and Selom. I would rather charge errors of this kind to the scribes than to the translators. Hebrew שלם.

units.la: Fratris uxorem accepit] jure propinquitatis, quod IBBUM vocant: quo tenebatur frater propinquus uxorem defuncti fratris in matrimonium assumere, quo ex ea semen excitaret. Fratris autem nomine intelligo fratrem [illegible, ~3 letters]. Qui si deerat, ibatur ad proximum agnatum. Poterat tamen is qui uxorem & liberos habebat, nuptias recusare.
units.tr: Fratris uxorem accepit] by the right of kinship, which they call IBBUM: by which the nearest brother was bound to take the wife of his dead brother in marriage, so that he might raise up seed from her. By the name of brother I understand a brother [illegible]. If he was lacking, one went to the nearest kinsman. Yet he who already had a wife and children could refuse the marriage.

units.la: Spermata in terram effunderet] duo hic miror. Primum quod usus sit voce Graeca, cum in mundo esset Latina: deinde quod cum de femine humano sermo fit, usurpat pluralem sperma-ta, & non singularem sperma, id est, femen. Nam Syrachides, loquitur quidem de femine humano, sed allegorice.
units.tr: Spermata in terram effunderet] I wonder at two things here. First, that he used a Greek word when there was a Latin one in the world; second, that when speaking of human seed he uses the plural spermata and not the singular sperma, that is, seed. For the son of Sirach does speak of human seed, but allegorically.

units.la: Meretricio habitu assumpto] nam faciem peplo velaverat more meretricum, ne a socero agnosceretur.
units.tr: Meretricio habitu assumpto] for she had veiled her face with a cloak, after the manner of harlots, so that she would not be recognized by her father-in-law.

units.la: Mista est] congressione. Sic Cicero in primo de Divinatione, corpus cum matre miscere.
units.tr: Mista est] in intercourse. So Cicero in the first book On Divination: to have intercourse with a mother.

units.la: Postero die editus est] fides historiae poscit, ut legamus contra codicum omnium fidem, posterior editus est. In fonte habetur, postea vero egressus est frater, qui manum cocco illigatam habebat, Id Graeci transtulerunt μετὰ τοῦτο[?]. Non ergo postero die editus est, sed eodem quo alter, nempe paullo post. Neque Sigonius annotat pro postero die. in Græcis esse statim, id est ἰωθὸς[?], cum hoc ibi dicatur de Phares, & non de Zare, qui posterior exivit. Res est non coniectura.
units.tr: Postero die editus est] the credibility of the history demands that we read, against the agreement of all the codices, "afterwards he was born." In the source it is said, "afterwards, indeed, the brother came out who had a hand bound with scarlet." The Greeks rendered this μετὰ τοῦτο [meta touto]. So he was not born on the following day, but on the same day as the other, namely a little after. Nor does Sigonius note, in regard to "on the following day," that in the Greek it is immediately, that is ἰωθός, since here it is said of Phares and not of Zara, who came out later. The matter rests on fact, not conjecture.

units.la: Phares] ut Habel: quod extra pausam scribunt Hebel. Sic Pheres, & in pausa Phares. Id nunc obtinet quando est nomen proprium. Sonat autem, interprete Aquila, ἁρπαγὴ[?], intercisio, diremptio, perruptio. Hiero. maceriam edidit. Idem in libro quæst. Ebrai. Pro maceria Aquila & Symmachus divisionem transtulerunt. Ab eo igitur quod diviserit membras nulam fecundinarum divisionis nomen accepit. Malim perruperit aut diruperit, & perruptionis nomen accepit. Nam διαπόρθω[?], divido, dirimo, perrumpo. Sed nolo contentionis funem propterea. Quæ sequuntur ibi, Vnde & Pharisæi qui se quasi justos a populo separaverant, divisi appellantur. Censura indiget. Nã Pharisæi vocantur פְּרוּשִׁים[?], non פְּרִישִׁים[?]. Sic dico, Phares ultimam habet S, Sade: unde פָּרִיצִים[?] latrones. Pharisæi a separando dicti, quod est ultima Sin. Syri eos vocant [illegible, ~5 letters], unde Pharisæorum appellatio. Vide Gene-fi. 28.29.
units.tr: Phares: as Habel (the form written Hebel outside a pause). So Pheres, but in pause Phares. This now holds when it is a proper name. It means, according to the translator Aquila, "plunder" [ἁρπαγή], interruption, division, breaking through. Jerome gives "wall" (maceria) in his edition. The same in his Hebrew Questions. For "wall", Aquila and Symmachus rendered "division". From the fact that he divided the membranes (?) of the afterbirth, he therefore received the name of division. I would prefer "broke through" or "tore down", and he received the name of breaking-through. For διαπορθώ [diaporthō] means to divide, to separate, to break through. But I do not wish to stir up a quarrel on that account. What follows there, "Whence also the Pharisees, who had separated themselves from the people as if they were just, are called divided", needs correction. For the Pharisees are called פְּרוּשִׁים [perushim], not פְּרִישִׁים [perishim]. So I say: Phares has the final letter S, Sade, whence פָּרִיצִים [paritsim] means robbers. The Pharisees were named from separating, which is the final Sin. The Syrians call them [illegible], whence the name Pharisees. See Gen. 28.29.

units.la: Zara] vel Zare. Sic Thara dicimus & Thare. Hieronymus in Traditio. Hoc nomen interpretatur oriens. Sive igitur quia primus apparuit, sive quia multi justi ex eo nati sunt, ut in libro Paralipomenon continetur, Zara, id est, oriens appellatus est. Alij à filo coccineo, quo manus ejus revincta erat, sic appellatum arbitrantur. Nicolaus de Lyra, ex fulgentia coccini ad manum ejus ligati. Zara enim refulgentiam sonat.
units.tr: Zara] or Zare. So we say Thara and Thare. Jerome in the Traditions. This name is interpreted as "rising". Whether because he appeared first, or because many righteous men were born from him, as is contained in the book of Chronicles, he was called Zara, that is, rising. Others think he was so called from the scarlet thread with which his hand was bound. Nicholas of Lyra, from the brightness of the scarlet bound to his hand. For Zara signifies brightness.

units.la: A curatore regio] curatorem regium appellat, quem supra dixerat, præpositum Pharaonis, qui a Mose vocatur eunuchus Pharaonis. Quomodo eunuchus, si uxorem habebat? An eunuchum dixit, qui minister & aulicus erat Pharaonis? Theodoritus, Eunuchi nominantur non soli sed etiam qui inter famulos sunt ἐυνουχεῖς[?], id est, benevoli possessoribus. Nonnulli autem dicunt solere AEgyptios eunuchos habere uxores propter libidinem & salacitatem. Quod Græce ἐυνουχίζει[?], id in vocabulo Ebræo סָרִיס[?] non habet locum. Quocirca debilior est hæc etymologia, quam ut ex ea probari possit quod vult ὁ Θεόλογος[?]. Sunt nihilominus qui Ebræa convertunt, aulicus Pharaonis, non magis audiendi, meo judicio, quam qui corrigunt, cubicularius Pharaonis. Si enim erat, ut Moses ait, princeps mactatorum, lanionum, aut carnificum & spiculatorum, quomodo potuit esse cubicularius regis. Tamen Eucherius in libros Regum, pag. 198. Fuit consuetudo & apud antiquos eunuchos vocare cubicularios & custodes palatii, qui uxores habebant, & abscisci corpore non fuerunt. Dixi mactatores, i. הַטַּבָּחִים [?] a Mose dici lanios vel carnifices, appellatio a mactando. Nam ut ei homines, ita illi pecudes mactabant. Hodie in Anglia, qui lanionet sive lanij sunt, iidem homines securi feriunt. Quod supplicii genus in viros principes ibi exercetur creberrime. Apud Josephum & LXX interpretes ἀρχιμάγειρος princeps coquorum: de quo extat judicium Hieronymi hujusmodi, In plærisque locis archimagiros, id est, cocorum principes, pro magistris exercitus Scriptura commemorat, ἀρχιμάγειροι quippe Græce interpretatur occidere. Et Augustini, quod habetur Quæst. in Genesin, Nolunt quidam præpositum coquorum interpretari, qui Græce ἀρχιμάγειρος dicitur, sed præpositum militiæ, cui esset potestas occidendi. Nam sic appellatus est etiam ille, quem Nabuchodonosor misit, penes quem potius invenitur primatus fuisse militiæ. Quidam hic edidit, rerum capitalium præsectus. Cui firmando quod in domo ipsius carter extiterit. Hic a Latinis dicitur etiam prætorianus judex, & quæstor rerum capitalium. Cetervm ἈΡΧΙΜΑΓΕΙΡΟΣ, de hominibus usurpatur Ies. 14.21. parare filius ejus mactationem.
units.tr: A curatore regio] He calls him the royal steward, whom he had said above was set over Pharaoh, and whom Moses calls the eunuch of Pharaoh. How a eunuch, if he had a wife? Or did he call him a eunuch who was a minister and courtier of Pharaoh? Theodoret: eunuchs are named not only those who are castrated but also those among the servants who are εὐνουχεῖς [eunoucheis], that is, well-disposed to their possessors. Some, however, say that the Egyptians were accustomed to have eunuchs with wives on account of lust and lewdness. The Greek εὐνουχίζει [eunouchizei] has no place in the Hebrew word סָרִיס [saris]. Therefore this etymology is too weak to prove what the Theologian wishes. Nevertheless there are some who render the Hebrew "courtier of Pharaoh", who in my judgment are no more to be heard than those who correct it to "bedchamber attendant of Pharaoh". For if he was, as Moses says, the chief of the slaughterers, butchers, or executioners and spearmen, how could he be the king's bedchamber attendant? Yet Eucherius, in his books on Kings, p. 198: it was also the custom among the ancients to call the chamberlains and guardians of the palace eunuchs, who had wives and were not cut in body. I have said "slaughterers", i.e. הַטַּבָּחִים [hattabbachim], which Moses calls butchers or executioners, a term from slaughtering. For as those men, so these slaughtered beasts. Today in England those who are butchers, or the butchers, are the same men who strike with the axe. This kind of punishment is most often carried out there on men of rank. In Josephus and the Seventy, ἀρχιμάγειρος [archimageiros], chief of the cooks. On this there is Jerome's judgment of this kind: "In many places Scripture speaks of archimagiroi, that is, chiefs of the cooks, as commanders of the army, for ἀρχιμάγειροι in Greek is interpreted as 'killers'." And Augustine's, found in the Questions on Genesis: "Some are unwilling to interpret the chief of the cooks, who is called archimageiros in Greek, as anything but the commander of the army, who had the power of killing. For that man also whom Nebuchadnezzar sent was so called, and in him the chief power of the army is found." Someone here published "prefect of capital cases", in support of which that he was in the house of the same man a jailer. Among the Latins he is also called the praetorian judge and quaestor of capital cases. Moreover ἀρχιμάγειρος is used of men in Isaiah 14:21: "prepare slaughter for his sons."

units.la: Pretio acceperat] id est, emerat.
units.tr: Had bought him for a price] that is, had purchased him.

units.la: Domumque ejus & familiam procuraret] per domum intelligit bona domestica: & per familiam, uxorem & liberos servosque reliquos. Alioqui domus quandoque pro familia ponitur, Gen. 30,5. Ab eo tempore constituit eum super domum suam & super omnia quæ habebat. Tales Latini scriptores appellant servos atrienses, quibus commissa cura familiæ ac totius domus. Græci οἰκονόμους vocant. Qua voce usi hoc loco sunt Jonathan & autor Jerosolymitanus. Est autem οἰκονόμος dispensator, œconomus vel œconomia præpositus. Aristoteles, [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐπίτροπος ἐργάτης: servus atriensis & operarius, id est, operam faciens domi aut in agro alibi ve.
units.tr: And would manage his house and household] By "house" he means his household goods, and by "household" his wife, children and remaining slaves. Elsewhere "house" is used for household, as in Gen. 30.5. From that time he set him over his house and over all that he had. Latin writers call such slaves atrienses, to whom the care of the household and of the whole house is entrusted. The Greeks call them stewards [οἰκονόμους]. Jonathan and the Jerusalem writer use this word here. An οἰκονόμος is a manager, a steward or one placed in charge of a household [οἰκονόμος]. Aristotle [illegible] calls him [ἐπίτροπος ἐργάτης]: a household slave and workman, that is, one who works at home or elsewhere in the field.

units.la: Vxoris domini] id est, heri fui.
units.tr: Wife of the master] that is, of my lord.

units.la: Male ergo in quibusdam libris Domini, cum D. majusculo. Nam tum est unum ex nomi[?]ibus Dei.
units.tr: So in some books, wrongly, "Lord" is written with a capital D. For then it is one of the names of God.

units.la: Oculos in se converterat] in amorem fui pellexerat, ob formae venustatem singularem, quia pollebat. Tradunt Ebraei, teste Hieronymo, emptum a Phutiphare Iosephi ob nimiam pulchritudinem in turpe ministerium. Quod quam facile dicitur, tam facile negari potest. Debet autem probare non is qui negat, sed qui dicit & affirmat aliquid. Nam quod iidem tradunt, eodem Hieronymo teste, a domino, virilibus ejus arefactis, postea electum esse juxta morem ἱεροφαντῶν[?], in pontificatum Heliopoleos, & hujus filiam esse Asenethi, quam postea Iosephi duxit uxorem, ex ipsis fo-tibus infirmari potest.
units.tr: Had caught her eyes] had enticed him into her love, because of his singular beauty, since he excelled in it. The Hebrews, as Jerome reports, say that Joseph was bought by Potiphar for a shameful service because of his excessive beauty. But as easily as this is said, it can as easily be denied. The burden of proof lies not with the one who denies, but with the one who says and affirms something. And what the same writers relate, again on Jerome's authority, that after his master's organs were dried up he was afterwards chosen, according to the custom of the hierophants [ἱεροφαντῶν], to be high priest of Heliopolis, and that Asenath, whom Joseph later took as his wife, was this man's daughter, can be refuted from the very sources.

units.la: Pag 18. Stuprum sibi intentatum] stuprum intentare conatum significat. Plus ergo est quam appellare aliquem de stupro, & minus quam stuprum cuiptam [?] inferre.
units.tr: Page 18. Had attempted to seduce him] to attempt to seduce means to try to commit fornication. So it is more than to accuse someone of adultery, and less than actually to commit adultery upon someone.

units.la: In carcerem conjectus est] regium qui erat in domo Phutiphari, in quem & regii ministri, quoties peccassent, includebantur. Unde apparet rectius existimare eos, qui hunc Phutipha-rem scribunt praefuisse non coquis aut laniis, sed regiis satellitibus spiculatoribusque: quippe penes quem jus regii carceris esset. Vide Gen.40 3.
units.tr: Was thrown into prison] the royal prison, which was in Potiphar's house, and into which the king's officials were also shut up whenever they offended. Hence it appears more correct to think that those who write that this Potiphar was over not cooks or butchers, but the royal guards and executioners, are right: since he had authority over the royal prison. See Gen. 40.3.

units.la: Ministri regis duo] qui eunuchi vocantur, Gen. 40.2. quorum unus erat pincerna sive pocillator, hoc est, princeps eorum qui regi vinum fundebant: alter pistor erat, hoc est princeps pistorum; quem ἀρχιοινοχόον[?] vocant Graeci. Sic alibi sacerdos ponitur pro summus sacerdos, & angelus pro archangelus. Quae ob-servatio lucem adfert huic loco Tobiæ, ego sum unus ex sep-tem angelis: quem vir doctus non capit, & ideo carpit. Nam ut sunt angeli innumerabiles, ita septem archangelos esse, quos Iohannes theologus spiritus appellat, religio a majoribus accepta tradit. Hiero in tradit. Ebra[?] Ubi nos posuimus principem vinariorum, in Ebræo scriptum habet M ASKE, quem nos possumus more vulgi vocare pincernam. Nec vile putemus officium, cum apud reges barbaros usq; hodie magnæ dignitatis sit regi poculum porrexisse.
units.tr: Two of the king's officials] who are called eunuchs, Gen. 40.2. one of whom was the cupbearer, or chief of those who poured wine for the king; the other was the baker, that is, chief of the bakers, whom the Greeks call the chief cupbearer [ἀρχιοινοχόον]. So elsewhere "priest" is put for high priest, and "angel" for archangel. This observation sheds light on the passage of Tobit, "I am one of the seven angels," which a learned man does not grasp and therefore criticises. For just as the angels are innumerable, so there are seven archangels, whom the theologian John calls the spirits; this is the belief handed down by our ancestors. Jerome in his translation. Where we have put "chief of the wine-stewards", the Hebrew text has mashqeh, which we may call, in common speech, the cupbearer. Nor should we think the office a small one, since among barbarian kings even today it is a matter of great dignity to hand the king a cup.

units.la: Futura ex somnio conjectans] quaeritur, an hoc sit licitum, & sciendum somnia duorum generum esse, Interna, Externa, In-terna vel ex phantasia oriuntur, vel ex complexione & constitutione corporis. Ex hac ultima specie medicus divinare potest, & ægroto aliquid certi praedicere, Externa vel ad corpus pertinent, vel ad spiritum. Ad corpus pertinent quae ἐπῳδαντικὰ[?] Graeci vocant, ex sympathia quadam, quae inter corpus nostrum & astra originem ducentia. Ad spiritum spectant, quae ex causa spirituali suntque duplicis generis. Nam alia divina, & alia diabolica. Divina a Deo proficiscuntur, diabolica ab ipso cacodaemone. Et his quae divina dixi & ἐπῳδαντικὰ[?] conjicere licet futura ex aliis non item, ut nec ex primi generis internis.
units.tr: Foretelling the future from a dream] It is asked whether this is lawful, and it must be known that dreams are of two kinds, internal and external. Internal dreams arise either from imagination or from the temperament and constitution of the body. From this last kind a physician can divine and foretell something certain to a sick man. External dreams relate either to the body or to the spirit. Those that relate to the body, which the Greeks call [ἐπῳδαντικὰ], arise from a certain sympathy between our body and the stars from which they derive their origin. Those that concern the spirit come from a spiritual cause and are of two kinds: some are divine and others diabolical. Divine dreams come from God, diabolical ones from the evil demon himself. From the things I have called divine and [ἐπῳδαντικὰ] it is permitted to conjecture the future, but not from other things, just as not from internal dreams of the first kind.

units.la: pistorem suspendio vitam finiturum.
units.tr: The baker would end his life by hanging.

units.la: ] pincernam liberandum crimine, propter quod in carcerem conjectus fuerat, & in locum muneris pristinum reponendum ac restituendum.
units.tr: The cupbearer would be freed from the charge on account of which he had been thrown into prison, and would be restored and reinstated in his former office.

units.la: Post biennium hoc adjecit, quoniam immemor bene de se meriti Iosephi pincerna tanto tempore nullam ejus memoriam apud regem usurpaverat.
units.tr: After two years he added this, because the cupbearer, forgetful of Joseph, who had deserved well of him, had for so long made no mention of him before the king.

units.la: Non posset absolvi pro eo habendum ac si dixisset, solvi declaratione aut interpretatione. Plautus, absolvere navem, & Varro promissum, & Tacitus, fidem.
units.tr: Could not be absolved to be taken as if he had said, "could be loosed by explanation or interpretation." Plautus uses "to absolve a ship," Varro "to absolve a promise," and Tacitus "to absolve faith."

units.la: Iosephi solvitur è vinculis.
units.tr: Joseph is released from his chains.

units.la: Quo metu rex perculsus mirum unde hoc hauserit. Nam in fonte non habetur. Metu quidem perculsus fuit cum vidisset somnium, sed hoc accidit antequam Iosephus illud interpretatus fuisset.
units.tr: By which fear the king was struck it is strange where he got this from, for it is not in the source. Indeed he was struck with fear when he saw the dream, but this happened before Joseph had interpreted it.

units.la: Aequato secum imperio si tamen solio extipiis[?]. 40 dumtaxat solio te major ero.
units.tr: Equal to me in power, if only in the throne. Gen. 41.40. Only in the throne will I be greater than you.

units.la: ] meminit hujus famis Iustinus historicus, lib. 36. ex Trogo Pompeio. Accidit autem, putante Orosio lib. 1. cap. 8. anno ante urbem conditam 1048.
units.tr: The historian Justin mentions this famine, book 36, drawing on Trogus Pompeius. It occurred, according to Orosius book 1 chapter 8, in the year 1048 before the city was founded.

units.la: Spes & salus Aegypti ipses[?] de salute AEgypti. Tmesis.
units.tr: The hope and salvation of Egypt concerning the salvation of Egypt. Tmesis.

units.la: ] filia Phutiphara sacerdotis vel magistratus Onij, quem multi eundem faciunt cum Phutiphar satellitum vel spiculatorum praefecto: meo judicio, non recte. Primum quia nomina diversa Phutiphara & Phutiphar: deinde quia Phutiphar in aula degebat, quae tum creditur fuisse apud Memphin. Ea distat ab Onio, ubi, ut credibile est, Photiphara habitabat, amplius quam viginti miliaribus. Notavit hoc S. Augustinus. Postremo causa est non levis cur credendum sit, si herifiliam duxisset, cum hoc ad honorem ejus non parum faciat, Mosen hoc tacuisse non fuisse. Scio in alia sententia fuisse olim Hieronymum: veruntaveruntamen, illud quidem certe negari non potest quin herus Iosephi סריס[?] fuerit. Quae vox si vere eunuchum denotat, non potest sacerdos Onij esse Phutiphar, cum eunuchi, licet id faciant quod viri solent cum mulieribus, tamen generare nequeunt. Ceterum Onij sacerdos vel princeps aut praefectus dici etiam potest Photifera & Phutifare: quae antiqua lectio est pro Phutifera: cuius ultima consonans in Ebraeo per Ain scribitur.
units.tr: daughter of Potiphar, priest or magistrate of On, whom many make the same as Potiphar, the captain of the guards or executioners: in my judgement, not rightly. First, because the names Potiphar and Potiphera are different; second, because Potiphar lived at court, which at that time is believed to have been at Memphis. That place is more than twenty miles from On, where, as is likely, Potiphera lived. St Augustine noted this. Lastly, there is no slight reason to believe that if he had married his master's daughter, Moses would not have kept silent about it, since this does no little to his honour. I know that Jerome was once of another opinion; but it cannot certainly be denied that Joseph's master was a saris [סריס]. If that word truly denotes a eunuch, Potiphar cannot be the priest of On, since eunuchs, although they may do what men usually do with women, cannot beget children. Moreover, the priest or chief or prefect of On may also be called Potiphera and Potiphare, which is the old reading for Potiphera, whose final consonant is written in Hebrew with an ayin.

units.la: Asenethl] ἀσενὲθ. Legitur & Asenath. Audi nunc & ride, Ionathan, Asenath, quam peperarat Dina Sichemo, & educaverat uxor Photiphare sacerdotis Onij. Vult dicere adoptaverat in filiam. Talibus ineptiis cum scateat Ionathan ille, non immerito mihi suspectus olim fuit & adhuc est.
units.tr: Asenath] [ἀσενὲθ]. It is also read Asenath. Now listen and laugh, Jonathan: Asenath, whom Dinah bore to Shechem, and whom the wife of Potiphera, priest of On, brought up. He means that she had adopted her as a daughter. Since that Jonathan abounds in such silliness, he was not undeservedly suspected by me long ago, and still is.

units.la: Duos filios genuit] antequam orta fames & annonae penuria esset, 41.50.
units.tr: He begot two sons before the famine and the scarcity of grain came on, 41.50.

units.la: Manassem] vel Manassen cum N in fine, a recto Manasse. Sed Graeci dicunt Manasses: unde Manassem cum M in fine. Id significat oblivionem inducens. Manasse, Manasses, ut Mose, Moses. Sic Iose, Ioses, Nominibus enim in vocali definentibus Graeci e addere solent, ut Iudas, Tobis, Iesus. Dictus ita ἀπὸ τοῦ נשה[?] oblivisci or, quod in participio secundae conjugationis, menasse, oblivisci faciens. Nam Deus Iosepho in Aegypto versanti dolorum omnium ipsiusque adeo patriae domus oblivionem attulerat.
units.tr: Manasseh] or Manassen with N at the end, from the correct Manasse. But the Greeks say Manasses, whence Manassem with M at the end. It means causing forgetting. Manasse, Manasses, as Mose, Moses. So Ise, Ises: for the Greeks are accustomed to add s to names ending in a vowel, as Judas, Tobis, Jesus. He was so named from [Hebrew nashah], to forget, because in the participle of the second conjugation, menasseh, meaning causing to forget. For God had brought upon Joseph, living in Egypt, forgetfulness of all his sorrows and even of his father's house.

units.la: Ephrem] antiquum est pro Ephraim. Qualia sunt Mesrem Aegyptius, apud Iosephum: Mozanem, bilances, apud Epipha-nium. Appellatio a fœcunditate. Nam Deus eum auxerat & fe-cundaverat in terra miseriae ipsius, hoc est in Aegypto.
units.tr: Ephraim] an old form for Ephraim, like Mesrem the Egyptian in Josephus, or Mozanem for balances in Epiphanius. The name is from fruitfulness, for God had increased and made him fruitful in the land of his affliction, that is, in Egypt.

units.la: Summam a rege potestatem] dominium in omnes Aegyptios, & in domum Pharaonis. In fonte habetur, cum staret coram rege. Gen. 41.46.
units.tr: Supreme power from the king lordship over all the Egyptians and over Pharaoh's house. It is in the source, when he stood before the king. Gen. 41.46.

units.la: Pag. 19. Septendecim] [illegible, ~6 letters]. Gen. 37.1. Quamquam in vulgata nostra Latina ledecim[?] tantum.
units.tr: Page 19. Seventeen] [illegible]. Gen. 37.1. Although in our Latin Vulgate only sixteen.

units.la: Gravis frumenti inopia] jugem & intolerabilem famem appellat Orosius lib. 1. cap. 8. qui eam accidisse tradit anno ante urbem conditam 1038. aut circiter, usus[?] hac in re autoritate Pompei historici, cujus abbreviator Iustinus Iosephi mentionem facit per haec verba, Minimus inter fratres Iosephi fuit. &c. Orosius addit fuisse hanc famem magnam sub rege Aegyptiorum Iapolito[?], cui nomen erat Amosis quo tempore Balaeus Assyrios, Argivos Apis regebat.
units.tr: Grievous shortage of grain] Orosius, book 1 chapter 8, calls it a continual and intolerable famine, which he reports happened in the year 1038 before the city was founded, or about then, relying in this matter on the authority of the historian Pompeius, whose epitomiser Justin makes mention of Joseph in these words: "He was the youngest among Joseph's brothers," etc. Orosius adds that this famine was great under the king of the Egyptians, Iapolito [?], whose name was Amosis, at the time when Balaeus ruled the Assyrians and Apis the Argives.

units.la: Annonæ arbitrium] id est, potestas, ut in illo.
units.tr: Annonæ arbitrium: that is, power, as in that line.

units.la: Te penes arbitrium nostræ vitæque necisque. Versus est Ovidianus.
units.tr: Te penes arbitrium nostræ vitæque necisque. It is a line of Ovid. In you lies the power over our life and death.

units.la: More regio adorant] ut subditi reges adorare solent. Adoratio ista civilis erat, siebatque corpore in terram prostrato, quod Græci dicunt προσκύνησιν. Hoc modo Persæ cum reges suos venerarentur, divinum honorem in exhibere dicuntur. Qua de re alias.
units.tr: More regio adorant: as subjects are accustomed to worship kings. This worship was civil, and was done by throwing the body prostrate on the ground, which the Greeks call προσκύνησιν [proskynēsin]. In this way the Persians, when they honoured their kings, are said to have offered divine honour. On this matter, more elsewhere.

units.la: Subdole] vafre ac fraudulenter.
units.tr: Subdole: craftily and deceitfully.

units.la: Loca] loca regionis minus firma: aut occulta & abdita. Nam interpretes variant. In Ebræo est ad verbum, nuditatem terræ. Sane Hiero. hoc enarrat, loca terræ immunita: Aquila vero & Symmachus τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς γῆς. Translatio a pudendis, quæ occulta sunt & sub veste latent.
units.tr: Loca: the less secure parts of the region, or hidden and concealed places. For the translators differ. In the Hebrew it is, word for word, the nakedness of the land. Jerome indeed explains it as the unprotected places of the land; but Aquila and Symmachus render τὰ κρυπτὰ τῆς γῆς [ta krypta tēs gēs]. The figure is taken from the private parts, which are hidden and lie concealed under clothing.

units.la: Simeon obses traditur] vinctus pro fratre retinebatur, ut si ille non adduceretur, Iosepho esset jus in eum quod vellet statuendi.
units.tr: Simeon obses traditur: he was kept bound as a hostage for his brother, so that if the other were not brought, Joseph would have the right to decide what he wished concerning him.

units.la: Deduxerunt] adduxerunt secum.
units.tr: Deduxerunt: they brought with them.

units.la: Frumentum gratis datum] id est, sine pecunia, quæ soluta quidem, sed ipsis insciis, in saccum cujusque reposita ac reddita. Ita gratis datum illis frumentum.
units.tr: Frumentum gratis datum: that is, without payment; the money was indeed paid, but without their knowledge, being put back and returned in each man's sack. So the grain was given to them free.

units.la: Male merentium] fratrum qui eum vendiderant.
units.tr: Male merentium: of the brothers who had sold him.

units.la: Oneratos frumento] improprie loquitur. Nam non ipsi onerati erant, sed jumenta ipsorum. Vide Gen. 42.26.
units.tr: Oneratos frumento: he speaks improperly. For they themselves were not loaded, but their beasts were. See Gen. 42.26.

units.la: Omni progeniæ ac familiæ] progeniem dicit liberos. Sic τέκνων & Camerarius interpretatur, mea progenies. Familiæ autem nomine uxores & servos designat. Alioqui progenies, id est genus cujusque, in familia continetur.
units.tr: Omni progeniæ ac familiæ: by progeny he means the children. So the Greek τέκνων [teknōn] is also rendered by Camerarius as "my progeny". By household he designates the wives and servants. Otherwise the progeny, that is, the kind of each, is contained within the household.

units.la: Ægyptiis] aulicis Pharaonis.
units.tr: Ægyptiis: the courtiers of Pharaoh.

units.la: Pag. 20. A diluvio autem an. M. CCC. & LX.] ita restituit olim Victor Gisselinus, prius erat M. CCC. & LX. Sigonius ad Gisselini numerum annos decem addit, ut sint M. CCC. & LXX. Quid hic sequendum? Videtur Gisselini emendatio vera esse. Nam Sigonij vitium continet ex falsa opinione, quam habuit de natali Iacob. Putavit enim Iacob natum esse anno 4, tatis Isaac LXX, cum natus fuerit anno ejusdem LX.
units.tr: Pag. 20. A diluvio autem an. M. CCC. & LX. Victor Gisselinus once restored it thus; it was previously 1360. Sigonius adds ten years to Gisselinus' number, to make 1370. What should be followed here? Gisselinus' correction seems to be true. For Sigonius' error arises from a false opinion he held about the birth of Jacob. He thought Jacob was born in the fourth year of Isaac's seventieth year, whereas he was in fact born in the sixtieth year of his age.

units.la: Series annorum a diluvio ad migrationem Israelitarum in Ægyptum.
units.tr: Series of years from the flood to the migration of the Israelites into Egypt.

units.la: A diluvio usque ad ortum Abrahæ supra numerat annos M. LXX.
units.tr: From the flood up to the birth of Abraham he counts above 1070 years.

units.la: Abraham annos natus centum genuit Isahacum
units.tr: Abraham, being a hundred years old, begot Isaac.

units.la: Isahac anno LX. ætatis genuit Iacob. His adde annos ipsius Iacob CXXX. Simul efficiunt an.
units.tr: Isaac, in his sixtieth year, begot Jacob. Add to these Jacob's own 130 years. Together they make the years

units.la: M. CCC. & LX.

Referuntur anni CCXV.] etiam hic erravit Sigonius emendans CCXXV. Error ipse ex eodem fonte manavit quo superior. Nam Iacob natus est cum Isahac annum ætatis ageret sexagesimum. Quod sic doceo. Duxit uxorem anno ætatis quadragesimo. Rebecca viginti annos continuos sterilis fuit. Exinde peperit geminos. Ceterum Abraham ingressus est terram Chanaan, anno ætatis 75. Anno autem centesimo genuit Isahacum. Superant anni viginti quinque. Quibus si addas, annos Isahaci LXX. & Iacobi CXXX. non sunt anni CCXXV. ut vult Sigonius; sed CCXV. tantum. Quocirca nihil hoc loco corrigendum est.
units.tr: The years are given as 215. Here too Sigonius erred in emending it to 225. The error itself came from the same source as the previous one. For Jacob was born when Isaac was in his sixtieth year. This I show as follows. He married at the age of forty. Rebecca was barren for twenty continuous years. After that she bore twins. Abraham, moreover, entered the land of Canaan at the age of 75, and in his hundredth year begot Isaac. Twenty-five years remain. If you add to these the 70 years of Isaac and the 130 of Jacob, you get not 225 years, as Sigonius wishes, but only 215. Therefore nothing here needs correcting.

units.la: Septimo & decimo anno] Sigonius emendat, septimo decimo, extrita copulante, quam infertam putat ab iis, quinque tas Sulpicianas, hoc est ea quæ Sulpicius per notas numerorum scripserat, explicuerunt.
units.tr: Septimo & decimo anno: Sigonius emends it to "seventeenth year", removing the connecting conjunction, which he thinks was inserted by those who explained the Sulpician numerals, that is, what Sulpicius had written by means of numerical notation.

units.la: Quam A Egypto advenerat] omisit præpositionem IN. quod huic scriptori familiare. Sic alibi dixit, A Egyptum descendeunt; pro in AEgyptum. Hoc primum: deinde promisque & sine discrimine vel cum accusandi vel cum auferendi casu hanc præpositionem jungit, contra Grammaticorum canones. Quod cum hic fecit, tum supra pag.13. Qua necessitate compulsus Isahac in Gerare ad regem Abimelech cesisit. Vide quæ notavimus ad illum locum.
units.tr: Quam A Egypto advenerat: he has omitted the preposition IN, which is characteristic of this writer. So elsewhere he wrote "they went down A Egypt" for "into Egypt". First, he joins this preposition without distinction with either the accusative or the ablative case, against the rules of the grammarians. He did this here, and also above on p. 13: "Driven by this necessity, Isaac withdrew to king Abimelech in Gerar." See what we have noted on that passage.

units.la: Sepulchro suo] sepulchro majorum suorum. quod in terra Chanaan in spelunca, quæ in agro Ephron Hetthæi, sive in spelunca quæ in agro Machphela, e regione Mamre, quam emerat Abraham ab Ephrone Hetthæo. Gen. 49. 18 & 30.
units.tr: Sepulchro suo: the sepulchre of his ancestors, which was in the land of Canaan, in the cave which is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, or in the cave which is in the field of Machpelah, opposite Mamre, which Abraham had bought from Ephron the Hittite. Gen. 49.18 and 30.

units.la: Tum Iosephi] prius Iosephi benedicendos filios Manasse & Ephraim obtulit patri: postea Iacob filium obtestatus est corpus, &c.
units.tr: Tum Iosephi: first Joseph presented to his father his sons Manasseh and Ephraim to be blessed; afterwards Jacob charged Joseph's son concerning his body, etc.

units.la: Benedictionis merito, &c.] quia sic meritus erat Ephraim ut fratri majori in benedictione præponeretur. Accidit hoc aliis multis, ut Habeli, Semo, Iacobo, Iosephho, Mosi, Davidi: qui prælati Caino, Iapeto, Esavo, Rubeni, Aharoni. Davidi autem licet licet minimus esset septem fratrum, tamen iis omnibus prælatus fuit.
units.tr: Benedictionis merito, etc.: because Ephraim had so merited that he was placed before his elder brother in the blessing. This happened in many other cases, as with Abel, Shem, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, David, who were preferred over Cain, Japheth, Esau, Reuben and Aaron. David, although he was the youngest of seven brothers, was nevertheless preferred over all of them.

units.la: Pro conscientia paventes] aurea est hæc dictio, & optimis autoribus usitata, pro conscientia; ut, pro re, pro tempore, pro periculo, pro copia rerum. Vult dicere, prout sibi male conscij erant. Vel pro, valet propter, quia, ut dialog. 1. pro eo tamen quod tibi est carissimus, non potest mihi non esse carus. Terentius Eunucho, ego pol te pro istis dictis ac factis scelus Ulciscar.
units.tr: Pro conscientia paventes: this is a fine expression, used by the best authors, "for conscience", as "for the thing", "for the time", "for the danger", "for the abundance of things".
