He means: as they were badly conscious of themselves. Or "pro" means "because" or "since", as in Dialogue 1: "since (pro) it is so that he is most dear to you, he cannot but be dear to me." Terence in the Eunuch: "By Pollux, for those words and deeds of yours I will avenge the crime."

units.la: Incredibile dictu] hoc incredibile non esse demonstrat Iob. Temporarius Chronologicarum demonstrationum lib. 2.
units.tr: Incredibile dictu: Iob. Temporarius demonstrates in book 2 of his Chronological Demonstrations that this is not incredible.

units.la: Quam cito numero aucti[?] sint] ingressa sunt Ægyptum ca-pita 70. egressa vero sunt armatorum ad millia sexcenta, præter imbellem turbam & vulgus promiscuum, quod innumerabile erat. Vide p. 24.
units.tr: Quam cito numero aucti sint: they entered Egypt with seventy persons, but they left as about six hundred thousand armed men, besides the unwarlike crowd and the mixed common people, which was countless. See p. 24.

units.la: Cito] spatio ducentorum & decem annorum, quem numerum annui putant verbo ירד[?] descendit. Res enim in numeris valet 200. Vau sex, Daleth quatuor. Simul efficiunt eum numerum quem dixi, hoc est, 216[?]. Cui firmando quod in Thargum Ierofo-lymitano, Et habitatio filiorum Israel qua habitarunt in Ægypto triginta semittarum erat, in quibus completi fuerunt anni quadringenti. Semitta (Hebraea vox est שָׁבוּעַ[?]) non solum septimum annum significat, sed ὅλων[?] annorum hebdomadam. Sonat autem ut si dicas ἄνεσις[?] remissio sive intermissio. Nam eo anno omne opus agriculationis intermittebatur. Porro triginta semitta, hoc est, annorum hebdomades, efficiunt annos 210. Rursum editio Chaldaica ad locum saltitans super montes, qui saltat merito patrum centum nonaginta annos. Quibus si addas annos, quibus fuerunt in Ægypto, emergunt anni 400. quos inchoant a nato Isahaco. Salmanticensis, traditio est in manu nostra annos captivitatis Ægyptiacæ numerari a die quo natus fuit Isahac. In qua supputatione consentiunt sapientes nationum, nec non eorum Chronica. Vide notas ad pag. 9. Sed & infra ad pag. 24 aliquid hac de re.
units.tr: Cito: in the space of 210 years, a number which some think is indicated by the Hebrew verb ירד [yarad] "descended". For the thing is worth 200 in numerals: Vau is six, Daleth four. Together they make the number I mentioned, that is, 216. To confirm this, the Jerusalem Targum has, "And the dwelling of the children of Israel, in which they dwelt in Egypt, was thirty semittas," in which the four hundred years were completed. A semitta (the Hebrew word is שָׁבוּעַ [shavua]) signifies not only a seventh year but a week of whole years. It means something like ἄνεσις [anesis] "release" or "intermission", for in that year all agricultural work was suspended. Now thirty semittas, that is, weeks of years, make 210 years. Again, the Chaldaic edition, on the passage "leaping upon the mountains", says that it refers to the patriarchs, who "leap" for 190 years. If you add to these the years they were in Egypt, you come to 400 years, which they reckon from the birth of Isaac. The Salamanca text: the tradition in our hands is that the years of the Egyptian captivity are counted from the day on which Isaac was born. In this reckoning the wise men of the nations agree, and so do their chronicles. See the notes on p. 9. But see also below, on p. 24, something on this matter.

units.la: Multiplicataque progenie] reptilium instar, non formicarum aut locustarum, ut annotat Galesinius. Quanquam formicæ inter reptilia, quæ יְשַׁרְצוּ[?] vocantur. Vide sis Exod. 1.7. Theodoretus, οὕτως ηὐξήθησαν ὡς ἀκρίδες [?] γῆς[?]. Hebraei scribunt singulas ternos aut quaternos & quandoque seaos peperiße.
units.tr: Multiplicataque progenie: like reptiles, not like ants or locusts, as Galesinius notes. Although ants are among the reptiles, which are called יְשַׁרְצוּ [yishretsu]. See Exod. 1.7. Theodoret says: οὕτως ηὐξήθησαν ὡς ἀκρίδες [houtōs ēuxēthēsan hōs akrides] … γῆς [gēs]: "they increased like the locusts of the earth." The Hebrews write that each woman bore three or four, and sometimes even six.

units.la: Defuncto rege] hic in historia Mephres nominatur, cuius anno nono Iosephi decessit, cum vixisset decem supra centum. Ex quo liquet ipsum cum imperio praefuisse Aegypto annos LXXX: Nam cum summa a rege potestatem accepit, annorum erat XXX. Interea in Aegypto fuerunt, ut proditum a nonnullis, reges quinque. Sed Eusebius quatuor tantum recensset. Hi sunt, Amosis, Chebron, Amenophis & Mephres. Vide sodes Chronicon ipsius.
units.tr: Defuncto rege: here in the history he is named Mephres, in whose ninth year Joseph died, having lived a hundred and ten years. From this it is clear that he himself held power over Egypt for eighty years, for when he received the sovereignty from the king he was thirty years old. Meanwhile, as some report, there were five kings in Egypt. But Eusebius lists only four. These are Amosis, Chebron, Amenophis and Mephres. See, if you please, his Chronicle.

units.la: Succedentium regum] horum nomina leguntur apud Funcium, Amenophis alter, cuius anno vigesimo sexto natus creditur Moses, Orus cognomento magnus, Aeengeres, Achorus, Cenchres sive Canchres, qui in mari rubro periit. Hunc Tacitus Bocchorin appellat.
units.tr: Succedentium regum: their names are read in Funcius: another Amenophis, in whose twenty-sixth year Moses is believed to have been born; Orus, surnamed the Great; Aeengeres; Achorus; Cenchres or Canchres, who perished in the Red Sea. Tacitus calls him Bocchoris.

units.la: Series regum Aegypti in dynastia XVIII.
units.tr: The series of the kings of Egypt in the eighteenth dynasty.

units.la: 1. Amosis, sub quo insignis illa fames fuisse creditur. Quanquam sunt qui eam sub Mephrem fuisse prodiderunt. Amosis regnavit annos. 25
units.tr: 1. Amosis, under whom that notable famine is believed to have occurred, though some have reported that it happened under Mephres. Amosis reigned 25 years.

units.la: 2 Chebron, qui in Glossa ordinaria Nebron vocatur, ann. 13
units.tr: 2. Chebron, who in the Glossa ordinaria is called Nebron, 13 years.

units.la: 3. Amenophis annos 21
units.tr: 3. Amenophis, 21 years.

units.la: 4. Mephres annos 12
units.tr: 4. Mephres, 12 years.

units.la: Hujus anno nono; aut, ut alij, undecimo, decessit Iosephus natus annos centum decem.
units.tr: In his ninth year, or, as others have it, his eleventh, Joseph died, aged 110.

units.la: 5. Misphar Mutosis (alias, Metusis; ita Glos. ordinaria) annos 36
units.tr: 5. Misphar Mutosis (otherwise Metusis, so the Glossa ordinaria), 36 years.

units.la: 6. Tuthemosis ann. 9
units.tr: 6. Tuthemosis, 9 years.

units.la: Ita Funccius. In Glos. ordin. vocatur Tithimosis, & octo tantum anni regno ipsius attribuuntur.
units.tr: So Funccius. In the Glossa ordinaria he is called Tithimosis, and only eight years are assigned to his reign.

units.la: 7. Menophis alter 31
units.tr: 7. Menophis the second, 31 years.

units.la: Hic ab aliis Memnon vocatur. Primus edictum de necandis Ebraeorum pueris proposuit. sub hoc natus est Moses.
units.tr: Others call him Memnon. He was the first to issue the edict concerning the killing of the Hebrew boys. Moses was born under him.

units.la: 8. Orus cognomento magnus ann. 38
units.tr: 8. Orus, surnamed the Great, 38 years.

units.la: 9. Acengeres annos 12
units.tr: 9. Acengeres, 12 years.

units.la: 10. Achorus annos 9
units.tr: 10. Achorus, 9 years.

units.la: 11. Cenchres sive Canchres, ann. 16
units.tr: 11. Cenchres or Canchres, 16 years.

units.la: Hic in mari rubro periit, ut dictum est.
units.tr: He perished in the Red Sea, as has been said.

units.la: Imperio] imo tyrannide. Nam iniquum & durum nimis imperium tyrannis est, deprimebantur autem in opposito habet extollebantur, adaugebantur.
units.tr: "Dominion": indeed, tyranny. For a dominion that is unjust and excessively harsh is tyranny. "Were oppressed" is set in opposition to "were raised up and increased."

units.la: Pag. 21. Aedificandarum civitatum] duas aedificarunt (armaria Pharaonis quidam eas vocant) videlicet Phithom & Ramesses, Exod 1. 11.
units.tr: Page 21. "To build cities": they built two (some call them Pharaoh's storehouses), namely Pithom and Raamses, Exod. 1.11.

units.la: Opus durum] & segne admodum, si non fallunt nos Ebraei, apud quos in proverbium abiit, Phitom & Raamesses, de opere segni ac tardo supra modum.
units.tr: "Hard labour": and very laborious, if the Hebrews do not mislead us, among whom it passed into a proverb, Pithom and Raamses, of work sluggish and slow beyond measure.

units.la: Ne quandoque libertatem, &c.] ne hostibus se conjungerent, aut sibi ex ea terra exitum bello quaererent.
units.tr: "Lest at some time they gain their freedom, etc.": lest they join themselves to the enemy, or seek a way out of that land by war.

units.la: Parvulos] mares. Hoc editum valde minuit numerum Ebraeorum in Aegypto, qui alioquin in majus potuissent excrescere. Nam ex jole Joseph nasci potuerunt eo spatio temporis, & quidem absque ullo miraculo, 2 5000000. bellatorum, ut quidem Temporarius demonstrat.
units.tr: "Little ones": males. This edict greatly reduced the number of Hebrews in Egypt, who otherwise could have grown larger. For from the seed of Joseph they could have been born in that span of time, and indeed without any miracle, 2,500,000 fighting men, as Temporarius demonstrates.

units.la: Filia Pharaonis] Termuth sive Thermuthin Josephus nominat. Pharao autem illo tempore Amenophis vocabatur, si credendum Eusebio, cujus anno vigesimo sexto natus fuit Moses. Quod sic doceo. Quum populares suos educeret ex Aegypto, agebat annum LXXX. Tum Aegypto praerat Pharao Cenchres, qui anno regni sui decimo sexto in mari rubro periit. Hunc antecessit Achorus, qui regnavit annos novem: Amenophis triginta annum. Subduc calculum, deprehendes eum natum fuisse anno regni Amenophis, quo dixi.
units.tr: "Pharaoh's daughter": Josephus names her Thermuthis or Thermuthin. Pharaoh at that time was called Amenophis, if we believe Eusebius, in whose twenty-sixth year Moses was born. I show this as follows. When Moses led his people out of Egypt, he was eighty years old. Then Cenchres, who in the sixteenth year of his reign perished in the Red Sea, ruled over Egypt. Achorus, who reigned nine years, preceded him, and Amenophis thirty. Work out the sum and you will find that he was born in the year of Amenophis' reign that I mentioned.

units.la: Infantem] filium Amram, quem ex Iochabed uxore genuerat. Hic Amram patrem habuit Caath, Levi filium, Iacobi nepotem. Fuit autem septimus a patriarcha Abrahamo. Quod significat Salmanticensis in libro Iohasin per haec verba, Moses doctor nosterfuper eum pax fuit septimus sanctorum patrum, itidem ut sabbathum. Hoc vult dicere, ut sabbathum septimus dierum est, ita Moses septimus patrum, id est, patriarcharum. Idem ibid. Natus est anno trigesimo septimo post obitum Levi, hoc est anno mundi condíti 1368. die quarto septimi mensis Adar, tertia hora diei, ut scriptum reliquit R. Abraham filius Hija Hisphanus.
units.tr: "The infant": the son of Amram, whom he begot of his wife Jochebed. This Amram had as his father Kohath, son of Levi, grandson of Jacob. He was seventh from the patriarch Abraham. The Salamanticensis, in the book Johasin, signifies this in these words: "Moses our teacher, peace upon him, was the seventh of the holy fathers, just as the sabbath is the seventh." He means this: as the sabbath is the seventh of the days, so Moses is the seventh of the fathers, that is, of the patriarchs. The same author, in the same place: he was born in the thirty-seventh year after the death of Levi, that is, in the year of the world's creation 1368, on the fourth day of the seventh month Adar, at the third hour of the day, as R. Abraham son of Hija Hisphanus left it written.

units.la: In flumine] in Nilo, qui peculiariter [illegible, ~3 letters], id est, rivus appellatur. Forte quia in multos rivos deducitur. Nihil affirmo.
units.tr: "In the river": in the Nile, which is peculiarly called [illegible], that is, a stream. Perhaps because it is divided into many streams. I affirm nothing.

units.la: Nutriendum pro filio curavit] matri eum tradidit nutriendum, quem per sororem Mariam, quae ad flumen stabat, ad se vocavit. Eandem nominavit eum Mosen, quod diceret, Ex aqua extraxi eum, Exod 2. 10. Vide sequentia.
units.tr: "He arranged for him to be nursed": he handed him over to his mother to be nursed, having called her to himself through his sister Miriam, who stood by the river. He named him Moses, because she said, "I drew him out of the water," Exod. 2.10. See what follows.

units.la: Nomen puero Moyses dedit] Quid vidit Galesinus theo Iogus cum scriberet, nomen hoc in circumcisione a parentibus ei impositum? Nam circumcisus fuit die octavo, ita jubente lege: nomen autem hoc inditum a filia Pharaonis, cum ex aqua, in quam projectus fuerat, eum eduxisset. Res est, non conjectura.
units.tr: "The boy's name Moses he gave": What did Galesinus the theologian see when he wrote that this name was given to him by his parents at circumcision? For he was circumcised on the eighth day, as the law commanded. This name was given by Pharaoh's daughter, when she drew him out of the water into which he had been cast. It is a fact, not a conjecture.

units.la: Moyses] varians scriptura Moses. Utraque reperitur in codicibus Græcis & Latinis. Hæc Ebræorum propria est. Appella-tio a [illegible, ~4 letters] extraxit, eduxit: non ex [illegible, ~5 letters] aqua et [illegible, ~5 letters] servatus, ut vult Iosephus. In circumcisione nominatus fuisse traditur Ioa-chim. Habuit præterea nomen aliud, videlicet Melchi. Quod notavit Clemens Alexandrinus. Unde habeat nescio. Vide Quæsita mea. Melchi sonat, si Latine velis interpretari, rex meus. Id nunc legunt Malchi. Antiquitates Philonis habent Melchil, vocavit, inquit (loquitur de filia Pharaonis) nomen ejus Mosés: mater autem eum vocavit Melchil. Alter Clemens, qui scripsit hoc nomen et datum postquam in cælum receptus esset. Ab Ægyptiis, teste Abenezra, vocabatur Monios. Omitto Saphenath Phanea, quod exponunt absconditorum repertor: alij mundi servator. Nam id sonat, teste Hierô. in lingua Ægyptiorum. Porro Moyses ita hodie pronuntiant, ut si esset vox trisyllaba Μωυσῆς, quam pronuntiationem adjuvat etymon Iosephi, de quo supra. [illegible, ~3 letters] enim id est, [illegible, ~3 letters] verbum est dissyllabum. Suspicari aliquis posset scripturam hanc manasse ex illo etymo. Quæ suspicio si vera, tum recte sic pronuntiant. Sed si diphthongus est ωυ in μωυσῆς, tum dissyllaba vox est pronuntianda [illegible, ~6 letters] ut monet Henricus Stephanus in Apologet. pro vet. ling. Græce pronuntiatione. Forte an aliquando lectum fuit [illegible, ~4 letters] per Vau scribere vocalem, quam interpretes per diphthongum ωυ expresserint. Sane ω & ου & ωυ in Vau permutantur. Qualis sensus in ου talis fere in ωυ consule Grammaticos.
units.tr: "Moses": the spelling varies, Moses. Both forms are found in Greek and Latin manuscripts. This form is peculiar to the Hebrews. The name comes from [illegible], "drew out" or "led out," not from [illegible] water and [illegible] "saved," as Josephus holds. At circumcision he is said to have been named Joachim. He had besides another name, Melchi, which Clement of Alexandria noted; whence he had it I do not know. See my Quaesita. Melchi means, if you wish to render it into Latin, "my king." Now they read Malchi. Philo's Antiquities has Melchil: "she called his name Moses" (he is speaking of Pharaoh's daughter), "but his mother called him Melchil." Another Clement, who wrote that this name was given after he had been received into heaven. By the Egyptians, according to Abenezra, he was called Monios. I omit Saphenath Phanea, which some explain as "discoverer of hidden things" and others as "saviour of the world"; for, according to Jerome, that is what it means in the language of the Egyptians. Further, they now pronounce Moyses as though it were a trisyllable, Μωυσῆς [Mōysēs], a pronunciation supported by the etymology of Josephus mentioned above. [illegible] is a disyllabic word. One might suspect that this spelling arose from that etymology. If that suspicion is true, then they pronounce it correctly. But if ωυ in Μωυσῆς is a diphthong, then the word must be pronounced as a disyllable, as Henricus Stephanus advises in his Apology for the Old Greek Pronunciation. Perhaps it was sometimes read as the vowel written with Vau, which the translators expressed by the diphthong ωυ. Certainly ω and ου and ωυ are interchanged with Vau. For the sense of ου is much the same in ωυ; consult the grammarians.

units.la: Cum viriles annos ageret] [illegible, ~6 letters] legitur in codicibus Græcis, sed [illegible, ~8 letters] & in Ebræo, magnus evalit, ut possis exponere, cum e pueris excelsisset. Sed [illegible, ~5 letters] etiam de viro dicitur. Quomodo hic accipiendum putarim. Nam agebat tum annum ætatis quadragesimum. Liquet ex narratione Stephani protomartyris, Act. 7. 23.
units.tr: "When he was of mature age": [illegible] is read in the Greek manuscripts, and in the Hebrew "grew great," so that you could explain it as "when he had grown up from boyhood." But it is also said of a man. How I think this should be taken here: for he was then in his fortieth year of life. It is clear from the account of Stephen the first martyr, Acts 7.23.

units.la: Hebræum] maritum Salomith filiæ Dabri. R Salomo. Quod tamen temere affirmatur. Nam non habet authoritatem de Scriptura. Quocirca quam affirmatur facile, tam facile negari potest.
units.tr: "A Hebrew": the husband of Shelomith, daughter of Dibri, says R. Solomon. Which, however, is rashly asserted, for it has no authority from Scripture. Wherefore what is as easily asserted can as easily be denied.

units.la: hunc putant fuisse ex præfectis regis, qui opera Iudæorum exigebant, morasque cessantium castigabant.
units.tr: This man they think was one of the prefects of the king, who exacted the labour of the Jews and punished those who shirked.

units.la: agnatum aut popularem.
units.tr: A kinsman or a fellow countryman.

units.la: Vide Act. 7.24.
units.tr: See Acts 7.24.

units.la: prostratum occidit & arena obruit, ne res innotesceret. Putabat enim neminem scire, cum undique circumspiciens neminem videret.
units.tr: He struck him down and buried him in the sand, so that the matter would not become known. For he thought no one knew, since, looking around on every side, he saw no one.

units.la: ubi rem cognitam esse intellexit, cum etiam Pharao rem audita ipsum ad supplicium quæreret. Id accidit die altero Exod. 2.13. Duos autem Hebræos inter se contendentes audaces Iudæi dicunt fuisse Dathan & Abirom. Ita Ionathan & R. Salomo. Pro die altero si vel secundo, Act. 7.16. εἰς τὴν ἐπιοῦσαν [?], id est, die sequenti.
units.tr: When he understood that the matter was known, and Pharaoh too, having heard the report, sought him for punishment. This happened on the next day, Exod. 2.13. The Jews say that the bold men who were quarrelling with each other were Dathan and Abiram. So Jonathan and R. Solomon. For "the next day," if it means "the second," see Acts 7.26: εἰς τὴν ἐπιοῦσαν [eis tēn epiousan], that is, the following day.

units.la: id est, post factum, ut cum dicimus ex illo tempore significamus, post illud tempus: vel certe propter factum. Nam (e) quoque propter significat, ut in epistola Cecilij ad Plinium, balneum etiam ex epistolis meis. notavit Linacer.
units.tr: That is, after the deed, as when we say "from that time" we signify "after that time"; or certainly "on account of the deed." For (e) also means "on account of," as in Caecilius's letter to Pliny: "the bath also on account of my letters," as Linacer noted.

units.la: Exod. 2.15. & sedit in terra Madian, Terram pro regione posuit: nam est nomen regionis. Quanquam Josephus urbem esse scribit in littore maris rubri si-tam. Eusebius in Locis duas urbes memorat ejus nominis. Prior, inquit, est trans Arabiam ad meridiem in deserto Saracenorum, contra orientem maris rubri: unde vocantur Madianæi & Madianæa regio. Alia est juxta Arnonem & Areopolim, cujus nunc ruinæ tantummodo demonstrantur. In hac Mosen exulasse scribit Hiero in locis Actio. Apostol.
units.tr: Exod. 2.15: "and he dwelt in the land of Midian." He put "land" for region, for it is the name of a region. Although Josephus writes that it is a city situated on the shore of the Red Sea, Eusebius in his Places mentions two cities of that name. The first, he says, is beyond Arabia to the south, in the desert of the Saracens, facing east toward the Red Sea; hence the Midianites and the region of Midian are named. The other lies near the Arnon and Areopolis, whose ruins alone are now pointed out. Jerome, in his Places of the Apostolic Acts, writes that Moses was exiled in this one.

units.la: nomen hoc scribi debet cum N in ultima. Quod autem in libris Græcorum μαδιὰμ, mendum est ab exscriptoribus: quale in Εὑ & similibus. Hodie Midjan & est dissyllabum.
units.tr: This name ought to be written with an N at the end. As for the Greek books' μαδιὰμ [Madiam], it is an error of the copyists, like the one in Eua [Εὕα] and similar forms. Today it is Midjan [Midjan] and has two syllables.

units.la: Raguel, non Iethro legitur, Exod. 2.17. quod Græci scribunt ῥαγουὴλ. Libri Latini variant. Nam in aliis Raguel, & in aliis Iethro. Quæ duo nomina Lyra confundit: etiam scholion quod in editione Romana, ῥαγουὴλ, ἰοθὼρ. Nam Iothor idem cum Iethro. Critici Ebræorum legunt Iether. Alijs Iethro pater erat, & Raguel avus. Quod autem in loco citato, ad Raguel patrem suum, id interpretantur ad Raguel auum suum. Sic Abeneʒra, R. Leui & alij. Nam pater Iethro dicebatur & Hobab. Sic dico Raguel pater Iethronis erat, & Iethro socer Mosis, cujus filiam Seppphoram in matrimonium acceperat. Vt pater pro avo, ita filius ponitur pro nepote. Sic mater est avia quandoque & filia neptis.
units.tr: Raguel, not Jethro, is the name read in Exod. 2.17, which the Greeks write ῥαγουὴλ [Ragouēl]. The Latin books vary: some have Raguel and others Jethro. Lyra confuses these two names, and so does the scholion in the Roman edition, which gives ῥαγουὴλ and ἰοθὼρ [Iothōr]. For Iothor is the same as Jethro. The Hebrew critics read Jether. Others held that Jethro was the father and Raguel the grandfather. What the passage cited says, "to Raguel his father," they interpret as "to Raguel his grandfather." So Abenezra, R. Levi and others. For Jethro was also called father, and so was Hobab. So I say that Raguel was the father of Jethro, and Jethro the father-in-law of Moses, whose daughter Zipporah he had given him in marriage. As "father" is put for "grandfather," so "son" is put for "grandson." Thus a mother is sometimes a grandmother, and a daughter a granddaughter.

units.la: Iethro] nihil immuto, tamen eo labor ut credam Severum, qui alioqui Græcos libenter sequitur, scripsisse Iotbor. nam ita vocatur hic sacerdos Exod. 2.18. in codicibus Græcis. Rei firmandæ est Iethor, quod in duabus editionibus, videlicet Basileensi & Parisiensi.
units.tr: Jethro] I change nothing here, yet I am inclined to believe that Severus, who otherwise willingly follows the Greeks, wrote Iotbor. For this priest is so called in Exod. 2.18 in the Greek codices. To confirm this, there is Iethor, which is found in two editions, namely the Basel and the Paris.

units.la: Sacerdotem] τὸν ἱερέα[?]. LXX. Iosephus, Hieronymus. Quod roborat Abenezra his verbis, omnis sacerdos est minister Dei aut idolorum. Ille autem erat Iethro minister Dei, quemadmodum adhuc declarabo. Quidam, principem regionis illius, in quem Oncelos paraphrastes Chaldæus. Sic Pho-tiphare, qui a veteribus vocatur sacerdos Omj, ab aliis dicitur princeps Omj, id est, præfectus aut gubernator. Eadem vox in Ebræo.
units.tr: Sacerdotem] the priest [τὸν ἱερέα]. So the Seventy, Josephus, Jerome. Abenezra confirms this in these words: every priest is a minister either of God or of idols. But that Jethro was a minister of God, as I shall show. Some take it to mean the prince of that region, and Onkelos the Chaldee paraphrast reads it so. So Potiphera, whom the ancients call priest of On, others call prince of On, that is, prefect or governor. The same word is used in Hebrew.

units.la: Sephoram] in libris quibusdam scriptum, Seppbora[?]. Sed Biblia Latina Sephora habent, Græca variant. Nam in aliis σεπφωρά[?], & in aliis σεπφώρα[?]: quam ego scripturam judico verio-rem esse. De hac Sepphora videndi sunt Eusebius Προπαρ.[?] lib. ix. pag. 257, & Theodoretus in Num. quæst. 22. In libro nomi-num Sephora, avis ejus vel pulchritudo. צִפּוֹר avis vel potius avicula aut passer; צְפוֹרָה pulchritudo. Nomina hæc di-versa sunt, quæ tamen in editione Latina confunduntur. Nam obstetrix Ægyptia Siphra sive Sephra, Exod. 1.15. Sephora vocatur. Tu distingue ut Sephra sit obstetrix, & Seppbora[?] uxor Mosis. Id sonat aviculam aut passerem. Origenes hom. 2. in Exodum, Sephora interpretatur passer.
units.tr: Sephoram] In some books it is written Seppbora. But the Latin Bibles have Sephora, and the Greek texts vary: some have σεπφωρά [Sepphōrá], others σεπφώρα [Sepphṓra], and I judge the latter spelling to be the truer. On this Zipporah see Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica, book 9, p. 257, and Theodoret on Numbers, question 22. In the book of names, Sephora means "her bird" or "beauty." The Hebrew ṣippor [צִפּוֹר] means a bird, or rather a little bird or sparrow; ṣipporah [צְפוֹרָה] means beauty. These names are different, yet in the Latin edition they are confused. For the Egyptian midwife Siphra or Sephra, Exod. 1.15, is called Sephora. Distinguish them so that Sephra is the midwife and Seppbora the wife of Moses. The latter means a little bird or sparrow. Origen, Homily 2 on Exodus, interprets Sephora as "sparrow."

units.la: Gerson] scribendum Gersom cum M in fine. Mendum quale in Phithon et Absalon & similibus. Contra peccatum in μαδιὰμ[?].
units.tr: Gerson] It should be written Gersom, with an M at the end. The error is like those in Phithon and Absalon and similar names, and unlike the error in Madian [μαδιὰμ].

units.la: Gerson cum N in fine alius est, Græci codices habent γηρσὰμ[?], id est, גֵּרְשׁוֹם[?] cum camets. Sic etiam in libro nominum. Critici Ebræorum elegerunt גֵּרְשָׁם[?]. Olim cum apices aberant tam hoc quam illo modo legi potuit. Iam vero dialectus Syriaca mutat Holem Ebræorum in camets, hoc est in a protensum sive longum. Hinc Gehennam, quod in libris punctatis Gehennom, id est, Vallis Hennom. Appellatio a גֵּר[?] expello. Nam quia pulsus erat Ægypto, ideo sic filium nominavit. Dicebat enim ἐγὼ ἐν γῇ ἀλλοτρίᾳ[?]: Quoniam advena sum in terra aliena.
units.tr: Gerson with an N at the end is a different name. The Greek codices have γηρσὰμ [Gērsam], that is, gērshām [גֵּרְשָׁם] with a qamets. So also in the book of names. The Hebrew critics chose gērshām [גֵּרְשָׁם]. When the vowel points were absent, either form could be read. Now the Syriac dialect changes the Hebrew holem into qamets, that is, into a long, drawn-out a. Hence Gehenna, which in the pointed books is Gehinnom [Gehinnom], that is, the Valley of Hinnom. The name comes from gēr [גֵּר], to expel. For because he had been driven out of Egypt, he so named his son. For he said, ἐγὼ ἐν γῇ ἀλλοτρίᾳ [egō en gē allotria], "I am a stranger in a foreign land."

units.la: Eliezer] Ἐλιέζερ[?]. Nomen hoc Moses dedit altero filio, quod Deus patrius ei subvenisset, eumque a Pharaonis gladio liberas-set. Verba clara sunt, Exod.18.4. quia Deus patris mei auxilio mihi fuit & liberavit me, &c.
units.tr: Eliezer] Ἐλιέζερ [Eliezer]. Moses gave this name to his second son, because the God of his father had helped him and freed him from Pharaoh's sword. The words are plain, Exod. 18.4: "because the God of my father was my help and delivered me," and so on.

units.la: Hoc tractu temporum] hac tempestate sive his temporibus (sic tractum corporis pro ipso corpore posuit Lucretius) vel magis hoc temporis intervallo ac spatio. Sic idem Lucretius, aevi labentia tractu. Nam trahere & extrahere tempus, veteres dicebant: atque ita cum tractus fere fit longa rerum extersio[?] etiam ad tempus id retulit novitate quadam insigni, ait Gifanius.
units.tr: "In this course of time": that is, in this age or these times (so Lucretius used tractus for the body itself), or rather in this interval and span of time. So Lucretius again: "of the passing course of the age." For the ancients said trahere and extrahere tempus, to draw out and prolong time. And so, when a long stretch of things is passed through, he applied it also to time, with a certain striking novelty, says Gifanius.

units.la: Iob fuit] Quo tempore Iob vixerit, incertum. Communis opinio tenet librum ipsum scriptum fuisse a Mose domino prophetarum. Quae si vera, necesse est ut vixerit patrum aevo ante Mosen, vel certe tempore Mosis. Quod autem alij afferunt tum fuisse in diebus Davidis, aut in deportatione Babylonica, id ita interpretatur Nomini bonus, qui Ebraice Sem-Tob, ac si dixissent, quovis tempore fuisse aliquem Iobum, hoc est virum bonum cui male fuerit. Ætatem produxit usque ad annum vigesimum supra du-centesimum. Quanto tempore Israelitae fuerunt in Ægypto. Unde in litteras relatum natum fuisse cum intrarent Ægyptum, & decessisse e vivis cum inde exirent. Vixit in terra Vz[?], quam Senes Aufitin[?] appellant, quae putatur esse non in Armenia, ut habet autor Thargum libri Iob, sed in Arabia vel Idumaea. Sunt qui sepulchrum ejus ostendi dicant Constantinopoli. Quod accipiendum non de Iob qui exemplum fuit patientiae; sed de alio qui vocatur Iob Alotsari[?], qui Constantinopolim venit anno primo post mortem Asin[?] ben eli, &c. cum 50. millibus virorum & 500. triremibus, ubi etiam occubuit in porta quae vocatur Igre capi. Venit autem anno quinquagesimo secundo ab adventu Mahometi. Notavit hoc Samuel Solem medicus ad librum Iohasin[?].
units.tr: When Job lived is uncertain. The common opinion holds that the book itself was written by Moses, the lord of the prophets. If this is true, Job must have lived in the age of the patriarchs before Moses, or at least in the time of Moses. As for others who assert that he lived in the days of David, or at the Babylonian deportation, the good Nominis [Nomini] interprets this, the one who in Hebrew is Sem-Tob [Sem-Tob], as though they meant that at some time there was a certain Job, that is, a good man to whom things went badly. He extended his life to the 220th year. He lived for as long as the Israelites were in Egypt. Hence it is recorded in writing that he was born when they entered Egypt and died when they left it. He lived in the land of Uz, which the old writers call Aufitis, and which is thought to be not in Armenia, as the author of the Targum of Job says, but in Arabia or Idumaea. Some say his tomb is shown at Constantinople. This must be understood not of the Job who was the example of patience, but of another, called Job Alotsari, who came to Constantinople in the first year after the death of Asin ben Eli, and so on, with 50,000 men and 500 triremes, and where he also fell at the gate called Igre capi. He came in the fifty-second year after the advent of Mahomet. Samuel Solem the physician noted this on the book of Iohasin.

units.la: Præditus opibus] habebat enim balantum sive ovium septem millia, camelorum tria millia: juga boum quingenta, & asinas totidem, copiosissimumque servitium. Denique orientalium omnium maximus erat, hoc est clarissimus ac locupletissimus.
units.tr: Endowed with wealth: for he had seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen and as many she-asses, and a very large household. In short, he was the greatest of all the men of the East, that is, the most famous and the richest.

units.la: Integris] salvis, nondum amissis.
units.tr: Integris: safe, not yet lost.

units.la: Diabolum] Satanam. Hoc Ebraicum est, illud Græcum. Nam Satan ἀπολλύων[?] vetusta declaratione.
units.tr: Diabolum: Satan. The first is Hebrew, the second Greek. For Satan means "destroyer" [ἀπολλύων], in an old explanation.

units.la: Diris] id est, sævis. q Deorum ira immissis.
units.tr: Diris: that is, savage, with the wrath of the gods let loose.

units.la: Vinci] ad versis superari. Hoc vult dicere, non potuit adduci ut præ[?] doloris impatientia, &c.
units.tr: Vinci: to be overcome, defeated. He means that he could not be brought, by impatience of grief, and so on.

units.la: Pag.22. In duplum recepit] tam dives evasit ut habuerit quatuordecim balantum sive ovium millia, camelorum sex mil-lia: mille boum juga ac totidem asinas, Iob. 42[?].
units.tr: Page 22. Received double: he became so rich that he had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen and as many she-asses, Job 42.

units.la: Spem auxilii a Deo exspectabant] vis in hoc sermone ut si diceret, cum ipse expectabant a Deo auxilium; vel potius, expecta-bant ut illis spem auxilij adferret. Spem expectare Cicero quoque dixit. Siquidem ad Atticum scribens, Ego quidem, inquit, aut rem; aut ne spem[?] quidem expecto.
units.tr: Hoping for help from God: the force of this phrase is as if he said that they themselves were looking to God for help; or rather, that they were waiting for him to bring them hope of help. Cicero also said "to expect hope." For writing to Atticus he says, "I expect neither the thing itself nor even hope of it."

units.la: Repente rubus ardere visa | mirabile erat videre ignem in interiore deserto: mirabilius videre rubum ardentem. Nam lignum viride non facile ignem concipit. Sed nihil tam admirabile, quam quod ardens rubus non consumeretur. Hoc significat cum ait,
units.tr: Suddenly a bramble seemed to burn: it was a wonder to see fire in the inner desert, but more wonderful to see a bramble burning. For green wood does not readily catch fire. But nothing was so admirable as that the burning bramble was not consumed. This is what he signifies when he says:

units.la: Flammis innoxiis] flamma innoxia, quæ minime nocet, hoc est, quæ materiam, quam semel corripuit, non consumit. Sic leo innoxius, saltus innoxius, a quo & in quo nullum periculum. Est etiam innoxius, cui minime nocetur.
units.tr: Harmless flames: a harmless flame is one that does no harm, that is, one that does not consume the material it has once seized. So we say a harmless lion, a harmless wood, from which and in which there is no danger. There is also the sense of harmless as applied to one who is not harmed at all.

units.la: Rubo propius accesit] pro, ad rubum. Sic Livius dixit, accedere mœnibus. Supra, turrim quæ cœlo accederet. Locus est pag.7.
units.tr: Approached the bramble nearer: that is, to the bramble. So Livy said "accedere moenibus," to approach the walls. Above, "a tower that would reach heaven." The place is on page 7.

units.la: Dominum se esse Abraham] malim, Deum se esse Abra-ham. Nā vocatur [illegible, ~8 letters] ,quod reddunt, Θεὸς Ἀβραάμ[?], &c. Sed novum non est huic autori ut Dominum pro Deum usurpet. Exempla passim obvia.
units.tr: I would prefer "that God himself was the God of Abraham," rather than "that the Lord himself was Abraham." For it is called (the text is damaged here), which they render as "the God of Abraham" [Θεὸς Ἀβραάμ], and so on. But it is not new for this author to use "Lord" for "God." Examples are everywhere.

units.la: Ad regem Ægypti] vocatur in divinis monumentis Pha-rao. Quod tamen non proprium ei nomen, sed commune regum Ægypti, ut diximus. Autores Manetho Ægyptius & Iosephus Ebræus. Dices, Quodnam ergo nomen proprium habebat? Cen-chren appellat Eusebius in Chronico: Amosin sive Amasin Cle-mens Stromat. 1. Omosin vel Amasin Iustinus, Orosius, Plu-tarchus. Bocchorim (alias Occhorim) Tacitus lib.5. historiarum.
units.tr: In the divine records he is called Pharaoh. This, however, is not a proper name for him, but a common title of the kings of Egypt, as we have said. The authors are Manetho the Egyptian and Josephus the Hebrew. You will ask, "What then was his proper name?" Eusebius in the Chronicle calls him Cenchres; Clement, in the first book of the Stromata, Amosis or Amasis; Justin, Orosius and Plutarch, Omosis or Amasis; Tacitus, in book 5 of the Histories, Bocchoris (otherwise Occhoris).

units.la: Cunctantem potestate confirmat, cunctabatur primum, quia se, quod disertus non esset, minus ad eam rem idoneum judicabat: deinde quia non credebat posse hoc popularibus suis per-suaderi. Ergo Deus ei se adfuturum dicit & socium dat Aharo-nem fratrem: tum etiam signis instruit, quibus fidem sibi conci-liare posset apud suos. Signa hæc faciebat mitio per virgam, ma-num & aquam fluminis,cum annum ageret ætatis octogesimum, tribus annis minor Aharone,qui tum agebat annum 83.
units.tr: Though he hesitated, God confirmed him in his commission. At first Moses hesitated because he judged himself unfit for the task, since he was not eloquent, and because he did not believe his own people could be persuaded. So God said that he would be with him and gave him Aaron his brother as a companion. He also equipped him with signs by which he could win the trust of his own people. Moses performed these signs with the staff, his hand and the river water, when he was eighty years old, and Aaron, who was three years younger, was then eighty-three.

units.la: Aaron] Graeca consuetudo scribit Ἀαρὼν[?] Ebraea vero Aharon cum aspiratione. Ceterum Aegyptius Moses in More part. 3. cap. 50 ab Adamo ad Mosen numerat annos circiter bis mille & quingentos. Vbi circiter posui, codex Ebraeus habet בקרב[?] quod sonat verbum e verbo, in propinquo. Notatum autem erat manu nescio cuius in margine 2513. expende.
units.tr: Aaron] The Greek writers spell it Ἀαρὼν [Aarōn] but the Hebrews write Aharon, with an aspirate. Moses the Egyptian, in the More part. 3, chap. 50, counts about two thousand five hundred years from Adam to Moses. Where I have put "about", the Hebrew manuscript has בקרב [bekarav], which word for word means "in the vicinity". In the margin someone, I know not who, has noted 2513. Take note.

units.la: Missum ie a Deo] est cur hic malim a Domino Deo Israel: ut mox, verbisque se Domini Dei Israel. Quae in textu Ebraeo per Tetragrammaton expressa.
units.tr: "Sent by God" I would prefer here "from the Lord God of Israel", as below, and "in the words of the Lord God of Israel." In the Hebrew text this is expressed by the Tetragrammaton.

units.la: Populum Hebraeum uti dimitteret] ad festum Domino agendum in deserto.
units.tr: "That the Hebrew people might be dismissed": to hold a feast to the Lord in the wilderness.

units.la: Ex virga draconem fecisset] hoc quia Aharon fecit jussu Moysis, Exod. 7. 9. ideo Moses fecisse non male dicitur.
units.tr: "Had made a serpent from the staff": Aaron did this at the command of Moses, Exod. 7:9, so it is not wrongly said that Moses did it.

units.la: Virga] vocatur virga Moysis, Exod. 4. 17. & Aharonis 7. 10. & Dei. Vide Nicolaum de Lyra ad locum, Tolle virgam tuam.
units.tr: "Staff": the staff is called the staff of Moses, Exod. 4:17, of Aaron, 7:10, and of God. See Nicolaus de Lyra on the passage, "Take your staff."

units.la: Aquas omnes] sunt qui censent aliquam aquam integram remansisse, quae postea conversa sit in janguinem a Chaldaeis: alij aliter hac de re opinantur.
units.tr: "All the waters": some think that some water remained untouched, and that it was later turned into blood by the Chaldeans; others hold different views on this matter.

units.la: Totamque terram] universam regionem Aegypti. Sic in sacris terrae nomen de illa debet accipi regione de qua sermo est.
units.tr: "And the whole land": the whole region of Egypt. So in Scripture the name "land" must be understood of the region under discussion.

units.la: Pag. 25. Chaldaeis] id est, magis Aegyptiorum. Maximus episcopus in sermone de Epiphania, Hodie Salvator a Chaldaeis est adoratus. Juvenalis, cum grege Chaldaeo Interpres vetus, cum magis aut mathematicis, Cato de re rustica, haruspicem, augurem, hariolum, Chaldaeum requem habeat. rusticus videlicet: & est sensus, ne habeat astrologum aut mathematicum. Chaldaei enim certe qui ex natalitio fidere futura praesagiunt, quod illa natio siderum observandorum peritissima fuerit. Praecipue autem in ea scientia excellebant Chaldaeorum sacerdotes. Quocirca & Chaldaei vocabantur. Vide quae scripsimus Observat. lib. 8. cap. 12. Hinc dici arbitrantur Ur Chaldaeorum, ut non gentis sit vocabulum, sed artis. Certe alio nomine Camarina dicebatur, in quo significatio Chamarim, id est, sacerdotum. proprie significat sacerdotes Deorum falsorum. Notavi alias.
units.tr: P. 25. "Chaldeans" that is, rather, the Egyptians' magicians. Bishop Maximus, in his sermon on the Epiphany: "Today the Saviour was worshipped by the Chaldeans." Juvenal: "with a Chaldean crowd". The old translator: "with magicians or mathematicians". Cato, On Farming: "a soothsayer, an augur, a diviner, a Chaldean", that is, a rustic, and the sense is that he should not have an astrologer or mathematician. Certainly the Chaldeans are those who foretell the future from a birth chart, because that nation was most skilled in observing the stars. The priests of the Chaldeans excelled especially in this science, and for that reason they too were called Chaldeans. See what I wrote in Observations, book 8, chap. 12. Some think Ur of the Chaldeans is named from this, so that the word denotes a craft rather than a nation. Certainly it was once called Camarina by another name, which signifies Chamarim, that is, priests; properly it means the priests of false gods. I have noted this elsewhere.

units.la: Facientibus similia] de hoc facto magorum videndi sunt Augustinus quaest. 21. & in tertio de trinitate, cap. 7. & 8. & in libro sententiarum 2. 4. Thomas 2. 2. quaest. 17. ar. 2. in corol. quaest. & super Matthaeum, cap. 24. Lippomanus in Catenapatrum, & alij. Magorum autem principes fuerunt Iannes & Mamres, Apostolo nominati 2.Timoth.3.18.quorum Numenius quoque meminit philosophus Pythagoricus. Mentio eorum & in Thalmud, tractatu de oblationibus, cap.9.
units.tr: "Doing the like": on this deed of the magicians, see Augustine, Questions 21, and On the Trinity, book 3, chaps. 7 and 8, and Sentences, book 2, dist. 4; Thomas, 2.2, q. 17, art. 2, in the corollary and on Matthew, chap. 24; Lippomanus, Catena Patrum, and others. The chief magicians were Jannes and Jambres, named by the Apostle in 2 Tim. 3:18, and the Pythagorean philosopher Numenius also mentions them. They are also mentioned in the Talmud, tractate On Offerings, chap. 9.

units.la: Ciniphibus] legitur & scíniphibus, De his Origenes, Hoc animal pennis suspenditur per aera volitans, sed ita subtile & minutum ut oculi visum, nisi ante cernentis, eludat.
units.tr: "Gnats": some read "scinifes". Origen on these: this creature flies through the air suspended on wings, but it is so fine and small that it escapes the eye unless one looks very carefully beforehand.

units.la: Corpus tamen, cum infiderit, acerbissimo terebrat stimu-lo, ut quem volantem videre quis non valet, sentiat stimu-lantem. Quæ verba paullo aliter leguntur apud S. Augustinum, serm.86. Vide Sigonium. Orosius, lib.7. cap.18. Tertia vexatio habuit scinifices (putarim leg. scinifes) muscula scilicet par-vissimas ac sævissimas: quæ mediis sæpe æstibus per loca squalida se coadunando ac vibrando densatæ nonnullo volatu allabi solent, capillisque hominum ac pecudum fetis cum urente morsu interseri Philo Iudæus, ζῷον ἐκ ἀγρίου βεαχύτατον, ἀλλὰ ὁμῶς ἀργαλεώτατον ἐκ γὰρ μόνον λυμαί-νεται τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν κἀσφαλῶς ἐπιδῆς τῶν βλαβερὰ-τὰς, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκ τὰς ἐντὸς βιαίως τῶν ἀμφὶ μυκτῆρας καὶ ὦτα. ἁιστήρ ἢ καὶ κόμας ὀφθαλμῶν ἀσπασάμενοι, ἡ μὴ Φυλάξαντο ὡς. Quidam scribunt cyniphes, & pedicnlos canonos interpretan-tur. Rupertus, Sunt igitur cyniphes muscæ minutissimæ, aculeis permolestæ. Vox Ebrea est פּוּנְחַה quam pediculos red-dunt. Sane a mulierculis Iudæorum pediculus hodieque Chinna vocatur. Quod eo significatu legitur in Nomenclatura Eliæ Le-vitæ Germani. Fagius arbitratur tale genus pediculorum fuisse quale hodie filizleuz vocamus. Belgice plat lups a latitudine. Est autem pediculus inguinalis, ita dictus, quod pubem & in-guina infestet. Sunt quiab Ebrea voce Latinam derivant: quos falli putò. Kniph & oxvip vermiculus est culici similis. Plinio certe culices sunt, qui a Græcis κνῖφες sive σκνῖφες vocantur. Inde ciniphes & scinifes. Ita mihi videtur Lexicon vetus, σκνιφ curculo, ὴ μυιὰγ, ἀκρῖς ἡ κάνναβ.
units.tr: Yet when it has settled on the body, it pierces with a most bitter sting, so that one who cannot see it flying still feels it stinging. These words are read somewhat differently in St Augustine, Sermon 86. See Sigonius. Orosius, book 7, chapter 18: "The third plague had scinifices (I would read scinifes), very tiny and very savage little flies, which often, in the midst of summer, gather in squalid places, and, massed together and buzzing, usually swoop down with a short flight and, with a burning bite, get tangled in people's hair and the bristles of cattle." Philo the Jew: "a creature very small, yet very troublesome [ζῷον ἐκ ἀγρίου βεαχύτατον, ἀλλὰ ὁμῶς ἀργαλεώτατον]; for it not only harms the surface and clings securely to what is hurtful, but also forcibly enters the inner parts around the nostrils and ears [ἐκ γὰρ μόνον λυμαίνεται τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν κἀσφαλῶς ἐπιδῆς τῶν βλαβερά τας, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐκ τὰς ἐντὸς βιαίως τῶν ἀμφὶ μυκτῆρας καὶ ὦτα], and the eyelashes and hair of the eyes, unless they guard against it." Some write cyniphes and render it as lice [pediculos canonos]. Rupert: "So cyniphes are very tiny flies, most troublesome with their stings." The Hebrew word is פּוּנְחַה [punḥah], which they render as lice. Certainly the Jewish women even today call a louse by the name chinna [חִנָּה]; this meaning is found in the Nomenclature of Elias the Levite, a German. Fagius thinks this kind of louse was what we today call the filzlaus, in Belgian "plat lups" from its flatness. It is a pubic louse, so called because it infests the pubic hair and groin. There are those who derive the Latin word from the Hebrew; I think they are mistaken. Kniph and oxvip are a little worm similar to a gnat [culex]. In Pliny they are certainly gnats, which the Greeks call κνῖφες or σκνῖφες. Hence cyniphes and scinifes. So the old lexicon seems to me to have: σκνιφ, a weevil; or a fly; or a gnat [ἡ μυῖα, ἡ ἀκρὶς ἡ κάνναβ].

units.la: Majestate divina ista fieri] Sic interpretatur quod apud Mo-sen, digitus Dei est. Paullo ante dixit, virtutem Dei, eodem sensu: quod magis se probat mihi.
units.tr: "These things were done by divine majesty": so one interprets what in Moses is "the finger of God". A little before he said "the power of God" in the same sense, which to me confirms this more.

units.la: Sed ubi clades exempta est ]id postquam ranas immissas evenisse Scriptura prodidit.
units.tr: "But when the plague was removed": Scripture reports that this happened after the frogs had been sent.

units.la: Impotens suæ animus] non potens animo suo moderari. In se] In se] ad ingenium suum.
units.tr: "Mind unable to control itself": not able to govern its own mind. "In himself": according to his own nature.

units.la: Decem plagis] has decem plagas metro comprehensas invenies apud Iohannem Saresberiensem in Polycratico, lib.8.cap.xi. Prima rubens unda, &c. // // //
units.tr: "Ten plagues": you will find these ten plagues summed up in verse by John of Salisbury in the Policraticus, book 8, chap. 11: "First, the red water," etc.

units.la: Quarum symbolum apud Ebraeos. דָּךְ עֵשׂ בְּאָחְ[?]
units.tr: Whose mnemonic among the Hebrews is [דָּךְ עֵשׂ בְּאָחְ]

units.la: Explicatio hujus Symboli
units.tr: Explanation of this Summary

units.la: Plaga I. דָּם[?], sanguis, in quem aquae omnes conversae. Quidam omnes exponunt pleraque, ut in illo, Omnes gentes habent praeputium. 2. צְפַרְדְּעִים rana. 3. כִּנִּים ciniphes. Hos alij pediculos fuisse tradunt. 4. עָרוֹב Arob, mixtio infectorum. 5. דֶּבֶר Deber, pestilentia, pecorum interitus. 6. שְׁחִין ulcus, pustula. 7. בָּרָד grando mixta horrendis aliis meteoris. 8. אַרְבֶּה locustarum omne genus. 9. חֹשֶׁךְ tenebrae palpabiles et triduanae. 10. בְּכוֹרוֹת primogenita.
units.tr: First plague: דָּם [dam] blood, into which all the waters were turned. Some interpret "all" as "most," as in that text, "All nations have foreskins." 2. צְפַרְדְּעִים [tsefardeim] frogs. 3. כִּנִּים [kinnim] gnats. Others report that these were lice. 4. עָרוֹב [arov] Arob, a mixture of noxious creatures. 5. דֶּבֶר [dever] Deber, pestilence, the death of the cattle. 6. שְׁחִין [shechin] sore, boil. 7. בָּרָד [barad] hail mixed with other terrifying meteors. 8. אַרְבֶּה [arbeh] locusts of every kind. 9. חֹשֶׁךְ [choshekh] darkness that could be felt, lasting three days. 10. בְּכוֹרוֹת [bekhorot] firstborn.

units.la: In precibus Ebraeorum laudatur Rabbi quidam Iuda ut autor hujus symboli. Videndus Orosius lib.1. cap.12.& lib.7 cap.18. ubi has decem plagas comparat cum decem vexationibus Christi-anorum, quas persecutiones vulgo vocant.
units.tr: In the prayers of the Hebrews a certain Rabbi Judah is praised as the author of this list. See Orosius, book 1, chapter 12, and book 7, chapter 18, where he compares these ten plagues with the ten vexations of the Christians, commonly called persecutions.

units.la: Rudis adhuc temporum] erras Severe. Nam prius annum ordiebantur a Thesri, qui ex parte septembri nostro respondet. Accidit ergo tibi, quod aliis multis viris doctis probisque, qui dum res Ebraeorum negligunt, in magnos & graves errores incidunt. Videndus ad hunc locum Iosephus: item Nicolaus de Lyra & alij. Quanquam Paulus Episcopus Burgensis pro hac Sulpicij sententia disputat. Adit.1.ad cap.12. Exod.Vide, si vacas Sunt qui mundum in autumno conditum autumant, quam opinionem sequuntur frequentes Ebrei, etiam Christiani doctiores. Minus audiendi, meo judicio, qui ejus originem referunt ad aequino-ctium vernum. Qua de re dicam alias.
units.tr: Still rude of the times] You are mistaken, Severus. For they formerly began the year from Tishri, which in part corresponds to our September. So it happens to you what has happened to many other learned and upright men, who, while neglecting the affairs of the Hebrews, fall into great and serious errors. Consult Josephus on this passage, likewise Nicholas of Lyra and others. Although Paul, bishop of Burgos, argues for Sulpicius' opinion. See Adit. 1 on Exodus chapter 12, if you have leisure. There are those who hold that the world was created in autumn, an opinion followed by many Hebrews and by the more learned Christians. In my judgment those who trace its origin to the spring equinox are less to be heeded. I shall speak of this matter elsewhere.

units.la: Mensem illum qui tum erat] cum Aegypto egrederentur: qui partim aprili nostro, partim Martio respondet, quem Nisan vocant vocabulo Syriaco an Persico? dicitur etiam mensis novo-rum, rum, Græce νέων[?], hoc est novarum frugum. Stephanus Gobarus apud Photium, cum tamen [illegible, ~12 letters] οἱ Ἐβδομάδοι [?] [illegible, ~10 letters]. Macarius AEgyptius eum appellat mensem florū, [illegible, ~20 letters]: in mense florum educit eas ex AEgypto. Mensis novorum incipien-te veris exordio meminit Hiero. in comment. Hag. 1.
units.tr: That month which was then] when they went out of Egypt. It corresponds partly to our April, partly to March. They call it Nisan, a Syriac or Persian word? It is also called the month of new things, Greek [νέων], that is, of new fruits. Stephanus Gobarus, in Photius... Macarius the Egyptian calls it the month of flowers... in the month of flowers he led them out of Egypt. Jerome, in his commentary on Haggai 1, mentions the month of new things as beginning with the opening of spring.

units.la: Sacrificium autem diei illius] intelligit Pascha: quod Iose-phus quoque sacrificium appellat, Orig. Iud. lib. 3. cap. 40. Sacri-ficium, inquit, quod tunc execuntes fecisse diximus, Pascha nominatum; quotannis instaurare lege jubemur. Cœnam puram vocant Augustinus & Chrysostomus.
units.tr: But the sacrifice of that day] he means the Passover, which Josephus also calls the sacrifice. Origen, Jewish Antiquities book 3, chapter 40: "The sacrifice," he says, "which we said they then performed, is called the Passover; we are commanded by law to renew it every year." Augustine and Chrysostom call it the pure supper.

units.la: In solennitatem consequentium seculorum] usque ad tempus Mesiæ, in quo finem accipiebant omnes cæremoniæ legis. Græce est, Exod. 12.14. [illegible, ~40 letters] & apud interpretem nostrum, celebra-bitis eam in generationibus vestris cultu sempiterno.
units.tr: For the solemnity of the following ages] until the time of the Messiah, at which all the ceremonies of the law came to an end. The Greek is in Exodus 12:14, and in our translator: "you shall celebrate it throughout your generations with a perpetual observance."

units.la: Seculorum] secula dixit, quas Ebraei [illegible, Hebrew] Græci αἰῶνας appellant, Latini autem ætates aut generationes. Alioqui seculum definitur spatium triginta vel centum annorum. Generatio seu ætas hominum est simul orientium & occidentium. Quod spatium vitæ humanæ continet annos 70. aut 80. secundum Davidem.
units.tr: Ages] he says ages, which the Hebrews and the Greeks call aeons, but the Latins call ages or generations. Otherwise an age is defined as a span of thirty or a hundred years. A generation or age of men is at once that of those rising and those falling. This span of human life contains seventy or eighty years, according to David.

units.la: Agnus immaculatus] expressit quod in plerisque codicibus Græcis ἄμωμον. Exod. 12.5. Sic etiam Hiero. agnus absque macula, id est, sine ullo vitio corporis. Quod noto, ne quis existimet hic sermonem esse de maculis, quæ in pelle μῶμος macula. Ebraice [illegible, Hebrew]. Iam est [illegible, Hebrew] in fonte quod reddunt integer, τέλειον.
units.tr: Unblemished lamb] he has expressed what in most Greek copies is ἄμωμον [amomon], Exodus 12:5. So also Jerome: a lamb without spot, that is, without any bodily defect. I note this so that no one thinks the talk here is of spots, which in the skin are μῶμος [momos], blemish. In the Hebrew... In the source they render it as "whole," τέλειον [teleion].

units.la: Agnus] Ibid. [illegible, ~20 letters] Unde Pyra dicit [illegible, Hebrew] etiam hædum significare. Sed hoc negat Paulus Burgensis episcopus.
units.tr: Lamb] Ibid. ... Whence Pyra says the word also means a kid. But Paul, bishop of Burgos, denies this.

units.la: Anniculus] filius anni, ἐνιαῖος. Quidam, filius anni fui. Quod in idem recidit. Quanquam nonnulli discriminent. Abe-zra, Dicit R. Iosua discrimen esse inter filium anni & filium anni sui. Nam de quo dicitur filius anni ei ascendit annus: filius autem anni sui significat id quod sonat. Et ecce in oblatione principum legimus, agnus unus filius anni sui: & post scriptum est, agnus filius anni. Hic agnus sumebatur ex ovibus aut ex capris. Quod in Ebræo, & ex capris: quale quale illud, qui percusserit patre aut matrem, vbi similiter(et) in fonte. In Hiero, iuxta quae ritu tolietis[?] & hoedu[?]. Quae versio[?] errandi causam nonnullis praebuit, ut existimarint una cum agno etiam hoedum immolatum fuisse. Sane haec de re Theodoritus, praecipit non ut utrumque simul immolent, sed ut is qui ovem habeat agnum immolet, qui vero caret ove, immolet hoedum. Memoriae proditum est hunc agnum anniculum usque ad decimum quartum diem, quo mactabatur[?], ad fulcrum sponde alligatum fuisse, ut omnium aspectui pateret, atque ita illis de redemptione sua inter se conferendi occasionem daret. Autor Fagius in notis ad Oncelum.
units.tr: Yearling] son of a year, ἐνιαῖος [eniaios]. Some read "son of my year." Which comes to the same thing, although some distinguish them. Abenezra: Rabbi Joshua says there is a difference between "son of a year" and "son of his year." For of whom it is said "son of a year," the year comes up to him; but "son of his year" means what it sounds like. Indeed in the offering of the princes we read "one lamb, son of his year," and afterwards it is written "lamb, son of a year." This lamb was taken from the sheep or from the goats. What is in the Hebrew, "or from the goats," is like that passage, "whoever strikes father or mother," where likewise in the source. In Jerome, "according to which you shall take..." and "a kid." This version gave some occasion for error, so that they thought a kid was sacrificed along with the lamb. Theodoret, indeed, on this matter instructs that they should not sacrifice both together, but that whoever has a sheep should sacrifice a lamb, and whoever lacks a sheep should sacrifice a kid. It is recorded that this yearling lamb was tied to the leg of the couch until the fourteenth day, when it was slaughtered, so that it lay open to everyone's sight, and thus gave them occasion to confer among themselves about their redemption. The authority is Fagius, in his notes on Onkelos.

units.la: Carnem penitus exedendam] in aliis epulis partes mittebant amicis & pauperibus. Quod hic fieri non poterat. Tota enim cena absumebatur. De carnibus loquor. Nam reliqua comburebantur, ne quid remaneret. Vide Thargum Ionathae, Exod. 12.46.
units.tr: To be eaten up entirely, the flesh] At other feasts they sent portions to friends and the poor, which could not be done here. For the whole supper was consumed. I speak of the flesh, for the rest was burned, so that nothing remained. See the Targum of Jonathan on Exodus 12:46.

units.la: Postes] portae domus, non cubiculi, in quo agnum edebant. Quaersu[?] haec? An ut angelus visio sanguine sciret esse domos Israelitarum, quas transfiliret? Aut potius hoc factum in contumeliam Aegyptiorum, qui arietem pro Deo colebant? prius verius videtur. Nam cum tenebrae essent, sanguis ille videri non poterat ab Aegyptiis, nisi postridie. Theodoretus, notandum quod Deus iussit postes sanguine tingi, ut cum exterminator transfiret ad Aegyptiorum primogenita perdendum, sanguinem super postes aspiciens, Ebraeorum domos illaesas transfiliret. Non quod his natura illa corporis expers indigeret, sed ut illi hoc signo docerentur quanta ergo illos esset Dei cura & providentia. Ceterum illinebatur praeter postes etiam limen superum, quod Graeci ὑπερθύρια[?] καὶ ἀναφλια[?] vocant.
units.tr: Doorposts] the doors of the house, not of the room in which they ate the lamb. Why was this? So that the angel, seeing the blood, would know which houses of the Israelites to pass over? Or rather was it done as an insult to the Egyptians, who worshipped a ram as a god? The former seems the truer. For when there was darkness, that blood could not be seen by the Egyptians until the next day. Theodoret: it is to be noted that God ordered the doorposts to be smeared with blood, so that when the destroyer passed through to slay the Egyptian firstborn, seeing the blood upon the doorposts, he would pass over the undamaged houses of the Hebrews. Not that this bodiless nature needed the sign, but that they might be taught by it how great was God's care and providence for them. Moreover, they smeared not only the doorposts but also the upper lintel, which the Greeks call ὑπερθύρια [hyperthyria] and ἀναφλια [anaphlia].

units.la: Os autem non conferendum] nempe ut eo celerius abire possent. Nam tempus requiritur ad confringenda ossa. Quod fit quum ex illis medullam educimus. Nam tum confringi solent.
units.tr: Nor was a bone to be broken] namely, so that they might leave the more quickly. For time is needed to break bones, which is done when we extract the marrow from them, for then they are usually broken.

units.la: Azymis uterentur] id est, infermentatis panibus, quos ἀζύμους Graeci vocant καὶ τὰ ἄζυμα. Hos edebant cum lactucis agrestibus, si modo מררים[?] sunt lactucae agrestes, quemadmodum Hiero. interpretatur. Cyprianus vocem Graecam retinuit, referens, cum picridibus: etiam Faustus apud Augustinum lib.32. cap.3. nisi quod in eo cum picridiis, tanquam a recto picridia. Vulgo σέγκις[?] exponitur intybum seu cichorium.
units.tr: Should use unleavened bread] that is, bread without leaven, which the Greeks call ἄζυμοι [azymoi] and τὰ ἄζυμα [ta azyma]. They ate these with wild lettuces, if indeed מְרֹרִים [merorim] are wild lettuces, as Jerome translates. Cyprian kept the Greek word, reporting "with picrides." So too Faustus in Augustine, book 32, chapter 3, except that in him it is "with picridia," as if from the nominative picridia. Commonly σέγκις [sengkis] is explained as endive or chicory.

units.la: Sed Gaza πιαρὰς alicubi laßucas agrestes & alibi amaragines transstulit. Plinius lib. 19. cap. 8. ubi de laßucæ generibus, pessimum autem genus cum exprobatione amaritudinis appella vere picrida. Sed est qui negat laßucas amaras esse, Hieronymum reprehendens: frustra. Nam sylvestrem lastucam habere folia amara, homines rei herbariæ periti prodiderunt. Qua de re fuse diximus in notis magnis ad Exodum.
units.tr: But Gaza translated πικράς [pikras] in some places as wild lettuces and elsewhere as bitter herbs. Pliny, book 19, chapter 8, where, on the kinds of lettuce, he calls the worst kind, with a reproach of bitterness, truly picris. But there is one who denies that lettuces are bitter, rebuking Jerome: in vain. For men skilled in herb lore have reported that wild lettuce has bitter leaves. On this matter we have spoken at length in the larger notes on Exodus.

units.la: Pag. 24. Suis copiis] id est, facultatibus. Sic Cicero, copiis locuples.
units.tr: Page 24. With their goods] that is, with their resources. So Cicero: rich in goods.

units.la: AEgyptispoliis] Exod. 3.22. & spoliabitis AEgyptios. Quod Græce redditum in ed. Rom. καὶ ἐκνλίνσατε. Rursum, Exod. 12.36. καὶ ἐσκύλευσαν τὰς Αἰγυπτίους.
units.tr: Spoil the Egyptians] Exodus 3:22, "and you shall spoil the Egyptians." Which in the Roman edition is rendered in Greek as καὶ ἐκνλίνσατε [kai ekdylinsate]. Again, Exodus 12:36, καὶ ἐσκύλευσαν τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους [kai eskyleusan tous Aigyptious].

units.la: Ex quinque & septuaginta] secutus est Græcos, qui ad numerum, qui in codicibus Ebræis, quinque addiderunt. Quod studione ab iis factum sit, an errore, nondum mihi compertum. Hoc scio in alio loco quodam illius editionis legi septuaginta tantum. Quod suspicionem de mendo non minuit, sed auget potius, cum sint qui τῶν τι factum putent ex ἀάντις, leviçula immutatione. Sane eadem vox superat in Iosepho, ubi Isabacum decessisse ait natum annos centum octoginta quinque.
units.tr: Of five and seventy] He followed the Greeks, who added five to the number found in the Hebrew codices. Whether they did this deliberately or by error is not yet clear to me. This I know: in another place of that edition I read only seventy. Which does not lessen the suspicion of a fault but rather increases it, since there are those who think τῶν τι [ton ti] arose from ἀάντις [aantis] by a slight alteration. Indeed the same word occurs in Josephus, where he says that Isaac died at the age of one hundred and eighty-five.

units.la: AEgyptum descenderant] pag. xix. in AEgyptum descendit, addita præpositione, quæ hic desiderari videtur, ut supra, mox annonæ inopia AEgyptum concessit.
units.tr: They had gone down into Egypt] Page 19 has "went down into Egypt," with the preposition added here, which seems to be needed, as above: "soon, because of a shortage of food, he withdrew into Egypt."

units.la: Ad millia virorum sexcenta] LXX. εἰς ἑξακοσίας χιλιάδας: quod a Hieronymo versum, sexcenta fere millia. Sed alius elegit, ad sexcenta millia: in quo sermone (ad) valet circiter. In Ebræo est Chaph, qua littera utuntur pro circiter siye ferme, id est, μικρὸν δέ. & cum aliquid ita affirmant ut de eo dubitari non possit. Vocant Chaph ὠλλᾶθ, cujusmodi forte hoc loco.
units.tr: Six hundred thousand men] The Septuagint has εἰς ἑξακοσίας χιλιάδας [eis hexakosias chiliadas]. Jerome translated this as about six hundred thousand. Another translator chose "to six hundred thousand," where the word "to" carries the sense of "about." In Hebrew there is Chaph, a letter they use for "about" or "nearly," that is, μικρὸν δέ [mikron de]. They also use it when they affirm something so that it cannot be doubted. They call Chaph ὠλλᾶθ [ōllath], and it may be of that kind here.

units.la: Virorum] peditum, præter imbellem turbam & vulgus promiscuum innumerabile. Quæri potest an tam brevi tempore, quo fuerunt in AEgypto, in tantam multitudinem excrescere potuerint? Qua de re vide sodes Augustinum, quæst. 43. sed imprimis chronologiam Temporarij, lib. 2. pag. 141. ubi schema propagationis Iacobæorum in AEgypto. Vide quoque quæ notavimus ad pag. 20.
units.tr: Men] that is, foot soldiers, apart from the unwarlike crowd and the countless mixed common people. One may ask whether they could have grown into so great a multitude in the short time they were in Egypt. On this question please see Augustine, Questions, 43, but above all the chronology of Temporarius, book 2, page 141, where there is a scheme of the propagation of the Jacobites in Egypt. See also what we noted on page 20.

units.la: Quo primum Abraham terram Chananæorum accesserat] imo, quo primum egressus est Vre Chaldæorum. Egressus autem est tem est anno ætatis LXX. Venit in Chananæa quinquennio post. hoc est anno ætatis LXXV. Nam quinque annis hæsit in itinere, videlicet apud Carras opidum Syriæ interamnis. Quinto & vigesimo anno post natum ei fuit Ijahac : a quo tempore computari debent anni quadringenti, de quibus pag ix. & alibi.
units.tr: Where Abraham first came into the land of the Canaanites] Indeed, where he first set out from Ur of the Chaldeans. He set out in his seventieth year. He came into Canaan five years later, that is, in his seventy-fifth year. For he stayed for five years on the journey, namely at Haran, a town of Syria between the rivers. In his twenty-fifth year after the birth of Ishmael, from which time the four hundred years should be counted, on which see page 9 and elsewhere.

units.la: Tricesimo & quadringentesimo[?] hic numerus habetur, Exod.12.40. et in Epiphanij Ancorato, & in quadam pervetusta editione, Atto. 7. 6. Proinde apud Lactantium Firmianum, lib. 4. cap. 10 ubi vulgo post annos trecentos triginta, legendum aio, post annos quadringentos triginta. Sane quidem erravit Lactantius, si aliter scripsit.
units.tr: This number, four hundred and thirty, is given in Exodus 12:40, in Epiphanius's Ancoratus, and in a very old edition, and in Acts 7:6. Therefore in Lactantius Firmianus, book 4, chapter 10, where the common reading is "after three hundred and thirty years," I say it should be read "after four hundred and thirty years." Certainly Lactantius erred, if he wrote otherwise.

units.la: A diluvio autem mille quingentis quinque & septuaginta] hic numerus concipitur & subducitur hac ratione. A diluvio ad ortum Abrahæ anni sunt 1070. pag. 8. Ab ortu Abrahæ usque ad ingressum in terram Chanaan 75, Gen 12.4. Inde ad egressum ex Ægypto anni 430. pag. 14. 1070 75 430 • Summa 1575. •
units.tr: From the Flood, however, to the year 1575 — this number is reached and calculated in this way. From the Flood to the birth of Abraham there are 1070 years (page 8). From the birth of Abraham to the entry into the land of Canaan, 75 years (Genesis 12:4). From there to the exodus from Egypt, 430 years (page 14). 1070 + 75 + 430 = total 1575.

units.la: Columna nubis interdiu] magis ut viam demonstraret, quam ut umbram præberet adversus æstum. Nam non tegebat castra Israelitarum, sed præcedebat ea. Noctu autem præferebatur præluccendi causa. Scire licet in deserto Arabiæ nulla vestigia hominum apparere, unde nec viæ ullæ. Ideo gnomone utun-tur qui per illa loca iter faciunt, perinde ut qui in mari navigant. Quod alias probabo, si Deus voluerit.
units.tr: The pillar of cloud by day] more to show the way than to give shade against the heat. For it did not cover the camp of the Israelites but went before it. At night, however, it was carried in front to give light. It should be known that in the desert of Arabia no traces of men appear, and so there are no roads. For this reason those who travel through those regions use a gnomon, just as those who sail on the sea. I shall prove this elsewhere, God willing.

units.la: Sinum maris rubri] qui Arabicus dicitur & oceanum influit maris Indici. Hoc mare duos sinus habet: quorum alter, videlicet is, qui ab oriente est, Persicus vocatur. Plinius lib. 6 cap. 23. Cur autem rubrum dicatur docet Brodæus Miscel lib. 3. cap. 9. Ebræi vocant mare Suph, id est, algosum aut caricosum.
units.tr: The gulf of the Red Sea] which is called the Arabian gulf and flows into the ocean of the Indian Sea. This sea has two gulfs: of which one, namely the one that lies to the east, is called the Persian. Pliny, book 6, chapter 23. Why it is called red, Brodaeus teaches in Miscellanies, book 3, chapter 9. The Hebrews call the sea Suph, that is, weedy or reedy.

units.la: Præter terram Philistim] ita locutus est, pag. 15. cum præter terram Edom iter destinaret. Terram autem Philisthim appellat regiunculam Philisthæorum, quæ Palestina vocatur, nomine strictius accepto, Ebraice פלשתים[?] olim a Chaphthoræis habitata.
units.tr: Beyond the land of the Philistines] He spoke in this way on page 15, when he intended to go by way of the land of Edom. He calls the land of the Philistines the little region of the Philistines, which is called Palestine, the name being taken in a narrower sense. In Hebrew it is פלשתים [Pelishtim], once inhabited by the Caphtorites.

units.la: Philistim] rectius, Philisthim, cum T, aspirato. Nam est Thau in scriptura Ebraica. Legitur & Philisthijm. Græci Allophylos vocant, nomine generis, ad certam speciem restrictio.
units.tr: Philistim] more correctly Philisthim, with an aspirated T. For in the Hebrew text there is Thau. It is also read Philisthijm. The Greeks call them Allophyloi, by a general name, restricted to a particular kind.

units.la: Eremum aspernantibus] nempe propter rerum omnium penuriam. Poterant etiam bellum aspernari, quod eis impedebat a Philisthæis, si per eorum regionem iter fecissent. Iosephus Orig. lib.2.cap.6. Duxit eos per mare rubrum, ne Palæstini, quos ob veterem simultatem infensos habebant, de hac professione certiores fieri possent. Vide sis, Exod.13.
units.tr: The desert, which they dreaded] namely because of the great scarcity of everything. They could also have dreaded war, which the Philistines would have caused if they had travelled through their region. Josephus, Antiquities, book 2, chapter 6: "He led them through the Red Sea, so that the Palestinians, whom they had reason to regard as hostile because of an old quarrel, could not be informed of this plan." Please see Exodus 13.

units.la: Ibi] ante Beelsephon. Exod.14. 2.
units.tr: There] before Baal-zephon. Exodus 14:2.

units.la: Nutu Dei] voluntate, imo iussu Dei.
units.tr: By the nod of God] that is, by the will of God, indeed by the command of God.

units.la: Exercitum] currnum sexcentorum (700. Iosephus) Exod.14. 7. equitum 50000. & peditum scutatorum 200000.
units.tr: The army] of six hundred chariots (700 according to Josephus), Exodus 14:7; of horsemen 50,000, and of shield-bearing foot soldiers 200,000.

units.la: Pag.25. Mare diuidit] in scissiones, ut quidam volunt, duodecim: ut alij, duas tantum: quarum una in latum, altera in longum fata. Psal.136.13. Qui scindit mare Suph in scissiones. Vide Davidem Camium ad hunc ultimum locum, & Nicolaum a Lyra, Exod.14.22.
units.tr: Page 25. The sea divided] into, as some want, twelve parts; as others, only two, one of which was cut lengthwise and the other across. Psalm 136:13: "who divided the Red Sea into parts." See David Kimchi on this last passage, and Nicholas of Lyra on Exodus 14:22.

units.la: Iter pervium fuit] per medium mare siccis pedibus transfe-untes egressi sunt, ut Iosephus ait, in adversum littus; ut alij putant, in idem littus. Siquidem Num. 33.7. ingressi leguntur mare ad fauces Hahiroth, quæ in solitudine Etham. Ibid. vers.8. egressi dicuntur e mari in solitudinem, & ambulasse tribus diebus per desertum Etham. Qua de re consule Lyram, Exod.14. & imprimis Burgensem in additionibus.
units.tr: The way was passable] Passing through the middle of the sea on dry feet, they came out, as Josephus says, onto the opposite shore; as others think, onto the same shore. For Numbers 33:7 reads that they went into the sea at the mouth of Hahiroth, which is in the wilderness of Etham. In the same passage, verse 8, they are said to have come out of the sea into the wilderness, and to have walked three days through the desert of Etham. On this matter consult Lyra on Exodus 14, and above all Burgensis in his additions.

units.la: Cum omni exercitu deletus est] Oforius lib.1. cap.12. Extant etiam nunc certissima horum monumenta gestorum. Nam tractus currumque rotarum orbitæ non solum in litore, sed etiam in profundo, quousque visus admittitur, peruidentur, &c. Cum exercitu etiam rex ipse periit. Fallit ergo nos Manetho Egyptius scribens Themosin regem post expulsos pastores (ita vocabant olim Ebræos) regnasse annis viginti & mensibus quatuor, ut refert Iosephus adversus Appionem, lib.1.
units.tr: Destroyed with his whole army] Osorius, book 1, chapter 12. Even now there are most certain monuments of these events. For the tracks and the ruts of the wheels can be seen not only on the shore but also in the deep, as far as the eye can reach, etc. The king himself perished with his army. Manetho the Egyptian therefore misleads us when he writes that King Thymosis, after the shepherds (as the Hebrews were once called) were driven out, reigned for twenty years and four months, as Josephus reports in Against Apion, book 1.

units.la: Virtuteque exultans] cuius quæso? hostiumne an suorum. Atqui hic nulla Israelitarum virtus: multo minus hostium, qui ad unum omnes in mari perierant. Quidam emendant, virtuteque Dei. Quid si, exitio hostium interituque exultans?
units.tr: Rejoicing in his strength] whose, I ask: that of the enemies or of his own people? Yet here there is no strength of the Israelites, much less of the enemies, who had all perished in the sea to a man. Some emend it to "strength of God." What if it was "rejoicing in the destruction and death of the enemies"?

units.la: Sed ingressus est emum] assentior Sigonio legenti, sed ingressos. Nam populus subaudiri non potest, cum sequatur urgebat. Dixisset enim certe, sed ingressum. Agerent] egissent malim. Nam tridui iter confecerant, cum aquæ penuria laborarent.
units.tr: But he entered the sea] I agree with Sigonius, who reads "but they entered." For "the people" cannot be understood, since "pressed on" follows. He would certainly have said "but he entered," yet I would prefer "had completed" to "had driven." For they had completed a three-day journey while suffering from lack of water.

units.la: Viui non erat] bibere eam non poterant ob amaritudinem: ex quo etiam locus ille Mara dictus est.
units.tr: The water was not drinkable] they could not drink it because of its bitterness; from this too that place was called Marah.

units.la: Ac tum primum, &c.] imo antea contumaces fuerant. Vide Sigonium.
units.tr: And then for the first time, etc.] Indeed they had been stubborn before. See Sigonius.

units.la: Lignum aquis intulit] Sirach 38. 5. nonne a ligno dulcuit aqua, ut cognoscei etur virtus ejus ab homine? Ex his verbis apparet ea vi praeditum fuisse hoc lignum ut aquam ex amara dulcem redderet. Nam agit ibi de proprietatibus naturalibus eorum quae e terra nascuntur. Iosephus autor fuisse frustum ligni casu ibi repertum, quod medium per ejus longitudinem scissum in aquam immisit Moses, qui etiam jusserit robustissimum quemque certatim puteum exhaurire, dicens, majore parte evacuata reliquum potabile fore, Orig. Iud. lib. 3. cap. 1. In historia ecclesiastica relatum, de sententia quorundam Ebraeorum, lignum hoc fuisse gustu amarissimum. Autor libri qui Mechiltha vocatur sol. 1 §. col. 2. R. Iohue dicit esse lignum Ialitis: R. Eliezer Modeita lignum oleae, quo nihil amarius: R. Iosua filius Corcha lignum Harduphne sive Hardiphne. Ionathan ei firmando esse potest, qui hoc loco edidit, arborem amaram Ardiphne. A quo non dissentit autor Ierosolymitanae referens, indicavit ei Deus arborem Ardiphne. Quid Ardiphne? In scriptura variante est Hardiphne cum aspiratione. Lexicon Chaldaicum Eliae, Arbor est quae flores profert similes liliis, & sunt illi flores amari valde. Moses Gerundensis annotat scribens lignum hoc natura, hoc est vi ac proprietate sua, fecisse aquam dulcem ex amara. Quod probat ex significatione verbi [illegible, ~3 letters] docuit. Nam non legitur, inquit, nisi in sensu [illegible, ~3 letters] doctrinae. Idem admonet de doctoribus, qui afferant lignum amarum fuisse. In Thanchuma sive Ilmedennu, Mos Dei benedicti ut dulce reddat amarum per id quod amarum est. Tolle amaritudinem & lege, ut dulce reddat quod amarum est, per id quod amarum est. His adde quod in Medras Mechiltha loco superius allegato, col. 3. R. Nathan dicit esse lignum cedri. Sunt qui dicant esse radicem ficus & radicem malogranati. Eadem habentur in Ilmed 30.1. Meminit & Alb. fer. 4 cap. 41.
units.tr: The wood put into the water] Sirach 38:5: "Was not the water made sweet by wood, so that its power might be known by men?" From these words it appears that this wood had the power of making sweet water out of bitter. For there it is speaking of the natural properties of things that grow from the earth. Josephus, the author, says that a piece of wood was found there by chance, which Moses put into the water after splitting it through the middle along its length. He also ordered the strongest of them to draw out the well vigorously, saying that when most of it was emptied the rest would be drinkable (Antiquities of the Jews, book 3, chapter 1). In the ecclesiastical history it is related, according to the opinion of some Hebrews, that this wood was extremely bitter in taste. The author of the book called Mechilta, section 1, column 2: Rabbi Johanan says it is the wood of Yalit; Rabbi Eliezer of Modeita the wood of the olive, than which nothing is more bitter; Rabbi Joshua son of Korcha the wood of Harduphne or Hardiphne. Jonathan, who published the paraphrase here, can be cited in support, since he calls it the bitter tree Ardiphne. The author of the Jerusalem Targum does not disagree with him, writing that God showed him the tree Ardiphne. What is Ardiphne? In the variant text it is Hardiphne, with an aspiration. The Chaldee lexicon of Elias: "a tree which bears flowers like lilies, and those flowers are very bitter." Moses of Gerona notes, writing that this wood, by its nature, that is, by its power and property, made the water sweet out of bitter. He proves this from the meaning of the verb [illegible, about three letters] "taught." For it is found, he says, only in the sense of teaching. He warns the same about the teachers who say the wood was bitter. In Tanchuma, or Ilmedennu: the way of the blessed God was to make the bitter sweet through what is bitter. Remove the bitterness and read: that he made sweet what was bitter, through what is bitter. To these add that in Mechilta, in the passage cited above, column 3, Rabbi Nathan says it is cedar wood. Some say it is the root of a fig tree and the root of a pomegranate. The same things are found in Ilmed 30.1. Albo also mentions it, sermon 4, chapter 41.

units.la: Cujus haec vis fuit] id est, natura, facultas. Augustinus, Genus ligni erat istam habens vim. ex glossa ordinaria.
