Videtur hoc lignum naturali vi ac facultate aquas fecisse dulces, vel secernendo adustas terrae partes quarum admixtione fit aquæ sapor; vel certe attrahendo & alliciendo ad sese imbibendoque amaras aquæ partes, si modo credimus Ebræis dicentibus fuisse lignum amarum, ut jam nunc probatum est. Adite[?] fis ad Franciscum Vallesium de sacra philosophia, cap. 15.
units.tr: "Of this was its power": that is, its nature and capacity. Augustine: "It was a kind of wood having this power," from the Glossa ordinaria. It seems that this wood, by its natural power and capacity, made the waters sweet, either by separating out the scorched parts of the earth whose mixture gives water its taste, or certainly by drawing in and attracting the bitter parts of the water and soaking them up, if we believe the Hebrews who say the wood was bitter, as has already been shown. Consult Francisco Vallesio, On Sacred Philosophy, ch. 15.

units.la: Apud Elim] mansio sexta, cuius meminit Eusebius de locis per hæc verba, Elim castra filiorum Israel, & locus in deserto, in quo duodecim fontes, & septuaginta palmarum arbores Moyses de mari rubro exiens repperit. Ceterum arbores illæ non admodum erant procerae propter loci ariditatem. Nam ne a fontibus quidem rigabantur. Neque multum fructus ferebant propter eandem aquarum inopiam. Iosephus Orig. lib. 3. cap. 7.
units.tr: "At Elim": the sixth station, which Eusebius mentions in his work On Places in these words: "Elim, the camp of the children of Israel, and a place in the desert, where Moses, coming out of the Red Sea, found twelve springs and seventy palm trees." Those trees were not very tall, because of the dryness of the place. For they were not even watered by the springs, and they bore little fruit on account of the same lack of water. Josephus, Antiquities, book 3, ch. 7.

units.la: 12. Fontibus aquarum] fontes illi non ita largi erant ut emissis rivulis humiditatem terra submini-strarent. Quare ad egerendas arenas versi sunt, &c. Vide Iosephum.
units.tr: "12. Springs of water": those springs were not so abundant as to supply moisture to the land by sending out streams. So they were reduced to digging out the sand, etc. See Josephus.

units.la: Aquarum] dulcium. Nam ut Ebræi annotant, palmæ non crescunt nisi secus aquam dulcem.
units.tr: "Of waters": sweet waters. For, as the Hebrews note, palm trees do not grow except beside sweet water.

units.la: Arboribus palmarum] prius legebatur arborum palmarum, in quo manifestius a manu, ut reor, aberrantis librarii fo-lacissimus. Arbores palmarum genus est loquendi, ut herba Lapathi, urbs Romæ, flumen Euphratis. Sic arbor palmæ. Hæ arbores, inquit Sulpicius, tantum in eremo, licet raro habentur. Vide sodes ejus dialogos, pag. 157. Strabo lib. 16. Pomponius continuum esse palmetum quoddam aquis abundans, & in magno honore haberi, propterea quod circumstans regio æstuosa sit & arida & umbrarum expers. Ibi, ut ait Artemidorus, mirum in modum sunt feraces palmæ.
units.tr: "Palm trees": previously it was read "trees of palms," an error, I think, made by a copyist who had strayed, and it is most easily corrected. "Palm trees" is a way of speaking, like "the herb lapathum," "the city of Rome," "the river Euphrates." So "the palm tree." Sulpicius says these trees are found only in the desert, though rarely. See his dialogues, p. 157. Strabo, book 16. Pomponius says there is a continuous grove of palms, abundant in water, held in great honour, because the surrounding region is hot, arid and without shade. There, as Artemidorus says, the palms are wonderfully fruitful.

units.la: Rursum populus famen conquerens] hoc accidit non in Elim, sed cum inde profecti venissent in desertum Sin, positum inter Elim & Sinai, Exod. 16. Eo pervenerunt decimoquinto die mensis secundi, ex quo Ægyptum reliquerant. Porro noster videtur Iosephum secutus, qui eodem modo hanc historiam narrat.
units.tr: "Again the people, complaining of hunger": this happened not at Elim, but when they had set out from there and come into the desert of Sin, which lies between Elim and Sinai (Exod. 16). They arrived there on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had left Egypt. Our author seems to have followed Josephus, who tells this story in the same way.

units.la: Grex cotarnicum] ὀρτυγάς[?], Iosephus, hoc est magna vis aut multitudo coturnicum. Locus est lib. 3. cap. 1, quem sic Latinum fecit Gelenius, Nec ita multo post magna vis coturnicum, quod genus avium præ ceteris Arabicus sinus alit, superato interjacente mari longo volatu sellarum[?], qui alioquin etiam non est sublimis, in Ebraeos defertur. Dio-dorus lib.1 de incolis Rhinocorura : [?]Greek text, not reliably readable: ταῦτα δὲ παρὰ τὴν ἀγγι-[?] ἀλλ' ἐπὶ πολλοὺς ταδ' οὐς[?] ἱστὶς τὰς θηρεύτας[?] ὀρτυγοῦ[?] ἔχοι αὐτὸ(φιλοῦντας γὰρ αὐτοὶ καὶ ἀγίλας μεζόνες[?]) ἐκ τῶν πελάγους[?] ἀνθρώποις ἀγὸς ἱκάνει ἐς ἁπλῶς αὐτοῖς.
units.tr: "A flock of quails": Josephus (the Greek word is possibly ortygas), that is, a great multitude or abundance of quails. The passage is in book 3, ch. 1, which Gelenius thus rendered into Latin: "Not long after, a great multitude of quails, a kind of bird which the Arabian gulf feeds more than others, crossed the intervening sea in a long flight and was carried down upon the Hebrews." Diodorus, book 1, on the inhabitants of Rhinocorura: the birds are caught on the shore, and ... men are brought to them from the sea ... (The Greek text of this quotation is too corrupt in the scan to be reliably rendered.)

units.la: Non est omittendum in Græcis voluminibus haberi ἱερογυοῦντρα quod Augustinus diversum quid esse dicit a coturnice. In Thesauro linguæ Græcæ ὀρτυγομήτρα exponitur coturnicum matrix. Hefychius interpretatur ὀρτυξ ὑπὸ μετίου[?] Plinius lib.10 cap. 23. Aura vehi volunt (corturnices migrantes); ropter pondus corporum, vireíque parvas. Aquilone ergo maxime volant, ortygometra duce. Vide Ariftotelem in historia animalium lib.8 cap.12.
units.tr: It must not be omitted that in the Greek books there is a word ortygometra, which Augustine says is something different from the quail. In the Thesaurus of the Greek language ortygometra is explained as "the mother of the quails." Hesychius interprets it as a bird. Pliny, book 10, ch. 23: "They want the quails to be carried on the wind when migrating, because of the weight of their bodies and their small strength. So they fly especially with the north wind, with the ortygometra as leader." See Aristotle, History of Animals, book 8, ch. 12.

units.la: Postero autem die, &c.] hæc paullo aliter Iofephus. Narrat enim, cum Moses precabundus pálmas attolleret, rorem e cœlo delapsum fuisse, qui manibus ipsius hærens concreverit, quemque degustaverit, suspicatus a Deo in alimoniam dimissum, &c.
units.tr: "Now on the next day, etc.": Josephus tells this a little differently. For he relates that when Moses, praying, lifted up his hands, a dew fell from heaven, which clung to his hands and hardened, and that he tasted it, suspecting that it had been sent down by God as food, etc.

units.la: Parvis quibusdam siliquis] manna tegebatur duplici rore, ut communiter tenent Ebræi. Hunc rorem siliquas appellat, Nam siliqua follicalus est seu integumentum, quo vestiuntur legumina, λοβὸς, κωμνυς, ἰδὲν. id est theca. Dicitur & concha, valvulus. Vide Lexicon Latino Græcum.
units.tr: "Certain small pods": the manna was covered with a double dew, as the Hebrews commonly hold. He calls this dew "pods," for a pod is a husk or covering in which pulses are enclosed, a husk, a shell, a case, that is, a sheath. It is also called a shell or a little valve. See the Latin-Greek lexicon.

units.la: Quarum species in modum coriandri feminis] fumus in oculis meis hæc verba. Nam fi per speciem aspectum intelligas, fallum videtur. Aspectus enim ad similitudinem bdellii accedebat, non feminis coriandri, cui simile erat manna quantitate duntaxat, hoc est magnitudine. Sic dico, femen coriandri nigrum est. Non ergo colore referebat hoc femen, sed figura (nam figuram habebat rotundam) item quantitate, ut dictum est. Sapor autem erat, qualis placentarum ex melle, five crufculi melliti. R. Salomo, Semen coriandri rotundum est, non album. Manna autem erat album; neque assimilatur feminis coriandri, nisi quatenus rotundum est. Nicolaus de Lyra, Quale femen coriandri, quantum ad quantitatem & figuram, non quantum ad colorem: unde subditur album (Exod. 16,31.) femen autem coriandri nigrum est. Aliter alij, & in his R. Levi.
units.tr: "Whose appearance was like coriander seed": this is smoke in my eyes, these words. For if by "appearance" you understand the look, it seems false. For the look of the manna was like bdellium, not like coriander seed, to which it was similar only in size, that is, in magnitude. Thus I say: coriander seed is black. So this seed did not resemble it in colour, but in shape (for the manna was round) and also in size, as has been said. Its taste, however, was like that of cakes made with honey, or of a honeyed wafer. Rabbi Solomon: coriander seed is round, not white. But the manna was white; nor is it compared to coriander seed except insofar as it is round. Nicholas of Lyra: "like coriander seed, as to size and shape, not as to colour: whence it is added 'white' (Exod. 16:31), whereas coriander seed is black." Others explain it otherwise, and among them Rabbi Levi.

units.la: In modum coriandri feminis] [?]Greek: ὡς σπέρμα κοριάνδρου, ut femen coriandri. Sequitur autem [?]Hebrew/Greek word, not reliably readable. Vide suspicor Sulpicium in ea. opinione fuisse ut exiftimarit hoc femen album fuisse. Quod de Gad vocabulo Ebraico asserit R. Levi. Vt ut fit, pro Graeca interpretatione faciunt interpretes Chaldaei duo Ionathan & Ierosolymitanus. Nam יָבֹל est coriandrum, quod Arabes יָבֹל vocant, teste Abenezra. In glossis Arabicis reperio Kusbor & Kasbara, & Kusbara & Kusibara. Adito sis ad notas magnas in Exodum.
units.tr: "In the likeness of coriander seed": [the Greek] "as coriander seed." What follows is a Hebrew word that is not reliably legible. I suspect Sulpicius was of the opinion that this seed was white. What Rabbi Levi asserts of the Hebrew word gad is so. However that may be, the Chaldee interpreters, Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum, follow the Greek rendering. For the word meaning coriander is what the Arabs call kusbara, as Abenezra testifies. In Arabic glosses I find Kusbor and Kasbara, and Kusbara and Kusibara. Consult the great notes on Exodus.

units.la: Glaciali albedine erat] ἀσυνὴν ὡσεὶ πάχνη ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, Exod. 16.14. pro quo in scholio πάχνη, id est, pruina. Quomodo ex Hebraeo interpretantur, sicut pruinam super terram, sive, ut vulgatus interpres habet, in similitudinem pruinae super terram. Quod nosler expressit his verbis, ut crebro hybernis mensibus superductis pruinis tegi terram videmus.
units.tr: "Was of the whiteness of ice": "as hoarfrost upon the earth" (Exod. 16:14), for which the scholium has "hoarfrost," that is, rime. This is how they translate it from the Hebrew, "as hoarfrost upon the ground," or, as the Vulgate translator has it, "in the likeness of hoarfrost upon the earth." Our version expresses this in the words "as we often see the earth covered with frost laid over it in the winter months."

units.la: Munere missum Dei] a Deo datum ad vitam sustentandam in deserto. Hinc quidam acceperunt etymon re Man. Nam מָן portio, donum, munus. Vide Quaestiones meas.
units.tr: "Sent as a gift of God": given by God to sustain life in the desert. Hence some have derived the etymology of the word manna from it. For man [מָן] means a portion, a gift, a present. See my Questions.

units.la: Tantum usurpare debere, &c.] ex aequo affaronis menstruam colligebant, nec licebat plus colligere. Hoc eo factum ne infirmioribus deesset, dum robustiores per avaritiam plus satis colligunt. Iosephus.
units.tr: "They were to gather only so much, etc.": they gathered a measure for each month, equal for all, and it was not permitted to gather more. This was done so that the weaker should not go short, while the stronger, through greed, gathered more than enough. Josephus.

units.la: Pro numero] videlicet gomor in singula capita, inita ratione numeri eorum qui erant in cujusque contubernio. Gomor autem continet decimam partem Ephi, ut habetur, Exod. 16. 36. Id sonat Aaron apud Iosephum, si modo vocabulum Ebraicum est עֶשֶׂר, in quo significatio numeri denarii. Decem enim sive עֶשֶׂר dicunt.
units.tr: "According to the number": namely, a gomer for each head, reckoned by the number of those in each tent. The gomer holds a tenth part of an ephah, as is stated in Exodus 16:36. Josephus's Aaron says this, if the Hebrew word is [עֶשֶׂר], in which there is the meaning of the number ten. For they say "ten" or [עֶשֶׂר].

units.la: Sexto tamen die] pridie sabbathi, qui nobis est dies Veneris & feria sexta. Atque hinc adagium, Qui colligit vespera sabbathi, vescetur in sabbatho. Vide Proverbia mea.
units.tr: "On the sixth day, however": the day before the sabbath, which for us is Friday, the sixth day of the week. Hence the proverb, "He who gathers on the evening of the sabbath will eat on the sabbath." See my Proverbs.

units.la: Quia sabbatho colligi non licebat: hinc licet perspicere sabbathi requiem observatam fuisse ante legem. Sunt qui ejus initium ad exordium originemque mundi referunt.
units.tr: "Because it was not permitted to gather on the sabbath": hence one may see that the rest of the sabbath was observed before the law. Some refer its beginning to the origin and beginning of the world.

units.la: Sabbatum] est cur malim Sabbathum, cum T aspirato. Nihil tamen mutavi, quia in Graecis voluminibus σάββατον, quod nunc secutus mihi videtur.
units.tr: "Sabbath": there is reason to prefer "Sabbathum," with an aspirated T. I have nonetheless changed nothing, because in the Greek books it is sabbaton, which now seems to me to have been followed.

units.la: Integra] neque foetebant, neque in iis vermes erant.
units.tr: "Whole": neither did they stink, nor were there worms in them.

units.la: Per XL. annos] Exod. 16. 35. Deficiebat primum cum Iordanem transfiffent, post celebratum Pascha in Galgalis. Tunc enim ceperunt vesci frugibus terrae Chanaan, Iof. 5. 11. Hujus cibi ea natura erat, ut qui eum haberet alium non desideraret, inquit Iosephus.
units.tr: "For forty years": Exodus 16:35. It ceased first when they had crossed the Jordan, after the Passover had been celebrated at Gilgal. For then they began to eat the fruits of the land of Canaan (Joshua 5:11). Josephus says the nature of this food was such that whoever had it did not desire another.

units.la: Cujus sapor melli proximus] sapor erat qualis crustuli ex melle, ut supra diximus. Igitur suavitate ad mellis dulcedinem proxime accedebat.
units.tr: "Whose taste was closest to honey": the taste was like a cake made with honey, as we said above. So in sweetness it came nearest to the sweetness of honey.

units.la: Nomen manna traditur] nam cum illud primum viderent, dicebant Man-hu. id valet antiqua declaratione, quid hoc est? Sed e recentioribus alij denum sive munus interpretantur, id est, manna: alij deducunt a verbo menna praeparo, quasi panem a Deo praeparatum dicas. Adhibe Quaestiones meas.
units.tr: The name manna is handed down] For when they first saw it, they said Man-hu. In the old explanation this means "What is this?" Some of the more recent writers interpret it as "gift" or "portion," that is, manna; others derive it from the verb menna, "to prepare," as if you were to call it bread prepared by God. Consult my Quaestiones.

units.la: Gomor plenum] quantum gomor caperet. Est autem Gomor sive Omer (nam Ebraice [illegible, ~3 letters]) genus mensurae decimam partem Ephi capiens, quod & Ιfaron dicitur: unde ἀσκαρτὸν Iosephi, cujus antea mentionem fecimus, pro quo Rufinus aſtarium edidit. Glossarium Philonis, Gomor mensura est Atticorum choenicum trium. Hieronymus, Gomor tres choenicas Atticaſ continet. Iosephus autor τρὶς ἡμιχοτύλους tres semicotylſ continere. Vide Theodoreti Quaest. in Exod. quaest. 20 Nicolaum Brabantinum, Exod. 16. Augustinum Eugubinum & alios.
units.tr: A gomer full] As much as a gomer would hold. The gomer, or omer (in Hebrew [עֹמֶר]), is a measure holding the tenth part of an ephah. It is also called isaron, whence the askarton [ἀσκαρτόν] of Josephus, which I mentioned earlier, for which Rufinus has published astarium. The Glossary of Philo says the gomer is a measure of three Attic choenices. Jerome says the gomer contains three Attic choenices. Josephus says it holds three half-cotylae. See Theodoret's Quaestiones on Exodus, question 20; Nicolaus Brabantinus on Exodus 16; Augustinus Eugubinus and others.

units.la: In vase aureo] ςαμύσ ... χωνεῖν appellant Graeci LXX. quos hic noster secutus est, adstipulante Apostolo in epistola ad Ebraeos. Errant ergo qui vas testaceum aut fictile fuisse putant, inter quos R. Salomo & Ionathan is cujus extat in Mosen portentosa paraphrasis. Abenezra fictile vel aereum fuisse scribit, ut alii vitreum, si modo [illegible, ~4 letters], quod in editionibus Chaldaicis, est vas vitreum, quemadmodum Iudaei hodie interpretantur. Ceterum ςάμυ non tam late patet quam vas Latinorum. Lexicon vetus, ςάμυ, matella, urceus, urna. Quidam hydriam exponunt. Vocem Ebraeam [illegible, ~3 letters] phialam alij & alij scutellam reddunt. Sunt etiam qui a [illegible, ~2 letters] deducunt, unde [illegible, ~3 letters] Sinna, parma, scutum. Ad ea quae de gomor supra notavi, addendum ex Oncelo, decima pars trium satorum, pro quo in Graeca editione legitur τὸ δὲ γόμορ τὸ δέκατον τῶν τριῶν μέτρων. R. Salomo, Epha continet tria fata, & fatum sex cabos & cabus quatuor logos, & logus sex ova. Sequitur hanc decimam partem Epha continere ova 43, cum parte quinta. Perpetram igitur Lyranus ad hunc locum, R. Salomo dicit quod continet quantitatem alij. ovorum.
units.tr: In a golden vessel] The Greeks, namely the Seventy, whom our author follows, call it [στάμνος], and the Apostle agrees with them in his Epistle to the Hebrews. Those therefore err who think it was an earthenware or clay vessel, among whom are Rabbi Solomon and Jonathan, whose monstrous paraphrase on Moses is extant. Abenezra writes that it was of clay or bronze, others of glass, as the Chaldee editions have it, a glass vessel, as the Jews interpret today. Moreover, [στάμνος] does not extend as widely as the Latin vas. An old lexicon gives [στάμνος] as chamber pot, pitcher, urn. Some explain it as a water-jar. Others render the Hebrew word as a bowl, and others as a dish. There are also those who derive it from another word, whence sinna, a shield. To what I noted above about the gomer, add from Onkelos: the tenth part of three measures, for which the Greek edition reads "the gomer is the tenth of three measures." Rabbi Solomon says an ephah contains three seahs, a seah six cabs, a cab four logs, and a log six eggs. It follows that this tenth part of an ephah holds 43 and a fifth part of eggs. Lyra therefore goes wrong at this place; Rabbi Solomon says it contains the quantity of other eggs.

units.la: Inde] ex deserto Sinaunde digressus populus venit in Daphca: inde in Alus: ab Alus demum venerunt in Raphidim, undecima mansione. Num.33.12.
units.tr: Thence] The people, departing from the desert of Sin, came to Daphca; thence to Alus; from Alus at last they came to Rephidim, the eleventh stop. Num. 33.12.

units.la: Ægre ab exitio ducis temperatum] parum aberat quin eum lapidarent.
units.tr: Hardly restrained from killing the leader] it was a near thing that they would stone him.

units.la: Apud locum, cui Oreb nomen est] scribendum Horeb vel Choreb. Nam in libris Græcorum χωρῆ[?], Qualia sunt Hermon & Chermon; Hebron & Chebron. Sic Rahab & Rachab. Horeb autem nomen loci esse videtur. Nam Exod.17.6. ecce ego sto ibi super petram in Horeb. Sensus est, quæ in Horeb. Quan-quam alij referunt, in sicco. Ut ut sit, scribendum Horeb cum aspiratione. Nam Oreb leniter scriptum aliud est. Quæ Moses aperte distinxit, ea non iunt confundenda, meo iudicio.
units.tr: Near the place called Oreb] It should be written Horeb or Choreb. In the Greek books the name is written with a different initial letter, as Hermon and Chermon, Hebron and Chebron, Rahab and Rachab. Horeb, however, seems to be the name of a place. For Exodus 17.6: "Behold, I stand there upon the rock in Horeb." The sense is "the one that is in Horeb." Others, however, refer it to "in the dry place." However that may be, it should be written Horeb with the aspirate, for Oreb written softly is something else. What Moses clearly distinguished should not, in my judgment, be confused.

units.la: Sed ubi Raphidim perventum] imo antea, cum aquam ex petra excuteret Moses, in Raphidim erant. Vide Sigonium. Eusebius de locis, Raphidim locus in deserto iuxta montem Horeb. Forte petra Horeb hinc nomen habuit; ut petra intelligatur quæ in monte Horeb. Hoc pono, non statuo.
units.tr: But when they had reached Rephidim] Indeed, earlier, when Moses drew water from the rock, they were already in Rephidim. See Sigonius. Eusebius, On Places: Rephidim is a place in the desert near Mount Horeb. Perhaps the rock of Horeb took its name from this, so that the rock is understood as the one that is on Mount Horeb. I propose this; I do not assert it.

units.la: Amalechitæ] melius, Amalecitæ. Nam est Coph in scriptura Ebraica.
units.tr: Amalekites] better, Amalekites, for the Hebrew text has Qoph.

units.la: Pag.27. Populum incursionibus vastabant] Sigonio magis arridet, vexabant: idem mihi quoque placet pro illo, vexabant.
units.tr: Pag. 27. They were laying waste the people with raids] Sigonius prefers "harassed," and I too like "harassed" better in place of that.

units.la: Cum Iesum bellantibus præfecisset] Iesum vocat post Græcos interpretes, qui ab Ebræis Iosua dicitur. Sic Iosua filius Iosedec ab iisdem Græcis Iesus nuncupatur. Unde perspicuum, quod tamen multi nimis impudenter negant, Iesus & Iosua unum idemque nomen esse.
units.tr: When he had set Jesus over those fighting] He calls him Jesus after the Greek interpreters; among the Hebrews he is called Joshua. So Joshua the son of Jehozadak is called Jesus by the same Greeks. Hence it is clear, though many too shamelessly deny it, that Jesus and Joshua are one and the same name.

units.la: Et Ur spectator] ponendum comma post Ur, ut fit Aharon & Ur, vel potius, Hur, spectator. & c. prius erat in vulgatis, & ut spectator. Hoc meadum ante me Sigonius notavit. Omnino scribendum, Aharon & Hur. Nam est הור in scriptura Ebraica, cum Heth in capite. Maritus erat Mariæ sororis Aharon & Mosis, qui Ωρα Græcis dicitur, quod similiter aspirandum Hor. Quanquam ambiguitas aliqua in hac scriptura. Nam Hor cum aspiratione simplici nomen est montis. Hoc loco Hor aspirationem habet geminatam, quam duplicē appellat Hieronymus Prior. He vocatur ab Ebræis: altera, Heth sive H, Heth. Vide sequentia.
units.tr: And Ur the spectator] A comma should be placed after Ur, so that it reads "Aaron and Hur," or rather Hur, the spectator, etc. Previously the common editions read "and as spectator." Sigonius noted this correction before me. It should certainly be written Aaron and Hur, for the Hebrew text has [הור], with heth at the beginning. He was the husband of Miriam, sister of Aaron and Moses, and is called Ōr by the Greeks, which likewise should be aspirated as Hor. There is some ambiguity in this spelling, for Hor with a single aspirate is the name of a mountain. In this place Hor has a doubled aspirate, which Jerome the Elder calls double. He is called by the Hebrews [הור], and the other, heth or H, heth. See what follows.

units.la: Montem conscendit] collis erat n[illegible, ~3 letters]mons, quæ Moses [illegible, ~3 letters] dicit, Græci autem βουνὸν reddunt, Exod.17.10. καὶ Μωϋσῆς, καὶ [illegible, ~25 letters] Est autem βουνός [?], collis. Lexicon vetus, βουνός [?], tumulus, collis. Chaldæi Ramatha vocant, quæ vox locum altum designat.
units.tr: He climbed the mountain] It was a hill, not a mountain, which Moses calls by one name, but the Greeks render [βουνόν], Exodus 17.10. Now [βουνός] means a hill. An old lexicon gives [βουνός] as mound, hill. The Chaldeans call it Ramatha, a word that designates a high place.

units.la: Dubio eventu] modo hus [?] modo illis vincentibus.
units.tr: With doubtful outcome] now one side, now the other, was winning.

units.la: Moysi precibus] pro Moysis, ut Achilli pro Achillis, quæ est antiqua declinandi ratio, qua dandi casum in talibus pro generandi ponebant. Sic Vlysi dicebant pro Vlysis. Sic Themistocli fuga, Aristoteli discipulus, Theophani consilia, Arriobarzani filius: quæ exempla magna ex parte extant apud Ciceronem, ut observavit olim Visiorius [?]. Vide Castigationes ejus, pag. 46. Apud Augustinum de doctrina Christiana lib. 2 [?]. cap. 8. reperitur etiam Moyseos, Græca declinatione nominis. Similiter Moseos impunitatem linguam dixit Faustus Manichæus, ut habetur in iis quæ idem Augustinus contra eum scripsit, lib. 14. cap. 1.
units.tr: By the prayers of Moysi] Moysi for Moysis, as Achilli for Achillis. This is the ancient method of declension, by which in such words they used the dative case in place of the genitive. So they said Vlysi for Vlysis, and likewise Themistocli's flight, Aristoteli's disciple, Theophani's counsels, Arriobarzani's son. Many such examples are found in Cicero, as Visiorius observed long ago; see his Castigationes, p. 46. In Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 8, we also find Moyseos, with the Greek declension of the name. Similarly Faustus the Manichaean spoke of "the impunity of Moseos's language," as is found in what Augustine wrote against him, book 14, chapter 1.

units.la: Hostes in noctem cecidit] usque ad noctem, ut pag. 14. in rubrum mare illati sunt: & mox, populum viæ errore in objectum mare devenisse. Sic bibere in diem, exponitur usque ad diem. Ceterum quamdiu Moses manus attollebat, tamdiu hostes cadebant. Attollebat autem, Aharone & Hur eas fulciente, usque ad occasum solis, Exod. 17.12. quo tempore vespera incipit. Noctis ergo vocabulo vesperam comprehendit, ut contra per vesperam nox significatur, Gen. 1 3 & alibi.
units.tr: The enemies he cut down into night] that is, until night, as on p. 14 they were carried into the Red Sea; and soon after, the people by a mistake of the way came to the sea that lay before them. So "to drink into the day" is explained as "until the day." Moreover, as long as Moses raised his hands, so long the enemies fell. He kept them raised, with Aaron and Hur supporting them, until sunset, Exodus 17.12, at which time the evening begins. So by the word night he comprehends the evening, just as conversely night is signified by evening, Gen. 1.3 and elsewhere.

units.la: Peridem tempus] incertum quando Iethro venerit ad Mosem. Quidam ante datam legem, alij post venisse tradunt. Priorem sententiam tuetur ex Hebræis R. Saadia, ex nostris Nicolaus de Lyra, ad quem te adire velim. Cum enim, inquit, mons Sinai non longe abesset a terra Madian, ut patet ex cap. 3. Exodi, non est credibile aut verisimile, locorum audita magnificentia generi per annum tardasse venire ad ipsum. Posteriorem defendit Abenezra, scribens eum venisse primum anno secundo post latam legem. Quod probat primum ex verbis quæ habentur, Exod. 17.12. obtulit ergo Iethro socer Mosi holocausta & hostias. Deinde quia non legimus Mosen extruxisse novum altare. Postremo quia scriptum, Exod. 17.16. nota facio præcepta Dei & leges ejus.
units.tr: At the same time] It is uncertain when Jethro came to Moses. Some say he came before the law was given, others that he came after. The former view is defended among the Hebrews by Rabbi Saadia, and among ours by Nicolaus de Lyra, to whom I would have you turn. For since Mount Sinai was not far from the land of Midian, as appears from Exodus chapter 3, it is neither credible nor likely that, having heard of the magnificence of those places, he delayed a year before coming to him. The latter view is defended by Abenezra, who writes that he came first in the second year after the law was given. He proves this first from the words in Exodus 17.12: "Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, offered burnt offerings and sacrifices." Then because we do not read that Moses built a new altar. Lastly, because it is written, Exodus 17.16: "I make known the precepts of God and his laws."

units.la: Iethro Mosi socer] alibi est, ex filiis Hobab soceri Mosis. Dicebatur & Iether, sive, ut antiqui legebant, Iothor. Indefatum Iethro, addita littera ex nomine Tetragrammato, quæ honoris ergo accessit, cum jam proselytus factus esset, ait R. Salomos [?]. qui etiam scribit eum septem nomina habuisse, Raguel, Iether, Iethro, Hobab, Heber, Cinaeus, Phutiel.
units.tr: Jethro, Moses' father-in-law] Elsewhere he is "of the sons of Hobab, Moses' father-in-law." He was also called Ieth er, or, as the ancients read it, Iothor. Jethro is a form with a letter added from the Tetragrammaton, which was added for honour, since he had already become a proselyte, says Rabbi Solomon. Who also writes that he had seven names: Raguel, Jether, Jethro, Hobab, Heber, Cinaeus, Phutiel.

units.la: Sephora] scribo Sepphora. Nam Sephora eo minus se mihi probat, quod una ex obstetricibus Aegyptiis ita nominetur in editione Hieronymi. Vide notata ad pag. 21.
units.tr: Zipporah] I write Sepphora. For I like Sephora less, because one of the Egyptian midwives is so named in Jerome's edition. See the notes on p. 21.

units.la: Domi reliederat] imo domum remissa fuit ex itinere. Notum hoc ex historia, quam sit diligentius & cum majore cura legisset Sulpicius, haec & alia quaedam paullo aliter scripsisset.
units.tr: He had returned home: but he was in fact sent home after the journey. This is known from the story, which Sulpicius would have related differently and in other ways had he read it more carefully and with greater attention.

units.la: Ordines populi distribuit[?] } hi magistratus erant singularum urbium, qui minores causas populi tractabant. Suberant autem principibus tribuum, quos Graeci φυλάρχας vocant. His omnibus praerat rex sive dux aut judex. Vide Carolum Sigonium de repub. Ebraeorum lib. 7 cap. 1 & deinceps. Caeterum in castris Israelitarum, cum hi ordines distribuerentur, tribuni erant 6000, centuriones 6000, semicenturiones 12000, decani sive decuriones 60000, notavit R. Salomo cognomine Pharsandatha, hoc est interpres legis. Sic audit vulgo apud suos.
units.tr: He distributed the orders of the people: these were the magistrates of the individual cities, who handled the lesser cases of the people. They were subordinate to the chiefs of the tribes, whom the Greeks call phylarchs [φυλάρχας]. Over all of them presided a king, or leader, or judge. See Carolus Sigonius, On the Hebrew Commonwealth, book 7, chapter 1 and following. Moreover, when these orders were distributed in the camp of the Israelites, there were 6,000 tribunes, 6,000 centurions, 12,000 half-centurions, and 60,000 decans or decurions. R. Solomon, surnamed Pharsandatha, that is, interpreter of the law, has noted this. This is how it is commonly heard among his people.

units.la: Tribunos centurionesque] χιλιάρχας καὶ ἑκατοντάρχας. Omisit semicenturiones, quos nonnulli quinquagenarios appellant, ut Graeci πεντηκοντάρχας[?].
units.tr: Tribunes and centurions: [chiliarchs kai hekatontarchas]. He has left out the half-centurions, whom some call quinquagenarians, as the Greeks call them pentekontarchs [πεντηκοντάρχας].

units.la: Decuriones] hos interpres Latinus decanos appellat, & Graeci δεκαδάρχας. Nomen acceperunt a numero eorum quibus praerant, praecipuum autem horum usus fuit in bello. Sed & in urbe jus reddebant, & causas leviores decidebant. Lex, Graeco-Lat. vetus, δεκάρχης decanus, δεκαδάρχης decurio, δεκάπρωτος decem primus: & Lat.Graec. decuriones, δεκάπρωτοι. In castris Romanorum, qui decanus erat, dicebatur alio nomine caput contubernij.
units.tr: Decurions: the Latin translator calls these decans, and the Greeks call them dekadarchs [δεκαδάρχας]. They took their name from the number of men they commanded, and their chief use was in war. But they also administered justice in the city and decided the lesser cases. In the old Greek-Latin lexicon, dekarchês [δεκάρχης] is "decan," dekadarchês [δεκαδάρχης] is "decurion," and dekáprōtos [δεκάπρωτος] is "first of ten"; and in the Latin-Greek lexicon, decuriones are dekáprōtoi [δεκάπρωτοι]. In the Roman camp, the man who was a decan was called by another name, head of the tent-group.

units.la: In patriam regressus] in urbem Madian, juxta Arnonem & Areopolim, quae erat patria ipsius. Est enim patria, ut Nonius Marcellus censet, urbs vel civitas parentum. Hiero. de locis Aflorum. Madian civitas juxta Arnonem & Areopolim, cujus nunc ruinae tantum modo demonstrantur, ubi Moyses apud Iethro socerum suum exulabat. Eadem scribit Eusebius. Aut nove dixit in patriam pro in terram Madian, ut Virgilius,
units.tr: Returned to his country: to the city of Midian, near the Arnon and Areopolis, which was his native place. For a native place, as Nonius Marcellus holds, is the city or state of one's parents. Jerome, On the Places of the Hebrews: Midian was a city near the Arnon and Areopolis, whose ruins alone are now pointed out, where Moses lived in exile with his father-in-law Jethro. Eusebius writes the same. Or perhaps he said "into his country" loosely for "into the land of Midian," as Virgil does,

units.la: -- qui sanguine nobis
units.tr: —who with their blood

units.la: Hanc patriam peperere suo[?], de Latio.
units.tr: Won this fatherland for us with their own blood, speaking of Latium.

units.la: Ad Sinam montem] culpatur hoc loco Sulpicius quod montem Sinam dixerit, cum Sina, ut aiunt, non montis nomen sit,
units.tr: To Mount Sina: Sulpicius is faulted here for calling it Mount Sina, since Sina, as they say, is not the name of a mountain,

units.la: sed desertis in quo mons ille fuit, qui propterea mons Sinai dicatur, id est, deserti Sinai. Quod Græce manifestius esset τὸ ὄρος τὰ σινά, non τὸ σινά. Hanc sententiam tuentur Hieronymus ab Oleastro & Carolus Sigonius. Sed ei repugnat primum Iosephus, Orig. lib. 3. cap. 4. deinde editio Græca τὸν ὄρ[?] in qua Exod. 19. τὸ ὄρος τὸ σινὰ legitur, & ὡς τὴν ἐρημίαν τῆς σινὰ [?]. Postremo Apostolus in epistola ad Galatas, cap. 4. vers. 25. Σινὰ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ: Sina mons est in Arabia. Hinc apparet nomen montis esse Sina, non deserti. Forte desertum Sinai, in quo mons ille. Nihil adfirmo. Theologi veteres scribunt hunc montem alia nomine Horeb dictum fuisse: potest esse ut Horeb pars fuerit montis Sinai. Sic differunt Sion & Moria, cum collis montis Sion proprie hoc nomine dicatur. De Sina monte Sulpicius noster dial. 1. cap. 11. ubi sic Postumianus ex oriente reversus, Rubrum mare vidi, jugum Sina montis ascendi: cujus summum cacumen coelo pene contiguum nequaquam adiri potest. Perventum autem fuit ad hunc montem tertio mense post exitum ex AEgypto.
units.tr: but of the desert in which that mountain lies, which is therefore called Mount Sinai, that is, of the desert of Sinai. This would be clearer in Greek as to oros ta sina [τὸ ὄρος τὰ σινά], not to sina [τὸ σινά]. This view is defended by Jerome, by Oleaster, and by Carolus Sigonius. But Josephus contradicts it first, in book 3, chapter 4 of the Antiquities; second, the Greek edition, where in Exodus 19 we read to oros to sina [τὸ ὄρος τὸ σινὰ], and "toward the desert of Sina" [εἰς τὴν ἐρημίαν τῆς σινὰ]. Last, the Apostle in the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 4, verse 25: Sina oros estin en tē Arabia [Σινὰ ὄρος ἐστὶν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ], "Sina is a mountain in Arabia." From this it is clear that the name of the mountain is Sina, not that of the desert. Perhaps it is "the desert of Sinai" in which that mountain stands. I affirm nothing. Ancient theologians write that this mountain was also called by another name, Horeb; it may be that Horeb was part of Mount Sinai. So Zion and Moriah differ, since the hill of Mount Zion is properly called by that name. Our Sulpicius speaks of Mount Sina in Dialogue 1, chapter 11, where Postumianus, returning from the East, says thus: "I saw the Red Sea, I climbed the ridge of Mount Sina, whose summit, almost touching heaven, can by no means be approached." They arrived at this mountain in the third month after the exodus from Egypt.

units.la: Sina] σινὰ ἐστὶ in codicibus Græcis vel σινα [?], errore, ut reor, exscribentium, pro σινᾷ, in quo iota subscriptum. Nam Ebraei dicunt Sinai. Simile mendum in σαρὰ [?], quod scribendum σαρὰ pro σαρᾷ [?], id est, Sarai. Ita conjicio: puto autem conjecturam meam non plane vanam esse. Græci vocant diphthongum improprium. Nam propria sonum habet duarum vocalium. Unde bivocalis appellatur. Porro Sinai nomen habere putatur a copia ruborum. Nam rubus סְנֶה vocatur.
units.tr: Sina: in the Greek manuscripts it is sina esti [σινὰ ἐστὶ] or sina [σινα], through an error, I think, of the copyists, for sinai [σινᾷ], with iota subscript. For the Hebrews say Sinai. A similar mistake occurs in sara [σαρὰ], which should be written sara [σαρᾷ], that is, Sarai. That is my conjecture, and I think it is not altogether empty. The Greeks call it an improper diphthong, since it has the sound of only one vowel, not two; hence it is called "two-vowelled" [bivocalis]. Moreover, the name Sinai is thought to come from the abundance of brambles there, for the bramble is called seneh [סְנֶה].

units.la: Populus ut sanctificaretur] more antiquo, qui sanctificabatur, vestimenta sua perluebat, seque ab uxore abstinebat. Qua de re alias.
units.tr: That the people might be sanctified: in the ancient manner, those who were being sanctified washed their garments and abstained from their wives. More on this matter elsewhere.

units.la: Tubarum] buccinaru potius. Nam est שׁוֹפָר, Exod. 19. 24.
units.tr: Of trumpets: rather of horns, for the word is shophar [שׁוֹפָר], Exodus 19:24.

units.la: Cum fulminibus] omisit tonitrua quæ Moses voces appellat, Exod. 19. 16. Alibi est, voces Dei eodem sensu. Nam tonitru a Deo.
units.tr: With lightnings: he has omitted the thunders, which Moses calls voices, Exodus 19:16. Elsewhere the voices of God are meant in the same sense, for thunder is from God.

units.la: Dominum propter constitit] Terent. hic propter hunc adsiste, id est, prope vel juxta hunc. Sic propter Dominum. Huc refer propter dormias, quod explicant similiter prope vel juxta dormias. Cicero, 6. in Ver. propter est spelunca quædam. Idem in Pisonem, qui propter te sedet.
units.tr: Stood near the Lord: Terence has "propter hunc adsiste," that is, stand near or beside him. So "propter Dominum" means near the Lord. Refer to this "propter dormias," which they similarly explain as "near" or "beside" you sleep. Cicero, in the sixth Verrine: "propter est spelunca quaedam," there is a certain cave nearby. The same in the speech against Piso: "qui propter te sedet," who sits beside you.

units.la: Lex lata] primum ore Dei pronuntiata fuit ex monte: deinde tabulis lapideis duabus comprehensa, & Mosi tradita ad populum deferenda. In his tabulis decem praecepta continebantur, quae decem verba Ebraei vocaut: unde Decalogi nomen. Verbum enim aliquando idem quod praeceptum, ut in historia Esther, secundum verbum regis, id est praeceptum, jussum, mandatum. R. Salomo autor in Decalogo comprehendi breviter omnia praecepta legis, quae sunt numero 613 explicata luculenter in libr.qui vocatur per sigla ΤΝΟ, id est, liber praeceptorum magnus. Legis vocabulo veniunt etiam judicia, quae noster paullo post edicta vocat & statuta, qui sunt ritus sacrorum caeremoniaeque. Quod noto, quia sunt qui legem multiplicem interpretantur triplicem. Quaenam haec triplex lex? una ad mores pertinet: quocirca moralis vocatur. Altera ad judicia fori spectat, quam ideo judicialem & forensem appellant. Tertia pertinet ad caeremonias ritusque sacros. Has tres leges significant his tribus nominibus, מִצְוֹת[?] προστάγματα ἢ ἐντολαί, praecepta sive mandata. מִשְׁפָּטִים[?] κρίματα, judicia. חֻקִּים[?] δικαιώματα καὶ νόμιμα, quod reddunt. Legitima.
units.tr: The law given: first it was pronounced by God's voice from the mountain; then it was comprised on two stone tablets and given to Moses to be delivered to the people. On these tablets were contained the ten precepts, which the Hebrews call the ten words; hence the name Decalogue. For the word sometimes means the same as precept, as in the story of Esther, "according to the word of the king," that is, the precept, command, or mandate. R. Solomon says that all the precepts of the law, which number 613, are briefly comprised in the Decalogue, and are clearly explained in the book called by the abbreviation TNO, that is, the great book of precepts. By the term law are also included judgments, which our author a little later calls edicts and statutes, which are the rites of the sacred things and ceremonies. I note this because there are those who interpret the law as having three kinds. What is this threefold law? One pertains to morals, and for that reason is called moral. Another concerns the judgments of the courts, which they therefore call judicial and forensic. The third pertains to ceremonies and sacred rites. These three laws are signified by these three terms: mitzvot [מִצְוֹת], prostagmata or entolai [προστάγματα ἢ ἐντολαί], precepts or commands; mishpatim [מִשְׁפָּטִים], krimata [κρίματα], judgments; chukkim [חֻקִּים], dikaiōmata kai nomima [δικαιώματα καὶ νόμιμα], which they render "legitimate things."

units.la: Etsæpe repetita] quam sæpe nescio, hoc scio repetitam semel Deut.5.6 paucis mutatis.
units.tr: And often repeated: how often I do not know, but I know it was repeated once, Deuteronomy 5:6, with a few words changed.

units.la: Mutatio omnis in verbis est, non in sensu. Verba inventa sunt ad sensum animi significandum. Ea habent rationem corporis, ut sensus anima, qui in verbis tanquam in vase quodam continetur. Quocirca sapientes de verbis non admodum solliciti fuerunt. Quidam verba similitudinem habere dicunt cum vagina, in qua gladius reconditus. Similiter sensus in verbis latet: unde verborum cognitio imprimis necessaria. Nam rerum cognitio pendet ab iis, ut recte monet Aristoteles.
units.tr: Every change is in the words, not in the sense. Words were invented to signify the sense of the mind. They stand to the sense as the body stands to the soul, the sense being contained in the words as in a kind of vessel. For this reason wise men were not very anxious about words. Some say that words resemble a sheath in which a sword is hidden; similarly the sense lies hidden in words, so that knowledge of words is above all necessary. For knowledge of things depends on them, as Aristotle rightly observes.

units.la: Pag, 28. Fontem iplum] codicem sacrum.
units.tr: Page 28. The fountain itself: the sacred codex.

units.la: Non erunt tibi, &c.] Scire licet verbum, quod in Ebraeo singulare esse, ut verti etiam possit, non erit tibi Deus alius. Quam ego sane versionem alteri praetulerim. Nomen enim Elohim tam Deum significat, quam Deos, licet construatur cum adjetivo ejusdem numeri.
units.tr: You shall not have, etc.: It should be noted that the verb, which in Hebrew is singular, may also be translated "you shall not have another God." I would certainly prefer this rendering to the other, since the name Elohim signifies God as well as gods, although it is construed with an adjective of the same number.

units.la: Alieni] ἕτεροι alii, id est, alieni. Sic Hiero. interpretatur. Sunt qui enarrant, alii a vero. Nam unus tantum est verus Deus. Ceteri non sunt dii, nisi opinione hominum, qui eos tales faciunt.
units.tr: Strange: [heteroi], other, that is, strange. Thus Jerome interprets. Some explain it as "other than the true one." For there is only one true God. The others are not gods, except in the opinion of men, who make them such.

units.la: Praeter me] ἀλλ' ἐμέ. Sic etiam Oncelos. In Ebraeo est לְפָנַי[?] quod Hiero. vertit coram me, & Lyra explicat, nullam unquam loco aut tempore. Id hausit ex R.Salomone. Coram me, quamdiu ego ero, ut coram sole, quamdiu erit sol, id est in aeternum.
units.tr: Besides me: [all' eme]. So also Onkelos. In Hebrew it is lefanai [לְפָנַי], which Jerome renders "before me," and Lyra explains as "in no place or time whatever." He drew this from R. Solomon: "before me," as long as I shall be, as before the sun as long as the sun shall be, that is, forever.

units.la: ἰδώλον, hoc est simulachrum numen aliquod re-præsentans, sive sculptile fuerit sive conflatile, non refert. Quantum in fonte tantum sculptile, id est, γλυπτὸν[?]. Id movit credo Senes, ut latiorem vocem ἰδώλου[?] usurparint: quos Sulpicius, ut solet, secutus est.
units.tr: Idol: [eidōlon], that is, an image representing some divinity, whether it was carved or cast, it makes no difference. Only in the fountain is it "carved," that is, [glyptos]. I think this led the Elders to use the wider term [eidōlou], which Sulpicius, as is his habit, followed.

units.la: non jurabis per Deum tuum. Si quis juraverit per caput regis, nec ratum habuerit juramentum suum, id ei capitale est. Hic mos obtinet hodieque in Ægypto. Quod si dederit pondo auri, non liberatur, quia sprevit regem palam. Si sic fit regi, qui est caro & sanguis, cujus initium vanitas, finis vanitas, & regnum quoque vanitas: quid fiet Deo qui millies millesies[?] rege major est?
units.tr: Thou shalt not swear by thy God. If anyone has sworn by the head of the king and does not keep his oath, it is a capital offence for him. This custom still prevails today in Egypt. But if he gives a pound of gold, he is not released, because he has openly despised the king. If this is how it is with a king, who is flesh and blood, whose beginning is vanity, whose end is vanity, and whose kingdom is vanity too, what will happen to God, who is greater than the king a thousand thousand times over?

units.la: ἐπὶ ματαίῳ[?]: quod Aquila dixit εἰς εἰκῆ. Vanum autem jurandum est quod temere fit & levi de causa. Nam quod violatur nec ratum habetur, perjurium dicitur. Ebraei certe discriminant inter juramentum vanum & falsum. Qua de re di-ximus alias.
units.tr: "In vain" [ἐπὶ ματαίῳ]: Aquila rendered this as "to no purpose" [εἰς εἰκῆ]. An oath is vain when it is sworn rashly and for a slight reason. What is violated and not kept is called perjury. The Hebrews certainly distinguish between a vain oath and a false one. I have discussed this matter elsewhere.

units.la: die septimo. Quod non notassem nisi scirem sabba-thum aliquando dici ipsam hebdomadam, ut ibi, jejuno bis in sabbatho. Hinc prima sabbathi, quod idem cum illo, prima dies hebdomadæ.
units.tr: "On the seventh day." I would not have noted this had I not known that the sabbath is sometimes called the week itself, as in the phrase "I fast twice in the sabbath." Hence "the first of the sabbath," which is the same as "the first day of the week."

units.la: Thomas annotat hoc præceptum partim esse morale, partim cæremoniale. Morale quatenus determinat aliquod tempus ad cultum divinum: cæremoniale quatenus diem Saturni ad hoc peculiariter destinat. Quocirca veteres Christiani in ejus locum primum diem hebdomadæ substituerunt, hoc est diem solis sive dominicum.
units.tr: Thomas notes that this precept is partly moral and partly ceremonial. It is moral insofar as it fixes a certain time for the worship of God; it is ceremonial insofar as it assigns the day of Saturn to this purpose in particular. For this reason the early Christians put the first day of the week in its place, that is, the Lord's day or Sunday.

units.la: servile aut mechanicum. Excipiuntur opera misericor-diæ, & quæ in templo fiunt a sacerdotibus, ut circumcidere in-fantem, unde dicunt, Circumcisio impellit sabbathum: item ægroto medicinam facere, & alia consimilia, de quibus alias. Debet etiam hic dies cultui divino consecrari. Sic dico, tum homo sacris vacare debet, ut etiam justitiæ, & abstinere ab omnibus operibus malis & vanis. Proinde Augustinus, Minus peccat, inquit, qui eo die arat, quam qui ludit.
units.tr: "Servile or mechanical." Works of mercy are excepted, and those done in the temple by the priests, such as circumcising an infant, whence they say, "circumcision overrides the sabbath"; likewise preparing medicine for the sick, and other similar things, of which elsewhere. This day ought also to be set apart for divine worship. So I say that a person ought to be free for sacred things, and also for justice, and to abstain from all evil and idle works. Accordingly Augustine says: "He who ploughs on that day sins less than he who plays."

units.la: Honorifica] Δοξάζω. Lexicon vetus, δοξάζω[?], glorifico, honorifico, magnifico, nobilito. Augustinus contra sermonem Arrianorum, Glorificare & honorificare & clarificare tria quidem verba, sed res una est, quod Græce dicitur δοξάζει[?], interpretum quidem varietate aliter atque aliter positum est in Latino. Usus est hoc verbo & interpres Sirachi-dis Ecclesiastici, io. 31. fili mi, in mansuetudine honorifica animam tuam. Quæ lucem accipiunt ex illo Salomonis, benefacit animæ suæ pius. Nam honorificat animam suam, hoc est seipsum, qui corpori ad vitam necessaria suppeditat: item qui legi operam dat. Itaque dicitant, populus terræ non est pius, nempe quia non dat operam legi, male meretur de anima sua. Sic parentes honorat, qui eis victum subministrat egentibus. Quæ de re lex est apud Judæos, Debet filius alere parentem pauperem: si nolit, judices cogunt eum. Idem sensus in Græco τιμᾷ[?], quod in editione τῶν[?] LXX. & in Latino Hiero. honora patrem, &c. Anselmus Matth 15.[?] ad locum, honora patrem & matrem. Honor ille non tantum in salutationibus & officiis deferendis, quantum in eleemosynis & munerum collatione sentitur. Quæ descripsit ex commentariis Hieronymi ad eundem locum. Vide, si placet, Idem Hiero in epist. ad Gerontiam, honor vel pro eleemosyna vel pro munere accipitur; ut est illud, presbyteri duplici honore digni habeantur: & in evangelio Dominus differt mandatum legis, honora patrem & matrem, non in verborum sono, qui inopiam parentum cassa potest adulatione frustrare, sed in victus necessariis administrandis debere intelligi.
units.tr: "Honour" [δοξάζω]. The old lexicon: δοξάζω means to glorify, honour, magnify, ennoble. Augustine, against the sermon of the Arians: "'to glorify,' 'to honour' and 'to clarify' are three words but one thing, which in Greek is called δοξάζει, and which has been rendered differently in Latin owing to the variety of translators." The translator of Ecclesiasticus also used this word, io. 31: "My son, honour your soul in meekness." These words receive light from that saying of Solomon, "the godly man does good to his own soul." For he honours his own soul, that is himself, who supplies his body with what is needed for life; likewise he who devotes himself to the law. Hence they say, "the people of the land is not godly," namely because it does not devote itself to the law, and so it deals ill with its own soul. In the same way he honours his parents who supplies them with food when they are in need. On this matter the Jews have a law: "a son ought to support a poor parent; if he is unwilling, the judges compel him." The same sense is found in the Greek τιμᾷ, which in the edition of the Seventy, and in the Latin of Jerome, is "honour your father, etc." Anselm on Matthew 15, on the words "honour father and mother." That honour is shown not only in greetings and services but in alms and the giving of gifts. He drew this from Jerome's commentary on the same passage. See, if you wish, Jerome himself in his letter to Gerontia: honour is taken either for alms or for a gift, as in the words "let elders be deemed worthy of double honour." And in the Gospel the Lord explains the commandment of the law, "honour father and mother," not as a matter of the sound of the words, which can cheat needy parents with empty flattery, but as something to be understood as providing for the necessities of life.

units.la: Non occides: non moechaberis: non furtum facies] se-cutus est ordinem quem libri antiqui præferunt & φονεύσεις· & μοιχεύσεις· & κλέψεις. Nam in aliis est, etiam in editione Romana, & μοιχεύσεις, non mœchaberis: & κλέψεις, non furtum facies: & φονεύσεις non occides.
units.tr: "Thou shalt not kill; thou shalt not commit adultery; thou shalt not steal." He followed the order which the old books present: φονεύσεις, μοιχεύσεις, κλέψεις. For in others, even in the Roman edition, it is μοιχεύσεις, "thou shalt not commit adultery," and κλέψεις, "thou shalt not steal," and φονεύσεις, "thou shalt not kill."

units.la: Occides] manu, lingua, veneno: item auxilio, consensu, odio. Ex quo illud, Qui fratrem suum odit, homicida est, Hiscuni[?] addit, silentio, ut si conscius consilij ejus qui alicui necem struit, non indicaverit illud. Jonathan hic edidit, non occides animam, id est, hominem, ut, octo animæ fuerunt in arca Noe. Male igitur Manichæi hoc præceptum extendebant ad bestias. Vide Augustinum de civit. Dei, lib. 1. cap. 20. & 21. Notabis in fonte verbum <bl>רצח[?]</bl> verbum esse quod dici ajunt proprie de cæde injusta. Aliud est <bl>הרג[?]</bl>, quod etiam occido reddunt. Id usurpatur tam de justa, quam injusta nece. Prohibetur ergo hic cæ<bl>des</bl> injusta tantum, non quæ a magistratu fit, cum supplicio afficit nocentem, aut in bello patratur a militibus. Iam vero aliquis occidit corpus tantum, ut homicida: aut animam tantum, ut falsus doctor & mendax: (scilicet illud, os quod mentitur, occidit animam) aut corpus & animam simul, ut qui seipsum necat.
units.tr: "Thou shalt not kill": by hand, by tongue, by poison; also by help, by consent, by hatred. Hence that saying, "he who hates his brother is a murderer." Hiscuni adds: by silence, as when one who knows of the plot of someone who is contriving another's death does not disclose it. Jonathan here rendered it "thou shalt not kill the soul," that is, the man, as in "there were eight souls in the ark of Noah." So the Manichaeans wrongly extended this precept to beasts. See Augustine, The City of God, book 1, chapters 20 and 21. Note that in the source text the word ratsach [רצח] is said to be a word properly used of unjust slaughter. Another, harag [הרג], which they also render "I kill," is used of both just and unjust killing. So only unjust slaughter is forbidden here, not that which the magistrate carries out when he punishes the guilty with death, or that which soldiers commit in war. Someone kills the body only, as a murderer; or the soul only, as a false teacher and liar (for "the mouth that lies kills the soul"); or body and soul together, as one who kills himself.

units.la: Non mœchaberis. <bl>Alij</bl>, non committes adulterium. idem est. Recentior interpretatio, non scortaberis, duabus de causis displicet. Una est quod ab antiqua temere nimis recedat: altera quod scortationem alio verbo significant. Sane ubi legimus, morte moriatur adulter & adultera, quis ferat interpretantem, morte moriatur scortator & scortatrix? Atqui idem verbum est in Ebræo, videlicet <bl>זנה[?]</bl> Scortari <bl>זונה[?]</bl> dicitur. Quæ aperte distinguuntur in Hosea, his verbis, Non animadvertam in filias vestras cum scortabuntur, neque in nurus vestras cum adulterium committent, sive cum mœchabuntur.
units.tr: "Thou shalt not commit adultery." Others: "thou shalt not commit adultery"; it is the same thing. The more recent rendering "non scortaberis" displeases for two reasons. One is that it departs too rashly from the ancient wording; the other is that they express fornication by a different word. Indeed, where we read, "let the adulterer and the adulteress be put to death," who could tolerate a translator who says, "let the whoremonger and the whore be put to death"? And yet the same word is used in Hebrew, namely zanah [זנה]; the word for a whore is zonah [זונה]. These are clearly distinguished in Hosea, in these words: "I will not punish your daughters when they play the harlot, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery."

units.la: Mitto veteres Ebræos, qui hoc præceptum ad <bl>מזיגות[?]</bl> restringiunt, alios concubitus alibi prohiberi dicentes. Quanquam Hiscuni vetari hic scribit omne illicitum concubitum, qui fit præter leges matrimonij. Idem censet Augustinus, & cum eo doctores catholici. Saadias gradus ponit in scortatione. Primus est in virgine viduaque: secundus cum uxore cujus menses profluunt: tertius cum uxore alterius: quartus cum altera, quæ non sit religionis Iudaicæ. Si semen, inquit, non dederit, debet proselyta fieri, ac tum potest eam ducere: si vero semen dederit, committit idololatriam. Quintus est cum masculo: sextus cum bestia. Infimus horum cum virgine & vidua. Summus cum bestia. Intermedii sunt quos dixi. Omisit autem in his gradibus concubitum cum sorore matre & filia, aliaque non nulla. Forte quod hæc incestu vocabulo significentur.
units.tr: I pass over the ancient Hebrews, who restrict this precept to mezigoth [מזיגות], saying that other kinds of intercourse are forbidden elsewhere. Yet Hiscuni writes that every illicit intercourse that happens outside the laws of marriage is forbidden here. Augustine thinks the same, and with him the Catholic teachers. Saadia sets out degrees in fornication. The first is with a virgin or a widow; the second with a wife whose courses flow; the third with another man's wife; the fourth with a woman who is not of the Jewish religion. "If he does not give seed," he says, "she must become a proselyte, and then he may take her; but if he gives seed, he commits idolatry." The fifth is with a male; the sixth with a beast. The lowest of these is with a virgin or widow; the highest is with a beast. The intermediate ones are those I have mentioned. He omitted from these degrees intercourse with a sister, a mother, a daughter, and some others, perhaps because these are signified by the word "incest."

units.la: Non furtum facies. <bl>prohibetur</bl> illicita rei alienæ ablatio, detentio. usurpatio: quæ cum clam fit, furtum: cum palam & aperte, rapina dicitur. <bl>Abenezra</bl>, Furtum proprie est ablatio pecuniæ in occulto: & est furtum capitale, cum quis hominem furatur. Iam vero furtum committitur in supputatione, mensura, pondere. Fur quoque dicitur, qui alterius cor suffuratur, ut Absalom. R. Salomo putat Scripturam hic loqui de fure hominum, ut alibi cum ait, ne furemini, de fure pe-cuniarum. Aliter doctores catholici. Vide Lyram.
units.tr: "Thou shalt not steal": forbidden is the unlawful taking away, keeping, or appropriation of another's property. When it is done secretly it is theft; when done openly and plainly it is called robbery. Abenezra: theft properly is the taking away of money in secret, and it is a capital theft when someone steals a man. Moreover, theft is committed in reckoning, in measure, in weight. One is also called a thief who steals another's heart, as Absalom did. R. Solomon thinks that Scripture here speaks of the thief of men, as elsewhere when it says "do not steal" of the thief of money. Catholic teachers take it otherwise. See Lyra.

units.la: Non falsum testimonium dices] falsum testimonium dicit & is qui per calumniam interpretatur dictum aliquod contra mentem ejus qui dixit, ut æmuli mei qui ea quæ de polygamia Davidis scripsit, de polygamia Christianorum interpretati sunt, falsum de me testantes, cum etiam Judæis concesserit fuerit libellus repudii, neque tamen ex eo sequatur etiam Christianis concessu esse, dicente Christo, ab initio non fuit sic. Consuetudo consuetudinē abrogavit, nova veterem, ut omittam pluralitate uxore pugnare videri cum prima institutione matrimonij. Tamen polygamiæ duo genera esse docuimus ex Augustino, cujus etiam verbis usi sumus contra nuperā quandā glossā legis illius, non multiplicabit sibi uxores. Quæ ibi scripsi vera sunt: non quod ita judicio nostro confidimus, sed quia ut nolumus adversus animi nostri sententiam verum oppugnare, sic adversum scilicet quorundam [?] sommnia illud cum Augustino aliisque doctoribus catholicis tueri nullum omnino periculum esse puto.
units.tr: "Thou shalt not bear false witness": one bears false witness also who by calumny interprets something said against the mind of the one who said it, as my rivals did, who applied to Christian polygamy what he wrote about David's polygamy, falsely testifying against me; although a bill of divorce was granted to the Jews, it does not follow that it is granted to Christians too, Christ saying, "from the beginning it was not so." Custom has abrogated custom, the new the old; not to mention that plurality of wives seems to clash with the first institution of marriage. Yet I have taught, from Augustine, that there are two kinds of polygamy, and I used his words against a recent gloss on that law, "he shall not multiply wives to himself." What I wrote there is true. It is not that I am so confident in my own judgment, but just as I am unwilling to oppose the truth against my own conviction, so I think there is no danger at all in defending that view against certain dreams of others, together with Augustine and other Catholic teachers.

units.la: Proximum tuum] πλησίον σου. Alibi socium, & alibi amicum tuum; quæ omnia significant alium quemvis, sive is amicus sit, sive inimicus. Absit enim ut liceat contra eum, qui amicus non est, falsum testari.
units.tr: "Neighbour" (Greek πλησίον σου). Elsewhere it means "companion" and elsewhere "your friend." All these terms mean any other person whatever, whether he is a friend or an enemy. Far be it from us to allow false witness against someone who is not a friend.

units.la: Non concupiscescquicquam proximi tui] ita ut frui velis eo quod concupiscis. Nam, si Chrysostomo credendum, voluntas debet accedere ad concupiscentiam. Siquidem concupiscere passionis est, velle arbitrij. Frequenter enim concupiscimus etiam quod nolumus. Si ergo inquit, non consentit voluntas, concupiscentia sola non damnat, expendant οἱ διαλογοι [?]. Ceterum in Deuteronomio præcedit, non concupiscesuxorem proximi tui. Quem ordinem hic LXX. servant, ut primum agat de bono deletabili, deinde de bono utili. Alioqui domus inter res immobiles ponitur: reliqua pertinent ad bona mobilia, quæ vocantur. Senes quoque possil[?]lud, non concupiscesdomum ejus, addunt ex Deuteronomio, οὔτε τὸν ἀγρὸν αὐτῆς [?], neque agrum ejus. Hoc primum: deinde post asinum ejus, addunt de juo, οὔτε πάντας κτήνους αὐτῆς [?], neque ullum pecus ejus.
units.tr: "Nor covet anything of your neighbour's," that is, so that you wish to enjoy what you covet. For, if we are to believe Chrysostom, the will must accompany the desire, since to desire belongs to the passions and to will belongs to the faculty of choice. We often desire even what we do not want. So if, he says, the will does not consent, desire alone does not condemn; let the dialecticians weigh this [οἱ διάλογοι]. Otherwise, in Deuteronomy the order is "Nor covet your neighbour's wife" first. The Septuagint keeps this order here, so that it first deals with the pleasant good and then with the useful good. Otherwise the house is placed among immovable goods, and the rest belong to what are called movable goods. The elders also add, after "Nor covet his house," the words from Deuteronomy, "nor his field" [οὔτε τὸν ἀγρὸν αὐτῆς], that is, "nor his field." This comes first; then, after "his ass," they add from Deuteronomy "nor any of his cattle" [οὔτε πάντας κτήνους αὐτῆς], that is, "nor any of his livestock."

units.la: Cum tubæ circumstreperent] sonitum buccinæ, habet Hieronymus Exod. 20. 18. ubi LXX. τὴν φωνὴν τῆς σάλπιγγος [?], vocem tubæ. Quod autem antecedit in Hiero, & populus videbat voces, id olim explicavi, nec adhuc muto, audiebat tonitrua. Sic cernere usurpatur in illo poeta veteris quod apud Nonium, vox illius certe est, idem omnes cernimus. Buccinae, τᾶς βυκάνης. Tuba propriè [Hebrew?] dicitur, & differt a buccina, quae [Hebrew?] appellatur. Nam buccina incurva erat, & tuba recta: item buccina ex cornu fiebat, unde κερατίνη dicitur: tuba ex aere vel argento.
units.tr: "The trumpets sounded all around" is in Jerome, Exodus 20:18, where the Septuagint has "the voice of the trumpet" [τὴν φωνὴν τῆς σάλπιγγος]. What comes before in Jerome, "and the people saw the voices," I explained before and still do not change: "they heard the thunders." So "to see" is used in that poet's old line, which is in Nonius, and it is certainly his phrase: "we all see the same thing." Buccinae [τᾶς βυκάνης]. The tuba is properly [Hebrew] so called, and differs from the buccina, which is called [Hebrew]. For the buccina was curved and the tuba straight; likewise the buccina was made of horn, whence it is called keratinē; the tuba of bronze or silver.

units.la: Lampades] [Hebrew?] id est, fulgura micantia vel coruscationes. Ex nuperis interpretibus alii faces, alii fulgetra ediderunt. Camij λάμψεις, [Hebrew?] lignum ardens: item fulgur. Quidam, lumina & ignes terribiliter ardentes.
units.tr: "Lamps" [Hebrew] means flashing lightning or flashes. Among recent translators some have given "torches," others "lightning-bolts." Camius [λάμψεις]: burning wood; likewise lightning. Some give "lights and fires burning terribly."

units.la: Edicta] [Hebrew?] judicialia, quae Moses [Hebrew?], interpres Hieron. judicia, id est, κρίματα vocant. LXX. δικαιώματα, id est, jura. Moneo tamen hac voce reddi ab iisdem interpretibus statuta, quae ab Ebraeis [Hebrew?] vocantur, & a Hiero. caeremonias. Sig. autem ritus sacros, totamque adeo caeremonialem legem. Hic agitur de iis quae ad civilem politiam & forenses controversias pertinent. Quaeritur utrum his legibus obstricti & obligati teneantur Christiani. Et respondetur communiter non teneri. Posse tamen magistratum Christianum in repub. jua, si velit, eas recipere. Secus judicandum de caeremoniis, quae penitus abolitae sunt, & quidem ita ut eas homo christianus observare nullo modo possit, dicente Apostolo, Si circumcidimini Christus nihil vobis proderit.
units.tr: "Judgements" [Hebrew] are the judicial laws, which Moses [Hebrew] calls, in Jerome's translation, "judgements," that is, κρίματα. The Septuagint has δικαιώματα, that is, "ordinances." I note, however, that the same translators render by this word the statutes which are called [Hebrew] by the Hebrews, and which Jerome calls ceremonies. Here, however, it means sacred rites and the whole ceremonial law. Here the subject is those things which pertain to civil polity and legal disputes. The question is whether Christians are bound and obliged by these laws. The common answer is that they are not. Yet a Christian magistrate may, if he wishes, adopt them in his commonwealth. It must be judged otherwise of ceremonies, which have been utterly abolished, and in such a way that a Christian cannot observe them in any way, since the Apostle says: "If you be circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing."

units.la: Hebraeus servus pecunia emptus] Exod. 21.2. Levit. 25. 39. Deut. 15.12. Ier. 34.14. De jure servorum multa in libro praeceptorum majore sol. 169. col. 1. Servus vedebatur vel a seipso vel a judicibus. Nemo poterat seipsum vendere, quamdiu aliquid ei supererat. Sed adito [?] ad locum illum. Hero mortuo servus manebat in servitute apud filium. Si filia haeres erat aut frater heri, aut alij, liber exibat, ib. 3.
units.tr: "A Hebrew servant bought with money": Exodus 21:2; Leviticus 25:39; Deuteronomy 15:12; Jeremiah 34:14. On the law of servants much is said in the Greater Book of Precepts, p. 169, col. 1. A servant was sold either by himself or by the judges. No one could sell himself as long as anything was left to him. But see the passage there. When the master died, the servant remained in servitude with the son. If the daughter were heir, or the master's brother, or another, he went out free, ib. 3.

units.la: Hebraeus] [Hebrew?] Israelita, lud us. Quae tria nomina se mutuo exponunt. Sic Deus Israel & Deus Ebraeorum synonyma sunt.
units.tr: "Hebrew" [Hebrew] means Israelite, or Judahite. These three names explain one another. Thus "God of Israel" and "God of the Hebrews" are synonyms.

units.la: Puer] παῖς, id est, servus, ut apud Terentium in Andria, etiam puerum inde abiens convenit Chremis. Cicero ad Atticum, eo die pueri tui mihi a te litteras reddiderunt.
units.tr: "Boy": παῖς, that is, servant, as in Terence's Andria, where on leaving, Chremes also meets the boy. Cicero to Atticus: "On that day your servants returned to me your letters."

units.la: Pecunia emptus] quem quis ab alio emerit, non qui seipsum pro paupertate vendiderit. Nam talis serviebat ad Iubilaeum, Levit. 25.39. Quidam hunc locum acceperunt de servo qui vendebatur. debatur a judicibus propter furtum suum, seu eo quod furtum fecerat, de quo Exod. 22.3.
units.tr: "Bought with money": whom someone has bought from another, not one who has sold himself because of poverty. For such a man served until the Jubilee, Leviticus 25:39. Some took this passage of a servant who was sold by the judges on account of his theft, or because he had committed theft, on which see Exodus 22:3.

units.la: Sex annis serviet] videlicet quot reliqui adhuc fuerint usque ad annum septimum. Nam si duo tantum supererant, tum annis duobus duntaxat serviebat. Sane in ipso anno remissionis liber erat, etiamsi anno praecedente primum emptus fuisset.
units.tr: "He shall serve six years": that is, as many years as remain up to the seventh year. For if only two remained, then he served only two years. Indeed, in the very year of release he was free, even if he had been bought in the preceding year.

units.la: Post haec liber erit] post annum sextum, ineunte videlicet septimo, sive in principio anni septimi, quem sabbatarium nonnulli vocant.
units.tr: "After this he shall go free": after the sixth year, that is, at the beginning of the seventh year, or at the start of the seventh year, which some call the sabbatical year.

units.la: Auris forabitur] subula, Exod. 21.6. Deut. 15.17. Ecce [?], aures perforasti mihi. Psal. 40.7, Ebraeo 10.5. Cui aures hoc modo forata erat, serviebat domino in seculum, id est, usque ad Jubilaeum, vel usque ad mortem heri.
units.tr: "His ear shall be bored": with an awl, Exodus 21:6; Deuteronomy 15:17. "Behold" [?], you have bored my ears, Psalm 40:7, Hebrew 10:5. The servant whose ear was bored in this way served his master forever, that is, until the Jubilee, or until the master's death.

units.la: Auris] dextera, Ionathan, R. Salomo. Id fiebat coram diis, hoc est judicibus, Exod. 21.5. & 6. Quomodo auris perforetur, vide [?]00 sol 169. col. 3.
units.tr: "Ear": the right one, according to Jonathan and R. Solomon. This was done before God, that is, before the judges, Exodus 21:5-6. On how the ear is bored, see p. 169, col. 3.

units.la: Qui hominem occiderit] Exod. 21.12. Haec lex in usu erat ante tempora Mosis. Gen. 9.6. Quicumq; fuderit sanguinem humanum, fundetur languis ejus. Sic leges civiles Romanorum, quarum collationem cum Mosaicis, vide, si placet, Tit. 1. Sigonius opinatur Sulpicium scripsisse qui prudens hominem occiderit. Nam apud antiquum scilicet interpretem esse, qui percusserit hominem volens occidere. Sed sciendum nihil tale in Ebraeo haberi, ac ne quidem in textu Graeco interpretum LXX. quos in hac historia praecipue sequitur Sulpicius. Sequentia tamen Sigonij opinionem firmant, & omnino tale quid intelligen-dum esse ipsa res clamat.
units.tr: "Whoever strikes a man": Exodus 21:12. This law was in use before the time of Moses, Genesis 9:6: "Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed." On the civil laws of the Romans, and their comparison with the Mosaic laws, see, if you like, Tit. 1. Sigonius thinks Sulpicius wrote "who by chance kills a man," for the old translator has "who strikes a man intending to kill him." But it should be noted that nothing of the kind is found in the Hebrew, nor even in the Greek text of the Seventy, whom Sulpicius especially follows in this history. Yet what follows confirms Sigonius's opinion, and the matter itself plainly cries out that something of this kind must be understood.

units.la: Capite poenas luet] non licebat judicibus hanc poenam condonare. Quod hodie nimis pervulgatum est. Utinam severius plecterentur homicidae. Non tot caedes passim committerentur. Vide Deut. 19. 13. & 100 sol. 64 col. 4.
units.tr: "He shall surely be put to death": the judges were not allowed to remit this penalty. This is now too commonly known. Would that murderers were punished more severely; then so many killings would not be committed everywhere. See Deuteronomy 19:13, and p. 100, col. 4 of the same book.

units.la: Qui imprudens] Paulus libro quinto sententiarum, titulo ad legem Corneliam de sicariis, Diffinitionem casus & voluntatis in homicidio servari rescripto Hadriani confirmatur. Verba rescripti, Et qui hominem occidit, absolvi solet, scili et si non occidendi animo id admisit: & qui non occidit, sed voluit occidere, pro homicida damnatur, &c.
units.tr: "Whoever unintentionally": Paul, in the fifth book of his Sentences, under the title on the Cornelian law concerning assassins: The definition of chance and will in homicide is upheld by a rescript of Hadrian. The words of the rescript: "He who kills a man is usually acquitted, if he committed the act without intending to kill; and he who does not kill, but wished to kill, is condemned as a murderer," etc.

units.la: Idem ibidem, Qui hominem occidit, aliquando absolvitur & qui non occidit, ut homicida damnatur. Consilium enim uniuscujusque nonfactum puniendum est. Ideo-que qui cum vellet occidere, casu aliquo perpetrare non potuit, ut homicida punitur: & is qui casu telo hominem ferierit, absolvitur. Gregorianus, Ea quae ex improviso casu potius quam fraude accidunt, fato plerumque, non noxae imputantur. Plura de his in collatione legum Romanarum & Mosaicarum, tit.1. Vide, si otium est.
units.tr: The same, in the same place: "He who kills a man is sometimes acquitted, and he who does not kill is punished as a murderer. For the intention of each person, not the deed, is to be punished. So he who, wishing to kill, could not carry out the deed by some accident, is punished as a murderer; and he who strikes a man with a weapon by chance is acquitted." Gregorian: "What happens unexpectedly by chance rather than by fraud is generally imputed to fate, not to guilt." More on these matters in the collation of Roman and Mosaic laws, tit. 1. See it, if you have the leisure.

units.la: Imprudens] nescius per errorem, casu nullo occidendi propo-sito. Hunc casum Graeci ἀτυχήματα[?] vocant.
units.tr: "Unintentionally": without knowledge, through error, by chance, with no purpose of killing. The Greeks call this kind of case ἀτυχήματα [misfortunes], that is, mishaps.

units.la: Rite] κατὰ θεσμόν[?], secundum leges.
units.tr: "Duly": according to the laws [κατὰ θεσμόν].

units.la: Exul erit] ad urbes exilio destinatas confugiet, aut ad aram. Nam in deserto nullae urbes erant, Jos.20 3. Proinde locus perfugii, cum in deserto versarentur, erat altare, ut multi putant: aut castra Levitarum, ut R. Salomon arbitratur. Post constituta sunt asyla, de quibus Num.35. Deut.19. Jos.20. Ratio, ut eo confugere possent, qui procul a magistratu aberant, donec de causa cognosceretur, ne a vindice opprimerentur. Altera ut ibi cognita causa usque ad mortem summi sacerdotis tuto ha-bitarent.
units.tr: "He shall flee": he shall take refuge in the cities appointed for exile, or at the altar. For in the wilderness there were no cities, Joshua 20:3. Therefore the place of refuge, while they were in the wilderness, was the altar, as many think, or the camp of the Levites, as R. Solomon supposes. Afterwards the cities of refuge were established, of which Numbers 35, Deuteronomy 19, and Joshua 20. The purpose was that those who were far from the magistrate could flee there, until the case was examined, so that they would not be crushed by the avenger. The other purpose was that, once the case had been decided there, they might dwell safely until the death of the high priest.

units.la: Qui patrem matremve pulsaverit, &c. ] duae leges sunt. Una, Qui parentes pulsaverit, id est percusserit, verberaverit: altera, Qui convitium eis dixerit. Utriusque poena capitalis erat, quamquam diversa. Nam percussor strangulabatur, convitiator lapidabatur. Proditum in capite ubi de suffocatis agitur, non esse reum percussionis nisi qui livorem fecerit. Jam vero qui percutit parentes post obitum eorum, liber est. Secus fit ubi quis maledixerit eis. Nam etiam qui post mortem eorum id faciebat, lapidabatur. Dicunt praeterea, Filius non debet pulsare parentes improbos, licet poenam capitalem propterea non subeat. Quod si parentes eum incitaverint ad cultum deorum falsorum, tum licet maledicere ei. Nam scriptum est, non parces, &c. Qui verbis aut nutu contemnit patrem matremve maledictus est, Deut.27 16. Proverb.30.17. item 23.22. Quod hic locus intel-ligi debeat de percussione minime levi docet R. Salomo, ita scribens, Non est filius reus, nisi percussio fuerit cum livore. Videatur Lyra. Nam quod in eo, nisi ex procussione[?] fiat ef-fusio sanguinis vel livor, non incurritur poena mortis, indiget examine. Siquidem effusionis sanguinis nulla mentio in Salomone illo. Jonathan hic habet, occidetur suffocatione sudarii, vult dicere, qua fit per sudarium. Quod genus supplicij [illegible, ~3 letters] appellant. Fiebat autem hunc in modum, Imponebant reum supino[?] usque ad genua, cujus collum duo mappa utrinque constringebant donec animam efflaret. R. Salomo. Vbi simpliciter & absolutè positum [illegible, ~2 words] morte afficitor, debet accipi de strangulatione: ubi vero additum est, sanguis ejus super eum esto, debet accipi de lapidatione.
units.tr: "He who strikes his father or mother, etc.": there are two laws. One: "He who strikes his parents," that is, who beats or wounds them; the other: "He who speaks abuse to them." The penalty for each was capital, though different. For the striker was strangled, the reviler stoned. It is recorded in the chapter on those who are suffocated that a person is not guilty of striking unless he left a bruise. Moreover, he who strikes his parents after their death is free. It is otherwise when someone has cursed them; for he who did this even after their death was stoned. They say further that a son ought not to strike wicked parents, although he does not undergo capital punishment for it. But if the parents have urged him to the worship of false gods, then it is lawful for him to curse them. For it is written, "Do not spare," etc. "He who by word or gesture despises his father or mother is cursed," Deuteronomy 27:16; Proverbs 30:17; likewise 23:22. That this passage must be understood of a very slight blow, R. Solomon shows, writing: "A son is not guilty unless the blow leaves a bruise." See Lyra. For that it is not the case that the penalty of death is incurred unless the blood flows or a bruise results from the blow, requires examination; for in that Solomon there is no mention of the shedding of blood. Jonathan here has "he shall be put to death by suffocation with a cloth," meaning that it is done by means of a cloth. This kind of punishment they call [illegible]. It was done in this way: they laid the accused on his back, with his neck tied by two cloths, one at each end, until he breathed out his soul. R. Solomon: where the sentence is stated simply and absolutely, he is put to death, it should be understood of strangulation; where, however, it is added, "his blood shall be upon him," it should be understood of stoning.
