units.la: Convitiumque eis dixerit] Exod. 21.17. Levit. 20.9. Qui maledixerit patri suo, &c. Hic est [illegible, ~3 letters] in Hebræo. Pœna erat lapidatio, ut diximus. Nam legimus Patri & matri maledixit, sanguis, ejus super eum esto. Id de lapidatione intelliguntur, quam [illegible, ~3 letters] vocant. Notabis in Mose (&) positum pro aut. Nam satis ad pœnam, si alterutri maledixisset. Id tamen fieri debebat per unum ex nominibus Dei propriis. Nam si per agnomen aliquod maledicebat, non incurrebat pœnam maledictionis. Non tamen plane immunis erat ab omni pœna. Nam subibat eandem cum iis qui alteri maledixisset. Similiter puniebatur qui avo suo aut avia maledixerat. Notata hæc sūt in [illegible, ~2 letters] sol.67. col.3.
units.tr: "And whoever shall curse them": Exod. 21.17; Lev. 20.9, "He that curseth his father, etc." The Hebrew here has [illegible]. The penalty was stoning, as we have said, for we read "He that cursed father or mother, his blood be upon him," which is understood of stoning, which they call [illegible]. Note that in Moses "or" (&) is put for "or" (aut). It was enough for the penalty if he had cursed either one of them. Yet he had to do this by one of God's proper names. If he cursed by some other appellation, he did not incur the penalty of the curse. Nor was he entirely free of every penalty, for he underwent the same as one who had cursed another. Likewise was punished one who had cursed his grandfather or grandmother. These points are noted in [illegible], sol. 67, col. 3.

units.la: Si quis Hebræum surreptum vendiderit] Vlpianus lib 8. de officio proconsulis, tit. ad legem Fabiam. Lege Fabia tenetur qui civem Romanum; eundemque qui in Italia liberatus sit, celaverit, vinxerit, vinctumque habuerit, vendiderit, emerit, quive in eam rem socius fuerit. Vide collationem legum, tit. 14.
units.tr: "If anyone shall steal a Hebrew and sell him": Ulpian, book 8, On the Office of the Proconsul, title on the Lex Fabia. Under the Lex Fabia is liable whoever has concealed, bound, kept in chains, sold or bought a Roman citizen who has been freed in Italy, or who has been an accomplice in that deed. See the Collatio legum, title 14.

units.la: Hebræum ]In fonte est [illegible, ~3 letters] virum, aut hominem. Sed LXX. ediderunt [illegible, ~10 letters] quemptam filiorum Israel. Oncelos quoque & Ionathan, animam ex filis Israel, id est, hominem Israelitam, vel si mavis, Ebræum. Locus est Exod. 21.17. Vide etiam Deut. 24.7. In collatione Romanarum legum cum Mosaicis citatur ex hoc loco. Quicumque plagiaverit quemquam in Israel & vendiderit eum, &c.
units.tr: "A Hebrew": in the source the word is [illegible], which means "man" or "person." The LXX rendered it "a soul of the sons of Israel." Onkelos and Jonathan also have "a soul from the sons of Israel," that is, an Israelite man, or if you prefer, a Hebrew. The place is Exod. 21.17; see also Deut. 24.7. In the comparison of Roman laws with Mosaic law, the Collatio cites this passage: "Whoever kidnaps anyone in Israel and sells him, etc."

units.la: Vendiderit] sive vendiderit eum, sive deprehensus fuerit in manu ejus ante venditionem, non refert. Hoc tamen arbitrarium esto. Nam pro, inventus fuerit in manu ejus. Hiero. edidit, convictus noxæ: & alius exponit, convincatur reus illius criminis.
units.tr: "Shall sell him": whether he sold him, or was caught in his hand before the sale, makes no difference. Yet this is open to debate. For "was found in his hand," Jerome rendered "convicted of the crime"; and another explains it as "let the accused be convicted of that crime."

units.la: Morti dabitur] Strangulabitur. Ionathan, R. Salomo. In collatione legum supra memoratarum, Sciendum est ex Novellis constitutionibus capitali sententia plagiatores pro atroatrocitate facti puniendos: quamvis Paulus crucis & metalli poenam hujusmodi reis irrogavit.
units.tr: "Shall be given to death": He shall be strangled. So Jonathan and R. Solomon. In the collation of the laws mentioned above, it should be noted that from the Novels, plagiarists are to be punished by capital sentence on account of the atrocity of the deed, although Paulus imposed the penalty of the cross and the mines on such defendants.

units.la: Si quis servum proprium] jure Romano, si dominus servum dolo occiderit, reus homicidii fit: sed punitur ut homicida servi, non ut homicida liberi hominis: & ex lege Cornelia, non ex plebiscito. Vide collationem legum illarum tit. 3, qui de jure ac ser-vitia dominorum. Vide etiam notas, pag. 82.
units.tr: "If anyone shall strike his own slave": By Roman law, if a master kills a slave by fraud, he becomes guilty of homicide; but he is punished as the killer of a slave, not as the killer of a free man, and under the Lex Cornelia, not under a plebiscite. See the collation of those laws, title 3, on the right and the servitude of masters. See also the notes, p. 82.

units.la: Servum] Chananæum, Ionathan alienigenam, alij etiam Ebræum, R. Salomo, si recte illum capio.
units.tr: "A slave": a Canaanite. Jonathan renders it "a foreigner," others also "a Hebrew," R. Solomon, if I understand him rightly.

units.la: Servamne] vel ancillam, Nicolaus de Lyra, Ista lex loquitur de servo vel ancilla gentilibus.
units.tr: "Male or female slave": or a maidservant. Nicholas of Lyra: this law speaks of male and female slaves who are gentiles.

units.la: Percusserit] baculo aut virga.
units.tr: "Strikes": with a staff or a rod.

units.la: Pag. 29. Reus judicio fiet] fons Ebræum habet vindicando vindicabitur; & Græcus, [illegible, ~12 letters], quod reddunt, poena punietur. Pœnæ genus indicant interpretes Ebræi, quam ajunt esse capitalem, Nam sic utique Ionathan, judicabitur judicio gladii. Verbum e verbo, occisionis gladij. q.d. damnabitur ad gladium: & R. Salomo vindicabitur morte gladij.
units.tr: p. 29. "He shall be punished": The Hebrew text has "shall be avenged, avenged," and the Greek has [illegible], which they render "shall be punished with a penalty." The Hebrew interpreters indicate the kind of penalty, which they say is capital. For Jonathan renders it "shall be judged by the judgment of the sword." Word for word, "of the killing of the sword," that is, "he shall be condemned to the sword." R. Solomon: "shall be avenged by death by the sword."

units.la: Sic alibi, gladius vindicans aut ulciscens. R. Levi, vindicabitur gladio, quemadmodum exponit ipsa lex, inquiens, Qui fuderit sanguinem hominis. &c. Nam effusio sanguinis fit gladio, juxta consuetum morem, & invenitur quoque verbum [illegible, ~3 letters] de gladio, ut gladius vindicans. Scholion Abenezræ est, Patres traditione acceperunt hunc locum intelligentiam habere ex illo, gladius vindicans. Quanquam vindicta fiat & aliis modis.
units.tr: So elsewhere, "the sword avenging or taking vengeance." R. Levi: "shall be avenged by the sword, as the law itself explains, saying, 'He who sheds the blood of a man, etc.'" For the shedding of blood is done with the sword, according to the usual custom, and the word [illegible] is also found of the sword, as "the avenging sword." The Scholion of Abenezra says: "The Fathers received by tradition that this place has its understanding from that: 'the avenging sword.'" Although vengeance is also taken by other means.

units.la: Si quis partum non deformatum] aut delenda negatio, aut aliqua quædam addenda, ut fit, Si quis partum non deformatum mulieri excusserit, multabitur: (in quantum maritus poposcerit aut judices constituerint) si deformatum, neci dabitur. Nam in mente habuit locum ex editione Græca, Exod. 21.22. ἐὰν δὲ μαχόντωσι δύο ἄνδρες, καὶ πατάξῃ γυναῖκα ἐγκύων, καὶ ἐξέλθῃ τὸ παιδίον αὐτῆς μὴ ἐξεικονισμένον, ἐπιζημιωθήσεται [?] καθότι ἂν ἐπιτιθῆται ὁ γυναικὸς ἀνὴρ αὐτοῦ, καὶ δώσει διὰ κριτῶν· ἐὰν δὲ ἐξεικονισμένον ᾖ, δώσει ψυχὴν ἀντὶ ψυχῆς, &c.
units.tr: "If anyone strikes out a child not yet formed": Either a negation is to be deleted, or something is to be added, as often happens: "If anyone strikes out a child not yet formed from a woman, he shall be fined (as much as the husband demands or the judges set); if it is formed, he shall be given to death." For he had in mind a passage from the Greek edition, Exod. 21.22: ἐὰν δὲ μαχόντωσι δύο ἄνδρες, καὶ πατάξῃ γυναῖκα ἐγκύων, καὶ ἐξέλθῃ τὸ παιδίον αὐτῆς μὴ ἐξεικονισμένον, ἐπιζημιωθήσεται [?] καθότι ἂν ἐπιτιθῆται ὁ γυναικὸς ἀνὴρ αὐτοῦ, καὶ δώσει διὰ κριτῶν· ἐὰν δὲ ἐξεικονισμένον ᾖ, δώσει ψυχὴν ἀντὶ ψυχῆς, &c.

units.la: Non deformatum] fœtus non formatus, qui nondum formam aut effigiem hominis accepit. David Psal. 139. [?] dixit, id est, imperfectum. Lexicon Suidæ, ἐξεικονισμένον, μιμοσφαιρωμένον, puta utero jam verminante. Mulieri] gravida.
units.tr: "Not formed": a fetus not formed, which has not yet received the form or image of a human being. David said it in Psalm 139 [?], that is, imperfect. In the lexicon of Suidas, ἐξεικονισμένον is μιμοσφαιρωμένον, that is, when the womb is already stirring. "To the woman": pregnant.

units.la: Neci dabitur] Id Ebræus dicit, dabit animam pro anima. tendit occidere hunc & occidit illum, liber est a morte: tantum pendit hæredibus occisi sanguines ejus ut fi venditus fuiflet in foro. Sed Abenezra, Quidam, inquit, dicunt 'mori debere percutere. Occiditur autem quia cogitavit occidere fratre suum. Quod demonstrant ex eo quod de natis dictum fit, multando multabitur: de morte autem mulieris dictum (consulendi sunt codices Ebrei: Nam hæc paullo aliter ibi referuntur, quam in textu Græco, aut apud noflrum Sulpitium) dabis animam pro anima. Quod ti de multa intelligitur, quid amplius imponitur ei qui occidit foeminam, atque ei qui occidit natos? Quod fi dixerimus etiam hos multæ subjacere, cur Scriptura mutat nunc sermonem, dicendo animam pro anima? Alia controversia est eorum qui dicunt eum qui intendit occidere hunc & occiditillum non affici morte. Mutat autem Scriptura sermonem ut dicat animam pro anima, quoniam multa animæ major est multo quam puerorum. Id probant conse-quæ verba, oculum pro oculo; quod intelligi non potest ad litteram, sed de redemptione per pecuniam. Haffenus R. Abraham. Videamus nunc quid Nicolaus hac de re scribat: Reddet animam pro anima, id est, morietur. Aliqui vero doctores Ebræi dicunt quod non per hoc intelligitur pœna mortis, eo quod non intendebat percutere mulierem vel fœtum ejus animatum interficere: sed fo-lum incurret pœnam pecuniæ fecundum taxationem judicum. Sed hoc videtur irrationabiliter dictum, cum uxor fit una caro cum viro quem intendebat percutere: & ideo prima expositio videtur melior, quia intelligitur pœna mortis cum dicitur, reddet animam pro anima.
units.tr: "Shall be given to death": The Hebrew says, "he shall give life for life." If he intends to strike this one and strikes that one, he is free from death; he only pays to the heirs of the slain whatever price he would have fetched if he had been sold in the market. But Abenezra: "Some, he says, say that the one who strikes must die. He is killed because he thought of killing his brother. They demonstrate this from what is said of the children: 'fining he shall be fined'; but of the death of the woman it is said (the Hebrew codices must be consulted, for these are reported there a little differently than in the Greek text or in our Sulpitius), 'you shall give life for life.' If this is understood of a fine, what more is imposed on one who kills a woman than on one who kills children? And if we say these too are subject to a fine, why does Scripture now change its wording, saying 'life for life'? There is another dispute about those who say that one who intends to kill this one and kills that one is not punished with death. Scripture changes its wording to say 'life for life,' since the fine for a soul is much greater than for children. The words that follow prove it: 'eye for eye,' which cannot be understood literally, but of redemption by money." Haffenus, R. Abraham. Now let us see what Nicholas writes on this matter: "He will give life for life, that is, he will die. But some Hebrew teachers say that this does not mean the penalty of death, because he did not intend to strike the woman or to kill her living fetus, but only incurs a monetary penalty according to the judges' assessment. But this seems to be said irrationally, since the wife is one flesh with the husband whom he intended to strike; and therefore the first explanation seems better, because the penalty of death is understood when it is said, 'he shall give life for life.'"

units.la: Si quis fervo oculum, &c.] de fervo Chananæo hæc dici censent, legemque extendunt ad præcipua membra corporis, ut sunt digiti manuum ac pedum, aures, nasus, membrum quo viri fumus. Ita R. Salomo. Vide collationem legum tit. 3. de domino-rum servitia cohibenda, Quibus addes ex l. Si in lege, etc. Etsi domidominus plenissimam servi habeat coercitionem, tamen nec inusitatis ministeriis artificium ejus corrumpere, nec cicatricibus deformare potest. Et ex L.1. §.3. de off. & praef. Si intolerabilis dominorum saevitia videtur, cogantur servos suos bonis conditionibus vendere. recte sane. Nam expedit reipub. ne quis resua[?] male utatur.
units.tr: "If anyone strikes out the eye of a slave, etc.": They think this is said of a Canaanite slave, and they extend the law to the principal members of the body, such as the fingers of the hands and feet, the ears, the nose, and the member by which a man is male. So R. Solomon. See the collation of laws, title 3, on restraining the servitude of masters. To this you may add from L. "Si in lege," etc.: although the master has the fullest power of coercing his slave, he can neither corrupt his skill with unusual services nor disfigure him with scars. And from L. 1 §3 de off. et praef.: "If the cruelty of masters seems intolerable, they shall be compelled to sell their slaves on good terms." Rightly so; for it is expedient for the commonwealth that no one should misuse his own property.

units.la: Servo] aut ancilla Chananaea. Chananaeam voco quae Judaea non est, hoc est alienigenam aut gentilem. Sic servus Chananaeus, qua vocabulo usi sunt Jonathan & R. Salomo, ab aliis exponitur alienigena vel gentilis. Quod postremum invenies in glossis Nicolai de Lyra.
units.tr: "Slave": or a Canaanite maidservant. I call Canaanite whoever is not of Judea, that is, a foreigner or gentile. So the Canaanite slave, a term used by Jonathan and R. Solomon, is explained by others as foreigner or gentile. You will find the latter in the glosses of Nicholas de Lyra.

units.la: Oculum aut dentem] idem censendum de aliis membris principalibus viginti quatuor, quae Judaei vocant Capita membrorum. Sunt autem digiti pedum decem, & digiti manuum totidem: item duae aures, nasus & membrum virile. Hoc ex traditione habere Judaeos autor Abenezra. Vide Nicolai de Lyra. Quod servii Ebraei attinet, de illo legimus, non exhibit, ut exire solent servi. ei illatum damnum retaliabatur ex Levit. 24.19.
units.tr: "An eye or a tooth": The same should be held of the other twenty-four principal members, which the Jews call the "heads of the members." These are the ten toes and as many fingers, likewise the two ears, the nose and the male member. The author Abenezra says the Jews have this from tradition. See Nicholas de Lyra. As for the Hebrew slave, we read of him that he shall let him go free, as slaves are wont to go out; the damage done to him was repaid by retaliation according to Lev. 24.19.

units.la: Vindicta liberabitur] Vindicta genus erat manumissionis apud Romanos: qua nunquam usi Ebraei, quod sciam. Quocirca male hoc loco id nomen inseruit, & rem obscuriorem reddidit. Apud Mosen, dimittet eum liberum pro oculo quem emit.
units.tr: Shall be freed by vindicta: a vindicta was a form of manumission among the Romans, which the Hebrews, as far as I know, never used. So the word was wrongly inserted here and has made the matter more obscure. Moses says he shall let him go free in exchange for the eye he has knocked out.

units.la: Taurus si hominem occiderit] haec lex antiquissima est. Nam legimus Gen. 9. Vestri sanguinis & ereptae vitae poenas expetam ex bestiis. Unde quod hic de tauro sive bove praecipitur, Ebrei extendunt ad omnes bestias, quae hominem occiderint. Augustinus quaest. 81. Quod de tauro positum est, a parte totum intelligendum est, quicquid de pecoribus usui humano subditis infestum est hominibus.
units.tr: If an ox gores a man: this law is very ancient. For we read in Gen. 9: "Of your blood and of your lost life I will require a reckoning from the beasts." Hence the Hebrews extend what is ordered here about the ox, or bull, to all beasts that kill a man. Augustine, Quaest. 81: what is said of the ox must be understood by a part for the whole: whatever among the animals subject to human use is dangerous to men.

units.la: Hominem] liberum videlicet. Nam si servus erat, tum in triginta drachmis pecunia domino servi numerabatur. Vide sequentia. Jam vero pro hominem, in fonte est, virum aut foeminam.
units.tr: A man: that is, a free man. For if he was a slave, then thirty shekels of money were counted to the slave's master; see what follows. But in the original the word for "man" means either a man or a woman.

units.la: Taurus] cornupeta sive petulcus.
units.tr: An ox: one that gores with its horns, or is prone to butting.

units.la: Si Dominus sciens bestiae vitium] si Dominus tauri, sciens eum petulcum esse, non consuluerit, id est, custodiverit eum.
units.tr: If the owner, knowing the beast's vice: if the owner of the ox, knowing it was prone to butting, did not take precautions, that is, did not keep it under guard.

units.la: Et ipse lapidabitur] etiam ipse lapidabitur cum tauro Graecum προσαποθανεῖται[?] simul morietur, accepit de lapidatione, cum posset extendi latius ad aliud genus supplicij. Sane in Ebraeo legitur [illegible, ~3 letters] morte afficietur aut occidetur. Id quidam narrant, occidetur cœlitus a Deo. Nam non poterat redimi, qui a judicibus morti adjudicatus erat. Alij, mortis reus erit, nisi se redemerit.
units.tr: He too shall be stoned: he too shall be stoned along with the ox. The Greek [προσαποθανεῖται] means "shall die with it." It is taken of stoning, though it could be extended more widely to another kind of punishment. Indeed in the Hebrew it reads [...] he shall be put to death or killed. Some explain that he shall be killed by God from heaven, for one who had been condemned to death by the judges could not be ransomed. Others take it as: he shall be liable to death unless he ransoms himself.

units.la: Servum] vel ancillam. Quæ de alienigenis interpretantur.
units.tr: A male slave, or a female slave. These things are interpreted of foreigners.

units.la: In triginta dragmis] suspicor Sulpicium edidisse, drachmis. Nam dragma huic loco non quadrat. Significat enim manipulum. Notum ut siclus in drachmam aliquando transferatur.
units.tr: For thirty drachmas: I suspect that Sulpicius printed drachmis. For the drachma does not fit this place, since it means a handful (manipulus). It is well known that the shekel was sometimes rendered as the drachma.

units.la: Sed forte legendum, didrachmis. Sic enim certe hoc loco habet editio Græca, ἀργυρίου τριάκοντα δίδραχμα δώσει τῷ κυρίῳ ἀὐλῶν[?]. Siclum didrachmum fuisse notius est quam ut probari debeat. De communi siclo loquor, non de sacro, qui tetradrachmus erat. Unde Budæus siclum esse ait numinum tetradrachmū, quantum vel stater valet.
units.tr: But perhaps one should read didrachmis, two-drachma pieces. For the Greek edition certainly has it this way in this place: "thirty didrachms of silver he shall give to the lord" [ἀργυρίου τριάκοντα δίδραχμα δώσει τῷ κυρίῳ]. That the common shekel was a didrachm is too well known to need proof. I speak of the common shekel, not the sacred one, which was a tetradrachm. Hence Budaeus says the shekel is the tetradrachm coin, as much as a stater is worth.

units.la: Si quis defoderit lacum] sensus est, si lacum, quem quis defoderit, non operuerit operculo. Lacum, id est, fossam aut foveam. Græci λάκκον appellant: Unde quidam existimant scribi debere laccum. Nam lacus aliud est in Latio. Ut noster defossum lacum, ita Virgilius dixit defossi specus, & Columella, scrobem defodere. Id fieri debebat in loco ubi communiter homines & jumenta versantur.
units.tr: If anyone digs a pit: the sense is, if he does not cover with a lid the pit which he has dug. A pit, that is, a trench or a hole. The Greeks call it [λάκκον], whence some think it should be written laccum, for lacus means something else in Latin. As our text has defossum lacum, so Virgil said defossi specus, and Columella scrobem defodere. This ought to be done in a place where men and beasts of burden commonly move about.

units.la: Pecasque[?] bos aut asinus, aut aliud animal humanis usibus deserviens. Augustinus, a parte totum intelligendum.
units.tr: Or an ox, or a donkey, or any other animal serving human use. Augustine: the whole must be understood from the part.

units.la: Non enim si equus ceciderit aut ovis, ideo non reddet, quia scriptum non est. Idem R Salomo. Videndus Lyra. Bovem Senes hoc loco βοῦν appellant, quem male vitulum reddunt.
units.tr: For if a horse or a sheep falls, he will not for that reason fail to repay, because it is not written. Rabbi Solomon says the same. See Lyra. Here the Seventy call the ox [βοῦν], which they wrongly render as a calf.

units.la: Pretium pecudis domino dabit] vel pecudis domino, vel pretium pecudis, id est, quanti æstimabitur pecus vivum, unde postea detrahebatur pretium mortui sive cadaveris.
units.tr: He shall give the price of the beast to its owner: either the beast itself to the owner, or the price of the beast; that is, what the living animal is valued at, from which afterwards the price of the dead animal or carcass was deducted.

units.la: Alterius taurum] τὸν ταύρον τῆς ἀλλοτρίας[?] bene interpretantur, taurum alterius. Minus bene Benzita[?] homo Ebræus, taurum fivebovem socium. Nam bos non habet socium, inquit, Abenezra, nisi forte ipsum Benzita.
units.tr: Another's ox: they translate well [τὸν ταύρον τῆς ἀλλοτρίας], "the ox of another." Less well is Benzita, a Hebrew man, who renders it "an ox or a companion ox." For, says Abenezra, an ox has no companion, unless perhaps Benzita himself.

units.la: Pecus] vivum, id est, bovem qui altero bove occiso vivus remansit.
units.tr: The living beast: that is, the ox which remained alive when the other ox was killed.

units.la: Peremptum etiam dividunt] occisum bovem partiuntur, hoc est dividunt in duas partes, quarum unam accipiet dominus vivi bovis, alteram habebit dominus occisi. Nicolaus, Dicit R. Salomo, quod lex ista intelligenda est de bobus æqualibus in valore. Aliter enim dominus bovis interficientis alium reportaret inde lucrum aliquando, quod effet contra rationem. Verbi gratia, si corium aut carnes bovis interfecti valerent sex libras (quia licet Iudæis esset illicitum comedere carnes illas, poterant tamen eas vendere gentilibus ad comedendum, quibus non erant prohibitæ) & bos interficiens valeret duas, si uterque dominus haberet medietatem utriusque pretii, sequeretur quod ille, cujus bos valebat solum duas libras, reportaret quatuor, &c
units.tr: They also divide the dead one: they divide the slaughtered ox, that is, split it into two parts, of which one will go to the owner of the living ox and the other to the owner of the dead one. Nicolaus: Rabbi Solomon says that this law must be understood of oxen equal in value. Otherwise the owner of the ox that killed the other would sometimes gain by it, which would be against reason. For example, if the hide or the meat of the slain ox were worth six pounds (since although it was unlawful for Jews to eat that meat, they could still sell it to Gentiles to eat, to whom it was not forbidden), and the goring ox were worth two, then if each owner had half of the value of both, it would follow that he whose ox was worth only two pounds would receive four, and so on.

units.la: Vitium tauri sciens] sciens taurum esse petulcum, & cornu ferire.
units.tr: Knowing the ox to be prone to butting, and to gore with its horn.

units.la: Non consuluerit] non custodierit eum.
units.tr: Did not keep it under guard.

units.la: Si quis vitulum subripuerit] & vendiderit aut macta-verit. Vitulum autem dicit, quem Græci μόσχον[?] interpretantur: quæ vox in hoc loco taurum vel bovem denotat. Certe in Ebræo est [illegible, ~3 letters]. Vitulum autem [illegible, ~3 letters] dicitur. Quæ confundenda non erant.
units.tr: If anyone steals a calf: and sells it or slaughters it. Now he says "calf" (vitulum), which the Greeks render [μόσχον]; in this place that word denotes an ox or a bullock. Certainly in the Hebrew it is [...]; but the calf is called [...]. These were not to be confused.

units.la: Quinque] pro uno quinque boves.
units.tr: Five: five oxen for one.

units.la: Ovem] πρόβατον[?]. Sic etiam Hiero. Alii, parvam pecudem. Ut ad bovem pertinent majora pecora, videlicet equi, asini, cameli: sic ad ovem minora, in quibus & capræ.
units.tr: A sheep: [πρόβατον]. So also Jerome. Others: a small beast. Just as the larger cattle, namely horses, asses and camels, belong to the ox, so the smaller belong to the sheep, among which are goats too.

units.la: Quadrupli pœna erit] quatuor oves restituet. Cur gravius punitur furtum bovis quam ovis? Utrum quia bos major est? an quia majus damnum accipit, qui bonem[?] amittit, cessante inte-rea agricultura, quæ sine bobus non fiebat. Antiqui enim bubus arabant. Quidam existimant oves, quia gregatim pascuntur facilius custodiri: contra boves facilius abduci. Nam ovis furem non sequitur. Debet eam humeris portare, quod molestum est. Bovem facilius ante se potest agere, aut sune ducere. Vide sis A-benezram.
units.tr: The penalty shall be fourfold: he shall restore four sheep. Why is theft of an ox punished more severely than theft of a sheep? Is it because the ox is larger? Or because he who loses the ox suffers the greater loss, agriculture meanwhile ceasing, which was not carried on without oxen? For the ancients ploughed with oxen. Some think it is because sheep, grazing in flocks, are more easily guarded, whereas oxen are more easily led away. For a sheep does not follow the thief; he must carry it on his shoulders, which is troublesome. He can more easily drive an ox before him, or lead it by a rope. Please see Abenezra.

units.la: Si viva pecora] boves, asini, oves.
units.tr: If living beasts: oxen, asses, sheep.

units.la: Penes abactorem[?] vel furem. Abactor, qui & abigeus & abigeator, quantitate à fure discernitur. Abactor enim est qui greges abducit: fur qui ovem aut bovem furatur. Claudius, Quantitas discernit furem ab abigeo. Qui enim unam suem surripuerit ut fur coercetur: qui gregem ut abigeus. Vide collationem legum, tit. XI.
units.tr: Found in the possession of a rustler or a thief. An abactor, who is also called abigeus and abigeator, is distinguished from a thief by quantity: an abactor is one who drives off flocks, a thief one who steals a sheep or an ox. Claudius: quantity distinguishes the thief from the rustler. For he who steals a single pig is punished as a thief, but he who steals a herd is punished as a rustler. See the Collatio legum, title 11.

units.la: Dupla restituet] duo reddet, videlicet id quod furto abstulit, & aliud ejus generis, vel falcem[?] valerem ipsius. R. Salomo, non reddet quod mortuū, est, sed vivum aut pretium ejus. In libro qui vocatur 200[?] fur testibus convictus duplū resti tuebat, videlicet pro uno denario duos, & pro uno came-lo aut asino duos: item pro uno tegumento duo. Si ipse prodebat furtum suum, tantum sortem pendebat. Hæc ibi,
units.tr: He shall restore double: he shall give back two, namely what he took by theft and another of the same kind, or its value. Rabbi Solomon: he does not restore what is dead, but the living animal or its price. In the book called 200[?], a thief convicted by witnesses paid double: for one denarius two, and for one camel or ass two, likewise for one covering two. If he himself confessed his theft, he paid only the principal. Thus far there.

units.la: Nocturnum furem] hæc lex habetur. Exod. 22 2, quam eo-dem modo interpretatur S. Augustinus. Vide glossam ordinariam ad hunc locum. Vlpianus lib. vij, ad edictum, si furem noctur-num, quem lex 12 tabularum omnimodo permittit occidere, aut diurnum, quem eadem lex permittit, sed ita demum, si se telo de-fendat, videamus an lege Aquilia teneatur. Adito jus ad collationem legum, tit. vij.
units.tr: A thief at night: this law is found at Exod. 22 2, which St Augustine interprets in the same way. See the ordinary gloss on this passage. Ulpian, book 7 on the Edict: "If we consider whether someone who kills a night thief, whom the Twelve Tables allow to be killed in any case, or a day thief, whom the same law allows to be killed only if he defends himself with a weapon, is liable under the Lex Aquilia." See the Collatio legum, title 7.

units.la: Furem] parietem domus noctu perfodientem, & in effossione deprehensum.
units.tr: A thief: one breaking through the wall of a house at night and caught in the act of digging through.

units.la: Occidi licet] percussor non erit reus sanguinis, id est, cædis: quod Græci dicunt [?] αὐτῷ φόνῳ [?]; Ebrai, non erunt ei sanguines. Nota Ebraismum.
units.tr: He may be killed: the striker will not be guilty of blood, that is, of murder, which the Greeks express as [αὐτῷ φόνῳ]; the Hebrews say, "there shall be no bloods for him." Note the Hebraism.

units.la: Diurnum non licet ) si post ortum solem deprehendebatur in furto, non licebat eum occidere. Qui occidebat, incurrebat pœnam homicidij. Fur autem hoc modo deprehensus si habebat unde reddaret, reddebat: sin non habebat, vendebatur pro suo furto. Deprehenso furto penes eum bovis, asini, ovis aut caprae viventis, duplum reddebat.
units.tr: A day thief may not be killed: if he was caught in the theft after sunrise, it was not lawful to kill him, and whoever killed him incurred the penalty for homicide. But a thief caught in this way, if he had the means, made restitution; if he did not, he was sold for his theft. If the stolen goods were found in his possession, living ox, ass, sheep or goat, he made restitution double.

units.la: Alterius [?]ata] agrum aut vineam. Ager feritur, vinea plantatur. Non ergo [?]ata tantum, sed etiam plantata.
units.tr: Another's [...]ata: a field or a vineyard. A field is sown, a vineyard is planted. So not only sown but also planted.

units.la: Eversa restituet] damnum farciet de optima parte agri sui aut vineæ suæ. Quod hic dictum de agro & vinea debet extendi latius, ut etiam de horto & oliveto, &c. intelligatur. Ceterum Ebraica veritas habet, Si quis depascı fecerit agrum aut vineam, &c. Qua lege non tenetur nisi qui pecus suum immiserit in aliena.
units.tr: He shall make restitution for what is destroyed: he shall make good the loss from the best part of his own field or vineyard. What is said here of field and vineyard should be understood more widely, so that it applies also to garden and olive grove, and so on. Moreover, the Hebrew truth has: "If anyone causes his beast to graze in a field or vineyard," and so on. By this law no one is bound except him who has let his own beast into another's land.

units.la: Si depositū perierit] depositū Græci vocat [?], quod quis apud alium deposuit, custodiendumque commisit sive pecunia fuerit aut vestes aliaque suppellectilia. Id si de domo surreptum, nec fur deprehensus fuerit, tum depositarius, inquit, jurabit se rem alterius non intervertisse. Id enim valet se nihil dolo egisse. Nam sensus est, dolo malo. Iusjurandum autem siebat coram dius, hoc est, judicibus aut magistratu. Deos enim vocant [illegible, ~6 letters] ut notatum a Theodorito. Quocirca minus recte hoc loco Seniores ediderunt [illegible, ~4 letters] τῷ Θεῷ. Iudices enim, cum plures essent, dij vocantur non Deus. Quanquam vox Ebraea Elohim ad utrumque ambigua sit. Ceterum in codicibus Ebraeis nulla mentio iurisiurandi, subintelligitur tamen ex verbis illis, applicabitur ad Deos. Nam, ut ait R. Salomo, applicatio nihil aliud est quam juramentum. Cui firmando R. Abraham ita scribens, in verbis illis, applicabitur ad Deos, continetur juramentum, quod fiebat coram judicibus.
units.tr: If a deposit is lost] The Greek calls a deposit [παρακαταθήκη], that which someone has placed with another and entrusted to his keeping, whether money, clothes, or other household goods. If it has been stolen from the house and the thief has not been caught, then, it says, the depositary shall swear that he has not misappropriated another's property. For this means that he has done nothing by fraud, that is, with evil intent. The oath was taken before God, that is, before the judges or the magistrate. For they call them gods [illegible], as Theodoret notes. Hence the Seventy have rendered this place less correctly as [τῷ Θεῷ], to God. For when there are several judges they are called gods, not God. Yet the Hebrew word Elohim is ambiguous and can mean either. In the Hebrew manuscripts, however, there is no mention of an oath, but it is understood from those words, "he shall be brought before the gods." For, as R. Solomon says, the bringing before is nothing other than an oath. In support of this, R. Abraham writes that in those words, "he shall be brought before the gods," an oath is contained, which was taken before the judges.

units.la: Nihil se dolo egisse] Nicolaus de Lyra. Custos depositi liber erit per juramentum suum, quod non commisit fraudem in illo depósito. Hiero. ex Ebraeo hoc refert, jurabit quod non excenderit manum in rem proximi sui, ad perpetrandam fraudem. Vide sequentia, & notas nostras ad hunc locum.
units.tr: He has done nothing by fraud] Nicholas of Lyra. The keeper of the deposit shall be free by his own oath, that he has not committed fraud in that deposit. Jerome reports this from the Hebrew: he shall swear that he has not put his hand upon his neighbour's property to commit fraud. See what follows, and our notes on this place.

units.la: Fur inventus, &c.] Exod. 22.7. ἐὰν εὑρεθῇ ὁ κλέπτης, ἀποτίσει τὸ διπλοῦν[?] loquitur autem de fure depositi.
units.tr: A thief found, etc.] Exod. 22.7. If the thief is found [ἐὰν εὑρεθῇ ὁ κλέπτης], he shall pay back double [ἀποτίσει τὸ διπλοῦν]. He is speaking, however, of the thief of a deposit.

units.la: Commendatum pecus] datum: ad custodiendum. Agitur autem de custode mercenario, ut si quis oves pastori tradat aut boves bubulco, certa mercede pactus cum eis.
units.tr: A beast entrusted] given: for keeping. The subject is a hired keeper, as when someone hands over sheep to a shepherd or oxen to a herdsman, having agreed with them on a fixed wage.

units.la: A bestia interceptum] hæc lex habetur, Exod. 22.13. ἐὰν δὲ θηρίον ὑπὸ θηρίου ἁλῶσι[?] id est, interprete Sulpicio, si a bestia interceptum fuerit. Pro טְרֵפָה[?] quod legerunt LXX. hodie legunt טְרֵפָה[?] hac sententia, adducet illud in testimonium, raptum non rependet[?] Iurisprudentes ita de hac re censent. Quod raptum a fele, vulpe aut mustela redditur: secus fit, si raptum fuerit a lupo, leone, ursò, serpente. Hæc R. Salomo. Quæ adduxi propter Sigonium, qui legendum hic opinatur ab hoste interceptum. Quæ diversa lex est, habetur autem Verf. 10. ἐὰν δὲ τις δῷ τῷ πλησίον ὑποζύγιον ἢ μόσχον ἢ πρόβατον ἢ πᾶν κτῆνος φυλάξαι, συντριβῇ ἢ τελευτήσῃ ἢ αἰχμάλωτον γένηται[?], &c. id est, ab hostibus captu. Quod Ebraei טְרֵפָה[?] dicunt.
units.tr: Torn by a beast] This law is found at Exod. 22.13. If they are torn by a beast [ἐὰν δὲ θηρίον ὑπὸ θηρίου ἁλῶσι], that is, in the translation of Sulpicius, if it has been seized by a beast. For the word [טְרֵפָה, torn], which the Seventy read, the Hebrews now read [טְרֵפָה] in this sense, and he will bring that in as evidence; what is torn he shall not restore. Jurists judge the matter thus: what has been seized by a cat, fox, or weasel is restored; it is otherwise if it has been seized by a wolf, lion, bear, or serpent. So R. Solomon. I have adduced these things on account of Sigonius, who thinks that here one should read "seized by an enemy." That is a different law, and it is found at verse 10: if anyone gives to his neighbour an ass, or an ox, or a sheep, or any beast to keep, and it is broken or dies or is taken captive [ἐὰν δὲ τις δῷ τῷ πλησίον ὑποζύγιον ἢ μόσχον ἢ πρόβατον ἢ πᾶν κτῆνος φυλάξαι, συντριβῇ ἢ τελευτήσῃ ἢ αἰχμάλωτον γένηται], etc., that is, captured by enemies. This the Hebrews call [טְרֵפָה].

units.la: Pag.30. Nondum desponsatam] alibi est, non desponsatam. Græce ἀμνηστεύτον[?]. Sed in Hiero. necdum desponsatam. Nam quæ desponsata pro uxore habetur, & ita vocatur pasim. Abenezra, desponsata licet non subierit jugum viri tamen vocatur uxor.
units.tr: Page 30. Not yet betrothed] elsewhere it is, "not betrothed." In Greek [ἀμνηστεύτον]. But in Jerome it is "not yet betrothed." For she who is betrothed is held to be a wife, and is so called everywhere. Abenezra: although a betrothed woman has not yet submitted to the yoke of her husband, she is nevertheless called a wife.

units.la: Corruperit] vitiaverit verbis seductam. Talis [illegible, ~4 letters] dicebatur. In [illegible, ~2 letters] 137.4. Qui verbis seduxerit virginem ita ut ultro consentiat, vocatur מפתה[?] id est, seductor. Vide sequentia. In fonte habetur. Qui lastaverit virginem non desponsatam, & concubuerit cum ea. Ipsa puella hoc modo corrupta dicebatur מפתה[?] seducta. Unde in libro citato, Quaecunque in urbe aliqua corrupta fuerit, habetur pro seducta, nisi testibus probaverit se vi oppressam fuisse. Vi oppressa vocabatur אנוסה[?] quod per vim vitiata esset. Hanc cogebatur qui vitiaverat, Deut. 22. 29. Quod si pater eius aut ipsa in nuptias consentire nolebat, tum raptor solvebat 50. siclos argenteos, tantundem videlicet quantum seductor. Sed plura hac de re in [illegible, ~5 letters] 138,1.
units.tr: Has violated] has debauched her by words, seduced. Such a woman [illegible] was called. In [illegible] 137.4. He who has seduced a virgin by words, so that she consents of her own accord, is called [מפתה], that is, a seducer. See what follows. It is found in the source: he who has lain with a virgin who is not betrothed and has slept with her. The girl herself, thus corrupted, was called [מפתה], seduced. Hence in the book cited: whichever woman in a city has been corrupted is regarded as seduced, unless she proves by witnesses that she was overpowered by force. A woman overpowered by force was called [אנוסה], because she had been violated by force. The one who had violated her was compelled to take her, Deut. 22.29. But if her father, or she herself, was unwilling to consent to the marriage, then the ravisher paid fifty shekels of silver, evidently as much as the seducer. But more on this matter in [illegible] 138.1.

units.la: Si pater puellae nuptias recusaverit] etiam ipsa puella nuptias recusare poterat. Sed & seductor, si nolebat convenire in nuptias, non cogebatur nisi ad multam solvendam.
units.tr: If the girl's father refuses the marriage] the girl herself too could refuse the marriage. But also the seducer, if he was unwilling to agree to marriage, was compelled only to pay a fine.

units.la: Raptor] corruptor, seductor. Abusus est voce Latina. Nam raptor proprie qui rapit virginem. Rapit autem qui vim adhibet. Hic a jureconsultis Ephraeis [illegible, ~3 letters] vocatur.
units.tr: Ravisher] corrupter, seducer. The Latin word is misused here. For "raptor" properly means one who snatches away a virgin. But one snatches who uses force. Here it is called [illegible] by the Ephraimite jurists.

units.la: Dotem dabit] ut fert dos virginum, hoc est quinquaginta siclos, ut habetur Deut. 22. 29. Sunt autem 50 sicli, viginti quinque coronata: Robertus Senalis, pag. 58. viginti quinque loachimici: Forsterus in [illegible, ~3 letters] viginti quinque taleri vulgares: Adrianus Junius in Nomenclatore.
units.tr: He shall give a dowry] as the dowry of virgins is, that is, fifty shekels, as found at Deut. 22.29. Now 50 shekels are twenty-five crowns: Robertus Senalis, p. 58; twenty-five loachimici: Forster in [illegible]; twenty-five common thalers: Adrianus Junius in his Nomenclator.

units.la: Pecudi se miscuerit] cum jumento coierit.
units.tr: Has lain with a beast] has had intercourse with a beast of burden.

units.la: Morti dabitur] mortis genus erat lapidatio, ut Hiscuni Ebræus annotat, quia in sectione Ciddusim[?] de hoc facti genere legitur, sanguis eorum super eos. Etiam bestia necabatur. Vide Lyram. Sunt qui hic per analogiam prohiberi volunt omnes nefarias libidines. Vide Levit. 18. 22. & 20. 25.
units.tr: He shall be put to death] the kind of death was stoning, as the Hebrew Hiscuni notes, because in the section Ciddusim concerning this kind of deed it is read, "their blood shall be upon them." The beast too was killed. See Lyra. Some want here, by analogy, that all unlawful lusts are forbidden. See Lev. 18.22 and 20.25.

units.la: Sacrificans] immolans, adolens, offerens, libans. Quae omnia contineri verbo זבח[?] sacrificio tollitur ex Salomone Trecense Ni-colaus de Lyra. Idem eximit ab hac poena eum qui verrit, orat, aquam spargit, ambelletur, deosculatur. Scribit autem Abenezra hanc legem pertinere peculiariter ad proselytum & advenam, qui ea conditione manebat inter Israelitas, ne diis, quibus consueverat, immolaret. Idem Hiscuni annotat. Ad eundem advenam referunt legem praecedentem, quia in more positum erat, (Hiscuni mihi autor est) apud quosdam populos, puta Syros, ut cum bestiis rem & consuetudinem haberent. Ceterum Israeli prohibita videtur idololatria per secundum praeceptum decalogi, non erit tibi Deus alius, &c.
units.tr: Sacrificing] slaughtering, burning, offering, pouring libations. That all these things are contained in the word [זבח], sacrifice, is taken from Solomon of Troyes; Nicholas of Lyra also exempts from this penalty the one who sweeps, prays, sprinkles water, mutters charms, or kisses. Abenezra, however, writes that this law pertains particularly to the proselyte and the sojourner, who on this condition lived among the Israelites, that he should not sacrifice to the gods to whom he was accustomed. Hiscuni notes the same. They refer the preceding law to the same sojourner, because (Hiscuni is my authority) it was the custom among certain peoples, for instance the Syrians, to have dealings and intercourse with beasts. Moreover, idolatry seems to be forbidden to Israel by the second commandment of the Decalogue, "you shall have no other god," etc.

units.la: Idolis] τοῖς θεοῖς ἐστι in LXX. sequitur autem ἄλλῳ κυρίῳ μόνῳ. Licet etiam vertere ex Hebræo, Deo alicui. ea vis articuli. Vocat autem idola gentium Deos, quia opinione hominum pro diis habentur. Oncelos quoque, idolis populorum, quæ ab errore sic vocantur in ea lingua אֱלִילִים[?].
units.tr: To idols] [τοῖς θεοῖς ἐστι] in the Seventy; it is followed by [ἄλλῳ κυρίῳ μόνῳ], to another Lord alone. It is also permissible to translate from the Hebrew, "to some god"; such is the force of the article. He calls the idols of the nations gods, because they are held to be gods by the opinion of men. Onkelos also, [for] the idols of the peoples, which in that language are called by their error [אֱלִילִים].

units.la: Pereat] in scholio est ἀναθεματισθήσεται[?], id est, delebitur & penitus excidetur; quod LXX. dixerunt ἀνάθεμα ἐξολεθρευθήσεται[?], morte exterminabitur, Ionathan occidetur gladio & facultates eius consumentur. Quidam, ut anathema delebitur. Nam חֵרֶם[?] anathema, exterminium. Hiero. in ea quam ad Algasiam scripsit, quæst. ix. Quod autem anathema interdum occisionem sonet, multis vet. test. testimoniis probari potest. Sane idem hoc loco vertit, occidetur. Sic etiam Santes.
units.tr: Let him perish] in the scholium it is [ἀναθεματισθήσεται], that is, he shall be destroyed and utterly cut off; what the Seventy rendered [ἀνάθεμα ἐξολεθρευθήσεται], shall be exterminated by death. Jonathan: he shall be killed by the sword and his goods shall be consumed. Some: "shall be destroyed as a anathema." For [חֵרֶם] is anathema, extermination. Jerome, in the question ix. which he wrote to Algasia, says so. That anathema sometimes signifies slaying can be proved by many testimonies of the Old Testament. Indeed here the same word is rendered "shall be killed." So also Santes.

units.la: Viduam & orphanum non premendos] non affligendos, non vexandos. Hæc lex extendi debet ad omnes alios, qui propter debilitatem virium se tueri non valent.
units.tr: The widow and the orphan not to be oppressed] not to be afflicted, not to be harassed. This law ought to be extended to all others who cannot defend themselves because of weakness of strength.

units.la: Pauperem debitorem] cui mutuo pecuniam dederis, & pauperem non quemlibet, sed Iudæum, qui populus Dei vocantur: aut populum meum, id est, pauperem. Nam pauperes appellantur peculiariter populus Dei.
units.tr: A poor debtor] to whom you have lent money, and not any poor man, but a Jew, who are called the people of God; or "my people," that is, the poor. For the poor are called, in a special sense, the people of God.

units.la: Non perurgendum] οὐκ ἐπ' αὐτὸν καταπονήσεις[?], id est, non urgebis solutionem ita ut nihil de iure tuo remittas. Ambrosius videtur legisse καταπονεῖν[?]. Nam vertit, non suffocabis eum.
units.tr: Not to be pressed hard] [οὐκ ἐπ' αὐτὸν καταπονήσεις], that is, you shall not press him for payment so that you remit nothing of your right. Ambrose seems to have read [καταπονεῖν], for he renders it, "you shall not suffocate him."

units.la: Pignore non accipiendum] non tam vetat accipere, quam iubet reddere ante solis occasum, Exod 22.25. Vt hic pro pignore accipere, ita Cicero dixit, salutem suam pro pignore tradunt ad explendas cupiditates. Vsitatius est pignori sive in pignus accipere.
units.tr: Not to be taken as a pledge] it forbids not so much the taking as commands the return before sunset, Exod. 22.25. As here "to take as a pledge," so Cicero said: they hand over their own safety as a pledge to satisfy their desires. "In pignus accipere" or "pignori accipere" is more usual.

units.la: Non increpandum] οὐκ ἐγκαλεῖς κακῶς[?] interpretatur, non increpabis: sed an recte? vix opinor. Nam increpare est reprehendere. Melius redditur, non maledices. Utrumque Græci exprimunt verbo λοιδορεῖν. Nam & increpare significat, & maledicere convitiarique & probris afficere aut insectari: unde λοιδόρημα, maledictum.
units.tr: Not to be reviled] [οὐκ ἐγκαλεῖς κακῶς] is rendered "you shall not revile," but is that correct? I hardly think so. For to revile is to reproach. It is better rendered "you shall not curse." The Greeks express both by the verb [λοιδορεῖν]. For it signifies both to reproach and to curse, and to abuse or assail with insults; hence [λοιδόρημα], a curse.

units.la: Principem populi tui] ἄρχοντα λαοῦ σου: quod Ebræus dicit, principem in populo tuo.
units.tr: Thy people's prince: the Greek has "ἄρχοντα λαοῦ σου" [ἄρχοντα λαοῦ σου], which the Hebrew renders as "prince in thy people."

units.la: Primogenita omnia] tam hominum quam pecudum: quorum illa redimebantur quinque siclis post trigesimum diem, hæc manebant apud matrem septem dies, die autem octavo dabantur Deo, hoc est sacerdoti Dei ministro. Nicolaus de Lyra, Primoge-nita hominum redimebantur quinque siclis argenti. Dicit autem hic R, Salomo quod quilibet siclus valet quinque solidos: tamen non dicit cujus monetae, & ideo melius videtur dicendum quod valor determinatus est nobis incertus, quia sicut frequenter dictum est, monetae & pondera auri & argenti multum variantur secundum tempora & varias regiones.
units.tr: The firstborn of all: of men as well as of beasts. The firstborn of men were redeemed for five shekels after the thirtieth day, while the firstborn of beasts stayed with their mother for seven days and were given to God on the eighth day, that is, to the minister of God, the priest. Nicholas of Lyra: "The firstborn of men were redeemed for five shekels of silver." Here the rabbi Solomon says that each shekel is worth five shillings, but he does not say of what coinage, and so it seems better to say that its exact value is uncertain to us, since, as has often been said, the values of gold and silver coins and weights vary greatly according to time and region.

units.la: A fera raptam ]θηριάλωτος a fera captam, id est, raptam. Nam capio interdum idem quod rapio. Codex Ebraeus habet, in agro raptam. Sed in Oncelo, a fera dilcerptam: & in Hiero. a bestijs praegustatam. Caro illa canibus projicienda erat.
units.tr: Torn by a beast: taken by a beast [θηριάλωτος], that is, seized or torn, since capio sometimes means the same as rapio. The Hebrew manuscript has "taken in the field." Onkelos has "torn to pieces by a beast," and Jerome "tasted beforehand by wild beasts." That flesh was to be thrown to the dogs.

units.la: Coitiones, &c.] ἡ συγκάλυψις vertit, non facies coitiones: quod alij reddunt non consentiēs; & alij, non dispones pactum, id est, συνθήκας. Nam συνθήκη pactum. Συγκατάθεσις proprie, simul pono calculum in urnam, in eadem sententiam descendo, assentior. Ebraice est, non pones manum cum improbo. Id explicant, ne auxilium ei praestes, vel, ne in societatem cum eo coeas. Praecedit autem, ne accipias auditionem vanam, sive rumorem vanum, qui saepe solet spargi de viris bonis & piis. Hanc theologiam si didicissent theologi quidam non tam facile essent ad accipiendam divulgandamque calumniam. Cave, inquit, calumniatori sidem habeas. Nam tam peccat qui admittit calumniam, quam qui dicit eam. Iudices quoque monentur hoc praecepto ne temere credant accusatori, sed alteram aurem accommodent reo.
units.tr: Coitiones, etc.: the Greek [ἡ συγκάλυψις] is rendered "do not make covenants" by one, which others render "do not agree," and others "do not set up a pact," that is, [συνθήκας]. For [συνθήκη] means a pact. [Συγκατάθεσις] properly means "I place my pebble in the urn together with another and descend into the same opinion, I assent." In Hebrew it is "do not put your hand with the wicked." They explain it as "do not give him help," or "do not enter into fellowship with him." It is preceded by "do not receive a vain report," or an empty rumour, which is often spread about good and pious men. If certain theologians had learned this teaching, they would not so readily receive and spread a slander. Beware, it says, of giving credit to a slanderer. For he who admits a slander sins as much as he who tells it. Judges too are warned by this precept not to believe an accuser rashly, but to lend the other ear to the accused.

units.la: Aut in quacumque malitia] ἐν κακία interpretatur cum Augustino, in malitia: cum possit exponi, ad malum. Sic Ebraeus codex, nisi quod ibi, ad mala pro ad malum. Forte legerunt He pro Thau. Nam affinitas aliqua inter has litteras. Κακία potius vitiositas. Nam malitia aliud est in Latio.
units.tr: Or in any malice: [ἐν κακία] is rendered, with Augustine, "in malice," though it could be explained as "to evil." So the Hebrew manuscript, except that there it reads "to evils" instead of "to evil." Perhaps they read He for Thau, for there is some affinity between these letters. [Κακία] means rather "vice," for "malice" is a different thing in Latin.

units.la: Inimici pecus errans] quidam hoc restringunt ad inimicum fratrem: ego latius patere non dubito. Ceterum bona ex hoc praecepto manant, si recte observetur, duo. Unum est quod pecus errans in viam reducitur, alioqui forte denorandum a feris: alterum quod occasio hinc inimico te amandi. Isidorus, Asinum reduci jubet, ut hac ratione odientis animum conciliet. Nam si omnino implacabilis & inexorabilis no fuerit, fieri non potest quin hac humanitate animus illius non mansuescat.
units.tr: The enemy's straying ox: some restrict this to a brother who is an enemy, but I do not doubt that it extends more widely. Moreover, two good things flow from this precept if it is rightly observed. One is that the straying animal is brought back to the road, otherwise perhaps to be devoured by wild beasts; the other is that it gives an occasion of loving your enemy. Isidore orders that the ass be brought back, so that by this means he may win over the heart of the one who hates. For if he is not wholly implacable and unyielding, it cannot be that his heart is not softened by such kindness.

units.la: Pecus] bovem aut asinum, aut aliud quodvis jumentum.
units.tr: Ox: an ox, or an ass, or any other beast of burden.

units.la: Reduces] ad inimicum. Multo magis ad eum qui non est inimicus. Sic alibi, Ciba hostem tuum. Si hostis cibandus, ergo & is qui hostis non est. Addita clausula, si elurierit. Similiter, si sitierit, da potum.
units.tr: Bring back: to the enemy. Much more to one who is not an enemy. So elsewhere, "Feed your enemy." If an enemy is to be fed, then also one who is not an enemy. A clause is added: if he hungers. Similarly, if he thirsts, give him drink.

units.la: Si animal inimici tui] ὑποζύγιον[?] vertit animal, proprie a-nimal sive immentum subjuge. Sed Senes peculiariter ad asinum restringunt hoc loco & Exod. 20.10, item Gen. 36.24. Sic Matth. 21. ὑποζύγιον, filium asinae.
units.tr: If the beast of your enemy: [ὑποζύγιον] is rendered "animal," properly "animal" or "beast put under the yoke." But the elders restrict this passage specially to the ass, as also Exodus 20:10 and Genesis 36:24. So in Matthew 21, [ὑποζύγιον] is "the colt of an ass."

units.la: Innocentem & justum] ἀθῷον[?] καὶ δίκαιον[?]. Videntur synonyma esse, sed non sunt. Nam innocens, qui sine culpa est, licet damnatus sit a judicibus. Iustus vero, qui culpam habet, licet a judicibus absolutus sit. Vide notationes nostras ad hunc locum.
units.tr: Innocent and just: [ἀθῷον] and [δίκαιον]. They seem to be synonyms, but they are not. For the innocent is one who is without fault, even if he has been condemned by judges. The just, however, is one who has fault, even if he has been acquitted by judges. See our notes on this passage.

units.la: Non justificabis impium pro muneribus] ὀυ δικαιώσεις τὸν ἀσεβῆ ἕνεκεν δώρων[?]. Sic Græci LXX. Sed in Hebræo aliter, quia non justificabo impium. Et, munera non accipies. Pro impium alij reponunt improbum. Sic vocatur reus sons ἢ ὑπο-δικος[?]. Unde lux Davidi, cum judicabitur, id est, litigabit, exeat improbus.
units.tr: You shall not justify the wicked for gifts: [οὐ δικαιώσεις τὸν ἀσεβῆ ἕνεκεν δώρων]. So the Greek Septuagint. But in the Hebrew it is otherwise, namely, "I will not justify the wicked." And "you shall not take gifts." Others substitute "the dishonest" for "the wicked." Thus the guilty defendant is called [ὑπόδικος]. Hence the saying of David's: "when he is judged," that is, when he goes to law, "let the wicked come forth."

units.la: Iustificabis] absolves.
units.tr: You shall justify: absolve.

units.la: Pro muneribus] additum a Græcis. Nam in Hebræo, ut dixi, Non justificabo improbum. Q.d. licet insons declaratus sit a judicibus, tamen a me non erit impunitus. Ego in illum suo tempore animadvertam, prout meretur. Hoc judicium mihi relinquendum erit. Aut, non justificabo improbum judicem, qui justum occiderit ullave injuria affecerit.
units.tr: For gifts: added by the Greeks. For in the Hebrew, as I said, it is "I will not justify the wicked." That is to say: although he has been declared innocent by the judges, yet he will not go unpunished by me. In his own time I will punish him, as he deserves. This judgment must be left to me. Or: I will not justify the wicked judge who has put a just man to death or done him any injury.

units.la: Advenam] tam eum qui per terram tuam iter fecit, quam eum qui in ea commoratur. Lex hæc habetur Exod. 23.9. quam nonnulli restringunt ad advenam prætereuntem. Alia lex est, Exod. 22.21, quam enarrant de advena qui apud nos habitat.
units.tr: The stranger: both him who has travelled through your land and him who dwells in it. This law is found in Exodus 23:9, which some restrict to the passing stranger. There is another law, Exodus 22:21, which they explain of the stranger who lives among us.

units.la: Expende diligentius.
units.tr: Consider this more carefully.

units.la: Benigne habendum] malim, non vexandum aut affli-gendum. Nam in textu Græco ξένῳ[?]. Editio Hiero. pere-grino non eris molestus.
units.tr: To be treated kindly: I would prefer "not to be vexed or afflicted." For in the Greek text it is [ξένῳ]. The Vulgate edition of Jerome: "you shall not be troublesome to the stranger."

units.la: Sabbato] id est, die septimo.
units.tr: Sabbath: that is, the seventh day.

units.la: Fructus septimi anni non metendos] videtur in eadem sententia fuisse cum Augustino, qui scribit licuisse quidem seminare hoc anno, sed non colligere fruges, cum aliud sonent verba Mosi, Exod. 23.11. Nam terra inculta penitus relinquebatur.
units.tr: The fruits of the seventh year not to be gathered: it seems to have been of the same opinion as Augustine, who writes that it was permitted indeed to sow in this year, but not to gather the crops, since the words of Moses, Exodus 23:11, sound otherwise. For the land was left entirely uncultivated.

units.la: Quod autem sponte nascebatur, id pauperibus cedebat. Ceterum annus ille ἀφέσεως[?], id est, remissionis & annus sabbata-rius dicebatur.
units.tr: Whatever grew of its own accord, however, went to the poor. That year was also called [ἀφέσεως], that is, the year of release, and the sabbatical year.

units.la: Altariumque sub duodecim lapidibus sub monte con-stituit] secutus est eos qui putant hoc altare extructum fuisse ex duodecim lapidibus juxta numerum tribuum, quae duodecim erant. Hujusmodi altare olim & Elias extruxit. Videndum Lyra, Exod. 14.10. Glossa interlinearis ad locum, Ædificavit altare Domino & duodecim titulos: In alia translatione legitur quod ex 12. lapidibus unum altare constructum fit. Editio Graeca ἀνοδόμησε[?] ἐκ τῶν δώδεκα λίθων εἰς τὰς δώδεκα φυλὰς τῶν Ἰσραήλ[?]. Lapides hoc est alij titulos, alij statuas vocant. Quod potius denotat vox Ebraea.
units.tr: And he set up an altar under twelve stones at the foot of the mountain: he followed those who think that this altar was built of twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes, which were twelve. Elijah too once built an altar of this kind. See Lyra on Exodus 14:10. The interlinear gloss on the passage: "He built an altar to the Lord and twelve titles." In another translation it is read that one altar was constructed out of twelve stones. The Greek edition has [ἀνοδόμησε ἐκ τῶν δώδεκα λίθων εἰς τὰς δώδεκα φυλὰς τῶν Ἰσραήλ]. Some call the stones "titles," others "statues." The Hebrew word rather indicates this.

units.la: Sub monte] ad radices montis.
units.tr: Under the mountain: at the foot of the mountain.

units.la: Ex 12. lapidibus] Hiscuni, Duodecim lapides statuit in altari ut testaretur omnes eos consensisse in foedere. Simile quid fecit Elias in monte Carmeli. Et accepit 12 lapides juxta numerum filiorum Israel.
units.tr: Of twelve stones: Hiscuni: He set up twelve stones on the altar to bear witness that they all had agreed to the covenant. Elijah did something similar on Mount Carmel, and took twelve stones according to the number of the sons of Israel.

units.la: Pag. 31. Nabad] leg Nadab litteris transpositis, vel ex editione Romana, in qua ναδαβ recte scriptum. Sic mox Abiu legendum pro Abiud, quod nunc scribunt Abibu, ut Aharon cum aspiratione, quia Graeci in medio fere omittunt. Vide Exod. 14.9.
units.tr: Page 31. Nabad: read Nadab, with the letters transposed, or from the Roman edition, in which [ναδαβ] is rightly written. So too shortly after, Abiu should be read for Abiud, which they now write as Abibu, and Aharon with an aspirate, since the Greeks mostly omit it in the middle. See Exodus 14:9.

units.la: Conscendit montem] septimo mensis Sivan, i. Maij.
units.tr: He went up the mountain: on the seventh day of the month Sivan, that is, May.

units.la: Non volentes Dominum intueri] Sigonius emendat, non valentes. probo vehementer, Paullo post, tanta claritudine faciei eius renidebat, ut intueri eum populus non valeret. Et in vita Martini, ultra accedere non valentes.
units.tr: Not willing to look upon the Lord: Sigonius emends it to "not able." I strongly approve. A little later: "so great a brightness shone from his face that the people could not look upon him." And in the Life of Martin: "not able to come nearer."

units.la: Locum tamen, in quo Dominus stabat] Exod. 24.10. in edit. Graeca, καὶ εἶδον τὸν τόπον οὗ ἑστήκει ὁ θεὸς τῆς Ἰσραήλ[?]. Sed in originali lingua, & viderunt Deum Israel, id est, gloriam Dei, ut quidem Chaldaei explicant.
units.tr: Yet the place in which the Lord stood: Exodus 24:10 in the Greek edition: [καὶ εἶδον τὸν τόπον οὗ ἑστήκει ὁ θεὸς τῆς Ἰσραήλ]. But in the original language it is "and they saw the God of Israel," that is, the glory of God, as the Chaldeans indeed explain it.

units.la: Cujus mirabilis forma] καὶ τὰ ὑπὸ τὴς ποδὰς αὐτοῦ ὡσεί[?] [illegible, ~40 letters] Exod. 14,10. Mox Verf. 17. Aspectus autem gloriae Domini erat sicut ignis vorans super cacumine montis, in oculis filiorum Israel.
units.tr: Whose wonderful form: [καὶ τὰ ὑπὸ τὴς ποδὰς αὐτοῦ ὡσεί] [illegible, about forty letters] Exodus 14:10. Shortly after, at verse 17: "The sight of the glory of the Lord was like a devouring fire on the top of the mountain, in the eyes of the sons of Israel."

units.la: Quae circum montem steterat] qua montem atque adeo ipsum Dominum obduxerat.
units.tr: Which had stood around the mountain: which had covered the mountain and indeed the Lord himself.

units.la: Huic tam praeciso operi] Vide quae scripsimus ad pag. 16.
units.tr: To this so carefully wrought work: See what we have written at p. 16.

units.la: Ducere] agere. transfigeret. Seneca dixit, diem somno du-cere. Hujus compositum, traduceret.
units.tr: To lead: to drive, to pierce through. Seneca said "to drive the day with sleep." Its compound is "traduceret," would lead across.

units.la: Ex metallis conflatis] ex uno aliquo metallo, videlicet auro, quod ex inauribus foeminarum conflatum erat. Vitulum fusilem appellat Moses. Quanquam in libris Graecis μόσχον χωνευτὸν[?], vi-tulum conflatilem.
units.tr: From melted metals: from one metal, namely gold, which had been melted down from the women's earrings. Moses calls it a molten calf. In the Greek books it is [μόσχον χωνευτόν], a cast calf.

units.la: Vituli caput] aureum caput bovis, quem Ægyptii, ad quo-rum profanos ritus animos transtulerant, Apim vocant. Lactantius[?] lib.4 cap.10. Hunc vitulum etiam David hymnogra-phus bovem appellat.
units.tr: The head of the calf: the golden head of an ox, which the Egyptians, whose profane rites had turned their minds, call Apis. Lactantius, book 4, chapter 10. The hymn-writer David also calls this calf an ox.

units.la: Hostias obtulit] hostias pro salute & holocausta.
units.tr: They offered sacrifices: offerings for peace and burnt offerings.

units.la: Vinoque se dedisset] perperam explicat & sedit populus bibere. Nam certe vinum non bibebant, quod in deserto nullum erat. Addit Scriptura, & surrexerunt ludere, de quo alias.
units.tr: And had given themselves to wine: he explains it wrongly; the people sat down to drink. For certainly they were not drinking wine, since there was none in the desert. Scripture adds, "and they rose up to play," which I discuss elsewhere.

units.la: Iusto dolore] aut magnum dolorem denotat, aut eum qui ex iusta causa Sic dicimus, iustum praelium, iustas inimicitias, iustum exercitum.
units.tr: With unjust grief: this either denotes great grief, or grief arising from a just cause. Thus we say a just battle, just enmities, a just army.

units.la: Et sacrilegio deditum] familiare Sulpicio ut cultum deorum falsorum, hoc est idololatriam, sacrilegium appellet. Sic infra pag.73. mirumque; id Eliae fuit qui solum se a sacrilegio immunem esse credebat. Et p.71. exprobatoque ei sacrilegio. Vide notas ad hunc postremum[?] locum. Alibi usurpat flagitium eodem sensu, ut p.69, invisum Domino flagitium expostu-latio consecuta.
units.tr: And given over to sacrilege: it is characteristic of Sulpicius to call the worship of false gods, that is, idolatry, sacrilege. So below, p. 73: "and wonderfully, this was Elijah's, who believed that he alone was free from sacrilege." And p. 71: "and the sacrilege was thrown in his face." See the notes on this last passage. Elsewhere he uses "flagitium" in the same sense, as on p. 69: "a disgrace hateful to the Lord followed by rebuke."

units.la: Pag.32. Multis tamen increpitis, Levitas] suspicor initio scriptum fuisse a Sulpicio, multis tamen increpitos Levitas. Sic infra pag 105. Is cum deprehendisset Iudæos gentilium connubiis permissos, multis increpitos, renunciare hujusmodi matrimoniis jubet. Plenum esset, multis verbis.
units.tr: P. 32. Yet with many rebuked, the Levites: I suspect that Sulpicius originally wrote "multis tamen increpitos Levitas," many Levites, however, rebuked. So below, p. 105: "When he had discovered that the Jews had been permitted marriages with Gentiles, and had rebuked many, he orders them to renounce such marriages." The sentence would be fuller with many words.

units.la: Sed queri potest cur increpuerit Levitas, quos extra culpam fuisse in hoc quidem peccato multi putant, in queis R. Salomo. An[?] quia populo permiserint adorare vitulum? nam impedire debuif-sent quo modo. Quidam censent ex Levitis aliquos culpæ affines fuisse. Id colligunt ex verbis illis, Exod. 31. 29. coniecra-viltis manus vestras hodie Domino quisque in filio suo & in fratre suo. Tum etiam quia Aharon vitulum ipsum fudisse legitur. Nam quid mirum si Levitæ peccarint, cum etiam Aharon princeps eorum non absque peccato fuisse deprehendatur? Sed hac de re alij aliter statuatur[?] quisque judicio suo.
units.tr: But it may be asked why he rebuked the Levites, who in this sin, at least, many think were free from blame, among whom is R. Solomon. Is it because they allowed the people to worship the calf? For they ought to have prevented it, but how? Some think that some of the Levites were implicated in the fault. They gather this from those words of Exodus 32:29, "Consecrate your hands today to the Lord, each in his son and in his brother." Then also because it is read that Aaron himself cast the calf. For what wonder if the Levites sinned, since even Aaron, their leader, is found not to have been without sin? But on this matter others decide differently, each according to his own judgement.

units.la: XXIII. millia] in libris Ebræorum, tria millia tantum. Sed & in Græcis εἰς τρισχιλίους ἄνδρας[?]. Latina exemplaria mire variant. Quædam habent, quasi triginta millia: alia, quasi viginti tria millia: alia, quasi tria millia, videlicet Biblia regia & novem manuscripta, præter Rabbanum.
units.tr: 23,000: in the Hebrew books only three thousand. But also in the Greek, "to three thousand men." The Latin copies vary greatly. Some have about thirty thousand, others about twenty-three thousand, others about three thousand, namely the Royal Bibles and nine manuscripts, besides the Rabbanum.

units.la: Tabernaculum] quod vocatur tabernaculum conventus, vel potius testorium, id est, Ohel. Nam tabernaculum [?]אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד[?] dicitur. Sed interpretes ista confundunt. Senes vocant, τὸ σκηνὴ τῆς μαρτυρίας[?] tabernaculum testimonii, (הָעֵדוּת אֹהֶל[?]) vocatur Num. 17. 8.) Eduth cum Moed confundentes.
units.tr: The tabernacle: which is called the tabernacle of meeting, or rather the tent of testimony, that is, Ohel. For it is called [אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד], the tent of meeting. But the translators confuse these things. The elders call it [הָעֵדוּת אֹהֶל], the tabernacle of testimony, which is mentioned in Numbers 17:8, confusing Eduth with Moed.

units.la: Extra castra] procul a castris, Exod. 33. 7. Ebræi scribunt abfuisse a castris spatio duorum millium cubitorum, quo spatio determinant iter sabbathi, cujus mentio in primo Actorum Apostolicorum. Adhibe quæstiones meas.
units.tr: Outside the camp: far from the camp, Exodus 33:7. The Hebrews write that it stood at a distance of two thousand cubits from the camp, which space they fix as the sabbath day's journey, the mention of which is in the first chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. Consult my questions.

units.la: Coram] facie ad faciem, id est, præsens præsentem, ut homines solent inter se. Idem dicit, ore ad os. Virumque proverbiale est, Abenmelech explicat, facie ad faciem, id est, familiariter & nullo angelo intermedio, optime & rectissime.
units.tr: Face to face: face to face, that is, present with the present, as men usually are with one another. He also says mouth to mouth. The expression is proverbial. Abenmelech explains "face to face" as familiarly and with no angel intervening, very well and very rightly.

units.la: Ut Dominum in majestate propria videret quod Ebræus dicit, ostende mihi gloriam tuam, id Græcus extulit ἐμφάνισόν μοι σεαυτὸν[?], ostende mihi teipsum. Libri tamen variant. Nam in aliis δεῖξόν μοι τὴν σαυτοῦ δόξαν[?] & apud S. Augustinum, ostende mihi tuam gloriam. Locus est Exod. 33. 18. Hanc gloriam Sulpicius majestatem propriam appellat, infrà facies vocatur & a nostro forma: quam ajunt significare veritatem essentiæ ipsius, quam nemo unquam asequi potuit.
units.tr: That he might see the Lord in his own majesty: what the Hebrew says is "show me your glory," which the Greek rendered [ἐμφάνισόν μοι σεαυτόν], show me yourself. Other books vary, however; in some it is [δεῖξόν μοι τὴν σαυτοῦ δόξαν], and in St Augustine, "show me your glory." The passage is Exodus 33:18. Sulpicius calls this glory "his own majesty"; below it is called a face, and by our author a form, which they say signifies the truth of his essence, which no one has ever been able to attain.

units.la: Formam ei, &c.] 33. 20. non poteris videre faciem meam: nam non videbit me homo & vivet. Quæ hic facies vocatur, noster[?] formam dixit. Quid causæ esse putabimus? An quia facies quandoque formam significat? Nam dicimus, vertere in omnes facies, pro eo quod est in omnes formas, & Plautis ait, in faciem versus est Amphitryonis Iupiter : quod mox dicit, mutavit se in formam ejus conjugis. (eterum duplex apprehensio divinitatis. Una est per priora, quae nunc vocatur facies Dei: altera est per posteriora, quae est cum ex operibus Dei cognoscimus ipsum. Hoc modo etiam nos videmus Deum.
units.tr: Form to him, etc.: Exodus 33:20, "You cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live." What is here called face our author called form. What cause shall we suppose? Is it because face sometimes signifies form? For we say "to turn into all faces" for "into all forms," and Plautus says, "Jupiter has turned into the face of Amphitryon." What he says next is: he changed himself into the form of his spouse. Moreover there is a twofold apprehension of divinity. One is through the former things, which is now called the face of God; the other is through the latter, which is when we know him from the works of God. In this way we too see God.

units.la: Sunt qui per faciem intelligunt divinam essentiam, ut per posteriora effectus divinae providentiae sive gubernationis, qui sunt proprie viae Domini, sic Paulus episcopus Burgensis. Nicolaus exponit, concedam tibi cognitionem mei, imperfectam tamen, sicut cum aliquis videt hominem a parte posteriore, sive a tergo, cognoscit quidem esse hominem, non tamen cognoscit quis sit. Sane ut duplex est Dei apprehensio, ita duplex est sciendi methodus. Una quae a natura cognitis et prioribus ad nobis nota et posteriora deducitur : altera quae eadem via ab ultimis ad prima recurrit. Haec ἀπὸ ὁδείξεως: illa ἐπαγωγὴ [?] colligitur. Innuit ergo Deum non cadere sub apodixin, cum eo nihil sit antiquius.
units.tr: Some understand by the face the divine essence, and by the hinder parts the effects of divine providence or government, which are properly the ways of the Lord; so Paul, bishop of Burgos. Nicholas expounds: "I will grant you a knowledge of me, yet imperfect, just as when someone sees a man from behind, or from the back, he indeed knows that it is a man, but does not know who he is." Indeed, as the apprehension of God is twofold, so the method of knowing is twofold. One proceeds from things prior by nature to the things posterior that are known to us; the other runs back by the same way from the last to the first. The former is [ἀπὸ ἀποδείξεως], by demonstration; the latter is [ἐπαγωγή], gathered by induction. He therefore hints that God does not fall under demonstration, since nothing is earlier than him.

units.la: Tabulaeque refectae] refectae fuerunt, hae tabulae partim a Deo, partim a Mose, qui eas sculpsit : Deus autem scripsit in iis decem praecepta, Exod. 34. 1.
units.tr: And the tablets were remade: these tablets were remade, partly by God and partly by Moses, who carved them; God, however, wrote on them the ten commandments, Exodus 34:1.

units.la: In hoc colloquio Dei]secundo. Nam his cum Deo locutus est in monte.
units.tr: In this conversation with God: secondly. For with these he spoke with God on the mountain.

units.la: Tanta claritudine, &c.] facies ejus resplendebat et radiabat ut cornu: unde cornuta pingitur. Vide Quaestiones meas.
units.tr: With such brightness, etc.: his face shone and radiated like a horn; whence he is painted horned. See my Quaestiones.

units.la: Renidebat] vel, renitebat: ut epist. 3. vu tus (B. Martini) luce clarior renitebat. pag. 237. edit. Plantiniana.
units.tr: Shone: or "shone out," as in epistle 3, the virtue of (St Martin) shone clearer than light, p. 237, Plantin edition.

units.la: Velamento] καλύμματι [?] velamen erat, quod Ebraei masve vocant : interpres Ierosolymitanus Sudara nuncupat, unde forte sudarij vox. Quanquam significatio diversa. Hoc velamento usus est cum ad populum verba faceret, propter splendorem vultus ejus, quem ferre non valebant : idem que abstulit, quando cum Deo loquebatur. Exod. 34 in extremo.
units.tr: With a veil: [καλύμματι], a veil, which the Hebrews call masveh; the Jerusalem interpreter calls it sudara, whence perhaps the word "sudary." Though the meaning differs. He used this veil when he addressed the people, because of the brightness of his face, which they could not bear; and he took it off when he spoke with God. Exodus 34, at the end.

units.la: Interiorumque ejus] quae sunt arca, mensa, candelabrum, altare thymiamatis, altare holocausti, labrum aeneum, atrium tabernaculi, pontificalia ornamenta et alia a Deo mandata.
units.tr: And its inner parts: these are the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering, the bronze laver, the court of the tabernacle, the priestly vestments, and the other things commanded by God.

units.la: Pag 43. Vtiplum Moyses aditu excluderet] nubes obumbrans tabernaculum. Mosen ab adito excludebat stans supra tabernaculum, eundem admittebat. Quoties vero recedebat, simul Israelitae castra movebant, dum eaconsisteret. Nam duce via nu-
units.tr: P. 43. Moses kept the people from the entrance: a cloud overshadowing the tabernacle. Standing above the tabernacle, it kept Moses from the entrance, yet it admitted him again. Whenever it withdrew, at the same time the Israelites moved camp, while it stood still. For the cloud served as their guide on the way.

units.la: I dem habebat interdiu, noctu vero praecedebat eos columna ignis.
units.tr: It did the same by day; but by night a pillar of fire went before them.

units.la: qui Ebræis Bresith a prima voce, Genesis vocatur quod mundi genesin & originem continet. Sunt etiam qui libros recti Genesin interpretentur, ut fit, recti pro rectorum fi-ve justorum. Nam rectum in metaphora quod justum est.
units.tr: Which the Hebrews call Bereshit from its first word; it is called Genesis because it contains the origin and beginning of the world. There are also those who interpret Genesis as "of the upright," as happens, taking "upright" for "of the upright or just," since in metaphor "upright" means what is just.

units.la: qui Ebræis Smoth & Veelle Smoth, id est, & hæc sunt nomina. Nam ita incipit apud eos.
units.tr: Which the Hebrews call Shemot, and Veelle Shemot, that is, "and these are the names"; for so it begins among them.

units.la: Hic liber ab Ebræis Vaicra nuncupatur, & liber sacerdotum, id est, [?]. Leviticus autem ideo a Græcis dicitur, quia Levitarum, quibus sacra ministeria tradita erant, officia complebantur.
units.tr: This book is called by the Hebrews Vayikra, and the book of the priests, that is, [?]. Leviticus is so called by the Greeks because the sacred duties, which had been committed to the Levites, were carried out by them.

units.la: id est, sacrificandi, ut pag. 40. idolis litaverunt & 67. idola eis ritu gentium suarum, quibus litaverat, constituit. & pag. 69. Vaccam auream in Bethel, alteram apud Dan constituit, quibus populus litaret. In his locis omnibus litare posuit pro sacrificare, cum proprie sit sacrificio facto Deum placare.
units.tr: That is, of sacrificing. As at p. 40 they "sacrificed" to idols, and at p. 67 he set up for them idols in the manner of their own nations, to which he had sacrificed; and at p. 69 he set up a golden calf at Bethel and another at Dan, for the people to sacrifice to. In all these places he uses "sacrifice" for "offer sacrifice," though properly it means to propitiate God by a sacrifice made.

units.la: tam moralis quam judicialis.
units.tr: Both moral and judicial.

units.la: sic infra pag. 38. Levitis sum assumptis. Quod sane capiendum. Nam soli Aharonitæ sacerdotio fungebantur. Aharonitas vocoposteros Aharonis, qui ex ipso genus ducebant: quibus reliqui Levitæ in templo ministrabant. Hi peculiariter Levitæ vocantur, ut alii sacerdotes, licet ambo eundem autorem generis haberent. Siquidem Aharon quoque ex filiis Levi erat. Aut sacerdotij vocabulo etiam Levitarum munus comprehendit. Sane pag. 53. Samuelem sacerdotem appellat, cum Levita tantum esset.
units.tr: So below, at p. 38: "I took the Levites." This must be understood with care, for only the sons of Aaron performed the priesthood. I call the descendants of Aaron, who traced their line from him, Aaronites; the rest of the Levites ministered to them in the temple. These are called Levites in a special sense, as the others are priests, though both had the same ancestor, since Aaron himself was also of the sons of Levi. Or else he includes the work of the Levites under the word "priesthood." Indeed, at p. 53 he calls Samuel a priest, though he was only a Levite.

units.la: Num. 2. 33. Levitæ non sunt numerati inter filios Israel.
units.tr: Num. 2.33: The Levites were not counted among the sons of Israel.

units.la: omisit minorem numerum. Nam in editione Græca, ἑξακόσιαι χιλιάδες [?] καὶ τριακόσιοι καὶ πεντήκοντα [?]: & in Latina, sexcenta tria millia quingenti quinquaginta. Sic etiam codices Ebræi.
units.tr: He has left out the smaller number. For in the Greek edition it reads six hundred thousand [?] and three hundred and fifty [?], and in the Latin, six hundred and three thousand five hundred and fifty. The Hebrew manuscripts also read so.

units.la: qui suavissimus erat, & mellis saporem referebat, aut humorem ex oleo, id est, שמן [?].
units.tr: Which was very sweet and tasted like honey, or a moisture of oil, that is, שמן [shemen].

units.la: pisces Ægyptios, cucumeres, pepones, porros, cepe & allia. Num. 11. 6.
units.tr: Egyptian fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic. Num. 11.6.

units.la: quod genus avium Arabicum sinus alit: quarum volatus non admodum sublimis est, sic ut manu facile prehendi possint.
units.tr: A kind of bird which the Arabian bay nourishes. Its flight is not very high, so that they can easily be caught by hand.

units.la: XX. & III. virorum millia
