units.tr: Twenty-three thousand men.

units.la: Eo, quem desiderabat, cibo punitus est Quanquam dubitari potest, sintne mortui ex cibo illo injelito, an vero Deus alia plaga eos affecerit, propter inordinatum appetitum carnium, pro quibus dulcissimum manna contemnebant
units.tr: He was punished with the very food he craved. Yet it may be doubted whether they died from that ill-omened food, or whether God struck them with some other plague because of their disordered craving for meat, for which they despised the sweetest manna.

units.la: Exploratoribus Hi ab Ebraeis [illegible, ~4 letters] vocantur, eratque primores tribuum suarum.
units.tr: These are called [illegible, about four letters] by the Hebrews, and they were the leaders of their tribes.

units.la: Gentes validas
units.tr: Strong peoples.

units.la: Tunc Iesus
units.tr: Then Joshua.

units.la: Chaleb
units.tr: Caleb.

units.la: Consciscis vestibus
units.tr: Rending their garments.

units.la: Flentes
units.tr: Weeping.

units.la: Hostes praedae potius
units.tr: Enemies, rather for plunder.

units.la: In perniciem eorum
units.tr: To their destruction.

units.la: Hostibus
units.tr: To enemies.

units.la: Exploratoribus interfectis ditionem conciverant. erant autem decem numero.
units.tr: Having killed the spies, they had stirred up the people against them. Now there were ten of them.

units.la: Dathan & Abiron ducibus] dux præcipuus erat Core, qui putatur pontificatum ambiisse. Dathan autem & Abirom offensi erant propter jus primogenituræ, ut vulgo creditum, quod ademptum illis datum erat filiis Iofeph. bis se socium jungebat quidam On filius Pheleth, de filiis Ruben.
units.tr: Dathan and Abiram, leaders: the chief leader was Korah, who is thought to have aspired to the high priesthood. Dathan and Abiram were aggrieved over the right of the firstborn, as is commonly believed, because it had been taken from them and given to the sons of Joseph. A certain On, son of Peleth, of the sons of Reuben, joined himself to them as a partner.

units.la: Abiron] ἀβιρὼν cum N in fine. sed scribendum ἀβιρὼμ[?] ex libris Ebræis, id est, Abirom, cum M in extremo. Mendum ergo est quale in Gerson pro Gersom, Abfalon pro Absalom. Contra lectum Edem pro Eden & Madiam pro Madian. Reperitur & Abiram, sicut dicimus Adam & Odom, Corbana & Corbona. Nam hodieque Syri quidam O pro A legunt, quod vocant Odom, & respondet τῆς[?] Camets Ebræorum. id valet a magnum sive longum.
units.tr: Abiron: ἀβιρών, with N at the end. But it ought to be written ἀβιρώμ according to the Hebrew books, that is, Abirom, with M at the end. So this is an error of the same kind as Gerson for Gershom, and Abfalon for Absalom. On the other hand, Edem for Eden and Madiam for Midian have been read. Abiram is also found, as we say Adam and Odom, Corbana and Corbona. For even today some Syrians read O for A, which they call Odom, and it corresponds to the Hebrew qamets. It means "great" or "long."

units.la: Quod erat nefas nisi sacerdotibus introire] videtur sub sacerdotum nomine Levitas etiam comprehendere. Nam & illis erat introire tabernaculum, ubi sacerdotibus ministrabant extra velum. Nam intra velum ad altare soli sacerdotes litabant. Sermo mihi de velo medio. Nam tria erant. Tabernaculum, ut hoc obiter notem, tres partes habebat: quarum intima vocabatur Sanctum sanctorum, quod solus pontifex ingrediebatur semel in anno. Media Sanctum dicebatur. Extima erat atrium quod fas erat ingredi omnibus Iudæis. Hœc ætas posterior distinxit in duas partes, quarum una dicebatur atrium virorum, altera atrium fœminarum, quod in eo sola fœminæ apparerent.
units.tr: That it was unlawful for any but priests to enter: he seems to include the Levites under the name of priests as well, for they too were allowed to enter the tabernacle, where they ministered to the priests outside the veil. For within the veil, at the altar, only the priests offered sacrifice. I am speaking of the middle veil, for there were three. The tabernacle, to note this in passing, had three parts. The innermost was called the Holy of Holies, which only the high priest entered, once a year. The middle was called the Holy Place. The outermost was the court, which all Jews were allowed to enter. A later age divided this into two parts, one called the court of the men, the other the court of the women, because only women appeared in it.

units.la: Pag.35. Irrumperent] expressit verba illa editionis LXX; καὶ ἐπῇλθον[?] ἐπὶ τὴν σκηνὴν τῆς μαρτυρίας[?]. Hic Ebræus habet וַיִּקָּהֲלוּ[?] & respexerunt ad tabernaculum conventus. Sed Hieronymus ad Mosen & Aaronem retulit, interpretans, fuerunt ad tabernaculum fœderis.
units.tr: Page 35. Rushed in: this renders the words of the Septuagint edition, καὶ ἐπῆλθον ἐπὶ τὴν σκηνὴν τῆς μαρτυρίας. Here the Hebrew has וַיִּקָּהֲלוּ, and they looked to the tabernacle of the assembly. But Jerome referred it to Moses and Aaron, translating "they went to the tabernacle of the covenant."

units.la: Populi exorta seditio est | hæc acciderunt in deserto Sin, in Cades, ubi & Maria soror Aaronis diem suum obiit.
units.tr: A sedition arose among the people: these things happened in the desert of Zin, at Kadesh, where also Miriam, the sister of Aaron, died.

units.la: Seditio] potius murmuratio, quam seditio erat.
units.tr: Sedition: it was rather a murmuring than a sedition.

units.la: Vt petram virga feriret] virga qua uti consuerat; quæ virga Dei & Mosis & Aaronis dicitur. Alias probabo.
units.tr: That he should strike the rock with the rod: the rod he was accustomed to use, which is called the rod of God and of Moses and Aaron. I will prove this elsewhere.

units.la: Aqua effluxit] quæ ab hoc eventu dicta aqua Meriba, id est, jurgij aut contradictionis.
units.tr: Water flowed out: from this event the water is called Meribah, that is, of strife or contradiction.

units.la: Non nisi iterato ictu] nam bis feriebat saxum, quod est signum diffidentiæ: quam arguunt & verba illa, An expetra Hac educemus aquam? R. Salomo scribit eum peccasse propter-ea quod virga percusserit rupem, cum potuisset solo verbo elice-re aquam. Sane jussus erat loqui ad petram, non ferire eam, Num.20,8.
units.tr: Only with a second blow: for he struck the rock twice, which is a sign of unbelief, as the words also show: "Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?" R. Solomon writes that he sinned because he struck the rock with his rod, when he could have drawn water by a word alone. Indeed he had been commanded to speak to the rock, not to strike it. Num. 20.8.

units.la: Præter Edom] id est, Idumæam. Supra, præter terram Philisthiim. Sic Livius, præter Caraliten amnem agmen ductum. Sic, præter mœnia ipsa fluere.
units.tr: Beyond Edom: that is, Idumaea. Above, "beyond the land of the Philistines." So Livy: "the army was led beyond the river Caralites." So, "flowing beyond the very walls."

units.la: Efau} qui & Edom unde Idumæi. Sic Iacob alio nomine Israel dicebatur, unde Israelitæ. Efau & Iacob fratres erant uterini. Proinde cognatio & jus sanguinis inter utramque gentem.
units.tr: Esau: who is also Edom, whence the Idumaeans. So Jacob was also called Israel, whence the Israelites. Esau and Jacob were full brothers, so there is kinship and blood relation between the two nations.

units.la: Transitum negavit] ex Deuteronomio contrarium verum videtur. Sed respondent transiisse Israelitas per fines terræ Edom, non per mediam terram ipsorum. Alij dicunt, cum præter illam regionem exercitus duceretur, Idumæos cibaria aliaque necessaria contulisse ac Israelitis vendidisse. Quo restringunt verba illa, Deut.2.29. sicut fecerunt filij Esau qui habitant in Seir. Vide quoque Deut.2.5.
units.tr: He refused passage: from Deuteronomy the contrary seems true. But they answer that the Israelites passed through the borders of the land of Edom, not through its middle. Others say that when the army was led past that region, the Idumaeans supplied food and other necessities and sold them to the Israelites. By this they restrict those words of Deut. 2.29, "as the sons of Esau who dwell in Seir did." See also Deut. 2.5.

units.la: In Or montem iter convertit] qui ad fines Idumææ, ubi Moses Aaronem fratrem amisit, ac jussu Dei Eleazarum ei sufficit. Pro Or scribe Hor. cum aspiratione, mendum quale superius in Vr, quod Hur emendavimus. Hor, id est, הר[?] qui & הר[?] Har interdum scio montem ita dici appellative: sed & proprium nomen montis est, ut Taurus, quæ vox in lingua Syra montem denotat. Dicunt enim certe תורא[?] & תורא[?] unde Taurus.
units.tr: He turned the journey toward Mount Or: which lies on the borders of Idumaea, where Moses lost his brother Aaron, and at God's command Eleazar was put in his place. For Or, write Hor with an aspirate, an error like the one above in Vr, which we corrected to Hur. Hor, that is, הר [har]. I know that har is sometimes used as a common noun for a mountain, but it is also the proper name of a mountain, like Taurus, a word which in the Syriac language denotes a mountain. For they certainly say תורא, whence Taurus.

units.la: Inter consanguineos] fratres appellat Scriptura.
units.tr: Between kinsmen: Scripture calls them brothers.

units.la: Regem gentis Chananæorum] perperam interpretatus est Mosen, in quo Chanani rege Arad, quod reddunt, Chananæus rex Arad, Num.21.1. Græci codices variant. Nam editio Basileensis ea quæ in octavo folio complicat, ὁ χαναναῖος[?] βασιλεὺς Ἀραδ[?]. Romana vero ὁ χαναναῖος[?], etc. Arad nomen est opidi. Hujus rex potuit esse ex una aliqua gentium terræ Chanaan. Nam hoc nomen quando late sumitur cōprehendit sex reliquas gentes, quæ terram promissam incolebant. Ideo Chananæus dicitur; cui roborando articulus qui præcedit. Nam in Ebræo ערד הכנעני[?]. Delevit ergo non regem gentis Chananæorum, sed Chananæum seu e gente Chananæorum regem Arad: quem portentosi Judæi Amalecum nominant.
units.tr: King of the nation of the Canaanites: he has translated the text wrongly. In Num. 21.1 it is rendered "the Canaanite king of Arad," and the Greek manuscripts vary. The Basel edition has, on its eighth page, ὁ Χαναναῖος βασιλεὺς Ἀραδ, but the Roman edition has ὁ Χαναναῖος, and so on. Arad is the name of a town. Its king could have been from one of the nations of the land of Canaan, for when this name is used broadly it covers the six other nations that inhabited the promised land. He is therefore called a Canaanite, and the article that precedes it strengthens this. For in Hebrew it reads ערד הכנעני. So he has deleted not "king of the nation of the Canaanites," but "the Canaanite, that is, of the nation of the Canaanites, king of Arad," whom the boastful Jews call Amalek.

units.la: Seon quisque] scribi debet Sehon vel Sihon. Nam in scriptura Ebraica duplex aspiratio, quam vocant Heth. Qua cum careant Latini, simplici utuntur. Græci utramque omittunt in medio. Posset tamen scribi Σνών. Nam in nonnullis dictionibus spiritum medium notant. Sane discimus ex Hesychio in nomine ἀώρα olim superscribi solitum spiritum tenuem hoc modo ἀώρ,ubi significabat ἀφόλωλοι: at densum ita ἁώρα, ubi pro ἀμεί ponebatur.[?]
units.tr: Sihon, each: it ought to be written Sehon or Sihon. For the Hebrew script has a double aspirate, which they call Heth. Since Latins lack it, they use a simple one; Greeks omit both in the middle. Yet it could be written Σνών, for in some words they mark a medial breathing. Indeed we learn from Hesychius that in the word ἀώρα a light breathing used to be written above in this way, ἀώρ, where it meant ἀφόλωλοι; but a rough one was written thus, ἁώρα, where it stood for ἀμεί.

units.la: Pag.34. Regem Amorrhæorum] Num. 21.22. qui rex Hesebon, Deut. 2.27. Amorrhæos autem critici Ebræorum nunc Emoræos legunt cum E in principio & unico R.
units.tr: Page 34. King of the Amorites: Num. 21.22, who was king of Heshbon; Deut. 2.27. The Hebrew critics now read Emorites, with E at the beginning and a single R.

units.la: Perculit] percussit, occidit.
units.tr: Smote: struck down, killed.

units.la: Balan quoque & Balac reges] videtur in ea sententia fuisse ut putarint Basan esse nomen regis. Quod si est, fallitur. Nam est nomen regionis cujus rex Og nominatur Num. 21.33. occurrit eis Og rex Basan. Forte sensus, devicit regem Basan, id est, terræ Basan. Nihil affirmo.
units.tr: Balan also and Balac, kings: he seems to have held the view that they thought Bashan was the name of a king. If so, he is mistaken, for it is the name of a region whose king is called Og, Num. 21.33: "Og king of Bashan met them." Perhaps the sense is that he defeated the king of Bashan, that is, of the land of Bashan. I affirm nothing.

units.la: Super Iordanem] id est, apud, prope, secus; ut super Numicum amnem, Num. 22.1. codex Ebræus habet בעבר cis Iordanem, nempe in campestribus Moab, in ea parte quæ respicit Ierichuntem urbem trans Iordanem sitam. Hoc in Græca editione legitur παραβάλον παρὰ τὴν Ἰορδάνην χ' Ἰεριχῶ, id est, apud Iordanem e regione Iericho.[?]
units.tr: Super Iordanem: that is, at, near, beside, as in super Numicum amnem (Num. 22.1). The Hebrew codex has בעבר on this side of the Jordan, namely in the plains of Moab, on the part facing the city of Jericho, which lies across the Jordan. This is read in the Greek edition [παρὰ τὴν Ἰορδάνην ἀπέναντι Ἰεριχῶ] beside the Jordan, opposite Jericho.

units.la: Balac devicit] nusquam hoc legitur: & tamen credibile est victum Balacum, cum legatur pugnasse in Israelitas Iof. 24.9. Erat autem rex Moabitarum.
units.tr: Balac defeated: this is nowhere read. Yet it is credible that Balak was defeated, since he is said to have fought against the Israelites (Josh. 24.9). He was king of the Moabites.

units.la: Adversus Madianitas certatum] quod bellum narratur, Num. 30. Gestum autem fuit jussu Dei ob fornicationem: tum etiam quia Madianitæ Deos suos adorandos Israelitis propo-fuerant.
units.tr: Fighting against the Midianites: this war is narrated in Num. 31. It was waged by God's command because of fornication, and also because the Midianites had urged the Israelites to worship their gods.

units.la: Moyses mortuus est] obiit in monte Abarim sive Nebo, septima mensis duodecimi, qui Adar nuncupatur, ut R. Salomo scribit. Vide Lyram Iof. 2. Salmanticensis, Mortuus est anno quadragesimo, mense Adar, septimo ejus mensis, meridie in robore diei. Sunt qui tradant eum decessisse in vespera sabbathi, anno mundi conditi bis millesimo, quadringentesimo, octogesimo octavo.
units.tr: Moses died: he died on Mount Abarim, or Nebo, on the seventh day of the twelfth month, which is called Adar, as Rabbi Solomon writes. See Lyra on Josh. 2 and the Salamanca commentary: "He died in the fortieth year, in the month of Adar, on the seventh day of that month, at midday in the strength of the day." Some hold that he died on the evening of the Sabbath in the year of the world 2488.

units.la: Hebræi] filij Israel Quamvis enim ab Heber sic dicti sint, tamen peculiariter hoc nomine veniunt Israelitæ sive posteri Israelis patriarchæ: qui & Israelitæ dicuntur, licet Esau, a quo Idumæi, Israelitæ quoque parentem habuerit. Contra fit, quando Iudæi vocantur. Nam hoc nomen angustius est. Peccato ejus adscribitur] de hoc peccato varie sunt expositorum sententiae. Vide sis episcopum Burgensem Num 10. in extremo capitis, ubi sententiam R. Mosis AEgyptij & aliorum recenset.
units.tr: Hebrews: the sons of Israel. Although they are so called from Eber, the name is used in a particular sense for the Israelites, or the descendants of the patriarch Israel, who are also called Israelites, although Esau, from whom the Edomites came, also had the same parent. The reverse happens when Jews are meant, for that name is narrower. Views on this sin vary among commentators. See the Bishop of Burgos on Num. 10, at the end of the chapter, where he reviews the opinion of Rabbi Moses the Egyptian and others.

units.la: De sepulchro ejus parum compertum] aliud nihil quam sepultum fuisse in valle quadam terrae Moab, e regione Bethphegor, Deut. 34. 6. de corpore autem ejus contendisse legitur diabolus cum Michaele archangelo Judae 9. quae historia sumpta creditur ex libro apocrypho, qui Ἀναβάσεις [?] vel Ἀνάληψις Μωυσέως inscribitur, de quo alias. Sepulchrum vero ejus hominibus ignotum fuit. Deut. 34. 6. ne Judei, qui ad idololatriam proni erant, in ventum corpus adorarent, eique divinos honores exhiberent, ut conjiciunt interpretes viri docti.
units.tr: Of his tomb little is known: we know nothing more than that he was buried in a certain valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-peor (Deut. 34.6). We are told that the devil contended with the archangel Michael over his body (Jude 9). This story is believed to be taken from an apocryphal book entitled the Ascension of Moses (Analepsis or Anabasis), about which more elsewhere. His tomb, however, was unknown to men (Deut. 34.6), lest the Jews, who were prone to idolatry, should worship the body and pay it divine honours, as learned interpreters conjecture.

units.la: Nave] Nαυή, quod corruptum esse diximus ex Nαυῆ, unius litterae immutatione. Nun, Naun, ut Ϝ, Αυζ: Reu, Ragau. Nota haec iis qui libros meos legerunt.
units.tr: Nave: Naue [Ναυή], which we said was corrupted from Nauē [Ναυῆ] by the change of a single letter; Nun, Naun, as [Ϝ, Αυζ]; Reu, Ragau. Note this for those who have read my books.

units.la: Virtutibus suis simillimum] fui legendum arbitratur Sigonius.
units.tr: Most like his own virtues: Sigonius thinks it should be read fuit ("was").

units.la: Dimissis per castra nuntius] nove vocat nuntios, qui a lxx γραμματεὺς τῆς λαοῦ, scribae populi: ab Ebraeis שֹׁטְרִים [?] vocantur. Hos in apparitores transfert Mosis erant autem Levitae, jussaque magistratuum exequebantur, & reos vinciebant, lorisque caedebant. Quocirca lictores quoque vocantur ab iis qui Ebraea in Latinum sermonem verterunt. Sed Hiero. principes interpretatur, & alij praefectos. Senes uno in loco habent ἀρχιτέκτονας [?], qui alios cogunt, & Aquila ἀρχισυνάγωγος [?] & alibi ἄρχοντας [?]. Nihil dico, si שׁוֹטֵר [?] non significat aliquando praefectum. Nam definiunt, qui a rege constituuntur aut praeficitur alicui loco.
units.tr: Heralds sent through the camp: he calls them by a new name. The Seventy call them scribes of the people [γραμματεὺς τοῦ λαοῦ], and the Hebrews call them shoterim [שֹׁטְרִים]. He renders them as attendants. They were Levites, who carried out the orders of the magistrates, bound offenders and beat them with thongs. For this reason, those who turned the Hebrew into Latin also call them lictors. Jerome, however, translates them as princes, and others as prefects. The Seventy, in one place, have [ἀρχιτέκτονας], who drive the others, and Aquila has [ἀρχισυνάγωγος], and elsewhere [ἄρχοντας] (rulers). I say nothing, unless shoter sometimes means a prefect; for they define it as one appointed by a king or set over some place.

units.la: Pag. 57. Frumentum uti pararent] תִּשְׂאָה [?] est in Ebraeo, ut apud Graecos LXX. ἐπισιτισμὸς, id est, commeatus, cibaria, viaticum. Id de manna usurpatur Psal. 78. 25. Sed hoc loco de manna intelligere eo minus placet quod manna in diem colligebatur: hic autem jubentur parare viaticum in tres dies. David Camius ait nomine תִּשְׂאָה [?] significari quemvis cibum, excepto pane.
units.tr: Page 57. To prepare provisions: in Hebrew it is [תִּשְׂאָה], as the Seventy have it [ἐπισιτισμός], that is, provisions, food, viaticum. This word is used of the manna in Ps. 78.25. But it is less fitting to understand manna here, because manna was gathered for each day, whereas here they are ordered to prepare provisions for three days. David Kimchi says that the name [תִּשְׂאָה] signifies any food except bread.

units.la: Iordanis] Qui Ebraeis Iarden, a Ionatha vocatur Iordena; unde Iordanis, id est, ἰορδάνης, qui & Iordanus, id est, ἰορδάνης [?]. Oritur ex radicibus montis Libani, aut ut alij volunt, e spelunca Phaneas, quod scribunt בָּנִיאָס [?]. Forte spelunca Phaneas intradicibus erat illius montis, & in tribu Dan, quod sonat Iordanis quasi descendens ex Dan. Alij dicunt nomen habere a duobus fontibus Ior & Dan.
units.tr: Jordan: the Hebrews call it Yarden [יַרְדֵּן], which Jonathan calls Yordena; hence Iordanis, that is [ἰορδάνης], also Iordanus. It rises from the roots of Mount Lebanon, or, as others hold, from the cave of Paneas, which they write [בָּנִיאָס]. Perhaps the cave of Paneas was at the foot of that mountain, in the tribe of Dan, so that the name Jordan means "descending from Dan." Others say the name comes from two springs, Ior and Dan.

units.la: De hoc enarrat R. David Psal. 74. 15, exficcasti numina fortia. Nam flumina de uno dici notius est quam ut probari debeat.
units.tr: Rabbi David comments on this in Ps. 74.15: "You dried up mighty rivers." It is too well known that "rivers" is said of a single river to need proof.

units.la: Est autem vadum locus in flumine tam exigua profunditatis, ut pedibus transiri facile possit. Solinus, flumen quod facile vadari poterat.
units.tr: A ford is a place in a river of such shallow depth that it can easily be crossed on foot. Solinus: a river that could easily be forded.

units.la: nam tempus messis erat, Ios. 3, 15. Aristeas de hoc fluvio, perinde ut Nilus messis tempore alveos excedens & exundans multum terrę irrigat. Vide Sirachidem 24, 36.
units.tr: For it was harvest time (Josh. 3.15). Aristeas says of this river, just as the Nile, at harvest time, overflows its banks and floods, watering much land. See Sirach 24.36.

units.la: cum sacerdotes arcam portantes starent in medio alveo, aqua superior mansit firma & immota instar muri: reliqua in mare defluxit mortuum. Ita per siccum copia traductæ, & Iordanis incisus fuit.
units.tr: When the priests carrying the ark stood in the middle of the channel, the upper water stayed firm and unmoved like a wall, while the rest flowed down into the Dead Sea. Thus the abundance was crossed on dry ground, and the Jordan was cut off.

units.la: aberat a Iordane, teste Iosepho, Radius 60. ab urbe 150. R. Salomo scribit Iordanem ab urbe distare itinere unius diei Iesa, 24. 16. Iter unius diei continet quatuor parasangas: quælibet autem parasanga decem milliaria. Elias.
units.tr: It was distant from the Jordan, according to Josephus, sixty stadia, and from the city a hundred and fifty. Rabbi Solomon writes that the Jordan is a day's journey from the city (Josh. 3.16). A day's journey contains four parasangs, and each parasang is ten miles. Elias.

units.la: Similiter peccatum in Hierusalem, Hieremias, Hesaias, & aliis sexcentis: Talia scri-bus imputanda, non interpretibus. Quocirca civitas lunæ vocatur. Dicitur & urbs palmarum.
units.tr: Sin was likewise committed in Jerusalem, and Jeremiah, Isaiah, and six hundred others; such things must be imputed to the writers, not to the translators. Hence the city is called the city of the moon. It is also called the city of palms.

units.la: Nec obsidioni facile] hoc de suo adjecit. Nam in textu sacro non habetur: nec ex eo id colligi potest.
units.tr: Nor easily besieged: he added this on his own, for it is not in the sacred text, nor can it be gathered from it.

units.la: Quot buccinæ, tot sacerdotes erant, qui arcam præibant.
units.tr: There were as many priests going before the ark as there were trumpets.

units.la: per septem dies quotidie circumlata fuit: septimo, qui dies sabbathi erat, muri ac turres conciderunt, opidum incensum. Quid hinc discimus? licere sabbatho urbes expugnare, & per consequens occidere. Si occidere licet, multo magis hominem servare.
units.tr: It was carried around daily for seven days; on the seventh day, which was the Sabbath, the walls and towers fell and the town was burned. What do we learn from this? That it is lawful to storm cities on the Sabbath, and consequently to kill. If killing is lawful, much more is saving a man.

units.la: omnia igne cremata, duntaxat auro, argento, æreisque ac ferreis vasis in erarium Domini relatis, Ios. 6.24.
units.tr: Everything was burned with fire, except the gold, silver, and vessels of bronze and iron, which were brought into the treasury of the Lord (Josh. 6.24).

units.la: Tum Iesus Dominum traditur] aliqua desunt, quæ sup-pleri possent[?] ex Ios. 6.26. tum Iesus ante Dominum tradi-tur adjurasse eum qui Iericho instaurare aggressus fuisset. Græca sunt, καὶ ὤρκισεν Ἰησοῦς ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ οὕτως Κυ-ρίῳ λέγων, Ἐπικατάρατος[?]. Vide notas Gisfelini nostri.
units.tr: Then Jesus is delivered before the Lord: some words are missing, which could be supplied from Josh. 6.26: then Jesus, before the Lord, put under oath the man who should undertake to rebuild Jericho. The Greek reads: "And Jesus swore on that day, saying thus to the Lord, Cursed" [καὶ ὤρκισεν Ἰησοῦς ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ οὕτως Κυρίῳ λέγων, Ἐπικατάρατος]. See the notes of our Gisfelin.

units.la: Adversus Geth] corrigo, adversus Gæ. Nam est γῆ in codicibus Græcis. Geth aliud est Γαί, Γαὶ, ut Ἰεσ[?], Ies. Restius scriberetur Gai: sed nos quid Sulpicius scripserit, non quid scribi debeat, nunc quærimus.
units.tr: Against Geth: I correct this to "against Gai", for the Greek codices have [γῆ]. Geth is something else, [Γαί], [Γαὶ], as in [Ἰεσ], Ies. More correctly it would be written Gai, but we are now asking what Sulpicius wrote, not what ought to be written.

units.la: A tergo urbis] εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω αὐτῆς[?]. Quod mox dicit ὀπίσω τῆς πόλεως[?], interpretantur, a tergo urbis. Hiero. maluit dicere, post eam, & post civitatem. Nam urbs tergum non habet proprie loquendo.
units.tr: "Behind the city" [εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω αὐτῆς[?]]. What he says a little later, ὀπίσω τῆς πόλεως[?], they render as "behind the city". Jerome preferred to say "after it" and "after the town", since, strictly speaking, a city has no back.

units.la: Qui in opido erant] rex Gai cum suis.
units.tr: Those who were in the town: the king of Ai with his men.

units.la: Qui in insidiis fuerant] inter Bethel & Gai sive Gæ.
units.tr: Those who were in ambush: between Bethel and Ai, or Gai.

units.la: Vacuam urbem cepere] Vacuam civibus cepere & suc-cendere.
units.tr: They took the city, emptied of its citizens, and set it on fire.

units.la: Summoque supplicio affectus] innuit supplicium crucis aut patibuli, quod Ebræis עֵץ[?] lignum aut arbor dicitur. Sic etiam crux in Latio vocatur. Interdum additur epitheton infelix, ut, arbori infelici suspendito. Quod sumptum ex libris ritualibus Latinorum. Græci hic legunt ἐπὶ ξύλου ἀδύμου[?], in ligno gemino. Nam duo ligna in cruce quæ se invicem intersecant, ut fila in stamine & subtegmine. Unde hodieque crux a Iudæis appellatur שְׁתִי וָעֵרֶב[?] stamen & subtegmen. Quidam crucem a patibulo ita distinguunt. Patibulum enim proprie ajunt esse, in quo suf-fixus homo expanditur, transverso tamen ligno: crucem vero, cum is erecto simplicique stipiti adfigitur sive infigitur. Tacitus, patibula, ignes, cruces.
units.tr: And subjected to the highest punishment: he hints at the punishment of the cross or gibbet, which in Hebrew is called [עֵץ], wood or tree. So too in Latium the cross is called the tree. Sometimes the epithet "unlucky" is added, as in "hang him on the unlucky tree," taken from the Latin ritual books. Here the Greeks read [ἐπὶ ξύλου ἀδύμου], "on a double wood," for there are two pieces of wood in the cross which cross each other, like threads in the warp and the weft. Hence even today the Jews call the cross [שְׁתִי וָעֵרֶב], warp and weft. Some distinguish the cross from the gibbet thus: they say that a patibulum is properly that on which a man is fastened and stretched out, with a transverse beam; but a cross is when he is fixed or fastened to an upright, single stake. Tacitus: "gibbets, fires, crosses."

units.la: Summo] extremo, ultimo, ut apud Ciceronem, vixit ad summam senectutem valitudine optima. Sic Virgilius, Ve-nit summa dies, &c.
units.tr: Summo: extremum, last, as in Cicero, "he lived to extreme old age in excellent health." So Virgil: "The last day has come," etc.

units.la: Vicinarum gentium] terra Chanaan, quæ septem erant; quanquam sex tantum memorentur, Ios. 9.1. Vnde terra septem gentium vocata. Hæ gentes cis Iordanem montana & campestria, totamque adeo maris oram Libano objacentem tenebant.
units.tr: Of the neighbouring nations: the land of Canaan, which had seven nations, though only six are named, Josh. 9.1. Hence the land is called the land of seven nations. These nations on this side of the Jordan held the hill country and the plains, and indeed the whole coast lying opposite Lebanon.

units.la: Pag.38. Gens valida ex urbe opulenta] Ios. 10.2. erat erim urbs magna Gabaon, ut una civitatum regalium, major opido Gai, omnesque viri ejus bellicosi.
units.tr: p. 38. A strong people from a wealthy city: Josh. 10.2. For Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities, larger than the town of Ai, and all its men were warlike.

units.la: Vltro se Hebræis dederunt] id est, dediderunt. Dare prodere potuit & pag. 62. cum se Abner David regi dedisset: & pag. 73. septem millia virorum esse adhuc pronuncians, qui se idolis non dediderunt.
units.tr: They surrendered themselves willingly to the Hebrews: that is, dediderunt (they gave themselves up). He could have used dare for prodere (to hand over). Also p. 62, when Abner had surrendered himself to King David, and p. 73, where he declares that seven thousand men were still left who had not surrendered themselves to idols.

units.la: Vtligna & aquam converterunt] ut lignatores essent & aquarii, inservirentque cœtui & Levitis in templo.
units.tr: They became woodcutters and water-carriers, serving the assembly and the Levites in the temple.

units.la: Proximarum urbium] Ierusalem, Hebron, Ierimoth, Lachis, Eglon. Hi quinque reges erant gentis Amorrhæorum.
units.tr: Of the nearby cities: Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon. These five kings were of the Amorite nation.

units.la: Gabaon] ita emendavimus. Prius erat Gabaoth in libris quos vidi.
units.tr: Gibeon: we have emended it so. Previously it was Gibeoth in the books I saw.

units.la: Merito fidei] hoc Apostolus dixit πίστει fide sive per fidem, Hebræo 9. Delendus autem accentus, quem editio prior habebat in merito, ne quis arbitretur adverbium esse, cum sit nomen in casu ultimo, qui ablativus dicitur.
units.tr: Deservedly, by faith: the Apostle said [πίστει], by faith, Heb. 9. The accent which the earlier edition placed on merito must be deleted, lest anyone think it an adverb, when it is a noun in the last case, which is called the ablative.

units.la: Dies perseveravit] sol stetit in medio cœli spatio circiter integri diei, sic ut nec antea nec postea unquam dies ullus longior fuerit.
units.tr: The day lasted on: the sun stood in the middle of the sky for about the space of a whole day, so that neither before nor after has any day been longer.

units.la: Quinque reges] videlicet Adonisedec rex Ierusalem, Oham rex Hebron, Pharan rex Ierimoth, Iaphia rex Lachis, Dabir rex Eglon.
units.tr: Five kings: namely Adonizedec king of Jerusalem, Oham king of Hebron, Piram king of Jarmuth, Japhia king of Lachish, Debir king of Eglon.

units.la: Vicinæ quoque urbes] Maceda, Lebna, Lachis, Eglon, Hebron, Dabir.
units.tr: The neighbouring cities too: Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, Debir.

units.la: In ordinem] usitatum magis, ordine.
units.tr: Into order: the more usual form is ordine.

units.la: Viginti & novem regna] secutus est (videtur certe) lectionem quæ in editione Romana lof. 12.14. ἐνοσωνία viginti novem cum albi sit, puta in edit. Veneta & Basileensi; ut etiam in Ebræo τεσσαρόμα ἡμῶν ἐς. Quam lectionem veram esse fide codicum Ebræorum, qui nihil hic variant, non dubitamus asserere.
units.tr: Twenty-nine kingdoms: he followed (certainly it seems so) the reading which, in Josh. 12.14, the Roman edition has as twenty-nine, though the white (the Venetian and Basel editions) has it differently, as also in the Hebrew, which has the same number. We do not hesitate to assert that this reading is true, on the authority of the Hebrew manuscripts, which vary nothing here.

units.la: Per undecim tribus] imo duodecim. Nam in locum tribus Levi successerunt filii Ioseph in duas divisis tribus Ephraim & Manasse. Vide lof. 14.4.
units.tr: Through eleven tribes: indeed twelve. For in place of the tribe of Levi the sons of Joseph succeeded, the tribe being divided into Ephraim and Manasseh. See Josh. 14.4.

units.la: Viritim] per singulos viros, καὶ ἀνδρα.
units.tr: Man by man: through single men, [καὶ ἀνδρα].

units.la: Levitis in sacerdotum assumptis] jam dixi, ex Levitis alii sacerdotes erant, alii sacerdotibus ministrabant. Hi peculiariter Levitæ dicebantur, ut illi sacerdotes qui ab Aharone genus ducebant. Sed Sulpicius videtur sacerdotij nomen latius accepisse, ut pisse, ut etiam Leuitarum functiones comprehendat. Sane Samuelem prophetam, qui Leuita tantum erat, sacerdotem appellat infra pag. §3.
units.tr: Levites taken into the priesthood: I have already said that some of the Levites were priests and others ministered to the priests. These were specially called Levites, as those priests who traced their descent from Aaron were called priests. But Sulpicius seems to have taken the name of priesthood more broadly, so as to include also the functions of the Levites. Indeed he calls the prophet Samuel, who was only a Levite, a priest, below p. §3.

units.la: Pag. 39. Nulla portio data] nulla pars aut hereditas vel possessio. Dicitur etiam sors, id est, κλῆρος: unde clerici nomen apud Christianos inuenerunt, quia hereditatem Domini adepti sunt. Nam κλῆρος hereditas. Hinc fratres a Latinis consortes diěti sunt, qui simul indiuisa hereditate agunt.
units.tr: p. 39. No portion given: no part, inheritance or possession. It is also called sors, that is, [κλῆρος]; whence Christians took the name clerici, because they obtained the inheritance of the Lord. For κλῆρος means inheritance. Hence brothers were called consortes by the Latins, since they hold an undivided inheritance together.

units.la: Quo liberius seruirent Deo] alia ratio expressa Iof.13.33. & Num.18.20. Vide quoque, Deut.18.
units.tr: So that they might serve God more freely: another reason is expressed in Josh. 13.33 and Num. 18.20. See also Deut. 18.

units.la: Ministris Ecclesiarum] hinc perspicimus ministrorum nomen, quae nunc utuntur, non esse recens aut bisce temporibus primum excogitatum. Nam Sulpicius vixit ante annos mille ducentos, ut suo loco videbimus.
units.tr: To the ministers of the churches: from this we perceive that the name of ministers, which they now use, is not recent or devised for these times for the first time. For Sulpicius lived 1200 years ago, as we shall see in its place.

units.la: Dum me horum temporum piget taedetque] Si nunc viueres, Seuere, magis tederet horum temporum. Etenim sunt qui Christum in ore habent & Machiauellum in pectore, qui calumniandi arte ipsum diabolum vincunt. Sed reprimam me. Nam veritas odium parit.
units.tr: While I am vexed and wearied by these times: If you were alive now, Severus, you would be even more wearied by these times. For there are those who have Christ on their lips and Machiavelli in their hearts, who with the art of slander surpass the devil himself. But I shall restrain myself, for truth breeds hatred.

units.la: Captiuo solo] innuit maiorem partem terrae Chanaan, quam ceperant. Nam universam non occuparunt eo tempore.
units.tr: Captured land: he means the greater part of the land of Canaan, which they had taken. For they did not occupy all of it at that time.

units.la: Eodem tractu] plenius alibi, eodem tractu temporis.
units.tr: In the same stretch: more fully elsewhere, in the same stretch of time.

units.la: Ieius mortuus est] absque prole masculâ: unde in Phesachint, non meruit habere filium. Sunt qui eum filias reliquisse scribant. Natus fuit anno mundi bis millesimo quadringentesimo sexto, ut habetur in Iohasin. Lege a Mose accepit cum ageret annum octogesimum secundum. Sunt qui litteris mandarunt ab eo ductam Rachab, ex qua filias suscepit, quae matres fuerunt prophetarum.
units.tr: He died without male offspring; whence in Pesachin it is said he did not deserve to have a son. Some write that he left daughters. He was born in the year of the world 2406, as is found in Yohasin. He received the law from Moses when he was eighty-two years old. Some have written that Rahab was taken by him, and that from her he had daughters, who were the mothers of prophets.

units.la: Anno aetatis decimo & centesimo] Iof.24.29. Iud.2.8.
units.tr: At the age of one hundred and ten: Josh. 24.29; Judg. 2.8.

units.la: Viginti & septem annis] cum Sulpicio sentit _Augustinus_ lib.xviij. de ciuit. Dei, cap.xi. Funccius ei attribuit annos triginta duos. Ex his septem consumpti sunt, inquit, in subigenda terra, & viginti quinque in eadem dividenda. Autor libri qui vocatur Series annorum mundi, Ebraice Seder Olam, locus rexit Israelem annis octo supra viginti. Salmanticensis, judicavit Israelem annis viginti octo, quemadmodum habetur in Seder Olam. Et mox, hoc notum duntaxat ex Cabbala, hoc est ex traditione maiorum. Idem refert Simeonem nem filium Semach Doran, in eo libro qui vocatur Clypeus pa-trum, duntaxat quatuordecim annos ejus imperio tribuere: quod etiam refutat.
units.tr: Twenty-seven years: Augustine agrees with Sulpicius in book 18 of the City of God, ch. 11. Funccius attributes to him thirty-two years. Of these, he says, seven were spent in subduing the land, and twenty-five in dividing it. The author of the book called The Series of the Years of the World, in Hebrew Seder Olam, says that he ruled Israel for twenty-eight years. The Salmanticensis judged that he ruled Israel for twenty-eight years, as is found in Seder Olam. And soon after: this is known only from the Cabbala, that is, from the tradition of the elders. The same author reports that Simeon son of Shemach Doran, in the book called The Shield of the Fathers, assigned only fourteen years to his rule; which he also refutes.

units.la: Pag.40. In excessum ejus] excessum absolute vocat mortem, id est, excessum e vita, ut Cicero in 1. de legibus. post excessum suum Romulus Iulio Proculo dixit se Deum esse.
units.tr: p. 40. At his passing: he calls death absolutely "excessus," that is, departure from life, as Cicero does in book 1 of On the Laws. After his passing, Romulus told Julius Proculus that he was a god.

units.la: Anni sunt M.DCCC.LXXX. & (III.] pro M. repono III. quod ante me Gifelinus annotavit. Sigonius autem pro IIII. admonet scribendum III, ut dicat, anni sunt ter mille octingenti octoginta & tres. Salmanticensis, mortuus est anno mundi bis millesimo quingentesimo decimo sexto. Id quadrat cum eo quod ante scripsi de anno nativitatis ipsius, expende, & verum esse comperies, quod dico.
units.tr: There are 1880 years, and (III.: I substitute III for M, as Gifelinus noted before me. Sigonius, however, advises writing III for IIII, so that the sense is three thousand eight hundred and eighty-three years. The Salmanticensis: he died in the year of the world 2516. This agrees with what I wrote before about the year of his birth. Weigh it, and you will find that what I say is true.

units.la: Sine duce agebat ] Senes tum rempub. administrabat, in quorum numero Chaleb, qui praecipuus erat, prout habetur in capite Sacerdos magnus & Nazirœus. Phinees quoque iis accense-tur, qui erat ex femine Ithamar, usque ad Eli sacerdotem. Vide librum Iohasin
units.tr: He governed without a leader: elders then administered the commonwealth, among whom Caleb was the most distinguished, as is found in the chapter "Great Priest and Nazirite." Phinehas is also counted among them, who was of the seed of Ithamar, down to Eli the priest. See the book Yohasin.

units.la: Iudas assumptis] malim Iuda. Nam de tribu sermo.
units.tr: Judah having been taken: I would prefer Iuda, since the discourse concerns the tribe.

units.la: Matrimonia ex viciis assumere] Iud. 3.6. Vt hic, assume-re matrimonia, sic pag.67. cum ex alienigenis conjugia sumpsisset, id est, uxores. Simile ut cum servitia ponimus pro ipsis servis.
units.tr: To take marriages from the nations: Judg. 3.6. As here "to take marriages" (assume matrimonia), so on p. 67, "when he had taken marriages from foreigners," that is, wives. It is like our use of "servitude" for the servants themselves.

units.la: Idolis] Baalem & Astharoth, quod aliter efferas Baalibus & Astartis, Iud.2.13. & 3.7.
units.tr: To idols: Baal and Ashtaroth, which you may render otherwise as Baals and Astartes, Judg. 2.13 and 3.7.

units.la: A rege Mesopotamiae] [?] , qui rex Syriae, Iud 3.10. & rex Assyriorum, Ant.hist.lib.5.cap.2. Hujus proprium nomen Chusan rasathaim, pro qua [?] in edit. Rom. [?] in Iosepho. & Cusardo in Rufini. Sunt qui apud Iosephum legant Chusathrem. In versione Latina Gelenii, a Cusarthe rege Assyriorum: qui obliquus est a [?], Chusarthes.
units.tr: By the king of Mesopotamia: [?], who was king of Syria, Judg. 3.10, and king of the Assyrians, Ant. hist. book 5, ch. 2. His proper name is Chushan-rishathaim, for which [?] in the Roman edition [?] in Josephus, and Cusardus in Rufinus. Some read Chusathres in Josephus. In Gelenius's Latin version it is "from Cusarthes, king of the Assyrians," which is the oblique form, Chusarthes.

units.la: VII. annis] corrige, VIII. annis. Nam Iud.3.8. [?] annis octo.
units.tr: Seven years: correct to eight years, for Judg. 3.8 has eight years.

units.la: Captivitatem pependerunt] infra pag. 68. aliquamdiu Salomoni servitutem pependerat. notabit juventus
units.tr: They endured captivity: below, p. 68, he had for some time endured servitude to Solomon. The young will note this.

units.la: Gothoniel duce] qui & Othoniel. Nam in scriptura Ebraica עָתְנִיאֵל[?] cum Ain in capite. Sic Gaza dicimus & Azza:Gomorra & Amorra. Hunc Iosephus Cenez appellat: male. Cenez enim erat nomen patris. Siquidem vocatur Othoniel filius Ce-nez. Id nostro more declinatum legitur in editione Gelenii Cenizus. Graecum exemplar habet κενιαζ[?]. Sed verior scriptura Cenezus sive Cenizus, κενιζ[?]. Salmanticensis, Othoniel filius Cenez, ut videtur, ex senioribus fuit, qui coepit judicare Israelem anno mundi 2533.
units.tr: Othniel as leader: who is also called Othoniel. In the Hebrew Scripture the name is [עָתְנִיאֵל], with Ayin at the beginning. So we say Gaza and Azza, Gomorrah and Amorrah. Josephus calls him Cenez, wrongly, for Cenez was the name of his father; indeed Othniel is read as son of Cenez. In our manner, declined, it is read in Gelenius's edition as Cenizus. The Greek copy has [κενιαζ], but the truer spelling is Cenezus or Cenizus, [κενιζ]. The Salmanticensis: Othniel son of Cenez, as it seems, was among the elders, who began to judge Israel in the year of the world 2533.

units.la: Per quinquaginta annos] quadraginta est Jud. 3.11. & apud Josephum. Nec interpretes dissentiunt. Salmanticensis, judicavit Israelem 40. annis. R. Jose autor Seder Olam, Othoniel filius Cenaz 40. annis. Sunt qui putant a Sulpicio adjectos decem annos, quo sic completeretur totum tempus, quod a morte Josuae effluxerat. Consule Sigonium.
units.tr: For forty years: forty is in Judg. 3.11 and in Josephus. Nor do the translators disagree. The Salmanticensis: he judged Israel for forty years. R. Jose, the author of Seder Olam: Othniel son of Cenaz, forty years. Some think that Sulpicius added ten years, so that the whole period which had elapsed since the death of Joshua would thus be completed. Consult Sigonius.

units.la: Ab Eglo enim rege] videtur declinasse Eglo ab Eglus, quod Graece esset Εγλός. Alioqui dixisset potius, ab Eglone enim rege, cum in fonte sit Eglon, id est, [illegible, ~4 letters]. Quanquam in LXX. Εγλωμ, cum M in fine. Eglom, ut Madiam, ut Edem, pro Madian & Eden. Contrario modo peccatum in Abfalon & Abiron. Eglom, Eglus: ut Charchom, Crocus. Scribi potest Eglo, nisi nomen Ebraicum esset. Sic male scribitur Simo pro Simon, nisi cum est nomen Graecum. Σιμών, Simo, ut Πλατών, Plato; Ξενών, Zeno, Ξενοφών, Xenopho, Κτησιφών, Ctesipho.
units.tr: From King Eglon] Eglo seems to be declined from Eglus, which in Greek would be Εγλός. Otherwise he would rather have said "ab Eglone," since in the source the name is Eglon, that is, [illegible, about four letters]. Yet in the LXX it is Εγλωμ, with M at the end: Eglom, as Madiam and Edem for Madian and Eden. The reverse happens in Abfalon and Abiron. Eglom, Eglus: as Charchom, Crocus. It can be written Eglo, unless the name were Hebrew. Thus Simo is wrongly written for Simon, unless it is a Greek name: Σιμών, Simo; as Πλατών, Plato; Ξενών, Zeno; Ξενοφών, Xenopho; Κτησιφών, Ctesipho.

units.la: Duodeviginti] octodecim. Jud.3 14.
units.tr: Eighteen] eighteen. Judg. 3.14.

units.la: Instinctu Dei] Qui eum ad hoc suscitaverat. Jud. 3.15.
units.tr: By the instigation of God] He who had raised him up for this. Judg. 3.15.

units.la: Pag. 41. Adon] corruptum ex Aod id est, Aod, quod hodie in editione Romana. Sed & in Hieronymo. Veritas scripturae Ahod, videlicet ex Ebraeo אחוד[?] quod nunc legunt Ebud. Alibi est Aoth, & in Polycratico Ajoth. lib. 8 cap. 2c. Salmanticensis. Anno mundi 2573. coepit Ahod, qui judicavit Israelem 80. annis. Hi anni mutantur in anno mundi 2653.
units.tr: Page 41. Adon] corrupted from Aod, that is, Aod, which today is in the Roman edition. But also in Jerome. The truth of Scripture is Ahod, evidently from the Hebrew אחוד, which they now read Ebud. Elsewhere it is Aoth, and in the Polycraticus Ajoth, book 8, chapter 2c. Salmanticensis: In the year of the world 2573 Ahod began, who judged Israel for 80 years. These years are shifted to the year of the world 2653.

units.la: Libertatem armis vindicavit] caesis sirciter decem millibus hostium.
units.tr: He vindicated liberty by arms] having slain about ten thousand of the enemy.

units.la: Per LXXX. annos] quibus inclusi anni quibus servierunt Moabitarum regi. Sic in annis judicatus Othonielis inclusi anni octo, quibus servitutem pependerunt regi Mesopotamiae. Alii aliter de hac re censent. Fruatur quisque judicio suo.
units.tr: For 80 years] within which are included the years in which they served the king of Moab. Likewise in the judgeship of Othniel eight years are included, during which they bore servitude to the king of Mesopotamia. Others judge this matter differently. Let each enjoy his own judgement.

units.la: Semigar] Samgar filius Anath. Jud. 3.31. In ed Rom. σαμεγαρ & apud Josephum σαμάγαρ, Putarim scribendum σαμάγαρ. Legitur & Semegar in Origine. De hoc scribit Josephus quod primo imperii sui, vel potius judicatus, anno mortem obi-erit. erit. Salmanticensis, Samgar præfuit anno uno. R. Iofe, In diebus Ahod erat Samgar filius Anath in fine dierum ejus. Eodem tractu temporis, videlicet in diebus Eglonis, accidit historia Ruth. Docti viderint,
units.tr: Semigar] Shamgar son of Anath, Judg. 3.31. In the Roman edition it is σαμεγαρ, and in Josephus σαμάγαρ; it should perhaps be written σαμάγαρ. Semegar is also read in Origen. Of him Josephus writes that he died in the first year of his rule, or rather of his judgeship. Salmanticensis: Shamgar presided for one year. R. Jose: In the days of Ahod, Shamgar son of Anath was, at the end of his days. In the same span of time, namely in the days of Eglon, the story of Ruth took place. Let the learned see to it.

units.la: Adversus allophylos] id est, Philistheos, quos ἀλλοφύλους Græci vocant, id est, alienigenas, nomine generis ad certam speciem revocato, ita passim interpretes LXX.
units.tr: Against the allophyles] that is, the Philistines, whom the Greeks call ἀλλόφυλοι, that is, foreigners, the generic name being applied to a particular species, as the LXX translators do everywhere.

units.la: Secundo eventu prælium fecit] alibi, secundum eventum, hac sententia, fecit prælium secundum eventu. Non omnino displicet. Magis tamen placet, secundo eventu, ut pag. 62. fe-cundis prælis repulit allophylos. & pag. 64. crebra deinde præliasecundo eventu habuit: & pag. 114. secundo eventu, perempto rege, gentem imperio adjungit. Rursum pag. 51. victores secundo prælio Allophyli.
units.tr: He fought a battle with a second outcome] elsewhere, "secundum eventum," in the sense "fought a battle according to the outcome"; this is not entirely displeasing. Yet "secundo eventu" pleases more, as on page 62, "with repeated battles he drove back the allophyles," and on page 64, "then he had frequent battles with a favourable outcome," and on page 114, "with a favourable outcome, the king having been slain, he joins the nation to his rule." Again on page 51, "the Allophyli were victors in the second battle."

units.la: Per viginti annos] Iud. 4. 3 qui annumerantur annis Debbo-ra. Hic Iabin Hasore regnabat.
units.tr: For twenty years] Judg. 4.3, which are counted among the years of Deborah. Here Jabin of Hazor was reigning.

units.la: Debbora] δεββώρα[?] quod apem sonat, & est antiqua lectio pro Debora, ut Mesias, quod nunc legunt & scribunt Mesia, id est ΝΠΨΩ. Cœpit judicare Israelem anno mundi 2654[?]. Videlicet anno post Semigar, non tantum judex erat, sed etiam Prophetes.
units.tr: Deborah] δεββώρα[?], which means bee, and is the old reading for Debora, as Mesias, which they now read and write Mesia, that is, ΝΠΨΩ. She began to judge Israel in the year of the world 2654[?]. That is, in the year after Shamgar; she was not only a judge but also a prophetess.

units.la: In typum ecclesiæ] mulier enim fortis typus est ecclesiæ secundum doctores theologos, ut apud Salomonem, mulierem fortem quis inveniat? Vide gloss. ordina. ad hunc postremum locum.
units.tr: As a type of the Church] for a strong woman is a type of the Church according to the theologian teachers, as in Solomon, "who can find a strong woman?" See the ordinary gloss on this last passage.

units.la: Cujus auxilio captivitas est depulsa] ergo Debbora typus fuit ecclesiæ, quæ captivitatem Satanæ depulit, ut illa gravissimam dominationem regis Iabin.
units.tr: By whose help captivity was driven off] so Deborah was a type of the Church, which drove off the captivity of Satan, as she drove off the most grievous domination of King Jabin.

units.la: XL. annis] Salmanticensis, Debbora judicavit quadraginta annis. Quod haustum ex Iud. 5 31.
units.tr: Forty years] Salmanticensis: Deborah judged for forty years. This is drawn from Judg. 5.31.

units.la: Duro imperio habebantur] per septem annos Iud. 6. 1. Salmanticensis, captivitas Madian duravit septem annos. Seder Olam, tradidit eos in manum Madian septem annis.
units.tr: They were held under a harsh rule] for seven years, Judg. 6.1. Salmanticensis: the captivity to Midian lasted seven years. Seder Olam: he handed them over into the hand of Midian for seven years.

units.la: Ita semper in secundis, &c.] nam facilius feruntur adversa, quam secunda. Sic dico, Res prosperæ[?] oblivionem inducunt Dei: ut adversæ recordationem.
units.tr: So always in prosperity, etc.] for adversities are borne more easily than prosperities. Thus I say: prosperous things bring forgetfulness of God, as adverse things bring remembrance.

units.la: Pag. 41. Christum ab his non esse receptum] quid mirum a Iudæis non esse receptum, qui a Christianis multi non recipiantur? Nam qui rejicit veritatem, rejicit Christum, qui est ipsa veritas. veritas, quam sigillum Dei vocant. Deus enim omnia sua obsig-
units.tr: Page 41. Christ not received by these] what wonder that he was not received by the Jews, when many are not received by Christians? For he who rejects the truth rejects Christ, who is the truth itself: the truth which they call the seal of God. For God seals all his

units.la: Addit Iosephus non ausum eum propter hostes propalam hoc in area facere.
units.tr: Josephus adds that he did not dare to do this openly on the threshing floor, because of the enemies.

units.la: Tam enim accipi potest de Deo, quam de Gedeone. De Deo videtur accepisse Augustinus re- ferens, potens in fortitudine: quod noster dixit, potens in virtute. De Gedeone autem Hiero, qui vertit, virorum for- tissime: & alius qui transtulit, miles strenuus. Ceterum in LXX. est ἰσχυρός δυνάμεως: in aliis, quos Sulpicius secutus est, δυνατὸς ἰσχύι potens robore, sive, quod idem, virtute. Nam virtus etiam pro robore sumitur. Verba Sulpicij accommodari possunt ad Gedeonem, si adverbium subaudias vocandi, ut dicat, o po- tens virtute. Idem sentiendum de Augustini declaramento seu interpretamento, quod superius adduxi. In fonte גבור החיל quod non male reddituur miles fortissime. Nam גבור miles: proprie robore valens. In virtute Graece diceretur, ἐν δυνάμει. Sic Κύριε δυνάμεων, Dominus virtutum. Locus est Iud.6.12.
units.tr: For it can be taken of God as well as of Gideon. Augustine seems to have taken it of God, when he renders "powerful in strength," which our author rendered "powerful in virtue." Of Gideon, Jerome, who translated it, gives "the bravest of men," and another translator gives "a vigorous soldier." In the LXX it is ἰσχυρός δυνάμεως; in others, whom Sulpicius followed, δυνατὸς ἰσχύι, "powerful in strength," or, which is the same, "in virtue," for virtue is also taken for strength. Sulpicius' words can be fitted to Gideon if you supply the adverb of address, so that he says, "O one powerful in virtue." The same should be thought of Augustine's declaration or interpretation, which I cited above. In the source it is gibbor ha-chayil [גבור החיל], which is not badly rendered "very brave soldier," for [גבור] means soldier, properly one strong in power. In Greek it would be said ἐν δυνάμει. So "Lord of hosts" (Κύριε δυνάμεων), the Lord of powers. The place is Judg. 6.12.

units.la: Ceterum in Ebraeo legitur, Est Dominus nobiscum? quod pronuntiatione ju vandum, ac si dicteret, Estne Dominus nobiscum? Graeci habent, καὶ ἔστι Κύριος μεθ' ἡμῶν; si est Dominus nobiscum? q d. minime. Vide sequentia.
units.tr: Moreover, in the Hebrew it reads, "Is the Lord with us?" which is to be pronounced as a question, as if he had said, "Is the Lord not with us?" The Greeks have καὶ ἔστι Κύριος μεθ' ἡμῶν; "if the Lord is with us?" i.e., by no means. See what follows.

units.la: Virtutumque] δυνάμεων, id est, fortium factorum.
units.tr: And of powers] δυνάμεων, that is, of brave deeds.

units.la: In hoc spiritu] ἐν τῇ ἰσχύι σου, in virtute aut sortitu- dine tua.
units.tr: In this strength] ἐν τῇ ἰσχύι σου, in your virtue or strength.

units.la: καὶ ἐγὼ ἐλάχιστος ... ἐν οἴκῳ πατρός μου. Ante quam verba, ἰδοὺ ἡ χιλιάς μου ἐν Μανασση. Seorsum ab aliis vertunt <bl>אֲנִי</bl> & <bl>ἐγώ</bl>: atque hinc elicuit Gedeonem in sua tribu chiliar- chum fuisse.
units.tr: "And I am the least ... in my father's house." Before these words, "Behold my thousand is in Manasseh." They translate ani [אֲנִי] and ἐγώ separately from the others, and from this they infer that Gideon was a chiliarch in his tribe.

units.la: Pag.43. Quam Baalis idolo Madianitæ sacraverant] quærendum unde habeat. Nam ex textu non potest aliud colligi, quam hanc aram a civibus Gedeonis fuisse sacratam quem propterea quod eam destruxisset, ad necem quærebant. Historia refertur, Iud.6.30.
units.tr: Page 43. Which the Midianites had consecrated to the idol Baal] one must ask where he gets this. For from the text nothing else can be gathered than that this altar had been consecrated by the citizens of Gideon, and that they sought his death for having destroyed it. The story is related in Judg. 6.30.

units.la: Baalis] Iovis Syrij. Nam Baal Iupiter, & Chochab Baal, Iupiter planeta. Sic Baalphegor, Iupiter Phegorius. Beel idem: Beelzebul Iupiter stercoreus. Sic vocabant principem daemoniorum ætate Christi.
units.tr: Baal] the Syrian Jupiter. For Baal is Jupiter, and Chochab Baal is Jupiter the planet. So Baal-peor, the Phegorian Jupiter. Beel is the same; Beelzebul, the dung Jupiter. Thus they called the prince of demons in the age of Christ.

units.la: Gens Amalech] scribo Amalec, ab Amalec filio Eliphaz, quem ei Thamna concubina peperit, sic appellatus. Moses Gerundensis arbitratur ab Horæo quodam, Amalec nomine, vocatos Amalecitæ. Strabus autem scribit Amalec fuisse filium Ismaël, quem ita sentientem prolixè refellit Nicolaus de Lyra, docens fuisse filium Eliphaz primogeniti Esau. Vide Glossas ejus, Exod.17. Gens hæc inter Idumæas pugnacissima, Gobolitidem regionem & Petram urbem incolebat. Iosephus Orig.Iud.lib.3.cap.2.
units.tr: The nation of Amalek] I write Amalec, named from Amalec the son of Eliphaz, whom his concubine Timna bore to him. Moses of Gerona thinks the Amalekites were called from a certain Horite named Amalec. Strabus, however, writes that Amalec was a son of Ishmael; Nicholas of Lyra refutes this opinion at length, teaching that he was a son of Eliphaz, the firstborn of Esau. See his glosses on Exod. 17. This nation was the most warlike of the Idumaeans, and inhabited the region of Gobolitis and the city of Petra. Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 3, chapter 2.

units.la: Ad triginta & II. millia] certum ex Iud.7.3. triginta duo millia fuisse. Quocirca male adjecit (ad) præpositionem, quæ hic circiter denotat, ut in illo Terentij, quasi talenta ad quindecim coegi. Sic infra pag.101. Nam fere ad LXX. erant, cum historia narret LXX. fuisse.
units.tr: To about thirty-two thousand] it is certain from Judg. 7.3 that there were thirty-two thousand. Hence he wrongly added the preposition "ad," which here denotes "about," as in that line of Terence, "as if I had gathered to fifteen talents." So below on page 101: for there were nearly seventy, since the story says there were seventy.

units.la: XX. & II millia] sic audaciter emendavimus. prius erat in libris XX. a castris recesserunt. Res est non conjectura. Vide Iud.7.3.
units.tr: Twenty-two thousand] thus we have boldly emended it. Before, the books read "twenty departed from the camp." The matter is not conjecture. See Judg. 7.3.

units.la: Media vigili] media vigilia incipiente, sive in principio ejus. Iud.7.19. Iosephus hic habet, circa quartam vigiliam, & ejus interpres Rufinus, circa primam. Mirum unde hæc varietas. De vigiliis vide quæ notavimus Observat lib.10. cap.10. Quibus addo, tres vigilias etiam a Macrobio statui, his verbis, Nox in tres vigilias distribuebatur, vigiliæ vero in quatuor horarum spatia. Manahem Ricinensis vigiliam mediam appellat custodiam secundam, quæ media nocte Tertiam autem definit, in qua homo fabulatur cum uxore sua. Videndus R.David & Psal.63.7. [?] Cetera vespertina & matutina vigilia mentio apud paraphrasten Chaldæum.
units.tr: In the middle watch] with the middle watch beginning, or at its start. Judg. 7.19. Josephus here has "about the fourth watch," and his translator Rufinus "about the first." It is strange where this variation comes from. On the watches see what we noted in the Observations, book 10, chapter 10. To these I add that Macrobius also set three watches, in these words: "The night was divided into three watches, and the watches into spans of four hours." Menahem of Recanati calls the middle watch the second guard, which at midnight ... and he defines the third, in which a man talks with his wife. Let R. David and Psalm 63.7 be consulted. The other, evening and morning, watch is mentioned in the Chaldee paraphrast.

units.la: Tuba] buccina. Sed confundi hæc scias.
units.tr: Tuba] trumpet. But you should know that these words are confused.

units.la: Neque cuiquam] Quidam codices, neque unquam: quod erratum typographicum esse puto.
units.tr: Neque cuiquam] Some manuscripts read "neque unquam" (nor ever), which I think is a typographical error.

units.la: Reges] reges Madian Zebee & Salmana, Iud. 8.13. Oreb & Zeb non reges erant, sed principes Madian.
units.tr: Reges] "the kings of Midian, Zebee and Salmana," Judg. 8.13. Oreb and Zeeb were not kings but princes of Midian.

units.la: XV. capta traduntur] imo remanserunt 15. millia, quae post caesa fuerunt, Iud. 8.11.
units.tr: XV. capta traduntur] Indeed, 15 thousand remained, those who were slain afterwards, Judg. 8.11.

units.la: Princeps] dux vel judex.
units.tr: Princeps] leader or judge.

units.la: Pag.44. Quam praecesse [?] suis] imo praefuit eis annis quadraginta, Iud. 8.28. Iosephus ad hoc eum coactum fuisse scribit, bis. ant. lib. 5. cap. 8.
units.tr: Pag. 44. Quam praecesse [?] suis] Indeed he ruled over them forty years, Judg. 8.28. Josephus writes that he was forced to this twice, Ant. book 5, chapter 8.

units.la: Fratribus interemptis] excepto Iotham minimo natu inter-emit fratres LXX.
units.tr: Fratribus interemptis] Except Jotham, the youngest, he killed the brothers, according to the Seventy.

units.la: Sichimorum] est cur malim Sicimorum, quod Graece scribitur τῶν σχιμων. Nam τὰ σχίματα dicimus. Quanquam in scriptura Ebraica Sechem sive Sichem, prima correpta. Sichem, Sichima, ut Chermel, Carmelus.
units.tr: Sichimorum] I have reason to prefer Sicimorum, which is written in Greek as τῶν σχιμων [tōn schimōn], for we say τὰ σχίματα [ta schēmata]. Yet in the Hebrew Scripture it is Sechem or Sichem, with the first syllable short. Sichem, Sichima, as Chermel becomes Carmelus.

units.la: Amisso opido] Thebes. Iud. 9.50.
units.tr: Amisso opido] Thebes. Judg. 9.50.

units.la: Saxo] fragmine molae. Iud. 9.53.
units.tr: Saxo] a fragment of a millstone. Judg. 9.53.

units.la: Duobus & viginti annis] Sic Eusebius. Nam in Graeca editione ἑξάκοντα ἔτη: & in Ebraeo tribus & viginti.
units.tr: Duobus & viginti annis] So Eusebius. For in the Greek edition it is ἑξήκοντα ἔτη [hexēkonta etē], sixty years, and in the Hebrew twenty-three.

units.la: Thola] Θωλὰ filius Phua filij patrui ejus, id est, [illegible, ~6 letters] , vel certe filij Dodonis, ut sit proprium viri nomen. Priorem interpretationem amplexi sunt LXX. & Hiero. Utraque autem invenitur in Chaldaeorum Thargumim, variantibus libris.
units.tr: Thola] Θωλὰ [Thōla], son of Phua, son of his uncle, that is, [illegible], or certainly son of Dodo, so that it is the man's proper name. The Seventy and Jerome adopted the former interpretation. Both, however, are found in the Chaldee Targumim, the manuscripts varying.

units.la: Iair] Galaadites, ὁ γαλααδίτης, pro quo nove lectum in editione Graeca ὁ γαλααδ̓ί̓της. Fortè mendum est librariorum.
units.tr: Iair] the Gileadite, ὁ γαλααδίτης [ho galaaditēs], for which a new reading appears in the Greek edition, ὁ γαλααδίτης with a different accent. Perhaps it is a scribal error.

units.la: Idolis] Diis Syriae, Sidonis, Moab, filiorum Ammon & Philistheorum: item Baalibus & Astartis, Iud. 10.6.
units.tr: Idolis] the gods of Syria, of Sidon, of Moab, of the sons of Ammon and of the Philistines; likewise the Baals and Astartes, Judg. 10.6.

units.la: Allophylis] Alienigenis, hoc est Philistheis. notatum alibi, nisi fallor.
units.tr: Allophylis] foreigners, that is, the Philistines. I have noted this elsewhere, unless I am mistaken.

units.la: Ammonitis] filiis Ammon. Ab his diversi videntur fuisse Ammonitae, qui [illegible, ~6 letters] vocantur. Qua de re dicam alias.
units.tr: Ammonitis] the sons of Ammon. The Ammonites seem to have been different from these, who are called [illegible]. I shall speak of this matter elsewhere.

units.la: Pag.45. Iepta duce] Scriptura haec a scribe est, non a Sulpicio, qui sine dubio Iephtha vel Iephthae scripsit, ita posterior prisca consuetudine.
units.tr: Pag. 45. Iepta duce] This spelling is the scribe's, not Sulpicius's, who undoubtedly wrote Iephtha or Iephthae; the later writer followed ancient custom.

units.la: Ad Ammon regem] veritas historiae postulat, ad regem filiorum Ammon. Sic est etiam in LXX consentientibus libris Ebraeis & Latinis, πρὸς βασιλέα υἱῶν Ammon, Iud 11.12
units.tr: Ad Ammon regem] The truth of the history requires "to the king of the sons of Ammon." So it is also in the Seventy, the Hebrew and Latin books agreeing: πρὸς βασιλέα υἱῶν Ammon [pros basilea huiōn Ammon], Judg. 11.12.

units.la: Holnam Deo dandam] veritas Ebraica, erit Domino & offeram illud in holocaustum. Sensus est, consecrabitur Domino, aut offeram illud, nempe si hujusmodi erit ut offerri possit per legem. LXX. καὶ ἐσται τῷ Κυρίῳ, ἀνοίσω αὐτὸν ὁλοκαύ-τωμα[?]. Omiserunt copulantem, quae hic desiungendi vim habet. Ceterum hostiam inter & holocautoma discrimen est. Nam holocautoma totum comburebatur: unde nomen accepit. Dicitur & holocaustum: Hostiae partem sacerdotes edebant. Sed latius hic sumitur hostiae vocabulum, vel certe pro holocausto posuit κατα-χρηστικῶς[?].
units.tr: Holnam Deo dandam] The Hebrew truth is: it shall be for the LORD, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering. The sense is: it shall be consecrated to the Lord, or I will offer it, namely if it is of such a kind that it can be offered under the law. The Seventy have καὶ ἔσται τῷ Κυρίῳ, ἀνοίσω αὐτὸν ὁλοκαύτωμα [kai estai tō Kyriō, anoisō auton holokautōma]. They omitted the conjunction, which here has the force of separating. Moreover there is a difference between hostia and holocaustum. For the holocaust was burned whole, whence it took its name. It is also called holocaustum; the priests ate part of the victim. But here the word hostia is taken more broadly, or certainly it is used for holocaust in a catachrestic sense.

units.la: Filia] quam unicam habebat, & per consequens charissimam. Quo gravior erat patri ejus sive mors sive perpetua virginitas. Scitum illud, Qui liberis caret pro mortuo habetur.
units.tr: Filia] whom he had as his only child, and consequently most dear. Her death, or her perpetual virginity, was therefore all the more grievous to her father. The saying is apt: he who has no children is counted as dead.

units.la: Non foeminea] id est, virili.
units.tr: Non foeminea] that is, manly.

units.la: Vt aequales suas prius videret] ut plangeret virginitatem una cum aequalibus. Hinc elicimus votum virginitatis, quod Deo vovetur, olim in usu fuisse.
units.tr: Vt aequales suas prius videret] that she might lament her virginity together with her companions. From this we gather that a vow of virginity, vowed to God, was in use in former times.

units.la: Hebon] in fonte Ebraeo Ebfan, quod nunc legunt Ibfan, ut Iosephus olim Abfan, Hiero, Abefan & LXX. ἀβασάν, quod Latine scribes Abassan. Ibfan, Ebfan, Abfan, ut Nimrod, Nemrod, Namrod. Saepe ita variabant in legendo antiqui. Possiet etiam scribi Ebfon, cum O in fine, Ebfan & Ebfon, ut Abiram & Abirom. Quin eo labor ut credam aliquando scriptum fuisse Ebefon. Nam Efebon notissimum nomen est, quod propterea cum alio minus noto ut fieri solet permutatum errore non tam interpretum, quam librariorum, ita mihi videtur.
units.tr: Hebon] In the Hebrew source it is Ebfan, which they now read as Ibfan; Josephus once read Abfan, Jerome Abefan, and the Seventy ἀβασάν [abasan], which in Latin you would write as Abassan. Ibfan, Ebfan, Abfan, as Nimrod, Nemrod, Namrod. The ancients often varied thus in reading. It could also be written Ebfon, with an O at the end, as Ebfan and Ebfon, as Abiram and Abirom. Indeed I am inclined to think that at some time it was written Ebefon. For Efebon is a very well-known name, which for that reason was, as usually happens, exchanged by error with another less known name, and this error seems to me to be due not so much to the translators as to the copyists.

units.la: Ailon] veritas lectionis Ailon. Nam sic est in codicibus Graecis ἀιλὼν, quod nunc legunt ex Ebraeo Elon. Hunc Eusebius in Chronico praetermisit eo loco ubi catalogum judicum recenset. In ipso autem Chronico ait, post Efebon in libro Ebraeorum fertur judex Adon rexisse populum annis 10. qui non habetur apud LXX interpretes. Mirari libet. Nam in editione Romana Iud. 12. 11. αἰλὼμ legitur, in quo mendum quale in Edem & Madiam. Reperio & ἀιλὰν. Ex ἀιλὼν factum Aialon, quod in Hiero. Ailon, Elon; ut Ailam, Elam. Sic Aingaddi & Engaddi: Ain-rogel & En-rogel. Notavi alias.
units.tr: Ailon] The true reading is Ailon. For so it is in the Greek manuscripts, ἀιλὼν [ailōn], which they now read from the Hebrew as Elon. Eusebius passed this over in the Chronicle where he lists the judges. But in the Chronicle itself he says that after Ebefon, in the book of the Hebrews, a judge named Adon is said to have ruled the people for ten years, and he is not found among the Seventy translators. It is a matter for wonder. For in the Roman edition at Judg. 12.11 αἰλὼμ [ailōm] is read, in which there is an error of the same kind as in Edem and Madiam. I also find ἀιλὰν [ailan]. From ἀιλὼν came Aialon, which in Jerome is Ailon, Elon, as Ailam is Elam. So Aingaddi and Engaddi, Ain-rogel and En-rogel. I have noted this elsewhere.

units.la: Abdon] filius Hellel Pharatbonites, perperam Elel in nostra vulgata Graece melius ἰλλὶλ, quod tamen aspirandum ut fit ἰλλελ Hellel.
units.tr: Abdon] son of Hillel the Pirathonite; our Vulgate wrongly has Elel. In Greek the better form is ἰλλὶλ [illil], which however must be aspirated, as in ἰλλελ, Hellel.

units.la: Pag 4€[?] Hujus mater] uxor Manoe.
units.tr: Pag 4€[?] Hujus mater] his mother, the wife of Manoah.

units.la: Sicera] hoc nomine denotari putant alij vinum vetus, alij Vinum purum, alij potum quemvis inebriantem Sunt etiam qui exponunt dicentes significare potum factitium ex pomis, quem Galli Sidre vocant: aut ex hordeo, qualis est nostra cerevisia. Quorum sententiam juvat quod hic & alibi passim sicera cum vino jungitur. Sed vide sodes Animadversiones meas.
units.tr: Sicera] Some think this word denotes old wine, others pure wine, others any intoxicating drink. There are also those who explain it as a made drink from fruit, which the Gauls call cider, or from barley, such as our beer. Their opinion is supported by the fact that here and elsewhere sicera is joined with wine. But please see my Animadversions.

units.la: Samson] Critici Ebraeorum legunt Simson. Cave putes hanc lectionem veriorem esse. Samson ita legitur ut Mariam, ut Namrod, ut Magdal; unde Maria Magdalene. Sic Cimchi dicimus & Camchi. Huc refer Phasga, quod antiqua consuetudine ita lectum pro Phisga.
units.tr: Samson] Hebrew critics read Simson. Do not think this reading is the truer one. Samson is read as Maria, as Namrod, as Magdal, whence Maria Magdalene. So we say Cimchi and Camchi. To this belongs Phasga, which by ancient custom was read thus for Phisga.

units.la: Pag. 47. Osse asini] maxilla sive mandibula asini.
units.tr: Pag. 47. Osse asini] the jawbone or lower jaw of an ass.

units.la: Ex osse] ex dente molari, qui erat in maxilla illa. τὸν λαμ-χὸν τὸν ἐν τῇ σιαγόνι appellant LXX.
units.tr: Ex osse] from a molar tooth that was in that jawbone. The Seventy call it τὸν λαμ-χὸν τὸν ἐν τῇ σιαγόνι [ton lamchon ton en tē siagoni], the jaw-tooth in the jawbone.

units.la: Samson Ebraeis praeerat] annis 20. Iud. 15. 20. Infra, cum XX. annis Ebraeis praefuisset. Videtur aliquando varietas fuisse in codicibus Ebraeis. Nam in Thalmud Ierosolymitano, Samson 20. tantum annis judicavit. Cur igitur 40. ei Scriptura tribuit? Ut hinc discas metum ejus per 20. annos continuos post obitum in Philisthaeis permansisse.
units.tr: Samson Ebraeis praeerat] for 20 years, Judg. 15.20. Below, it says he had ruled the Hebrews for twenty years. Perhaps there was sometimes variation in the Hebrew manuscripts. For in the Jerusalem Talmud it says Samson judged only twenty years. Why then does Scripture attribute forty to him? So that you may learn that his fear remained among the Philistines for twenty continuous years after his death.

units.la: Vxorem ejus quam ille postea acceperat] Dalila vocatur libris Ebraeis & Latinis, sed in Graecis est Dalida id est, Δαλιδὰ. Sic casida & casila. Nam D et L communem familiam habent. Iosephus Dalale scribit. Hodie legunt Delila, quod est דלילה in scriptura originali.
units.tr: Vxorem ejus quam ille postea acceperat] She is called Dalila in the Hebrew and Latin books, but in the Greek it is Dalida, that is, Δαλιδὰ [Dalida]. So casida and casila; for D and L belong to a common family. Josephus writes Dalale. Today they read Delila, which is דלילה [Delilah] in the original Scripture.

units.la: Pecunia corrumpunt] Iud. 16. 5. quod si feceris, dabimus tibi mille & centum argenteos. Vide locum.
units.tr: Pecunia corrumpunt] Judg. 16.5: "If you do this, we will give you eleven hundred pieces of silver each." See the passage.

units.la: Diu eludentem] ter eludentem.
units.tr: Diu eludentem] deceiving him three times.

units.la: In crinibus] quos, utpote Naziraeus, intonsos gerebat.
units.tr: In crinibus] in his hair, which, as a Nazirite, he wore uncut.

units.la: Compedibus] catenis aereis vinctus detinebatur Gazae ad molendum.
units.tr: Compedibus] he was kept bound in bronze fetters at Gaza, grinding at the mill.

units.la: Crinem ejus abstulit] pro crinem ejus, alij referunt, capillamentum ejus. In fonte habetur, septem cincinnos [?] capitis ejus.
units.tr: Crinem ejus abstulit] for "his hair," others refer it to his hair covering. In the source it is found as "the seven locks of his head."

units.la: Opperiebatur] editio Coloniensis, operiebatur, unico P, quod duplici scribunt LL. VV. & Virgilius Carpensis.
units.tr: Opperiebatur] The Cologne edition has operiebatur, with a single P, whereas they write it with a double P, and so does Virgil of Carpentras.

units.la: Erat Allophylis moris] hujus moris nec Scriptura meminit, nec etiam Iosephus. Unde vero habeat incertum.
units.tr: Erat Allophylis moris] Neither Scripture nor even Josephus mentions this custom. Where he got it is uncertain.

units.la: Pag. 48. Idoli] Dagon, quod vel a pisce ita dictum, vel certe a frumento. Idenim Dagan Ebrai vocant, ut Dagon sit ζεὺς ἀὀρ[illegible, ~3 letters] quem Philo Byblius in historia Phœnicum Σιτων interpretatur,
units.tr: Pag. 48. Idoli] Dagon, which is so called either from fish or certainly from grain. For the Hebrews call it Dagan, so that Dagon is Zeus [illegible], which Philo of Byblos, in his History of the Phoenicians, renders as Σιτῶν [Sitōn].

units.la: Cum XX. annis Ebræis præfuisset] numerus hic quadrat cum eo qui habetur, Iud. 15 20. Quanquam Thalmudici videntur ibi legisse olim XL. pro XX. Vide quæ notavimus ad pag. 47. Quibus addo ex Salmanticensi, Samson judicavit 20. annis, licet in Ierosolymitano dicatur in scriptura ipsorum invenire quod judicaverit 40 annis. Nam etiam de sententia eorum sunt 20. tantum. Quippe dicunt, ipse judicavit 20. annis, & quomodo dicit Scriptura 40 annis. Docet post mortem 20. annis durasse metum ejus apud Philistæos.
units.tr: Cum XX. annis Ebræis præfuisset] This number agrees with what is found at Judg. 15.20, although the Talmudists seem once to have read forty there instead of twenty. See what I noted at p. 47. To these I add, from the Salamanca [edition], that Samson judged twenty years, though in the Jerusalem [Talmud] it is said that in their scripture one finds that he judged forty years. For they also hold that it was only twenty. Indeed they say: he judged twenty years, and how does Scripture say forty years? It teaches that his fear lasted twenty years after his death among the Philistines.

units.la: Huic Simmichar succesfsit] infra, nam quum post Samson judicem Semigar fuerit. Hanc scripturam veriorem esse arbitror. Semigar, id est, [illegible, ~5 letters], quod nunc legunt Samgar. Hujus mentio supra pag. 41. & Iud. 3, 31.
units.tr: Simmichar succeeded him] Below, for after the judge Samson there was Semigar. I think this reading is the truer one. Semigar, that is, [illegible, ~5 letters], which they now read as Samgar. Mention of him above, p. 41, and Judg. 3:31.

units.la: sine duce] Iud. 18, 1.
units.tr: without a leader] Judg. 18:1.

units.la: Iudas] tribus Iuda.
units.tr: Judah] the tribe of Judah.

units.la: Annum unum imperii ejus] Semigar, qui tamen Abodja-dici, non Samsoni successit, anno imperij primo vitam cum morte commutaverit, Iosephus.
units.tr: One year of his rule] Semigar, who succeeded Samson, though he was Abodja-dici and not Samson's successor, ended his life in the first year of his rule, according to Josephus.

units.la: Annotarunt] Sigonius mavult, annotaverunt: ego nihil mutandum putarim. Nam & infra pag. 66. annotarim legitur pro annotaverim.
units.tr: The authors have noted] Sigonius prefers "annotaverunt." I think nothing should be changed, since below, p. 66, "annotarim" is read for "annotaverim."

units.la: Plerique ita eum præterierunt] Eusebius, Augustinus & alij.
units.tr: Most have passed him over in this way] Eusebius, Augustine and others.

units.la: Heli sacerdotem] rectius scribitur Eli sine aspiratione. Sacerdotem autem appellat eum qui summus sacerdos sive pontifex erat, ut pag. 9. a Melchisedec sacerdote benedicitur. Sic sacerdotium pro pontificatu positum invenitur.
units.tr: Eli the priest] It is more correctly written Eli, without the aspirate. He calls him priest because he was the chief priest or high priest, as on p. 9 he is blessed by Melchizedek the priest. So "priesthood" is also found used for the high priesthood.

units.la: Civile bellum] inter tribum Benjamin & alias undecim.
units.tr: Civil war] between the tribe of Benjamin and the other eleven.

units.la: In oppido Gabaa] quod est oppidum tribus Benjamin, & alter Gaba dicebatur: unde Gaba Benjamin, Iud. 20, 10. [illegible, ~4 letters] Gabaa, ut [illegible, ~4 letters] Samson, & [illegible, ~4 letters] Gaba seu potius Gabe, ut [illegible, ~5 letters] Photifara seu Photiphare. Nunc legunt Geba.
units.tr: In the town of Gibeah] which is a town of the tribe of Benjamin, and was also called Gaba; hence "Gaba of Benjamin," Judg. 20:10. [illegible, ~4 letters] Gibeah, as [illegible, ~4 letters] Samson, and [illegible, ~4 letters] Gaba, or rather Gabe, as [illegible, ~5 letters] Photifara or Photiphare. Now they read Geba.

units.la: Pag. 49. A Benjamitis] a filiis Iemini. Iud. 19, 16. Nota Benjamitas dici filios Iemini non filios Benjamin. Quod quia non vum, ideo prætereundum non erat.
units.tr: p. 49. By the Benjamites] by the sons of Jemini. Judg. 19:16. Note that the Benjamites are called sons of Jemini, not sons of Benjamin. Since this is not an unimportant point, it should not be passed over.

units.la: Senex quidam] ex monte Ephraim. Stupro eum subdere] imo, occidere. Iud. 20.5.
units.tr: A certain old man] from the mountain of Ephraim. To subject her to outrage: nay, to kill her. Judg. 20:5.

units.la: Ægreque exhortati] Sigonius emendat, exorati. probo ve-hementer.
units.tr: And with difficulty persuaded] Sigonius emends to "prevailed upon." I strongly approve.

units.la: An verecundia] ita legendum, non, ut in exemplari, quod secutus sum, verecundiae.
units.tr: Out of modesty] so it should be read, not "of modesty," as in the copy I followed.

units.la: Viso viro] imo priusquam vidisset virum animam effudit[?]. Nam simulac ostium aperuisset mortuam comperit, quam adhuc viuere putabat, Iud. 19.28.
units.tr: When he saw the man] nay, before he had seen the man she gave up her soul. For as soon as he had opened the door he found her dead, whom he still thought to be alive, Judg. 19:28.

units.la: Per 12. tribus] etiamne per tribum Benjamin? videtur. Quidam tamen negant, sed eos errare puto. Vide sis Nicolaum de Lyra. In fonte habetur, per omnes terminos Israel.
units.tr: Through the twelve tribes] Does this include the tribe of Benjamin too? It seems so. Some deny it, but I think they are mistaken. See Nicholas of Lyra. In the source it is found: through all the borders of Israel.

units.la: Iudas] tribus Iuda, ut pag. 40. dux belli Iudas assumptus est.
units.tr: Judah] the tribe of Judah, as on p. 40, where Judah was taken as leader of the war.

units.la: Regum libri sequuntur] numero quatuor, quorum priores in ritualibus Ebraeorum Samuelis tribuuntur, posteriores Regum nomine inscribuntur. Nota hos omnes libros in codicibus Graecis titulum habere βασιλειῶν[?], id est, regnorum: unde paulo post, Eli etiam sacerdos libris regnorum fuisse referatur. Hiero. epist. §2[?].
