Asa also fell ill in the 39th year of his reign, with a most severe pain in his feet; yet in his sickness he did not seek the Lord, but relied rather on the art of physicians. These are the words of the Vulgate translator, in the passage cited above.

units.la: Initio regni huius] si Josepho credendum, secundo jam anno regni Asa cxIIo [?]. Scribit hoc Josephus Orig. lib. 8. cap. 5. Quod tamen verum non videtur. Nam legimus 1 Reg. 15. 25. Nadab filius Ieroboam regnavit super Israel anno secundo Asa regis Iuda.
units.tr: At the beginning of this reign: if we are to believe Josephus, in the second year of Asa's reign, the 112th [?]. Josephus writes this in Origen book 8, chapter 5. This does not seem true, however. For we read at 1 Kings 15.25, "Nadab the son of Jeroboam reigned over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah."

units.la: Maternis meritis] assentior Sigonio legenti, paternis meritis. Nam quia Ieroboam cultum vitulorum instituerat, ideo progenies ejus in vita Domino erat. Vide 3 Reg. 15. 30.
units.tr: For his mother's merits: I agree with Sigonius, who reads "for his father's merits." For because Jeroboam had instituted the worship of calves, his line was for that reason alive to the Lord. See 3 Kings 15.30.

units.la: Banachiæ filium] olim emendavi, nec adhuc pœnitet, Baasa Achiæ filium. Vix dubito quin Severus ita scripserit. Vide 3 Reg. 15. 27.
units.tr: The son of Banachia: I corrected this long ago, and I still do not regret it: Baasha the son of Ahijah. I scarcely doubt that Severus wrote it so. See 3 Kings 15.27.

units.la: Is [?] textu & vigesimo imperij anno defunctus est] ex eo-dem dem loco legendum quarto & vigesimo. Nam diserte ibi εβερ 33. regnavit Baasa filius Ahiæ super omne Israel in Thersa 24. annis. Nec differunt LXX. ubi ἐνέτη καὶ τιοτάγα ἐτη Idem numerus est in Eusebio, nisi quod in Latinis Scaligeri leftum XXIX. pro XXIV. Nam etiam Græcum exemplar habet ἐτη κδ. Vide, si otium.
units.tr: He died in the text and in the twenty-first year of his reign: from the same passage, one should read the fourth and twentieth. For there it is plainly stated, "Baasha the son of Ahijah reigned over all Israel at Tirzah for 24 years" (3 Kings 15.33). The LXX do not differ, where [Greek] for twenty-four years. The same number is in Eusebius, except that in Scaliger's Latin editions XXIX is read for XXIV. For the Greek copy too has 24 years [Greek]. See, if you have leisure.

units.la: Ad Helam filium] scribendum hoc nomen absque aspiratione, ad Elam filium, nisi magis placet, ad Ela filium. Nam est ꞌꞌꞌꞌ in textu Ebræo, 3 Reg. 16. 6. Græce ἡλὰ υἱὸς Βααςὰ. Quod cum leniter ibi scriptum sit, mirum cur Sulpicius aspiraverit. An exemplari usus fuit, in quo ἡλὰ videtur.
units.tr: To Hela his son: this name should be written without the aspirate, to Ela his son, unless it pleases more, to Ela his son. For in the Hebrew text it is spelled without the aspirate, 3 Kings 16.6; in Greek, Ela son of Baasha. Since it is written lightly there, it is strange why Sulpicius aspirated it. Perhaps he used a copy in which Hela appears.

units.la: Zambri] antiquum est pro Zamri. Sic Mambre pro Mamre; Ambri pro Amri. His adde Nembrod quod nunc scribunt Nemrod. Ceterum in uno codice offendi, lambri.
units.tr: Zambri: an old form for Zamri. So Mambre for Mamre, Ambri for Amri. To these add Nembrod, which they now write Nemrod. Moreover, in one codex I found Lambri.

units.la: Princeps equitum] dux media partis equitum.
units.tr: Commander of the cavalry: leader of the half of the cavalry.

units.la: Ab hoc pars populi secessit] non a Zamri secessit, sed post excessum ejus populus divisus est in partes duas; quarum una Thebni secuta eum regem facere statagebat, altera vero Amri sequebatur, quæ etiam prævaluit. Vide 3. Reg. 16 21.
units.tr: Part of the people seceded from him: it did not secede from Zamri; but after his departure the people was divided into two parts. One part, following Tibni, was striving to make him king; the other followed Omri, and this prevailed. See 3 Kings 16.21.

units.la: Thamni cuidam] Θαμνὶ habent codices Græci, sed in Ebræo ꞌꞌꞌꞌ Thebni sive Thabni, ut quidem antiqua lectio erat. Josephus Thamanum appellat. error natus, ut credibile est, ex antiquo charactere. Qualis & in στιναχηςέμ. Vide sis Castigationes nostras in historiam Tobiæ
units.tr: To a certain Thamni: the Greek codices have [Greek] Thamni, but in the Hebrew it is Tibni or Tabni, as was indeed the older reading. Josephus calls him Thamanus. The error arose, as is credible, from an ancient character, such as also in [Greek]. See, if you please, our Castigations on the history of Tobias.

units.la: Sed lambri] veritas Scripturæ Amri, quod nunc legunt Omri. Amri, Ambri, ut Zamri, Zambri, simile mendum i. Machab 9. 36. in Ιαμβρι. Nam emendant Αμβρι: recte an secus, viderint eruditi.
units.tr: But Lambri: the truth of Scripture is Amri, which they now read as Omri. Amri, Ambri, as Zamri, Zambri; a similar error at 1 Macc. 9.36, in [Greek] Iambri. For they emend it to [Greek] Ambri. Whether rightly or not, let the learned judge.

units.la: Ante hunc septem annos, & cum eodem duodecim regnavit] cum bona venia, cumque pace tua Severe, Amri regnavit duntaxat duodecim annos, videlicet sex in Thersa & totidem in Samaria a se condita, 3. Reg. 16. 23. minus certum, quod de Thamni scribit. Nam quamdiu regnaverit non est proditum sacris monumentis.
units.tr: Before him seven years, and with the same, twelve years he reigned: with good leave, and with your peace, Severus: Omri reigned only twelve years, namely six in Tirzah and as many in Samaria, which he himself founded, 3 Kings 16.23. What he writes of Tibni is less certain. For how long he reigned is not recorded in the sacred records.

units.la: Afab mortuo] Asa mortuus est anno regni sui quadragesimo primo, 2. Paralip. 16. 13. Quanvis in editione Græca ἐν τῷ Διαςαρακοσῷ ἐτες τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ. In Chronico Eusebii, Hebræorum Juda rex quintus Asa, ann. XLI.
units.tr: Asa being dead: Asa died in the forty-first year of his reign, 2 Chron. 16.13. Although in the Greek edition it is [Greek] in the forty-third year of his reign. In Eusebius's Chronicle, "the fifth king of the Hebrew Judah, Asa, 41 years."

units.la: Vir religiosus virtutibus] est qui mavult, religionis virtutibus: ego nihil mutandum putarim.
units.tr: A man religious in his virtues: it is one who prefers "of the virtues of religion." I would think nothing should be changed.

units.la: Is cum lambri pacem habuit] potestne hoc ita esse? Nam Amri ante Iosaphatum fato functus est. Id liquet ex 3.Reg.16. 29. Achab autem filius Amri sive Omri regnavit super Israel anno trigesimo octavo Asa regis Iuda, ut habetur 3.Reg.16.29.
units.tr: He had peace with Lambri: can this be so? For Omri died before Jehoshaphat. This is clear from 3 Kings 16.29: "Ahab the son of Omri or Amri reigned over Israel in the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah," as is stated in 3 Kings 16.29.

units.la: Cum regnasset annos V. & XX.] Sic 2 Paralip. 20.31, & in Chronicis Eusebij, Hebraeorum Iuda rex sextus Iosaphat religiosus ann.25. Quod ibi religiosus, id est, εὐσεβὴς[?], hic dicitur, religiosis virtutibus clarus.
units.tr: When he had reigned 25 years: so 2 Chron. 20.31, and in Eusebius's Chronicle, "the sixth king of the Hebrew Judah, Jehoshaphat, pious, 25 years." What is there called pious, that is [Greek], is here called distinguished for the virtues of religion.

units.la: Vltra omnes] id est, supra omnes. Sic alibi, ultra modum pro supra modum. Sic ultra famam, & pag.137. ædem sacratam ultra omnia mortalia illustrem. In vita Martini, ultra humanum modum.
units.tr: Beyond all: that is, above all. So elsewhere "beyond measure" for "above measure." So "beyond fame," and on page 137, a temple consecrated, illustrious beyond all mortal things. In the Life of Martin, "beyond human measure."

units.la: Pag.71. Basæ regis ex Sidone] aut Basæ delendum, aut Ethbaal pro eo reponendum. Sic enim vocatur, 3.Reg.16.31. Quanquam in libris Græcorum Ἰεζιβάαλ[?]. Iosephus Iethobalem vocat, lib.8. cap.7. Apud Menandrum Ephesium, Ἰεζιβάαλ[?] ὁ τῆς Ἀσσυρίας[?] βασιλεύς[?].
units.tr: Page 71. Of King Basa from Sidon: either Basa must be deleted, or Ethbaal put in its place. For so he is called at 3 Kings 16.31, though in the books of the Greeks [Greek]. Josephus calls him Ethbaal, book 8, chapter 7. In Menander of Ephesus, [Greek], king of Assyria.

units.la: Baali] id est, Iovi Syrio. Iupiter ille in Babylonia Bel dicebatur. Qua de re diximus alibi.
units.tr: Baali] That is, to Syrian Jupiter. That Jupiter was called Bel in Babylonia. I have discussed this matter elsewhere.

units.la: Helias] leniter scribendum Elias. Nam est Aleph in scriptura Ebraica.
units.tr: Helias] It should be written more lightly as Elias, since there is an Aleph in the Hebrew text.

units.la: Oratione cœlum conclusit] in epistola catholica Iacobi apostoli, cap.5. verf 17. Elias homo erat eisdem quibus nos passionibus obnoxius, & precibus precatus est ne plueret: & non pluit super terram annos tres & sex menses.
units.tr: Oratione cœlum conclusit] In the catholic epistle of the apostle James, chapter 5, verse 17: "Elias was a man subject to the same passions as we are, and he prayed earnestly that it would not rain; and it did not rain upon the earth for three years and six months."

units.la: Cibum] carnes & panem.
units.tr: Cibum] Meat and bread.

units.la: Torrens proximus] torrens Carith contra Iordane positus.
units.tr: Torrens proximus] The brook Cherith, situated opposite the Jordan.

units.la: Inde] postquam aruisset torrens.
units.tr: Inde] After the brook had dried up.

units.la: Saraptæ opidum ] locutio est ut, urbs Romæ: alioqui dixisset, Saraptam opidum. Sed est cur malim Saraphtham, haud nescius in Bibliis Græcis esse Σαρεφθὰ[?] Σιδωνίας[?].
units.tr: Saraptæ opidum] This is a usage like "the city of Rome"; otherwise he would have said "Sarepta the town." But I have reason to prefer Saraphtha, since I am well aware that in the Greek Bibles the reading is Σαρεφθά [Sarephtha] of Sidon.

units.la: Nisi pusillum farris] eo labor ut credam Severum scripsisse, pugillum farris: tamen non adseverο. Movet me primum quod in editione LXX. ἐξ ἀλεύρου[?] ἐν τῇ ὑδείᾳ[?]: deinde quod apud Hieronymum, quantum pugillus capere potest. δράξ enim est pugillus, quantum videlicet pugno comprehendi potest. Mirum autem cur pro farina, far posuerit.
units.tr: Nisi pusillum farris] I am inclined to believe that Severus wrote "a handful of meal" (pugillum farris), though I do not assert it. I am moved first by the fact that the Septuagint has "from the flour [ἐξ ἀλεύρου] in the jar [ἐν τῇ ὑδρίᾳ]"; and then by the fact that Jerome has "as much as a handful can hold." For δράξ [drax] means a handful, that is, as much as can be grasped with the fist. It is strange, however, why he put "far" for "flour."

units.la: Vna cum filiis] [illegible, ~8 letters] μὲν ἐστι in LXX. qui [illegible, ~3 letters] legerunt pro לִבְנִי[?], id est filio meo. Sic apud Hoseam ijdem legerunt filios meos, ubi nunc in Ebraeo, ex Aegypto vocavi filium meum.
units.tr: Vna cum filiis] [illegible] In the Septuagint it is ... (the Greek word for "is" or "indeed") ... they read לִבְנִי [livni], that is, "my son," instead of it. So too in Hosea the same translators read "my sons," where the Hebrew now has "out of Egypt I called my son."

units.la: Nec hydriam farre] videtur farris vocabulum pro farina usurpare. Hoc primum: deinde hydriam appellat quem Ebraei cadum indigitant, quia videlicet in Bibliis Graecis legerat, ὑδρίαν ἀλεύρου[?]; & hydria farina.
units.tr: Nec hydriam farre] He seems to use the word "far" (spelt) for "flour." First, this: then he calls the jar (hydria) what the Hebrews designate as a cadus, because he had evidently read in the Greek Bibles "a jar [ὑδρίαν] of flour"; and "hydria" means a jar of flour.

units.la: Nec vas oleo esse minuendum] hoc vas Ebraeis dicitur קַנְקַן[?], Graecis interpretibus καψάκης, quae & κάψα i. capsa. In Hiero. est lecythus.
units.tr: Nec vas oleo esse minuendum] This vessel is called by the Hebrews קַנְקַן [kankan], by the Greek translators καψάκης [kapsakēs], which is also κάψα [kapsa], i.e. "box." In Jerome it is "lecythus" (oil flask).

units.la: Tantum accrescceret] est cur malim, tantum accrevit.
units.tr: Tantum accrescceret] I would prefer "so much increased" (tantum accrevit).

units.la: Ejusdem videns filium] liber est inter opera B. Augustini, cui titulus, De mirabilibus Scripturae. In eo scriptum lectum, Ebraei censent Ionam fuisse filium illius viduae, quem Elias e mortuis suscitavit. Quod verum an falsum sit, aliis expendendum relinquo.
units.tr: Ejusdem videns filium] There is a book among the works of St. Augustine, titled On the Wonders of Scripture. In it is written and read that the Hebrews hold that Jonah was the son of that widow, whom Elijah raised from the dead. Whether this is true or false I leave for others to weigh.

units.la: Mortuum] miraculum hoc elevant qui vere mortuum fuisse negant, in qua opinione videtur fuisse Moses Cordubensis, cognomento Aegyptius. Nam quod in textu, & anima ejus non relicta in eo, tale quid legimus in Daniele, cujus haec verba sunt, & anima non relicta fuit in me. Id certius in morbis accidere, certius est quam ut probari debeat. Adito sis ad More part. 1. c. 42. & lege quae interpres Sem Tob annotavit ad illud caput.
units.tr: Mortuum] Those who deny that he was truly dead explain away this miracle. In this opinion Moses of Cordoba, surnamed the Egyptian, seems to have been. For the words in the text, "and his soul was not left in him," we read something similar in Daniel, whose words are, "and his soul was not left in me." That this happens more surely in illnesses is more certain than that it ought to be proved. Consult More, part 1, chapter 42, and read what the commentator Sem Tob has noted on that chapter.

units.la: Pag. 72. Exprobratoque ei sacrilegio] accipio ut pag 31. populumque luxui & sacrilegio dedidum, id est, idololatriae. Amat enim Sulpicius nostrer cultum idolorum sacrilegium vocare. Nam cultus ille honorem Deo debitum, quae res sacra est, legit ac furatur. Vide quoque 37. 81. & 85. Sed & pag. 75. ait, mirum id Eliae fuit, qui se solum a sacrilegio immunem esse crediderat.
units.tr: Pag. 72. Exprobratoque ei sacrilegio] I take it as on page 31: "and the people given over to luxury and sacrilege," that is, to idolatry. For our Sulpicius likes to call the worship of idols sacrilege. For that worship steals and robs God of the honour owed to Him, which is a sacred thing. See also 37, 81 and 85. But on page 75 he also says it was a wonder in Elijah, who had believed himself alone free from sacrilege.

units.la: Sacerdotibus CCCC fere & L.] suo more addidit fere, quod hic plane redundat. Nam prophetae Baal erant numero quadringenti & quinquaginta. Praeterea non optima fide haec refert cum ait, accitis idolorum & lucorum sacerdotibus CCCC & L. Nam praeter idoli Baal sacerdotes CCCC & L, erant etiam luci sive lucorum sacerdotes C C C C. Vide 3. Reg. 18. 19.
units.tr: Sacerdotibus CCCC fere & L.] In his usual way he added "about," which here is wholly superfluous. For the prophets of Baal were four hundred and fifty in number. Moreover, he does not report this in good faith when he says, "with the priests of the idols and groves, 400 and 50 were summoned." For besides the 450 priests of Baal, there were also 400 priests of the groves. See 1 Kings 18:19.

units.la: Domini fui] Dei sui.
units.tr: Domini fui] "of his God."

units.la: Tum forte] adverbium forte otium agit. Vide Sigonium.
units.tr: Tum forte] The adverb "by chance" (forte) here expresses leisure. See Sigonius.

units.la: Cæsum] in partes dissectum
units.tr: Cæsum] Cut into pieces.

units.la: Vitulum] bovem est in nostra vulgata & פר [?] in Ebræo, id est, juvencum. Quas ætates sub uno nomine μόσχου [?] Græci comprehendunt.
units.tr: Vitulum] In our Vulgate it is "ox" (bovem), and in the Hebrew פר [par], that is, a young bull. The Greeks comprehend these ages under the one name μόσχος [moschos].

units.la: Sacrarium] aquæductum, qui circum altare. Vocat autem sacrarium quia locus erat sacratus Deo. Ceterum aquam effudit super holocaustum tanta copia ut circum aram redundaret ipsamque scrobem (aquæductum alij vocant,) quæ circum altare, repleret.
units.tr: Sacrarium] The water channel around the altar. He calls it a sacrarium because it was a place consecrated to God. Moreover, he poured so much water over the burnt offering that it overflowed around the altar and filled the trench itself (which others call the water channel) that surrounded the altar.

units.la: Cum hostia] cum holocausto.
units.tr: Cum hostia] With the burnt offering.

units.la: Pag.73. Ad torrentem] Cifon, qui torrens est Galilææ inferioris, ad radices montis Thabor unde oritur.
units.tr: Pag.73. Ad torrentem] The Kishon, a brook of Lower Galilee, at the foot of Mount Tabor, where it rises.

units.la: Regem prophetaprosecutus est] donec veniret in Iezrael.
units.tr: Regem prophetaprosecutus est] As far as Jezreel.

units.la: Ad remotiora secessit] in disertum Bersabee, quod in fini-bus Iudææ.
units.tr: Ad remotiora secessit] Into the desert of Beersheba, which is on the borders of Judea.

units.la: Qui se idolis non dedissent] pro, dedidissent. Vide 3. Reg. 19.18.
units.tr: Qui se idolis non dedissent] For "had given themselves over." See 1 Kings 19:18.

units.la: Vineam Nabuthæi] suspicor initio scriptum fuisse, Nabutha. Nam in edit. Græca ναβουθαί. Solet autem nomina Ebraica indeclinata relinquere. Apud Iosephum invenio Nabuthus, ut in nostra vulgaria, Naboth. Nabuthæus aliud est. Sane Nabuthæi Arabes appellantur, quos ναβαταῖους [?] Græci vocant, 1. Mach 9.35.
units.tr: Vineam Nabuthæi] I suspect that originally it was written "Nabutha." For in the Greek edition it is ναβουθαί [nabouthai]. Moreover, he usually leaves Hebrew names undeclined. In Josephus I find "Nabuthus," as in our vernacular "Naboth." "Nabuthæus" is something else. Indeed, the Nabatheans are Arabs, whom the Greeks call ναβαταῖοι [nabataioi], 1 Maccabees 9:35.

units.la: Adhærentem sibi] id est, palatio suo. Tale est, ivit ad Pompeium pro ad domum Pompeij.
units.tr: Adhærentem sibi] That is, to his palace. The usage is like "he went to Pompey" for "to the house of Pompey."

units.la: Dolis Iezabel interfectus est] falsis subornatis testibus, qui dicebant eum Deo ac regi maledixisse, lapidibus obrutus est.
units.tr: Dolis Iezabel interfectus est] By false witnesses suborned by Jezebel, who said that he had cursed God and the king; he was stoned to death.

units.la: Cum tamen Nabuthæi morte doluisse referatur] 3.Reg. 21.16. καὶ ἐγένετο ὡς ἤκουσεν Ἀχαὰβ ὅτι τέθνηκεν Ναβουθαί ὁ Ἰεζραηλίτης, καὶ διέρρηξε τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ καὶ περιεβάλετο σάκκον. Hæc non habentur in Ebræo, nec apud Hieronymum. Sumpta autem videntur ex vers.27. ejusdem capitis, ubi Græci, καὶ περιεβάλετο σάκκον ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἡ ἐπάταξεν τὸν ναβουθαί [?]. Alter Iosephus, qui narrat ipsum exiluisse gaudio & ad visendum id prædium se consessim contulisse, lib 8. cap.7.
units.tr: Cum tamen Nabuthæi morte doluisse referatur] 1 Kings 21:16: καὶ ἐγένετο ὡς ἤκουσεν Ἀχαὰβ ὅτι τέθνηκεν Ναβουθαὶ ὁ Ἰεζραηλίτης, καὶ διέρρηξε τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ καὶ περιεβάλετο σάκκον [And it came to pass, when Ahab heard that Naboth the Jezreelite was dead, that he rent his clothes and put on sackcloth]. These words are not found in the Hebrew, nor in Jerome. They seem to have been taken from verse 27 of the same chapter, where the Greek has: "and he put on sackcloth in the day that he smote Naboth." The other Josephus relates that he leapt for joy and at once went to view that estate, book 8, chapter 7.

units.la: Actis deinde obsessorum rebus] Sigonius reponit Fractis. Quid si arctis, ut infra pag.116 arctis suorum rebus? nisi sane respexit ad illud Terentij, actum est.
units.tr: Actis deinde obsessorum rebus] Sigonius proposes "broken" (fractis). What if "straitened" (arctis), as below on page 116, "the straitened circumstances of his own people"? Unless perhaps he had in mind that line of Terence, "it is all over."

units.la: Fœminas] uxores & filios. Hæc historia refertur in libris Ebræorum cap.20. & in libris Græcorum cap.21. post occisum Naboth. Hos ut solet, secutus est Sulpicius. Nam secundum Ebraeos Samaria obsessa fuit antequam Naboth occideretur.
units.tr: Fœminas] Wives and sons. This story is related in the Hebrew books in chapter 20, and in the Greek books in chapter 21, after the killing of Naboth. Sulpicius, as usual, followed these. For according to the Hebrews Samaria was besieged before Naboth was killed.

units.la: CXX. millia] in fonte est centum millia duntaxat. Quem numerum etiam Graeca editio agnoscit 3. Reg. 21.29. Sed & Iosephus lib. 8. cap. 8. Eodem tempore fuerunt ruina muri oppressa in Aphec viginti septem millia, ut fortasse Sulpicius ediderit CXXVII. millia.
units.tr: CXX. millia] In the source it is only one hundred thousand. The Greek edition also acknowledges this number, 1 Kings 21:29. Josephus too, book 8, chapter 8, says that at the same time twenty-seven thousand were crushed by the falling of a wall at Aphek. So perhaps Sulpicius published 127 thousand.

units.la: A propheta] a propheta quodam, qui & unus de filiis prophetarum dicitur. 3. Reg. 20.35. Quod noto ut discas filios prophetarum etiam prophetas vocari.
units.tr: A propheta] By a certain prophet, who is also called one of the sons of the prophets. 1 Kings 20:35. I note this so that you may learn that the sons of the prophets were also called prophets.

units.la: Pseudoprophetarum impulsu] qui numero erant circiter quadringenti viri. 3 Reg. 22. 6.
units.tr: Pseudoprophetarum impulsu] who were about four hundred men in number. 1 Kings 22:6.

units.la: Spreto Michaea] est cur praetulerim Michaia. Nam in μιχαία, unde vulgatum Michaeas, non est diphthongus Graeca, ut vulgus existimat. Quid igitur? Ebraei scribunt מִיכָיְהוּ in qua Scriptura prius Iod quiescit, posterius legitur & est j. consonans. Ex quo liquet sonandum esse Michaja per j. consonam, & non Michaeas per diphthongum.
units.tr: Spreto Michaea] There is reason for my preferring "Michaia." For in μιχαία [Michaia], whence the vulgar "Michaeas" comes, the "ai" is not a Greek diphthong, as the common people think. What then? The Hebrews write מִיכָיְהוּ [Mikhayehu], in which the first yod is silent, and the second is read and is a consonantal j. From this it is clear that "Michaja" must be sounded with a consonantal j, and not "Michaeas" with a diphthong.

units.la: Ochoziae filio imperium reliquit] 3. Reg. 22.40. και ἐβασίλευσεν ἀντ' αὐτοῦ Critici Ebraeorum legerunt Achaziam.
units.tr: Ochoziae filio imperium reliquit] 1 Kings 22:40: καὶ ἐβασίλευσεν ἀντ' αὐτοῦ [and he reigned in his place]. The Hebrew critics read "Ahaziah."

units.la: Is aeger corpore] ex casu quodam, de quo 4. Reg. 1.2.
units.tr: Is aeger corpore] From a certain accident, of which see 2 Kings 1:2.

units.la: Idolum] numen Accaronitarum, Beelzebub dictum sive Baal-Zebub: quod Latine sonat muscae dicas, Iupiter mutca. Nam Baal, Iupiter: & Zebub, musca, id est, μυῖα. Graeci certe hic legunt ἐν τῷ Βάαλ μυῖαν θεὸν ἀκκαρών.
units.tr: Idolum] The deity of the Ekronites, called Beelzebub or Baal-Zebub, which in Latin sounds like "fly-lord" or "Jupiter the fly." For Baal is Jupiter, and Zebub is fly, that is, μυῖα [myia]. The Greeks certainly read here: ἐν τῷ Βάαλ μυῖαν θεὸν ἀκκαρών [in Baal-myian, god of Ekron].

units.la: A Deo monitus] per angelum.
units.tr: A Deo monitus] Through an angel.

units.la: Sed misisti] duo πεντηκόνταρχοι, hoc est quinquagenarij sive semicenturiones cum militibus ipsorum.
units.tr: Sed misisti] Two πεντηκόνταρχοι [pentēkontarchoi], that is, captains of fifty or half-centurions, with their soldiers.

units.la: Coelesti igne absumpti] desideratur verbum substantivum ut dicat, absumpti sunt. Similis locus pag. 65. Vide quae scripsimus ad illum.
units.tr: Coelesti igne absumpti] The verb "to be" is missing here, so it should read "were consumed." A similar passage is on p. 65; see what I wrote on it there.

units.la: Pag. 75. Obiit] sine prole, sive, ut cum Tertulliano loquar, improlis aut illiberis. Itaque in regnum ei successit Ioram frater ejus, anno secundo Ioram filij Iosaphat regis Iuda.
units.tr: Pag. 75. Obiit] Without offspring, or, to use Tertullian's words, improles or illiberi. So his brother Joram succeeded him in the kingdom, in the second year of Joram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah.

units.la: Duodecim annis imperio potitus est] 4. Reg. 3. 1. Καὶ Ἰωράμ υἱὸς Ἀχαζίου ἐβασίλευσεν ἐν Ἰσραὴλ ἐν ἔτει δευτέρῳ Ἰωράμ υἱοῦ Ἰωσαφὰτ βασιλέως Ἰούδα, ἡνίκα ἐβασίλευσε δώδεκα ἔτη.
units.tr: Duodecim annis imperio potitus est] 2 Kings 3:1. And Joram, son of Ahaziah, reigned over Israel in the second year of Joram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and he reigned twelve years. [Καὶ Ἰωράμ υἱὸς Ἀχαζίου ἐβασίλευσεν ἐν Ἰσραὴλ ἐν ἔτει δευτέρῳ Ἰωράμ υἱοῦ Ἰωσαφὰτ βασιλέως Ἰούδα, ἡνίκα ἐβασίλευσε δώδεκα ἔτη.]

units.la: Annis duodeviginti] id est, octodecim, cum octo tantum regnaverit. gnaverit, 1.Paralip.21.5. triginta duorum annorum erat Ioram cum regnare coepisset, & octo annis regnavit in Ierusalem. Si fides habenda Davidi Camio, Ioram iste una cum patre regnavit annis septem. Siquidem Ioram rex decem tribuum coepit regnare anno secundo huius Ioram, 4.Reg.1.17. qui erat decimus octavus Iosaphati, 4 Reg.3.1. Iosaphat autem regnavit annis XXV. Adito fis ad commentarium ejus in hunc locum.
units.tr: Annis duodeviginti] that is, eighteen, although he reigned only eight. (2 Chronicles 21:5:) Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. If we may trust David Chytraeus, this Joram reigned together with his father for seven years. For Joram, king of the ten tribes, began to reign in the second year of this Joram (2 Kings 1:17), who was the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat (2 Kings 3:1). Jehoshaphat, however, reigned twenty-five years. See his commentary on this passage.

units.la: Post hunc Ochozias] qui Achazias Hieronymo. Sic etiam Ebraei hoc nomen legunt & scribunt.
units.tr: Post hunc Ochozias] who is called Achazias by Jerome. The Hebrews also read and write this name in the same way.

units.la: Hoc regnante Helias translatus refertur] de tempore quo translatus fuit Elias nihil mihi lectum praeter quod Iudaeus Salmanticensis observavit in libro Iohasin, cujus verba non pigrabor Latina facere: Ascensio Eliae fuit anno mundi 3047. anno decimo octavo regni Iosaphat, quando regnabat Ioram filius Achab. Videtur autem quod Elisaeus tunc acceperit patrum traditiones ab Elia. Ceterum ex libris praeteritorum apparet quod venerit epistola ab Elia ad Ioram filium Iosaphat circa annum 3061. mundi conditi, translato jam ante Elia. Nam Iosaphat pater ejus & Ioram filius Achab venerunt ad Elisaeum prophetam. Sed in Seder Olam relatum allatam fuisse illam epistolam in principio regni filii Iosaphat, septem videlicet annis post quam raptus est.
units.tr: Hoc regnante Helias translatus refertur] Nothing I have read about the time when Elijah was taken up has come to my notice, except what the Spanish Jew noted in the book Yohasin. I will not hesitate to render his words into Latin: The ascension of Elijah took place in the year of the world 3047, in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat's reign, when Joram, son of Ahab, was reigning. It seems, however, that Elisha then received the traditions of the fathers from Elijah. Moreover, from the books of the Former Prophets it appears that a letter came from Elijah to Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, about the year 3061 of the created world, Elijah having already been taken up earlier. For Jehoshaphat, his father, and Joram, son of Ahab, came to the prophet Elisha. But in Seder Olam it is related that this letter was brought in the beginning of the reign of Jehoshaphat's son, that is, seven years after he was taken up.

units.la: Et aliquanto post, Videtur ex textu quod Elisaeus mortuus sit anno trigesimo septimo regni Ioas regis Iuda, qui est annus mundi 98. secundum aeram minorem. Quod si ei̇t, vixit Elisaeus annum unum supra quinquaginta post ascensionem Eliae. Et iterum, Ex Seder Olam discimus anno decimo Ioas regis Israel, qui fuit septimus post obitum Ioas regis Iuda, vita functum Elisaeum. Quod si verum, vixit Elisaeus 61. annos post raptum Eliae. Et rursum, Autor Seder Olam ait Eliam revelandum quum venerit Messias, qui mox iterum abscindetur & postea revelabitur ubi venerint Gog & Magog. Hastenus Salmanticensis. De ipso Elia variant quoque sententiae doctorum. Alii fatentur ei fuisse translatum, & quidem R. Levi contendit eum Phinees fuisse, quem sequitur universus Israel, ait idem, quem modo nominavi, Salmanticensis. Alii scribunt oriundum ex Gad tribu, in qua Galaad. Certum autem fuisse ex inquilinis Galaad. Patrem habuit, ut alii volunt, ex eadem tribu, matrem ex Benjamin: unde alibi de seipso, Ego, inquit, sum ex filiis filiorum ipsius Ra-chel. Quicquid horum verius, inquit Iudæus ille, cum venerit, ipse indicabit nobis.
units.tr: Et aliquanto post, It seems from the text that Elisha died in the thirty-seventh year of Joash, king of Judah, which is the year of the world 98 according to the lesser era. If that is so, Elisha lived fifty-one years after Elijah's ascension. And again: From Seder Olam we learn that in the tenth year of Joash, king of Israel, which was the seventh after the death of Joash, king of Judah, Elisha had died. If that is true, Elisha lived sixty-one years after Elijah was taken up. And again: The author of Seder Olam says that Elijah will be revealed when the Messiah comes, who will soon be cut off again and afterwards revealed when Gog and Magog come. Thus far the Spaniard. Opinions of the learned also vary about Elijah himself. Some admit that he was taken up; indeed R. Levi maintains that he was Phinehas, whom, the same man whom I have just named, the Spaniard, says, all Israel follows. Others write that he was descended from the tribe of Gad, in which Gilead lies, though it is certain that he was one of the sojourners of Gilead. He had a father, as some want, from the same tribe, and a mother from Benjamin; hence he says elsewhere of himself: I am, he says, of the sons of the sons of Rachel. Whichever of these is more true, that Jew says, when he comes he himself will show us.

units.la: Translatus] Iudæorum vulgus & sapientes credunt eum translatum in hortum Eden, hoc est in Paradisum, ibique vivere cum anima & corpore: a quibus diversi abeunt recentiores Rabbini, & in his R. David, qui scribit eum turbine raptum e terra in aerem usque ad sphæram ignis, ibique consumptum corpus ejus, spiritum autem rediisse ad Deum, qui dedit ipsum.
units.tr: Translatus] The common people of the Jews and their wise men believe that he was taken up into the garden of Eden, that is, into Paradise, and that he lives there with soul and body. More recent rabbis differ from them, among whom is R. David, who writes that he was caught up by a whirlwind from the earth into the air as far as the sphere of fire, where his body was consumed, but his spirit returned to God who gave it.

units.la: Helisæus] scribo. Elisæum; quod factum putarim ex Hebræo Elisæ Latina declinatione. Nam ex Græco Ἐλισαῖος [?] esset Elisæus, cum diphthongo. Quanquam in editione Romana Ἐλισαῖ [?]. אֱלִישָׁע [?] Elisa, & ἐλισαῖος [?] Elisæ, ut יְלִישָׁע [?] Thare.
units.tr: Helisæus] I write Elisaeus; I suppose this was made from the Hebrew, following the Latin declension of Elisa. For from the Greek Ἐλισαῖος [?] it would be Elisaeus, with a diphthong. Although in the Roman edition it is Ἐλισαῖ [?]. אֱלִישָׁע [?] Elisa, and ἐλισαῖος [?] Elisae, just as יְלִישָׁע [?] Thare.

units.la: Multis signis potens] apud Nicolaum de Lyra recensentur miracula sedecim edita ab Elisæo, cum Elias tantum octo ediderit. Quo accommodant duplum, quo præditus fuit, spiritum Elisæi. Quem tamen locum alij aliter enarrant. Habetur autem, 4.Reg.2.9.
units.tr: Multis signis potens] According to Nicholas of Lyra, sixteen miracles performed by Elisha are listed, although Elijah performed only eight. To these they apply the double spirit with which Elisha was endowed. Other interpreters explain this passage differently. It is found at 2 Kings 2:9.

units.la: Ab eo est viduæ filius resuscitatus] enumerat nunc aliquot signa sive miracula Elisæi, sed plura Scholastici recensent ex libris Ebræorum.
units.tr: Ab eo est viduæ filius resuscitatus] He now lists some of the signs or miracles of Elisha, but the Scholastics enumerate more from the books of the Hebrews.

units.la: Sedecim Elisæi miracula.
units.tr: The sixteen miracles of Elisha.

units.la: 1. Iordanis divisio.
units.tr: 1. The dividing of the Jordan.

units.la: 2. Aquarum sanatio.
units.tr: 2. The healing of the waters.

units.la: 3. Puerorum laceratio.
units.tr: 3. The mauling of the boys.

units.la: 4. Aquæ impetratio pro tribus regibus.
units.tr: 4. Obtaining water for the three kings.

units.la: 5. Olei multiplicatio.
units.tr: 5. The multiplication of the oil.

units.la: 6. Sunamitidis fœcundatio.
units.tr: 6. The fertility of the Shunammite woman.

units.la: 7. Filii ejus suscitatio.
units.tr: 7. The raising of her son.

units.la: 8. Pulmenti dulcoratio.
units.tr: 8. The sweetening of the pottage.

units.la: 9. Panum multiplicatio.
units.tr: 9. The multiplication of the loaves.

units.la: 10. Naaman leprosi curatio.
units.tr: 10. The cleansing of Naaman the leper.

units.la: 11. Gtezi [?] infectio.
units.tr: 11. The infection of Gehazi.

units.la: 12. Ferri natatio.
units.tr: 12. The floating of the iron.

units.la: 13. Oculorum pueri sui apertio ad videndum equos & currus igneos &c.
units.tr: 13. The opening of his servant's eyes to see the horses and chariots of fire, etc.

units.la: 14. Adversariorum excæcatio.
units.tr: 14. The blinding of the adversaries.

units.la: 15. Abundantia commeatus inopinata in porta Samariæ.
units.tr: 15. The unexpected abundance of provisions at the gate of Samaria.

units.la: 16. Suscitatio mortui ad tactum ossium ejus.
units.tr: 16. The raising of the dead by touching his bones.

units.la: Viduæ] Sunamitidis.
units.tr: Widow] of the Shunammite.

units.la: Syrus] Naaman princeps exercitus regis Syriæ: qui a Græcis vocatur ῥαμμὰν ὁ ἀρχῶν τῆς δυνάμεως Συρίας, aut Variantibus libris ὁ ἀρχιστράτηγος βασιλέως Συρίας.
units.tr: Syrian] Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, who is called by the Greeks [ῥαμμὰν ὁ ἀρχῶν τῆς δυνάμεως Συρίας], or in other books [ὁ ἀρχιστράτηγος βασιλέως Συρίας], the commander-in-chief of the king of Syria.

units.la: In usum trium exercituum] Israel, Iuda & Edom. Hæc habentur, 4. Reg. 3. 16.
units.tr: For the use of three armies] Israel, Judah and Edom. These things are found in 4. Reg. 3. 16.

units.la: De exiguo olei immodicis incrementis solutum &c.] historia extat, 4. Reg. 4. 7.
units.tr: Concerning the little oil that was multiplied beyond measure and sold, etc.] the story is found in 4. Reg. 4. 7.

units.la: Ochozias] filius Ioram.
units.tr: Ochozias] son of Joram.

units.la: Ioram] frater Ochoziæ, 4. Reg. 1. 17. filius Achab, 4. Reg. 3. 1.
units.tr: Joram] brother of Ochozias, 4. Reg. 1. 17; son of Ahab, 4. Reg. 3. 1.

units.la: Syros] Hazael regem Syriæ.
units.tr: Syrians] Hazael, king of Syria.

units.la: Iehu] puto Sulpicium scripsisse leu Nam sicGræci inou. Quam- vis in edit. Rom. ieu.
units.tr: Jehu] I think Sulpicius wrote Ieu (leu), for so the Greeks have [ιου]. Although in the Roman edition it is ieu.

units.la: Per prophetam] Elisæum.
units.tr: By the prophet] Elisha.

units.la: Pag. 76. Posito Ochozia] id est, sepulto. Sepultus autem fuit cum patribus suis in civitate David. Vide 4. Reg. 9. 24. Aut posito, id est, mortuo: quod in Euangelio, animam ponere.
units.tr: Page 76. Ochozias having been placed] that is, buried. He was buried with his fathers in the city of David. See 4. Reg. 9. 24. Or "placed", that is, dead, as in the Gospel, "to lay down one's life".

units.la: Iehu tenuit] annis viginti octo.
units.tr: Jehu reigned] twenty-eight years.

units.la: Gotholia] γοθολία. Sic Græci olim legerunt, ut Hiero. A- thalia. Quomodo & critici Ebræorum Masforitæ. Hujus Athal- iæ furorem evasit Ioas a Iosaba sorore Ochoziæ occultatus 4. Reg. 11. 2.
units.tr: Gotholia [γοθολία]. So the Greeks once read it, as Jerome has Athalia; and so also the Masoretic critics of the Hebrews. Joash escaped the madness of this Athaliah, being hidden by Jehosheba, sister of Ochozias, 4. Reg. 11. 2.

units.la: Post octo fere annos] Iosaba filia Ioram, habuit occultum Ioas annos sex, 4. Reg. 11. 3. Septimo restitutum et fuit regnum per Iojada pontificem. Quomodo igitur verum esse potest quod ait, post octo fere annos? An scripsit, post sex fere annos? Nam fere in hoc autore plurimum redundat.
units.tr: After about eight years] Jehosheba, daughter of Joram, kept Joash hidden for six years, 4. Reg. 11. 3. In the seventh year he was restored and the kingdom was given back through Jehoiada the high priest. How, then, can what he says be true, "after about eight years"? Did he write "after about six years"? For "about" (fere) abounds greatly in this author.

units.la: Per sacerdotem] per Iojada pontificem, qui uxorem habebat Iosaba, id est, יהוֹשַׁבְעַת quæ 2. Paralip. 22. 11. Iosabeth vocatur, id est יְהוֹשַׁבְעַת cum Thau in fine. Hujus pontificis meminit Eusebius in Chronico per hæc verba, Iojadas apud Hebræos insignissimus erat pontifex, qui solus post Moysen vixit annos centum triginta. Vide 2. Paralip. 24. 15.
units.tr: By the priest] by Jehoiada the high priest, who had as his wife Jehosheba, that is [יְהוֹשַׁבְעַת], who is called Jehosabeth in 2 Paralip. 22. 11, that is, with a Tau at the end. Eusebius, in the Chronicle, mentions this high priest in these words: "Jehoiada was the most distinguished high priest among the Hebrews; he alone lived after Moses for 130 years." See 2 Paralip. 24. 15.

units.la: Hic initio regni] quamdiu doctorem Iojada sacerdotem habuit 4. Reg. 12. 2. immo cunctis diebus Iojadæ sacerdotis. 2. Paralip. 24. 2.
units.tr: Here at the beginning of his reign] as long as he had Jehoiada the priest as his teacher, 4. Reg. 12. 2; nay, all the days of Jehoiada the priest, 2 Paralip. 24. 2.

units.la: Adulatione principum] principes Iudæ intelligit, quorum adulatione corruptus a pietate defecit. 2. Paralip. 24. 17.
units.tr: By the flattery of princes] he means the princes of Judah, by whose flattery he was corrupted and fell away from piety. 2 Paralip. 24. 17.

units.la: Azael] scribendum aspirate Hazael. Nam in fonte חזאל[?]. Historia hæc habetur, 4 Reg. 12. 17 & 18.
units.tr: Azael] it should be written with an aspirate, Hazael; for in the source it is [חזאל]. This story is found in 4 Reg. 12. 17 and 18.

units.la: Facti invidia] cujus facti? an quod pacem auro templi redemisset? Scriptura dicit eum interfectum ob cædem Zachariæ filij Iojadæ pontificis, 2. Paralip. 24.25.
units.tr: Envy of the deed] what deed? Perhaps that he had bought peace with the gold of the temple? Scripture says he was killed on account of the murder of Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the high priest, 2 Paralip. 24. 25.

units.la: Asuis] servis sive aulicis, in quibus Iozachar filius Samaath, & Iozabad filius Somer, 4. Reg 12.21. Vide quoq; 2. Paralip. 24.26. ubi pro Iozachar legitur Zabad, & pro Somer, Samarith[?] Moabitidis.
units.tr: Servants] that is, attendants or courtiers, among whom were Jozachar son of Shimeath and Jozabad son of Shomer, 4. Reg. 12. 21. See also 2 Paralip. 24. 26, where for Jozachar we read Zabad, and for Shomer, Shimrith the Moabitess.

units.la: Amasia] prope est ut credam Sulpicium edidisse Amessia sive Amessias. Nam ita est in editione τῶ[?] ο; ut etiam apud Eusebium in libris veteribus. Quanquam in aliis Amasias, ut & in Latina nostra vulgata.
units.tr: Amasia] I am almost inclined to think that Sulpicius published Amessia or Amessias. For so it is in one edition, as also in old copies of Eusebius. Though in others it is Amasias, as in our Latin Vulgate.

units.la: Ioachas] prætulerim Ioachaz. Nam sic est in Bibliis Græcis ἰωάχαζ, cum ζ in ultima. Ioachas se tuetur consuetudine illa qua postrema nominis barbari in σ mutatur, ut Annibal, Ἀννίβας.
units.tr: Joachas] I would prefer Joachaz. For so it is in the Greek Bibles, [ἰωάχαζ], with a zeta at the end. Joachas is supported by that custom by which the final syllable of a foreign name is changed to sigma, as Hannibal, [Ἀννίβας].

units.la: Ioæ filio | Ioas, Ioa; ut Iudas, Iudæ; Thomas, Thomæ. regnavit XVI. annis.
units.tr: To the son of Joas] Joas; genitive Joa, as Judas, Judae; Thomas, Thomae. He reigned sixteen years.

units.la: Civile bellum intulit] non bellum ei intulit, sed illatum excepit. Vide Sigonium, & 4. Reg 14.11.
units.tr: He brought civil war] not that he made war upon him, but that he received the war when it was brought against him. See Sigonius, and 4. Reg. 14. 11.

units.la: Amalsiæ[?]] editio Paris, Amaliæ.
units.tr: Amalsia] the Paris edition has Amalia.

units.la: Pag.77. Quantum in libris Regnorum reperi] errat. Nam 4.Reg.14. ἀχοζι χρῷ ἐτίᾳ[?], id est, viginti novem.
units.tr: Page 77. As far as I have found in the books of Kings] he is wrong. For in 4. Reg. 14 the Greek has the number that is twenty-nine.

units.la: In Paralipomenis \ 2 Paralip.25.1.
units.tr: In the Paralipomena] 2 Paralip. 25. 1.

units.la: Annotatum est] alibi, annotatum, absque verbo substantivo. Quod in his libris novum non est.
units.tr: It has been noted] elsewhere it is "annotatum" without a verb substantive, which is not new in these books.

units.la: Ioram enim rex decem tribuum] adhuc quæro ubi Ieroboam in Paralipomenis Ioram vocetur. Affirmat hoc quidem Sigonius, sed affirmat tantum: non probat. Quod sic affirmatur, eodem modo negari potest. Sed quæramus amplius.
units.tr: For Joram, king of the ten tribes] I still ask where Jeroboam is called Joram in the Paralipomena. Sigonius affirms this, but he only affirms it; he does not prove it. What is affirmed in this way can be denied in the same way. But let us inquire further.

units.la: Octavo anno] quinto decimo 4.Reg.14.23.
units.tr: In the eighth year] the fifteenth year, 4. Reg. 14. 23.

units.la: Ozia Amasiæ filio; Ozias vocatur 2. Paralip. 26.1. qui 4 Reg 2 4.2.[?] & 15.8. Azarias dicitur. Fuit ergo Ἀζαρίας[?], id est, binomius.
units.tr: Ozia, son of Amasia] Ozias is called so in 2 Paralip. 26. 1, and in 4. Reg. 15. 8 and 2 Kings 14. 21 he is called Azarias. So he was [Ἀζαρίας], that is, two-named.

units.la: Quarto imperij ejus anno] reponunt, trigesimo octavo imperii ejus anno. rectè an secus, ubi plus otij erit, videro.
units.tr: In the fourth year of his reign] they read "in the thirty-eighth year of his reign." Whether rightly or not, I will consider when I have more leisure.

units.la: Regi Amasiæ effecit] Eusebium intelligit, qui in Chronicis ita scribit, Ebræorum Iudæ Amaliæ[?] anno. XXXIX.
units.tr: To king Amasia he made] he means Eusebius, who in the Chronicle writes thus: "of the Hebrews, of Judah, in the year 39 of Amalia."

units.la: Ioram] Ieroboam, sub quo Amos prophetavit. Amos 1.1. Supra, Ioram enim rex 10. tribuum unum & quadraginta annos imperium tenuisse traditur. Quod firmatur autoritate Scripturæ. Vide 4. Reg. 14. 23. In Eusebio tamen, Hebræorum Israel XII. Ieroboam ann. XLII. Nec aliter est in exemplari Græco.
units.tr: Joram] Jeroboam, under whom Amos prophesied, Amos 1. 1. Above, it is said that Joram, king of the ten tribes, held the kingdom for forty-one years, which is confirmed by the authority of Scripture; see 4. Reg. 14. 23. In Eusebius, however, it is "of the Hebrews, Israel, XII, Jeroboam, year XLII." Nor is it otherwise in the Greek copy.

units.la: Pag. 78. Zacharia propheta] secutus est eos qui 2. Paralip. 26. 5. legunt intelligens in visionibus Dei. Nam diversa lectio alium sensum continet. Vide si vacas, Observat. lib. 14. cap. 20. & cap. 22.
units.tr: Page 78. The prophet Zechariah] he followed those who read "understanding in the visions of God", 2 Paralip. 26. 5. For a different reading contains another sense. See, if you have leisure, Observations, book 14, chapters 20 and 22.

units.la: Adversus finitimos] Philistheos.
units.tr: Against neighbouring peoples] the Philistines.

units.la: Arabas] qui in Gurbaal habitabant.
units.tr: Arabs] those who dwelt in Gurbaal.

units.la: Obtulit] offerre voluit. Nam quo minus offerret impeditus fuit a sacerdotibus. Sic alibi, pugnavit, exponitur pugnare cogi-tavit. Nam verba quandoque conatum duntaxat designant.
units.tr: He offered] he wished to offer. For he was prevented from offering by the priests. So elsewhere "he fought" is explained as "he intended to fight", for words sometimes denote only an attempt.

units.la: Per Azariam] comitatum 8o aliis sacerdotibus.
units.tr: Through Azariah] accompanied by eighty other priests.

units.la: Sacerdotem] pontificem. Notavi alias. Sic Ebraïs כהן sa-cerdos usurpatur pro כהן sacerdos summus. Sic angelus pro archangelus; ὁ ἄγγελος pro ἀρχάγγελος: pisor pro pisorum principe.
units.tr: Priest] high priest. I have noted this elsewhere. Thus among the Hebrews the word for priest [כהן] is used for high priest; thus "angel" for archangel, [ὁ ἄγγελος] for [ἀρχάγγελος]; "pisor" for the prince of the pisors.

units.la: Decessit] non e vita sed abiit templo.
units.tr: He departed] not from life, but he went out from the temple.

units.la: Ioatl.-e filio] Ioatham Græci scribebant pro Iotham; unde obliquus Ioathæ: cujus scripturæ rationem nondum investigare potui.
units.tr: Son of Joatham] the Greeks wrote Ioatham for Iotham, whence the oblique case Ioathae; I have not yet been able to work out the reason for this spelling.

units.la: Admodum sanctus] admodum pius, hoc est ὅσιος, non ὁσιώτατος. Quam vis nitrumque vox Latina significet.
units.tr: Very holy] very pious, that is [ὅσιος], not [ὁσιώτατος], although the Latin word signifies both.

units.la: Gentem Ammonitarum] filios Ammon, a quibus diversi Ammonitæ, licet interpretes hæc nomina confundant. Vide 2. Paralip. 20. 1.
units.tr: The nation of the Ammonites] the sons of Ammon, from whom the Ammonites are distinct, although the interpreters confuse these names. See 2 Paralip. 20. 1.

units.la: Stipendium] tributum, ut pag. 68. cum laxari sibi stipendium popofciflet. Erant autem 100 talenta argenti 1000 cororum tritici & totidem bordei.
units.tr: Tribute] a tax, as on page 68, when they asked that the tribute be relaxed for them. Now the tribute was 100 talents of silver, 1000 cors of wheat and as many of barley.

units.la: Circa hæc tempora] quartus liber Regum e Slendit Ionam sub Ieroboam Ioas filio vixisse, 4. Reg. 14. 25. Atque ita exposuit quoque Iosephus, & post eum S. Hieronymus. A quibus non dissidet Funccius, qui missum fuisse scribit Ionam ad Ninivitas tempora Vzia sive Ozia. Nam Ozias & Ieroboam filius Ioas, qui secundus & junior dicitur, una regnaverunt. Vide Iosephum lib. 9. cap. 11.
units.tr: About this time] the fourth book of Kings seems to show that Jonah lived under Jeroboam, son of Joash, 4. Reg. 14. 25. Josephus also explained it so, and after him St Jerome. Funccius does not dissent from them; he writes that Jonah was sent to the Ninevites in the time of Uzziah or Ozias, for Ozias and Jeroboam, son of Joash, who is called the second and younger, reigned together. See Josephus, book 9, chapter 11.

units.la: Seon filio] nihil etiam dubitans lego Sem filio. Nam Affur filius filius Sem Gen 10,22. Hic Niniven primus condidit, Gen. 10 & 11. Eucherius, Allur Assyrij, ab Assur filio Sem. Hi urbem Ninum ex nomine[?] Nini regis condiderunt, quae nunc Ninive vocatur.
units.tr: Son of Seon] without any doubt I read "son of Sem", for Asshur was the son of Shem, Gen. 10. 22. He first founded Nineveh, Gen. 10 and 11. Eucherius, "Allur" the Assyrians, from Asshur, son of Shem. These founded the city Ninus from the name of king Ninus, which is now called Nineveh.

units.la: Alens virorum millia C, & XX.] imo hominum qui non poterant discernere inter dextram & sinistram, hoc est puerorum. Si verum hoc, ut est verisimum, quantus, putas, erat numerus aliorum, qui discernere poterant inter utramque manum?
units.tr: A hundred and twenty thousand men] indeed, of men who could not tell the difference between right and left, that is, of children. If this is true, as it is likely, how great, do you suppose, was the number of the others who could tell the difference between either hand?

units.la: Sicut olim Sodoma, &c.] hoc de suo adjecit & ex ingenio prompsit: aut ex commentario aliquo sumpsit. Sane in scholiis[?] Cammij Ebraei, evertetur quemadmodum eversæ fuerunt Sodoma & Gomorra. Nam opera eorum similia operibus Sodomitarum
units.tr: Like Sodom of old, etc.] he added this from his own imagination and drew it from his own wit, or else took it from some commentary. Certainly in the scholia of the Hebrew Cammius: "it will be overthrown as Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown, for their works were like the works of the Sodomites."

units.la: Sed præscientia qua] alibi est, quia. Vide Ion. 4.2.
units.tr: But the foreknowledge which] elsewhere it is "because" (quia). See Jonah 4. 2.

units.la: Tharsos] Tharsum Ciliciæ Iosephus. Sed vide an legendum sit Tharsis. Nam sic est Ion. 1. in edit. Græca ηγὶ ἀνίσῃ ἰωνᾶς τὸ φυγεῖν εἰς Θαρσὸς[?]. Adhibe Lectiones meas.
units.tr: Tharsos] Josephus says Tarsus of Cilicia. But see whether it should be read Tarshish, for so it is in Jonah 1 in the Greek edition: "Jonah wished to flee to Tharsos" [εἰς Θαρσὸς]. Consult my readings.

units.la: A ceto] a magno aliquo pisce, quem lamiam fuisse nonnulli putant. Nam balena, quod fauces angustiores habeat, hominem integrum vorare nequit.
units.tr: From the sea-monster] from some great fish, which many think was a shark. For a whale, since its throat is rather narrow, cannot swallow a man whole.

units.la: Post triduum fere] redundat fere. Nam Ion. 2.1. fuit Io-nas in viscenibus piscis tres dies & tres noctes.
units.tr: About three days later] is almost redundant. For in Jonah 2.1 Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

units.la: Ninivitarum littoribus] historia narrat illum in aridam ejectum, nulla mentione facta littorum, in quæ ejectus fuerit.
units.tr: onto the shores of the Ninevites] The narrative says he was cast up on dry land, with no mention made of the shores onto which he was thrown.

units.la: Triduo perituram] expressit lectionem Græcam ἔτι τρεῖς, quam corruptam esse indicat Theodoritus, legendumque τεσσαρακοντα[?] adhuc quadraginta dies: cui assentior. Licet eam excusare conetur Augustinus de civit. Dei lib. 18 cap. 44. Prosper Aquitanus.
units.tr: to perish in three days] He expresses the Greek reading [ἔτι τρεῖς], which Theodoret shows to be corrupt, and says it should be read [τεσσαράκοντα] "still forty days", to which I agree. Although Augustine, in The City of God book 18 chapter 44, tries to excuse it. Prosper of Aquitaine.

units.la: Sic Ninive monitis Ionæ sub tempore cladis Credidit, & tribus in luctu jejuna diebus Promeruit morum excidio consistere regno,
units.tr: So Nineveh, at Jonah's warning, believed in the time of disaster, and by fasting in mourning for three days, earned that its kingdom should stand, though its manners were destroyed.

units.la: Pag. 80. Sellia quidam] Sellum filius Iabes, qui in Græcis Bibliis σαλλοῦμ vocatur. 4. Reg. 15.10 Hic regnavit in Samaria μνᾶ ἡμισ[illegible, ~3 letters], hoc est interprete Hieronymo, mensem unum. Ceterum in Eusebio est dies tres.
units.tr: Page 80. Sellia, a certain man] Sellum, son of Jabesh, who in the Greek Bibles is called [σαλλοῦμ]. 4 Kings 15.10. He reigned in Samaria [the Greek number here is illegible], that is, according to Jerome's interpretation, one month. But in Eusebius it is three days.

units.la: Mane] Alibi, Manes. Manem, Manes; ut Iosephi, Iosef, & est contractum ex Manahem. Aut Mane, ut Iose, in quo abjecta ultima ex Iosephi. Manem, Mane, ut Iosephi, Iose. Sic Goliath, Golias
units.tr: Mane] Elsewhere, Manes. Manem, Manes; as Joseph, Josef, and it is contracted from Manahem. Or Mane, as Jose, in which the last syllable of Joseph is dropped. Manem, Mane, as Josephi, Jose. So Goliath, Golias.

units.la: Mariam, Maria. Paulo ante Manae insidiis, qui est obliquus a Mane. nisi legendum Mane insidiis. Porro in contra&ione Manem pro Manahem nullum est mendum, ut quidam censent. Nam fi- milis contra&io in Manaim pro Mahanaim, id est, castra.
units.tr: Mariam, Maria. A little before, "Manae insidiis", which is an oblique form from Mane, unless it should be read "Mane insidiis". Moreover, in the contraction Manem for Manahem there is no error, as some think. For a similar contraction occurs in Manaim for Mahanaim, that is, camp.

units.la: Filioque Pache reliquit] Phaceia est 4.Reg.15.25 Phaceas in chronico Eusebij. regnavit ann.10.
units.tr: and he left Pekah] Phaceia is at 4 Kings 15.25; Pekah in Eusebius's chronicle. He reigned ten years.

units.la: Phace quadam ejusdem nominis] hic in fonte Phacee dicitur, nomine quidem affini & cognato, sed tamen alio diverso que, Græci quoque in bis nominibus variant. Nam Phaceia in eorum libris vocatur Φακεσιας [?]: alter autem Φακεσ [?] ϊὸς [?] ϱοιτλιε [illegible, ~6 letters]. Sicedit Rom. quam nunc solam consului. Hic Phacee regnavit ann. XX. Sub hoc Theglath Phalaffar rex Assyrius magnam partem populi transplantavit in Affyriam, 4.Reg.15.29.
units.tr: Pekah, a certain man of the same name] here in the source he is called Pekah; indeed the name is related and kindred, but nevertheless a different person, and the Greeks also vary in these names. For in their books Phaceia is called [Φακεσιας]; the other, however, [Φακεσ... ] [illegible]. So the Roman edition, which alone I have now consulted. This Pekah reigned twenty years. Under him Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, transplanted a great part of the people into Assyria, 4 Kings 15.29.

units.la: Ac Ofee ieremptus] vocatur Hofee filius Ela & Δαξιαος [?] εἰκα [?]. Nam alius erat propheta filius Beeri: cujus prophetia extat.
units.tr: and Hoshea, who was slain] he is called Hoshea son of Elah and [Δαξιαος] [εἰκα]. For there was another prophet, son of Beeri, whose prophecy survives.

units.la: Hic ultra omnes reges superiores impius] Aliud colliga ex 4.Reg 17.2.
units.tr: He, impious beyond all the earlier kings] Gather the other point from 4 Kings 17.2.

units.la: Salmanaffar] hunc Eusebius perperā cum Sennacheribo confundit. Sane in historia Ebraica Tobiae Salmanaffar, quem Græ. ea Enemeffarum appellat, pater est Sennacherib, qui filio impe- rium reliquit. Sub hoc Tobias in captivitatem duftus fuit.
units.tr: Shalmaneser] Eusebius wrongly confuses him with Sennacherib. Indeed, in the Hebrew history of Tobit, Shalmaneser, whom the Greeks call Enemessarum, is the father of Sennacherib, who left the kingdom to his son. Under him Tobit was led into captivity.

units.la: Rex Assyriorum] Idem regem Chaldæorum eundem appellat: quam recte, viderint qui harum rerum intelligentiam habent.
units.tr: king of the Assyrians] The same author calls him king of the Chaldeans. Whether this is correct, let those who understand these matters judge.

units.la: Iegemque Æthiopum] quærendum unde hoc habeat. Nam 4.Reg.17.4. vocatur rex Ægypti. Nomen ei in codicibus Ebraeis <bl>ו</bl> So, quod orientales Iudæi legunt <bl>סי</bl> Si. Quanquam in Hieronymo Sua: & in edit. Romana σνγὼς βασιλεὺς αἰγύπτιος. Iosephus habet, Noam Ægyptiorum regem. Chryfoftomus hom XXX.in Iohannem, Huic (Salmanaffari) Ofee primum parum: inde defectione facta Æthiopibus confœderatus est. Quod cum Assyrius intelligeret, sentem illam obser- fam cepit, neque amplius illic habitare permisit, ecce nihil difhidet a neftro Sulpicio. Mirum unde bauferint. Porro Ægyp- tum tunc obtinebat (Eusebius mihi autor Bocchoris, cujus an- nus XXXIII aut XXXIV incidit in nonum Hofee. Regnavit autem anno XLIV quem Sacalon. Æthiops devicit, ejufquere- gnum occupavit. Hæc indigent diligentiore inquisitione. Vtinam mihi nunc tempus & otium superesset.
units.tr: and the king of the Ethiopians] One must ask where he gets this. For in 4 Kings 17.4 he is called king of Egypt. His name in the Hebrew codices is So [ו], which the eastern Jews read as Si [סי]. Although in Jerome it is "Sua", and in the Roman edition the king of Egypt is named by a Greek word. Josephus has Noam, king of the Egyptians. Chrysostom, homily 30 on John: To this Shalmaneser Hoshea at first paid little; then, having revolted, he allied himself with the Ethiopians. When the Assyrian learned this, he seized that siege and no longer allowed him to live there. Behold, this differs in nothing from our Sulpicius. I wonder where they drew it from. Moreover, Egypt was then held by Bocchoris (Eusebius is my authority), whose thirty-third or thirty-fourth year fell in the ninth of Hoshea. He reigned forty-four years, and was conquered by the Ethiopian Sabacon, who occupied his kingdom. These things need more careful inquiry. I wish I had time and leisure now.

units.la: Vrbemque excidit] cepit, non excidit penitus. Adito fis ad ipsum fontem.
units.tr: and he destroyed the city] He took it; he did not destroy it completely. Go to the source itself.

units.la: In regnum suum] in Assyriam, 4.Reg.17.6. in Halach & Chabor, flumine Gozan & urbibus Mediae, ibid. Chalach de opinione quorundam sunt Colchi, & Chabor Iberi. Viderint eruditi.
units.tr: into his kingdom] into Assyria, 4 Kings 17.6: into Halah and Habor, by the river Gozan and in the cities of Media, ibid. Halah, in the opinion of some, are the Colchians, and Habor the Iberians. Let the learned judge.

units.la: Assyriis in hostili solo ad custodiam positis] Iosephus ait fuisse gentem Persicam ex eo tractu, qui ab amne Chutho denominatus est. Orig. Iud. lib. IX. cap XIV. Forsan Assyrios appellat quia subditi erant regi Assyriorum. Siquidem coloni erant ex Chutha & Babylonia: item ex Ava, Hemath & Sepharuaim, 4.Reg.17.24.
units.tr: Assyrians placed on hostile soil as guards] Josephus says it was a Persian people from that region which was named after the river Chuthus. Origen, Jewish Antiquities book 9 chapter 14. Perhaps he calls them Assyrians because they were subjects of the king of the Assyrians. For indeed they were colonists from Chutha and Babylonia, likewise from Ava, Hamath and Sepharvaim, 4 Kings 17.24.

units.la: Exinde ea pars Samaria appellata] non exinde, o bone; sed ab urbe ejus nominis, quae a monte vocitata, ut & mons, a quodam Semer. Res est certa. Tamen Isidorus Orig. lib. 15. Samariam Sennacherib rex construxit vocavitque Samariam, id est, custodiam, quia quando Israel transtulit in Medos, ibi custodes constituit. Haec omnia indigent patrocinio Serarij. Nam ut quidam advocati sunt malarum causarum, sic ille patronus est falsarum & absurdarum opinionum, quae in patribus. Primum enim Sennacherib non transtulit Israelem in Medos; sed ejus pater Salmanassar. Deinde non construxit Samariam, quam longe ante conditam scimus[?]. Nomen etiam Samariae ante haec tempora in usu fuisse certum est quam ut probari debeat. Postremo non constituit ibi custodes, sed transtulit colonias ex Chutha & aliunde.
units.tr: Thence that part was called Samaria] Not thence, good sir; but from the city of that name, which was called after the mountain, as the mountain too was named after a certain Shemer. The matter is certain. Nevertheless Isidore, Origins book 15: King Sennacherib built Samaria and called it Samaria, that is, a guard, because when he transferred Israel to the Medes he set guards there. All these claims need the defence of Serarius. For as some are advocates of bad causes, so he is the patron of false and absurd opinions, which are found in the Fathers. For first, Sennacherib did not transfer Israel to the Medes; his father Shalmaneser did. Next, he did not build Samaria, which we know was founded long before. The name Samaria was in use before these times, as is certain and needs no proof. Lastly, he did not set guards there, but transferred colonists from Chutha and elsewhere.

units.la: Quod lingua Assyriorum custodes Samaritas vocant] Eusebius in Chronicis, Sennacherib rex Chaldaeorum ad custodiendam regionem Iudaeae accolas misit Assyrios, qui aemulatores Iudaeae legis facti Samaritae nuncupati sunt: quod in Latina lingua exprimitur custodes. Quam multa hic male fana. Adesdum[?] Serari. Defende sis Eusebium, qui Salmanassar & Sennacherib in unum confundit: qui Samariam regionem Iudaeae vocat: Sennacheribum regem Chaldaeorum appellat: Samaritas Iudaeae legis aemulatores dicit. Non inficior aliqua ex his a me defendi posse, sed tibi potius, qui otio abundas, haec provincia convenit. Ego interim alios patres adducam, qui ab Eusebio in hac etymologia non dissentiunt. Epiphanius contra
units.tr: Which in the Assyrian language they call the Samaritans, guards] Eusebius in the Chronicle: King Sennacherib of the Chaldeans sent Assyrian settlers to guard the region of Judea, who, having become rivals of the law of Judea, were called Samaritans, which in Latin is expressed as "guards". How many errors are here! Come now, Serarius. Defend, I pray, Eusebius, who confuses Shalmaneser and Sennacherib into one; who calls the region of Samaria Judea; who calls Sennacherib king of the Chaldeans; who says the Samaritans were rivals of the law of Judea. I do not deny that I can defend some of these, but this task suits you better, who abound in leisure. Meanwhile I will adduce other Fathers, who do not dissent from Eusebius in this etymology. Epiphanius against

units.la: hæresies, lib.1.tom. 1. Interpretari possest Samaritas custodes propterea quod custodum locum in terra obtinebant: aut quod custodes essent constituti secundum legem Mosi. Eucherius pag. 185. Samaritæ custodes, eo quod a Babylonis illic ad custodiam collocati essent ludæorum. Ceterum Samar verbum est Ebraicum, non Assyrium. Assyrij & Chaldæi pro eo Natarii usurpant. Vnde in ea lingua custodes potius Natarita dicerentur.
units.tr: Heresies, book 1, volume 1. The Samaritans could be interpreted as guards because they held the place of guards in the land, or because they were appointed as guards according to the law of Moses. Eucherius, page 185. The Samaritans are guards, because the Babylonians had placed them there to guard the Jews. Moreover, Samar is a Hebrew word, not an Assyrian one. Assyrians and Chaldeans use Natarii for it. Hence in that language they would rather be called Natarita, guards.

units.la: Ex quibus plerique divinas cæremonias receperunt, reliquis in errore gentilitatis perseverantibus] hæc ita restituit possent ad veritatem historiæ, qui divinas cæremonias receperunt, & simul in errore gentilitatis perseverarunt. Nam cum Dominum colerent (verba sunt interpretis antiqui, 4. Reg. 17.33.) diis quoque suis serviebant juxta consuetudinem gentium, de quibus translati fuerant Samariam. His adde quod in eodem capite verf. 41. Fuerunt igitur gentes isti timentes quidem Dominum, sed nihilominus & idolis suis servientes: nam & filii eorum & nepotes sicut fecerunt patres sui, ita faciunt usque in hodiernum diem.
units.tr: Of whom most received divine rites, the rest persisting in the error of paganism] These could be restored thus to the truth of history: those who received divine rites and at the same time persisted in the error of paganism. For while they worshipped the Lord (the words of the ancient translator, 4 Kings 17.33), they also served their own gods according to the custom of the nations from whom they had been brought to Samaria. To this add that in the same chapter, verse 41: these nations feared the Lord, but nevertheless also served their idols; for their sons and grandsons, just as their fathers did, do so to this day.

units.la: Divinas cæremonias] lege præceptas, quam solam recipiebant, rejectis prophetis & hagiographis.
units.tr: Divine rites] that is, the prescribed law, which alone they received, the prophets and the Hagiographa being rejected.

units.la: Achas] cum in libris Græcorum fit ἀχάζ, putarim Sulpicium scripsisse Achaz: tamen non adversus eam consuetudinem quam notavi Observat lib.IX cap.IX. Sic in hoc libro reperies Ioachas, qui est obliquus a recto Ioachas. Sic ἰωάχ pro ἰωάχ legitur apud Iosephum, & alibi Iosæs pro Iosephi. Quod tamen & aliam rationem habet. Nam etiam Iose dicimus, unde potest esse Iosæs, ut ex Iesu factum Iesus, Græca & Latina declinatione.
units.tr: Ahaz] Since in the Greek books it is [ἀχάζ], I should think Sulpicius wrote Achaz; yet this is not against that custom which I noted in my Observations, book 9 chapter 9. Thus in this book you will find Ioachas, which is an oblique form of the nominative Ioachas. So in Josephus one reads one Greek form for another, and elsewhere Iosaes for Josephi. This, however, has another explanation. For we also say Iose, whence Iosaes may come, as Iesu became Iesus, by Greek and Latin declension.

units.la: Finitimorum] Syrorum & Israelitarum.
units.tr: Neighbours] The Syrians and the Israelites.

units.la: Deos gentium] Moloch 4. Reg. 16.3. Baalim 2. Paralip 28. 2. & Deos Dammasci sive Darmasci, 4. Reg. 28.23.
units.tr: Gods of the nations] Moloch, 4. Reg. 16.3; the Baalim, 2. Paralip. 28.2; and the gods of Damascus or Darmascus, 4. Reg. 28.23.

units.la: Eorum illæ] gentes videlicet.
units.tr: Those nations] that is, the nations.

units.la: Piaculo] id est, crimine. Proprie crimen ob quod expiatio fieri debet.
units.tr: Guilt] that is, the crime. Properly, the crime for which expiation must be made.

units.la: Ezechias] rectius scribitur Ezecias. Primum quia Græci sic scribunt Ἑζεκίας: deinde quia est Coph in Ebræo characterere, quam consonantem antiqui expresserunt semper per C, simplex. Vide Alphabetum nostrum vetus.
units.tr: Hezekiah] It is more correctly written Ezecias. First, because the Greeks write it [Ἑζεκίας]; second, because the Hebrew has the letter Coph, which the ancients always expressed by a simple C. See our old alphabet.

units.la: Decem tribus in captivitatem nuper abductæ] hæc dicere tunc non potuit. Siquidem oratio hæc habita fuit anno Ezeciæ primo: tribus autem abductæ primum anno septimo ejusdem. Loquor de annis regni ejus.
units.tr: The ten tribes recently carried off into captivity] He could not have said this at that time. For this speech was given in the first year of Ezechias, but the tribes were carried off only in his seventh year. I am speaking of the years of his reign.

units.la: Sacrilegii] idololatriæ, ut 31. 72. & 85.
units.tr: Sacrilege] idolatry, as at 31, 72 and 85.

units.la: Levitas sacerdotesque] maluissem, Sacerdotes levitasque. Nam digniores primo loco nominandi. Quod tamen ubique non observatur. Hic perspicue discriminat sacerdotes a levitis, ut dubitare nunc incipiam de iis quæ scripsi pag. 53. ad Samuel sacerdos. Nam eo labor ut potius credam Sulpicium errasse, qui putarit Samuelem revera sacerdotem; &, si quid sapio in his rebus, etiam pontificem fuisse.
units.tr: The Levites and the priests] I would have preferred "the priests and the Levites", for the more worthy ought to be named first. Yet this is not observed everywhere. Here he plainly distinguishes priests from Levites, so that I now begin to doubt what I wrote at p. 53 on "Samuel the priest". For my labour inclines me rather to believe that Sulpicius erred in thinking Samuel was really a priest; and, if I have any sense in these matters, that he was even high priest.

units.la: Pag.82. Celebrarique Pascha instituit] hoc Pascha cele-bratum fuit mense secundo. Primum quia sacerdotes nondum e-mundati erant mense primo: deinde quia populus tunc adhuc universus non convenerat: postremo quia lustratio templi primum absoluta fuit die decima sexta mensis primi, ut habetur 2. Paralip. 30. 3.
units.tr: Page 82. And he ordered the Passover to be celebrated] This Passover was celebrated in the second month. First, because the priests had not yet been purified in the first month; second, because the whole people had not yet gathered; lastly, because the cleansing of the temple was first completed on the sixteenth day of the first month, as is found in 2 Paralip. 30.3.

units.la: Per omnem terram] Israel & Iuda.
units.tr: Throughout the whole land] Israel and Judah.

units.la: Conventus diem] decima quarta mensis Iar, qui secundus est Nisan in anno Mosaico.
units.tr: The day of the assembly] the fourteenth day of Iar, which is the second month, Nisan in the Mosaic year.

units.la: Edixit] libri quidam, indixit.
units.tr: He proclaimed] some books read "indixit" [he announced].

units.la: Vrbis obsidionem urgebat] Ierosolymorum urbem significat, ideoque scripsit hoc nomen littera majuscula.
units.tr: He pressed the siege of the city] It signifies the city of Jerusalem, and therefore he wrote this name with a capital letter.

units.la: Rex Assyrius portis assultans] hoc fecit per duces suos, in quibus erat Rabsaces, quos Ierosolymam cum valido exercitu miserat, dum Lachis obsideret. Historia refertur, 4. Reg. 18. 17.
units.tr: The Assyrian king assaulting the gates] He did this through his commanders, among whom was Rabshakeh, whom he had sent to Jerusalem with a strong army while he himself was besieging Lachish. The story is told in 4. Reg. 18.17.

units.la: Arma suppressisse] sumpsisse pro suppressisse legendum censet Sigonius: id quod sententia mirabiliter confirmat.
units.tr: Had hidden their arms] Sigonius thinks that "sumpsisse" [had taken up] should be read instead of "suppressisse", which the sense wonderfully confirms.

units.la: Efaiam] antiquum est pro Iesaiam. Sic Ezeciel dicebant pro Iezeciel, prima nominis prorsus abjecta.
units.tr: Esaias] an old form for Isaiah. So they said Ezeciel for Iezeciel, the first letter of the name being dropped altogether.

units.la: Tirchac rex Aethiopum] Tharaca est in editione Latina, & in Graeca Θαρακα[?] Ief. 37. 9. & 4. Reg. 19. 9. Sed in Ebraeo Tharbaca, quod nunc legunt Tbirhaca. Iosephus autor regem hunc, quem Tharsicem[?] nominat, suppetias tulisse Aegyptiis contra Sennacheribum, qui tunc Pelusium obsidebat. Sennacheribum autem, cum ab Aegyptiaco bello soluta obsidione reverteretur, in itinere comperisse exercitum suum, quem in Iudaea sub Rabsacis imperio reliquerat, pestilentia divinitus immissa deletum prima nocte.
units.tr: Tirhakah, king of the Ethiopians] Tharaca is in the Latin edition, and in the Greek [Θαρακα]: Isa. 37.9 and 4. Reg. 19.9. But in the Hebrew it is Tharbaca, which they now read Tirhaqa. Josephus, the author, says that this king, whom he calls Tharsis, came to the aid of the Egyptians against Sennacherib, who was then besieging Pelusium. He also says that Sennacherib, when he was returning from the Egyptian war with the siege lifted, found on the way that his army, which he had left in Judea under Rabshakeh's command, had been destroyed in the first night by a pestilence sent by God.

units.la: postea quam urbem oppugnare occeperat, Haec Iosephus lib.10,c.2. Vide Sigonium.
units.tr: after he had begun to attack the city, This is from Josephus, book 10, chapter 2. See Sigonius.

units.la: Æthiopum] non eorum qui supra Ægyptum, ubi nunc regnum Abyssinum; sed eorum qui in Arabia degebant, quam Chusaam appellant, unde & Zara erat rex Æthiopum, de quo alias.
units.tr: Ethiopians] not those who lived beyond Egypt, where the kingdom of Abyssinia now is, but those who dwelt in Arabia, which they call Chusaam; whence also Zara was king of the Ethiopians, about whom elsewhere.

units.la: regnum Assyriorum invadit] non invasit regnum Assyriorum, sed egressus erat ad pugnandum contra Sennacherib, qui tum Lobnam obsidebat; vel certe contra ipsius ducem Rabsacem, qui validis copiis Ierosolymam premebat, ejusque cives ad deditionem sollicitabat.
units.tr: invades the kingdom of the Assyrians] not "invaded the kingdom of the Assyrians", but he had gone out to fight against Sennacherib, who was then besieging Libnah; or at least against his commander Rabshakeh, who was pressing Jerusalem with strong forces and urging its citizens to surrender.

units.la: Se paullo post rebus domi compositis] haec aliter textus. Nam haec litterae missae ante cladem Ierosolymitanam, quam subsecuta est abitio, vel potius fuga Sennacheribi.
units.tr: Himself a little later, with affairs at home settled] The text has these things differently. For these letters were sent before the disaster at Jerusalem, which was followed by Sennacherib's departure, or rather his flight.

units.la: Multa hominum millia letho dedit] centum octoginta quinque millia 4 Reg 19 35 & Iesai 37,36.
units.tr: He gave many thousands of men to death] one hundred and eighty-five thousand; 4 Reg. 19.35 and Isa. 37.36.

units.la: A filius] Arammelech & Sarasar. Interfectus autem est in templo Dei sui Nesroch, post quem regnavit filius Asarhaddon, 4 Reg.19,37.
units.tr: By his sons] Arammelech and Sarasar. He was killed, however, in the temple of his god Nisroch, after whom his son Asarhaddon reigned, 4 Reg. 19.37.

units.la: Ignem se exitium tulit] suspicari aliquis posset Sulpicium initio scripsisse, ignem se exitium tulit: sed nihil mutemus.
units.tr: Brought fire-ruin upon himself] One might suspect that Sulpicius originally wrote "ignem se exitium tulit"; but let us change nothing.

units.la: Morbo incubuerat] morbus ipse letalis erat. Quod significat γραφή[?], cum ait, in diebus illis aegrotavit Ezechias rex usque ad mortem. 4 Reg.20.
units.tr: Had taken to his sickbed] The illness itself was deadly. This is what the Scripture [γραφή] signifies when it says, "In those days Hezekiah the king was sick unto death," 4 Reg. 20.

units.la: Verbum Domini annunciavit] vide num scripserit, verbo Domini annunciaret.
units.tr: Announced the word of the Lord] See whether he wrote "might announce the word of the Lord".

units.la: Culturas impias exercuit] alius hoc diceret, idola coluit. Nam impius omnis cultus, qui tribuitur idolis.
units.tr: Practised impious cults] Another would say "worshipped idols". For every cult that is given to idols is impious.

units.la: Pag 84. Ob quod in potestatem Assyriorum traditus] qui eum vinctum duxerunt Babylonem, 2 Paralip. 33, 22. Vide, si otium
units.tr: Page 84. Whereupon he was handed over into the power of the Assyrians] They took him bound to Babylon, 2 Paralip. 33.22. See, if you have leisure.

units.la: Helchia sacerdote] scribo Helcia. Nam in fonte [illegible, ~4 letters]. Rursum hic sacerdotis nomen usurpat pro sacerdote summo, quem pontificem appellant.
units.tr: Hilkiah the priest] I write Helcia. For in the source [illegible, about four letters]. Again, here he uses the word "priest" for the high priest, whom they call pontifex.

units.la: Librum verbi Dei] id est, legis. Nam lex & verbum Dei se invicem explicant. Aliter pag. 85. cumque Esaias ei verbum Domini annunciasset.
units.tr: The book of the word of God] That is, of the Law. For law and the word of God explain each other. Otherwise, p. 85: "and when Isaiah had announced the word of the Lord to him."

units.la: Sacrilegia] culturas Deorum falsorum, quas modo superius culturas impias dixit: nos idololatrias vocamus.
units.tr: Sacrileges] the worships of false gods, which just above he called impious worships; we call them idolatries.

units.la: Per Ollam prophetissam] emendo, per Oldam prophetissam, quam LXX. τὴν προφῆτιν[?]. Hieto. prophetidem appellat. Scribi autem debet Holda, cum aspiratione. Græce Ολδά. 4.Reg 22.14.
units.tr: Through Olla the prophetess] I emend to "through Oldah the prophetess", whom the Seventy call [τὴν προφῆτιν]; Jerome calls her "prophetess". It ought to be written Holda, with an aspirate; in Greek [Ολδά]: 4. Reg. 22.14.

units.la: Vtioli ac lunæ divinos honores darent] τῷ ἡλίῳ καὶ τῇ σελήνῃ καὶ τοῖς μαζούραις[?] καὶ πάσῃ τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ οὐρανοῦ[?]. In Latina vetere, & soli & lunæ & duodecim signis & omni militiæ cœli, 4.Reg 23.5.
units.tr: That they should give divine honours to the sun and moon] [τῷ ἡλίῳ καὶ τῇ σελήνῃ καὶ τοῖς μαζούραις καὶ πάσῃ τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ οὐρανοῦ]. In the old Latin: "to the sun and to the moon and to the twelve signs and to all the host of heaven", 4. Reg. 23.5.

units.la: Pag.85. Quibus in pulverem redactis[?] ] quomodo in pulverem redacta si ex metallis & quænam hæc sacraria? An fana & delubra? Sed ea ex metallis non fiunt. An potius altaria excelsa ... 4.Reg 23.4. legimus, [?]praecepit rex Helciæ pontifici & sacerdotibus secundi ordinis & janitoribus, ut proicerent de templo Domini vasa omnia, quæ fecerant Baal & luco & universæ militiæ cœli: & combusit ea extra Ierusalem in convalle Cedron, & tulit pulverem eorum in Bethel. Quem locum si non habuit in mente, tum certe respexit ad eum qui habetur in eodem capite versu 15. Insuper & altare quod erat in Bethel & excelsum quod fecerat Ieroboam filius Nabat, qui peccare fecit Israel: & altare illud excelsumque destruxit atque combusit & comminuit in pulverem, succenditque etiam lucum.
units.tr: Page 85. Which, having been reduced to dust] How can things made of metal be reduced to dust, and what are these shrines? Temples and sanctuaries? But these are not made of metal. Or rather, we read of high altars at 4. Reg. 23.4: "The king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, and the priests of the second order, and the doorkeepers, to cast out of the temple of the Lord all the vessels that had been made for Baal and for the grove and for all the host of heaven; and he burned them outside Jerusalem in the valley of Kidron, and carried their dust to Bethel." If he did not have this passage in mind, then certainly he looked to the one in the same chapter, verse 15: "Moreover the altar that was at Bethel, and the high place which Jeroboam the son of Nebat had made, who made Israel sin, that altar and high place he pulled down and burned, and beat it to powder, and also burned the grove."

units.la: Ne sepulchris quidem impiorum pepercit] qui in monte prope Bethel erant. 4.Reg. 23.16.
units.tr: Nor did he spare even the tombs of the impious] which were on the mountain near Bethel. 4. Reg. 23.16.

units.la: A propheta] a propheta quodam ex tribu Iuda, 3.Reg 13.2.
units.tr: By a prophet] by a certain prophet from the tribe of Judah, 3. Reg. 13.2.

units.la: Octavo & decimo] 2 Paralip. 35.9[?].
units.tr: On the eighteenth] 2. Paralip. 35.9.

units.la: Pascha] quod Ebræi Phase vocant. Id habetur in edit vulgata, loco citato. Errant qui Pascha dictum existimant a verbo Græco πάσχειν, non minus sane quam qui nomen Iesus derivant παρὰ τὸ ἰαω ἰάσω[?]. Nam utrumque Ebraicum est, Iesus dictus a salvando, & Pascha a transeundo. Phase in forma Chaldaica פסחא[?], quod antiquitus legebant Phalcha & aspirata in tenuem versa Pascha. Nihil verius. Sic ex Chermel fit Charmel factum Carmelus, id est, Καρμηλος[?].
units.tr: Passover] which the Hebrews call Phase. This is in the Vulgate edition, in the passage cited. Those are wrong who think Pascha is named from the Greek verb πάσχειν [paschein], no less than those who derive the name Jesus from [παρὰ τὸ ἰαω ἰάσω]. For both are Hebrew: Jesus is named from saving, and Pascha from passing over. Phase is in the Chaldean form pasha, which they formerly read as Phalcha, the aspirate having been changed into the tenuis, giving Pascha. Nothing is truer. So from Chermel comes Charmel, made Carmelus, that is [Καρμηλος].

units.la: Post triennium fere] nihil mutandum. Nam halucinatus fuit noster, qui hunc regnasse scribit ann. XXI. cum regnarit ann. XXXI. Ex quo sequitur hæc accidisse tredecim annis post celebratum Phase. Siquidem Pascha celebratum fuit, ut habetur.
