units.tr: After about three years] Nothing is to be changed. For our author went astray in writing that this man reigned twenty-one years, when he reigned thirty-one. From this it follows that these things happened thirteen years after the Passover was celebrated; for the Passover was celebrated, as is found in the text.

units.la: 2. Paralip. 25. 19. decimo octavo anno imperij Iosiæ. Nihil certius.
units.tr: 2. Paralip. 25.19, in the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah. Nothing is more certain.

units.la: Adversus Nechao] Pharao Nechao, 4. Reg. 23. 29. Hic ab Ebraeis Necho vocatur, voce monosyllaba. Siquidem scheva non constituit syllabam apud eos. Græce est Φαραώ νεχαώ, & 2. Paralip. 35. 20. νεχαώ.
units.tr: Against Necho] Pharaoh Necho, 4. Reg. 23.29. He is called Necho by the Hebrews, in a single syllable, since the shewa does not form a syllable among them. In Greek it is [Φαραώ νεχαώ], and in 2. Paralip. 35.20 [νεχαώ].

units.la: Priusquam inter se acies concurrerent] dum aciem instruunt ab uno cornu ad alterum vehitur, ictus fuit sagitta cujusdam Ægyptij. Iosephus.
units.tr: Before the battle lines joined: while he was drawing up his line and riding from one wing to the other, he was struck by an arrow shot by a certain Egyptian. Josephus.

units.la: Cum regnasset annos I & XXX] modo monui legendum esse I & XXX. Quod ita esse difcessex 4. Reg. 22. 1.
units.tr: When he had reigned thirty-one years: I have just pointed out that it should be read as thirty-one. That this is so is clear from 4 Kings 22:1.

units.la: Ioachas] ut supra Achas pro Achaz, sic hoc loco est Ioachaz pro Ioachaz, ex ea consuetudine quam ibi notavimus.
units.tr: Ioachas: just as above Achas stands for Achaz, so here Ioachas stands for Ioachaz, by the same practice we noted there.

units.la: Regnum adeptus est] opera populi, 2. Reg. 33. 30. Tulit-que populus terræ Ioachaz filium Iosiæ & unxerunt eum & constituerunt eum regem pro patre suo. Viginti trium annorum erat Ioachaz cum regnare cœpisset, & tribus mensibus regnavit in Ierusalem.
units.tr: He obtained the kingdom: by the action of the people, 2 Chron. 33:30. "And the people of the land took Joachaz the son of Josiah, and anointed him, and made him king in his father's stead. Joachaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem."

units.la: Vinctum] vinctum duxit in Rebla sive Reblatha, quæ est in terra Hamath.
units.tr: Bound: he led him in chains to Riblah, or Reblatha, which is in the land of Hamath.

units.la: Nec multo post in vinculis diem fuit defunctus est] apud Ægyptios, 4. Reg 33. 34.
units.tr: Not long after, he died in chains: among the Egyptians, 4 Kings 33:34.

units.la: Stipendium annuum] centum argenti talenta & unum auri, 4 Reg. 23. 33.
units.tr: Annual tribute: one hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold, 4 Kings 23:33.

units.la: Eliachim] Eliacim potius, qui erat frater Ioachaz & filius Iosiæ: frater, inquam, major natu.
units.tr: Eliachim: Eliakim rather, who was the brother of Joachaz and son of Josiah; a brother, I say, older by birth.

units.la: Ioachis vocitatus est] nomen ei mutatum ab ipso Pharao, ne Nechao sic Nabuchodonosor mutavit nomen Danielis in Balthasar. Similiter mutavit & omnia sociorum ejus. Mos iste perantiquus est. Debet autem scribi Ioacis, per C simplex. Nam in Ebraeo Ioacim. Notum Græcos ultimam nominis barbari in S, mutare. Quod ex libris meis ita tritum ut nihil magis. Hoc primum: deinde Ioachis, qui & Ioachin & Iechonias, non filius erat Iosiæ, sed nepos. Qui certe in unum confundendi non sunt. Nam nepotem eundem facere cum filio imperitiæ est Severianæ. Cá veant qui verum amant.
units.tr: He was called Ioachis: his name was changed by Pharaoh himself, just as Nebuchadnezzar changed Daniel's name to Belteshazzar. He changed the names of all his allies in the same way. The custom is very ancient. It should be written Ioacis, with a simple C, for in Hebrew it is Ioacim. It is well known that the Greeks change the final letter of a foreign name into S; this is so familiar from my books that nothing could be more so. That is the first point. Second, Ioachis, who is also Ioachin and Jechoniah, was not the son of Josiah but his grandson. Certainly these must not be merged into one, for to make the grandson the same as the son is the ignorance of Severus. Let those who love the truth beware.

units.la: Hic Ioachæ fratris Iosiæ F fuit] falsum. conjicio leg. hic Ioachæ frater, Iosiæ F. fuit. Iosias enim quatuor filios habuit, Iohannem, qui a nonnullis Ioachaz esse creditur, Ioacim, Sedecias. tiam & Sellum. Doctores Ebraei scribunt Ioacim, qui & Eliacim, duobus circiter annis majorem fuisse Ioachazo. Quod sic probant. Textus ait, filius viginti trium annorum erat Ioachaz cum regnare inciperet: & alibi, filius viginti quinque annorum erat Ioacim cum regnare inciperet. Idem ait, Ioachaz tribus tantum mensibus regnasse 2. Paralip. 36.2. Haec manifesta sunt. Aliud argumentum, 4. Reg. 23.30. Tulit populus terrae Ioachaz filium Iosiae & unxerunt eum. Cur unxerunt? Nam filij regum non ungebantur, nisi ob certam causam. Respondent Ebraei, quia Ioacim natu major erat. Addunt doctores, quia implebat locum patrum suorum, quod non faciebat Ioacim. Dixi Ioachaz a nonnullis credi eundem esse cum eo qui in Paralipomenis Iohannes vocatur. Obstare videtur quod Iohannes ipse nominetur primogenitus. Respondent ideo fieri quod adoptione primogenitus esset. Nam in regno praelatus fuit ipsi Ioacim. Abenezra censet Iohannem primogenitum non regnasse, Sellum autem esse Ioachaz. Secus R. David, qui Sellum opinatur esse Ioachin, nepotem Iosiae. Moris enim esse ut nepotes filiorum nomine censeantur. Sic in primo librorum Mosis, quae fecerat ei filius ejus minimus, id est, nepos Chanaan. Idem scribit, quum diem suum obiret Iosias, Ioachaz egisse annum 13.[?] & Sedeciam 24.[?] & Ioacim 25.[?] Addit Sedeciam a patre regem constitutum fuisse post a populo Ioachaz ei praelatum. Qua de re alias plura, si Deus permiserit.
units.tr: Here Joachaz was the brother of Josiah's son: false. I conjecture that we should read: "Here Joachaz was the brother, son of Josiah." For Josiah had four sons: Johanan, who by some is thought to be Joachaz; Joakim; Zedekiah; and also Shallum. The Hebrew teachers write that Joakim, who is also Eliakim, was about two years older than Joachaz. They prove this as follows. The text says, "Joachaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign," and elsewhere, "Joakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign." The same text says that Joachaz reigned only three months, 2 Chron. 36:2. These points are clear. Another argument is 4 Kings 23:30: "The people of the land took Joachaz the son of Josiah and anointed him." Why anoint him? For the sons of kings were not anointed except for a certain reason. The Hebrews answer that Joakim was the elder by birth. The teachers add that Joachaz filled the place of his fathers, which Joakim did not do. I said that some believe Joachaz to be the same as the one called Johanan in Chronicles. What seems to stand in the way is that Johanan himself is named the firstborn. They answer that he was firstborn by adoption, for Joakim was preferred to him in the kingdom. Abenezra holds that Johanan the firstborn did not reign and that Shallum is Joachaz. R. David, on the other hand, thinks Shallum is Jehoiachin, the grandson of Josiah, for it is the custom that grandsons are counted under the name of sons. So in the first book of Moses: "what his youngest son had done to him," that is, his grandson Canaan. The same writer says that when Josiah died, Joachaz had lived 13 [?] years, Zedekiah 24 [?] and Joakim 25 [?]. He adds that Zedekiah was made king by his father, after the people had preferred Joachaz to him. More on this matter elsewhere, if God permits.

units.la: Rex Babylonius] ab aliis dicitur rex Chaldaeorum. Rex autem Babylonis vocatur, 4. Reg. 24.1. βασιλεὺς Βαβυλῶνος.
units.tr: The Babylonian king: others call him the king of the Chaldeans. But he is called king of Babylon, 4 Kings 24:1 [βασιλεὺς Βαβυλῶνος].

units.la: Iudaeam terram occupavit armis, una cum regione sive terra etiam regem subegit, qui propterea vocatur servus Nabuchodonosori, triennij spatio. Nam post rebellionem fecit.
units.tr: He seized the land of Judea by arms, and subdued along with the region, or land, also its king, who for this reason is called a servant of Nebuchadnezzar, for a space of three years. For after that he rebelled.

units.la: Pag. 86. Filio ejusdem nominis] non plane ejusdem nominis. Nam vel in Graeca editione pater Ἰωαχείμ[?] vocatur, filius Ἰωαχείμ[?] sive Ἰωαχίμ[?]. Ecce discrimen in una littera quale apud Ebraeos, qui ultimam insuper efferunt per N. Scribunt enim Ioachin, unde Ioachis, ut ex Ioacim factum Ioacis. Sulpitius autem qui haec confundit non est audiendus.
units.tr: Page 86. To a son of the same name: not plainly of the same name. For even in the Greek edition the father is called Iōachim [Ἰωαχείμ] and the son Iōachim or Iōachin [Ἰωαχίμ]. Here is a difference in one letter, such as the Hebrews make, who moreover pronounce the final letter with an N. For they write Ioachin, whence Ioachis, as from Ioacim was made Ioacis. Sulpicius, who confuses these, is not to be heard.

units.la: Nabuchodonolor Ierofolymam cum exercitu ingressus] prius servi Nabuchodonosoris expeditionem fecerant contra Ierosolymam, cumque urbs in obsidionem venisset, & ipse Nabuchodonosor ad urbem a suis obsessam venisset, egressus Ioachin ad eum cum matre,&c. Dedidit se ei anno octavo regni Nabucho-donosor, qui erat mensis tertius, a quo regnare cœperat Ioachin Ierofolymæ. Habentur ista 4.Reg.24.11.&12.
units.tr: Nebuchadnezzar entered Jerusalem with an army: earlier the servants of Nebuchadnezzar had made a campaign against Jerusalem, and when the city had been put under siege, and Nebuchadnezzar himself came to the city besieged by his men, Jehoiachin went out to him with his mother, etc. He surrendered to him in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, in the third month, from which Jehoiachin had begun to reign at Jerusalem. These things are found in 4 Kings 24:11–12.

units.la: Jngressus) hoc admodum credibile est, licet Scriptura diserte non exprimat. Quid enim vetat Ioachin primum egressum esse ad Nabuchodono-sor in castra extra urbem, & ipsum Nabuchodono-sor postea ingressum esse urbem? Simul haec vera esse possunt, & sunt professo, si non fallitur aut fallit nos noster Sulpicius.
units.tr: Entered: this is very credible, although Scripture does not state it expressly. For what prevents Jehoiachin from first going out to Nebuchadnezzar in the camp outside the city, and Nebuchadnezzar himself entering the city afterwards? These things can both be true, and they are professed, if our Sulpicius is not mistaken or does not mislead us.

units.la: Vrbem murosque ac templum solo stravit] falsum est.
units.tr: He levelled the city, its walls and the temple to the ground: this is false.

units.la: Auri immensum modum] abstulit inde omnes cum templi tum regiae thesauros: adhæc confregit vasa aurea omnia, quæ Salomo rex fecerat ad templum Domini, 4 Reg.13.13.
units.tr: An immense amount of gold: he carried off from there all the treasures both of the temple and of the palace. Moreover he broke all the golden vessels which King Solomon had made for the temple of the Lord, 4 Kings 24:13.

units.la: Puberesque omnes] omnem juventutem ex urbe captivam duxit, Josephus: totam Ierofolymam, omnes milites numero 10. M. omnesque fabros & artifices. 4.Reg 24.14.
units.tr: And all the adult males: he led all the youth of the city away captive. Josephus: the whole of Jerusalem, all soldiers, numbering 10,000, and all the craftsmen and smiths. 4 Kings 24:14.

units.la: Sedechias] melius, Sedecias, Hic patruus erat Ioachin, & prius Mattanias dicebatur, quod nomen ipse Nabuchodonosor postea mutavit, imposito ei Sedeciae nomine. Vide 4.Reg.24.17.
units.tr: Zedekiah: Zedekiah is better. He was the uncle of Jehoiachin, and was previously called Mattaniah, a name which Nebuchadnezzar himself later changed, giving him the name Zedekiah. See 4 Kings 24:17.

units.la: Inani tantum umbra regij nominis concessa] hæc ex in-genio Sulpicij manarunt, non ex sacris libris.
units.tr: Granted only the empty shadow of the royal name: these things flowed from the invention of Sulpicius, not from the sacred books.

units.la: Tribus mensibus] & decem diebus.
units.tr: For three months: and ten days.

units.la: Cum populo] cum matre, uxoribus, eunuchis & dynastis Iudæae.
units.tr: With the people: with his mother, wives, eunuchs and the nobles of Judea.

units.la: Trigesimum post annum] desiderantur septem anni. Nam[?] 4.Reg. 25.27. diserte; Factum est anno tricesimo septimo transmigrationis Ioachin regis Iudæ, mense duodecimo, vigesima septima die mensis,&c. Adhibe Sigonium.
units.tr: The thirtieth year after: seven years are missing. For 4 Kings 25:27 says expressly: "It came to pass in the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month," etc. Consult Sigonius.

units.la: A rege] Evilmerodach. Hoc actidit anno primo regni ejus.
units.tr: By the king: Evil-merodach. This happened in the first year of his reign.

units.la: Consiliis participatus] Sic participare aliquē sermone dixit Plautus, & prandio Apulejus.
units.tr: Made a sharer in counsels: thus Plautus spoke of making someone a sharer in conversation, and Apuleius of sharing a dinner.

units.la: Pag.87. Turbae inutilis] tenuis plebeculæ. Supra quæ turba inutilis servitio, exercendis colendisq; agris, ne inculrum esset solum, deputata. Alio sensu Homerus dixit [illegible, ~8 letters] & alius, inutilia pondera terræ.
units.tr: Of the useless crowd: of the humble common people. Above, a useless crowd was assigned to servitude, to working and cultivating the fields, lest the land be left uncultivated. In another sense Homer used the phrase [illegible], and another writer spoke of "useless weights of the earth."

units.la: Postremis malis debitus] qui debebat extrema mala pati. Sic, mors naturæ debita: &, cœlo debita progenies.
units.tr: Owed to the last evils: who ought to suffer the final calamities. So "death owed to nature," and "offspring owed to heaven."

units.la: Post novem annos] anno nono regni ejus, mense decimo, decimo die mensis, 4 Reg.25.1.
units.tr: After nine years: in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, 4 Kings 25:1.

units.la: Triennio obsedit] rescribendum ex historia biennio fere. Nam biennium integrum nondum exactum erat. Siquidem obsessa fuit mense decimo anni noni, capta autem mense quarto anni undecimi, nona die mensis.
units.tr: He besieged it for three years: this should be corrected from history to almost two years. For a full two years had not yet been completed. For it was besieged in the tenth month of the ninth year, and captured in the fourth month of the eleventh year, on the ninth day of the month.

units.la: Tum vero Sedecias, &c.] haec paullo aliter narrantur Ierem. 37. 16. Nam conjectus fuit in carcerem ante ol[?] jam urbem non a rege, sed a praeceribus; cum eum Ierias quidam in porta Benjamitica comprehendisset, objecto crimine quod ad Chaldaeos transfugeret. Sed pro Sulpicio factum quae habentur, Ierem. 32. 3. Vide, si vacas.
units.tr: Then indeed Zedekiah, etc.: these things are related a little differently in Jeremiah 37:16. For he was thrown into prison before the city fell, not by the king but by the princes, when a certain Irijah had seized him at the Benjamin Gate on the charge that he was deserting to the Chaldeans. But what is found in Jeremiah 32:3 was done for Sulpicius. See it, if you have leisure.

units.la: Specialem poenam denuncians] Ierem. 37. 16. in manus regis Babylonis traderis.
units.tr: Announcing a special punishment: Jeremiah 37:16, "you shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon."

units.la: Iudaeorum principibus] Ierem. 34. 4.
units.tr: To the princes of the Jews: Jeremiah 34:4.

units.la: In lacum immensi profundi] qui erat in vestibulo carcer-is. Lacum autem dicit λάκκον, qui Ebraeis est [?], id est, locus subterraneus in carcere.
units.tr: Into a pit of immense depth: which was in the vestibule of the prison. He calls the pit [λάκκον], which in Hebrew is [?], that is, an underground place in the prison.

units.la: Sed rex] monitus ab eunucho Abdemelech.
units.tr: But the king, having been warned by the eunuch Abdemelech.

units.la: Sacerdotibus] principibus.
units.tr: For "the priests", read "the princes."

units.la: Opidum captum] undecimo anno Sedeciae, mense quarto, nona mensis. Ierem. 39. 2. anno mundi conditi 3338. Salmanticensis.
units.tr: "The city was taken": in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month. Jer. 39. 2. In the year of the world 3338. Salmanticensis.

units.la: Princeps regius] hic in fonte dicitur magister lanionum seu carnificum. Id interpretantur quidam praefectus satellitum: alij, magister equitum. Hiero. magister militiae. Ierem. 40. 1.
units.tr: "Royal officer": here in the source he is called master of the butchers or executioners. Some interpret this as commander of the guard, others as master of the horse. Jerome has master of the soldiery. Jer. 40. 1.

units.la: Reliqui fecerat] videtur folaecismus esse pro reliquos fecerat: quales nonnulli sunt in Cicerone. Sigonius tamen conjicit legendum, reliquit fecerat, & Vittor Gisselinus, reliquias fecerat. Iudicium est penes eruditos. Ego in folaecismum eo magis inclino quod sciam vitium hoc orationis in Sulpicio novum aut insolens non esse. Ergo impuit praefat. in vitam B. Martini, cum primum animum ad scribendum appuli, quia nefas putarem tanti viri latere virtutes, apud me ipse didici ut folaecismus non erubescerem: quia nec magnam iturum unquam rerum sciebam contigisse, & si quid ex his studiis olim fortasse libasset, totum id desuetudine tanti temporis perdidisset. Diximus in Cicerone aliquos esse folaecismos. Si non sunt, tamen esse videntur, ut in his verbis, Quo in discrimine mirifica Senatus, incredibilis Italiae totius, lingularis bonorum omnium consensus. Nam in orationis cursu ea vox exit, quae parum respondet superiori structurae. Quocirca est quod metuant Serarij ferulam cum ipse Sulpicius, tum etiam princeps Latinae eloquentiae Cicero. Nam in pueriles Grammatii-vorum leges ambo peccarunt.
units.tr: "Reliqui fecerat": this seems to be a solecism for "reliquos fecerat", of the kind some are found in Cicero. Sigonius nevertheless conjectures that we should read "reliquit fecerat", and Vittor Gisselinus "reliquias fecerat". The judgement rests with the learned. I incline to the solecism all the more because I know that this fault of expression is neither new nor unusual in Sulpicius. Thus in the preface to his Life of St Martin, when I first turned my mind to writing, he says, because I thought it wrong for the virtues of so great a man to lie hidden, I learned for myself not to blush at a solecism, since I knew I would never attain a great knowledge of things, and if he had perhaps once tasted something of these studies, he had lost all of it through disuse over so long a time. We have said that there are some solecisms in Cicero. If they are not solecisms, they at least seem to be, as in these words: "In this crisis, the remarkable zeal of the Senate, the incredible zeal of all Italy, and the singular consensus of all good men." For the sentence runs on to a word that corresponds poorly to the preceding structure. Hence the Serarii have reason to fear the ferule, both Sulpicius himself and also the prince of Latin eloquence, Cicero. For both of them sinned against the childish rules of the grammarians.

units.la: I. DRVSII AD Librum secundum HISTORIAE SACRAE commentarius sive nota.
units.tr: I. Drusius's commentary or note on the second book of the SACRED HISTORY.

units.la: Pag 89. Captivitatis tempora] captivitates quatuor fuerunt. In secunda abductus fuit Daniel, quae accidit anno quarto Ioacim, qui fuit primus Nabuchodonosori. Sed vide sis interpretes Ebraeos, Dan. 1.1.
units.tr: Page 89. The times of captivity] There were four captivities. In the second, Daniel was carried off, which happened in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, who was the first of Nebuchadnezzar's years. But please consult the Hebrew interpreters on Dan. 1.1.

units.la: Prophetarum vaticiniis] Ieremiae, Ezechielis & Danielis.
units.tr: By the prophecies of the prophets] Of Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel.

units.la: In absolutionem Sufannae divino consilio] Sigonius emendat, divinum consilium. Quod ut non damno, ita dico retineri posse vulgatam lectionem, si deleas (in) ut dicat, & absolutionem Sufannae divino consilio: quae facta est divino, non humano consilio.
units.tr: The acquittal of Susanna by divine counsel] Sigonius emends this to "divine counsel" (divinum consilium). I do not condemn this, but I say the common reading can be kept if you delete the "in" so that it reads "the acquittal of Susanna by divine counsel": it was brought about by divine, not human, counsel.

units.la: Ioachim] Ioacim. Sigonius. Res ipsa. Vide Dan. 1.1.
units.tr: Joachim] Jehoiakim (Ioacim), as Sigonius has it. The fact itself. See Dan. 1.1.

units.la: Ananias, Misael & Azarias] quorum mutata, ut moris tum erat, nomina in Sidrach, Misach & Abdenago.
units.tr: Ananias, Misael and Azarias] Whose names were changed, as was the custom at that time, into Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego.

units.la: Alphanae eunucho] ut supra Ioachae filio. Est autem obliquus ex Atheo Asphanes, quod Ebraei Asphanez scribunt. Dan. 1.3.
units.tr: To Alphanas the eunuch] As above, the son of Joachas. The oblique form Asphanes comes from Atheo; the Hebrews write Ashpenaz. Dan. 1.3.

units.la: Paternarum traditionum] Sic loquendo significat traditiones patrum, id est, majorum: qui a Graecis dicuntur παραδόσεις πατρικαί Galat. 1.14. aemulator existens ζηλωτὴς ὑπάρχων τῶν πατρικῶν μου παραδόσεων.
units.tr: Ancestral traditions] In this way of speaking he means the traditions of the fathers, that is, of ancestors, which the Greeks call ancestral traditions [παραδόσεις πατρικαί] Gal. 1.14, "being a zealot of my ancestral traditions" [ζηλωτὴς ὑπάρχων τῶν πατρικῶν μου παραδόσεων].

units.la: Paternarum] malim patriarum: sed tamen nihil muto. Nam & infra sic locutus est, ut pag. 106. qui paternae urbis status esset: & pag 109. admonita ne paternarum traditionum immemor. Sic apud interpretem nostrum, 1. Petr. 1.18. paternę traditionis.
units.tr: Ancestral] I would prefer "of the fathers" (patriarum), but I change nothing. For he also speaks this way below, as on page 106, "what was the state of the ancestral city," and on page 109, "warned not to be forgetful of ancestral traditions." So our interpreter also has "ancestral tradition" at 1 Pet. 1.18.

units.la: Id faciebat per Malasar, quem Danieli praeposuerat, Dan.1.11.
units.tr: He did this through Malasar, whom he had set over Daniel, Dan. 1.11.

units.la: Per idem tempus Sufanna quae iam huius historiae in Iohafin per haec verba, Sedeciae regis aevo condita fuit Marilia, eodemque tempore fuit Sufanna filia Helciae uxor Ioacim. Cum hac voluerunt duo senes iudices concumbere. Sed cum noluit, accusarunt eam adulterii. Nam testabantur se vidisse concumbentem cum juvene quodam. Daniel autem sapientia sua eam liberavit. Forte hi senes erant Achab filius Coliae, & Sedecias filius Maasiae.
units.tr: At the same time Susanna, who had already been in this history, in Iohafin, by these words, founded Marilia in the age of King Zedekiah, and at the same time Susanna, daughter of Helcias, was the wife of Joakim. Two old men, judges, wanted to lie with her. But when she refused, they accused her of adultery, for they testified that they had seen her lying with a certain young man. But Daniel freed her by his wisdom. Perhaps these old men were Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah.

units.la: & hic scribo Ioacim. Nam est Ἰωακὶμ in textu Graeco, & apud Salmanticensem.
units.tr: And here I write Joakim, for it is Ioakim (Ἰωακὶμ) in the Greek text and in the Salamanca edition.

units.la: A duobus presbyteris appetita] a duobus senioribus, quos Ebraei appellant, & est nomen dignitatis. Nam sic vocabantur magistratus, quos nunc seniores aut consules dicimus. Habebant enim in Babylonia magistratum ex Iudaeis. Quod mirum videri nemini debet, cum etiam Alexandriae olim habuerint.
units.tr: Sought by two elders] By two seniors, whom the Hebrews call elders, and this is a title of dignity. For magistrates were so called, whom we now call seniors or consuls. For they had a magistracy in Babylonia made up of Jews. This should seem strange to no one, since they also once had one in Alexandria.

units.la: Diserte Strabo, citante Iosepho Antiquit. lib. 14. cap. 12. Par Aegyptum iane etiam coloniae sunt ejus gentis, absque eo quod Alexandrinae urbis magna pars eis assignata est. Habet enim proprium magistratum, qui suae gentis res administret, & controversias ex jure dirimat, & contractus atque pacta rata habeat, non aliter quam sit in absoluta republica. Rei firmandae est Thalmud Babylonicum, quo continentur leges & jura in Babylonia usurpari solita a Iudaeis: infirmandae vero est dictum illud, ubi non est sacerdos, non est judicium: &, Iudicia non exercentur extra terram. Sed vide, si vacas, Mosem Geruudensem in Numeros, sol. 283.
units.tr: Strabo says so plainly, citing Josephus, Antiquities book 14, chapter 12. Likewise, there are colonies of that nation in Egypt, besides the large part of the city of Alexandria assigned to them. For they have their own magistrate, who manages the affairs of his nation, settles disputes according to law, and holds contracts and agreements valid, no differently than in an independent commonwealth. To confirm this there is the Babylonian Talmud, in which are contained the laws and rights that the Jews were accustomed to use in Babylonia. To weaken it, however, there is the saying, "where there is no priest there is no judgment," and "judgments are not carried out outside the land." But see, if you have leisure, Moses of Gerona on Numbers, fol. 283.

units.la: In remotis locis] est cur malim, in occultis locis intelligit autem loca horti sive pomarii, Dan. 13.37. in editione Theodotionis, quam Ecclesia prisca recepit, Greek: ἡ ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἀν τὸν κῆπον, ὃς ἦν κεχρυμμένος, ἡ ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ αὐτῆς: venitque ad eam adolescens, qui erat absconditus, & concubuit cum ea.
units.tr: In remote places] There is reason to prefer "in hidden places"; he means the places of a garden or orchard. Dan. 13.37, in Theodotion's edition, which the early Church received: but the young man came to her, who was hidden in the garden, or rather from her [ἡ ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἀν τὸν κῆπον, ὃς ἦν κεχρυμμένος, ἡ ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ αὐτῆς]: and the young man, who was hidden, came to her and lay with her.

units.la: de adulterio latam, Deut. 22.
units.tr: Concerning adultery, given in Deut. 22.

units.la: quotum annum egerit historia non prodidit: tantum dicit fuisse Greek: παῖδαριον νέον τεσσάρων, ἦ puerulum juniorem. Quaereudum igitur unde hae habeat Severus. Morti dedisent] ad mortem damnassent, morti adjudicassent.
units.tr: The history does not reveal how old he was; it says only that he was a young child of four [παῖδαριον νέον τεσσάρων], or a younger little child. It must therefore be asked where Severus got this. They would have given him to death] would have condemned him to death, would have adjudged him to death.

units.la: Maiores natu] senes vel judices, quos & presbyteros appellat.
units.tr: The eldest] old men or judges, whom he also calls elders.

units.la: Vnumque ex eis] unum atque alterum ex eis, legendum conjicit Sigonius. Quid si, unumque ex eis & post alterum interrogat? Certe aliquid abesse videtur: nisi legamus, utrumque ex eis. Quod mihi se valde probat.
units.tr: And one of them] Sigonius conjectures "one and another of them." What if it reads "and one of them" and then asks about the other? Surely something seems to be missing, unless we read "each of them," which pleases me greatly.

units.la: Pag. 91. Ex varietate responsi] [illegible, ~20 letters] reddit: alter [illegible, ~10 letters] sub lentisco: alter [illegible, ~8 letters] sub ilice. Vide Ælium Antonium Nebrissensem, Annot. cap. X. Apud Salmanticensem, Daniel sapientia sua liberavit eam per scrutinium quo deprehendit nos concordare testimonia ipsorum.
units.tr: Page 91. From the variance of the answer] [illegible] gives; the one [illegible] under the mastic tree; the other [illegible] under the holm oak. See Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis, Notes, chapter X. In the Salamanca edition: Daniel freed her by his wisdom through an examination by which he detected that their testimonies agreed.

units.la: Chaldæos, qui magicis artibus] mirum ni scripsit, quique magicis artibus, ut magos innuat, quos a Chaldaeis distinguit interpres vetus Dan. 4 5. & 5, 7. magi, & haldæi & arusprices. Græca sunt [illegible, ~12 letters], Infra 98. magos & Chaldæos advocat.
units.tr: Chaldeans, who by magical arts] I would not be surprised if he wrote "and who by magical arts," so as to indicate the magi, whom the old interpreter distinguishes from the Chaldeans, Dan. 4.5 and 5.7: magi, Chaldeans and soothsayers. The Greek words are [illegible]. Below, on page 98, he calls on the magi and Chaldeans.

units.la: Extisque hostiarum] qui extis hostiarum futura prædicunt, vocantur a Græcis [illegible, ~10 letters]: a Latinis haruspices & extispices. Priore vocabulo usus est Theodotio, Dan. 2. posteriore Symmachus, itemque Herodianus. Loquor de Græcis, non de Latinis vocibus. Magos & haruspices Daniel clare discrimi-nat a Chaldæis, ut dictum est. Quid nosteri? Si non est mendum in hoc loco, usus est vocabulo Chaldæorum late, ut etiam haruspices & magos comprehendat. Sane magos Ægyptiorum superius Chaldæos appellat.
units.tr: And by the entrails of victims] Those who foretell future things from the entrails of victims are called by the Greeks [illegible]; by the Latins haruspices and extispices. Theodotion used the former word, Dan. 2; Symmachus used the latter, as did Herodian. I speak of the Greek words, not the Latin ones. Daniel clearly distinguishes the magi and haruspices from the Chaldeans, as has been said. What about our own writers? If there is no error in this place, he has used the word "Chaldeans" in a broad sense, so as to include the haruspices and magi too. Certainly he calls the magi of the Egyptians Chaldeans above.

units.la: Futura præcinere] prædicere: aut præcinere, quia vates etiam canunt, dum versus rhythmica ratione compositos cantando pronunciant. Similiter poetæ canere dicuntur eadem de caussa: ex quo illud, Arma virumque cano.
units.tr: To foretell future things] To predict; or "to sing before," because prophets also sing when they pronounce verses composed in rhythmic measure by chanting. Poets are likewise said to sing for the same reason, whence that line, "Arms and the man I sing."

units.la: Si vera in his divinatio esset] somniis videlicet. Videtur hoc velle, si vera ex somniis divinare possent, aut, si vere divini essent
units.tr: If divination in these matters were true] Namely from dreams. He seems to mean: if they could divine truly from dreams, or if they were truly diviners.

units.la: Tantam molem] tantam difficultatem, ut apud Virg. lib. 1, Æneid, Tantæ moli erat Romanam condere gentem.
units.tr: Such a mass] Such a difficulty, as in Virgil, Aeneid book 1: "So great was the effort to found the Roman race."

units.la: Humanæ opis] humanæ facultatis, aut humanarum virium.
units.tr: Human aid] Human ability, or human powers.

units.la: Rex motus] si nihil deest, debet subaudiri fuit: & motus, id est, id est, commotus iracundia.
units.tr: The king was moved] If nothing is missing, "was" should be understood: and moved, that is, roused by anger.

units.la: Interficiebantur] jam interfeciendi erant, & interfecti sine dubio fuissent nisi Daniel intercessisset. Quod colligitur ex participio [illegible, ~5 letters] quo usus est Daniel cap 2. com 13 Idem im licet sit præsentis temporis, tamen aliquando significat paullo post futurum tempus, ut Ion. 1.3. invenit navem euntem Tharsis, id est, moxituram.
units.tr: Were being killed] They were already to be killed, and without doubt would have been killed had Daniel not interceded. This is gathered from the participle [illegible], which Daniel used in chapter 2, verse 13. Although the same form is of the present tense, it sometimes signifies a time shortly to come, as in Jonah 1.3: "he found a ship going to Tarshish," that is, about to go.

units.la: Regis proximum] maluissem regis præfectum. Nam præfectus erat rerum capitalium, quem Theodotio ἀρχιμάγειρον appellat. An proximus regis fuerit nescio. Hoc scio in fonte habeberi מַכְבָּר? רַב טַבָּחִים magistrum mactatorum, id est, satellitum aut carnificum. Nomen ei Arioch, Dan. 2.14. Forte proximum vocat quia semper in aula prope regem erat. Sic enim certe loquendo aulicos innuere videtur supra pag. 90. prudentia & disciplina brevi omnibus regis proximis antelati.
units.tr: Nearest to the king] I would have preferred "the king's prefect." For he was prefect of capital matters, whom Theodotion calls archimageiros (ἀρχιμάγειρον). Whether he was the king's nearest I do not know. This I know: in the source there is מַכְבָּר? רַב טַבָּחִים [rab tabbachim], the master of slaughterers, that is, of guards or executioners. His name was Arioch, Dan. 2.14. Perhaps he calls him "nearest" because he was always in the court near the king. For so, certainly, he seems to indicate courtiers by speaking as he does above on page 90: "prudence and discipline soon set him above all the king's nearest."

units.la: Mysterio] arcano, secreto. Sane quod propheta Daniel רָז appellat, ejus interpres Theodotio μυστήριον vocat. Innuit autem somnium cum interpretatione. Hoc somnium, quia erat occultum & absconditum, reste mysterium vocatur, cujus origo vocis Hebraea est, videlicet [illegible, ~6 letters]: unde in tertia conjugatione præteritum מִסְתַּר abscondit & participium generis passivi מִסְתָּר, quod legunt musthar sive mysthar. Hinc mysterium, q. res abscondita & quæ homines vulgo latet.
units.tr: Mystery] Secret, hidden. Indeed, what the prophet Daniel calls רָז [raz], its interpreter Theodotion calls mystery (μυστήριον). He means the dream together with its interpretation. Because this dream was hidden and concealed, it is rightly called a mystery. The origin of the word is Hebrew, namely [illegible], whence in the third conjugation the past tense מִסְתַּר [mistar], "he hid," and the passive participle מִסְתָּר [mistar], which they read musthar or mysthar. Hence "mystery," that is, a hidden thing, one which lies hidden from men in general.

units.la: Statuam] prius erat, imaginem. Galesinius reposuit, statuam. Id excuderunt Parisienses & Coloniëses. Nam in editione Plantiniana, imaginem, ut etiam in Græca Theodotionis εἰκὼν μία, id est, imago una. Quod etiam (hoc pono, non statuo) in editione τῶν ὁ. Nam solus Symmachus edidit statuam. Testis mihi Hieronymus ita scribens, Pro statua, id est, ἀνδριάντα, quod solus interpretatus est Symmachus, ceteri imaginem transstulerunt, volentes hoc nomine similitudinem ostendere futurorum. Scire licet Græcos Danielem juxta Theodotionis editionem legere. Quod forte ignorâ vit autor hujus scholij, LXX. interp. ἐκ τῶν ὁ? Nam potest fieri ut existimarit Danielem, qui nunc in Bibliis Græcis, LXX interpretum esse. Nihil temere adsirmandum.
units.tr: Statue] Previously it was "image." Galesinius restored "statue," and the Parisian and Cologne editions printed it. For in the Plantin edition it is "image," as also in Theodotion's Greek, "one image" (εἰκὼν μία). This also (I put this forward, I do not assert it) is in the edition of the ... For Symmachus alone gave "statue." Jerome is my witness, writing thus: "For 'statue,' that is, ἀνδριάντα, which Symmachus alone translated; the others rendered 'image,' wishing by this name to show a likeness of future things." It must be noted that the Greeks read Daniel according to Theodotion's edition. Perhaps the author of this note did not know that the Seventy translators had ... ? For it may be that he thought Daniel, which is now in the Greek Bibles, to be by the Seventy translators. Nothing is to be asserted rashly.

units.la: Brachiisque] plenum esset, pectore brachiisque.
units.tr: And with its arms] it would be full, with breast and arms.

units.la: Cruribus] tibiis Hiero. In edit, Græca est κνημῖδες. Lex. vet. κνήμη, sura, tibia. Testum] alij, testam. Sed vulgatam lectionem tuentur consequa verba, inter confusum coire non poterat. Vide sis pag. 93.
units.tr: Cruribus] Jerome has "shins" (tibiis). The Greek edition has κνημῖδες [knēmīdes]. The old lexicon gives κνήμη [knēmē] as shin or shinbone. Testum] others read "testam." But the received reading is supported by the words that follow, since things mixed together could not cohere. See p. 93.

units.la: Primum & opulentissimum fuisse accepimus] Sunt qui Assyriorum imperium primum fuisse tradant. Forte simul hæc legenda, primum & opulentissimum. Nam ante non fuit opulentius, quod sciam. Aut sub Chaldæorum imperio etiam Assyriorum comprehendit. Scilicet hæc nomina inter se confundi. Nam Assyrij dicuntur, qui Chaldei proprie loquendo & contra Chaldæi, qui Assyrij. Quomodo excusari posset Eusebius in Chronicis Sennacheribum regem Chaldæorum appellans, qui Isidoro lib. XV. & aliis rex Assyriorum dicitur. Vicinæ adeo hæ gentes, ut nemini mirum videri hoc debeat. Sic Persæ & Medi se invicem explicant propter vicinitatem. Sane Medus acinaces, & bellum Medicum pro Persico inveniri apud autores notius est quam ut probari debeat.
units.tr: We have heard that it was the first and most wealthy] Some hold that the empire of the Assyrians was the first. Perhaps these words should be read together, "first and most wealthy," for as far as I know nothing was richer before it. Or, under the rule of the Chaldeans, the author includes the Assyrians as well. These names are plainly confused with one another. Those called Assyrians are, properly speaking, Chaldeans, and conversely the Chaldeans are Assyrians. How could Eusebius in his Chronicle be excused for calling Sennacherib king of the Chaldeans, when Isidore in book 15 and others call him king of the Assyrians? These nations were so close that this should seem no wonder to anyone. So the Persians and Medes are used for each other because of their proximity. Certainly that the "Median scimitar" and the "Median war" are found in authors for "Persian" is too well known to need proof.

units.la: Macedoniæ vindicavit] quod ideo regnum Macedonium dicitur, aut Græcorum. Nam Macedones inter Græcos, qui autem post ipsum regnarunt in Asia, Syro Macedones appellati sunt, eorumque ditio Iavan dicta, id est, Græcia. Vnde lux primo Macchabæorum, cap. 1. com. 1. regnavit pro eo primus in Græcia. Siquidem de Alexandro loquitur, qui primus regnavit pro Dario in Græcia, h. c est in Syro-Macedonia. Id regnum Græcorum idem historicus appellat.
units.tr: He subdued Macedonia] This is why it is called the Macedonian kingdom, or that of the Greeks. For the Macedonians were among the Greeks, but those who afterwards reigned in Asia were called Syro-Macedonians, and their dominion was called Javan [יָוָן], that is, Greece. Hence the first book of Maccabees, ch. 1 v. 1, says that he reigned first in Greece in place of Darius. It speaks of Alexander, who was the first to reign in Greece in place of Darius, that is, in Syro-Macedonia. The same historian calls that kingdom the kingdom of the Greeks.

units.la: Omnibus ante regnis validissimum] melius & Latinius, omniu.n ante regnorum val difsimum.
units.tr: The most powerful of all the kingdoms before it] The better and more Latinate reading is "of all the kingdoms before it, the most powerful."

units.la: Pedes vero partim Ferrei & c.] alter Hiero Regnum, in quit, quartum, quod perspicue pertinetad Romanos, ferrum est; quod commi nuit ac domat omnia: ied pedes ejus & digiti ex parte ferrei & ex parte sunt fictiles: quod hoc tempore manifestissime comprobatur. Sicut enim in prin- cipio nihil imperio Romano fortius & durius fuit, ita in fine rerum nihil imbecillius: quando & in bellis civilibus & adversum diversas nationes aliarum gentium barbarorum indigemus auxilio. Hucusque Hieronymus.
units.tr: The feet, partly iron, etc.] Jerome, in another place: "The fourth kingdom, which clearly pertains to the Romans, is iron, which breaks and subdues all things; but its feet and toes are partly iron and partly clay, which is most clearly proven at this time. For just as at the beginning nothing was stronger or harder than the Roman empire, so at the end of things nothing is weaker, since in civil wars, and against various nations, we need the help of other barbarian peoples." Thus far Jerome.

units.la: Semper pacis specie] se per pacis speciem emendat Sigonius, quod mihi se valde probat.
units.tr: Always under the appearance of peace] Sigonius emends this to "through the appearance of peace," which I strongly approve.

units.la: Postrema tempora] extremitatem dierum vocant sacræ litteræ. Dicuntur etiam ultima, itemque novissima tempora, & extremi dies & aevum Messiae & seculum futurum: ex quo illud, neque in hoc neque in futuro [?] seculo, quod proverbialiter usurpant pro nunquam. Credebant enim omnia peccata in hoc seculo remissum iri.
units.tr: The last times] Holy Scripture calls them the extremity of the days. They are also called the last, and likewise the latest times, the last days and the age of the Messiah and the future age; hence that saying, "neither in this age nor in the future," which they use proverbially for never. For they believed that all sins would be forgiven in this age.

units.la: In mores nostros] malim, in ritus nostros. Nam mores ad vitam, ritus ad religionem spectant proprie.
units.tr: Into our customs] I would prefer "rites." For customs properly concern life, while rites concern religion.

units.la: In lapide vero sine manibus abscissus, &c.] Hieronymus in commentario super Danielem, In sine autem horum omnium regnorum, auri, argenti, aeris & ferri, abscissus est lapis Dominus atque salvator, sine manibus, id est absque cointu humano, de utero virginali, & contritis omnibus regnis, factus est mons magnus & implevit universam terram: quod Iudaei & impius Porphyrius male ad populum referunt Israel, quem in fine seculorum voluntate fortissimum & omnia regna conterere & regnare, &c.
units.tr: But in the stone cut out without hands, etc.] Jerome in his commentary on Daniel: "But at the end of all these kingdoms, of gold, silver, bronze and iron, the stone was cut out, the Lord and Saviour, without hands, that is, without human seed, from a virgin's womb; and when all the kingdoms were crushed, it became a great mountain and filled the whole earth. The Jews and the impious Porphyry wrongly refer this to the people of Israel, which they say will in the end of the ages, by its own will, most strongly crush all kingdoms and reign, etc."

units.la: Siquidem non ex voluntate viri] hoc de regeneratis extulit Euangelista Ioh. 1.13.
units.tr: Which was not of the will of man] The evangelist John (1:13) said this of the regenerate.

units.la: Pag.94, Futurum seculum] post resurrectionem. Nam est aliud post hanc vitam. Vocatur etiam futurum seculum tempus Messiae, ut dictum est. De his Don Isahac Abarbenel in libro qui Possessio patrum inscribitur.
units.tr: Page 94. The future age] After the resurrection. For there is another age after this life. The time of the Messiah is also called the future age, as has been said. On these matters see Don Isaac Abarbanel in the book entitled The Possession of the Fathers.

units.la: Ejus suffragio] rogatu potius. Nam suffragium aliud est. Vide Dan.2.49.
units.tr: By his support] At his request, rather. For suffragium means something else. See Dan. 2:49.

units.la: Resurrectionis mysterio] utrum respexit ad caput trigesimum septimum Ezechielis (ita scribendum, non Ezechielis) quod nonnulli de generali resurrectione intelligunt? cum potius ibi agat de restitutione captivitatis Babylonicae, quae quasi mors quaedam civilis est. Sed & moritur qui in calamitates incidit. Unde lucem faciunt Salomoni, cum ait, iustitia liberat a morte. Nam id enarrant, a variis calamitatibus.
units.tr: The mystery of the resurrection] Did he perhaps look to chapter 37 of Ezekiel (so it should be written: Ezekiel, not Ezechielis), which some understand of the general resurrection? Yet there he speaks rather of the restoration from the Babylonian captivity, which is a kind of civil death. But he also dies who falls into calamities. Hence they shed light on Solomon when he says, "righteousness delivers from death." For they explain it as deliverance from various calamities.

units.la: Ismael quodam duce] qui de femine regio erat, ac propterea aegre ferebat alium sibi a Chaldaeis praelatum, Ierem. 40. & 41.
units.tr: Under a certain leader, Ishmael] who was of royal seed and therefore took it badly that another had been set over him by the Chaldeans: Jer. 40 and 41.

units.la: At hi qui extra noxiam fuerant] Iohannes Careae filius & alij, Ierem. 41.12.
units.tr: But those who had been outside the guilt] John son of Kareah and others: Jer. 41:12.

units.la: Pag.95. Ammonitas] filios Ammon. Quod notandum, quia Ammonitae proprie dicuntur, a quibus diversi sunt filij Ammon, id est, בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן [?] Quanvis interpretes hos populos inter se confundant. Vide 2.Paralip. 20.1. Quid de ea postea actum sacris litteris siletur] non plane fileiur. Nam pars in AEgypto periit, pars rediit in terram Iuda, Ierem.44.17. pars Babylonem ducta fuit, Iosephus Ant. lib.10.cap.11. Quinto post excidium Ierosolymitanum anno, qui fuit regni Nabuchodonosoris, &c. AEgyptum est ingressus, occisoque qui tunc regnabat, (vocatur Pharao Ephree. Ierem.44.30.) & alio rege constituto, repertos ibi Iudaeos rursum captivos Babylonem abduxit.
units.tr: Page 95. The Ammonites] The sons of Ammon. This should be noted, because the Ammonites are properly so called, and the sons of Ammon, [בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן], are different from them, although the translators confuse these peoples. See 2 Chron. 20:1. What became of them afterwards is passed over in silence in Holy Scripture] Not entirely silent. For part perished in Egypt, part returned to the land of Judah (Jer. 44:17), and part was led off to Babylon. Josephus, Antiquities book 10 ch. 11: in the fifth year after the destruction of Jerusalem, which was the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, he entered Egypt, killed the king then reigning (called Pharaoh Hophra, Jer. 44:30), and after setting up another king, led the Jews found there captive back to Babylon.

units.la: Rebus secundis] victoriis quas obtinuerat de Syria, Iudaea & AEgypto.
units.tr: In prosperous circumstances] Through the victories he had won over Syria, Judaea and Egypt.

units.la: Immensae magnitudinis] altitudine cubitorum sexaginta, latitudine vero sex.
units.tr: Of immense size] Sixty cubits in height and six in breadth.

units.la: Posuit] in campo Dura provinciae Babylonis. Sic vulgatus interpres Dan.3.1. Sed moneo verba Ebraea verti etiam posse, in campo Dura, in urbe Babylonis. Nam Medina tam urbem quam provinciam denotat. Hiero. ad hunc locum Pro Dura, Theodotio Deira, Symmachus Doraum (Dora [illegible, ~3 letters]) LXX, [illegible, ~9 letters] transtulerunt: quod nos vivarium vel conclusum locum dicere possumus.
units.tr: He set it up] In the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon. So the Vulgate translator at Dan. 3:1. But I warn that the Hebrew words can also be rendered "in the plain of Dura, in the city of Babylon," since Medina denotes both a city and a province. Jerome on this passage: for Dura, Theodotion has Deira, Symmachus Doraum (Dora [illegible]), and the Seventy [illegible] translated; we may call it an enclosed or walled place.

units.la: Ut sacram effigiem] hoc adjecit, quoniam adoratio quaedam in oriente civilis erat, quae sine sacrilegio, aut, ut alibi loquitur, nefariae mentis piaculo fiebat. Hoc modo Abraham patriarches adoravit olim populum terrae.
units.tr: That they should worship the sacred image] He added this because a certain worship was civil in the East, which was performed without sacrilege, or, as he says elsewhere, without the guilt of an impious mind. In this way Abraham the patriarch once worshipped the people of the land.

units.la: Pag.96. Piaculum committere] statuam adorare. Sic alibi cultum idolorum nefariae mentis piaculum vocat. Alio sensu dixit pag.151. non aliua piacula pronteri.
units.tr: Page 96. To commit sacrilege] To worship the statue. So elsewhere he calls the worship of idols an offence of an impious mind. In another sense he said on p. 151 that no other offences are shown.

units.la: Vincti pedibus] fatis erat vinctis simpliciter, i. [illegible, ~5 letters]. Nam [illegible, ~3 letters] vincio, ligo. Sed expressit participium Graecum [illegible, ~12 letters], cujus thema [illegible, ~5 letters], compedio. Sic Hieronymus, justit ut ligatis pedibus mitterent eos. Ego imbibi non solum pedes vinctos fuisse, sed etiam manus: fuitque aliquando tempus cum legendum putarem, vincti compedibus. Quod Graecum [illegible, ~10 letters] proprie significat.
units.tr: Bound at the feet] It would have been enough simply to say bound, i.e. [illegible]. For [illegible] means to bind or tie. But he rendered a Greek participle whose stem [illegible] means to fetter. So Jerome: he ordered them to be sent with their feet bound. I once was persuaded that not only the feet but also the hands were bound, and there was a time when I thought one should read "bound with fetters," which the Greek word properly signifies.

units.la: Psalmum] hymnum, quem Azariae dixit, ut habetur in editione Graeca, Dan.3.
units.tr: The psalm] The hymn which Azariah spoke, as it stands in the Greek edition, Dan. 3.

units.la: Specie angeli] imo viri, qui similis erat filio Dei, quem paullo post angelum vocat, cum ait, misit angelum suum. Verba sunt Nabuchodonosoris vers.95.
units.tr: In the form of an angel] Rather, of a man, who was like the Son of God, whom a little later he calls an angel when he says, "he sent his angel." These are the words of Nebuchadnezzar, verse 95.

units.la: Filium Dei] similem filio Dei. Sic enim certe Theodotio
units.tr: The Son of God] Like the Son of God. For so Theodotion certainly renders it.

units.la: Potestate regia abjecta, sed cum ex hominibus depelleretur, simul amisit dignitatem illam. Hoc accidit anno regni ejus trigesimo primo, ut quidem Funccius putat: octavo autem supra trigesimum, eodem teste, in regnum restitutus fuit.
units.tr: With royal power cast off; but when he was driven out from among men, he at the same time lost that dignity. This happened in the thirty-first year of his reign, as Funccius indeed thinks; but in the thirty-eighth year, on the same witness, he was restored to the kingdom.

units.la: Egisse poenitentiam traditur, dum adhuc mente valeret. Quod etiam Hiero. opinatus videtur: & idcirco, inquit, usque ad mensem duodecimum in eum est dilata sententia. Herbam autem comedit ut bos, cum jam furore caecatus esset. Ita Theodoretus opinatur.
units.tr: He is said to have done penance while he still had his wits. Jerome also seems to have thought this, and therefore, he says, the sentence was deferred against him for twelve months. But he ate grass like an ox when he was already blinded by madness. Thus Theodoret thinks.

units.la: Post septem annos in Daniele, post finem annorum: & paulo ante, septem tempora. Vt per tempora R. Saadia menses intelligit, Abenezra vero annos: alij dies, alij hebdomadas. Sed tam breve spatio non possunt pili & ungues a deo increscere. Vide Dan 4.30. Tempus autem pro anno sumitur & in illo, tempus & tempora & dimidium temporis.
units.tr: After seven years in Daniel, after the end of the years; and a little before, seven times. Through "times" R. Saadia understands months, Abenezra years, others days, others weeks. But hair and nails cannot grow by God's power in so short a space. See Dan. 4:30. Time is also taken for a year, and in that sense "a time and times and half a time."

units.la: Post deviētum Sedeciam regnasse traditur ann. VI & XX. Sedecias deviētus fuit anno undecimo regni sui, qui fuit Nabuchodonosoris (ita quidam opinantur) decimus nonus. Regnavit ergo Nabuchodonosor ante deviētum Sedeciam ann. XIX. Quibus si addideris hos viginti sex, simul efficiunt ann. XLV. quos Nabuchodonosoro tribuit Megasthenes Persa, ut Sigonius observat: in quo male pro Megasthenes Metasthenes legitur. Alii, Nabuchodonosoro tribuunt tantum ann. XLIII. in quem numerum veniunt anni tredecim quibus cum patre Nabopollassaro regnavit. Solus enim duntaxat cum imperio fuit ann. XXX. Quae de re alias, cum plus otij habebo.
units.tr: After Sedecias was defeated, he is said to have reigned twenty-six years. Sedecias was defeated in the eleventh year of his reign, which was (so some think) the nineteenth of Nebuchadnezzar. Nebuchadnezzar therefore reigned nineteen years before the defeat of Sedecias. If you add these twenty-six years, they make forty-five in all, which Megasthenes the Persian assigns to Nebuchadnezzar, as Sigonius observes; in that passage "Metasthenes" is wrongly read for Megasthenes. Others assign to Nebuchadnezzar only forty-three years, reached by adding the thirteen years in which he reigned together with his father Nabopolassar. For he held sole power for thirty years. I will say more on this matter elsewhere, when I have more leisure.

units.la: Regum Babyloniorum tempora] quae sic quidam digerunt ex Megasthene & Berofo. Nabopollassarus ann. XXIX. Nabuchodonosorus ann. XXX. post patrem Evilmeradochus ann. II. Neriglissoorum affinis Evilmaradochi ann. IV. Baltasar, qui & Laborofoarchodos. Nabuchodonosoris ex filia nepos, mens. IX.
units.tr: The reigns of the Babylonian kings, which some arrange thus from Megasthenes and Berosus: Nabopolassar, 29 years; Nebuchadnezzar, 30 years; after his father, Evilmerodach, 2 years; Neriglissoor's kinsman by marriage, Evilmaradochus, 4 years; Baltasar, who is also Labrosoarchodos, Nebuchadnezzar's grandson through a daughter, 9 months.

units.la: Siquidem & chronicis consentirent] Si Eusebij chronica intelligit, non video qui hoc verum esse possit. Nam Ex-
units.tr: "For if they agreed with the chronicles." If he means the Chronicle of Eusebius, I do not see how this can be true. For Ex-

units.la: Prius erat in LXX. [?] ἀγγέλου θεοῦ, id est, similis angelo Dei. Notatum hoc in editione Romana.
units.tr: It was earlier in the Septuagint [?] "of an angel of God", that is, "like an angel of God". This is noted in the Roman edition.

units.la: Provulgavit] promulgavit.
units.tr: "Provulgavit": read promulgavit.

units.la: Potestate regia abjecta] non ipse abjecit potestatem regnum.
units.tr: "The king had cast off royal power": the king did not himself lay aside the kingdom's power.

units.la: Egisse poenitentiam traditur] dum adhuc mente valeret.
units.tr: "He is said to have undergone repentance": while he was still of sound mind.

units.la: Pag. 97.
units.tr: Page 97.

units.la: Iam interpolato] melius in interpolato. sebius[?] longe aliter supputat annos captivitatis. Vide si habes & si vacas.
units.tr: "Already interpolated": better read "in interpolato". Eusebius reckons the years of the captivity quite differently. See, if you have it and have time.

units.la: Usque in primum Cyri regis annum LXX annos] hos annos alij dinumerant a capto Iechonia. Eusebius qui a captivi-tate Sedeciæ incipit, eos desinere scribit in annum secundum Da-rij. Funccius hoc modo eos putat. Nabuchodonosorus post captum Sedeciam regnavit ann.XXVI. Evilmerodach XXX. Rega-far III. Labofardach VI. Balsafar IV. ecce LXIX. Nam septua-gesimo anno redierunt in terram patriam, qui fuit primus annus Cyri. Aliter Sigonius, quem te adire volo. Vide quoque Io-sephum.
units.tr: "Until the first year of King Cyrus, seventy years": some count these years from the capture of Jechoniah. Eusebius, who begins from the captivity of Sedecias, writes that they end in the second year of Darius. Funccius thinks they are counted thus: Nebuchadnezzar reigned 26 years after the capture of Sedecias; Evilmerodach 30; Regasar 3; Labosardach 6; Balsasar 4; behold 69. For in the seventieth year they returned to their homeland, which was the first year of Cyrus. Sigonius reckons differently, and I want you to consult him. See also Josephus.

units.la: Quem in Chronicis Evilmarodac fuisse vocitatum reperi] imo sic vocatur, Ierem. §2.31 & 4. Reg 25 27. Scribendum autem Evilmarodach sive Evilmerodach, cum C, aspirato in ultima: quod Græci declinant Εὐιλμαροδόχ[?]ῳ Evilma-rodochus.
units.tr: "Which I find in the Chronicles was called Evilmarodac": indeed he is so called, Jer. 52.31 and 2 Kings 25.27. It should be written Evilmarodach or Evilmerodach, with the C aspirated at the end; the Greeks decline it as [Εὐιλμαροδόχῳ], Evilmarodochus.

units.la: Duodecimo imperij anno] disserit a Iosepho, qui scribit eum præfuisse ann.XVIII. Megasthenes vero & Berosus Babylo-nius et tributum duntaxat ann.II.
units.tr: "In the twelfth year of his reign": this differs from Josephus, who writes that he ruled for eighteen years. Megasthenes and Berosus the Babylonian gave him only two years of tribute.

units.la: Fratri minori, qui Balthasar dictus est, locum fecit] Sic Eusebius, Mortuo Nabuchodonosor Babyloniorum rege suscepit imperium Evilmarodach, cui successit frater e-jus Balthafar: sub quo Daniel eam scripturam, quæ in pa-riete apparuerat, interpretatus est, significantem impe-rium Chaldæorum in Medos & Persas transferendum.
units.tr: "He made way for his younger brother, who was called Balthasar": thus Eusebius: on the death of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, Evilmarodach took up the empire, and his brother Balthasar succeeded him. Under him Daniel interpreted the writing that had appeared on the wall, signifying that the empire of the Chaldeans was to be transferred to the Medes and Persians.

units.la: Alij scribunt Balthasarem non fuisse fratrem Evilmarodochi, sed sororis filium. Sane a Berosfo & Megasthene vocatur Λαβοσαρδάχος[?] Ναβυχοδονοσόρου υἱὸς, id est, ex filia nepos. Is est Balthasar.
units.tr: Others write that Balthasar was not the brother of Evilmarodochus but the son of his sister. Indeed Berosus and Megasthenes call him Labosardachos [Λαβοσαρδάχος], "son of Nebuchadnezzar" [Ναβυχοδονοσόρου υἱὸς], that is, a grandson through a daughter. This is Balthasar.

units.la: Balthasar] vel potius, Baltasar. Nam Dan. 5.1. in edit. Græca Βαλτάσαρ[?] ὁ βασιλεύς[?]. Sed legendum ex Hiero. & codicibus Ebræis Balsafar. Nam Baltasar nomen est Danielis. Nabuchodonosor enim ita eum vocavit de nomine Dei sui, hoc est idoli Bel sive Balsale igitur faciunt, meo judicio, qui nomina talia imponunt filiis suis. Nam hoc modo refricant memoriam Deorum falsorum, quod sacræ litteræ fieri vetant. Sane David ait, non usurpabo nomina eorum labiis meis. Proinde causa nulla est cur mihi succensear aut irascatur bipedum nequissimus Baltasar. Nam si Hercules, si mediusfidius exulare debent ab ore ChristiaChristianorum, cur non etiam Bel?
units.tr: Balthasar: or rather Baltasar. For in Dan. 5.1 the Greek edition has [Βαλτάσαρ ὁ βασιλεύς]. But one should read Balsafar, as in Jerome and the Hebrew manuscripts, for Baltasar is Daniel's name. Nebuchadnezzar gave him that name after his god, that is, the idol Bel. So, in my judgement, those do wrong who impose such names on their sons, for in this way they revive the memory of false gods, which the sacred letters forbid. David indeed says, "I will not take up their names on my lips." So there is no reason for me to be angry with or incensed at that most wicked biped, Baltasar. For if Hercules, if Medius Fidius, ought to be banished from the mouths of Christians, why not Bel as well?

units.la: Quarto & decimo anno] Iosephus autor hæc accidisse anno regni ejus decimo septimo: a quo dissentiunt non parum qui ei tantum annos quinque assignant. Qui Laborosoarchodum eundem faciunt cum Balsasare tribunt imperio ejus menses IX. duntaxat: quod Iosephus prodidit de Labosardacho[?] (sic eum appellat) quem diversum facit a Balsasare, qui Babylonius, inquit, Nabonandel nominatur. Alibi est Nabonidus sive Labonidus pro eodem. Sed vide sequentia.
units.tr: "In the fourteenth year": Josephus is the authority that these things happened in the seventeenth year of his reign, and not a few who assign him only five years dissent from him. Those who make Laborosoarchodus the same as Balsasar give his rule only nine months, which Josephus stated of Labosardachus (as he calls him), whom he distinguishes from Balsasar, who, he says, is called the Babylonian Nabonandel. Elsewhere Nabonidus or Labonidus is put for the same man. But see what follows.

units.la: Pag. 98 Omnis virilis ac muliebris sexus uxores]- Sigonius mavult, Omnes virilis ac muliebris sexus uxores. Quod ut non improbo, ita scio veteres scripsisse omnis & omneis pro omnes. Sic quis & quei pro quibus scribebant.
units.tr: "All the wives of every male and female sex": Sigonius prefers "omnes virilis ac muliebris sexus uxores". I do not object to this, but I know that the ancients wrote omnis and omneis for omnes, just as they wrote quis and quei for quibus.

units.la: Inversum ductæ literæ] Idem suspicatur Sulpicium edidisse, in candelabrum versum. Ita Cicero dixit, in forum versus.
units.tr: "The letters inverted": the same Sigonius suspects that Sulpicius published "turned into a candelabrum" (in candelabrum versum). So Cicero said "turned toward the forum" (in forum versus).

units.la: Regina] avia. Iosephus.
units.tr: "Queen": grandmother, Josephus says.

units.la: Qui sacra Deo vasa temerasset] in uno codice desideratur, vasa. Paullo ante, sacra vasa proferri imperavit. Hæc vasa temerabat, hoc est contaminabat ac profanabat, cum ipse, uxores, concubinæ, ceterique conviviæ promiscue ut uterentur bibendo ex eis.
units.tr: "Who had defiled the sacred vessels": one manuscript lacks "vasa". A little before, he ordered the sacred vessels to be brought out. He was defiling these vessels, that is, polluting and profaning them, when he himself, his wives, his concubines and his other guests drank from them indiscriminately.

units.la: Medis ac Persis datum] primum Dario Medo, qui suscepit regnum oblatum sibi a Babyloniis: deinde Cyro Persæ ejusque posteris. Vide Dan. 5. 31.
units.tr: "Given to the Medes and Persians": first to Darius the Mede, who took the kingdom offered to him by the Babylonians; then to Cyrus the Persian and his descendants. See Dan. 5.31.

units.la: Balthasar interiit] occisus fuit in convivio a conjuratis, significato conjurationis Nabonido Mede, qui & Darius Medus. Quædam sunt qui Nabonidum eundem faciunt cum Balthasare.
units.tr: "Balthasar perished": he was killed at a banquet by conspirators, the conspiracy being that of Nabonidus the Mede, who is also Darius the Mede. Some make Nabonidus the same as Balthasar.

units.la: Regnumq; ejus Darius Medus occupavit] adjutus a Cyro cognato suo, Iosephus: accepit traditum a Babyloniis, Daniel, Berosus, alij: quem Cyrus post in arce Borsippena expugnavit, Scaliger.
units.tr: "And Darius the Mede seized his kingdom": aided by Cyrus his kinsman, says Josephus; received it handed over by the Babylonians, says Daniel, Berosus and others; which Cyrus afterwards stormed in the citadel of Borsippa, says Scaliger.

units.la: Natione Medus] incertum an natione Medus fuerit. Vocatur quidem Darius Medus, sed ex eo non sequitur gente Medum fuisse. Forte Medus dicitur quia patre Medo erat oriundus, aut quia vixerat apud Medos. Sic Vrias Hethæus vocatur, & Doeg Idumæus. Darius iste filius fuit Asveri de semine Medorum. Dan. 9.1. Asverus autem is esse creditur, qui a Græcis Cyaxares vocatur, vel certe Astyages. Iosephus lib. 10. cap. 13. Darius
units.tr: "A Mede by nation": it is uncertain whether he was a Mede by nation. He is indeed called Darius the Mede, but it does not follow from this that he was of the Median people. Perhaps he is called a Mede because he was descended from a Median father, or because he had lived among the Medes. So Uriah is called the Hittite, and Doeg the Edomite. That Darius was the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes (Dan. 9.1). Ahasuerus is believed to be the one whom the Greeks call Cyaxares, or certainly Astyages. Josephus, book 10, chapter 13. Darius

units.la: Astyagis F. qui Babyloniorum principatum destruxit. Scaliger [scribit hunc a Berofo Nabonidum, ab Herodoto vero Labynitum dici: regnavit annis septendecim.
units.tr: Son of Astyages, who destroyed the power of the Babylonians. Scaliger writes that Berosus calls him Nabonidus, but Herodotus calls him Labynitus; he reigned seventeen years.

units.la: Universo imperio praeposuit] erat unus ex tribus principibus, quos Sarchin appellabant, et alij praesides interpretantur, qui praeerant centum viginti satrapis Dan.6.1. Hinc emaculandus Iosephus, in quo, erat unus ex tribus summis satrapis, qui sub se habebant alios CCCLX. satrapas: totenim a Dario primum instituti sunt.
units.tr: "He set him over the whole empire": he was one of the three chief princes, whom they called Sarchin, and whom others interpret as prefects, who presided over the 120 satraps (Dan. 6.1). Hence the passage in Josephus must be corrected, where he says that Daniel was one of the three highest satraps who had 360 other satraps under them; for these were first instituted by Darius.

units.la: Pag 99. Velte purpurea & torque aureo] Tertullianus, purpura & aurum, cervicis ornamentum apud AEgyptios & Babylonios, insignia sunt dignitatis.
units.tr: "A purple robe and a golden collar": Tertullian says that purple and gold, an ornament of the neck among the Egyptians and Babylonians, are insignia of dignity.

units.la: Tertium regni principem] rex jussit ut tertius in regno princeps proclamaretur Dan.5.29.
units.tr: "The third ruler in the kingdom": the king ordered that a third prince in the kingdom be proclaimed (Dan. 5.29).

units.la: Qui una cum eo rerum potentes erant] praesides, de quibus supra, & satrapae Dan 6.3. Mox, principes appellat.
units.tr: "Who together with him were powerful in affairs": the prefects mentioned above, and the satraps (Dan. 6.3). Soon after, he calls them princes.

units.la: Exagitati invidia] recte sic emendavit olim VictorGisellinus, cum prius legeretur exagitati in Iudaea fine ullo commodo sen. Iosephus, itaque cum tam carus & honoratus effet apud regem, qui et tanquam divino de quovis negotio consulenti pareret, non effugit ceterorum invidiam, quemadmodum fieri solet inter eos, qui aliquem sibi a rege praeferri non patiuntur aequo animo. Vt hic, exagitati invidia, ita superius dixit pag.13. Agente invidia; & inferius pag.106. flagrante invidia.
units.tr: "Harassed by envy": this was correctly emended long ago by Victor Gisellinus, when it was previously read "harassed in Judaea without any advantage". Josephus says that, since he was so dear and honoured by the king, who consulted him on any matter as if he were a god, he did not escape the envy of the others, as usually happens among those who cannot patiently bear that someone is preferred to them by the king. As here, "harassed by envy"; so above he said, on page 13, "envy at work"; and below, on page 106, "envy blazing".

units.la: Dominum nisi regem precari] petere quicquam a Deo quocunq; aut ab ullo homine, nisi a rege solo. Hoc faciebat Daniel quum quotidie ter genua flectebat, Deumque precaretur in caenaculo suo. Ceterum qui aliquid petit ab alio, non propterea ei exhibet divinum honorem. Quocirca miror cur[?] scripserit hoc loco, ut sibi divini honores darentur: & stultitia regum omnium, qui sibi divina vendicant: & rursum, igitur Daniel non rudis neque inscius Deo preces, non homini deferendas. Imo etiam preces hominibus deferuntur. Sed aliter Deo, aliter hominibus.
units.tr: "To pray to no lord except the king": to ask anything from God, or from any man, except from the king alone. Daniel did this when he knelt three times a day and prayed to God in his upper room. But one who asks something of another does not thereby give him divine honour. Wherefore I wonder why he wrote in this place that divine honours were given to himself, and about the folly of all kings who claim divine things for themselves; and again, "therefore Daniel, not rude nor ignorant, that prayers must not be offered to a man." Indeed, prayers are even offered to men, but differently to God and differently to men.

units.la: In lacum] Graeci vocant τὰς λάκκους[?] τῶν λεόντων[?], quod in eo leones asservarentur.
units.tr: Into the den: the Greeks call it [τοὺς λάκκους τῶν λεόντων], because lions were kept in it.

units.la: Accusatores] cum uxoribus & filiis.
units.tr: The accusers: with their wives and children.

units.la: Deputari] delegari, assignari: unde deputati. Gallice de-putés. putés. Verbum minus usitatum hoc sensu Latinis autoribus, eo tamen usus fuit & supra 86. Quae turba inutilis servitio, exercendis colendisque agris, ne incultum esset solum, deputata.
units.tr: Deputed: sent off, assigned, whence "deputati" (in French, "députés"). Latin authors seldom use the word in this sense, but he used it above at p. 86: "This useless crowd, deputed to serve, to cultivate the fields, lest the soil be left uncultivated."

units.la: Pag. 110. Seculorum ordinem] regnorum sive monarchiarum seriem. Sunt autem visiones ejus in universum decem.
units.tr: P. 110. The order of the ages: the succession of kingdoms or monarchies. Now his visions are ten in all.

units.la: Annorum etiam numerum complexus, &c. ] Dan. 9. 16.
units.tr: Also taking in the number of years, etc.: Dan. 9. 16.

units.la: post bebdomadas sexaginta duas excidetur Mesias ([illegible, ~6 letters]) & non propter se, id est [illegible, ~4 letters] culpa sua, aut ob peccata sua. Sic in primo librorum Mosis [illegible, ~4 letters] quod enarrant [illegible, ~5 letters] in meam gratiam, vel de me. Sunt qui malint, & non erit, ut [illegible, ~3 letters] redundet in Latio. Sed tum potius dixisset, meo judici, [illegible, ~4 letters] & non ipse, ut Gen. 5. Ambulavit Henoch cum Deo, & non fuit. Alij aliter. Nam quot interpretes, tot sententiae. Ego meam pono tantum, nihil statuo.
units.tr: After sixty-two weeks the Messiah will be cut off ([illegible]) and not for himself, that is [illegible], through his own fault, or on account of his own sins. So in the first book of Moses [illegible], which they relate [illegible] for my grace, or concerning me. Some prefer that "and it will not be" [illegible] abounds in Latium. But then he would rather have said, in my judgment, [illegible], and not himself, as in Gen. 5: "Enoch walked with God, and he was not." Others take it otherwise, for there are as many interpreters as opinions. I put forward only my own and settle nothing.

units.la: Venturumque Antichristum manifeste exposuit] Dan. 7. 14. & 25. ad quem locum Hiero.
units.tr: And that Antichrist will come he clearly expounded: Dan. 7. 14 and 25, on which passage Jerome [...]

units.la: Antichristus in tantam erigetur superbiam ut leges Dei & caeremonias mutare conetur, & elevetur supra omne quod dicitur Deus, religionem cunctam suae subjiciens potestati. Theodoretus sive Theodoritus, decem reges circa finem exurgent, & postremus Antichristus exorietur, regnumque obtinere contendet ac tres illos evertet. Nec contentus victoria, quam de hominibus retulerit, etiam maledicta contra Deum altissimum conjiciet & sanctos supplicio afficiet & putabit se posse pietatem, quae tunc vigebit, evertere & rempub. com-mutare.
units.tr: Antichrist will rise to such pride that he will try to change the laws and ceremonies of God, and will exalt himself above everything called God, subjecting all religion to his own power. Theodoret (or Theodoritus) says that ten kings will arise near the end, and the last Antichrist will appear and seek to gain the kingdom and overthrow those three. Not content with the victory he will have won over men, he will also hurl blasphemies against the Most High God, will put the saints to torture, and will think he can overthrow the piety that will then flourish and change the commonwealth.

units.la: Duodeviginti] id est, octodecim. Alij unum dumtaxat annum regnasse tradunt, alij septemdecim, in quibus Iosephus Scaliger vide quae scripsit heros ille in De temporum emendatione, pag. 280.
units.tr: Eighteen: that is, eighteen. Others report that he reigned only one year, others seventeen. On this see what that hero Joseph Scaliger wrote in De emendatione temporum, p. 280.

units.la: Patrem habuit Asverum, qui ab aliis Xerxes Medus & Axares vocatur, & pleniore vocabulo Cyaxares, addita videlicet syllaba Cu, quae in ea lingua dynastam aut principem denotat.
units.tr: He had as his father Asuerus, who by others is called Xerxes the Mede and Axares, and with the fuller name Cyaxares, the syllable Cu being added, which in that language denotes a lord or prince.

units.la: Astiages] melius, Astyages. Hic etiam Cyaxarem patrem habuit. Forte frater erat Darij Medi.
units.tr: Astiages: better, Astyages. This one also had Cyaxares as his father. He was perhaps the brother of Darius the Mede.

units.la: Ex filia] Mandana, quae Cambyse Persae nupserat: unde Cyrus.
units.tr: By a daughter: Mandane, who had married the Persian Cambyses; hence Cyrus.

units.la: Babylonij quoque in potestatem ditionemque ejus concessere] vitto Dario Medo, quem expugnatum in arte Borsip-pena Carmaniæ præfecit, agentem tum annum ætatis octogesi-mum, Berosus.
units.tr: The Babylonians too came under his power and dominion, after Darius the Mede had been overcome, whom he placed as governor of Carmania in the citadel of Borsippa, then in his eightieth year of age, according to Berosus.

units.la: Dat potestatem Iudæis in solum patrium redeundi] post exactos annos LXX. de quibus Ierem. 29 10, & alibi.
units.tr: He gives the Jews power to return to their native land after the seventy years had run out, of which Jer. 29:10, and elsewhere.

units.la: Sacra etiam vasa] quæ numerantur Ezræ 1.10. & deinceps.
units.tr: The sacred vessels also, which are listed in Ezra 1:10 and following.

units.la: Pauci tum in Iudæam regressi] quadraginta duo millia trecenti sexaginta, exceptis servis eorum & ancillis, qui erant septem millia trecenti triginta septem. Ezræ 2.64. & 65.
units.tr: Few then returned to Judea: 42,360, besides their male and female servants, who were 7,337. Ezra 2:64 and 65.

units.la: Beli antiquissimi regis] Hiero. in comment. Hof /2. 16. [?]
units.tr: Of Bel, the most ancient king: Jerome in his commentary on Hosea 2:16?

units.la: Primum omnium Asiæ regnasse Ninum Beli filium omnes & Græcæ & Barbaræ narrant historiæ. Lactantius lib. 1. cap. 23. [?]
units.tr: All Greek and barbarian histories relate that Ninus, son of Belus, first of all reigned over Asia. Lactantius, book 1, chapter 23.

units.la: Theophylus in libro de temporibus ad Autolycum scripto, ait in historia sua Thalum dicere, quod Belus, quem Babylonij & Assyrij coluerunt, antiquior Trojano bello fuisse invenitur C.CXXII [?] annis.
units.tr: Theophilus, in his book To Autolycus on the times, says that Thallus, in his history, says that Belus, whom the Babylonians and Assyrians worshipped, was found to be older than the Trojan War by 1122 years.

units.la: Beli] Græca nominis forma ex Bel, quod scribunt בל [?], & est contractum ex Beel. Id Sidonij & Phœnices reliquique Syri enuntiant Baal & Bal. Vide sequentia.
units.tr: Belus: the Greek form of the name, from Bel, which they write [בל], and which is contracted from Beel. The Sidonians, the Phoenicians and the remaining Syrians pronounce it Baal and Bal. See what follows.

units.la: Quod superstitione hominum consecratum] Hiero. in loco superius allegato, Ninus in tantam pervenit gloriam ut patrem suum Belum referret in Deum, qui Ebraice dicitur Bel, & in multis prophetis, maximeque in Daniele & juxta Theodotionem sub idolo Babylonis hoc appellatur nomine. Et post aliquanto, didicimus exordium dæmonis, imo hominis in dæmonem conversi. Omnia enim idola ex mortuorum errore creverunt.
units.tr: Which was consecrated by the superstition of men: Jerome, in the passage cited above: Ninus rose to such glory that he referred his father Belus to God, who in Hebrew is called Bel; in many prophets, and especially in Daniel, and according to Theodotion under the idol of Babylon, he is called by this name. And a little later: we have learned the origin of a demon, or rather of a man turned into a demon. For all idols grew out of the error of the dead.

units.la: Cuius etiam Virgilius meminit] aut glossema est ex margine, ut vult Sigonius: aut, quod magis puto, confundit Belum Babylonium cum Tyrio. Sic etiam Hieronymus in loco citato, Belum Sidonij & Phœnices appellant Baal: unde & Dido Sidonia regij generis, cum Æneâ suscepisset hospitio, hac patera Iovi vinum delibat.
units.tr: Virgil also mentions him. Either this is a gloss from the margin, as Sigonius holds, or, what I think more likely, he confuses the Babylonian Belus with the Tyrian. So Jerome too, in the passage cited, says that the Sidonians and Phoenicians call Belus Baal; hence Dido, of Sidonian royal stock, when she had received Aeneas as her guest, poured wine from this bowl to Jupiter.

units.la: Qua Belus & omnes a Belo soliti.
units.tr: With which Belus and all who came after Belus were wont (to make their libations).

units.la: Cyrus] Darius. Historia Ebraica.
units.tr: Cyrus] Darius. The Hebrew history.

units.la: Antistitum ejus] sacerdotum ejus.
units.tr: Its priests: its sacrificing priests.

units.la: Pag. 101. Pensitationem] a pensito, id est, solvo. Ita vocat id quod quotidie in Belum impendebatur. Erant autem similæ artabæ duodecim, oves quadraginta & vini metretæ sex: aut, ut est apud Gorionis F. compositorem historiae Ebraicae, juven-cus unus, decem arietes & centum columbi, totidemque agni, cum septuaginta placentis panis, totidemque cadis vini.
units.tr: P. 101. Pensitation: from pensito, that is, to pay. So he calls what was paid out every day to Bel. Now there were twelve artabae of fine flour, forty sheep and six metretae of wine; or, as in Gorionides, the compiler of the Hebrew history, one bullock, ten rams and a hundred pigeons, and as many lambs, with seventy cakes of bread and as many jars of wine.

units.la: Fere ad septuaginta] redundat fere. Nam in Daniele, erant autem sacerdotes Bel septuaginta. Sic pag. 43. ad triginta duo millia. Vide notas ad illum locum. In historia Ebraica, misit qui comprehenderent septem sacerdotes Belo ministrantes. <bl>nyɔw</bl> pro <bl>ɔ'yɔw</bl>. Forte mendum est. Nam ne septuaginta quidem potuissent eam pensitationem absumere, nisi uxores & parvulos in societatem ascivissent.
units.tr: About seventy: "about" is redundant, for in Daniel "the priests of Bel were seventy." So on p. 43 "to thirty-two thousand." See the notes on that passage. In the Hebrew history he sent men to seize seven priests who ministered to Bel; the Hebrew word is misprinted. Perhaps this is an error, for not even seventy could have consumed that pensitation unless they had taken their wives and little children into partnership.

units.la: Inferre] cibum & potum.
units.tr: To bring in: food and drink.

units.la: Signo regis] sigillo regis & Danielis, Gorionides.
units.tr: By the king's seal: by the seal of the king and of Daniel, says Gorionides.
