units.la: Pavimentum cinere aspersisset] jussitq; Daniel ut clauderent fores templi Bel, & portas ejus, excepta porta per quam ingressus fuerat rex. Tunc dixit Daniel: Adferte mihi cinerem, sparseruntque cinerem illum super pavimentum templi Bel, insciis sacerdotibus. Post egressi sunt rex & Daniel per portam, quam intraverant, ipsi & pueri eorum: quam clauserunt jussu Danielis, obsignavitque eam rex annulo suo & annulo Danielis, &c. Idem qui supra.
units.tr: And had ashes strewn over the pavement: and Daniel ordered them to shut the doors of the temple of Bel and its gates, except the gate through which the king had entered. Then Daniel said: "Bring me ashes." And they scattered the ashes over the pavement of the temple of Bel, the priests being unaware. Afterwards the king and Daniel went out through the gate they had entered by, they and their boys, which they shut at Daniel's command, and the king sealed it with his ring and Daniel's ring, etc. The same as above.

units.la: Pag. 102. Ita omnes jussu regis interfecti, &c.] haec pa-rallelo aliter historia Ebraica, misit qui comprehenderent septem sacerdotes ministrantes Belo, quos rex adjuravit, dicendo, nisi verum indicaveritis mihi, scitote vos moritu-ros. Igitur ostenderunt ei ingressus obscuros, per quos illi nocte ingrediebantur in templum, comedentes instru-ctam mensam ejus. Ibi rex cognita veritate eorum, jussit dirui templum Bel funditus, ita ut nihil quicquam remanserit.
units.tr: P. 102. So all were put to death at the king's command, etc.] The Hebrew history gives this in a parallel account: he sent to seize seven priests who ministered to Bel, whom the king adjured, saying, "Unless you tell me the truth, know that you will die." So they showed him the hidden entrances through which they used to enter the temple by night, eating the table laid out for him. There the king, having learned the truth, ordered the temple of Bel to be razed to the ground, so that nothing whatever remained.

units.la: Danieli in potestatem datum] Dan 14.21. Occidit ergo illos rex, & tradidit Bel in potestatem Danielis: qui subvertit eum & templum ejus.
units.tr: Given into Daniel's power: Dan. 14:21. So the king killed them, and handed Bel over to Daniel's power, who overthrew him and his temple.

units.la: Donec centesimo fere anno] recte. Nam ab anno primo Cyri usque ad Artaxerxem, cognomento Longimanum, qui μακρόχειρ Graecis, anni sunt nonaginta septem totidemque menses. Quod ex hac tabula perspicuum fiet. Cyrus rerum potitus est ann. 31 Cambyses ejus filius anu. 9 Magi duo mensibus | 7 Darius Hystaspis F. ann. | 36 Asverus sive Xerxes ann. | 2ℓ Summa ann. 97. mens. 7.
units.tr: Until about the hundredth year: rightly. For from the first year of Cyrus until Artaxerxes, surnamed Longimanus, who is [μακρόχειρ] to the Greeks, there are ninety-seven years and as many months. This will be clear from the following table: Cyrus reigned 31 years; Cambyses his son 9; the two Magi 7 months; Darius son of Hystaspes 36 years; Xerxes or Asuerus 21 years. Total: 97 years, 7 months.

units.la: Imperitante] codex Coloniæ impressus, imperante. Sed non displicet imperitante. Sic pag. 5. vocitata dixit pro vocata. Vide Eyre 4-7.
units.tr: Ruling: the printed Cologne copy has imperante, but imperitante is not objectionable. So on p. 5 he wrote vocitata for vocata. See Eyre, 4–7.

units.la: Locis] vicinis.
units.tr: Places] neighbouring ones.

units.la: Darij regis] Darij Nothi, qui medius inter duos Artaxerxes. Porro Artaxerxen Ebrei Artaxata vocant. Horum regum alius cognominabatur μακρόχειρ, id est, Longimanus, & alius, qui posterior, μνήμων, id est, Memor sive Recordans, ut quidem Hieronymus interpretatur.
units.tr: Of King Darius: Darius Nothus, who came between two Artaxerxes. The Hebrews call Artaxerxes "Artaxata." Of these kings one was surnamed [μακρόχειρ], that is Longimanus, and the other, the later one, [μνήμων], that is Mindful or Remembering, as Jerome interprets it.

units.la: Qui reges Persis imperaverint] præter Severum nostrum, etiam Hieronymus, qui Persis imperaverint, quatuordecim recenset Dan. 7. cuius verba non pigrabor ascribere, Post Cyrum, qui regnavit annis triginta, scimus apud Persas regnasse Cambysen filium ejus, & fratres Magos, & deinceps Darium: cuius secundo anno coeptum est ædificari templum in Ierusalem: quintum, Xerxen, filium Darij: sextum, Artabanum: septimum, Artaxerxen, qui μακρόχειρ, id est, Longimanus cognominatus est: octavum, Xerxen: nonum, Sogdianum: decimum, Darium cognomento Nothum: undecimum, Artaxerxen, qui appellatus est μνήμων, id est, Recordans: duodecimum alium Artaxerxen, qui & ipse cognominatus est Ochus: tertium decimum, Arsen Ochi filium: quartum decimum, Darium Arsami filium, qui ab Alexandro Macedonum rege superatus est.
units.tr: Who reigned over the Persians] Besides our Severus, Jerome also lists fourteen kings who ruled the Persians, in Daniel 7. I will not hesitate to copy his words: "After Cyrus, who reigned thirty years, we know that Cambyses his son reigned over the Persians, and the Magi, two brothers, and then Darius. In the second year of Darius the building of the temple in Jerusalem was begun. Fifth, Xerxes, son of Darius. Sixth, Artabanus. Seventh, Artaxerxes, who was surnamed Longimanus [μακρόχειρ]. Eighth, Xerxes. Ninth, Sogdianus. Tenth, Darius, surnamed Nothus. Eleventh, Artaxerxes, who was called Memor [μνήμων], that is, Mindful. Twelfth, another Artaxerxes, who was himself surnamed Ochus. Thirteenth, Arses, son of Ochus. Fourteenth, Darius, son of Arsames, who was defeated by Alexander, king of the Macedonians."

units.la: Pag. 301. Cyrus uno et triginta] huic ab Eusebio, Hieronymo & Iustino triginta anni, ab aliis novem tantum tribuuntur. Magis autem Iosephus tribuit annum unum integrum.
units.tr: Page 301. Cyrus, thirty-one years] Eusebius, Jerome and Justin give him thirty years; others assign him only nine. Josephus gives him one full year, which is more likely.

units.la: Scythis bellum inferens in prælio cecidit] Tomyris enim eo tempore Scytharum regina, compositis insidiis, ducenta millia Persarum una cum ipso rege trucidavit, ita ut ne nuntius quidem tantæ cladis superfuerit. Caput Cyri amputatum, in utrem humano sanguine plenum conjectum fuit, cum hac exprobatione, satia te sanguine, quem sitisti.
units.tr: Waging war on the Scythians, he fell in battle] For Tomyris, queen of the Scythians at that time, by laying an ambush, slaughtered two hundred thousand Persians together with the king himself, so that not even a messenger survived so great a disaster. Cyrus's head was cut off and thrown into a skin full of human blood, with this taunt: "Now satisfy yourself with the blood you thirsted for."

units.la: Secundo anno postquam Tarquinius Superbus Romæ regnare coeperat] Aliter sensisse videtur Hieronymus in prologo in Haggaum prophetam, quando secundum annum Darij Hystaspis incidere ait in annum vigesimum septimum huius Tarquinij. Verba sunt, Quo tempore apud Romanos septimus a Romulo regnabat Tarquinius Superbus, habens annum imperij vigesimum septimum: qui post octo annos expulsus est a Bruto, ac deinde rempub. per annos quadringentos sexaginta quatuor usque ad Iulium Cæsarem consules administrarunt.
units.tr: In the second year after Tarquin the Proud had begun to reign at Rome] Jerome seems to have held a different view in his preface to the prophet Haggai, where he says that the second year of Darius Hystaspis falls in the twenty-seventh year of this Tarquin. His words are: "At that time, among the Romans, Tarquin the Proud, the seventh from Romulus, was reigning, in the twenty-seventh year of his rule. He was expelled eight years later by Brutus, and then the consuls administered the state for four hundred and sixty-four years, down to Julius Caesar."

units.la: Annos novem] sex, Iosephus: septem, Functius: octo alij. Vide pag 112.
units.tr: Nine years] Josephus gives six, Functius seven, others eight. See page 112.

units.la: Casu seipsum vulneravit,&c,] gladio sua sponte evagi-nato in femore graviter vulneratus occubuit. Iustinus lib.1.
units.tr: He wounded himself by accident, etc.] He fell, mortally wounded in the thigh, when his sword slipped from its scabbard of its own accord. Justin, book 1.

units.la: Magi duo fratres] Cometes & Oropastes. Idem.
units.tr: Two Magi, brothers] Cometes and Oropastes. The same source.

units.la: Menses septem] annum integrum Iosephus.
units.tr: Seven months] Josephus says a full year.

units.la: Septem nobilissimi Persæ] quorum nomina extant apud Herodotum libro 3. Sunt autem Otanes, Intaphernes, Gobrias, Megabyzus, Aspathines, Hydarnes, Darius Hystaspis, cujus pater Persis præerat.
units.tr: Seven most noble Persians] Their names are given by Herodotus, book 3. They are Otanes, Intaphernes, Gobryas, Megabyzus, Aspathines, Hydarnes, and Darius Hystaspis, whose father was governor of Persia.

units.la: Darius Hystaspis filius] sub hoc qui extrussum [?] putant templum Ierosolymitanum, falluntur. Non enim de hoc Dario intelligendi prophetæ, sed de alio, qui fuit inter duos Artaxarxes, quem Nothum appellitant. Res est, non conjectura.
units.tr: Darius, son of Hystaspes] Those who think that the Jerusalem temple was built under this Darius are mistaken. The prophet is not to be understood of this Darius, but of the other, who came between two Artaxerxes and is called Nothus. This is a matter of fact, not of conjecture.

units.la: Natus ex fratre patruele Cyri] pater Cyri erat Cambyses, Hystaspis Arsamenes. Ergo Cambyses et Arsamenes fratres erant, & horum filij fratres patrueles. Natu maximus filiorum Hystaspis Darius, occiso Pseudosmerdi, Persarum regnum e magorum manibus vindicavit, equeque sui hinnitu rex declaratus est.
units.tr: Born of Cyrus's paternal cousin] The father of Cyrus was Cambyses, and of Hystaspes Arsames. So Cambyses and Arsames were brothers, and their sons were first cousins. Darius, the eldest son of Hystaspes, after Pseudosmerdis was slain, rescued the Persian kingdom from the hands of the Magi, and was declared king by the neighing of his horse.

units.la: Quod Cyro in Scythiam expeditionem facienti longe ante revelatum fuerat in somnis. Vide Herodotum lib.1.
units.tr: This had been revealed to Cyrus in a dream long before, when he was about to make his expedition into Scythia. See Herodotus, book 1.

units.la: Apud Marathonem pugnavit] Herodotus lib.1. Thucydides 1.& 6 Iust 2,
units.tr: He fought at Marathon] Herodotus, book 1. Thucydides, books 1 and 6. Justin, book 2.

units.la: Sexagesimo] sexagesimo secundo. Functius.
units.tr: In the sixtieth [year]] In the sixty-second. Functius.

units.la: Macherino & Augurino consulibus] T. Geganio Macherino & P. Minutio Augurino: qui consules fuerunt, teste Livio, anno urbis CCLIX.
units.tr: In the consulship of Macherinus and Augurinus] Titus Geganius Macerinus and Publius Minucius Augurinus. They were consuls, according to Livy, in the year 259 from the founding of the city.

units.la: DCCC. LXXX. & VIII.] Scaliger addit biennium solidum. Nam a consulatu, inquit, Macerini & Augurini ad consulatum Stilliconis, anno Christi Dionysiano CCCC. indictione XIII anni sunt præcise DCCCXC.
units.tr: 888] Scaliger adds a full two years. For, he says, from the consulship of Macerinus and Augurinus to the consulship of Stilicho, in the year of Christ 400 according to the Dionysian reckoning, in the thirteenth indiction, there are precisely 890 years.

units.la: Omne tempus in Stiliconem consulem direxi] Fl. Stilicho consul fuit anno Christi 400. mundi vero, ut quidem e Sulpicio noster Gifelinus computat, 5869. vel potius 5819. imperante Honorio.
units.tr: I have reckoned all time down to the consul Stilicho] Flavius Stilicho was consul in the year of Christ 400. In the world, according to Sulpicius, our Gifelinus computes it as 5869, or rather 5819, under the reign of Honorius.

units.la: Pag 104. Xerxes] qui Asverus vocatur Ezræ 4.6. de sententia Scaligeri, quam firmat res ipsa. Nam post eum commemoratur Artoxerxes, cui Darius successit, sub quo templum ædificatum fuit.
units.tr: Page 104. Xerxes] who is called Ahasuerus in Ezra 4:6, according to Scaliger's view, which the facts themselves confirm. For after him is mentioned Artoxerxes, whom Darius succeeded, and under whom the temple was built.

units.la: Vno & viginti annis] perperam in Sigonio uno & triginta. Chronicon Eusebij, Persarum quintus Xerxes filius Darij ann. XX. Exemplaria, quæ vidi, nihil hodie variant. Videntur tamen olim variasse. Nam quæ sequuntur, quanquam in plerisque exemplaribus viginti & quinque annos imperij ejus fuisse reperi, de Eusebianis vulgo interpretantur. Quanquam fieri potest ut alia Chronica in mente habuerit. Vt ut fit, sunt qui Xerxi viginti octo annos imperij tribuant. Ceterum o-misit successorem Xerxis Artabanum, quia menses tantum se-ptem regnavit, qui menses in ordine annorum reputantur, ait Eusebius.
units.tr: Twenty-one years] Wrongly printed in Sigonius as thirty-one. In Eusebius's Chronicle, the fifth king of the Persians, Xerxes, son of Darius, reigned twenty years. The copies I have seen today show no variation, though they seem once to have varied. For although in most copies I have found that his reign lasted twenty-five years, which is commonly taken from the Eusebian text, it may be that he had other chronicles in mind. However that may be, some assign Xerxes twenty-eight years. Eusebius says that he omitted Xerxes' successor Artabanus, because he reigned only seven months, and such months are counted in the sequence of years.

units.la: Artaxerxes] qui & Artoxerxes, Ebraice autem Artbachsa-tha. Duo autem fuerunt hujus nominis, quorum prior, de quo hic sermo, μακρόχειρ[?], id est, Longimanus cognominabatur: posterior, qui Dario Notho successit μνήμων, id est, Memor, sive, ut Hiero interpretatur, Recordans. Vide quæ notavimus ad pag 102.
units.tr: Artaxerxes] also Artoxerxes; in Hebrew, Artachshatha. There were two of this name. The first, the one spoken of here, was surnamed Longimanus [μακρόχειρ]. The second, who succeeded Darius Nothus, was Memor [μνήμων], that is, Mindful, or, as Jerome explains, Recalling. See what we noted on page 102.

units.la: Cum inhiberi ædificationem] Ezræ 4.7.
units.tr: When the building was forbidden] Ezra 4:7.

units.la: Annos unum & quadraginta] in Eusebio quadraginta tantum.
units.tr: Forty-one years] In Eusebius only forty years.

units.la: Xerxes] alter sive secundus.
units.tr: Xerxes] the second, or younger.

units.la: Sucdianus] alibi Sogdianus, quod magis arridet. Hos duos reges plerique omittunt. Sane Thucydides statim a morte Artaxerxis Darium regnasse scribit.
units.tr: Sucdianus] elsewhere Sogdianus, which is the more usual form. Most writers omit these two kings. Certainly Thucydides writes that Darius reigned immediately after the death of Artaxerxes.

units.la: Septem mensibus] sic etiam Eusebius. Quanquam in exemplari quod Henricus Stephanus excudit, Sogdianus menses 8. Sequitur in eodem, sic per menses diversos his superioribus annus accrescit.
units.tr: Seven months] so also Eusebius. Yet in the copy printed by Henri Estienne, Sogdianus has eight months. In the same copy the years increase in this way through the various months above.

units.la: Darius deinde] cognomento Nothus. Eusebi.
units.tr: Darius then] surnamed Nothus. Eusebius.

units.la: Sub quo templum est restitutum] anno regni ejus altero, Cui Ochus tum nomen erat] Darius Ochus, ut Artaxerxes Ochus. Vox haec in lingua Persarum magnum significat. Quod notatum Ebraeis in Achaveros. Nam Ochos & Achas idem valent. Darius ergo Ochus, id est magnus. Sic Alexander magnus, Pompeius magnus, Carolus magnus. Omne enim magnificum magnum dicebant, ut mater magna, dij magni, rex magnus.
units.tr: Under whom the temple was restored] in the second year of his reign, when he was then called Ochus. Darius Ochus, as Artaxerxes Ochus. This word means "great" in the Persian language. This was noted by the Hebrews in the case of Ahasuerus, for Ochus and Achas have the same meaning. So Darius Ochus means great. Thus Alexander the Great, Pompey the Great, Charlemagne (Carolus Magnus). For they called everything magnificent "great", as in "great mother", "great gods", "great king".

units.la: Ex Ebraeis tres adolescentes] Zorobabel ex Ebraeis erat. Etiamne ceteri mihi nusquam id lectum, quod meminerim. Historia refertur, 3 Ezrae 3. & apud Iosephum lib. 11. c. 4. itemque in historia Ebraica sol.11. col.2.
units.tr: Three young men from the Hebrews] Zerubbabel was a Hebrew. I do not remember reading this anywhere else. The story is told in 3 Ezra 3, and in Josephus, book 11, chapter 4, and in the Hebrew history, sol. 11, col. 2.

units.la: Corporis custodes] σωματοφύλακες, οἱ φυλάσσοντες τὸ σῶ-μα τοῦ βασιλέως[?]: corporis custodes, qui custodiebant corpus regis, 3 Ezrae 3.3. שֹׁמְרֵי רֹאשׁ הַמֶּלֶךְ[?] capitis regij custodes, sive, qui custodiebant caput regis. Historia Ebraica.
units.tr: Bodyguards] σωματοφύλακες, those who guard the body of the king: bodyguards, who guarded the king's body, 3 Ezra 3:3. שֹׁמְרֵי רֹאשׁ הַמֶּלֶךְ the guardians of the king's head, or those who guarded the king's head. Hebrew history.

units.la: Unusque ex his] Zorobabel, qui eo loco erat apud hunc regem, quo Daniel fuerat apud alios: cujus elogium habetur in historia Ebraica. An vidistis in universa terra (verba sunt Darij ad principes suos) similem huic Zorobabelo, virum intelligentem & sapientem, spiritu Danielis praeditum, &c? Ad hunc locum Sigonius annotat, Videndum est autem Sal-picio, num recte Zorobabel dici adolescens, regnante Dario secundo possit, qui centum amplius annos ipso supputante haberet. Scire licet duos Zorobabeles fuisse. Quod observatum Galatino de arcanis catholicae veritatis lib. 7. cap. 12. Vide si placet. Ut ut sit, Zorobabel hic egit cum Dario secundo, & non cum primo. Liquet ex eo quod Darius, sub quo vixit, inter duos Artaxerxes ponatur. Quis autem ille nisi Darius secundus?
units.tr: Each one of these] Zerubbabel, who was at that king's court where Daniel had been at the courts of others. His praise is recorded in the Hebrew history. "Have you seen in the whole land" (these are Darius's words to his nobles) "anyone like this Zerubbabel, a man of understanding and wisdom, endowed with the spirit of Daniel," etc.? On this passage Sigonius remarks: But it must be examined by Salpicius whether Zerubbabel can rightly be called a young man under the reign of Darius the Second, when, by his own reckoning, he would have been more than a hundred years old. It is well known that there were two Zerubbabels. This was observed by Galatinus, On the Secrets of Catholic Truth, book 7, chapter 12. See it if you like. However that may be, this Zerubbabel dealt with Darius the Second and not the first. This is clear from the fact that Darius, under whom he lived, is placed between two Artaxerxes. And who else could that be but Darius the Second?

units.la: Prudentiae documento] nam cum quaestio mota esset, Quae-nam res majores vires haberet, & unus dixisset vinum, alter regem: Zorobabel tertius intulit mulierem, & supra omnia veritatem: cujus prudentiam rex admiratus, dedit ei optionem petendi quod vellet.
units.tr: A proof of wisdom] For when a question had been raised, which thing had the greatest strength, and one man said wine, another the king, Zerubbabel, the third, put forward women, and above all things truth. The king, admiring his wisdom, gave him the choice of asking for whatever he wished.

units.la: Copiam restituendæ urbis] id est, licentiam, facultatem. Inferius pag.106. daret sibi eundi & restituendæ ejus potestatem.
units.tr: The opportunity of restoring the city] that is, permission, the power. Below, page 106. that he might give him leave to go and the authority to restore it.

units.la: Restitutendæ urbis] & ædificandi templi. Nam utrumque rex voverat, 3 Ezrae 4.43 & 44. Quadrennio] nam anno secundo Darij cœptum, sexto demum consummatum fuit, 3. Ezræ 6.2 et 7.5.
units.tr: "Of restoring the city": and of building the temple. For the king had vowed both (3 Esdras 4.43 and 44). "Four years": it was begun in the second year of Darius and only finished in the sixth, (3 Esdras 6.2 and 7.5).

units.la: Eldras] qui Ebraeis Ezra. Ezra Ezras, ut Iuda Iudas. Hoc primum; deinde ζ in f d mutavit, more Dorico. Dores enim certe ευχιτδα[?] dicunt pro ευχιζω.
units.tr: Eldras: who is called Ezra by the Hebrews. Ezra becomes Ezras, as Iuda becomes Iudas. This is the first change; then he changed the ζ into d, in the Doric manner. For the Dorians certainly say ευχιτδα [?] for ευχιζω.

units.la: Scriba legis] legisperitus: etiam sacerdos erat.
units.tr: Scribe of the law: a learned man in the law; he was also a priest.

units.la: Post viginti fere annos] redundat fere, ut sæpe in hoc libro. Nam anno sexto Darij consummatum fuit templum.
units.tr: Some twenty years later: "nearly" is superfluous, as often in this book. For the temple was finished in the sixth year of Darius.

units.la: Ab eo tempore Darius vixit ann. 13. Septimo autem Artaxarxis Mnemonis Ezras Babylonia profectus est. Ecce viginti anni solidi. Nam 13. & 7. faciunt 20. Esdras ipse a Iudæis perlibetur fuisse admodum sanctus et mansuetus: unde ob morum similitudinem Hellel vocatur discipulus ipsius Ezræ. Sunt etiam qui Malachiam prophetam eundem faciunt cum Ezra; de quo alias.
units.tr: From that time Darius lived thirteen years. In the seventh year of Artaxerxes Mnemon, Ezra set out from Babylon. See, twenty full years, for thirteen and seven make twenty. The Jews hold that Ezra himself was very holy and gentle; hence, because of the similarity of their characters, Hellel is called the disciple of Ezra. There are also those who make the prophet Malachi the same man as Ezra; more on this elsewhere.

units.la: Vnum de viginti annis] fictitiam Eusebius & alij
units.tr: The one year out of the twenty: Eusebius and others regard it as fictitious.

units.la: Artaxarxis secundi] qui Mnemon sive Memor cognominatur. Hæc acciderunt anno regni ejus septimo. Ezræ 7.7.
units.tr: Of Artaxerxes the Second, who is surnamed Mnemon or Memor. These things happened in the seventh year of his reign (Ezra 7.7).

units.la: Multitudine eum secuti] vulgo, multisque eum secutis: quæ lectio si recipitur, scribendum cum Galesinio, Hierosolymam pervenit.
units.tr: "Following him in a multitude": the common reading is "and many following him." If that reading is accepted, one should write with Galesinus, "he came to Jerusalem."

units.la: Cum duodecim levitis] Ezræ 8.24.
units.tr: With twelve Levites (Ezra 8.24).

units.la: Gentilium] gentium terræ Chanaan: item Ammonitarum, Moabitarum & Ægyptiorum, 1. Ezræ 9.1.
units.tr: Of the Gentiles: of the peoples of the land of Canaan; likewise of the Ammonites, Moabites and Egyptians (1 Ezra 9.1).

units.la: Veteris legis ritum agebat] lex quæ vetat ducere uxores alienigenas habetur, Exod. 34.16.
units.tr: He was observing the rite of the old law: the law forbidding marriage with foreign wives is found at Exod. 34.16.

units.la: Ceterum Esdram nihil super reficienda urbe egisse comperio] nam ea cura Nehemiæ fuit. Unde dicitant, Zorobabel templum extruxit: Ezras disciplinam reformavit: Nehemias urbem restituit.
units.tr: But I find that Ezra did nothing about rebuilding the city, for that concern belonged to Nehemiah. Hence they say: Zerubbabel built the temple, Ezra reformed the discipline, and Nehemiah restored the city.

units.la: Erat ea tempestate] anno vigesimo regni Artaxarxis secundi.
units.tr: At that time: in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the Second.

units.la: Nechemias] inferenda aspiratio ut sit Nehemias. Huic pater erat Hachalias, & cognomentum Hatharsatha.
units.tr: Nechemias: an aspirate should be inserted so that it reads Nehemias. His father was Hachaliah, and his surname was Hatharsatha.

units.la: Minister regius] minister vinarius, Chronicon Eusebij, הַמַּשְׁקֶה[?] pincerna sive pocillator regis, Nehem. 1.11.
units.tr: Royal minister: cupbearer (the wine-steward), as in Eusebius's Chronicle; [הַמַּשְׁקֶה] the cupbearer or taster of the king, Neh. 1.11.

units.la: Apud Babylonian] imo apud Susas. Nam diserte Nehem. 1.1. ego eram in Susan Habbira: quod reddi potest, Susis in arce vel castro. Quamquam sunt qui malunt, in metropoli.
units.tr: In Babylon: indeed, rather in Susa. For Neh. 1.1 plainly says, "I was in Susa the palace" [Susan Habbira], which may be rendered "at Susa, in the citadel or fortress." Some, however, prefer "in the capital city."

units.la: Pag.106. Iudæos] Ἰουδαῖος[?], id est, Iudæos. Sic Græci LXX. Sed & pleraque Latina exemplaria habent, viri Iudaei licet in aliis sit, ut etiam in fonte Ebræo, ex Iuda. Quæ lectio ambiguitatem habet. Nam potest sensus esse, viri ex Iuda, id est, Iudæi: vel, venit Hanani & viri (alij cum eo) ex Iuda, id est, Iudæa.
units.tr: Page 106. Jews: [Ἰουδαῖος], that is, Jews. So the Greeks of the Seventy. But most Latin copies read "men of Judah" (viri Iudaei), though in some it is as it is in the Hebrew source, "from Judah." This reading is ambiguous. For the sense can be "men from Judah, that is, Jews," or "Hanani came, and men (others with him) from Judah, that is, from Judea."

units.la: Paternæ urbis] id est, patriæ. Aut paternæ quoniam a patribus habitata, hoc est a majoribus ejus. Sic traditio paterna, quæ a majoribus tradita. Nam hos patres Ebræi vocant.
units.tr: Of the city of his fathers: that is, of his country. Or "of the fathers," because it was inhabited by the fathers, that is, by his ancestors. So "paternal tradition" is tradition handed down by the ancestors, for the Hebrews call these the fathers.

units.la: Patriam] Ierosolymam.
units.tr: His country: Jerusalem.

units.la: Inter epulas] quum ei vinum funderet.
units.tr: During the feast: when he was pouring wine for him.

units.la: Extra solitum] præter solitum. Sic Terent. extra unam ancillulam.
units.tr: Beyond what was usual: contrary to custom. So Terence: "except for one little maidservant."

units.la: Per annos fere ducentos & quinquaginta] Sigonius emendat, & sexaginta. Nam anni erant, inquit, præcise, ducenti & quinquaginta octo. Ideo adjectum fere. Mendum, ut credibile est, e notis numerorum.
units.tr: For nearly two hundred and fifty years: Sigonius emends this to "and sixty," for he says the years were exactly two hundred and fifty-eight. Hence "nearly" was added. The error, as is credible, arose from the numeral notation.

units.la: Potestatem] copiam pag 104. Alius diceret, licentiam, facultatem.
units.tr: Authority: opportunity, see p. 104. Another would say licence, permission.

units.la: Cum præsidio equitum] Nehem.2.9.
units.tr: With an escort of horsemen (Neh. 2.9).

units.la: Quo tutius iter ageret] agere iter phrasis est minus usitata: tamen Sulpicius utitur etiam dialog.1.segm.4. iter cum eo, dum dioeceses visitat, agebamus. Nec Ovidius de arte lib.2. eam abhorruit.
units.tr: That he might travel more safely: "to make a journey" (agere iter) is a rather uncommon phrase, yet Sulpicius uses it too, in Dialogue 1, section 4: "we were travelling with him while he visited the dioceses." Nor did Ovid shrink from it in the second book of the Art of Love.

units.la: Ad prætores] subreguli & præsides vocantur, pag 104.
units.tr: To the governors: they are called petty kings and presidents, p. 104.

units.la: Gentium] Arabum, Ammonitarum, Samaritanorum & Azotiorum.
units.tr: Of the nations: of the Arabs, Ammonites, Samaritans and Ashdodites.

units.la: Conspirant opera interrumpere] Sic lib.1. in bellum conspirant Ebræos armis depellere; & alibi, conspirant; subvertere. Vide Gijelinum.
units.tr: They conspire to hinder the work: so in book 1, "they conspire to drive the Hebrews away by arms," and elsewhere "they conspire to overthrow." See Gijelinus.

units.la: Pag.107, Cœpta explicuit] ut lib.1. opus vigesimo anno explicuit, id est, absolvit. Vide quæ scripsimus ad illum locum.
units.tr: Page 107. He finished what he had begun: as in book 1, "he finished the work in the twentieth year," that is, completed it. See what we have written on that passage.

units.la: Consummatoque] excidit vox, quam Sigonius supplet, consummatoque muro, historia id mirabiliter comprobante.
units.tr: And when it was completed: a word has dropped out, which Sigonius supplies as "and when the wall was completed," the history wonderfully confirming this.

units.la: Ad quinquaginta millia] numerus civium erat 42360. Servorum & ancillarum 7337. Cantorum & cantatricum 245. Summa 49937. Eorum autem qui Nehemiæ septimo expresse numerati sunt summa est 31389.
units.tr: Nearly fifty thousand: the number of citizens was 42,360; of male and female servants 7,337; of singers, men and women, 245. Total 49,937. Of those expressly numbered in the seventh chapter of Nehemiah, however, the sum is 31,389.

units.la: Immani numero] id est, magno, ingenti. Sic Varro in 3. de rerustica, immanis numerus annorum.
units.tr: In vast number: that is, great, immense. So Varro in the third book of De re rustica: "an immense number of years."

units.la: Hæ duæ tribus] Iuda & Benjamin. Adde sis tribum Levi, quæ hoc residuo etiam continetur. Nam una cum duabus abdu-cta[?], cum ijsdem postliminio rediit in terram patriam.
units.tr: These two tribes: Judah and Benjamin. Add, if you like, the tribe of Levi, which is also included in this remnant, for it was led away along with the other two and returned with them by postliminy to the homeland.

units.la: CCC & XX.] Sigonius e libris regum contrahit hunc numerum ad CLXXX. Verone an falso alias examinabimus. Nunc ad alia properamus.
units.tr: 320: Sigonius, from the books of Kings, reduces this number to 180. Whether rightly or wrongly we shall examine elsewhere; now we hasten on to other matters.

units.la: Per Parthos, Medos, Indos atque Æthiopas] omisit Af-syrios[?]. Indorum atque Æthiopum nulla mentio in sacris litteris. Vide 4. Reg. 17.6. & 18.10. item 1. Paralip. 5. 26. In his mentio Colchorum & Iberiæ fluviisque Gozan & urbium Mediæ. Parthos autem videtur Persas dicere. Iosephus Orig. lib. 9. cap. 14. Salmanasar populum traduxit in Mediam & Persidem.
units.tr: Through the Parthians, Medes, Indians and Ethiopians: he omitted the Assyrians. There is no mention of Indians or Ethiopians in Holy Scripture. See 4 Reg. 17.6 and 18.10, and likewise 1 Paralip. 5.26. In these passages there is mention of the Colchians and Iberia, the rivers of Gozan, and the cities of Media. But he seems to mean the Persians by "Parthians." Josephus, Antiquities book 9, chapter 14: Shalmaneser transferred the people into Media and Persia.

units.la: Sane Persas Hesychius Parthos appellat, propter horum populorum vicinitatem. Sic bellum Persicum, in quo Iulianus occubuit, Ammianus procinctum Parthicum vocat, pauloque post scribit Iulianum tradidisse Procopio propinquo suo paludamentum purpureum, mandasseque arripere fidentius principatum, si se interiisse didicisset apud Parthos, cum tamen de Persis proprie loquatur.
units.tr: Indeed, Hesychius calls the Persians Parthians, on account of the nearness of these peoples. So Ammianus calls the Persian war in which Julian fell the Parthian campaign, and shortly after he writes that Julian handed his purple cloak to his kinsman Procopius and bade him seize the sovereignty more boldly if he should learn that Julian had perished among the Parthians, although he is properly speaking of the Persians.

units.la: XXX & II.] legendum XXXII. deleta computante. Hic numerus extat Nehem. 5. 14. qui est in libris nostris secundus Esdræ. Unde medicinam facies Eusebio, in quo Nehemiam, qui muros Ierusalem construxerat, confummasse opus tricesimo anno Artaxerxis regis Esdras memorat. Nam & in alia editione trigesimo primo, et tollit omnem omnino dubitationem ipse Eusebius in eodem loco, cum ait, Nehemias Hebræus [?]nister vinarius Artaxerxis regis Persarum, vicesimo e-s[?] anno de Babylone venit in Iudæam, & tricesimo se-cundo anno muros urbemque restituit.
units.tr: Thirty-two: read XXXII, the reckoning having been struck out. This number occurs at Neh. 5.14, which in our books is the second book of Esdras. Hence you may find a remedy for Eusebius, in whom Ezra records that Nehemiah, who had built the walls of Jerusalem, completed the work in the thirtieth year of King Artaxerxes. For in another edition it is the thirty-first, and Eusebius himself removes all doubt in the same place, when he says: "Nehemiah the Hebrew, cupbearer of Artaxerxes king of the Persians, came from Babylon into Judea in the twentieth year, and in the thirty-second year restored the walls and the city."

units.la: Fusium & Rubellium consules] C. Fufius Geminus & C. Rubellius Geminus consulatum gesserunt anno urbis 781 ut Funcius, aut 782. ut Sigonius, Christus autem passus est anno 784. teste eodem Funcio. Sed Chronologi hac in re variant. Vide Sigonium.
units.tr: Fufius and Rubellius, consuls: Gaius Fufius Geminus and Gaius Rubellius Geminus held the consulship in the year of the city 781, according to Funck, or 782 according to Sigonius; but Christ suffered in the year 784, on the testimony of the same Funck. But the chronologers differ on this point. See Sigonius.

units.la: CCC XCVIII.] hic annus incidit in annum urbis CCC LXXVIII. Vide, si placet, Sigonium.
units.tr: 398: this year falls in the year of the city 378. See Sigonius, if you like.

units.la: A restitutione templi] quæ fuit anno Darij sexto, ut diximus. Quamvis Iosephus eam factam scribat anno Xerxis vi-gesimo gesimo octavo, mense nono. Orig. Iudaic. lib.11. cap.5.
units.tr: From the restoration of the temple: which was in the sixth year of Darius, as we said, although Josephus writes that it was done in the twenty-eighth year of Xerxes, in the ninth month. Antiquities of the Jews, book 11, chapter 5.

units.la: Pag.108. Consule Augusto] Fl. Vespasiano Augusto. Hic erat annus imperij ejus secundus.
units.tr: Page 108. In the consulship of Augustus: Flavius Vespasian Augustus. This was the second year of his reign.

units.la: LX & IX. hebdomadas] quae faciunt annos praedictos: quibus si septem addideris, erunt hebdomadae LXX. Eusebius in Nehemia, Si quis autem ab hoc tempore (quo videlicet Ierusalem constructa fuit) LXX hebdomadas a Daniele[?] scriptas numeret, quae faciunt annos CCCXC reperiet eas in regno Herodis expletas: sub quo obsideri Ierusalem coepta secundo postea Vespasiani anno capitur. Et in Herode, Ab instauratione templi sub Dario usque ad Hyrcanum & centesimam octogesimam sextam Olympiadem, annis CCCCLXXXIII in medio transactis, quos Daniel quoque significat, dicens: & scies & intelliges ab initio sermonis restaurandi et aedificandi Ierusalem, usque ad Christi principatum hebdomades septem et hebdomades sexaginta duo, quae hebdomades LXIX faciunt annos CCCC LXXXIII. Vide sequentia.
units.tr: Sixty-nine weeks: these make the aforesaid years; if you add seven to them, there will be seventy weeks. Eusebius, in his work on Nehemiah: "If anyone counts the seventy weeks written by Daniel from this time (namely, when Jerusalem was built), he will find that they make 390 years, and that they were completed in the reign of Herod, under whom the siege of Jerusalem began, and it was taken in the second year of Vespasian afterwards." And in his work on Herod: "From the restoration of the temple under Darius to Hyrcanus and the 186th Olympiad, with 483 years intervening, which Daniel also indicates, saying: 'Know therefore and understand, that from the going forth of the word to restore and build Jerusalem unto Christ the Prince shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; the weeks, sixty-nine, make 483 years.'" See what follows.

units.la: A die autem captivitatis, etc.] ab anno undecimo Sedeciae regis Iuda usque ad annum XXXII Artarxerxis Memoris. Scire licet Sulpicium ab anno illo undecimo Sedeciae numerare annos LXX. quibus Iudaei fuerunt in captivitate Babylonica usque ad annum primum Cyri regis Persarum. Alij aliter numerant annos illos.
units.tr: But from the day of the captivity, etc.: from the eleventh year of Zedekiah king of Judah to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes Memor. You may know that Sulpicius counts the seventy years from that eleventh year of Zedekiah, during which the Jews were in Babylonian captivity, until the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians. Others count those years differently.

units.la: Hoc temporum tractu Esther atque Iudith fuisse arbitramur] falleris. Nam Esther fuit sub Asvero. Quis autem Asverus nisi Xerxes? cuius uxor Amestris vocatur in historia Herodoti. Utraque vox Persica est. Nam Ebraicum nomen erat Hadassa, quo vocabatur antequam in aulam regis assumpta esset. Amestris quasi [illegible, ~7 letters] De Iudith major dubitatio est. Sunt qui eam vixisse putant sub principatu Manasse: quod mihi non fit verisimile. Nam tempore huius regis Iudaei Babylonis satis noti erant: tempore Iudith non item. Colligo ex iis verbis quae habentur Iud 5.20. Adhaec sub Iudith templum destructum fuisse doceo ex 5. 10. secundum editionem Complutensem. Ait enim ibi Achior, [illegible, ~20 letters] Iuditha honorificam mentionem facit Clemens Stromat lib. 4. ejus historiam confictam esse arbitratur Beroaldus Chronologiae suae lib. 1. cap.4. Dubitatum de ea olim fuisse paret ex verbis Hiero. Hag. 1. sicut et in Iudith (si quis tamen vult librum recipere mulie-ris) et parvuli siti[?] perierunt. Vide sis Augustinum de civit. Dei / 8.26.
units.tr: We think Esther and Judith lived in this period.] You are mistaken. For Esther lived under Ahasuerus. Who is Ahasuerus but Xerxes, whose wife is called Amestris in the history of Herodotus? Both words are Persian. Her Hebrew name was Hadassah, by which she was called before she was taken into the king's court. Amestris, as it were [illegible] As for Judith, there is a greater doubt. Some think she lived under the reign of Manasseh, which does not seem probable to me. For in the time of this king the Jews were well known to Babylon; in Judith's time they were not. I gather this from the words in Judith 5:20. Moreover I show from Judith 5:10, according to the Complutensian edition, that the temple was destroyed under Judith. For Achior says there, [illegible] Clement in Stromateis book 4 makes honourable mention of Judith. Beroaldus, in book 1, chapter 4 of his Chronology, thinks her history is fabricated. That there was doubt about her once is clear from the words of Jerome on Haggai 1: Hiero. Hag. 1. "as also in Judith (if anyone nevertheless wishes to receive the book of a woman) and little ones perished of thirst." See Augustine, City of God, 8.26.

units.la: Hesther] scribendum leniter Esther. Nam est Aleph in scrip-ptura Ebraica, cujus litera vim exprimit spiritus lenis apud Græcos. Similiter peccatum ab antiquis in Habraam, Helias & similibus.
units.tr: Hesther] It should be written lightly: Esther. For there is an aleph in the Hebrew text, whose letter expresses the breathing which the Greeks call smooth. Similarly the ancients wrote Habraam, Helias and similar forms.

units.la: Iudith] nomen mulieris, Gen.26.34. & est contractum pro Iehuduth. Significat etiam in genere Iudæam fœminam, a mas-culino יְהוּדִי[?] Iudæus. Similis contractio in Iuda, quod textus semper scribit יְהוּדָה[?] Iehuda. Nota ut alias.
units.tr: Iudith] a woman's name, Gen. 26:34, and it is contracted from Jehudith. It also means, in general, a Jewish woman, from the masculine Jehudi, Jew. A similar contraction occurs in Judah, which the text always writes as Jehudah. Note as elsewhere.

units.la: Quarum quidem actus ]supra lib. 1. pag. 3. Apostolorum-que actus. Nunc acta potius dicimus, id est, πράξεις.
units.tr: Quarum quidem actus] see above, book 1, p. 3. And the Acts of the Apostles. Now we rather say acts, that is, praxeis [πράξεις].

units.la: Sub Artaxerxe] Sic Græci Asverum appellant. Nec aliter Iosephus. Alij melius Asverum Xerxem esse conjiciunt.
units.tr: Under Artaxerxes] Thus the Greeks call Ahasuerus. Josephus does the same. Others more plausibly conjecture that Ahasuerus is Xerxes.

units.la: Duos hujus nominis Persarum reges fuisse reperi] prior μακρόχειρ dictus est, quod manum dexteram haberet altera longiorem: posterior Mnemon, id est, Memor, ut antea monuimus. Hic prius Arsicas nominabatur, cujus vitam descripsit Plutarchus. Præter hos Ochus etiam appellatus fuit Artoxerxes. Vide sis Ælianum, itemque Diodorum in extremo libri decimi quinti.
units.tr: I have found that there were two Persian kings of this name. The first was called Longimanus, because one of his hands was longer than the other. The second was Mnemon, that is, Memor, as we noted earlier. The first was formerly called Arsicas, and his life was described by Plutarch. Besides these, Ochus was also called Artoxerxes. See Aelian, and likewise Diodorus at the end of book 15.

units.la: Quæ ante fuit verisimilis, etc.] hunc locum perspicue cor-ruptum ita restituit doctissimus Sigonius, quia haud fuit veri-simile, si sub priore Artaxerxe fuisset, qui ejus tempora complexus est, nullam tam illustris fœminæ mentionem retulisse. Gisselinus accedit propius ad vulgatam lectionem, quia haud fuit verisimile, ut, si sub priore Artaxerxe suis-set, qui hujus tempora complexus est, nullam tam illustris fœminæ mentionem retulisset.
units.tr: "Which earlier was probable," etc.] The learned Sigonius restored this evidently corrupted passage thus: "since it was not likely that, if it had been under the earlier Artaxerxes, who spanned her times, he would have recorded no mention of so illustrious a woman." Gisselinus comes closer to the common reading: "since it was not likely that, if it had been under the earlier Artaxerxes, who spanned her times, he would have recorded no mention of so illustrious a woman."

units.la: Qui ejus tempora complexus est] Ezram intelligit.
units.tr: Who spanned his times] He means Ezra.

units.la: Vastis quædam ] Vasti, Vastis, ut Tobi, Tobit: Levi, Levis, id est λευις[?] Sed melius hoc nomen scribitur Vasthis, cum t, aspirato. Ebraice enim est וַשְׁתִּי[?] Vasthi.
units.tr: Vastis some] Vasti, Vastis, as Tobi, Tobit; Levi, Levis, that is, Levis [λευις]. But this name is better written Vasthis, with an aspirated t, for in Hebrew it is Vashti.

units.la: Die quodam ]anno tertio imperij sui.
units.tr: On a certain day] In the third year of his reign.

units.la: Publicum convivium] hoc convivium dabat cum appa-raret expeditionem in Græciam: eoque proceres suos excipit, Esther 1.
units.tr: Public banquet] He gave this banquet when he was preparing the expedition against Greece, and there he received his nobles, Esther 1.

units.la: Pudens virorum oculis, etc.] aliam causam allegat Iose-phus cum ait hoc vetare leges Persarum. Patruele fratre]errat Sigonius exi-stimans Mardochæum fuisse patruum Esthera cum fuerit filia patrui ejus, id est [?]Θυγα-τὴρ ἀδελφῆς παιδὸς αὐτῆς [?]. Unde suspicio mihi legendum in editione nostra Latina, filiam fratris patris sui: ubi vulgo, filiam fratrisfui, Esth. 2, 7. Ceterum patruelem fratrem dicit imitatione Ciceronis, qui sic locutus est in quinto de finibus, fratèr noster cognatione patruelis, amore germanus.
units.tr: Modest in the eyes of men, etc.] Josephus gives another reason, saying that the laws of Persia forbade this. Paternal cousin] Sigonius is wrong to think Mordecai was Esther's paternal uncle, when she was the daughter of his brother, that is, [θυγατὴρ ἀδελφῆς παιδὸς αὐτῆς]. Hence I suspect that in our Latin edition we should read "filiam fratris patris sui" (daughter of her father's brother), where the common text has "filiam fratris sui", Esth. 2:7. Moreover, he calls him patruelis frater in imitation of Cicero, who spoke thus in the fifth book of De finibus: "our brother by cousinship, a full brother in love."

units.la: Regales nuptias] Sic pag. 98. regales usus &, regale covivium, id est rege dignum. Pratulerim tamen, regias nuptias.
units.tr: Royal weddings. So on p. 98 he has "regales usus" and "regale convivium", that is, worthy of a king. I would prefer, however, "regias nuptias".

units.la: Paternarum traditionum] quas a patribus, id est, majoribus acceperat. Græci eas vocant [?]παλ[?]ιοπαραδότας ἱστολὰς [?]. Vide quæ scripsimus ad pag. 89.
units.tr: Paternal traditions] which they had received from their fathers, that is, from their ancestors. The Greeks call them [παλαιοπαραδότας ἱστορίας]. See what we wrote at p. 89.

units.la: Gentilium cibis participaret] quære unde habeat. Gentiles autem dicit gentes, ut antea notatum Sic in vita Martini, segm. X gentilium turba: & segm. XVI Profani ac gentilis domum adire posse: & alibi, parentibus secundum seculi dignitatem non infimis, gentilibus tamen. Hinc gentilitas, gentium religio. Ibid. seg. 3. Matrem gentilitatis absolvit error: & paullo ante, parentesque, quos adhuc gentilitas detinebat: & segm. XVI. Nam Tetradius eodem tempore adhuc gentilitatis errore implicitus tenebatur. Alius paganissimum diceret.
units.tr: Should share in the food of the Gentiles.] Inquire where he got this. He calls the nations "gentes", as noted before. So in the Life of Martin, section 10, "a crowd of gentiles"; section 16, "that a profane and gentile man could enter the house"; and elsewhere, "parents not of humble station according to worldly rank, yet gentiles." Hence "gentility", the religion of the nations. Ibid., section 3: "the error of gentility freed the mother"; a little before, "and the parents whom gentility still held"; section 16: "for Tetradius at that same time was still held entangled in the error of gentility." Another would say "most pagan".

units.la: [?]iuncta[?] regi] connubio scilicet.
units.tr: [Joined] to the king.] Namely by marriage.

units.la: Veste purpurea] diademate Esther 1. 17. ubi [?]τὸ διάδημα τὸ γυναικεῖον appellatur Josephus quoque διάδημα vocat Antiquit. lib. 1. cap. 6. & Esther in sua ad Deum precatione [?]σημεῖον τῆς ἐπιφανείας μου, ὅ εἰσι ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς μου[?]. Vide Brisso-nium de regno Persarum, pag. 76.
units.tr: Purple robe.] A diadem, Esther 1:17, where it is called the women's diadem [τὸ διάδημα τὸ γυναικεῖον]. Josephus also calls it a diadem, Antiquities book 1, chapter 6; and Esther, in her prayer to God, calls it [σημεῖον τῆς ἐπιφανείας μου, ὅ εἰσι ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς μου], "the sign of my splendour, which is upon my head." See Brissonius, on the kingdom of Persia, p. 76.

units.la: (inter proximos regis erat] inter amicos regis necessarios, Josephus. Neutrum habetur in historia Ebraica. Quærendum ergo unde hauserint.
units.tr: (He was among the king's intimates.) Among the king's close friends, says Josephus. Neither is found in the Hebrew history. We must therefore inquire where they drew it from.

units.la: Pro virili portione negotiorum familiarum curator] expressit verbum Græcum [?]ἐπιστάτην[?] Esther 2.11 quod inter alia curare significat. Interpres Latinus editionis Romanæ vertit, serviebat. Vsurpatur de liberali obsequio quo quis alium demeretur. Sed eo loco veritas Ebraica habet, sedebat in porta regis, id est, morabatur, manebat. Nam Persarum optimates & proceres regum limina terebant, et quotidie in porta versabantur, quam nunc aulam vocant. Vnde aulici omnes generali [?]τῶν ἐπὶ[?]
units.tr: Curator of the family's affairs according to his share.] He has rendered the Greek word [ἐπιστάτην], Esther 2:11, which among other things means "to take care of". The Latin interpreter of the Roman edition translates it "served". It is used of the courteous service by which someone wins another's favour. But in that place the Hebrew text has "sat in the king's gate", that is, dwelt, remained. For the Persian nobles and grandees wore out the king's thresholds and were daily in the gate, which they now call the court. Whence all courtiers are generally called [τῶν ἐπὶ ...]

units.la: Εὐνοῦχοι βασιλέως [?] nomine nuncupantur. Quod à Cyro constitutum olim fuisse annotat vir sane peraccuratus Barnabas Brissonius de regno Persarum lib. 1. pag. 20. Vide, si tibi otium.
units.tr: [Eunuchs of the king] are called by this name. Brissonius, a most accurate man, notes that this was instituted by Cyrus. See De regno Persarum, book 1, p. 20. See it, if you have the leisure.

units.la: A duobus spadonibus] Bagathan & Tharès eunuchis, custodibus liminis, vel, ut alij, supellectilis. Quanquam in editione Græca ἀρχισωματοφύλακες [?], id est, principes eorum qui corpus regis custodiebant. Vetus interpres, quem vulgatum indigetant, Qui janitores erant, & in primo palatij limine præsidebant.
units.tr: Two eunuchs] Bagathan and Tharas, eunuchs, guards of the threshold, or, as others say, of the furniture. Though in the Greek edition they are called [ἀρχισωματοφύλακες], that is, the chiefs of those who guarded the king's body. The old interpreter, whom they call the Vulgate, has "who were doorkeepers and presided at the first threshold of the palace."

units.la: Insidias prodiderat] quas Barnobazus Iudæus alterius eunuchi servus domesticus ei patefecerat. Iosephus.
units.tr: Had betrayed the plot] which Barnabazus, a Jew, the household servant of the other eunuch, had disclosed to him. Josephus.

units.la: Pag.110. Summisque honoribus donatus] falsum. Nam Esth. 6. 3. Quid factum est honoris Mardochæo? & dixerunt pueri ejus ministri ejus, Non est factum cum eo quicquam. Vide quæ notavimus olim ad hunc locum.
units.tr: p. 110. And honoured with the highest honours] False. For Esther 6:3 says, "What honour has been done to Mordecai?" And his young servants, his ministers, said, "Nothing has been done for him." See what we noted long ago on this passage.

units.la: Haman quidam] Hamadathi filius, Agagæus.
units.tr: Haman a certain] son of Hammedatha, the Agagite.

units.la: Adorari] quod Græci προσκυνεῖν [?], Latini etiam venerari dicunt. Id qui faciebat, corpus totum in terram prosternebat, sicut mento quandoque solum contingeret
units.tr: To be worshipped] which the Greeks call [προσκυνεῖν], and the Latins also call venerari. Whoever did this prostrated his whole body on the ground, so that sometimes his chin alone touched the earth.

units.la: More regum] Persarum. Iustinus lib. 6. Conon a regis conspectu & colloquio prohibitus est, quod eum more Persarum adorare nollet. Lampridius in Alexandro Severo, Adorari se vetuit regum more Persarum.
units.tr: After the manner of kings] of the Persians. Justin, book 6: Conon was barred from the king's sight and conversation because he refused to adore him in the Persian manner. Lampridius, in the life of Alexander Severus: he forbade himself to be adored in the manner of the Persian kings.

units.la: Odia Persæ] Persam vocat, quem Additiones apocryphae Ma-cedonem: alij Amalecitam fuisse tradunt, ut qui genus duxerit ab Agag, quondam Amalecitarum rege. Sic fere Hebræi. Sed & Iosephus lib. 11. cap. 6.
units.tr: The Persian hatred] He calls him a Persian, whom the apocryphal Additions call a Macedonian. Others say he was an Amalekite, as one descended from Agag, once king of the Amalekites. Roughly so the Hebrews. But see also Josephus, book 11, chapter 6.

units.la: Ad perniciem Hebræi] Mardochæi, atque adeo Ebræorum omnium. Nam parum esse ratus uni manum adferre, conatus est omnes Ebræos, quotquot erant in toto Asveri regno, perdere. Id evincunt consequa verba.
units.tr: To the destruction of the Hebrews] of Mordecai, and indeed of all the Hebrews. For thinking it too little to lay hands on one man, he tried to destroy all the Hebrews, as many as there were in the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus. The words that follow prove this.

units.la: Hominum genus] Iudæos intelligit, quos Mardochæi populares esse dicerat.
units.tr: Race of men] He means the Jews, whom he had said were Mordecai's compatriots.

units.la: Externis legibus utens] imo propriis, quæ tamen externæ Persis aliisque gentibus erant.
units.tr: Using foreign laws] Indeed, their own, which nonetheless were foreign to the Persians and the other nations.

units.la: Per omne regnum] per centum viginti septem provincias, quæ illo tempore Persæ parebant.
units.tr: Throughout the whole kingdom] through the hundred and twenty-seven provinces that at that time obeyed the Persians.

units.la: Pag.111. Reginæ introire ad regem, nisi accersitæ, non licet] imo nulli viro aut fœminæ. Puellæ autem virgines admit-tebantur. tebantur per vices. Quod autem in Sulpicio, nec tamen cum fuerit regi libitum, sed statuto tempore admittitur, addi-tum videtur ex ingenio ejus. Dubito etiam an cum fide historiæ conveniat.
units.tr: They were admitted in turn. What is said in Sulpicius "nor yet when it pleased the king," but at an appointed time they are admitted, seems to have been added from his own disposition. I also doubt whether it agrees with the faithfulness of the history.

units.la: Separata a conspectu regis haberetur] non vocata a rege esset. Esth.4.11.
units.tr: That is, unless she were called by the king. Esth. 4:11.

units.la: Aulam regis] atrium interius, quod in aula, quæ in hac hi-storia non semel porta vocatur. Sic imperatores Turcarum hodieque suam aulam appellant.
units.tr: The inner court, which in this history is more than once called the gate in the hall. Thus the emperors of the Turks still call their court to this day.

units.la: Barbarus re insolita perculsus] Quanquam nihil horum in textu Ebreo, tamen ex Græca editione colligimus ipsam regi-nam perculsam fuisse, quod rex eam irato vultu primum in-tueretur.
units.tr: Although none of this is in the Hebrew text, we gather from the Greek edition that the queen herself was struck with alarm, because the king first looked at her with an angry face.

units.la: Blandimento muliebri delinitus] protendit ei sceptrum aureum, quod qui tangebat, ἀχινδύν[?] ἢ, ut est apud Iosephum.
units.tr: He held out to her the golden sceptre, which whoever touched [ἀχινδύν ἢ], as it is in Josephus.

units.la: Iudææ gentis infestus] plus est quam inimicus. Sed Galesi-nius legendum suspicatur potius, Iudææ genti infestus.
units.tr: It is more than hostile. But Galesinius suspects that one should rather read "hostile to the Jewish nation."

units.la: Quum jam post epulas multis poculis convivium cale-recoepisset] circuitione usus est, ut significaret id quod Ebræi dicunt in convivio vini. Vide notas meas in Estheram, quas Pagnus edidit, anno 1586.
units.tr: He used a circumlocution to signify what the Hebrews call "the wine of the banquet." See my notes on Esther, which Pagninus published in 1586.

units.la: Ultra] præterea vel amplius.
units.tr: Moreover, or further.

units.la: Arrepto tempore] captata occasione.
units.tr: Seizing the opportunity.

units.la: Hamanis mortem flagitat in ultionem gentis quam perditam cupierat] totum hoc a Sulpicio confictum videtur. Vide Esth. 7. 6.
units.tr: All this seems to have been invented by Sulpicius. See Esth. 7:6.

units.la: Modicum fecesit] in hortum arboribus consitum.
units.tr: He withdrew a little into a garden planted with trees.

units.la: Appetitam] ad fluprum.
units.tr: To lust.

units.la: Tum regi compertum erat] ex indicio Harbona, qui unus erat ex eunuchis coram rege, id est regis. Esth. 7. 9. Geminum in Latio, sacerdos in æde pro sacerdos ædis.
units.tr: From the information of Harbona, who was one of the eunuchs before the king, that is, the king's. Esth. 7:9. A Latin double construction: "sacerdos in aede" for "sacerdos aedis."

units.la: Crucis] Crucem appellat, quam Hebræi [illegible, ~2 letters] id est lignum fi-ve arborem, Græci ξύλον & ξύλον δ' ἀ[illegible, ~3 letters]ρ, Latini arborem infelicem. Dicitur etiam patibulum & lignum suspendii.
units.tr: He calls it a cross. The Hebrews call it wood or a tree, the Greeks xylon, and the Latins an unlucky tree. It is also called a gibbet and a hanging-wood.

units.la: Cruci affigitur] Græce σταυροῦτω[?]; vel, si mavis, σταυρῶσθαι[?]: quod verbum usurpant hoc loco interpretes Græci σταυρωσάντα[?] αὐτὸν: crucifigatur in eo. Sic editio Latina, quam Roma dedit. Nam in Latina Hieronymi, appendite eum in eo. Sic etiam Ebræi.
units.tr: In Greek [σταυροῦται], or if you prefer [σταυρωθῆναι]; the Greek translators use the word [σταυρωσάντα αὐτόν]: let him be crucified on it. So the Latin edition which Rome published. For in Jerome's Latin it reads, "hang him on it." So also the Hebrews.

units.la: Omniaque bona ejus Mardochæo data] non Mardochæo, sed Esterae reginæ, quæ postea Mardochæum eis præfecit. Esth. 8. 1. & 2. Vide, si placet.
units.tr: Not to Mordecai but to Queen Esther, who afterwards set Mordecai over them. Esth. 8:1 and 2. See, if you like.

units.la: Annos duos & sexaginta] In hunc numerum consentit Plutarchus Artoxerxe, Eusebius ei tribuit annos XL tantum: unde suspicatur Sigonius Sulpicium edidisse duos & quadraginta, er-rore, ut fit, ex numeris orto XLII & LXII: sed fallit eum ac decipi opinione liquet ex pag. 18. Vide quæ notavimus ad illam paginam.
units.tr: Plutarch agrees with this number for Artaxerxes. Eusebius gives him only forty years, so Sigonius suspects that Sulpicius wrote forty-two by error, as happens, arising from the numerals XLII and LXII. But it is clear from p. 18 that he is mistaken and misled by opinion. See what we noted on that page.

units.la: Ochus] qui & Artaxerxes. Eusebius in Chronicis: Aelianus de varia historia lib. 6. cap. 8. Hic plurimos Iudæorum in Hyr-caniam ad mare Caspium deportavit, ubi etiamnum habitare creduntur: atque inde aliquando erupturos opinio est. Orosius lib. 3. cap. 7.
units.tr: Ochus, who is also Artaxerxes. Eusebius, Chronicle; Aelian, Varia Historia bk 6 ch. 8. He carried many of the Jews to Hyrcania by the Caspian Sea, where they are believed to live even now, and there is an opinion that they will one day break out from there. Orosius bk 3 ch. 7.

units.la: Iudith actus[?] conferam] legendum, conferam. Infra 121, ut temporum ordo consertus[?] sit. Idem Epistola secunda, ut est confertus apostolis & prophetis: & Dialog. 1. segm 1. Neque gravabor quam libet conferte vobiscum, ut poscitis, fabulari.
units.tr: Read "conferam" (I will compare), as below at p. 121, so that the order of the times is set out. The same in the second Epistle: "compared with the apostles and prophets"; and in Dialogue 1, segment 1: "I will not be reluctant to converse with you as much as you ask."

units.la: Traditur enim post captivitatem fuisse] Iudith. 5. 23. Nuper autem reversi ad Dominum Deum suum, ex dispersione, qua dispersi fuerant, adunati sunt, &c. Paullo ante in editione Græca fit mentio templi destructi. his verbis, ὁ ναὸς τῆς ἁγιωσύνης αὐτῶν ἐγυμνώθη, εἰς ἔδαφος[?]. Unde convinci erroris possunt, qui sentiunt hanc historiam accidisse sub Manasse rege Iuda cum Diocles, qui Ecbatana ædificavit, Medis imperaret. Vide Bellarminum de verbo Dei l. 1. cap. 12.
units.tr: For it is handed down that it was after the captivity. Judith 5:23: "Lately returned to the Lord their God from the dispersion in which they had been scattered, they were gathered together," etc. A little before, in the Greek edition, mention is made of the destroyed temple in these words: "the temple of their holiness was laid bare to the ground." Whence those who think this history happened under Manasseh, king of Judah, when Diocles, who built Ecbatana, ruled the Medes, can be refuted in their error. See Bellarmine, De verbo Dei, bk 1 ch. 12.

units.la: Nisi ob impatientiam et pariles conatus quicum ille rex] autore Sigonio legendum, nisi ii ob impotētiam & pares co-natus, quicunque ille rex fuerit, Nabuchodonosor &c. Sed vide sodes vitiorem Gifelinum.
units.tr: According to Sigonius one should read: "unless they, because of impotence and equal attempts, whoever that king was, Nebuchadnezzar, etc." But please see the more faulty Gifelinus.

units.la: Pariles conatus] id est similes. Usus est hac voce Dialogo tex-tu, segm. 10. Visam, certum est, pariles quodammodo columnam ruere de cœlo. Frustra igitur Sigonius reponit pa-res: licet hoc magis usitatum sit.
units.tr: That is, similar. He used this word in the text of the Dialogue, segm. 10: "I saw, it is certain, a column somehow equal falling from heaven." Sigonius therefore vainly replaces it with "pares," although that is more usual.

units.la: Plerique tamen Cambysem[?] ambyfem, Cyri regis filium, putant esse] in queis Eusebius. Vide Chronicon ejus. Sed & venerabilis Beda de temporibus ita scribit, Cambyses Cyri majoris F. ab Ebræis secundus Nabuchodonosor vocatur, & sub eo co-tigerunt. tigerunt quæ de Iudith narrantur. Nec longè abit ab hac sententia B. Augustinus de civit. Dei, lib. 18[?].cap.19.
units.tr: Most, however, think Cambyses, son of King Cyrus, is meant, among whom is Eusebius. See his Chronicle. But also the venerable Bede, in On Times, writes thus: "Cambyses, son of the elder Cyrus, is called by the Hebrews the second Nebuchadnezzar, and under him what is narrated about Judith happened." Nor is St Augustine far from this opinion, De civitate Dei, bk 18 ch. 19.

units.la: Hanc opinionem refellit Bellarminus de verbo Dei, l.1.cap.2. quem locum supra meminimus. Vide, si vacas & si habes. Nam mihi Bellarminus iam non est ad manum.
units.tr: Bellarmine refutes this opinion, De verbo Dei, bk 1 ch. 2, which passage we mentioned above. See it, if you have leisure and if you have it. For Bellarmine is not now at hand for me.

units.la: Vt in secularibus quibusdam scriptis legi Mox ait, Quod scriptores secularium litterarum nihil ex his quæ sacris voluminibus scripta sunt attigerint, id est profanarum.
units.tr: As I read in certain secular writings. Soon he says that writers of secular letters have touched on none of those things which are written in the sacred volumes, that is, of profane writers.

units.la: Infra 118. fuit autem (Ochus) ultra omnes cruentus & plusquam barbaro animo. Nam, ut alia omittam, sororem Ochum, eandemque & socrum, viuam capite defodit: patruum cum centum liberis ac nepotibus telis impe-ravit transfigi, quod in his maximam apud Persas probitatis laudem consistere videret. Ælianus de varia historia l.2 c.17. Οἱ μὲν Πέρσαι μάγοι πρὸς αὐτὸν [?] τῶν Ωχου [?] ἀνδρείας [?] καὶ τὸ Φοινικῶν [?] αὐτῶν [?] &c.
units.tr: Below 118. Ochus was more cruel than all others and of more than barbarous mind. For, to omit other things, he buried his sister, who was also his mother-in-law, alive up to the head; he ordered his uncle to be pierced with arrows along with a hundred children and grandchildren, since he saw that the greatest praise of uprightness among the Persians consisted in such things. Aelian, Varia Historia bk 2 ch. 17. The Persian magi [Οἱ μὲν Πέρσαι μάγοι] … [Ωχου] [ἀνδρείας] [καὶ τὸ Φοινικῶν] [αὐτῶν] etc.

units.la: Phœnicibus & Iudæis.
units.tr: To the Phoenicians and Jews.

units.la: Eusebius in Chronico, Ochus anno XIV Ægyptum tenuit, Nectenabo in Aethiopiam pulso, in quo Ægyptiorum regnum distructum est: & mox anno XVII Sidonem subvertit atque Ægyptum suo iunxit imperio. Et bene recuperavit. Nam a Persis defecerat, proprio rege ascito.
units.tr: Eusebius in Chronicle: Ochus held Egypt in the fourteenth year, Nectanebo having been driven into Ethiopia, in which the kingdom of the Egyptians was destroyed; and soon, in the seventeenth year, he overthrew Sidon and joined Egypt to his empire. And he recovered it well, for it had revolted from the Persians, having taken a king of its own.

units.la: Et Apim in Deum receptum]
units.tr: And Apis received as a god.

units.la: nomen regis, quem sub vivi bovis imagine colebant Ægyptij, qui corpore niger, candida fronte, in tergore alba nota insignis, duplicibus pilis in cauda, & lingua cantharo notatus erat. De hoc Deo videndi sunt Herodotus & alij.
units.tr: The name of the king whom the Egyptians worshipped under the image of a living ox, which was black in body, with a white brow, marked with a white sign on its back, with double hairs on its tail, and marked with a beetle on its tongue. On this god see Herodotus and others.

units.la: Βαγώας ὁ εὐνοῦχος αὐτοῦ, ὡς Αἰγύπτιος. Ælianus de varia historia, lib.4.cap.8.
units.tr: Bagoas, his eunuch, being an Egyptian. [Βαγώας ὁ εὐνοῦχος αὐτοῦ, ὡς Αἰγύπτιος.] Aelian, Varia Historia, bk 4 ch. 8.

units.la: infra 118. Hunc Bagao ægrotantem venenis sustulit. Ælianus loco citato, nisi fallor, Bagoas[?] non satis fuit occidisse Ochum, sed ex ejus femoribus gladiorum manubria fecit, ut ipsius animum ad caedes propensum demonstraret. Idem lib. 6. cap. 8. Odio eum habuit, quod Apim in Agypto trucidarat.
units.tr: Below 118. Bagoas carried him off, sick, with poison. Aelian in the place cited, unless I am mistaken, Bagoas was not satisfied with having killed Ochus, but made sword-handles from his thighs, to show his own mind inclined to slaughter. The same, bk 6 ch. 8. He hated him because he had slaughtered Apis in Egypt.

units.la: Historia divina] sic vocat historiam Iudith apocryphām, sive quod eam pro canonica haberet, sive quod libri apocryphi etiam divini nuncupantur. Sic enim eos a libris profanis distinguunt. Nam sacrum, sive quod idem, divinum, et profanum opponuntur.
units.tr: So he calls the apocryphal history of Judith "divine," either because he held it canonical, or because the apocryphal books are also called divine. For thus they distinguish them from profane books, since "sacred," or what is the same, "divine," and "profane" are opposed.

units.la: Holofernes] alibi Olofernes. Sic edit. Rom. Legitur et Oloferues, ut ὁλίβαν[?] καὶ ὁλείβαν[?]. Nam λ et ε alternant.
units.tr: Elsewhere Olofernes. So the Roman edition. Oloferues is also read, like ὁλίβαν and ὁλείβαν, since λ and ε alternate.

units.la: Sub quo Baguam fuisse] plures fuerunt hoc nomine. Nam et Alexander quendam Bagoam turpiter adamavit. Sunt qui scribant, in lingua Persica spadonem Bagoa dici.
units.tr: Under whom Bagoas was. There were several of this name, for Alexander also shamefully loved a certain Bagoas. There are those who write that in the Persian language a eunuch is called bagoa.

units.la: Mundiales historici] Iustinus, Aelianus, Plutarchus in Artaxerxe. Ceterum vocabulo mundialis, ab ecclesiasticis scriptoribus mutuato, usus est praeter alios Prudentius. Latini dicerent profani historici. Nam (seculares) vocabulum etiam ecclesiasticum est, hoc quidem sensu. Nota mundum aliquando ita dici ut ab ecclesia separetur: ex quo illud, totus mundus in maligno est: &, mundus odit vos: aliquando ipsam Ecclesiam includit, ut cum Christus mortuus esse legitur pro peccatis totius mundi. Priore significatu sumitur paullo post in his verbis, quae separata a mundi negotiis & sacris tantum vocibus proferenda: nam est periphrasis historiae sacrae. Mundiales ergo historici, qui tractant mundi negotia, & non ecclesiae.
units.tr: Profane historians: Justin, Aelian, Plutarch in Artaxerxes. Moreover, the word "mundane," borrowed from ecclesiastical writers, was used, among others, by Prudentius. Latin writers would say "profane historians," for "secular" is also an ecclesiastical word in this sense. Note that the world is sometimes so called as separated from the Church, whence "the whole world lies in evil" and "the world hates you"; sometimes it includes the Church itself, as when Christ is read to have died for the sins of the whole world. In the former sense it is taken a little later in these words, "to be uttered separated from the affairs of the world and only with sacred words," for it is a periphrasis of sacred history. Profane historians, therefore, are those who treat the affairs of the world and not of the Church.

units.la: Illud nemini mirum esse oportebit, &c.] Ptolemaeus Phi-ladelphus de Demetrio Phalereo quaerens cur nemo historicus aut poeta sacrae legis mentionem fecisset, respondit neminem ausum eam attingere quam constaret divinam esse & omni venerazione dignissimam: & punitos esse quosdam a coelesti numine, qui eam temere attrectare non essent veriti. Theopompum enim volentem inde quaedam suis scriptis inserere, mente motum fuisse diebus triginta, & per intervalla insaniae precibus Deum pla-casse, facile conjicientem quae morbi causa fuerit, atque etiam in somnis admonitum haec ideo ipsum pati, quod fuisset circa res divinas curiosior, eaque voluisset proferre profanis hominibus. Quare cum a coepto desitisset, sanam mentem ei fuisse redditam.
units.tr: It will be no cause for wonder that no one... Ptolemy Philadelphus, asking Demetrius of Phalerum why no historian or poet had mentioned the sacred Law, answered that no one had dared to touch what was known to be divine and worthy of all reverence, and that some who had handled it rashly had been punished by the heavenly power. Theopompus, wishing to insert some of it into his writings, was struck in his mind for thirty days, and during intervals of madness he appeased God with prayers. Guessing easily the cause of his illness, he was also warned in dreams that he suffered this because he had been too curious about divine things and had wanted to reveal them to profane men. When he desisted from his undertaking, his sound mind was restored to him.

units.la: Theodectae etiam poetae, cum in quadam tragedia vellet aliquid e sacris efacris[?] libris admiscere, oculos glaucomate suffusos caligasse, &c. cum erratum agnovisset, exorato Deo redditam aciem. Habentur hæc apud Iosephum Antiquit. Iudaic. lib. 12. cap. 2. circa finem. Quæ Gelenij verbis nunc exhibuimus, cum non vacaret Græcum inspicere textum
units.tr: The poet Theodectes too, when in a certain tragedy he wished to mix something from the sacred books, had his eyes clouded with a cataract and went blind, etc. When he recognised his error and God was entreated, his sight was restored. These things are found in Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, book 12, chapter 2, near the end. I have given them now in Gelenius's words, since I had no time to consult the Greek text.

units.la: Pag. 114. Ac per Iudith gesta] Sigonius corrigit, Ac Iudith gesta: vel certe, Atque Iudith gesta. Fateor hoc Latinius & elegantius dici: sed tamen Sulpicij ævo ita loquebantur. Orosius lib. 1. cap. 8. Hæc idem Moyses plenius veriusque, tanquam per ie suosque gesta, conscripsit. Idem cap. 12. quæ per Mosen strenuè acta sunt: & mox, sicut quæ per eum gesta.
units.tr: Page 114. And the deeds through Judith Sigonius corrects this to "And the deeds of Judith," or certainly "Atque Judith gesta." I admit this is said more neatly and elegantly in Latin, but still in Sulpicius's age they spoke thus. Orosius, book 1, chapter 8. The same Moses wrote these things more fully and truly, as through himself and his own deeds. The same, chapter 12: which were done bravely through Moses; and soon after, as the things done through him.

units.la: Rex Persarum Medis bellum intulit] Quia sub Ocho hæc gesta putavit, ideo eum appellat regem Persarum, qui Iudith 1. 5. rex Assyriorum vocatur. Quam multa hic quæ debilitant opinionem Sulpicij. Primum enim Ochi tempore nullum regnum Assyrium, nullus erat rex Assyriorum. Deinde ut demus Persarum regem ibi regem Assyriorum dici, tamen is non regnabat Ninivæ, quæ regia tum esse diu ante desierat. Postremo bellum eo tempore nullum Medis illatum, cum Persæ & Medi unum regem haberent. Unde Arphaxad rex Medorum esse non potuit, nisi fortasse regem appellat, qui satrapa duntaxat erat, quem Latini autores regulum vocant. Quod si conceditur, tunc illud mirum belli hujus Medici nullam mentionem fieri apud autores.
units.tr: The king of the Persians made war on the Medes. Because he thought these things were done under Ochus, he calls him king of the Persians, whom Judith 1.5 calls king of the Assyrians. How many points here weaken the opinion of Sulpicius! First, in Ochus's time there was no Assyrian kingdom and no king of the Assyrians. Second, granting that the king of the Persians could there be called king of the Assyrians, yet he did not reign at Nineveh, which had long before ceased to be the royal city. Last, no war was waged on the Medes at that time, since the Persians and Medes had one king. Hence Arphaxad could not have been king of the Medes, unless perhaps he is called king because he was merely a satrap, whom Latin authors call a petty king. But if this is conceded, then the remarkable silence of the authors about this Median war is strange.

units.la: Arfaxat] nomen hoc Ebraicum esse scribique debet Arphaxad cum d in fine. Sic enim certè scribitur Gen. 10. 22. Nec variat editio nostra vulgata Iudith 1. 1. Græca quoque habet Ἀρφαξάδ, ut dubitare de vera scriptura nemo jam debeat.
units.tr: Arfaxat This name is Hebrew and ought to be written Arphaxad, with a d at the end. For so it is certainly written in Genesis 10.22, and our printed Vulgate does not differ in Judith 1.1. The Greek also has Ἀρφαξάδ, so that no one should now doubt the true spelling.

units.la: Acie conflixit, secundo eventu: perempto rege, &c] ita distinximus, cum prius legeretur in exemplari, quod secutus sum, acie conflixit: secundo eventu, perempto rege, gentem imperio adjungit.
units.tr: He joined battle, with a successful outcome: the king having been killed, etc. I have punctuated thus, since in the copy I followed it was read first as "he joined battle: with a successful outcome, the king having been killed, he added the nation to his empire."

units.la: Et Arabiam] vide num sit legendum, & Mesopotamia: quam bello vastatam narrat historia Iudith 1. 1. 4. Quam vis in eodem capite, καὶ ἦλθεν εἰς ὁ ἐν Ἰαφθ[?], τὰ πρὸς νότον, κατὰ πρόσωπον τῆς Ἀραβίας, καὶ ἐκύκλωσεν πόλεις τὰς γῆς Μα-διὰν, &c.
units.tr: And Arabia. See whether we should read "and Mesopotamia," which the history of Judith 1.1, 4 relates as laid waste by war. Although in the same chapter: καὶ ἦλθεν εἰς ὁ ἐν Ἰαφθ, τὰ πρὸς νότον, κατὰ πρόσωπον τῆς Ἀραβίας, καὶ ἐκύκλωσεν πόλεις τὰς γῆς Μαδιάμ, etc. [and he came to ... toward the south, facing Arabia, and surrounded the cities of the land of Midian].

units.la: Ad templum frequentes concurrunt] Iudith 4. 2. Ἰεροσολύμων καὶ τὸ ἱερὸν τοῦ Κυρίου [illegible, ~8 letters] αὐτῶν ἐπικαλεῖσθαι[?] ἐν[?] συνηγμένων[?]: &c. vers.9 intantes[?] prostraverunt contra faciem templi Do-mini. Quæ perspicue convellunt sententiam eorum qui hæc acci-disse scribunt sub Cambyse. Nam templum consummatum fuit primum anno sexto Darij Nothi, ut supra demonstratum est.
units.tr: Crowds gather at the temple. Judith 4.2: "...Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord..., calling upon him..." ver. 9: "...prostrated themselves before the face of the temple of the Lord." These things clearly overthrow the opinion of those who write that these things happened under Cambyses. For the temple was first completed in the sixth year of Darius Nothus, as was shown above.

units.la: Iamque Damascum admotus exercitus Iudith 2. 17.[?] Et post hæc descendit in campos Damasci in diebus messis, & succendit omnia fata omnesque arbores & vineas fecit incidi: & cecidit timor illius super omnes inhabitantes terram. Verba sunt ex editione Hiero. Græce habetur, καὶ κατα-[?]βῆ εἰς πτόλιν Ἀσμαθ[?], &c.
units.tr: And now the army was brought near Damascus. Judith 2.17: "And afterwards he went down into the plains of Damascus in the days of harvest, and burned all the fields and grain and orchards, and cut down all the trees and vines, and the fear of him fell upon all who dwelt in the land." These are words from Jerome's edition. In Greek it reads: καὶ κατα-βῆ εἰς πτόλιν Ἀσμαθ [and he went down into the city Asmath], etc.

units.la: Servitio nuper exemptis] captivitatem Baby-lonicam intelligit, e qua non ita pridem reversi erant, Paullo an-te: pertis quippe usque ante captivitatis mala.
units.tr: Recently freed from servitude: he means the Babylonian captivity, from which they had not long before returned, as he said a little earlier; for the evils of the captivity were still fresh.

units.la: [?]abitis] desideratur, & Ammonitis; vel, si mavis, fi-que Ammon. Nam. Achior, de quo mox, dux erat filiorum
units.tr: [illegible] is lacking, and "of the Ammonites," or, if you prefer, "or the sons of Ammon." For Achior, of whom soon, was leader of the sons

units.la: Accitor quidam] Achior vocatur Iudith 5. 5. etiam in Græca editione Αχιωρ ut mirum sit cur ipse Accitor scripserit. An mendum est librariorum?
units.tr: A certain man named Accitor: Achior is he called in Judith 5.5, and in the Greek edition too he is Αχιωρ, so it is remarkable why he himself wrote "Accitor." Is it a scribal error?

units.la: Dei cultores] Dei, non Deorum: & Dei veri, quem Deum patrum suorum vocabant, qui sunt Abraham, Isaac & Iacob. Alio sensu Achior dicit, deserentes itaque cæremonias pa-trum suorum, quæ in multitudine Deorum erant: qui se ipse explicat cum ait, populus iste ex progenie Chaldæorum est. Hic primum in Mesopotamia habitavit, quoniam noluerunt sequi Deos patrum suorum, qui erant in terra Chaldæorum.
units.tr: Worshippers of God: of God, not of gods, and of the true God, whom they called the God of their fathers, who are Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Achior speaks in another sense when he says: "they therefore deserted the ceremonies of their fathers, which were in a multitude of gods." He explains himself when he says: "this people is from the stock of the Chaldeans. They first dwelt in Mesopotamia, because they refused to follow the gods of their fathers, who were in the land of the Chaldeans."

units.la: Pependisse servitium] pag.4o. captivitate pependerunt: & pag 6 *. de Ieroboamo servo Salomonis, aliquandiu Salomo-ni servitutem pependerat.
units.tr: Had endured servitude: at p. 40, "they had endured captivity," and at p. 6 (*), concerning Jeroboam the servant of Solomon, "for some time he had endured servitude to Solomon."

units.la: Omnibus gentibus devictis[?]] terræ Chanaan quæ septem erant: unde terra septem gentium. In his præcipui erant Chana-næi & Amorrei[?].
units.tr: All the nations conquered: of the land of Canaan, which were seven; whence "the land of the seven nations." Among these the chief were the Canaanites and Amorites.

units.la: Majoribus] Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo; quos supra patres appellavit.
units.tr: Ancestors: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whom he above called the fathers.

units.la: Vario rerum statu floruisse] sub Iudicibus.
units.tr: Had flourished in a varied state of affairs: under the Judges.

units.la: Secundum merita] id est, facta eorum bona vel mala.
units.tr: According to their merits: that is, their good or evil deeds.

units.la: In castra Hebræorum] si castra erant, ea erant Bethuliæ in ipsa urbe. Bethuliam autem putarim esse quæ in libris Canonicis Bethel dicitur. Quod tamen dubitans pone, non adfirmo.
units.tr: Into the camp of the Hebrews: if they were a camp, it was at Bethulia in the city itself. I would suppose Bethulia to be what in the canonical books is called Bethel. Yet, though doubting this, I put it forward without affirming it.

units.la: Vinctum ] ad arborem.
units.tr: Bound: to a tree.

units.la: In collem perducunt] Bethuliam, quæ in colle, velpotius in monte sita. Nam collis humilior & depressior est quàm mons.
units.tr: They lead him up to the hill: to Bethulia, which lies on a hill, or rather on a mountain. For a hill is lower and more depressed than a mountain.

units.la: Parem exitum opperiebatur] expectabat parem exitum cum Iudæis Bethulienfibus.
units.tr: He awaited a similar end: he expected a like end with the Jews of Bethulia.

units.la: Iudæus factus est] proselytus factus est. Tales etiam Iudæos vocabant: unde verbum <bl>[illegible, ~5 letters]</bl> Iudaizabant, id est, sacra Iudæorum suscipiebant. Interdum qui proselytus evaserat, dicebatur proselytus justitiæ. Nam proselyti nomen in lingua Græca quemlibet advenam denotat. Sic etiam <bl>[illegible, ~2 letters]</bl> in lingua Mosis.
units.tr: Became a Jew: became a proselyte. Such people were also called Jews; whence the verb [illegible] "they were Judaizing," that is, they took up the rites of the Jews.
