Sometimes one who had become a proselyte was called a proselyte of righteousness, for the name proselyte in the Greek language denotes any stranger. Thus also [illegible] in the language of Moses.

units.la: Montes militibus circumdat] quibus cincta erat Bethulia. Sic de Ierosolyma legimus, montes circum eam. Nam pars Iudææ montosa erat: quæ ideo montana sive montes Iudææ vocatur. In hac Bethulia erat.
units.tr: He surrounds the mountains with soldiers: by which Bethulia was enclosed. So we read of Jerusalem, "mountains around it." For part of Judea was mountainous, and for this reason it is called the mountain country or the mountains of Judea. Bethulia was in this region.

units.la: Aquationibus prohibet] nam incidi curavit aquæductum eorum: tum etiam custodes posuit fontium, ne haurirent aquam ex eis.
units.tr: He forbids the water supply: for he took care to cut off their aqueduct, and also posted guards at the springs so that they could not draw water from them.

units.la: Ad Oziam] Michæ filium ex tribu Simeonis. Iudith.7.12.
units.tr: To Ozias: son of Micah, of the tribe of Simeon. Judith 7.12.

units.la: Quintodecimo die] quærendum unde hoc habeat. Nam Iudith 7 23 quinto die. Etiam in Græco nihil legitur. Forte Severus initio scripserat, quinto demum die.
units.tr: On the fifteenth day: one must ask where this comes from. For Judith 7.23 says "on the fifth day," and nothing of the kind is read in the Greek either. Perhaps Severus had originally written "only on the fifth day."

units.la: Viro viduæ] virum habuerat nomine Manassem, qui genus suum referebat ad Simeonem patriarcham. Vidua vero manserat domi suæ tres annos & quatuor menses, vel, sequendo Hieronymum, sex menses. Iudith 8.3.
units.tr: Husband of a widow: she had a husband named Manasseh, who traced his lineage to the patriarch Simeon. She had remained a widow in her house for three years and four months, or, following Jerome, six months. Judith 8.3.

units.la: Tum in castris erat] Bethuliæ, ubi erant castra Ebræorum. Supra, propelli Acritor[?] in castra Hebræorum jubet.
units.tr: Then he was in the camp: at Bethulia, where the camp of the Hebrews was. Above, he orders Achior to be driven into the camp of the Hebrews.

units.la: Comitæ ancilla] Iudith 10.2, vocavit abram suam, id est, ancillam, famulam. Proprie ita vocantur ancillæ honestiores. Legitur hæc vox ἀβρὰ, ἢ ἀβραὰ[?] (nam anceps scriptura) Gen. 24. in editione τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα: item Exod. 2. αἱ ἀβραὰι[?] αὐτῆς, id est, ancillæ ipsius.
units.tr: Her maid: Judith 10.2, she called her maid, that is, a handmaid, servant. Properly, such are the names for more honourable maidservants. The word ἀβρὰ, or ἀβραὰ (for the writing is ambiguous), is read in Genesis 24 in the Septuagint edition, likewise in Exodus 2: αἱ ἀβραὰι αὐτῆς, that is, her maidservants.

units.la: Pag.117. Abuti] malim, abutendi.
units.tr: Page 117. To abuse: I would prefer "of abusing."

units.la: Persam facile permoverat] id est, Holofernem, quem Persam appellat eo modo quo supra Nabuchodonoforum Persarum regem esse dixit.
units.tr: Had easily moved the Persian: that is, Holofernes, whom he calls a Persian in the same way as above he said Nebuchadnezzar was king of the Persians.

units.la: Per Baguam eunuchum deduxerunt] est cur malim, de-ducitur. ducitur. Baguam autem interpres noster vulgatus Vagao nomi-nat. Hujus meminit vir doctus per hæc verba, Fuit litteris pro-ditum reges Persarum, qui spadones in regnum aliciti fue-re, Bagoas nuncupare.
units.tr: They led him through the eunuch Bagoas. I would prefer to read "deducitur" (he is led). Our translator, the Vulgate, calls him Vagao. A learned man mentions him in these words: "It has been recorded in writings that the kings of Persia, who had enticed eunuchs into the kingdom, called them Bagoas."

units.la: Multo fe vino-obruit] tantum vini hausit quantum nun-quam per totam vitam uno die hauserat.
units.tr: He drowned himself in wine: he drank as much wine as he had never drunk in a single day in his whole life.

units.la: caput hostis defecat] pugione fi ve acinace ipsius Holofer-nis, qui ad columellam lecti pendebat.
units.tr: He cut off the enemy's head with a dagger or scimitar, the one belonging to Holofernes himself, which hung by the little post of the bed.

units.la: Defuperioribus] de pinnis murorum.
units.tr: "From above" means from the battlements of the walls.

units.la: Tabernaculum ducis frequentes assistunt] nemo audebat cubiculum pulsare, aut introeundi excitandi ve caussa fores ape-rire. Tandem accedens Bagoas, tabernaculi atrium pulsat, suspi-catus eum cum Iudith dormire. Sed cum nullum jacentis motum auribus perciperet, ingressus cubiculum propius ad lectum acce-dit, subductaque cortina deprehendit eum in lecto jacentem trun-cum sine capite.
units.tr: Many stood about the commander's tent. No one dared knock at the bedchamber or open the doors to go in or to wake him. At last Bagoas came forward and knocked at the outer court of the tent, suspecting that he was sleeping with Judith. But when he perceived no movement from the man lying there, he went into the bedchamber, came nearer to the bed, drew back the curtain and found him lying on the bed, headless.

units.la: Pag.118. Castris ac præda potiti] sub.sunt. Quod verbum in hac historia quandoque desideratur. Post hæc poni velim non, comma, sed punctum.
units.tr: Page 118. "They took possession of the camp and the spoil": "sub. sunt" (supply: "are"). This word is sometimes missing in this story. After these words I would have a full stop placed, not a comma.

units.la: Centum & quinq; annos vixisse traditur] Iudith 16.28.
units.tr: He is said to have lived one hundred and five years. Judith 16.28.

units.la: Anno imperij ejus duodecimo] decimo tertio. Iudith 2.1.
units.tr: In the twelfth year of his reign. It should be the thirteenth. Judith 2.1.

units.la: A tempore Hierosolymæ restitutæ usque in id bellum fuerunt anni duo & viginti] imo duo & quadraginta. Nam Ierofolyma restituta anno Artaxerxis XXXII.pag. 107. qui re-gnavit annos LXII.pag.112. Adde duodecim Ochi faciunt XLII. Sciendum pag.112. ubi vulgo LXII. Sigonium legere XLII. Si recte, tum nihil hic mutandum. Nam X Artaxerxis & XII Ochi simul efficiunt XXII. Nihil verius.
units.tr: From the time when Jerusalem was restored until that war there were twenty-two years. Rather forty-two. For Jerusalem was restored in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes (p. 107), who reigned sixty-two years (p. 112). Add the twelve of Ochus and the total is forty-two. Note that on p. 112 the common reading is LXII, but Sigonius reads XLII. If that is right, nothing here needs changing, for the ten years of Artaxerxes and the twelve of Ochus together make twenty-two. Nothing could be truer.

units.la: Viginti & tres] & sex. Eusebius, Funccius.
units.tr: Twenty-three. It should be twenty-six. So Eusebius and Funccius.

units.la: Fuit autem ultra omnes cruentus] Plutarchus in Arto-xerxe, Ochus sævitia & crudelitate omnes superavit. Iusti-nus lib.10. hæreditas regni Ocho tradita, qui timens pa-rem conjurationem, regnum cognatorum cæde & itrage principum replet, nulla non sanguinis, non sexus, non æ-tatis misericordia permotus.
units.tr: He was also more bloodthirsty than all the others. Plutarch, in the Life of Artaxerxes: Ochus surpassed all in savagery and cruelty. Justin, book 10: the kingdom passed by inheritance to Ochus, who, fearing a similar conspiracy, filled the realm with the slaughter and butchery of his relatives and princes, moved by no pity for blood, sex or age.

units.la: Vltra omnes] supra omnes.
units.tr: "Beyond all" should read "above all."

units.la: Arxes] Arses Ochi F. Eusebio.
units.tr: Arxes: Arses, son of Ochus, according to Eusebius.

units.la: Triennio] quadriennio. Eusebius, alij.
units.tr: "For three years" should be "for four years," so Eusebius and others.

units.la: Darius] ultimus, Arsami F. qui Codomannus. Est autem Arsami obliquum a recto Arsames. Sic Vlyssi dicimus a recto Vlysses. Quidam Arsanes scribunt, per N. Ceterum Arsami F. obviam in Eusebio, ut Codomannus vel magis Codomanus in Iustino historico. Sic nominabatur antequam regnum adeptus esset, Vide Iustinum, lib. 10. Ex privata enim fortuna (fuerat enim ἀςράτης [?] siue ἀσπάτης [?], id est, ὑπερόβερμος [?], ut interpretatur Hesychius) ad regnum pervenit, Darij nomine, nequid regiæ maiestati deesset, honoratus. Siquidem in more positum erat olim ut ad imperium accedentes reges nomina mutarent. Regnum autem consecutus fuit beneficio Bagoæ eunuchi. Quod sig. Alexander apud Curtium per hæc verba: Ne Darius quidem Persarum accepit imperium, sed in sedem Cyri beneficio Bagoæ castrati hominis admissus.
units.tr: Darius the last, son of Arsames, who was called Codomannus. The oblique form Arsami is from the nominative Arsames, just as we say Ulysses in the nominative for Vlyssi. Some write Arsanes, with an N. Eusebius has "son of Arsames", and Codomanus, or more often Codomanus in the historian Justin, is the name he bore before he obtained the kingdom (see Justin, book 10). For he rose from private fortune (he was [ἀσράτης] or [ἀσπάτης], that is [ὑπερόβερμος], as Hesychius explains) to the kingdom, and was honoured with the name Darius, so that nothing should be lacking to royal majesty. For it was an old custom that kings on accession changed their names. He obtained the kingdom through the favour of the eunuch Bagoas. Alexander also signifies this in Curtius in these words: "Darius did not receive the Persian empire either, but was admitted to the seat of Cyrus through the favour of Bagoas, a castrated man."

units.la: Annos quatuor] sex. Eusebius & alij. Cum Sulpicio facit Iustinus, qui scribit Alexandrum Asiæ imperium rapuisse quinto post acceptum regnum anno. Quintus autem Alexandri incidit in quartum Darij Codomanni.
units.tr: "For four years" should be "for six years," so Eusebius and others. Justin agrees with Sulpicius, who writes that Alexander seized the empire of Asia in the fifth year after receiving the kingdom. Alexander's fifth year falls in the fourth year of Darius Codomannus.

units.la: Alexander acie conflixit] bis cum eo conflixit. Semel ad Issum in Cilicia; iterum deinde in Arbellis apud Gaugamela.
units.tr: He fought with him twice. Once at Issus in Cilicia; then again at Arbela, near Gaugamela.

units.la: Annos ducentos & quinquaginta] ut hic numerus constet, debet legi, pag. 112 annos LXII. Alioqui tantum essent anni CCXXX. Quod ex subjecta tabula clare perspicies. Cyrus regnavit ann. | 31 Cambyses ann. | 9 Magi fratres menses. | 7 Darius Hystaspis ann. | 36 Xerxis ann. | 21 Artaxerxes μακρόχειρ [?] ann. | 41 Xerxes alter mens. | 2 Sogdianus mens. | 7 Darius Ochus ann. | 19 Artaxerxes Mnemon ann. | 62 Ochus ann. | 23 Arxes sive Arses ann. | 3 Darius ultimus ann. | 4 Summa ann. 450. mens. 4.
units.tr: So that this number stands, it should be read on p. 112 as sixty-two years; otherwise there would be only 230 years, as you will see clearly from the table below. Cyrus reigned 31 years; Cambyses 9; the Magian brothers 7 months; Darius Hystaspis 36; Xerxes 21; Artaxerxes Macrocheir 41; Xerxes the second 2 months; Sogdianus 7 months; Darius Ochus 19; Artaxerxes Mnemon 62; Ochus 23; Arses or Arxes 3; Darius the last 4. Total: 450 years, 4 months.

units.la: Ita Salpicius; alij aliter. Nam sunt qui tantum CC annos hoc imperium stetisse volunt. Sunt etiam qui CCXXX & alij CC XXV annos sti assignant. Vide Brif. de regno Persarum pag. 2. Adisse[?] Hierosolymæ templum dicitur] pontifice Iaddua, qui Ebræis Simeon Iustus, si modo ijdem sunt, & non alius hic ab illo Iaddua pontifex in historia Ebraica Hananel nomina- tur. Salmanticensis, Simeon Iustus pontifex fecit duas vac- cas, & ipse fuit e viris magnæ synagogæ, vocaturque Iad- dua (Iddo est in Ebræo) eiusmodi Ioïuæ filij Iosedec iummi sacerdotis. Et mox, eum honoravit Alexander Macedo a- doravitque.
units.tr: Thus Sulpicius; others differ. For some want this empire to have lasted only 200 years, some assign 230 and others 225 years. See Brisson, On the Kingdom of the Persians, p. 2. He is said to have entered the temple at Jerusalem in the time of the high priest Jaddua, who for the Hebrews is Simeon the Just, if indeed they are the same person and this high priest Jaddua in Hebrew history is not someone else, named Hananel. The Salmanticensis: Simeon the Just, high priest, made two heifers; he was one of the men of the Great Synagogue, and is called Jaddua (Iddo in Hebrew), son of Jeshua, son of Jozadak the high priest. And soon after: Alexander the Macedonian honoured him and worshipped him.

units.la: Vt Iudæis ibidem degentibus liberum esset in patriam reverti] Hoc Persarum reges liberum fecerant. Quid igitur? Iudæis petentibus ut patriis legibus vivere sibi liceret, utque septimo quoque anno concederetur tributorum immuni- tas, concessit omnia. Iosephus Orig.lib.1 1. cap 8-
units.tr: So that the Jews dwelling there might freely return to their homeland. The kings of Persia had granted this freedom. What then? When the Jews asked that they be allowed to live by their ancestral laws, and that immunity from tribute be granted every seventh year, he granted everything. Josephus, Antiquities, book 11, chapter 8.

units.la: Dubitatum an 1 ānus[?] Arsami fuerit filius.
units.tr: It is doubted whether Anus was the son of Arsames.

units.la: Darium ultimum, quem Alexander devicit, supra ex Eusebio Arsami filium diximus. Eusebij sententiam firmat vir magnus, ita scribens, Videtur hoc fatale Dario fuisse, ut eodem an- no & ipse & eversor imperij ejus Alexander, imperium simul avitum inirent. Nam, eodem attestante, Darius inivit imperium eodem anno quo Philippus Macedo fuit interfectus, Olympiade CXI paullo ante Philippi ipsius mortem. De his om- nibus dubitare nos facit testimonium Alexandri quod supra ex Curtio produximus, tum etiam locus Iustini e libro X ibidem allegati, ubi scribit post mortem Ochi Codomannum (ita nomina- batur cum adhuc privatus esset) in memoriam pristinæ virtutis regem a populo constitutum, Darij nomine, ne quid regiæ majes- tati deesset, honoratum. Hæc antea mihi observata. Quibus nunc addo aliud testimonium Alexandri Macedonis ex Arriani lib. III. ubi Dario per epistolam exprobat quod occiso Arse, Bagoæ ἐπέρα[?], imperium occupasset ᾧ δικαίως[?], ἀλλ' ἐκ τῶν Περσῶν νόμων[?].
units.tr: We said above, following Eusebius, that Darius the last, whom Alexander defeated, was the son of Arsames. A great man confirms Eusebius's opinion, writing thus: "It seems this was fated for Darius: in the same year both he and Alexander, the overthrower of his empire, entered upon their ancestral empire together. For, as the same author attests, Darius entered on the empire in the same year in which Philip of Macedon was killed, in the 111th Olympiad, a little before Philip's own death." All these things make us doubt the testimony of Alexander which I brought forward above from Curtius, and also the passage of Justin from book 10 cited there, where he writes that after the death of Ochus, Codomannus (for so he was named while still a private man) was set up as king by the people in memory of his former virtue, and honoured with the name Darius, lest anything be lacking to royal majesty. These points I had noted before. To them I now add another testimony, that of Alexander the Macedonian, from Arrian, book 3, where he reproaches Darius in a letter that, after Arses was killed, he seized the empire by the hand of Bagoas, [οὐ δικαίως, ἀλλ' ἐκ τῶν Περσῶν νόμων], not justly but against the laws of the Persians.

units.la: Similiter Strabo lib. XV ejus spadonis opera Darium ἐκ ἀρχῆς τῆς γένους τῶν βασιλέων[?], regem factum scribit. Sed & Diodorus Siculus lib. XXVII ait post Ochi & Arsis ejus filij cædem ἐπὶ τῆς βασιλείας οἴκου[?], καὶ μηδενὸς ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τῆς γένους[?] ἀναξίνου τῷ ἀνδρὶ[?], cum nemo ex Ochi liberis, ad quem regnum lege rediret, superesset Darium regnum Bagoæ eunuchi beneficio adeptum esse. Pergamus nunc ad alia.
units.tr: Similarly, Strabo, book 15, writes that by the work of this eunuch Darius was made king, not [ἐκ τῆς γένους τῶν βασιλέων], from the royal family line. Diodorus Siculus, book 27, also says that after the slaughter of Ochus and of his son Arses, when none of Ochus's children survived to whom the kingdom would return by law, Darius obtained the kingdom through the favour of the eunuch Bagoas. Let us now go on to other matters.

units.la: Duodecimo imperij anno ] regnavit Alexander annos 12. & mortuus est. Eusebius in Chronicis addit menses sex. Alij scribunt anno decimo tertio vita functum esse. Rursum Eusebius, Alexander regnum Asiae anno regni sui septimo occupat & tenet omnia annis duodecim. At Sulpicius, septimo, posteaquam Darium devicerat, apud Babyloniam defunctus est. Quomodo hoc verum esse potest, si tenuit omnia annis duodecim? expende, erudite lector. Nam mihi nunc non vacat.
units.tr: In the twelfth year of his reign] Alexander reigned twelve years and died. Eusebius in the Chronicle adds six months. Others write that he departed this life in his thirteenth year. Again Eusebius: Alexander took over the kingdom of Asia in the seventh year of his reign and held everything for twelve years. But Sulpicius says that in the seventh year, after he had defeated Darius, he died at Babylon. How can this be true if he held everything for twelve years? Consider this, learned reader. For I have no leisure for it now.

units.la: Defunctus est] anno aetatis suae XXXII. Eusebius, alij.
units.tr: He died] in the thirty-second year of his age. Eusebius, others.

units.la: Regnum amici ejus, &c.] alibi est, servi ejus, id est, aulici, & alibi, satrapae [?] ejus. Significat autem principes & duces exercitus Macedonici, qui ejus venerationis ac virtutis erant ut singulos reges esse putarent, ait Iustinus, lib. XIII. Fumus in oculis meis quod 1. Machab. 1. 7. Et vocavit pueros suos illustres, qui una secum enutriti fuerant a juventute, & divisit illis regnum suum, dum adhuc viveret. Quid aut quem secutus est autor ille, alioqui non malus, cum haec scriberet? An in mente habuit locum Danielis, Dum ipse adhuc staret [?], confractum fuit regnum ejus, & divisum fuit in quatuor ventos coeli? Nam de Alexandro loquitur, & staret [?] et interpretantur vi-veret. Sed vide notas meas ad illum locum.
units.tr: Elsewhere it reads "his servants", that is, courtiers, and elsewhere "his satraps". He means the princes and commanders of the Macedonian army, who were held in such reverence and esteem that each was thought to be a king, as Justin says, book 13. A smoke in my eyes, 1 Macc. 1.7. "And he called his illustrious boys, who had been brought up with him from youth, and divided his kingdom among them while he was still alive." What or whom did that author, otherwise not a bad one, follow when he wrote this? Did he have in mind the passage of Daniel, "While he himself still stood, his kingdom was broken and divided into the four winds of heaven"? For he speaks of Alexander, and "stood" is interpreted as "lived." But see my notes on that passage.

units.la: Partiti sunt] Appianus in Syriacis, Amici Alexandri gentes subactas diviserunt in satrapias, Perdicca divisore, ex autoritate Philippi: nec multo post mortuis regibus regnarunt ipsi satrapae. Orosius lib. 3. cap 21. Alexander per duodecim annos trementem sub te orbem ferro pressit. Principes vere ejus XIV annis dilaniaverunt, & veluti opima praedam a magno leone prostratam avidi discerpsere catuli, seque ipsos in rixam invicem irritatos praedae aemulatione fregerunt.
units.tr: Partiti sunt]: Appian in the Syriaca: The friends of Alexander divided the subjugated nations into satrapies, with Perdiccas as divider, by the authority of Philip; and not long after the kings died, the satraps themselves reigned. Orosius, book 3, chapter 21: Alexander pressed the world, which trembled beneath you, under the sword for twelve years. But his chief men tore it apart for fourteen years, and like greedy whelps that have dragged down a rich prey from a great lion, they broke themselves in strife with one another, stirred up by rivalry over the spoil.

units.la: Sine usurpatione regali] alius dixisset, sine usurpatione regia. Nemo enim se regem appellabat, aut regis nomen usurpabat, quandiu aliquis ex stirpe Philippi Alexandrive in vi-vis erat.
units.tr: Sine usurpatione regali]: another writer would have said "sine usurpatione regia" (without royal usurpation). No one called himself king or assumed the title of king as long as anyone of the line of Philip or Alexander was still alive.

units.la: Arridaeo quodam Philippo] proprium ei nomen Arridaeum sive Aridaeus, id postea mutatum in Philippum, amore, ut creditur Philippi, cujus stirpem Macedones unice amabant. Iustinus, cum equites quoque idem fecissent, pedites indignati, nullas sibi consiliorum partes relictas, Aridaeum Alexandri fratrem regem appellant, satellitesque illi ex tribu sua legunt, &c. nomine Philippi patris vocari iubent. Arrideo] malim Arrideo. Iuflinus hoc nomen scribit Aridæo, unica R, & Appianus Aridæo, cum duplici D. Cui perimbecillo verbo datum imperium videbatur] nomen regium penes illum erat, autoritas penes alios. Vide Iuflinum lib. XIII. Sic dico, nihil præter nomen habebat, quod Sulpicius appellat imbecille verbum, cum mentis non satis compos esse crederetur. Appianus, Aridæus amore stirpis Philippi electus fuit, quamvis mentis, ut putabatur, non satis compos esset, cum adhuc Alexandri filii essent sub educatoribus. Nam & mater prægnans observabatur.
units.tr: Arridaeo quodam Philippo]: His proper name was Arridaeus or Aridaeus, later changed to Philip, supposedly out of love for Philip, whose line the Macedonians alone loved. Justin: when the cavalry had done the same, the infantry, indignant that no share in the counsels was left to them, called Aridaeus, Alexander's brother, king, and chose attendants for him from their own tribe, etc., and ordered that he be called by the name of his father Philip. Arrideo]: I would prefer Arrideo. Justin writes this name Aridaeo, with a single R, and Appian Aridaeo, with a double D. Cui perimbecillo verbo datum imperium videbatur]: the royal name was in his keeping, the authority in the hands of others. See Justin, book 13. Thus I say he had nothing but the name, which Sulpicius calls an imbecile word, since he was thought not sufficiently sound of mind. Appian: Aridaeus was chosen out of love for the line of Philip, although he was, as was supposed, not altogether sound of mind, while Alexander's sons were still under guardians. For his pregnant wife was also kept under watch.

units.la: Omnesque se reges appellari maluerunt] 1. Machab. 1. 9. Alexandro mortuo servi ejus, occupato suo quisque loco, omnes sibi diadema imposuerunt, nec non eorum posteri per multos annos. Primus in Asia Antigonus, victo Ptolemæo, ab exercitu rex appellatus fuit, extinctis tum regibus Aridæo Philippi atque Alexandri filiis. Mox etiam Ptolemæum regem suum appellavit exercitus, ne ob cladem videretur victori cedere.
units.tr: Omnesque se reges appellari maluerunt]: 1 Maccabees 1.9: After Alexander died, his servants each took his own place, and all of them put a diadem on themselves, and so did their descendants for many years. Antigonus was the first in Asia to be called king by the army, after Ptolemy had been defeated, the kings Aridaeus, son of Philip and Alexander, having then been done away with. Soon the army also called Ptolemy its king, so that it should not seem to yield to the victor because of the defeat.

units.la: Primus in Syria post Alexandrum Seleucus rex fuit] hoc verum non videtur. Nam initio Syria paruit Ptolemæis regibus Ægypti. Respondeo Asiæ et Syriæ satrapa prima fuisse Antigoni. Eum bello vicerunt Seleucus & Ptolemæus: unde contentio inter hos duos de regno Syriæ. Qua de re videndus lib. V. Polybius, ubi inter alia Antiochus queritur de injuria quam sibi fecerat Ptolemæus in occupandis Syriæ locis. Antigonum enim Monoculum & Seleucum, qui primi ea loca occupaverant, verissimos ac justissimos dominos fuisse ajebat. Ideoque ad se, non ad Ptolemæum Syriæ regnum quasi hereditario jure pertinere. Quippe Ptolemæum adversus Antigonum pugnasse non sibi, sed Seleuco eorum locorum imperium quærentem. Præterea communem omnium regum consessionem in medium afferebat. Nam quo tempore, superato Antigono, dividere inter se regna Cassander & Lysimachus & Seleucus voluerunt, Seleuci esse omnem Syriam judicavere. Hæc ibi: quæ fortasse moverunt Eusebium (nam hunc Sulpicius sequitur) ut scripserit Seleucum primum in Syria regnasse ann. XXXII. Vide Sigonium.
units.tr: Primus in Syria post Alexandrum Seleucus rex fuit]: This does not seem true. For at first Syria obeyed the kings of Egypt, the Ptolemies. I answer that the first satrap of Asia and Syria was Antigonus. Seleucus and Ptolemy defeated him in war, whence arose the dispute between these two over the kingdom of Syria. On this matter see Polybius, book 5, where, among other things, Antiochus complains of the wrong Ptolemy did him in seizing the places of Syria. He said that Antigonus Monophthalmus and Seleucus, who first occupied those places, were the truest and most just lords, and therefore the kingdom of Syria belonged to him, not to Ptolemy, by something like hereditary right. Ptolemy, he said, had fought against Antigonus not for himself but for Seleucus, who sought dominion over those places. Besides, he brought forward the common agreement of all the kings. For when, after Antigonus was overthrown, Cassander, Lysimachus and Seleucus wished to divide the kingdoms among themselves, they judged that all Syria belonged to Seleucus. So far Polybius. These are perhaps what moved Eusebius (for Sulpicius follows him) to write that Seleucus first reigned in Syria for thirty-two years. See Sigonius.

units.la: Seleucus] cognomento Nicanor, Eusebius: Nicator, alij. Quæ putatur esse vera Macedonica dialectus. Appellatio a victoriis quas habuit. Alij dictum ita putant a Nicatore quodam cæso. Subiecta eidem Perside ac Babylone] cum esset rex Syriae subjecit ei (* videlicet) Persidem ac Babylonem. Primum fuit satrapa Babyloniorum: postea factus est rex Babyloniae Medìaeque, Appianus: Babyloniae & superiorum locorum, Eusebius. Idem aliter. Nam superiora loca vocantur Media ac Persia, ut 1. Machab. 6.1. Rex Antiochus perambulans superiores regiones audivit esse civitatem Elymaida in Perside nobilissimam.
units.tr: Seleucus] surnamed Nicanor by Eusebius, Nicator by others. The latter is thought to be the true Macedonian form. The name is from the victories he won. Others think it was so called from a certain Nicator who was slain. Subiecta eidem Perside ac Babylone]: since he was king of Syria, he placed under him (that is) Persia and Babylon. He was first satrap of the Babylonians; afterwards he became king of Babylon and Media: Appian. Eusebius says "of Babylon and the upper regions." The same thing in other words, for the upper regions are called Media and Persia, as in 1 Maccabees 6.1: King Antiochus, travelling through the upper regions, heard that there was a city in Persia, Elymais, most noble.

units.la: Trecenta argenti talenta] annuum vectigal sive tributum, quod Judaei Seleuco dabant, erant trecenta talenta non auri, sed argenti, aut eo plus. Infra 12 4. Nam deficientibus Judaeis ab eo, qui ei ultra trecenta argenti talenta annua pensitaverant.
units.tr: Trecenta argenti talenta]: The yearly revenue or tribute which the Jews paid to Seleucus was three hundred talents, not of gold but of silver, or more. See below, 12.4. For when the Jews had defected from him, those who had paid him yearly more than three hundred talents of silver.

units.la: Per ternos magistratus] non displicet conjectura Sigonii legentis, externos pro ternos. Nam vulgata scriptura nullum commodum sensum habet, nisi per ternos magistratus intelligas ternos judicum confessus, qui civibus jus reddebant. Erant autem in autoritate summa & res graviores tantum tractabant, judices Sanhedrin, numero LXX, quibus rex aut princeps, quem [?] nasi vocabant, praeerat. Proximi ab his Judices viginti tres, qui consessus medium erat inter consessum majorem & minorem, qui ex tribus judicibus constabat, resque leviores absolvebat.
units.tr: Per ternos magistratus]: Sigonius's conjecture reading "externos" for "ternos" is not unwelcome. For the received text makes no sensible sense, unless by "ternos magistratus" you understand the three courts of judges who rendered justice to the citizens. These were of the highest authority and dealt only with weightier matters: the Sanhedrin of seventy judges, over which the king or prince, whom they called nasi, presided. Next below these were the twenty-three judges, who held a place between the greater and the lesser council; the lesser consisted of three judges and settled the lighter cases.

units.la: Per sacerdotes suos] id est, pontifices. Justinus lib. XXXVI. Semper exinde hic mos apud Judaeos fuit ut eosdem reges & sacerdotes haberent: quorum justitia religione permixta incredibile quantum coaluere. Non tantum apud Judaeos hic mos obtinuit, sed etiam, si Servio credendum, apud alias gentes. Qua de re sic ille ad hunc Virgilii locum,
units.tr: Per sacerdotes suos]: that is, high priests. Justin, book 36: From then on this custom always prevailed among the Jews, that the same men were their kings and priests; and from the mixing of justice with religion they grew incredibly strong. This custom prevailed not only among the Jews, but also, if Servius is to be believed, among other nations. On this point he says as follows on this line of Virgil:

units.la: Rex Anius, rex idem hominum Phoebique sacerdos, Majorum, inquit, haec erat consuetudo ut rex esset etiam sacerdos vel pontifex: unde hodieque imperatores, pontifices dicimus. Ceterum quando primum coeperit hic mos in Judaea, incertum. Darii quidem Nothi aevo suos adhuc duces habebant: sed post ratio regiminis immutata fuit, cum Alexandri tempore sacerdotis Jaddua imperio subessent. Nullius certe ducis aut principis tum mentio usurpatur apud autores. Post Machabaei sacerdotes dicti sunt ethnarchae. Primus Aristobulus diadema sumpsit. Quamvis in historia Ebraica Judas & fratres ejus reges nominentur.
units.tr: Rex Anius, rex idem hominum Phoebique sacerdos, It was, he says, the custom of the ancients that the king should also be priest or pontiff; whence even today we call emperors pontiffs. But when this custom first began in Judaea is uncertain. In the time of Darius Nothus they still had their own leaders; but afterwards the form of government was changed, since in the time of Alexander they were subject to the rule of the high priest Jaddua. Certainly no mention of any leader or prince is then made by the writers. After the Maccabees the high priests were called ethnarchs. Aristobulus was the first to take the diadem. Yet in the Hebrew history Judas and his brothers are called kings.

units.la: Sub rege Seleuco] Seleucus iste fuit septimus rex Syriæ, cognomento Philopator sive Philopater: cui Epiphanes successit anno CCCXXXVII regni Græcorum, quod a Seleuco Nicatore initium ducit.
units.tr: Sub rege Seleuco]: This Seleucus was the seventh king of Syria, surnamed Philopator or Philopater; he was succeeded by Epiphanes in the 137th year of the kingdom of the Greeks, which takes its beginning from Seleucus Nicator.

units.la: Series regum Syriæ usque ad Antiochum Epiphanem.
units.tr: Succession of the kings of Syria down to Antiochus Epiphanes.

units.la: 1. Seleucus Nicator ann. | 32
units.tr: 1. Seleucus Nicator, 32 years.

units.la: 2. Antiochus Soter ann. | 19
units.tr: 2. Antiochus Soter, 19 years.

units.la: 3. Antiochus Theus ann. | 15
units.tr: 3. Antiochus Theus, 15 years.

units.la: 4. Seleucus Callinicus ann. | 20
units.tr: 4. Seleucus Callinicus, 20 years.

units.la: 5. Seleucus Callinici F. ann. | 3
units.tr: 5. Seleucus, son of Callinicus, 3 years.

units.la: 6. Antiochus frater Callinici, cognomine Magnus ann. | 36
units.tr: 6. Antiochus, brother of Callinicus, surnamed Magnus, 36 years.

units.la: 7. Seleucus Philopator, quem Iafo Cyrenæus regem Asiæ vocat, ann. | 12 Summa | 137
units.tr: 7. Seleucus Philopator, whom Iafo the Cyrenaean calls king of Asia, 12 years. Total: 137.

units.la: Dissidet aliquantum Sulpicius noster. Nam Callinico tribuit annos viginti duos, & Antiocho Callinici fratri triginta septem. Qui reliquis additi efficiunt 139.
units.tr: Our Sulpicius differs somewhat. For he assigns twenty-two years to Callinicus and thirty-seven to Antiochus, brother of Callinicus. Added to the rest, these make 139.

units.la: Oniam sacerdotem] Oniam tertium, Simonis secundi F. ad quem Areus sive Arius rex Lacedæmoniorum legatos misit. Ita Eusebius & Iosephus. A quibus dissentit doctissimus Scali-ger, qui ab Ario legatos missos ait ad Oniam Iaddua F. sub Se-leuce Nicanore, quo tempore Arius quoque ille erat in vivis, post quem nullus alius Arius in familia regia fuit.
units.tr: Onias the priest] Onias the third, son of Simon the second, to whom Areus, or Arius, king of the Lacedaemonians, sent envoys. So Eusebius and Josephus. The most learned Scaliger dissents from them. He says that Arius sent envoys to Onias, son of Jaddua, under Seleucus Nicanor, at which time that Arius was still alive, and that after him there was no other Arius in the royal family.

units.la: Series pontificum ab Alexandro usque ad Antio-chum Epiphanem.
units.tr: Succession of the high priests from Alexander down to Antiochus Epiphanes.

units.la: 1. Iaddus sive Iaddua.
units.tr: 1. Jaddus, or Jaddua.

units.la: 2. Onias Iaddua F.
units.tr: 2. Onias, son of Jaddua.

units.la: 3. Simon Oniæ F. cognomento Iustus.
units.tr: 3. Simon, son of Onias, surnamed the Just.

units.la: 4. Eleazarus, Oniæ item F. frater Simonis.
units.tr: 4. Eleazar, also son of Onias, brother of Simon.

units.la: 5. Onias Simeonis Iusti F.
units.tr: 5. Onias, son of Simon the Just.

units.la: 6. Simon Oniæ F. cujus meminit Sirachides.
units.tr: 6. Simon, son of Onias, whom the son of Sirach mentions.

units.la: 7. Onias Simeonis F.
units.tr: 7. Onias, son of Simon.

units.la: De Simeone Iusto, quem cum Iaddua confundunt scribit Sal-manticensis, Chronica Christianorum dicunt Iustum[?] cog-nominatum esse propterea quod erat clemens erga popu-lum, non sicut priores. Quæ verba illustrabis ex Chronico Eu-sebij, ubi mentio hujus Simeonis per hæc verba, Iudæorum pontifex maximus Simon Oniæ F. clarus habetur: cui cognomentum Iusto fuit propter sollicitam in Deum religionem & cives suos pronam clementiam.
units.tr: Concerning Simon the Just, whom they confuse with Jaddua, Salmanticensis writes that the Christian chronicles say he was surnamed Just because he was kind to the people, unlike his predecessors. You will illustrate these words from the Chronicle of Eusebius, where mention of this Simon is made in these words: "Simon, son of Onias, is regarded as the famous high priest of the Jews. He had the surname Just on account of his zealous piety toward God and his readiness to show kindness to his citizens."

units.la: Virum sanctum & integrum] אִישׁ תָּמִים וְיָשָׁר [?], id est ὅσιος καὶ ἄμωμος καὶ τέλειος [?], id est, immaculatum, sine macula. Hujus memihit Breviarium Iasonis, cap. 3. τῆς ἁγίας πόλεως καὶ τῶν νόμων ἐπὶ κάλλιστα συνηρμοσμένων [?] Ὀνίᾳ ἀρχιερεῖ [?] ἐπιτῆς ἐκχύσεως [?] ἀπὸ τῶν βασιλέων [?] φυλακῆς [?] πρὸς τὸν τόπον [?]. Vide sequentia.
units.tr: A holy and upright man] Hebrew ish tamim veyashar [אִישׁ תָּמִים וְיָשָׁר], that is, Greek hosios kai amomos kai teleios [ὅσιος καὶ ἄμωμος καὶ τέλειος], that is, blameless, without blemish. The Breviary of Jason mentions him in chapter 3: the holy city and the laws being most finely ordered under the high priest Onias, after the outpouring [...] from the kings [...] guard [...] toward the place [...]. See what follows.

units.la: Simon quidam] idem liber, Σίμων ὁ τῆς Βενιαμὶν φυλῆς προστάτης τοῦ ἱεροῦ [?]. Hinc discimus primum Benjamitam fuisse: deinde præpositum templi. Vide 2.Ma-chab. 4.1.
units.tr: Simon, a certain man] The same book: Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin, prefect of the temple [Greek Simōn ho tēs Beniamin phylēs prostatēs tou hierou]. From this we learn first that he was a Benjamite, and then that he was head of the temple. See 2 Maccabees 4:1.

units.la: Exquirere nequiverat] extinguere legendum conjicit Sigonius. An hoc egerit Simon, nescio: hoc scio [?]Machab. 3.5. haberi, καὶ πίστεως τὸν ὀνόματα [?] τὸν ὑπὲρ τὸ ἀνθρώπων [?]. Proinde legendum putarim hoc loco, vincere nequiverat. Sed tamen amplius deliberandum censeo. Nam quæ initio valde placent, aliquando post admodum displicent.
units.tr: Could not find] Sigonius conjectures that exquirere should be read as extinguere, to extinguish. Whether Simon actually did this I do not know. What I do know is that at 2 Maccabees 3:5 a Greek phrase occurs [...] beyond human [...]. So I think vincere, "could not overcome", should be read here. But I think the matter needs further consideration, for things that at first please greatly often afterwards displease greatly.

units.la: Iafon fratet Oniæ] qui sic vocari maluit quam Iesus: quod est nomen Ebraicum, ut illud Græcum sive Hellenisticum, unde scripserim libentius Iasō. Ἰάσων, Iasō; ut Πλάτων, Plato. Sic Zeno. Similiter scribi posset Simo, nempe ex Græco Σίμων. Nam Ebraicum Simon non abjicit N. Moris erat illo tempore ut nomina Ebraica cum Græcis permutarent. Sic ex Iesus factum Ἰάσων. Similiter frater ejus Oniæ dictus est Menelaus. Nihil dico, si non Tarphon ex ea consuetudine mutavit in Τρύφων, qui Latine Trypho diceretur. Sic hodieque quidam Ianus dicunt pro Iohannes: quam recte viderint. Mihi talis novitas nunquam arrisit.
units.tr: Jason, brother of Onias] who preferred to be called this rather than Jesus, which is the Hebrew name, just as the Greek or Hellenistic form is Iasōn [Ἰάσων], whence I would more willingly write Iasō, as Plato is written for Πλάτων. So with Zeno. Likewise Simo could be written, from the Greek Σίμων, since the Hebrew Simon does not drop the final N. At that time it was the custom to exchange Hebrew names for Greek ones. So from Jesus came Iasōn. Similarly his brother Onias was called Menelaus. I say nothing of whether Tarphon was changed by the same custom into Trýphōn [Τρύφων], which in Latin would be Trypho. So even today some write Ianus for John, and how rightly they may have seen. Such novelty has never pleased me.

units.la: Antiochum regem] cognomento Ἐπιφανῆ, id est, Illustrem, qui post Ἐπιμανὴς dictus est, id est, Insanus. Hæc acciderunt post excessum Seleuci, anno regni Græcorum, id est, Syro-Macedonum, 137.
units.tr: King Antiochus] surnamed Epiphanes [Ἐπιφανής], that is, Illustrious, who was afterwards called Epimanēs [Ἐπιμανής], that is, Madman. These things happened after the death of Seleucus, in the year 137 of the Greek era, that is, of the Syro-Macedonians.

units.la: Pag. 120. Augmentum stipendij pollicens] talenta tria millia sexcenta sexaginta [?]. Iosephus τὰ ἀνδρόγυνα [?]. Tre-ceta quinquaginta, et ex reditibus aliis talenta LXXX. Epitoma Iasonis. Hic denuo stipendium dixit pro tributo aut vectigali.
units.tr: Page 120. Promising an increase of the tribute] three thousand six hundred and sixty talents [?]. Josephus gives [...]. Fifty-three, and from other revenues eighty talents. Epitome of Jason. Here again he says stipendium for tribute or tax.

units.la: Perpetuo sacerdotio perfungi] lege, perpetuo sacerdotio fungi: aut cum Sigonio, non perpetuo sacerdotio. perfungi. Nam usque ad hæc tempora pontificatus fuerat perpe-tuus. Sequentia quoque corrupta esse judicat Sigonius, atque ita corrigit, tamen rex avaritia prævalente Oniam depulit, & Iasoni pontificatum concessit.
units.tr: To hold the priesthood for life] read perpetuo sacerdotio fungi, to discharge the priesthood for life; or with Sigonius, non perpetuo sacerdotio perfungi, not to hold the priesthood for life. For up to this time the high priesthood had been held for life. Sigonius also judges what follows to be corrupt, and corrects it thus: "yet the king, his greed prevailing, drove out Onias and granted the high priesthood to Jason."

units.la: Sacerdotium est mandatum] & una principatus. Nam ea ætate penes pontificem etiam principatus erat. Id colligo ex 2. Machab. 4. 10 ubi summum sacerdotium diserte principatus appellatur. Porro sacerdotium hic est ἱερωσύνη[?], & idem valet atque ἀρχιερωσύνη[?]. Sic ἱερεὺς[?] usurpatur pro ἀρχιερεὺς[?], ut Act. 5. 24[?]. Sed & 1. Machab. 15. 1. Σίμων ἱερεύς[?], mox se explicat cum ait, ἱερεὺς μέγας[?].
units.tr: The priesthood is entrusted] and with it the principate. For in that age the high priest also held the principate. I gather this from 2 Maccabees 4:10, where the high priesthood is expressly called a principate. Moreover, the priesthood here is hierōsynē [ἱερωσύνη], and it means the same as archierōsynē [ἀρχιερωσύνη]. So hiereus [ἱερεὺς] is used for archiereus [ἀρχιερεὺς], as at Acts 5:24. But also at 1 Maccabees 15:1, Simōn hiereus [Σίμων ἱερεύς], which he then explains when he says hiereus megas [ἱερεὺς μέγας].

units.la: Is fœde admodum cives patriamque lacerà vit] initio ritus Græcanicos introduxit & gymnasium Ierosolymæ instituit: postcum Menelaus ei esset suffectus, urbem cædibus implevit. Vide 2. Mach. 5. 6.
units.tr: He most shamefully tore apart the citizens and the fatherland] At first he introduced Greek customs and set up a gymnasium at Jerusalem. Afterwards, when Menelaus had been substituted for him, he filled the city with slaughter. See 2 Maccabees 5:6.

units.la: Simonis illius fratrem] Sic Iasō Cyrenæus. Aliter Iosephus Orig. lib. 12. cap. 6. & Eusebius in Chronico. Scribunt enim hunc fuisse fratrem Iasonis alio nomine Iesum dictum.
units.tr: That brother of Simon] So Jason the Cyrenaean. Josephus in Book 12, chapter 6, and Eusebius in the Chronicle say otherwise. For they write that this man was the brother of Jason, called by another name Jesus.

units.la: Iisdem attibus[?]) emit pontificatum, ut antea Iasō fecerat, trecentis argenti talentis eum supergressus, 2. Machab. 4. 24. Obtinuerat] obtinuit. Sigonius probo vehementer.
units.tr: By the same means] he bought the priesthood, as Jason had done before, outbidding him by three hundred talents of silver, 2 Maccabees 4:24. Obtinuerat] obtinuit. I strongly approve Sigonius here.

units.la: Lysimachus substituitur] frater Menelai, 2. Machab. 4. 29. Patria excessit] fugit ad Ammanitas sive Ammonitas, 2. Machab. 4. 26. profugus in Ammanitidem expulsus est regionem. Vbi notabis Ammanitidem dici, quæ vulgo Ammonitis. Sic Ammanitæ qui & Ammonitæ. Crebrum hoc in editione τῶν ἑβδομήκοντα[?].
units.tr: Lysimachus is substituted] the brother of Menelaus, 2 Maccabees 4:29. He left his country] he fled to the Ammanites, or Ammonites, 2 Maccabees 4:26; he was driven out as a fugitive into the region of Ammanitis. Here you will note that the region is called Ammanitis, which is commonly Ammonitis. So Ammanitae are also Ammonitae. This is frequent in the edition of the Seventy.

units.la: Plerique populariū] in quibus Tobiæ filij, qui a Menelai partibus stabant. Iosephus Ant. lib. 12. cap. 6.
units.tr: Most of the common people] among whom were the sons of Tobias, who sided with the party of Menelaus. Josephus, Antiquities, Book 12, chapter 6.

units.la: More gentilium] ritu Græcanico. Iosephus, maior populi pars factionem Iasonis sequebatur; quorum vim non sustinentes Menelaus & Tobiæ filij secesserunt ad Antiochum, dicentes se velle religionis patriis institutis ac legibus religionem regis & Græcanicos ritus assumere. Vide sequentia lib. 12. cap. 6.
units.tr: In the manner of the Gentiles] in the Greek fashion. Josephus says that the greater part of the people followed the faction of Jason. Unable to withstand their strength, Menelaus and the sons of Tobias withdrew to Antiochus, saying that they wished to adopt the religion of the king and the Greek rites, abandoning the religion of their fathers' institutions and laws. See what follows in Book 12, chapter 6.

units.la: Legem profanare] introductis externis ritibus. Nam & præputia sibi adducebant, ut nudi quoque non essent Græcis dissimiles. Iosephus in loco citato.
units.tr: To profane the law] by introducing foreign rites. For they even drew the foreskin over, so that they would not be unlike the Greeks in being naked. Josephus in the place cited.

units.la: Regi Ægyptio] Ptolemæo Philometori.
units.tr: To the Egyptian king] Ptolemy Philometor.

units.la: Quod iussu senatus & P R. deposuit] res ita se habet. Cum Ptolemaei fratres a senatu auxilia petiissent, missus est legatus Popilius ad Antiochum, qui abstinere illum ab Aegypto, aut si iam incessisset, excedere iuberet. Quum in Aegypto eum invenisset, osculumque ei rex obtulisset (nam coluerat inter ceteros Popilium Antiochus, cum Romae obses esset) tunc Popilius facessere interim privatam amicitiam iubet, cum mandata patriae intercedant: prolatoque senatus decreto & tradito, cum cunctari eum videret, consultationemque ad amicos referre, ibi Popilius virga, quam in manu gerebat, amplo circulo inclusum ut & amicos caperet, consulere iubet, nec prius inde exire quam responsum senatui daret aut pacem aut bellum cum Romanis habiturum. Adeoque haec austeritas animum regis fregit, ut parituarum se senatui responderit. Haec Iustinus lib. XXXIV.
units.tr: Which, by order of the Senate and the Roman people, he laid down] the matter stood thus. When the brothers of Ptolemy had asked the Senate for help, Popilius was sent as envoy to Antiochus, to order him to keep away from Egypt, or, if he had already entered it, to withdraw. When Popilius found him in Egypt, the king offered him a kiss (for Antiochus had cultivated Popilius among others when he was a hostage at Rome). Then Popilius bade him put aside private friendship for the time being, since the commands of his country stood in the way. Presenting the Senate's decree and handing it over, and seeing that the king hesitated and wished to refer the matter to his friends for consultation, Popilius drew a large circle around him with the staff he carried in his hand, so as to enclose the friends too, and ordered him to give an answer before leaving the circle, whether he would have peace or war with the Romans. Such sternness so broke the king's spirit that he replied he would obey the Senate. Thus Justin, Book 34.

units.la: templum spoliavit inde vasis sacri ministerij, & inter cetera candelabris aureis, altari aureo, mensaque propositionis, quam vocant, ac neaulaeis quidem reliquit, quae e cocco & bysso constabant. Iosephus. Nec thesauris etiam pepercit: nam abstulit e templo mille octingenta talenta. Breviarium Iasonis.
units.tr: He stripped the temple of the sacred vessels of the ministry, and among other things of the golden candlesticks, the golden altar, and the table of the showbread, as they call it, and he did not even leave the curtains, which were made of scarlet and fine linen. Josephus. Nor did he spare the treasures, for he carried off eighteen hundred talents from the temple. The Breviary of Jason.

units.la: Tanta enim virorum mulierumque occisio, tanta virginum ac puerorum fata caedes est, ut tribus non amplius diebus, octoginta hominum millia perierint. Iaso Cyre-næus[?]: direptaque tota urbe, habitatores partim necavit, partim captivos una cum liberis & uxoribus abduxit, usque ad decem millium numerum. Iosephus lib. 2. cap. 7.
units.tr: For the slaughter of men and women was so great, and the fate and slaughter of virgins and boys so great, that in no more than three days eighty thousand people perished. Jason the Cyrenaean. Having plundered the whole city, he partly killed the inhabitants and partly led them captive, together with their children and wives, to the number of ten thousand. Josephus, Book 2, chapter 7.

units.la: Seleucus post novem annos in Syria rex est appellatus, sunt anni CLI. Iosephus Antiochum urbem ingressum scribit anno centesimo quadragesimo tertio, ex quo primum ad Seleuci familiam Syriae regnum devenerat, & biennio post urbem captam accidisse hanc cladem, regni ejus fa-miliae CXLV, vigesima quinta mensis Chasleu, Olympiade CLIII.
units.tr: Seleucus was called king in Syria nine years later; these are 151 years. Josephus writes that Antiochus entered the city in the one hundred and forty-third year, from which the kingdom of Syria first passed to the family of Seleucus, and that this disaster happened two years after the city was taken, in the 145th year of that family's reign, on the twenty-fifth day of the month Chasleu, in the 153rd Olympiad.

units.la: Post quinquennium fere quam Antiochus regnare coe-[?] perat] superfluit dictio fere, ut sæpe alias. Nam Antiochus re-gnare cœpit anno Græcorum CXXXVII, a quo quintus est annus CXLII. Consule priorem Machabæorum.
units.tr: About five years after Antiochus had begun to reign] The word "fere" (about) is superfluous, as often elsewhere. For Antiochus began to reign in the year 137 of the Greeks, and the fifth year from that is 142. Consult the former book of the Maccabees.

units.la: Defuncto rege Alexandro, &c ] autor prioris Machabæo-rum scribit vivo adhuc Alexandro id factum esse. Quæ de re di-ximus antea. Nam videtur Danielem secutus. Ceteri tamen cum Sulpicio consentiunt, etiam Iosephus.
units.tr: Alexander being dead, etc.] The author of the first book of the Maccabees writes that this happened while Alexander was still alive. We have discussed this matter before. For he seems to have followed Daniel. The others, however, agree with Sulpicius, and Josephus too.

units.la: Seleucus] ab hoc regnum Seleucidarum appellatum, quod & regnum Græcorum. Hujus Seleuci & sæpra meminimus. Urbes aliquot in Syria condidit, Iosephus lib. 12. cap. 3.
units.tr: Seleucus] The kingdom of the Seleucids was named after him, and it is also called the kingdom of the Greeks. We have mentioned this Seleucus above as well. He founded several cities in Syria, Josephus, book 12, chapter 3.

units.la: Annos duos & triginta] sic etiam Eusebius.
units.tr: Thirty-two years] So also Eusebius.

units.la: Antiochus filius ejus] cognomento Soter, qui novercam amavit, & postea Gallos in Asiam irrumpentes repulit.
units.tr: Antiochus, his son] surnamed Soter, who loved his stepmother, and afterwards drove back the Gauls who burst into Asia.

units.la: Qui & Theus cognominatus est] id est Deus. Hunc pater ex noverca genuit, quem postea uxor ejus veneno sustulit. Theum autem primi cognominavere Milesij, quia Timarchum eorum tyrannum occiderat, Appianus.
units.tr: Who was also surnamed Theus] that is, God. His father had him by his stepmother, and his wife later removed him with poison. The Milesians were the first to give him the surname Theus, because he had killed their tyrant Timarchus, Appian.

units.la: Callinicus] Gallinicus est apud Eusebium et Funccium. Hunc pater Antiochus e Laodice genuit.
units.tr: Callinicus] In Eusebius and Funccius it is Gallinicus. His father Antiochus had him by Laodice.

units.la: Pag. 122. Seleucus filius [Callinici] cognomine Ceraunus. Imperio præfuit annos tres, nec a valetudine firmus nec ab opibus. Quocirca exercitum continere in officio non potuit. Appianus autor eum sublatum fuisse veneno purpuratorum perfidia post exactum annum regni alterum.
units.tr: Page 122. Seleucus, son [of Callinicus] surnamed Ceraunus. He ruled for three years, firm neither in health nor in resources. For this reason he could not keep the army in obedience. Appian, the author, says that he was removed by poison through the treachery of the purple-clad nobles after the second year of his reign was completed.

units.la: Antiochus frater Callinici] hic est Antiochus Magnus, quem Lucius Scipio parte Asiæ, quæ cis Taurum, multavit: unde Asiatici cognomen accepit.
units.tr: Antiochus, brother of Callinicus] This is Antiochus the Great, whom Lucius Scipio punished by taking the part of Asia that lies this side of the Taurus. From this he received the surname Asiaticus.

units.la: Imperii parte multatus est] pacis leges Antiocho ita datæ fuerunt, ut Europa omni abstineret, Asiaque omni, quæ cis Taurum montem est, decederet: pro impensis autem in bellum factis XVM talentorum Eubicorum daret, mille talenta per XII annos penderet. In Chronico Eusebij, Post prælium quo in Thermo-phylis est victus Antiochus, hoc inter Romanos & eum convenit, ut mille talenta per annos singulos vectigalis nomine eis solveret.
units.tr: Deprived of part of his empire] The terms of peace were laid on Antiochus thus: he was to keep out of all Europe and withdraw from all of Asia this side of the Taurus mountain. In return for the expenses incurred in the war he was to pay fifteen thousand Euboic talents, paying a thousand talents over twelve years. In the Chronicle of Eusebius: after the battle at Thermopylae, in which Antiochus was defeated, this was agreed between the Romans and him, that he should pay them a thousand talents every year under the name of tribute.

units.la: Et Antiochum] Epiphanem, quem Polybius Epimanem appellat, id est furibundum & mente captum.
units.tr: And Antiochus] Epiphanes, whom Polybius calls Epimanes, that is, raging and out of his mind.

units.la: Seleucus] Philopator sive Philopater.
units.tr: Seleucus] Philopator or Philopater.

units.la: Filius natu minor] propter absentiam natu majore, qui Romæ Romæ obses erat, ut dictum est.
units.tr: The younger son] because the elder, who was at Rome, was absent as a hostage, as has been said.

units.la: Insimulatum diximus] pag. 119.
units.tr: We have said "accused"] page 119.

units.la: Post quinquennium quam regnare coeperat] cum ex Ægypto, quam subito inuaserat, Senatus mandato reces-sisset. Id gestum est anno regni Græcorum CXLIII, ut habetur 1 Machab. 11.21, unde videtur potius leg. post lexennium. ita Funcc-ius.
units.tr: Five years after he had begun to reign] when, at the Senate's command, he had withdrawn from Egypt, which he had suddenly invaded. This was done in the 143rd year of the Greek kingdom, as is found in 1 Maccabees 11:21, whence it seems better to read "after eleven years" (post lexennium). So Funccius.

units.la: Grave Romanis stipendium pensitans] gravi tributo pacis a Romanis victus oneratusque. Iustinus. Vide quæ notavimus ad illud, imperij parte multatus est.
units.tr: Paying the heavy tribute to the Romans] overcome and burdened by the heavy tribute of peace imposed by the Romans. Justin. See what we noted on the phrase "deprived of part of his empire."

units.la: Post biennium deinceps] anno CXLV regni Græcorum, 1. Machab. 1.57 & 5.14 & 2 Machab 5.11.
units.tr: Two years afterwards] in the 145th year of the Greek kingdom: 1 Maccabees 1:57 and 5:14; 2 Maccabees 5:11.

units.la: Pag. 123. Præsidium arci imposuit] quam extruxerat in superiore urbe, quæ a David nominata vocatur enim civitas David, 1. Mach. 1.35. Demolitus mœnia in inferiore urbe arcem condidit, erat enim editiore loco sita, ipsi templo imminens. Quapropter bene prius firmatæ mœnibus ac turribus Macedonicum præsidium imposuit. Admixti tamen erant ex impiis Iudæis Icelestisimi, a quibus plurimum vexata fuit civitas. Iosephus Antiquit. lib. 12 cap. 7. Arx hæc acra dicitur, id est, ירושלם & ἀκρόπολις. Probatum alias.
units.tr: Page 123. He placed a garrison in the citadel] which he had built in the upper city, the one called David's, for it is called the city of David, 1 Maccabees 1:35. Having torn down the walls in the lower city, he built the citadel there, for it lay on higher ground, overhanging the temple itself. Therefore, having first strongly fortified it with walls and towers, he placed a Macedonian garrison in it. Some of the impious Jews, the Hellenizers, were however mixed in with them, and by them the city was very greatly harassed. Josephus, Antiquities, book 12, chapter 7. This citadel is called "acra," that is, ירושלם [Jerusalem] and ἀκρόπολις [citadel]. Proved elsewhere.

units.la: Mittit edictum] 1. Machab. 1 43.
units.tr: He sends an edict] 1 Maccabees 1:43.

units.la: Sacra etiam leges & prophetarum volumina igne cremata] legis vocabulo intelligit quinque libros Mosis, & prophetarum etiam Hagiographos, qui latiore significatione propheta fuerunt. Autor More (is est Moses Ægyptius) de his, omnes scripti erant θεοπνευστοι, & omnes vocantur prophetæ. Ita sumes in illo, h. betis legem & prophetas.
units.tr: The sacred laws and the books of the prophets burned with fire] By the word "law" he means the five books of Moses, and by the prophets also the Hagiographa, which in a wider sense were prophets. The author Maimonides (that is, Moses the Egyptian) says that all these writings were θεόπνευστοι [divinely inspired], and all are called prophets. So you will take it in that: "you have the law and the prophets."

units.la: Matathias Iohannis F. sacerdos erat] Mathathias patrem habuit Iohannem, avum Simonem. Neuter horum pontifex fuit. Quocirca non est credibile Mathathiam pontificem fuisse. Quod tamen Ebræi temere nimis adfirmant. Nam ea tempestate summum sacerdotium venale erat, quod pessimi quique consequebantur. Cognomen ei erat Hasamonæus: unde Hasamonæus & filij ejus: &, fœdus quod inter Romanos & Iudam filium Hasamonæi, id est, Mathathiæ. Hinc origo nominis Hasamonæorum, quo posteri ejus omnes appellantur, quos nos Machabæos vocamus. Diserte R. David ad vocem Hasmannim, quæ habetur Psal. 68. 31. Mathathias filius Iohannis vocatur
units.tr: Mattathias, son of John, was a priest] Mattathias had John as his father and Simon as his grandfather. Neither of these was high priest. Therefore it is not credible that Mattathias was high priest, though the Hebrews affirm it too rashly. For at that time the high priesthood was for sale, and the worst men obtained it. His surname was Hasmonaeus, whence Hasmonaeus and his sons, and the covenant which the Romans made with Judas, son of Hasmonaeus, that is, of Mattathias. Hence comes the name of the Hasmonaeans, by which all his descendants are called, whom we call the Maccabees. Rabbi David explains this clearly at the word Hasmannim, which occurs in Psalm 68:31. Mattathias, son of John, is called

units.la: {P} ... Hafamonæus, & similiter filij ejus omnes vocantur Hafa-monæi. Minus bene Iosephus, Mathathias filius Iohannis,qui fuit Simeonis ex Hasfamonæo geniti. Nec melius autor Chronici Eusebius, Matthathias quidam ex sacerdotibus filius Hafamonæi.
units.tr: {P} ... Hasmonaeus, and likewise all his sons are called Hasmonaeans. Josephus is less accurate: Mattathias, son of John, who was born of Simeon, of Hasmonaeus. Nor does the author of the Chronicle, Eusebius, do any better: Mattathias, a certain one of the priests, son of Hasmonaeus.

units.la: Matathias] Græce est ματαθίας[?]. prætulerim ματαθιας[?], id est, Matthathias, vel certe Mathathias. Nam in historia Ebraica מַתִּתְיָה[?]. Legitur et מַתִּתְיָה[?], unde ματαθίας[?], id est, Mathathias. Quod in codice Aldino & apud Iosephum. Addam pro collario. In Iohasin sol. 14 pag. 2. Anno mundi 3611 rebellavit Mathathias filius Iohannis sacerdotis magni: & ipse est qui cognominatur Hasamonæus. Alibi est in eodem libro, Mathathias qui vocatur Hasmonæus: &, qui est principium Hasmonæorum.
units.tr: Mattathias] In Greek it is ματαθίας. I would prefer ματαθιας, that is, Matthathias, or at any rate Mathathias. For in the Hebrew history it is read מַתִּתְיָה, and also מַתִּתְיָה, whence ματαθίας, that is, Mathathias. This is what stands in the Aldine codex and in Josephus. I will add as a corollary: in Yoma, folio 14, page 2: "In the year of the world 3611 Mattathias, son of John the great priest, rebelled, and he himself is the one surnamed Hasmonaeus." Elsewhere in the same book: "Mattathias, who is called Hasmonaeus, and who is the beginning of the Hasmonaeans."

units.la: Sacerdos] sacerdos erat ex vice Ioarib, sive Ioiarib 1. Mach. 2. 1. Etiamne pontifex? non videtur. Nam in catalogo pontificum nulla ejus memoria usurpatur. Quanquam in historia Ebraica, Mathathias filius Iohannis iummus sacerdos. Quæ tamen verba ambigua sunt in Ebraeo. Nam verti possunt, filius Iohannis sacerdotis summi. Sed tollit omnem omnino dubitationem locus alter, Ipse est Mathathias summus sacerdos, qui sustulit manum suam primus contra regnum Græcorum, & qui præcepit ut Iudæi sabbatho pugnarent. Eadem habentur in Salmanticensi, & apud alios Iudæos. Quæ ex eodem fonte hausta, ab uno tantum autoritatem accipiunt, nempe a Iosepho Gorionis F. quem conflat in multis multifarie halluci-natum, ac proinde cum judicio legendum esse.
units.tr: Priest] He was a priest of the course of Joarib, or Joiarib, 1 Maccabees 2:1. Was he also high priest? It seems not, for no mention of him is made in the catalogue of high priests. Yet in the Hebrew history it says "Mattathias, son of John, the chief priest," though those words are ambiguous in Hebrew, for they can be rendered "son of John the chief priest." But another passage removes all doubt: "He himself is Mattathias the high priest, who first raised his hand against the kingdom of the Greeks, and who commanded that the Jews fight on the Sabbath." The same things are found in the Salmanticensis and among other Jews. These, drawn from the same source, derive their authority from one man alone, namely Josephus, son of Gorion, who is known to have often hallucinated in many ways, and so must be read with judgment.

units.la: Cum a regis cogeretur edicto parere] quorum dux erat Philippus quidam, Historia Ebraica, Chronicon templi secundi: Appelles, quem una cum Iudæo profanante Mathathias occidit, Iosephus.
units.tr: When he was compelled by the king's edict to obey] whose leader was a certain Philip. The Hebrew history, the Chronicle of the Second Temple, calls him Appelles, whom Mattathias killed together with the Jew who was profaning the sacrifice. Josephus.

units.la: Profanantem] profana sacra facientem. Historia Ebraica refert eum porcum immolasse. Quod si verum, dupliciter peccabat. Primum quod diis gentium sacrificabat: deinde quod suem immolabat, animal luto amicum immundumque.
units.tr: Profaning] performing profane sacrifices. The Hebrew history relates that he sacrificed a pig. If this is true, he sinned twice: first because he sacrificed to the gods of the nations, and then because he sacrificed a swine, an animal unclean and fond of mud.

units.la: Opido egressus] opidum vocat quod Iosephus κώμην[?], id est, vicum appellat, historia Machabæorum πόλιν[?], & Ebraica montem. Quomodo & interpres nostri, 1. Macbab. 2. 1. consedit in monte Modin. Hoc nomen alij Modein scribunt, id est, μα[illegible, ~6 letters] alij Modeim [illegible, ~6 letters]. In Chronico templi secundi & in historia Ebraica reperio [illegible, ~6 letters] Modeith, id est, [illegible, ~6 letters]. In comment. super Aboth, cap. 3. R. Eliezer Hammodei, id est, ex monte Hammodei, qui est prope Ierosolymam, quemadmodum dixerunt doctores nostri felicis memoriæ. Eusebius de locis, Modim, vicus juxta Diospolin, unde fuerunt Machabæi, quorum hodieq; ibidem sepulchra monstrantur. Modim, id est, [illegible, ~6 letters]: quomodo scriptum hoc nomen in Iosepho 12,8. Quanquam in Rufino Modin, id est, [illegible, ~6 letters]. Sed rectum puto [illegible, ~6 letters] ut Nun addita sit a librariis, sicut in [illegible, ~6 letters] et similibus. Ceterum egressus est opido in montes vicinos, ad quem confluebant quicunque pietatis ac recti studio ducebantur tanto numero ut justi exercitus speciem efficerent.
units.tr: He went out of the town] He calls it a town (opidum), which Josephus calls κώμη [village], the history of the Maccabees calls πόλις [city], and the Hebrew text calls a mountain. Our translators likewise, at 1 Maccabees 2:1, say "he settled in the mountain of Modin." Others write this name Modein, that is, μα[text illegible in scan], and others Modeim [text illegible in scan]. In the Chronicle of the Second Temple and in the Hebrew history I find [text illegible in scan] Modeith, that is, [text illegible in scan]. In the commentary on Aboth, chapter 3, Rabbi Eliezer Hammodei, that is, from the mountain of Hammodei, which is near Jerusalem, as our teachers of blessed memory have said. Eusebius, in his book on places: Modim, a village near Diospolis, whence the Maccabees came, whose tombs are still shown there today. Modim, that is, [text illegible in scan]: so this name is written in Josephus, 12.8. Though in Rufinus it is Modin, that is, [text illegible in scan]. But I think [text illegible in scan] is right, and that a Nun was added by the copyists, as in [text illegible in scan] and similar cases. Moreover, he went out of the town to the neighbouring mountains, and to him flocked all who were moved by zeal for piety and righteousness, in such numbers that they gave the appearance of a righteous army.

units.la: Id faciebat suggerentibus Ptolemæis. Vide 1.Mach. 6. 8.
units.tr: He did this at the urging of the Ptolemies. See 1 Mac. 6. 8.

units.la: ac tandem etiam occidebat. Sint pro exemplo duæ mulieres quæ infantes suos circumciderant, quas suspensis de mammis infantibus, publicè per urbem circumductas de muro præcipitarunt. Historia refertur, 2. Machab. 6. 10.
units.tr: And at last he even put them to death. For example, there were two women who had circumcised their infants. With the infants hanging from their breasts, they were paraded publicly through the city and hurled down from the wall. The story is told in 2 Mac. 6. 10.

units.la: horum historiam Iosephus peculiari libello complexus est, cui titulus, [illegible, ~8 letters] quod animus sit qui in nobis imperium habet. Vocatur etiam [illegible, ~8 letters], teste Eusebio Ecclef. hist. lib. 2. cap. 10. Nam hi fratres peculiariter Machabæi nuncupantur, ut & omnes alij, qui ea tempestate propter ritus patrios sævitiam Antiochi & ducum ejus experti sunt.
units.tr: Josephus treated their history in a separate little book, titled [illegible], that reason is what holds sway within us. It is also called [illegible], as Eusebius attests in Ecclesiastical History book 2, chapter 10. For these brothers are called the Maccabees in particular, as are all the others who in that period suffered the cruelty of Antiochus and his commanders on account of their ancestral rites.

units.la: Hannam vocat compositor historiæ Ebraicæ, quæ post filios ultima interiit: quam historiam invenies & 2. Machab. 7. 1. usque ad finem capitis.
units.tr: The compiler of the Hebrew history calls her Hannah, who died last, after her sons. You will find this history also in 2 Mac. 7. 1 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Ducem Iudam Quod epitheton Christiani commune fecerunt cum Iuda reliquis Hassamonæis: sed quam recte, viderint. Nam Ebræi soli Iudæ tribuunt.
units.tr: Judas the leader: Christians have made this epithet common to Judas and the other Hasmoneans, but let them consider how rightly. For only the Hebrews attribute it to Judas alone.

units.la: Apollonium præfectum Samariæ, Iosephus: [illegible, ~8 letters], Idem in Maccabaico. Huic Iudas ensem ademit, quo semper postea in bellis usus est.
units.tr: Apollonius, governor of Samaria, Josephus [calls him ...]. The same in the Maccabean book. Judas took his sword from him, which he afterwards always used in his wars.

units.la: Qui tum Syriæ præerat [illegible, ~10 letters].
units.tr: Who then governed Syria [illegible].

units.la: dux exercitus Syriæ, 1. Machab. 3. 13. Coelosyriæ præfectus, Dux exercitus Macedonici, Compositor historiæ Ebraicæ. Hæc fuit secunda expeditio Iudæ.
units.tr: commander of the Syrian army, 1 Mac. 3. 13. Governor of Coele-Syria; commander of the Macedonian army; compiler of the Hebrew history. This was Judas's second campaign.

units.la: Multiplicatis legionibus] hoc vocabulum mutuo sumpsit a militia Romana. Siquidem nullæ erant legiones in exercitu Syro-Macedonum. Quid igitur? Phalanges erant, quas appellat legiones. Sic interpres noster, quem vulgatum dicimus, legionem posuit pro phalange, 1. Machab. 9. 12. Nam in Græco ἢ φαλάγξ [?]. Octingentis ferme amisis] ἐξ ἀνδρῶν [illegible, ~6 letters] 1. Machab. 3. 14. ceteri fugerunt in terram Philistæorum.
units.tr: Multiplied legions: he borrowed this word from the Roman army, since there were no legions at all in the Syro-Macedonian army. What, then? They were phalanxes, which he calls legions. So our translator, whom we call the Vulgate, rendered "legion" for "phalanx" at 1 Mac. 9. 12, for in the Greek it is ἡ φάλαγξ [?]. Almost eight hundred lost: [ἐξ ἀνδρῶν ...] 1 Mac. 3. 14. The rest fled into the land of the Philistines.

units.la: F xhaustis penitus thesauris] condita deficiente pecunia, 1. Machab. 3. 39. Vide quoque 1. Machab. 1. 43. & Iosephum Ant. lib. 12. cap. 11.
units.tr: The treasuries utterly exhausted: money failing, as the reserves ran out, 1 Mac. 3. 39. See also 1 Mac. 1. 43 and Josephus, Antiquities book 12, chapter 11.

units.la: Qui ex ultra trecenta argenti talenta annua pensitave-rant] Supra 119. Qua tempestate Iudæi annuum stipendium trecenta argenti talenta regi dabant.
units.tr: Who had paid more than three hundred talents of silver a year: see above, p. 119. At that time the Jews paid the king an annual tribute of three hundred silver talents.

units.la: Ne Gentilibus quidem] Hæc includenda parenthesi usque ad, illis quidem, ut recte monuit Sigonius. Quare autem Christiani veteres maluerint dicere gentiles quam gentes, & ethnicos quam ἔθνη viderunt, quorum interest hæc scire. Ego scio gentes dici antiquissimis Ebræis, quos posterior ætas ἕλληνας, id est, Græcos appellavit: Christiani etiam paganos vocitarunt.
units.tr: Not even to the Gentiles: this clause should be enclosed in parentheses, down to "to those indeed", as Sigonius rightly observed. Why the early Christians preferred to say gentiles rather than nations, and pagans rather than ethnē, is something those who care to know should see for themselves. I know that the most ancient Hebrews used "gentes", which a later age called Hellēnes, that is, Greeks. Christians also called them pagans.

units.la: Inveteratas superstitiones] supra 121, cum dicit populum superstitionibus suscèptis reperiret. Innuit autem religiones gentilium, quas superstitiones appellat, quia religio propria veri Dei est. Qui religiosus est Deum veretur, qui superstitiosus timet. Quod tamen discrimen interpretes Bibliorum non observant.
units.tr: Long-established superstitions: see above, p. 121, where he says the people found superstitions adopted. He means the religions of the Gentiles, which he calls superstitions, because religion belongs to the true God. The religious man reveres God; the superstitious man fears. Yet the translators of the Bible do not observe this distinction.

units.la: Illis quidem] Iudæi, inquit, facile reliquebant Antiochum, apud quem nihil sancti erat.
units.tr: Indeed to those: the Jews, he says, readily abandoned Antiochus, with whom nothing was sacred.

units.la: Omnibus] tam Gentilibus quam Iudæis. Ipse olim omnibus regibus opulentior] [illegible, ~10 letters] 1. Machab. 3. 30. Quæ verba sic interpretatur Sebastianus Castalio, reges omnes superaverat largitione superaverat. Sed aliter interpres vulgatus.
units.tr: To all: both to the Gentiles and to the Jews. He himself once richer than all kings [illegible] 1 Mac. 3. 30. Sebastian Castalio renders these words thus: he had surpassed all kings in largesse. But the Vulgate translator renders them otherwise.

units.la: Copias cum Lysia partitur] homine nobili & regio genere orto. 1. Machab. 3. 32. Ex historia Ebraica colligimus fuisse filium patris Antiochi. Nam compositor illius historiæ Gorionides appellat. pellat eum filium patrui sive patruelem Eupatoris. Erant ergo Lysias & Eupator duorum fratrum filij hoc est ἀδελφιδοί[?]. Quod Appianus scribit de Demetrio & Eupatore:
units.tr: He shares his forces with Lysias, a man of noble birth and of royal stock, 1 Mac. 3. 32. From the Hebrew history we gather that he was the son of the father of Antiochus. For the compiler of that history calls him Gorionides, the son of the paternal uncle, that is, the cousin of Eupator. So Lysias and Eupator were the sons of two brothers, that is, adelphidoi. What Appian writes of Demetrius and Eupator:

units.la: Eique Syriam, &c.] constituit eum super negotia regia a flumine Euphrate usque ad flumen Aegypti: tum etiam filium nutriendum ei reliquit.
units.tr: And to him he gave Syria, &c.: he appointed him over royal affairs from the river Euphrates to the river of Egypt, and then left his son to him to be brought up.

units.la: Ipse in Persas profectus] anno Graecorum centesimo qua-dragesimo septimo.
units.tr: He himself set out against the Persians in the year 147 of the Greeks.

units.la: Doronem] delendum videtur: nisi Sulpitius edidit, Ptolemaeum Dorymenis, Gorgiam & Nicanorem. Quae conjectura Sigonij robur accipit a Josepho Ant.lib. 12.cap. 1. sed magis ex 1.Machab 3.30[?].
units.tr: Doron seems to need deleting, unless Sulpicius edited "Ptolemy, Dorymenes, Gorgias and Nicanor". Sigonius's conjecture gains strength from Josephus, Antiquities book 12, chapter 1, but more from 1 Mac. 3. 30 [?].

units.la: Tum Iudas] tertia expeditio Iudae.
units.tr: Then Judas: the third campaign of Judas.

units.la: Bene pugnatum] id est, feliciter.
units.tr: Fought well: that is, successfully.

units.la: Fusae hostium copiae] occisa sunt ad tria millia. Haec in Ma-spha acciderunt. Vide 1.Machab.4.23.
units.tr: The enemy forces routed: about three thousand were killed. This happened at Mizpah. See 1 Mac. 4. 23.

units.la: Tyriarum opum] purpurae marinae.
units.tr: Of the wealth of Tyre: sea purple.

units.la: Pag.116. Ex nunciis] ex iis qui evaserant.
units.tr: P. 116. From the messengers: from those who had escaped.

units.la: Immani exercitu] in quo erant LX millia peditum & VM equitum. Haec est quarta expeditio Iudae.
units.tr: With a huge army: in which there were 60,000 foot and 5,000 horse. This is the fourth campaign of Judas.

units.la: Ierosolymam regressus] anno regni Syriae sive Graecorum CXLVIII.
units.tr: He returned to Jerusalem in the year 148 of the Syrian or Greek reign.

units.la: Quod eversum ab Antiocho] triennio ante. Eversum autem templum dicit propter abolitam ibi deletamque religionem. Eam Iudas restituere animum intendit purgareq; templum quod prophanatum fuerat superstitione gentilium. Hoc praedictum a Daniele volunt Dan.8.14.& 12.,12.
units.tr: Which had been overthrown by Antiochus: three years before. He says the temple was overthrown because the religion there had been abolished and destroyed. Judas set himself to restore that religion and to cleanse the temple, which had been defiled by Gentile superstition. Some hold that this was foretold by Daniel: Dan. 8. 14 and 12. 12.

units.la: Quae continua templo] quae templo superstabat. Iosephus 12.14 Sed vide num potius legendum sit, quae contigua templo. Arcem autem dicit quam superius acram & acropolim vocari diximus. Unde in libro jejunij filij Acrae vocantur, qui illic in praesidio sedebant.
units.tr: Which stood next to the temple: which overlooked the temple. Josephus 12. 14. But see whether it should rather be read "which was contiguous to the temple". He calls the citadel which we said above is called the acra and the acropolis. Hence in the Book of Fasting the sons of Acra are named, who sat there in garrison.

units.la: Et loci natura superior] non ergo in urbe inferiore sita erat, sed in superiore, hoc est in civitate David. Nam templum subjectum habebat, quod in clivo montis Sion, Moria dicto.
units.tr: And the nature of the place was higher: so it was not situated in the lower city but in the upper, that is, in the city of David. For it had the temple lying below it, which was on the slope of Mount Zion, called Moriah.

units.la: Subjecta] loca circa templum.
units.tr: Surrounding: the places around the temple.

units.la: Crebris eruptionibus] eorum qui in arce erant.
units.tr: By frequent sallies: of those who were in the citadel.

units.la: At Lysias multiplicato exercitu] quinta expeditio, de qua nihil mihi adhuc lectum, nec apud Josephum, nec apud alios.
units.tr: But Lysias, with his army multiplied: the fifth campaign, of which I have read nothing so far, neither in Josephus nor in others.

units.la: Quærendum ergo unde habeat. Sigonius ad hunc locum annotat, Lysias, postquam semel victus recessit Antiochiam, elegit quidem milites, ut multiplicatis eis rursus veniret in Iu-dæam: verum venisse non dicitur, neque ab autore libri Machabæorum, neque a Iosepho, sed multa præl[?]ia fecun-da cum finitimis gentibus fecisse, quæ deinceps quinto ca-pite explicantur.
units.tr: We must ask, then, where he got it. Sigonius annotates on this passage: Lysias, after being once defeated, withdrew to Antioch, indeed chose soldiers so that, with his forces multiplied, he might come again into Judaea. But it is not said that he came, neither by the author of the Maccabean book nor by Josephus; rather, he fought many successful battles with the neighbouring peoples, which are explained afterwards in the fifth chapter.

units.la: Opidum Elymum] Elymaidem, 1. Machab. 6. r. Elymaida Iosephus 12. 13. Pertsepolim, 2. Machab. 9. 2. Ceterum Elymais esse videtur, quæ in libris canonicis Elam vocatur.
units.tr: The town of Elymus: Elymais, 1 Mac. 6. 1. Elymais, Josephus 12. 13. Persepolis, 2 Mac. 9. 2. Elymais seems to be what the canonical books call Elam.

units.la: Fanumque ibi situm] fanum Veneris, Appianus: Diane, Iosephus 12. 13. Verba Appiani sunt τὸ τῆς Ἐλυμαΐδος ἀφεδρῶ-νος τῆς ἱερῶν ἱεροῦ ἀγόν ... ψιλᾶ ἐνεπλησὶν ... Λυκ. [?]ἡ ἁγίου [?] Euergetes. Hieronymus commentario in Daniele ex Polybio et Diodoro refert Antiochum, cum templum Dianæ in Elymaide spoliare conaretur, oppressum a custodibus templi et vicinis gentibus, quibusdam phantasiis in amentiam versum, morbo interiisse in Tabes opido Perfidis. Iustinus lib. 31.
units.tr: And the temple situated there: the temple of Venus, Appian; Diana, Josephus 12. 13. Appian's words are: [τὸ τῆς Ἐλυμαΐδος ... ἱεροῦ ...]. Jerome, in his commentary on Daniel, drawing on Polybius and Diodorus, reports that Antiochus, when he tried to plunder the temple of Diana in Elymais, was overwhelmed by the temple guards and the neighbouring peoples, was driven into madness by certain phantasms, and died of disease at Tabae, a town of Persis. Justin, book 31.

units.la: Interea in Syria rex Antiochus, cum gravi tributo pacis a Romanis victus oneratusque esset, seu inopia pecuniæ compulsus, seu avaritia folicitatus, qua sperabat se, sub specie tributariæ necessitatis excusatius sacrilegia com-missorum, adhibito exercitu, nocte templum Didymæi Iovis aggredi-tur. Qua re prodita concursu incolarum cum omni militia interficitur. Quæ conciliabis, si hos loqui dixeris de Antiocho magno aut Sidete, et illos de Antiocho Epi-phane. Magnus enim et Sidetes perierunt in Perside: Epiphanes fugatus ex mærore animi corporis morbo incubuit. Qua de re dictum alias, si Deus voluerit.
units.tr: Meanwhile in Syria King Antiochus, weighed down and overcome by the heavy tribute imposed by the Romans for peace, whether compelled by lack of money or spurred on by avarice, by which he hoped under the pretext of tributary need to excuse the sacrileges committed, with an army brought up, attacks by night the temple of Didymaean Jupiter. The plot being betrayed, he is killed by the gathering of the inhabitants together with all the soldiery. These things you may reconcile, if you say that the former speak of Antiochus the Great or Sidetes, and the latter of Antiochus Epiphanes. For the Great and Sidetes perished in Persia; Epiphanes, put to flight, fell sick of bodily illness from grief of mind. About this matter I have spoken elsewhere, if God wills.
