units.la: Pag 127. Vel a Lyfimacho] Quis ille Lyfimachus? An qui Menelao successit in pontificatu, cujus mentio pag. 120? Sigonius legit, res a Lysia improspere gestas, reliqua superare arbitratur a gloriosa mate. [?]
units.tr: P. 127. Or by Lysimachus: Who is that Lysimachus? Is he the one who succeeded Menelaus in the priesthood, whose mention is on p. 120? Sigonius reads "the affairs unsuccessfully handled by Lysias," and thinks the rest surpass by reason of the glorious [?].

units.la: Post paucos dies moritur] obiit Babylonia anno Græcorum CXLIX. 1. Machab. 6. 16. Sed vide fis Iosephum lib. 12. cap. 13, et 2. Machab. 9. Vide quoque historiam Ebraicam, quam nunc Latinam facere per otium non licet. Propero enim ad alia.
units.tr: After a few days he dies: he died in Babylon in the year 149 of the Greeks. 1 Mac. 6. 16. But see also Josephus, book 12, chapter 13, and 2 Mac. 9. See also the Hebrew history, which I have no leisure to turn into Latin now; for I hasten on to other matters.

units.la: Cui Eupator nomen erat] Sic appellatus fuit a Syris propter patris virtutem, Appianum: a Lysia educatore 1. Machab. 6. 17. Eupa-
units.tr: Cui Eupator nomen erat] So he was called by the Syrians on account of his father's virtue, Appian; from Lysias, his tutor 1 Macc. 6:17. Eupa-

units.la: 17. Eupator autem potius erat cognomen, quam nomen proprium. Aut mutatum ei fuit nomen in regno more apud veteres tralatitio. Hunc juniorem Antiochum appellat Eusebius.
units.tr: 1 Macc. 6:17. Eupator, however, was a surname rather than a proper name. Or his name was changed when he became king, as was the common custom among the ancients. Eusebius calls him the younger Antiochus.

units.la: Ea tempestate] anno post obitum Antiochi Epiphanis, qui Graecorum erat CL.
units.tr: In that season] in the year after the death of Antiochus Epiphanes, which was the 150th year of the Greeks.

units.la: Cum centum millibus] videtur legendum, cum peditum centum millibus.
units.tr: With a hundred thousand] it seems we should read "with a hundred thousand foot soldiers."

units.la: Elephantis] triginta duobus, 1. Machab 6. 30. Iosephus lib. 12. cap. 4. octoginta, historia Ebraica.
units.tr: Elephants] thirty-two, 1 Macc. 6:30. Josephus, book 12, ch. 4, says eighty; the Hebrew history too.

units.la: Quia infido ingenio, &c. ] legendum opinor, qua pro quia, ut pax subintelligatur. Qua pace, inquit, infido ingenio male usus est: perfidiam consecuta ultio. Constat enim verbum substantivum (est) in hac historia saepius desiderari. Qui hoc nescit, nihil scit.
units.tr: Because of his faithless nature, etc.] I think we should read "qua" for "quia", so that "peace" is understood. "By that peace," he says, "he misused his faithless nature; vengeance followed his treachery." It is well established that the substantive verb (est) is often omitted in this history. Whoever does not know this knows nothing.

units.la: Demetrius Seleuci filius] Appianus in Syriacis hunc Demetrium ait fuisse Σελεύκου μὲν γὰρ υἱὸν, Ἀντιόχου δὲ Ἐπιφανοῦς ἀδελφιδοῦν, γαμβρὸν δὲ τῆς μεγάλης Ἀντιόχου, ἀνεψιὸν τοῦ [?] non ergo patruus erat Antiochi Eupatoris, ut Iustinus lib. XXXIV scriptum reliquit: sed patruelis, ut recte Appianus eum appellat. Erant enim duorum fratrum filij. Adito sis ad locum illum Appiani, & ad Epitomen Livij.
units.tr: Demetrius, son of Seleucus] Appian in the Syriaca says this Demetrius was the son of Seleucus [Greek: Σελεύκου μὲν γὰρ υἱὸν], but the nephew of Antiochus Epiphanes [Greek: Ἀντιόχου δὲ Ἐπιφανοῦς ἀδελφιδοῦν], son-in-law of Antiochus the Great [Greek: γαμβρὸν δὲ τῆς μεγάλης Ἀντιόχου], and cousin of ... So he was not the paternal uncle of Antiochus Eupator, as Justin wrote in book 34, but a cousin, as Appian rightly calls him. For they were the sons of two brothers. Go to that passage of Appian, and to the Epitome of Livy.

units.la: Seleuci filius] non Antiochi magni, ut existimasse videtur Iustinus. Nam Antiochum Epiphanem appellat fratrem Demetrij, cum fuerit fratris filius. Seleucus enim & Antiochus ille germani fratres erant. Horum filij Eupator & Demetrius. Nihil certius.
units.tr: Son of Seleucus] not of Antiochus the Great, as Justin seems to have thought. For he calls Antiochus Epiphanes the brother of Demetrius, though he was his brother's son. Seleucus and that Antiochus were full brothers, and their sons were Eupator and Demetrius. Nothing is more certain.

units.la: Ut audivit Antiochum decessisse] Audita morte Antiochi, cujus loco Romae obses fuerat, petivit primo ut se in regnum reducerent, secundo ut saltem obses esse desineret, quandoquidem permutatus esset patruelis, qui tum defunctus erat. Quum ne hoc quidem impetraret, aufugit navigio. Appianus.
units.tr: When he heard that Antiochus had died] On hearing of the death of Antiochus, in whose place he had been a hostage at Rome, he first asked that they restore him to the kingdom; second, that at least he be released from being a hostage, since the cousin for whom he had been exchanged had now died. When he did not obtain even this, he escaped by ship. Appian.

units.la: Quod cum ei negatum fuisset] nam Romani conducibilius esse sibi ducebant si Syria ab Antiocho tum puero adhuc regeretur, quam a Demetrio, eo tempore annum ingressio tertium & vigesimum.
units.tr: When this was refused him] for the Romans thought it more advantageous for themselves if Syria were ruled by Antiochus, then still a boy, than by Demetrius, who at that time was entering his twenty-third year.

units.la: Clam Roma profugit] specie venandi ab urbe profectus Hostiae navem conscendit.
units.tr: Fled secretly from Rome] setting out from the city on the pretext of hunting, he boarded a ship at Hostia.

units.la: In Syriam venit] ubi exceptus fuit a Syris magna gratulatione, regnumque adeptus est, Lysia primum occiso, deinde puero & Ti{a}Timarcho, qui Babylonis præfecturam male administrave-rat. Quamobrem Soter appellatus est, orto a Babyloniis initio.
units.tr: He came into Syria] where he was welcomed by the Syrians with great rejoicing and gained the kingdom. Lysias was killed first, then the boy, and Timarchus, who had mismanaged the governorship of Babylon. Hence he was called Soter, a title that began with the Babylonians.

units.la: Antiocho filio] puero malim, nisi scripsit, Antiocho Antiochi F. Similis defectus Igitur Demetrij filius. Nam legendum, Demetrius Demetrij filius Puer ætate erat, cum interficeretur, decennis, postquam novennis, id est, cum sustulit, ut est in Appiano, ad regnum pervenisset. Unum ergo duntaxat annum regnavit. Quibus nosfer adjecit sex menses. Quanquam in Eusebiano 2.
units.tr: "Antiochus the son"] I would prefer "the boy", unless he wrote "Antiochus, son of Antiochus". There is a similar defect: so "Demetrius, son of Demetrius" should be read. He was a boy of ten, after nine, when he was killed; that is, when he removed him, as is in Appian, he had come to the kingdom. He therefore reigned only one year. Our author added six months, though in the Eusebian ... 2.

units.la: Hoc regnante primum Iudæi a populo Romano amicitiam fœdusque petiere] 1.Machab.8. Iosephus, Ant. lib. 12. cap.17. Gorionides lib.4.cap.23.
units.tr: During his reign the Jews first sought friendship and a covenant with the Roman people] 1 Macc. 8. Josephus, Ant. book 12, ch. 17. Gorionides, book 4, ch. 23.

units.la: Et Alchimum [Iudæum] scribo Alcimum. Nam Græce Ἀλκίμος, et in historia Ebraica <bl>...</bl> Alio nomine Iacimus dicebatur, teste Iosepho. Utrumque nomen extat in sacris. Nam Alcimus est Eliacim, et Iacimus, Ioacim, qui Ebræis Iehoiacim sive Ioiacim, Alcimus ipse, ut est in historia Ebraica, tempore Antiochi, mutata lege, carnes suillas comederat. Sunt qui scribant ipsum ex familia Aharonis fuisse, sunt rursum qui negant. Ut ut sit, constitutus fuit sacerdos a Demetrio 1.Machab.7.9. Videatur Iosephus lib.12.cap.15. cui dissidium cum priore Machabæorum. In quo, inquies? In eo quod scribit post excessum Alcimi populum communibus suffragiis pontificatum Iudæ tradiffe, qui eum per triennium administrarit. Nam Alcimus diu post Iudam vixit. Successit enim Lysimacho an Menelao? quem Menelaum rex suasu Lysiæ misssum in Beroeam occidi curaverat. Quare offensus Onias Menelai filius in Ægyptum concessit, ibique, impetrato a Ptolemæo rege loco in præfectura Heliopolitana, templum simile Ierosolymitano extruxit.
units.tr: And for "Alchimum [Iudaeum]" I write "Alcimum". In Greek it is [Alkimos], and in the Hebrew history ... He was also called Iacimus by another name, according to Josephus. Both names occur in Scripture. Alcimus is Eliakim, and Iacimus is Joiakim, who in Hebrew is Jehoiakim or Ioiakim. Alcimus himself, as the Hebrew history says, had eaten pork in the time of Antiochus, when the law was changed. Some write that he was of the family of Aaron; others deny it. Be that as it may, he was appointed priest by Demetrius, 1 Macc. 7:9. See Josephus, book 12, ch. 15, where there is a disagreement with the earlier book of Maccabees. In what, you ask? In that Josephus writes that after the death of Alcimus the people, by common vote, handed the high priesthood to Judas, who administered it for three years. For Alcimus lived long after Judas. Did he succeed Lysimachus or Menelaus? The king, at the urging of Lysias, had ordered Menelaus, whom he had sent to Beroea, to be killed there. Offended by this, Onias, son of Menelaus, withdrew into Egypt, and there, having obtained from King Ptolemy a place in the prefecture of Heliopolis, he built a temple like the one at Jerusalem.

units.la: Volt Nicanor in bello occubuit] historia habetur apud Iosephum lib.12.cap.17. Gorionidem lib.4 cap.24. Vide quoque 1.Machab.7.26, et 2.Machab.14.
units.tr: Nicanor fell in the war] the story is found in Josephus, book 12, ch. 17, and in Gorionides, book 4, ch. 24. See also 1 Macc. 7:26 and 2 Macc. 14.

units.la: Adversum Iudam confligunt] hæc gesta sunt anno Græcorum CLII; et in hac pugna Iudas occubuit, 1.Machab.9, Iosephus 12.18.
units.tr: They engage in battle against Judas] these things happened in the year of the Greeks 152; and in this battle Judas fell, 1 Macc. 9; Josephus 12:18.

units.la: Interea Alchimus, cum fœde Ierosolymam vastasset, moritur] 1.Machab.9.55. Iosephus 12.17. Hunc Alcimum a genere sacerdotali alienum fuisse scribit Eusebius: quod dextre capiendum. Nam ἡγ[?]ὼ ἱερανχὸς posuit pro ἀρχιερατικός, id est, pontificale. Sic ἱερεὺς pro ἀρχιερεύς, & ἱερωσύνη pro ἀρχιερωσύνη. Notavi alias non semel.
units.tr: Meanwhile Alcimus, after he had foully laid waste Jerusalem, dies] 1 Macc. 9:55. Josephus 12:17. Eusebius writes that this Alcimus was foreign to the priestly line, which must be understood rightly. For he used [hiarchikos] for [archieratikos], that is, pontifical; so [hiereus] for [archiereus], and [hierosynē] for [archierosynē]. I have noted this elsewhere more than once.

units.la: In locum Iudae Ionathan fratrem eius deligunt] non statim a caede Iudae, sed aliquanto post, cum se tota fere regio Bacchidi tradidisset.
units.tr: They choose Jonathan, his brother, in Judas's place] not immediately after Judas was slain, but some time later, when almost the whole region had surrendered to Bacchides.

units.la: Qui propositis conditionibus data] inter conditiones erat, neutrum arma moturum in alterum.
units.tr: Who, after terms were proposed] among the terms was that neither side would take up arms against the other.

units.la: Pertugas captivosque] captivi utrimque redditi fuerunt. De transfugis reddendis nulla mentio nec apud Iosephum, nec in libris Machabaeorum.
units.tr: Prisoners and captives] captives were returned on both sides. There is no mention of returning deserters, either in Josephus or in the books of the Maccabees.

units.la: Adolescens quidam] hoc accidit anno Graecorum, sive Selencidarum, CLX.
units.tr: A certain young man] this happened in the year 160 of the Greeks, or Seleucids.

units.la: Nomine Alexander] Alexander Balas, sive Bales. Iosepho dicitur Balles: aliis ὁ βαλάς, id est, filius Balae: quibusdam Veles. De hoc Appianus in Syriacis, Adversus Demetrium exortus est quidam Alexander falso in Seleucidarum gentem se inserens: quem Ptolemaeus Aegypti rex fovebat odio Demetrii, atque ita conniventibus Aegyptiis Alexander Demetrium regno expulit. Qui postquam in exilio defunctus est, filius paterno nomine Demetrius regnum recepit, & quia vicit alienum a sua familia, Nicatorem Syri cognominaverunt, ut secundum post Seleucum, a quo descenderunt reges Syriae. Et Iustinus lib XXXV. Antic-chenses adjuvantibus Ptolemaeo rege Aegypti,& Attalo rege Asiae, & Ariarathe Cappadociae, bello a Demetrio lacessiti, subornant propalam quendam loitis extremae juvenem, qui Syriae regnum velut paternum armis repeteret, & nequid contumeliae decesset, nomen ei Alexandro inditur, genitusque ab Antiocho rege dicitur. Tantum odium Demetrii apud omnes erat, ut aemulo ejus non vires regiae tantum, verum etiam generis nobilitas consensu omnium tribueretur.
units.tr: Named Alexander] Alexander Balas, or Bales. Josephus calls him Balles; others [ho Balas], that is, son of Bala; some Veles. Of him Appian in the Syriaca says: "Against Demetrius there arose a certain Alexander, who falsely inserted himself into the Seleucid line. Ptolemy, king of Egypt, favoured him out of hatred for Demetrius, and so, with the Egyptians conniving, Alexander drove Demetrius from the kingdom. When he died in exile, his son, with his father's name Demetrius, recovered the kingdom; and because he conquered one foreign to his family, the Syrians surnamed him Nicator, as second after Seleucus, from whom the kings of Syria descended." And Justin, book 35: The Antiochenes, attacked in war by Demetrius, and aided by Ptolemy, king of Egypt, Attalus, king of Asia, and Ariarathes of Cappadocia, openly put forward a certain youth of the lowest rank, who would reclaim the kingdom of Syria by arms as if it were his paternal inheritance. Lest anything of disgrace be lacking, he was named Alexander and said to have been born of King Antiochus. So great was the hatred of Demetrius among everyone that his rival was granted, by the consent of all, not only royal power but also noble birth.

units.la: Antiochi] Epiphanis. Historia Machabaeorum vocat filium Antiochi, quia videlicet habebatur pro filio ejus. Sic in Evangelio Iosephi appellatur pater Iesu. Sic etiam idola Dij nuncupantur.
units.tr: Of Antiochus] Epiphanes. The history of the Maccabees calls him son of Antiochus, because he was evidently regarded as his son. So in the Gospel of Joseph, Joseph is called the father of Jesus. So also idols are called gods.

units.la: Annos XIII] XI habet Iosephus. Vide Antiquitates ejus 13.5. in fine. Fœdus cum Ionatha fecerat] cui etiam pontificatum detulit, anno quarto postquam occisus est Iudas. Iosephus loco citato, ἀξιώσας δὲ τὸν Ἰωνάθην συνθήκην ποιήσασθαι μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ [?] τοῦ ἐπιστολῶν [?] ... ἐν τῷ πολέμῳ, τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιστάσεως [?] ...
units.tr: Thirteen years] Josephus has eleven. See his Antiquities 13:5, at the end. He had made a covenant with Jonathan, to whom he also offered the high priesthood in the fourth year after Judas was killed. Josephus, in the place cited, says that he thought Jonathan worthy to make an agreement with him [Greek: ἀξιώσας δὲ τὸν Ἰωνάθην συνθήκην ποιήσασθαι μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ] ... in the war, of his own oversight ...

units.la: Vide 1. Mach. 10. 18. et deinceps.
units.tr: See 1 Macc. 10:18 and following.

units.la: Veste purpurea] quæ amicis regum dari solebat, unde purpuratorum nomen. In Iosepho est [?] πορφύραν.
units.tr: Purple robe] which was customarily given to the friends of kings, whence the name "purpurati". In Josephus it is [porphyran].

units.la: Inlignibus regiis] in eodem, ἱμάτιον [?] στέφανον [?] χρυσοῦν [?] & coronam auream.
units.tr: In royal insignia] in the same passage: [himation], [stephanon] [chrysoun], and a golden crown.

units.la: Ita quinquennio quo rerum potitus est] Alexander vi-delicet. Mox ait, cum regnasset annos quinq;. Vide quæ scri-psimus ad illum locum.
units.tr: So for the five years in which he held power] Alexander, namely. Soon he says, "when he had reigned five years." See what we have written on that passage.

units.la: Res Iudæorum tranquillæ fuerunt] 1. Mach. 9. 73. & cessavit gladius ab Israel. Quod pro eo habendum ac si dixisset, res eorum tranquillæ fuerunt, sive quies eis fuit a bello.
units.tr: The affairs of the Jews were quiet] 1 Macc. 9:73: "and the sword ceased from Israel." This should be taken as if he had said that their affairs were quiet, or that they had rest from war.

units.la: Igitur Demetrij filius] historia posci ut legamus, Demetrius Demetrij filius. Hic a Syris Nicanor sive Nicator cognominabatur. Caussam supra ex Appiano produximus.
units.tr: Therefore the son of Demetrius] the history requires that we read "Demetrius, son of Demetrius". He was called by the Syrians Nicanor or Nicator. We brought forward the reason from Appian above.

units.la: Hortante Lasthene] sumpsit ex Iosepho. Vide illum Orig. Iud. lib. 13. cap. 8. Sed & Iustinum, lib. 35. Hujus Lasthenis, si me non fallit augurium, meminit prior Machabæorum cap. 11. vers. 31.
units.tr: Lasthenes urging] Taken from Josephus; see Antiquities of the Jews, book 13, ch. 8. But also Justin, book 35. Of this Lasthenes, if I am not mistaken about the augury, the first book of Maccabees, ch. 11, vers. 31, makes mention.

units.la: Iam tum genero infestum] propter insidias, quas ei struxerat per Ammonium quendam. Iosephus.
units.tr: already then hostile to his son-in-law] because of the plots which he had laid against him through a certain Ammonius. Josephus.

units.la: Quam spe Syriæ occupandæ] 1. Machab. 11. 1. quærebat obtinere regnum Alexandri dolo, & addere illud regno suo.
units.tr: who, with the hope of seizing Syria] 1 Macc. 11.1: he sought to obtain the kingdom of Alexander by trickery and to add it to his own kingdom.

units.la: Filiam] Cleopatram.
units.tr: his daughter] Cleopatra.

units.la: Vincitur Ptolemæus, cadit Alexander, &c.] locum hunc ita interpolat ad historiæ fidem Sigonius, Vincitur Alexander, cadit Ptolemæus. Vincitur Alexander, & paullo post interficitur. Cui firmando consequa verba, cum regnasset annos quinque. Quæ de Ptolemæo accipi nullo modo possunt.
units.tr: Ptolemy is conquered, Alexander falls, etc.] Sigonius alters this place to fit the facts of history: "Alexander is conquered, Ptolemy falls." Alexander is conquered, and shortly after is put to death. In support of this follow the words "when he had reigned five years." These cannot in any way be understood of Ptolemy.

units.la: Cadit Ptolemæus] non in prælio cecidit: sed aliquot diebus post ex vulneribus in caput jacentis influxis, cum equus, quo vehebatur, barritu elephanti consternatus eum excussisset, extinctus est. Livius lib. 52. Ptolemæus in caput graviter vulneratus inter curationem, dum ossa medici terebrare contendunt, expiravit. Et paullo post interficitur] a Zabelo Arabum dynasta, ad quem fugerat: qui caput ejus misit ad Ptolemaeum, quod is ante mortem cum voluptate spectasse traditur.
units.tr: Ptolemy falls] He did not fall in battle, but some days later, from wounds to the head, when the horse on which he was riding, startled by the trumpeting of an elephant, threw him off; he died. Livy, book 52: Ptolemy, gravely wounded in the head, died during treatment while the doctors were trying to bore through the bone. And shortly after he is put to death by Zabelus, prince of the Arabs, to whom he had fled; Zabelus sent his head to Ptolemy, who is said to have looked upon it with pleasure before he died.

units.la: Annos quinque] consentit Iosephus, non item Eusebius, qui annos decem ei tribuit cum septem mensibus.
units.tr: Five years] Josephus agrees, but not Eusebius, who gives him ten years and seven months.

units.la: Regnum adeptus] indeptus est in Lu[?]iae impressis: ceteri habent adeptus.
units.tr: obtained the kingdom] In the printed editions of [?] it reads "indeptus"; the others have "adeptus".

units.la: Iudaeos legibus suis reddidit] non legibus, sed immunitate donavit. Nam prius cum religione leges recuperaverant: tributa & vectigalia regibus Syriae adhuc persolvebant. Ea remisit in gratiam Ionathae Demetrius, Iosephus lib.13.cap.8.& 1. Machab.11.28. Vide sequentia.
units.tr: He restored the Jews to their own laws] Not with laws but with immunity he granted them. For before this they had recovered their laws along with their religion; they still paid tributes and taxes to the kings of Syria. Demetrius remitted these out of favour to Jonathan: Josephus, book 13, ch. 8, and 1 Macc. 11.28. See what follows.

units.la: Tryphon, qui partium Alexandri fuerat] Diodotus cognomine Tryphon genere Apamenus. Iosephus lib.13.cap.9. Diodotum etiam vocat Appianus, lib.16. & Strabo, lib.14. Verba Appiani sunt, Nicator in expeditione Parthica captus vixit in Phraatae regia, regis sorore Rodogina ducta in matrimonium. Ceterum Syriae regiam tum vacuam occupavit servus regum Diodotus, inducto Alexandro puero Alexandri Nothi ex Ptolemaei nata filio: quo mox sublato ipse regnare ausus est, ascito sibi novo Tryphonis nomine. In Orosio lib.5. cap.2. perperam Diodorus legitur pro Diodotus. Alexandrum filium autem dicit quem Appianus Alexandrum puerum appellat. Nam duo erant, pater & filius. Quocirca nihil mutandum in his verbis. Demetrio capto Diodotus quidam cum Alexandri filio regnum ejus & regnum nomen usurpavit: qui postea ipsum Alexandrum filium, quem participem periculi in pervadendo habuerat, ne in obtinendo consortem haberet, occidit.
units.tr: Tryphon, who had been on the side of Alexander] Diodotus, surnamed Tryphon, of Apamean birth. Josephus, book 13, ch. 9. Appian also calls him Diodotus, book 16, and Strabo, book 14. Appian's words are: "Nicator, taken on the Parthian expedition, lived in the court of Phraates, having married Rodogyna, the king's sister. But the royal seat of Syria, then empty, was seized by Diodotus, a slave of the kings, who brought in Alexander the boy, son of Alexander Nothus by Ptolemy's daughter; when he was soon removed, Diodotus himself dared to reign, taking the new name Tryphon." In Orosius, book 5, ch. 2, "Diodorus" is wrongly read for "Diodotus". He says "the son Alexander", whom Appian calls "Alexander the boy", for there were two, father and son. Therefore nothing in these words should be changed. After Demetrius was captured, a certain Diodotus, with the son of Alexander, usurped his kingdom and royal title; he afterwards killed the son Alexander himself, whom he had had as a partner in the danger of seizing power, so that he would not have a colleague in holding it.

units.la: Tryphon] vel Trypho, quod ita scribitur a Latinis, ut Plato, ut Zeno, quae Graece Τρύφων, Πλάτων & Ζήνων scribuntur cum N fine. In talibus Latina consuetudo locum habet potius, quam Graeca.
units.tr: Tryphon] or Trypho, which is how the Latins write it, as with Plato and Zeno, which in Greek are written with a final N [Τρύφων, Πλάτων, Ζήνων]. In such cases Latin custom has more place than Greek.

units.la: Praef[?]ctus Syriae regno post haec verba punctum esse ponendum admonuit nos Carolus Sigonius. Subintelligitur autem erat, aut aliquid tale. Quod fugit non effugit. Supra ex Appiano Alexandri filium Alexandrum appellavimus. Id refellit prior Machabaeorum. Nam in eo Antiochus nominatur, 1.Machab.11. §4. Si recte, tum legendum in Orosio, Alexandri filio & Alexxandri filium.
units.tr: Prefect of Syria] Carolus Sigonius reminded us that a full stop should be placed after these words. "Was" or something like it is understood. What has slipped by has not slipped away. Above, from Appian, we called the son of Alexander "Alexander". The earlier book of Maccabees refutes this, for in it Antiochus is named: 1 Macc. 11. §4. If that is right, then in Orosius we should read "Alexandri filio" and "Alexandri filium".

units.la: Contra[?]] vicissim: adverbium est, non praepositio.
units.tr: Contra] in turn: it is an adverb, not a preposition.

units.la: Terribilis XL millium exercitu] 1. Machab. 12. 41. Et exivit Jonathas obviam illi cum quadraginta millibus virorum electorum in prælium.
units.tr: Terrible, with an army of 40,000] 1 Macc. 12.41. And Jonathan went out to meet him with forty thousand chosen men for battle.

units.la: Ptolemaidam] potius Ptolemaidem, a recto Ptolemais, Dicitur & Tholemais: unde Tholemaidenses. Quod historiam attinet, primum comprehendit eum, postea occidit Bascamæuna cum duobus filiis 1. Machab. 13. 23.
units.tr: Ptolemais] rather Ptolemaidem, from the nominative Ptolemais. It is also called Tholemais, whence the Tholemaidenses. As regards the history, he first took him prisoner, and afterwards killed Bascamauna with his two sons 1 Macc. 13.23.

units.la: Ad Simonem] qui Thasi cognominabatur. Ionathan autem Iudæis præfuit, si Iosephum sequimur, annis duodeviginti, interfectus anno pontificatus sui decimo quarto.
units.tr: To Simon] who was surnamed Thasi. Jonathan, however, ruled the Jews, if we follow Josephus, for eighteen years, and was killed in the fourteenth year of his high priesthood.

units.la: Is funus fratris magnifice curavit] collegit ossa ejus & sepelivit ea in Modin, urbe patrum ejus 1. Machab. 13. 25. Hinc dicimus Modin fuisse patriam Hasamonæi Mattathiæ. Nam qui eum Ierosolymæ natum fuisse tradunt, ex hoc loco convincuntur erroris.
units.tr: He honoured his brother's funeral magnificently] he gathered his bones and buried them at Modin, the city of his fathers 1 Macc. 13.25. Hence we say Modin was the native place of the Hasmonean Mattathias. Those who report that he was born at Jerusalem are refuted in error by this passage.

units.la: Septemque illas pyramidas] de quibus 1. Machab. 13. 27[?]. Morem hunc ex Ægypto profectum notavit Diodorus. Vide Sigonium.
units.tr: And those seven pyramids] concerning which 1 Macc. 13. 27[?]. Diodorus noted that this custom came from Egypt. See Sigonius.

units.la: Annua ejus] Iudæa videlicet. Sed placet conjectura Gisellini nostri legentis eis pro ejus.
units.tr: Its yearly] that is, Judaea. But the conjecture of our Gisellinus, who reads "eis" for "ejus", pleases me.

units.la: In perpetuum remittit] anno primo Simonis, quem Iosephus vocat ἐτῷ τῆς ἐλευθερίας καὶ τῶν ἀνεσφόρων [?], qui in annum Græcorum CLXX incidit. Hoc anno primum Iudæi plenam immunitatem consecuti sunt, cum prius, tributa semper & vectigalia regibus victimis pependissent.
units.tr: He remits in perpetuity] in the first year of Simon, which Josephus calls the year of liberty and of the exempt [ἐτῷ τῆς ἐλευθερίας καὶ τῶν ἀνεσφόρων], which falls in the Greek year 170. In this year the Jews first obtained full immunity, whereas before they had always paid tributes and taxes to the kings.

units.la: Id gestum Demetrij regis anno secundo] qui fuit primus Simonis ethnarchæ, & CLXX regni Syriæ, ut diximus.
units.tr: This was done in the second year of King Demetrius] which was the first year of Simon as ethnarch, and the 170th of the kingdom of Syria, as we said.

units.la: Unde 1. Machab. 13. 4. Anno centesimo septuagesimo ablatum est jugum gentium ab Israel. Vide Iosephum Antiq. lib. 13. cap. 1.
units.tr: Whence 1 Macc. 13.4. In the 170th year the yoke of the nations was removed from Israel. See Josephus, Antiquities, book 13 ch. 1.

units.la: Abanorum regum] intelligit reges Syriæ, quorum imperium in Asia.
units.tr: Of the Abanian kings] he means the kings of Syria, whose rule was in Asia.

units.la: Qui Iudæis vel pontifices vel reges fuerunt] malim, vel principes vel reges fuerunt. Nam qui reges etiam pontifices erant. Sic Simon & qui eum secuti sunt usque ad Aristobulum cum pontificatu principatum administrarunt. Primus Aristobulus diadema sibi sumpsit: a quo deinde reges & pontifices. Iure pontificis] & principis. vel si eum ducem aut ethnarcham libet appellare, quæ in idem recidunt. Sic vocatur 1. Mach. 15 1. Σίμωνι ἱερέα καὶ ἐθνάρχῃ τῶν Ἰουδαίων: quæ vetus interpres convertit, Simoni sacerdoti & principi gentis Iudæorum. Nam ἐθνάρχης, princeps gentis.
units.tr: Who were for the Jews either high priests or kings] I would prefer "either leaders or kings", for those who were kings were also high priests. Thus Simon and those who followed him, down to Aristobulus, administered the leadership together with the high priesthood. Aristobulus was the first to take the diadem for himself; from him kings and high priests followed. By right of high priest] and leader, or if one prefers to call him commander or ethnarch, which come to the same thing. Thus he is called 1 Mach. 15.1: to Simon, priest and ethnarch of the Jews [Σίμωνι ἱερέα καὶ ἐθνάρχῃ τῶν Ἰουδαίων]. The old translator renders this, "to Simon the priest and prince of the nation of the Jews," for ethnarch means prince of the nation.

units.la: Tum a suis tum a populo Romano] 1.Machab. 14.25 ubi Latina editio, populus Romanus, Græca habet ὁ δῆμος simpliciter. Quod reflius intelligitur de populo Iudæo, quam de populo Romano. Sane historiæ veritas postulat ut hic legamus potius, tum a suis tum a regibus. Nam honos ipse delatus est fuit a regibus Alexandro & Demetrio 1.Machab. 11 27. & 14.38.
units.tr: From his own people and from the Roman people] 1 Macc. 14.25, where the Latin edition has "populus Romanus", while the Greek simply has [ὁ δῆμος]. This is more readily understood of the Jewish people than of the Roman people. Indeed the truth of history requires that we read here rather "from his own people and from the kings", for the honour itself was conferred by the kings Alexander and Demetrius, 1 Macc. 11.27 and 14.38.

units.la: Post octo annos] Si cœpit præesse anno CLXX, ut apparet ex 1.Machab. 13.41. præfuit duntaxat septem annis. Nam anno CLXXVII occisus fuit, infidus generi sui circum ventus, 1.Machab. 16.14.
units.tr: After eight years] If he began to rule in the year 170, as appears from 1 Macc. 13.41, he ruled only seven years. For he was killed in the year 177, treacherously ensnared by his son-in-law, 1 Macc. 16.14.

units.la: Infidius Ptolemæi circum ventus] generi sui, qui vocatur Ptolemæus Abobi F. quem Chronicon templi secundi perperam regem Ægypti facit historia extat, 1.Machab. 16.11.
units.tr: Treacherously ensnared by Ptolemy] of his son-in-law, who is called Ptolemy son of Abobus, whom the Chronicle of the Second Temple wrongly makes king of Egypt; the history is in 1 Macc. 16.11.

units.la: Huic Iohannes filius successit] fecundus natu. Nam Iudas & Mathathias interfecti fuerunt una cum patre 1.Machab 16. 14. Hunc Iohannem Eusebius non semel Ionathan appellat: in quo memoria lapsus mihi videtur.
units.tr: John his son succeeded him] the second by birth, for Judas and Mattathias were killed together with their father, 1 Macc. 16.14. Eusebius more than once calls this John Jonathan; in this I seem to see a lapse of memory.

units.la: Qui cum adversum Hyrcanos, gentem validissimam, egregie pugnasset Hyrcani nomen accepit] Secutus videtur Eusebium ita scribentem in Chronico suo, Simoni successit filius Iohannes, qui victis Hyrcanis, Hyrcanus cognomen accepit. Iit, Iohannes dux Iudæorum & pontifex adversus Hyrcanos (ita legendum: vulgo perperam, adversus Hyrcanum) bellum gerens Hyrcani nomen accepit, & a Romanis ius amicitiæ postulans decreto senatus inter amicos relatus est. Hinc apparet membrum illud, gentem validissimam, a Sulpicio ex ingenio additum esse. Ex ingenio, imo ex opinione. Nam opinatus est Eusebium loqui de gente Hyrcanorum, quæ procul aberat a Iudæa, ut non fit verisimile Hyrcanum adversus eam gentem bellum gessisse. Quid igitur? Aut loquitur de Hyrcania, vico Palæstinæ juxta Iudæam, Stephano memorata: aut fallit nos ipse imbutus falsa opinione de hoc nomine. Quod eo libentius credo, quia scio alios hoc nomine vocatos, in quis Hyrcanus filius R. Eliezer filij Hyrcani, & R. Iosua filius Hyrcani. Abben Gorion autor maximum natu filiorum Simonis Hyrcanum appellatum fuisse, eoque interempto, idem nomen Io-hanni attributum a seniorib. Israel. Scribit hoc, si bene meminì, lib. 4. cap. 27.
units.tr: Who, having fought splendidly against the Hyrcanians, a most powerful people, received the name Hyrcanus] He seems to have followed Eusebius, who writes thus in his Chronicle: "Simon was succeeded by his son John, who, having conquered the Hyrcanians, received the surname Hyrcanus." Also: "John, leader of the Jews and high priest, waging war against the Hyrcanians (so it should be read; commonly, wrongly, against Hyrcanus), received the name Hyrcanus, and, asking the Romans for the right of friendship, was by decree of the senate placed among the friends." Hence it appears that the clause "a most powerful people" was added by Sulpicius from his own mind. From his own mind, nay, from his own opinion. For he supposed that Eusebius spoke of the Hyrcanians, a people far away from Judaea, so that it is not likely Hyrcanus waged war against that people. What then? Either he speaks of Hyrcania, a village of Palestine near Judaea, mentioned by Stephanus, or he himself, imbued with a false opinion about this name, misleads us. I believe the latter the more readily, because I know that others were called by this name, among them Hyrcanus, son of R. Eliezer, son of Hyrcanus, and R. Joshua, son of Hyrcanus. Abben Gorion, the author, writes that the eldest of Simon's sons was called Hyrcanus, and that when he was killed the same name was given to John by the elders of Israel. He writes this, if I remember rightly, in book 4, ch. 27.

units.la: Annos V.1 & XX rerum potitus] Sic Eusebius: sed Io-sephus et tribuit ann, XXXI. Hunc Funccius sequitur.
units.tr: Twenty-five years he held power: so Eusebius. But Josephus gives him thirty-one years, and Funccius follows him.

units.la: Aristobulus pontifex] hic Græcos unice diligebat, unde φιλέλλην[?] dictus est.
units.tr: Aristobulus the high priest: he loved the Greeks above all others, and for this reason was called philhellene [φιλέλλην].

units.la: Regnum nomen assumpsit] Iofephus libro XIII. Antiq. cap. XIX. Defuncto Hyrcano patre natu maximus Aristobu-lus volens principatum in regni formam vertere, diadema sibi primus imposuit, post CCCCLXXXI annos & menses tres, ex quo de captivitate Babylonica liberatus populus ad pristinas sedes postliminio reversus est.
units.tr: Regnum nomen assumpsit: Josephus, Antiquities book 13, chapter 19. When his father Hyrcanus died, the eldest, Aristobulus, wishing to change the principate into the form of a kingdom, was the first to place a diadem on his own head, 481 years and three months after the people, freed from Babylonian captivity, returned by postliminy to their former seats.

units.la: Diadema ]fascia erat tenuis candidaque circundans caput; quam a Libero patre inventam Plinius notavit. Valerius lib. 6. cap. 2. Cui candida fascia crus colligatum habenti Favonius, Non refert, inquit, qua in parte corporis fit diadema.
units.tr: Diadem: it was a thin white band encircling the head, which Pliny noted was invented by Father Liber. Valerius, book 6, chapter 2: to Favonius, who had a white band tied around his leg, he said, "It does not matter," he said, "on what part of the body the diadem is worn."

units.la: Alexander ]qui Ebræis ינאי[?], id est, Iannæus. Sic etiam Iofephus eum vocat. Post Aristobuli obitum, inquit, Saiome e-jus uxor, quam Græci Alexandram nominant, solutis eius fratribus, quos ipse, ut diximus, vinxerat. Iannæum, qui & Alexander est, regem constituit, ætate ceteros præcedentem atque modestia. Vide sequentia. Habentur autem lib. 13. cap. 20. Vide quoq; historiam Ebraicam, cap XXX. & Chronicon templi secundi, sol. 39 col. 3.
units.tr: Alexander: who in Hebrew is [ינאי], that is, Jannaeus. Josephus also calls him this. After Aristobulus's death, he says, his wife Salome, whom the Greeks call Alexandra, released his brothers, whom he himself, as we said, had bound, and made Jannaeus, who is also Alexander, king, he being older than the others and more moderate. See what follows. These things are found in book 13, chapter 20. See also the Hebrew history, chapter 30, and the Chronicle of the Second Temple, p. 39, col. 3.

units.la: Filius ejus ]imo frater. - Nam Hyrcanus tres filios habuit, Aristobulum, Antigonum, Alexandrum. Aristobulus exactō anno diem funétus est. Quod in historia Ebraica regnavit annum unum solidum. Unde corriges Chronicon templi secundi, in quo regnavit biennio dierum, pro anno dierum. Antigonus periit ante mortem Aristobuli. Historia nota est. Alexander, licet in magno fratris odio fuisset, tamen eisuccessit in regno. Unde in Chronico illo, Alexander frater ejus regnavit pro eo.
units.tr: His son: nay, his brother. For Hyrcanus had three sons, Aristobulus, Antigonus and Alexander. Aristobulus died when exactly one year had passed; that is why the Hebrew history says he reigned one full year. Hence you should correct the Chronicle of the Second Temple, which says he reigned two years of days, to read one year of days. Antigonus perished before Aristobulus's death; the story is well known. Alexander, although he had been greatly hated by his brother, nevertheless succeeded him in the kingdom. Hence in that Chronicle it says, "Alexander, his brother, reigned in his place."

units.la: Eadem invenies in historia Ebraica. Vide quinetiam Iofephum lib. 13. cap. 20.
units.tr: You will find the same in the Hebrew history. See also Josephus, book 13, chapter 20.

units.la: Regnavit annis VII & viginti] Sic etiam Iofephus & alij.
units.tr: He reigned for twenty-seven years: so also Josephus and others.

units.la: Præter crudelitatem] unde interroganti, Quidnam faciendo sibi plebis conciliaret, responsum est, Si mererentur. Ob hanc crudelitatem Iudæum Θεανίδων[?] cognominarunt: pro quo in editione Rufini Crucifixor. Nam octingentos Pharisæos uno tempore eruci affixit. Vide Iosephum 13.22. Obiit in obsidione Ragabæ castelli, quod in Gerasenorum finibus, ultra Iordanem.
units.tr: Besides his cruelty, when someone asked by what means he might win over the people, the answer was, "If they deserved it." Because of this cruelty they called him the Jew [Θεανίδων], in place of which the edition of Rufinus has "Crucifier". For he crucified eight hundred Pharisees at one time. See Josephus 13.22. He died during the siege of the fortress of Ragaba, which lies in the territory of the Gerasenes, beyond the Jordan.

units.la: Solima] quum hoc nomen habeat ab Eusebio, videtur legendum Salina. Nam in eo Σαλίνα, consentientibus libris. Hieronymus quoque Oan.11[?]. Alexandra, quæ & Salina vocatur. Nec aliter Epiphanius. Iosephus tamen Salomen eam appellat, id est, Σαλώμην[?]: quod rectum esse puto. Consule Antiquitates ejus lib.13.cap.20.
units.tr: Solima: since Eusebius gives this name, it seems we should read Salina, for in him it is Σαλίνα [Salina], as the manuscripts agree. Jerome also has, "Alexandra, who is also called Salina", and Epiphanius likewise. Josephus, however, calls her Salome, that is Σαλώμην [Salōmē], which I think is correct. Consult his Antiquities, book 13, chapter 20.

units.la: Fœda inter fratres de regno certamina] In textu Sigonij, certamina orta. Hic rursum desideratur verbum substantivum fuerunt.
units.tr: Foul contests between the brothers over the kingdom: in Sigonius's text it reads "contests arising". Here again the verb "were" (fuerunt) is missing.

units.la: Pag. 132. Ac primum Hyrcanus imperium obtinebat] Vivente adhuc Alexandra pontificatus ei obvenit, ea mortua imperium obtinuit: erat enim natu major. Quocirca mater moriens testamento ei regnum reliquit. Id menses tenuit tres dumtaxat. Erat autem tertius hujus nominis, ut notatum in historia Ebrai-ca. Tertius, inquam pontificum, vel certe Hasamonæorum[?]. Nam alij fuerunt hoc nomine præterea, in queis Iosephi ἀρχιτελώνης[?] filius, qui primus sacerdotum Hyrcanus nominatus fuit. autor Iosephus. Unde colligimus nomen hoc apud Iudæos vulgatissimum fuisse.
units.tr: p. 132. And first Hyrcanus held power: while Alexandra was still alive, the high priesthood fell to him, and after her death he obtained the rule, for he was the elder. Accordingly his dying mother left him the kingdom in her will. He held it for three months only. He was, as noted in the Hebrew history, the third of this name: the third, I say, of the high priests, or at least of the Hasmoneans. For there were others of this name besides, among whom was the son of Josephus, the archtelōnēs [ἀρχιτελώνης], who was the first of the priests to be called Hyrcanus, according to Josephus. Hence we gather that this name was very common among the Jews.

units.la: Mox ab Aristobulo fratre pulsus] accidit hoc, Iosepho teste, anno tertio septimæ ac septuagesimæ, supra centesimam, Olympiadis, Q. Hortensio & Q. Metello Cretico consulibus.
units.tr: Soon driven out by his brother Aristobulus: this happened, according to Josephus, in the third year of the 177th Olympiad, in the consulship of Q. Hortensius and Q. Metellus Creticus.

units.la: Confugit ad Pompeium] primum ad Aretam regem A-rabum, deinde ad Pompeium Magnum, qui tum Syriam occupaverat. Hæc fratrum contentio de regno Iudæam quoque Romanis tributariam fecit, ut non temere dictum sit, Concordia res-parvæ crescunt: discordia magnæ dilabuntur.
units.tr: He fled to Pompey: first to Aretas, king of the Arabs, and then to Pompey the Great, who had then occupied Syria. This contention of the brothers over the kingdom also made Judaea tributary to the Romans, so that it was not rashly said: "By concord small things grow; by discord great things fall apart."

units.la: Quitum[?] Mithridatico bello confecto] consule Sigonium hoc loco. Scribendum autem Mithridatico cum aspiratione potius quam Mitridatico. Nam dicimus Mithridates Quidam præfeunt[?] Mithradates, quia videlicet Græci dicunt Μιθραδάτης. Proba-rem, nisi scirem a Latinis quandoque A in I mutari. Sane Massilia Græcis est Μασσαλία, & Catina, Κατάνη, & Agrigentum, Ἀκράγας.
units.tr: When the Mithridatic war was finished: consult Sigonius on this point. One should write "Mithridatico" with the aspirate rather than "Mitridatico", for we say Mithradates, some prefer Mithradates, because the Greeks say Μιθραδάτης [Mithradátēs]. I would approve, were I not aware that the Latins sometimes change A into I. Indeed Massilia is Μασσαλία [Massalía] for the Greeks, Catina is Κατάνη [Katánē], and Agrigentum is Ἀκράγας [Akrágas].

units.la: Incendij] in uno codice incendi : quod scribendum incendi, sum I maju[culo. Nam ita veteres quandoque scribebant duplex, sive geminatum,
units.tr: "Incendij": in one manuscript it is "incendi", which should be written "incendi" with a capital I. For the ancients sometimes wrote the letter doubled, or geminated.

units.la: Igitur Hyrcanum libens excepit] historia prolixa est, quam nostrer in pauca contraxit: Invenies autem eam apud Iosephum, si non pigebit ejus Antiquitates consulere.
units.tr: Therefore he gladly received Hyrcanus: the history is long, and our author has condensed it into a few words. You will find it, however, in Josephus, if you do not mind consulting his Antiquities.

units.la: Vrbe capta] non tantum cepit urbem, sed etiam moenia ejus diruit, sicut & Ptolemæus primus Ægypti rex quoudam fecerat. Autor Appianus, qui eam dicit fuisse urbem maximam & sanctissimam in ea regione, ut Plinius clarissimam totius Orientis. Cæterum capta fuit Ierosolyma Olympiade CLXXIX. anno primo, ut Iosephus: aut, ut alij censent, anno secundo.
units.tr: City taken: he not only captured the city but also tore down its walls, just as Ptolemy the First, king of Egypt, once did. The author Appian says it was the greatest and holiest city in that region, and Pliny calls it the most famous of the whole East. Jerusalem was taken, however, in the first year of the 179th Olympiad, according to Josephus, or, as others think, in the second year.

units.la: Templo pepercit] vult dicere, non spoliavit illud. Iosephus 14.8. Cum in sacræ pecuniæ thesauris ejus circiter talentorum duo millia, nihil horum præ pietate attigit. Cicero, Cn. Pompejus, captis Iero-olymis, victor ex illo fano nihil attigit. Imprimis hoc, ut multa alia, sapienter in tam superstitiosa & malefica civitate locum sermoni obtrectatorum non reliquit. Non enim credo religionem Iudæorum & hostium impedimento præstantissimo imperatori, sed pudorem fuisse. Sua cuique civitati religio, Læli, est; nostra nobis. Eusebius in Chronico, reserato tempio usque ad sancta sanctorum accesssit. Quæ verba docent ipsum ulterius non progressum esse. Non ergo vidit arcam fœderis, ut quidam volunt. Nam arca, in qua tabulæ fœderis & super eas Cherubim, in sancto sanctorum erat; non in sancto: quod tantum ingressus videtur Pompeius.
units.tr: He spared the Temple: he means that he did not plunder it. Josephus 14.8: "Although from the treasuries of the sacred money there were about two thousand talents, out of piety he touched none of these." Cicero: "Gnaeus Pompey, when he had captured Jerusalem, as victor touched nothing from that temple." Above all, in this he wisely, as in many other things, left no room for the tongues of detractors in such a superstitious and malicious city. For I do not believe it was the religion of the Jews that hindered that excellent commander, but his modesty. "Each city has its own religion, Laelius; ours is for us." Eusebius in his Chronicle says that, with the temple opened, he approached as far as the Holy of Holies. These words show that he did not go any further. Therefore he did not see the ark of the covenant, as some maintain. For the ark, in which were the tables of the covenant and, above them, the cherubim, was in the Holy of Holies, not in the Holy Place, which Pompey seems to have entered only.

units.la: Aristobulum vict in Romam misit] imo secum adduxit vinctum. Sic Eusebius. Sed legendum utrobique vinctum, id est, Iosephus diserte, abduxitque secum Aristobulum vinctum cum duabus filiabus & totidem filiis 14.8.
units.tr: Aristobulus, once defeated, he sent to Rome: nay, he led him away with him in chains. So Eusebius. But "bound" (vinctum) should be read in both places. Josephus says plainly that "he led Aristobulus away with him, bound, together with two daughters and as many sons", 14.8.

units.la: Imposito[que] Iudæis stipendio] id est, tributo censum vocant. Erat autem didrachmus in singula capita. Male igitur Hiero. in comment. Matth. 17. 25. Fuit Augustum Iudæa tributaria, & omnes censi capite ferebantur. Nam ante Augustum erat vectigalis, vel, si mavis, tributaria. Nec sub Augusto censum fuisse populum certius est quam ut probari debeat quomodo eo post Augustum omnes censi capite, & tunc primum Iudæa facta tributaria? non persuadet. Qui patres unquam errasse negat, negat solem lucere in meridie.
units.tr: Tribute imposed on the Jews: that is, they call the tribute a census. Now the didrachm was paid per head. Hence Jerome is wrong in his commentary on Matthew 17:25: "Judaea became tributary under Augustus, and all were enrolled by head." For before Augustus it was a vectigal, or, if you prefer, tributary. Nor is it so certain that the people were enrolled under Augustus that one must prove how, after Augustus, all were enrolled by head and Judaea first became tributary. That does not persuade. Whoever denies that the Fathers ever erred also denies that the sun shines at midday.

units.la: Procuratorem] Iudaea, Sigonius: Palaestina, Eusebius. Ab hoc tempore Iudaea semper habuit procuratores, qui praetoribus aut subconsulibus Syriae suberant. Talis Christi aevo erat Pontius Pilatus.
units.tr: Procurator: Judaea, according to Sigonius; Palestine, according to Eusebius. From this time Judaea always had procurators, who were subordinate to the praetors or sub-consuls of Syria. Such was Pontius Pilate in the age of Christ.

units.la: Antipatrum | qui & Antipas, eodem quo pater ipsius nomine vocabatur, Iosephus: a quo distentit Eusebius Africanum secutus, qui hujus Antipatri patrem Herodem nominat, quem ait fuisse Ascalone ἱεροδούλος[?], hoc est sacerdotem in templo Apollinis. Iosephus autem scribit eum ab Alexandro ejusque uxore constitutum ducem totius Idumaeae, amicitias Arabum, Gazaeorum & Ascalonitarum coluisse, multisque illos sibi conciliasse muneribus. Ab utroque diversus abit Nicolaus Damascenus Antipatri genus deducens a primatibus Iudaeorum, qui postliminio in Iudaeam reversi sunt e Babylonia.
units.tr: Antipater: who was also called Antipas, bearing the same name as his father, according to Josephus. Eusebius differs from him, following Africanus, who names this Antipater's father Herod, and says he was a hierodoulos [ἱεροδούλος] at Ascalon, that is, a priest in the temple of Apollo. Josephus, however, writes that he was appointed by Alexander and his wife as commander of all Idumaea, cultivated the friendship of the Arabs, Gazaeans and Ascalonites, and won them over to himself with many gifts. Nicolaus of Damascus differs from both, deriving Antipater's family from the leaders of the Jews who returned to Judaea from Babylon by postliminy.

units.la: Ascalonitem] Quomodo Ascalonita si erat Idumaeus! An patria ei Ascalon, & parentes ex Idumaea? Scire licet Ascalonem fuisse urbem superioris Idumaeae. Quod affirmat idem, quem supra nominavi, Iosephus lib. 3. cap. 3.[?] Aut patria erat Idumaea & Ascalon locus commorationis parentum ipsius.
units.tr: Ascalonite: how could he be an Ascalonite if he was an Idumaean? Was Ascalon his homeland, with his parents from Idumaea? One may know that Ascalon was a city of Upper Idumaea, as the same Josephus whom I named above affirms, book 3, chapter 3. Or his homeland was Idumaea, and Ascalon was the place where his parents lived.

units.la: Quatuor & triginta annos] Secutus est Eusebium, qui hos annos putat ab eo tempore quo primum Hyrcanus pontificatum adeptus est, vivente adhuc matre Alexandra. Sic autor Glossae ordinariae prioris Machabaeorum: Hyrcanus, inquit, animo de-fessus, adjuvante Antipatro procuratore, tenuit pontificatum ann. XXXI V. Sigonius huic summae detrahit decem, legendumque putat XXIV pro XXXIV: quia videlicet horum annorum aliud initium ponit. Nam eos numerat a restitutione Hyrcani quae per Pompeium facta. Hoc docent consequa ipsius verba, Tot enim sunt a consulatu M. Tullii Ciceronis, usque ad con-sulatum C. Asinij Pollionis. Quo tempore Herodes rex a senatu appellatus est. Iosephus haec paullo aliter lib. 15. cap. 9. Hyrca-nus vivente adhuc matre Alexandra pontifex Iudaeorum creatus, per novem annos eum honorem obtinuit: cum defunctae cum in regnum successisset, elapsis tribus mensibus, ab Aristobulo fratre pulsus est, ac deinde Pompei ope restitutus receptisque omnibus honoribus quadraginta annos in eis exegit.
units.tr: They followed Eusebius, who reckons these years from the time when Hyrcanus first obtained the high priesthood, while his mother Alexandra was still alive. So the author of the ordinary gloss on the first book of Maccabees: Hyrcanus, he says, weary of spirit, with the help of Antipater the procurator, held the high priesthood for thirty-five years. Sigonius subtracts ten from this sum and thinks we should read twenty-four for thirty-four, because he sets a different starting point for these years. He counts them from the restoration of Hyrcanus, which was done by Pompey. The words that follow confirm this: "For there are so many years from the consulship of Marcus Tullius Cicero to the consulship of Gaius Asinius Pollio, in which time Herod was called king by the senate." Josephus says this a little differently in the fifteenth book, chapter 9: Hyrcanus was made high priest of the Jews while his mother Alexandra was still living, and held that honour for nine years. When she died and he succeeded to the kingdom, after three months he was driven out by his brother Aristobulus, and then, restored by the help of Pompey and given back all his honours, he spent forty years in them.

units.la: Herodes] fecundus filiorum Antipatri ex uxore, quam Iosephus Cypron vocat, quæ illustri inter Arabas genere nata erat. Unde Arabissum appellat Eusebius.
units.tr: Herod: the second of Antipater's sons by his wife, whom Josephus calls Cypros, who was born of an illustrious Arab family. For this reason Eusebius calls him "the Arabian."

units.la: Alienigena] Quomodo alienigena si erat Iudæus? An quia patrem habuit Ascalonitam? Nam tales peculiariter alienigenæ vocabantur. Res notior est quam ut probari debeat. Alienigena, id est, ἀλλόφυλος. Sic eum appellat Eusebius. Sed & alij multi. Vocatur etiam proselytus. Quod pariter culpant. Nam qui Iudæus erat, nec proselytus dicebatur nec alienigena. Sed maiores ejus proselyti fuerant, imo alienigenæ. Nam Idumæi, priusquam sacra Iudæorum suscepissent, alienigenæ dicebantur. Hoc verum est. Non tamen a Iudæis ideo vocatur alienigena, sed servus Hasmonæorum. Ego sic sentio, Idumæos, licet Iudæi essent religione, gente tamen Idumæos fuisse a Iudæis distinctos. Tales etiam proselyti vocantur.
units.tr: "Foreigner": how could he be a foreigner if he was a Jew? Perhaps because his father was from Ascalon? For such people were specially called foreigners. The matter is too well known to need proof. "Foreigner," that is, allophylos in Greek. So Eusebius calls him, and many others too. He is also called a proselyte, and they blame this equally. For one who was a Jew was called neither a proselyte nor a foreigner. But his ancestors had been proselytes, indeed foreigners. For the Idumaeans, before they had accepted the sacred rites of the Jews, were called foreigners. This is true. Yet he is not called a foreigner by the Jews for this reason, but as a slave of the Hasmoneans. My view is this: although the Idumaeans were Jews in religion, they were nevertheless distinguished from the Jews by nation. Such people are also called proselytes.

units.la: Chronicon templi secundi, Antipater erat vir prudens, &c sed radix ejus non erat ex filiis Israel, verum ex Idumæis, qui servi ceciderunt in manum Israel: & ipsi sunt proselyti tantum, & non filij nobilium. Sic forte R. Aquiba vocatur proselytus iustitiæ, quia erat ex filiis filiorum Sifaræ. Idumæi ergo proselyti. Si proselyti cur non etiam alienigenæ? Nam antequam proselyti essent, alienigenæ fuerant. Hic originem spectamus, hoc est, ut Ebræi loquuntur, radicem gene-ris. Duæ fuerunt opiniones de Antipatro Herodis patre. Una Iosephi qui eum Idumæum fuisse scribit: altera Nicolai Damasceni, qui genus ejus deducit a primatibus Iudæorum, qui postliminio in Iudæam reversi sunt e Babylonia. Hanc probare videtur autor historiæ Ebraicæ ita scribens, Antipater accepit uxorem e femine regio Idumæam. Ideo dixerunt scriptores antiqui eum fuisse Idumæum. Sed Nicolaus scriptor fidelis ait eum fuisse Iudæum: id verum est. Fuit enim ex ingenuis Iuda, ex iis Iudæis qui redierunt e Babylonia Ierosolymam, in diebus Nehemiæ filij Hachaliæ & Ezræ sacerdotis.
units.tr: The Chronicle of the Second Temple: Antipater was a prudent man, etc., but his root was not from the sons of Israel but from the Idumaeans, who fell as slaves into the hand of Israel; and they are proselytes only, not sons of nobles. Thus perhaps R. Akiba is called a proselyte of righteousness, because he was of the sons of the sons of Sisera. So the Idumaeans were proselytes. If they were proselytes, why not also foreigners? For before they were proselytes they had been foreigners. Here we look at the origin, that is, as the Hebrews say, the root of the stock. There were two opinions about Antipater, Herod's father. One, that of Josephus, who writes that he was an Idumaean; the other, that of Nicolaus of Damascus, who traces his descent from the leading men of the Jews, who returned to Judea from Babylon by right of return. The author of the Hebrew history seems to support this, writing thus: "Antipater took a wife of royal blood from Idumaea." Therefore the ancient writers said he was an Idumaean. But Nicolaus, a trustworthy writer, says that he was a Jew, and this is true. For he was of the free-born men of Judah, of those Jews who came back from Babylon to Jerusalem in the days of Nehemiah the son of Hachaliah and Ezra the priest.

units.la: Externum regem] non Iudæum, sed Idumæum. Aut externum sive alienum a regno. Non enim erat e stirpe Davidis, nec ex genere sacerdotali. Eusebius in Chronico, Siquidem Herodes post eum (Antigonum) a Romanis constitutus est princeps alienigena, & nihil omnino pertinens ad Iudæam. Quod intelligentiam habet ex superioribus. Alioqui durum est il-lud, nihil omnino pertinens ad Iudæam. Secundum vaticinia prophetarum] nam Iacob patriarcha prophetes erat, cujus illud [illegible, ~9 letters], non recedet sceptrum de Iuda, &c. Quod induxit nonnullos ut crederent Herodem Messiam esse. Hos Herodianos appellant. Quanquam Herodiani videntur potius fuisse milites Herodis, ita dicti ut Herculanos dicimus & Iovianos & Theodosianos. Priorem sententiam tuetur Hiero. adversus Luciferianos, cap. 8: his verbis, Herodiani Herodem regem suscepere pro Christo. Alibi eam castigat, Latinorum commentum esse dicitans. Huc refer Vaticinium Haggaei prophetae, adhuc unum, modicum illud est, quod interpretantur de regno Hasmonaeorum, quod non adeo diu duravit. Quo deleto venit desiderium omnium gentium, hoc est Christus. Lege locum illum.
units.tr: "A foreign king": not a Jew, but an Idumaean; or foreign, that is, alien to the kingdom. For he was not of the line of David, nor of the priestly family. Eusebius in the Chronicle: "For after Antigonus, Herod was appointed by the Romans as a foreign ruler, having nothing at all to do with Judea." This is clear from what goes before; otherwise the phrase "having nothing at all to do with Judea" is harsh. "According to the prophecies of the prophets": for the patriarch Jacob was a prophet, and his words are, "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah," etc. This led some to believe that Herod was the Messiah. These they call Herodians, though the Herodians seem rather to have been soldiers of Herod, named as we say Herculians, Jovians and Theodosians. Jerome supports the former view against the Luciferians, chapter 8, in these words: "The Herodians received King Herod as Christ." Elsewhere he rebukes this, saying it is an invention of the Latins. Refer here the prophecy of the prophet Haggai, "Yet once, it is a little while," which they interpret of the kingdom of the Hasmoneans, which did not last so long. When that was destroyed, the desire of all nations came, that is, Christ. Read that passage.

units.la: Sub hoc Herode] qui Magnus cognominabatur ad differentiam aliorum. Ebraei scribunt Orodes & Harodes. Quae scriptura nominis invenitur etiam in Appiano
units.tr: Under this Herod: who was called "the Great" to distinguish him from others. The Hebrews write "Orodes" and "Harodes." This spelling of the name is also found in Appian.

units.la: Anno imperij ejus tertio & trigesimo] secundo & trige-simo Eusebius, qui fuit Augusti XLII: a quo Tertullianus paululum dissidet, qui Christum natum scribit anno Augusti XLI. Idem Eusebius a nato Abrahamo usque ad nativitatem Christi annos ponit MMXV.
units.tr: In the thirty-third year of his reign: Eusebius has the thirty-second year, the forty-second of Augustus; Tertullian differs from him a little, who writes that Christ was born in the forty-first year of Augustus. Eusebius also places from the birth of Abraham to the birth of Christ 2015 years.

units.la: Pag.133. Sabino & Rufino conss.] C. Calvisio Sabino ii, & L. Pasieno Rufo sive Rufino: qui consules fuerunt anno urbis DCCL. Hic consulatus, teste Sigonio, incidit in annum XXXIV Herodis, & imperij Augusti, si triumviratum annumeres, XL. Quocirca Eusebius, inquit, in historia & Epiphanius lib.2. contra haereses ostendunt eum natum esse Augusto tertium decimum & Silvano consulibus, ipsius Augusti anno XLII, qui erit urbis DCCLII. Quam supputationem Chronographi fere omnes hoc tempore non sine ratione sequuntur.
units.tr: Page 133. In the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus: Gaius Calvisius Sabinus, twice, and Lucius Pasienus Rufus or Rufinus, who were consuls in the year 750 from the founding of the city. This consulship, according to Sigonius, falls in the thirty-fourth year of Herod and, if you count the triumvirate, the fortieth year of Augustus's rule. Hence Eusebius says, in his history, and Epiphanius in the second book against heresies, show that he was born in the thirteenth year of Augustus, in the consulship of Silvanus, in the forty-second year of Augustus himself, which will be the year 752 from the founding of the city. Nearly all the chronographers of this time follow this reckoning, not without reason.

units.la: Ceterum a mundo condito usque ad Christum natum supp[?]tant annos, Eusebius | 5190. alias 5109 Beda de temporibus | 3952 Iosephus | 4191 mens. 6 Suidas | 5600 Augustinus | 5351[?] Cassiodorus | 4697 Hieronymus in Quæst.Ebra. | 3941 Isidorus | 5110 [?] Sulpitius Severus | 5414 Philo Iudæus | 3962 Paulus Orosius | 5049 Metheodorus [?] | 5000 Epiphanius contra Manich. | 5029 Albumasar & alij astronomi | 5328 Thalmud | 3784
units.tr: Moreover, from the creation of the world to the birth of Christ they count the years: Eusebius 5190, otherwise 5109; Bede, On Times 3952; Josephus 4191, six months; Suidas 5600; Augustine 5351; Cassiodorus 4697; Jerome, in Hebrew Questions 3941; Isidore 5110; Sulpicius Severus 5414; Philo Judaeus 3962; Paulus Orosius 5049; Methodius 5000; Epiphanius against the Manichaeans 5029; Albumasar and other astronomers 5328; the Talmud 3784.

units.la: VIII Kalend. Ianuarias] Scaliger in Eusebium.
units.tr: On the eighth day before the Kalends of January] Scaliger on Eusebius.

units.la: Omnis ecclesia in partibus Orientis, seculo Eusebij & antecedenti & sequenti, credidit Christum natum VIII Kalend. Ianuarij. Nisi erratum est operarum, aut properantis calami, alia fuit haec de re Orientalium ecclesiarum & alia Occidentalium opinio.
units.tr: Throughout the seventh century of Eusebius, the one before it and the one after it, every Church in the regions of the East believed that Christ was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. Unless it is a printer's error or a hasty pen, the opinion of the Eastern churches on this matter was one thing and that of the Western churches another.

units.la: Ne quid forma praecisi operis] supra 16. cujus progeniem in hoc tam praecisso opere inferendam non putavi: & pag. 311. Quae ego, quia prolixa admodum videbantur, inserenda huic tam praecisso operi non putavi.
units.tr: Lest anything be lost from the form of the work] See above, 16, whose offspring I did not think should be inserted into this so abridged work; and p. 311, "Since these matters seemed very lengthy, I did not think they should be inserted into this so abridged work."

units.la: Herodes post nativitatem Domini regnavit annos quatuor] quinque, Eusebius: alij aliter.
units.tr: Herod reigned four years after the birth of the Lord] Eusebius says five; others differ.

units.la: Nam omnie imperij ejus tempus VII & XXX anni fuerunt] Sic Eusebius, Iosephus, Gorionides & alij. Chronicon tertii secundi, vixit Herodes postquam occidisset Antipatrum filium suum octo dies & mortuus est. Omne autem tempus regni ejus quadraginta anni.
units.tr: For the whole time of his rule was thirty-seven years] So Eusebius, Josephus, Gorionides and others. The Chronicle of the Third Temple says: Herod lived after he had killed his son Antipater, and died eight days later. The whole time of his reign, however, was forty years.

units.la: Archelaus Tetrarcha] ducem vocat Eusebius: ut Ethnarcham Iosephus 17.13. Caesar paucis post diebus Archelaum non regem declarat, sed, dimidia parte ditionis quae Herodis fuerat ei concessa, Ethnarcham eum constituit, regnum quoque pollicitus, quam primum ille se talem honore dignum redderet. Potest etiam Toparcha dici. Nam in secundo belli Iudaici, cap. 9. portionem ejus idem Iosephus τετραρχίαν [?] appellat.
units.tr: Archelaus, tetrarch] Eusebius calls him a leader, as Josephus calls him ethnarch, 17.13. Caesar a few days later declared Archelaus not king, but, granting him half of the dominion that had belonged to Herod, appointed him ethnarch, promising him the kingdom also as soon as he should show himself worthy of that honour. He could also be called toparch. For in the second book of the Jewish War, ch. 9, Josephus himself calls his portion tetrarchy [τετραρχίαν].

units.la: Annis IX] Eusebius, Archelaus nono anno regni sui in Viennam urbem relegatur. Iosephus autor hoc accidisse anno principatus Archelai decimo. Vide Archaeolog. lib. 17. cap 15. Vbi in textu Graeco τῆς ἀρχῆς Ἀρχελάου [?]. Ergo Archelaus etiam princeps, id est, ἐθνάρχης [?]: Nam regnum ei tribuere cum Eusebio non ausim. Herodes ann. XX & IIII.] id est, annis viginti quatuor, perperam anno in quadam editione. In Sulpicio Sigonij, XXX & IIII. Nescio an mendu sit operarum. Innuit autem Herodem Antipam Tetrarcham Galilaeae quem Caius Caesar perpetuo damnavit exilio apud Lugdunum urbem Galliae. Compositor historiae Ebraicae prius hunc Antipatrum appellatum scribit, & postea, cum Tetrarcha factus esset, Herodem nominatum; quem ait fuisse fratrem Archelai, id est, [illegible, ~2 letters] sive [illegible, ~2 letters], pro quo mendose in codice Veneto [illegible, ~3 letters] legitur, littera Hethin Thau versa. Caeterum Antipas vocatus fuit etiam Herodis Magni pater, qui postea Antipatrum se nominavit. Quidam scribunt Antipatrem. Autor Chronici T.S. Octavianus Augustus regnare fecit Antipam fratrem Archelai pro eo, vertitque nomen ejus in nomen Herodis.
units.tr: In the ninth year] Eusebius says that in the ninth year of his reign Archelaus was banished to the city of Vienne. Josephus states that this happened in the tenth year of Archelaus' rule. See Antiquities, book 17, ch. 15, where the Greek text has "of the rule of Archelaus" [τῆς ἀρχῆς Ἀρχελάου]. So Archelaus was also a prince, that is, an ethnarch [ἐθνάρχης]. I would not dare to grant him a kingdom with Eusebius. Herod, twenty-four years] that is, twenty-four years; in one edition it is wrongly printed as twenty-four years in another way. In Sulpicius of Sigonius it reads thirty-four. I do not know whether this is a printer's error. He means Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, whom Caius Caesar condemned to perpetual exile at Lugdunum, a city of Gaul. The compiler of the Hebrew history first writes that this man was called Antipater, and afterwards, when he had become tetrarch, was named Herod; he says that he was the brother of Archelaus, that is, [illegible] or [illegible], for which the Venetian codex wrongly reads [illegible], the letter Heth being turned into Tau. Moreover, Antipas was also called the father of Herod the Great, who afterwards called himself Antipater. Some write Antipater. The author of the Chronicle of T.S. says that Octavian Augustus made Antipas, brother of Archelaus, reign in his place, and changed his name into the name of Herod.

units.la: Herodes hic est ille qui Philippi fratris uxorem in matrimonium accepit, & Iohannem Baptistam, qui eum propterea reprehendebat, occidit. Quam historiam aliter Euangelista, aliter Iosephus narrat. Pro Euangelistis facit historia Ebraica, cap. 63.
units.tr: This is that Herod who took to wife the wife of his brother Philip, and killed John the Baptist, who for this reason rebuked him. The Evangelist and Josephus relate this story differently. The Hebrew history, ch. 63, supports the Evangelists.

units.la: Herodes Antipas occidit multos ex sapientibus Israel, & in his Iohannem sacerdotem magnum, propterea quod dixisset, Non licet tibi ducere uxorem fratris tui Philippi. Hic est Iohannes ille qui baptizatus fuit. Sed & Chronicon templi secundi, Herodes accepit uxorem Philippi fratris sui, quae ei genuerat duos filios. Quem ob hanc abominationem redarguit R. Iochanan sacerdos magnus. Ideo per-cussit & occidit cum Antipas. Verba illa, Non licet tibi du-cere uxorem fratris tui, accipienda sunt cum hac conditione, Si ipse adhuc vixerit. Nam post mortem licebat hoc facere, imo tenebatur frater defuncti ducere uxorem ejus viduam, si erat improles sive illiberis, hoc est si liberos nullos ex eo suscepserat. Vide nunc, si placet, Iosephum Ant. lib 18. cap 7.
units.tr: Herod Antipas killed many of the wise men of Israel, and among them John the high priest, because he had said, "It is not lawful for you to take your brother Philip's wife." This is that John who was baptized. But also the Chronicle of the Second Temple: Herod took the wife of his brother Philip, who had borne him two sons. R. Johanan the high priest rebuked him for this abomination. Therefore he struck and killed him, together with Antipas. Those words, "It is not lawful for you to take your brother's wife," must be understood with this condition: if he himself were still alive. For after his death it was lawful to do this; indeed, the brother of the deceased was bound to take his widow as wife, if she was childless, that is, if he had had no children by her. Now see, if you please, Josephus, Antiquities book 18, ch. 7.

units.la: XX & II.] In historia Ebraica est XX & I. ex qua emendabis Chronicon templi secundi, in quo [?] II. pro [?] 21. sol.54. col.4.
units.tr: Twenty-two.] In the Hebrew history it is twenty-one, from which you will correct the Chronicle of the Second Temple, in which [?] two stands for [?] twenty-one, sol. 54, col. 4.

units.la: Anno regni octavo & decimo, quo tempore Christus agebat annum XXXIII. Incidit autem hic annus in annum mundi 5232 secundum supputationem Eusebij, quem Sulpicius nunc secutus mihi videtur. Ceterum Tertullianus autor Chri-stum pas-sum anno Tiberij XV. a quo diversus abit Eusebius passionem ejus cõjiciens in annum Tiberij XVIII. cum triennio ante baptismatus fuisset a Iohanne.
units.tr: In the eighteenth year of his reign, at which time Christ was living in his thirty-third year. This year fell in the year of the world 5232 according to the reckoning of Eusebius, whom Sulpicius now seems to me to follow. Moreover, the author Tertullian places Christ's suffering in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, from which Eusebius differs, placing his passion in the eighteenth year of Tiberius, since three years had passed after his baptism by John.

units.la: Regni] regnum etiam Ebraei vocant, quæ proprie tetrarchia vel ethnarchia, aut certe ἐθνάρχης[?], id est, principatus. Regis enim nomen latissime patet apud eos.
units.tr: Of the reign] The Hebrews also call a kingdom a reign, which properly means tetrarchy or ethnarchy, or certainly [ἐθνάρχης], that is, a principality. For the name of king is applied very broadly among them.

units.la: Fufio Gemino & Rubellio Gemino conss.] hoc est quod quidam dicunt Christum passum duobus Geminis conss. approbante Tertulliano. Alij secus opinantur. Nam a consulatu Sabini & Rufini usq; ad hoc consules numerātur anni duntaxat XXXI, cum Christus passus perhibeatur ætatis suæ anno XXXIII vel certe XXXIV.
units.tr: In the consulship of Fufius Geminus and Rubellius Geminus] this is what some say, that Christ suffered in the consulship of the two Gemini, with Tertullian's approval. Others think otherwise. For from the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus up to this one, only thirty-one years are counted, whereas Christ is said to have suffered in the thirty-third or certainly the thirty-fourth year of his age.

units.la: ubellio] alibi est Rebellio. Nondum scio utra scriptura melior verior sit.
units.tr: Rubellio] elsewhere it is Rebellio. I do not yet know which spelling is the better and truer.

units.la: Sunt anni CCCLXXII] demptis quinque, Sigonius reponit CCCLXVII; quibus additi anni XXXIII efficiunt CCCC. In quem annum Christi diximus incidere consulatum Stiliconis.
units.tr: There are 372 years] with five removed, Sigonius restores 367; to these, adding thirty-three years, makes 400. In this year, as we said, the consulship of Stilicho fell in the year of Christ.

units.la: Vsque in tempus quo Paulus[?] Romam deductus est] hoc est, inquit Sigonius, usque ad annum Christi LVIII, qui erat imperij Neronis tertius. Exorsus autem est suam historiam ab eo die quo Christus in cœlum ascendit, quo tempore spiritus sanctus missus fuit in Apostolos. Is erat annus Christi, eodem Sigonio supputante, XXXIII. Continent ergo Actus Apostolorum historiam annorum XXV, aut XXVI.
units.tr: Until the time when Paul was taken to Rome] that is, says Sigonius, until the year of Christ 58, which was the third year of Nero's reign. He began his history from the day on which Christ ascended into heaven, at which time the Holy Spirit was sent upon the Apostles. By Sigonius' reckoning, that was the year 33 of Christ. The Acts of the Apostles therefore covers a history of twenty-five or twenty-six years.

units.la: Dignus extitit qui persecutionem, &c.] Bella imperatorum in Christianos persecutiones et vexationes vocantur: eæ fuerunt, ut quidam volunt, inter quos Optatus Milevitanus lib. 3. quatuordecim, qui initium faciunt ab ea qua Stephanus diaconus martyrij coronam emeruit. Sed alij, quos Sulpicius noster sequitur, decem tantum agnoscunt, quas comparant cum decem plagis Ægypti. Earum prima est quam Nero exercuit. Eusebius in Chronico, Primus Nero super oīa scelera sua etiā persecutione in Christianos facit, in qua Petrus & Paulus gloriosè Romæ occubuerunt. Orosius lib. 7. cap. 5. Auxit hanc molem facinorum eius temeritas impietatis in Deum. Nam primus Christianos supplicijs & mortibus affecit, ac per omnes provincias pari persecutione excruciari imperavit, ipsumque nomen extirpare conatus beatissimos Christi apostolos Petrum e uce, Paulum gladio occidit.
units.tr: He proved worthy to suffer persecution, etc.] The wars of emperors against Christians are called persecutions and vexations. There were, as some hold, among whom is Optatus of Milevis, book 3, fourteen of them, beginning with the one in which the deacon Stephen won the crown of martyrdom. But others, whom our Sulpicius follows, acknowledge only ten, which they compare with the ten plagues of Egypt. The first of these is the one that Nero carried out. Eusebius in the Chronicle: "Nero first of all, above all his crimes, made a persecution against the Christians, in which Peter and Paul died gloriously at Rome." Orosius, book 7, ch. 5: "His reckless impiety against God increased this mass of crimes. For he was the first to inflict punishments and deaths on Christians, and commanded that they be tormented with equal persecution throughout all the provinces, and tried to wipe out the very name, and killed the most blessed apostles of Christ, Peter by crucifixion and Paul by the sword."

units.la: Christianos] discipuli, qui primum Nazaraei dicebantur, vocati sunt primum Christiani Antiochiæ Act. 11. 26. Appellatio a Christo, non ab unctione spirituali. Nam ab ea Christi vocantur, non Christiani. Vt ab Augustino Augustiniani sic a Christo Christiani. Res est, non conjectura. Theodoretus in Genesin, quæst. XLVII. ἡμεῖς δὲ τὸ [?]διηκότον [?]χρηστοῦ προσηγορίας χριστιανοὶ καλούμεθα. Hos pagani per imperitiam Chrestianos appellabant. Sic Chrestus dicebant pro Christus. Tacitus, Iudæos, Chresto duce tumultuantes, Roma expulit.
units.tr: Christians] The disciples, who were at first called Nazarenes, were first called Christians at Antioch, Acts 11.26. The name comes from Christ, not from spiritual anointing. For they are not called Christs from him, but Christians. Just as Augustine's followers are called Augustinians, so from Christ they are called Christians. This is a matter of fact, not of conjecture. Theodoret on Genesis, question 47: "But we are called Christians from the name of the kindly [ἡμεῖς δὲ ... χρηστοῦ προσηγορίας χριστιανοὶ καλούμεθα]. The pagans, through ignorance, called these people Chrestians. Thus they said Chrestus for Christus. Tacitus: "Rome expelled the Jews, who were rioting at the instigation of Chrestus."

units.la: Primus inciperet] nam Claudius eos urbe tantum expulerat Suetonius, Tacitus, alij, Tertullianus, Consulite commentarios vestros, in illis reperietis Neronem primum in hanc sectam tum maxime Romæ orientem Cæsariano gladio ferocissime.
units.tr: The first to begin] for Claudius had only expelled them from the city, as Suetonius, Tacitus and others say. Tertullian: "Consult your records; in them you will find that Nero was the first to rage most fiercely against this sect, then at its height in Rome, with the imperial sword."

units.la: Explerit] id est, expleturus sit. Ita exponendum esse docent ea quæ mox sequuntur.
units.tr: Will fulfil] that is, is about to fulfil. This is how the things that immediately follow teach it should be explained.

units.la: Siquidem opinione multorum receptum fit ipsum Antichristum venturum] eadem fuit opinio quorundam Christianorum de Domitiano, cui cognomentum Neroni fuit, qui sævitia Neronem vel æquabat, vel superabat. Unde alter Nero & Nero calvus convicio populi vocabatur. Hiero. Dan. 11. Multi nostrorum putant ob sævitiæ ac turpitudinis magnitudinem Domitianum Neronem antichristum fore. In glossa ordinaria, 1. Machab. ubi eadem hæc verba legitur, Domitianum sive Neronem. Præteulerim, aut Neronem ut dicat, opinione quorundam Christianorum alterutrum Antichristum fore. Nam ambo sævitiæ nota insignes fuerunt. Haymo scribit Neronem umbram fuisse Antichristi, sicut David Christi. Scribit hoc ad locum Apostoli 2. Thessal. 2,7. Iam nunc mysterium operatur iniquitatis, Vbi Nicolaus de Lyra, Hoc mysterium exerceri coepit a temporibus Neronis, vel quia Nerotypus erat Antichristi, ut Haymo scribit: vel quia tunc primum jacta sunt fundamenta tyrannidis ecclesiasticæ. Si typus & umbra fuit, non erit Antichristus. Similiter David non erit Christus, hoc est Messias ille qui patribus promissus fuit. Meliore jure aliquis Antichristum Neronem vocaret aut Neronem fore diceret, hoc est hominem sævum & crudelem. Nam tales Neros hodie dicimus, nomine proprio in appellationem verso. Certerum Neronem venturum in fine sæculi credidit etiam B. Martinus, sed idem eundem ab Antichristo discriminat. Verba Sul[?]icij hac de re habentur in Dialogis, fegm XVI. Cum ab eo de tune sæculi quærerémus, aut nobis, Neronem & Antichri-stum prius esse venturos; Neronem in Occidentali plaga regibus subiectis decem imperaturum: persecutionem autem ab eo hactenus exercendam, ut idola gentium coli cogat. Ab Antichristo vero Orientale imperium esse ca-piendum: qui quidem sedem & caput regni Ierosolymam esset habiturus, ab illo urbem & templum esse reparandum. Illius autem persecutionem futuram esse ut Christum Do-minum cogat negari, sed potius Christum esse confirmans: omnesque secundum legem circumcidi iubeat, & ipsum denique Neronem ab Antichristo esse perimendum; atque sub illius potestate universum orbem, cunctasque gentes esse redigendas, donec adventu Christi impius opprima-tur. Non esse autem dubium, quin Antichristus malo spiritu conceptus, esset etiam (forte jam) in annis puerilibus constitutus, a tate legitima iumpturus imperium. Similia somniant Iudæi de suo [illegible, ~8 letters] quem Romæ nunc vivere credunt inter pauperes. Profecto ita est, Sabini somniant quicquid volunt.
units.tr: For by the opinion of many it is received that Antichrist himself is to come] The same opinion was held by some Christians about Domitian, who had the surname of Nero, and who either equalled or surpassed Nero in cruelty. Hence he was called the second Nero and bald Nero by the people's reproach. Jerome on Daniel 11: "Many of our people think that Domitian, or Nero, will be Antichrist because of the greatness of his cruelty and wickedness." In the Glossa Ordinaria on 1 Maccabees, where these same words are read, "Domitian or Nero"; I would rather it say "or Nero," so that by the opinion of some Christians one or the other will be Antichrist, for both were notably marked with the stamp of cruelty.
