Haymo writes that Nero was a shadow of Antichrist, as David was of Christ. He writes this on the passage of the Apostle, 2 Thessalonians 2:7, "The mystery of iniquity is already at work," where Nicholas of Lyra says: "This mystery began to be at work from the times of Nero, either because Nero was a type of Antichrist, as Haymo writes, or because then for the first time the foundations of ecclesiastical tyranny were laid. If he was a type and a shadow, he will not be Antichrist; similarly David will not be Christ, that is, that Messiah who was promised to the fathers." With better right someone might call Antichrist Nero, or say that Nero will be, that is, a cruel and savage man. For we today call such people Neros, turning a proper name into a common appellation. Moreover, blessed Martin also believed that Nero would come at the end of the age, but he distinguishes the same man from Antichrist. Sulpicius' words on this matter are found in the Dialogues, 16: "When we asked him about the end of the age, whether Nero or Antichrist would come first: Nero will rule in the western region over ten subject kings, and he will carry out persecution until then, forcing the idols of the nations to be worshipped. But Antichrist is to seize the eastern empire, and he will have Jerusalem as the seat and head of his kingdom, and the city and temple are to be rebuilt by him. His persecution will be such that he compels Christ the Lord to be denied, yet he is to confirm Christ rather than deny him; and he will order all men to be circumcised according to the law; and finally Nero himself is to be destroyed by Antichrist, and the whole world and all nations are to be brought under his power, until the impious one is crushed at the coming of Christ. There is no doubt that Antichrist, conceived by an evil spirit, is also (perhaps already) established in childish years, and will take up the empire at legitimate age." The Jews dream similar things about their own [illegible] whom they now believe to be living at Rome among the poor. Truly, it is so: the Sabines dream whatever they please.

units.la: Pag.134. Peromniafœdissima & crudelissima] Orosius lib.7. cap 5. Crudelitatis autem rubie ita efferatus est, ut plurimam senatus partem interfecerit, equestrem ordinem pœne destituerit: sed ne parricidiis quidem abstinuit, matrem, fratremque, sororem, uxorem, ceterosque cognatos & propinquos sine hæsitatione profravit.
units.tr: Page 134. Most foul and most cruel in every respect] Orosius, lib. 7, cap. 5. In his cruelty Nero was so enraged that he killed most of the senate and nearly destroyed the equestrian order. Yet he did not even refrain from parricide, but without hesitation destroyed his mother, brother, sister, wife, and his other kinsmen and relatives.

units.la: Eo processisse ut matrem interficeret] unde [illegible, ~9 letters] appellatus est in hoc versu,
units.tr: That he went so far as to kill his mother; whence [illegible] is called in this verse,

units.la: [illegible, ~18 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Et in illo, qui a populo decantatus olim ut vere Sybillinus,
units.tr: And in the one which was once sung by the people as truly Sibylline,

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Xiphilinus e Dione scribit nonnullos culeum de nocte in quadam statua ipsius suspendisse, ut eo significarent Neronem ut matricidam in culeum projici oportere: aliosque exposuisse pueru-lum in foro, alligata ad eum tabella in qua scriptum fuerit, non te tollo, ne matrem occidas. Notum & illud,
units.tr: Xiphilinus, following Dio, writes that some people hung a sack on a statue of him at night, to signify that Nero, as a matricide, ought to be thrown into a sack; and others exposed a little boy in the forum with a tablet tied to him, on which was written, "I do not raise you up, so that you may not kill your mother." It is also well known that

units.la: Quis negat Æneæ magna de stirpe Neronem,Sustulit hic matrem, sustulit ille patrem.
units.tr: Who denies that Nero springs from the great stock of Aeneas? He killed his mother; he killed his father.

units.la: Matrem] etiam uxorem & Senecam præceptorem, & Lucanum sum fratrem ejus. Salmanticensis, Post Claudium imperavit Nero, anno mundi MMMVcCCXIX[?], qui dictus est Nero crudelis, quia occidit matrem suam & praeceptorem suum Senecam, & fratrem ejus Lucanum.
units.tr: His mother] also his wife, and Seneca his tutor, and Lucan his brother. The Salmanticensis: After Claudius, Nero reigned in the year of the world 3519, who was called Nero the Cruel because he killed his mother, his tutor Seneca, and his brother Lucan.

units.la: Pythagorae cuidam nuberet] Post crudelitatis exemplum adfert nunc alterum foeditatis ac turpitudinis insignis. Xiphilinus in Nerone, Quanquam ipse nupsit Pythagorae liberto, dotemque ei per syngraphan constituit (hoc Sulpicius significat, cum ait, in modum solennium conjugiorum) quas nuptias populus Romanus celebravit una cum ceteris gentibus: & post, Ex eo tempore duo simul cum Nerone coibant, Pythagoras pro viro, Sporus pro uxore, ac Nero praeter cetera domina & regina vocabatur. Orosius, Virum in uxorem duxit, ipse a viro ut uxor acceptus est. Suetonius, Doryphoro liberto, sicut ipsi Sporus, ita ipse denupsit.
units.tr: That he married a certain Pythagoras] After an example of cruelty, he now adduces another, notable for its foulness and shamelessness. Xiphilinus, on Nero, Although he himself married Pythagoras, a freedman, and settled a dowry on him by contract (Sulpicius indicates this when he says, in the manner of solemn marriages), a marriage which the Roman people celebrated together with the other nations. And afterwards: "From that time two men at once lay with Nero, Pythagoras as husband, Sporus as wife, and Nero was called, among other things, lord and queen." Orosius: He took a man as his wife, and was himself received by a man as a wife. Suetonius: Just as Sporus was to him, so he was married to the freedman Doryphorus.

units.la: Indiumq;[?] imperatori flammeum, &c.] Sex. Victor, Nero eo progressus est, ut neque suae neq;e aliorum pudicitiae parcens, ad extremum amictus nubentium virginum speciem palam convocato senatu, dote dicta, cunctis de more frequentantibus nuberet.
units.tr: And to the emperor a bridal veil, etc.] Sextus Victor: Nero went so far that, sparing neither his own chastity nor that of others, he finally, dressed in the guise of a bride, with the senate openly summoned, and a dowry named, married in the customary way while all present took part.

units.la: Reliqua vero ejus] quale illud quod Suetonius refert, suam quidem pudicitiam usque adeo prostituit, ut contamina-tis poene omnibus membris, novissime quasi genus lusus, excogitaret: quatenus ferae pelle contectus emitteretur e cavea, virorumque ac foeminarum ad stipitem deligatorum inguina invaderet: & Xiphilinus Dionis abbreviator, Illud vero quis digne mirari potuit? quid cum adolescentes ac puellas nudas alligaret palo, capiebat pellem ferae: deinde quasi devoraturus aliquid, in eos irruebat petulanter.
units.tr: As for the rest of his conduct] such as what Suetonius reports: he so prostituted his own chastity that, having defiled almost every part of his body, he finally devised a kind of game: covered with the skin of a wild beast, he was let out of a cage and attacked the groins of men and women tied to a stake. And Xiphilinus, the abbreviator of Dio: "What could anyone rightly wonder at? When he tied naked young men and girls to a post, he put on the skin of a beast, and then, as though about to devour something, he rushed wantonly upon them."

units.la: Primus Christianum nomen tollere aggressus est] vide quae scripsimus ad praecedentem paginam, tum etiam Iohan. Saresberiensem in Polycratico lib. 8. cap. 18. Coepit saevire, inquit Sigonius, anno Christi LXV, Lecanio Licinioque consulibus, culpa incendii urbis in Christianos innocentes collata, ut Tacitus quoque memoriae prodidit. Alij aliter, Vide Scaligeri Animadversiones in Chronicon Eusebij, pag. 181. col.1.
units.tr: He was the first to undertake to abolish the Christian name] See what we wrote on the preceding page, and also John of Salisbury, Policraticus, book 8, chapter 18. "He began to rage," says Sigonius, in the year of Christ 65, in the consulship of Lecanius and Licinius, the blame for the fire of the city being laid on innocent Christians, as Tacitus also recorded. Others otherwise. See Scaliger's Animadversions on Eusebius's Chronicle, p. 181, col. 1.

units.la: Divina] id est, Christiana. Sic patrum scripta divina dici-possent[?]. Nam & libri apocryphi divini dicuntur & disputatiotheologica apud Anglos divina vocatur, qui etiam ipsam theo-logiam Divinitatem appellant.
units.tr: Divine] i.e. Christian. Thus the writings of the Fathers could be called divine. For apocryphal books too are called divine, and a theological disputation is called "divine" among the English, who also call theology itself "Divinity."

units.la: Ab injusto præsulis judicio] Festum intelligit, qui Felici successit. malim ergo, præsidis, ut pagina, quæ proxime sequitur, præsidis sui Gesij Flori injurias non ferentes.
units.tr: By the unjust judgment of the prelate] He means Festus, who succeeded Felix. I would rather read "of the governor" (praesidis), as in the page immediately following, "not enduring the wrongs of their governor Gessius Florus."

units.la: Romam deducto] sub militari custodia.
units.tr: Led to Rome] under military guard.

units.la: Adversus Simonem] est ille, qui vulgo Simon Magus appellatur: cui statua olim posita Romæ inter duos pontes, cum hac inscriptione, Simoni Deo Sancto[?]. Vide sis[?] Eusebii hist. eccles. lib. 2. cap. 13. Mentio hujus & in Iohafin, per hæc verba, In diebus Petri Apostoli erat Simon Samarita magus, de cujus nomine vocata est Simonia, quando aliquis vendit sanctitatem suam, id est, sacerdotium suum.
units.tr: Against Simon] This is the one commonly called Simon Magus, for whom a statue was once set up at Rome between two bridges, with this inscription: "To Simon the holy god." See Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 13. He is also mentioned in John, in these words: "In the days of the apostle Peter there was Simon the Samaritan magician, from whose name simony is called, when someone sells his holiness, that is, his priesthood."

units.la: Magicis artibus] Augustinus in sermone de sanctis, cum enim Simon se Christum diceret, & tanquam Christus ad patrem assereret se posse conscendere, atque elatus subito magicis artibus volare cœpisset: tunc Petrus fixis genibus precatus est Dominum, & precatione sancta vicit magicam levitatem. Nam velut vinctum eum de sublimi aere depositus, & quodam præcipitio in saxa elidens crura confregit. Meminit hujus congressionis & Apnobius[?] per hæc verba, Viderunt Romani currum Simonis magi & quadrigas igneas Petri ore diffiatas[?], & nominato Christo evanuisse. Pag.135. Dæmonibus] legitur & dæmoniis
units.tr: By magic arts] Augustine, in his sermon on the saints: When Simon said that he was Christ, and claimed, as Christ, that he could ascend to the Father, and being suddenly lifted up began to fly by magic arts, then Peter, kneeling, prayed to the Lord, and by holy prayer overcame the magical lightness. For he brought him down from the high air as one bound, and dashing him upon the rocks by a headlong fall broke his legs. Arnobius also mentions this contest in these words: "The Romans saw the chariot of Simon the magician and his fiery team scattered by Peter's word, and vanish at the name of Christ." Page 135. Daemonibus: the reading is also daemoniis.

units.la: Nerone apud Antium constituto] mutatus hoc est a Tacito, qui de hac re ita scribit, Incendium forte an dolo principis conflatum fuerit in incerto fuit. eo certe tempore Antij agens Nero non ante in urbem regressus est, quam domui ejus, qua Palatium & Mecænatis hortos continuaverat, ignis propinquaret.
units.tr: Nero being at Antium] This is borrowed from Tacitus, who writes about this matter thus: "Whether the fire was started by chance or by the emperor's treachery was uncertain. At any rate, Nero, who was then staying at Antium, did not return to the city until the fire came near his house, which joined the Palace and the gardens of Maecenas."

units.la: Gloriam innovandæ urbis] Idem Tacitus lib. XV Annalium, Videbaturq; Nero condendæ urbis novæ & cognomento suo appellandæ gloriam quærere.
units.tr: The glory of renewing the city] The same Tacitus, Annals book 15: "And Nero seemed to seek the glory of founding a new city and naming it after himself."

units.la: Neque ulla re Nero efficiebat] rursum Tacitus, Sed non ope humana, non largitionibus Principis, aut Deum placamentis, decedebat infamia, quin jussum incendium crederetur.
units.tr: And by nothing could Nero accomplish] Again Tacitus: "But neither by human means, nor by the emperor's largesse, nor by appeasing the gods, did the infamy depart, so that the fire was still believed to have been ordered."

units.la: Igitur vertit invidiam in Christianos] Idem qui supra, Ergo abolendo rumoriNero subdidit reos & quæsitissimis[?] poenis affecit, quos per flagitia invisos vulgus Christianos appellabat.
units.tr: Therefore he turned the odium onto the Christians] The same as above: "Therefore, to quash the rumour, Nero put forward as guilty, and punished with the most exquisite torments, those whom the common people called Christians, hated for their crimes."

units.la: Vt ferarum tergis contecti] Sunt ipsissima verba Taciti, Et pereuntibus addita ludibria, ut ferarum tergis conte-cti, laniatu canum interirent: aut crucibus affixi, aut flammandi, atque ubi defecisset dies in usum nocturni luminis urerentur.
units.tr: Covered with the hides of wild beasts] These are the very words of Tacitus: "And mockery was added to their deaths, so that they perished covered with the skins of wild beasts, torn by dogs, or were fixed to crosses and set on fire, and when daylight failed they were burned to serve as nocturnal light."

units.la: Vt cum defecisset dies, &c.] ut tunica molesta induti per-totam noctem ardentes vigilibus essent vicem ignium excubiarum. Sed vide Scaligerum in Chronicon Eusebij 18i. 1. cujus a-nimadversiones compilare nolo.
units.tr: When the day had failed, etc.] so that, clothed in tunics of pitch, they were to burn all night as watch-fires in place of lamps. But see Scaliger on the Chronicle of Eusebius, 18i. 1; I do not wish to compile his animadversions.

units.la: Datis legibus] latis pro datis legendum censet Carolus Sigonius.
units.tr: Laws given] Carolus Sigonius thinks that latis should be read instead of datis.

units.la: Petrus in crucem sublatus est] Salmanticensis, Nero sus-pendit Petrum Joan in ligno. [illegible, ~5 letters] , id est, Petrum Johannis, τὸ Ἰωάνης[?], qui & Ἰωσᾶ[?]: unde Bar jona. Est autem contractio pro Johana.
units.tr: Peter was raised up onto the cross] The Salmanticensis: Nero hanged Peter John on a tree. [illegible], that is, Peter son of John, the Ioannes [Ἰωάνης], who is also Iosas [Ἰωσᾶ]: whence Bar-jona. It is, however, a contraction for Johanna.

units.la: Felti Flori] In Eusebio, Ceftij Flori: sed legendum ex Josepho Gesij Flori. Vide Ant. ejus, lib. 20. cap. 9.
units.tr: Felix Florus] In Eusebius it reads Cestius Florus, but it should be read as Gessius Florus from Josephus. See his Antiquities, book 20, chapter 9.

units.la: Pag. 136. Adversus eos Vespasianus proconsulari imperio missus] Eusebius, Contra Iudæos, qui Cestij Flori avaritiam non ferentes rebellabant, Vespasianus magister militiæ a Nerone transmittitur.
units.tr: Page 136. Against them Vespasian was sent with proconsular power] Eusebius, Against the Jews: Those who, not enduring the greed of Cestius Florus, were rebelling, Vespasian, master of the soldiery, is sent out by Nero.

units.la: Humanis rebus eximitur] extinctus est VIII Eid. Junij, anno & XXII diebus ante initium Vespasiani. Scaliger in Eusebium.
units.tr: He is removed from human affairs] He died on the eighth day before the Ides of June, in the year ... and 22 days before the beginning of Vespasian's reign. Scaliger on Eusebius.

units.la: Incertum an ipse sibi mortem conscíverit] imo certissimum. Nam cum audisset Galbam in Hispania ab exercitu imperatorem declaratum, hostis a senatu judicatus, ex urbe fugiens, semet ipsi[?] gladij transegit, adjuvante trepidantem manum eunucho Sporo: cum prius nullo reperto exclamaret, Itane? nec inimicum habeo nec amicum: dedecorose vixi, turpius pererrem, Suetonius, alij. Cum a senatu quaereretur ad poenam e Palatio fugiens, ad quartum urbis milliarium in suburbano liberti sui inter Salariam & Numentanam viam semet interficit, anno ætatis suæ XXXII. Eusebius in Chronico.
units.tr: It is uncertain whether he brought about his own death] On the contrary, most certain. For when he heard that Galba had been declared emperor by the army in Spain, and had been judged a public enemy by the senate, he fled from the city and ran himself through with a sword, his trembling hand being helped by the eunuch Sporus, after first finding no one and exclaiming: "Is it so? I have neither enemy nor friend; I lived shamefully, and I shall die more shamefully." Suetonius, and others. When he was sought by the senate for punishment, fleeing from the Palace, he killed himself at the fourth milestone from the city, on an estate in the suburbs of his freedman, between the Salarian and Nomentan roads, in the thirty-second year of his age. Eusebius, in the Chronicle.

units.la: Curato vulnere ejus servatus] dixerat, incertum an ipse sibi mortem conscíverit. Nam secundum opinionem quorumdam se ipse vulneravit, e quo vulnere postea curatus fuit, unde adhuc vivere creditur. Samuel Solem ad librum Iobafin[?], Commentarij de vitis regum dicunt partim Neronē mortuum esse, partim fugitiue[?],nec sciri locum quo fugerit: usq; adeo ut Augustinus episcopus afferat ipsum adhuc vivere.
units.tr: Having had his wound treated, he was saved] He had said: it is uncertain whether he brought about his own death. For according to the opinion of some, he wounded himself, and from that wound he was afterwards healed, whence he is believed to be still alive. Samuel Solem, on the book ..., the Commentaries on the lives of the kings, say that Nero partly died and partly fled, and that the place where he fled is not known; so much so that Augustine the bishop asserts that he is still alive.

units.la: Et plaga mortis ejus curata est} ita legendum ex Apoca-lyp. 13.3 prius erat in libris, Vt plaga mortis ejus curat- est. Quem locum nonnulli de Nerone interpretati sunt: sed male, meo judicio. Augustinus de civit. Dei, lib. 20. cap. 19. Quidam putant hoc (intelligit locum Apostoli, Nam mysterium jam operatur iniquitatis) de imperio Romano dictum esse, & propterea Paulum apostolum ea aperte scribere noluisse, ne calumniam incurreret, quod imperio Romano male optaret, quod speraretur æternum: & ut hoc quod dixit, jam enim mysterium iniquitatis operatur, Neronem voluerit intelligi, cujus jam facta velut Antichristi videbantur.
units.tr: "And his mortal wound was healed": so it should be read, from Revelation 13:3. Earlier printed editions had "that the wound of his death was healed." Some have interpreted this passage of Nero, but in my judgment wrongly. Augustine, De civitate Dei, book 20, chapter 19: "Some think that this (he means the passage of the Apostle, For the mystery of iniquity already works) was said of the Roman empire, and that for this reason the apostle Paul did not wish to write it plainly, lest he incur the charge of wishing ill to the Roman empire, which was hoped to be eternal. And by the words 'for the mystery of iniquity already works' they meant Nero, whose deeds already seemed like those of Antichrist."

units.la: Unde nonnulli ipsum resurrecturum & futurum Anti-christum suspicantur. Alij vero non eum occisum putant, sed subtractum potius ut putaretur occisus & vivum ec-cultari in vigore ipsius ætatis, in qua fuit cum crederetur extinctus, donec suo tempore reveletur & restituatur in regnum. sed multum mira hæc opinantium præsumptio. Quæ adduxi propter Samuelem Iudæum, quem supra laudavi, qui Augustinum non bene intellexit, si unquam legit.
units.tr: Hence some suspect that he will rise again and be the future Antichrist. Others, however, do not think he was killed but rather withdrawn, so that he would be thought dead, and that he is hidden alive in the vigour of the age he was in when he was believed to have died, until at his appointed time he is revealed and restored to the kingdom. But the presumption of those who hold these opinions is very strange. I have adduced these things on account of the Jew Samuel, whom I cited above, who did not understand Augustine well, if he ever read him.

units.la: Vt mysterium iniquitatis exerceat} hoc est, ut fit Anti-christus. Nam per eum exercebitur mysterium iniquitatis, de quo Apostolus 2. Thessal 2.7. Vide quæ notavimus ad pag. 133.
units.tr: That he may work the mystery of iniquity: that is, so that he becomes Antichrist. For through him the mystery of iniquity will be carried out, of which the Apostle speaks in 2 Thessalonians 2:7. See what we have noted on page 133.

units.la: Post excessum Neronis] Sarisberiensis de nugis Curialium lib. 8. cap. 19. Nero sextus a Iulio omnium immanissimus & vilissimus hunc exitum habuit. Postquam enim defor-mitate veterum officiorum & angustiis flexurisq; viarum offensus, ut prædictum est, urbem incendit, ab omni po-pulo, sicut Suetonius refert, desertus est: & cum ingressus in cubiculum quæreret percussorem & non inveniret (omnes quippe discesserant[?]) Ergo ego, inquit, nec amicum nec inimicum habeo. Idem paullo antequam se confoderet scrobem coram se fieri præcepit ad corporis sui mo-dulum, componique in ea si qua invenirentur marmoris frusta, & aquam simul & ligna ad curandum cadaver, flens [?]itens ad singula atque identidem dictitans, Qualis artifex pereo? Vide sequentia.
units.tr: After the death of Nero: Sarisbury, De nugis curialium, book 8, chapter 19: "Nero, the sixth from Julius, the most savage and worthless of all, had this end. For after he, offended by the deformity of the old buildings and the narrowness and winding of the streets, as has been said, set fire to the city, he was deserted by all the people, as Suetonius reports. And when he went into his bedchamber and looked for an assassin and did not find one (for all had indeed departed), he said: 'So I have neither friend nor enemy.' Shortly before he stabbed himself, he ordered a pit to be dug in front of him to the measure of his body, and pieces of marble, if any could be found, to be put in it, along with water and wood to tend the corpse, weeping at each thing and repeating again and again: 'What an artist I die!'" See what follows.

units.la: Vitellius in Gallias] res poscit ut legamus e Galliis, de quo nos admonuit doctissimus Sigonius. Ceterum a morte Neronis usque ad imperium Vespasiani Xiphilinus e Dione ponit annum unum & menses 11.
units.tr: Vitellius into the Gauls: the matter requires that we read "from the Gauls" (e Galliis), as the most learned Sigonius reminded us. Moreover, Xiphilinus, from Dio, gives one year and eleven months from the death of Nero until the rule of Vespasian.

units.la: Postquam ad Vespasianum delata] Suetonius in Vespasiano, Tiberius Alexander praefectus Ægypti primus in verba Vespasiani legiones adegit Kalendis Iulij: qui principatus dies in posterum observatus est.
units.tr: After the news reached Vespasian: Suetonius, in Vespasian: Tiberius Alexander, prefect of Egypt, first bound the legions to the oath to Vespasian on the Kalends of July, and that day of the beginning of his rule has been observed since.

units.la: Cum se Vitellius[?] interfecisset] Si Eusebio credendum, non se interfecit, sed a Vespasiani ducibus occisus est. Verba Eusebij habentur in Chronico, Vitellius octavo imperij sui mense a Vespasiani ducibus occisus in Tiberim proiicitur. Idem Galbae, Othoni & Vitellio assignat annum unum & menses sex.
units.tr: When Vitellius had killed himself: If Eusebius is to be believed, he did not kill himself, but was slain by Vespasian's commanders. Eusebius's words are found in the Chronicle: "Vitellius, in the eighth month of his reign, was slain by the commanders of Vespasian and thrown into the Tiber." The same author assigns one year and six months to Galba, Otho and Vitellius together.

units.la: Imperium confirmavit] sex menses post occisum Vitellium. Sigonius.
units.tr: He confirmed his rule: six months after Vitellius was killed. Sigonius.

units.la: Ne humanis quidem corporibus pepercerunt] nam mulier quaedam, nomine Maria Eleazari filia, proprium filium occidit, coxit & comedit ex parte. Iosephus ἀλώσ[?]. lib.7. cap.8.
units.tr: They did not even spare human bodies: for a certain woman, named Mary, daughter of Eleazar, killed her own son, roasted him and ate part of him. Josephus, The Jewish War, book 7, chapter 8.

units.la: In diem Paschae] quo Iudaei omnes undique sacrorum causa Ierosolymam confluebant, ut & in reliquis duobus festis, quae Regalim appellantur.
units.tr: At the day of Passover: when the Jews from everywhere gathered at Jerusalem for the sacred rites, as also at the other two feasts, which are called pilgrim feasts.

units.la: Vt eo tempore quo Dominum, &c.] Eusebius in Chronico, oportuit enim iisdem diebus Paschae eos interfici, in quibus Salvatorem crucifixerunt. Idem scribit in historia Eccles. lib.3. cap.5.
units.tr: So that at the same time when they crucified the Lord, etc.: Eusebius in the Chronicle: "For they had to be killed on the same days of Passover on which they crucified the Saviour." He writes the same in the Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 5.

units.la: Pharisaei aliquantisper pro templo acerrime restiterunt] non est dubium quin inter eos quoque Saducaei fuerint, & fortasse an etiam Heseni[?]. Proditum est litterarum monimentis, quod tamen ubi legerim nescio, Anani pontificem, qui tum erat, Saducaeum fuisse. Fallit me memoria, si secus est.
units.tr: The Pharisees for a time resisted most fiercely on behalf of the temple: there is no doubt that Sadducees were among them too, and perhaps also Essenes. It has been handed down in written records, though I do not remember where I read it, that Ananus the high priest, who was then in office, was a Sadducee. My memory fails me if this is not so.

units.la: Numerus peremptorum ad undecies centena millia referetur] debuisset dicere mortuorum. Nam sequitur Iosephum, & (ad) in eo saepe otium agit. Iosephus Ἀλώ.7.17. numerus mortuorum per omne tempus obsidionis undecies centum millia. Mortuorum, hoc est eorum qui fame aut gladio perierunt. Eusebius in Chronico, Iosephus vero scribit. undecies centena millia fame & gladio periisse. Iosephus Iudaeus scribit undecies centena millia Iudaeorum gladio & fame periisse. De numero peremptorum sive interfectorum conveniunt Suetonius & Tacitus. Idem Orofius, Sexcenta millia Iudaeorum eo bello interfecta Cornelius & Suetonius referunt. Et Eusebius, Titus Iudaea capta & Ierosolymis subversis sexcenta millia virorum interfe-cit. Quid Egesippus sive Hegesippus ? Caesa, inquit, per omne tempus obsidionis decies centena millia, aut CX myriades, ut plerique asserunt. Centum & decem myriades sunt undecies centena millia. Ea mortua, non caesa Iosephus asserit. Quid ergo vidit, cum talia scriberet? Professo scriptor ille meritò suspectus est viris eruditis.
units.tr: The number of those slain is said to be eleven hundred thousand: he ought to have said "of the dead." For he follows Josephus, and in him he often takes his ease. Josephus, The Jewish War 7.17: the number of the dead through the whole time of the siege was eleven hundred thousand. "Dead," that is, of those who perished by famine or sword. Eusebius in the Chronicle, but Josephus writes that eleven hundred thousand perished by famine and sword. The Jewish historian Josephus writes that eleven hundred thousand Jews perished by sword and famine. Suetonius and Tacitus agree on the number of those slain or killed. Likewise Orosius: "Six hundred thousand Jews were killed in that war," as Cornelius and Suetonius report. And Eusebius: "Titus, having taken Judea and overthrown Jerusalem, killed six hundred thousand men." What does Hegesippus, or Egesippus, say? "Slain," he says, "throughout the whole time of the siege, a thousand times a hundred thousand, or 110 myriads, as most assert." A hundred and ten myriads is eleven hundred thousand. Josephus asserts that these were dead, not slain. What, then, did he see when he wrote such things? That writer, as a professed author, is rightly suspected by learned men.

units.la: Capta vero ū[?] millia ac venundata] ex Iosepho scribendum, ad centum millia. Nam erant XCVII millia. Quem numerum etiam Hegesippus agnoscit. Sed in Eusebio, & alia centum millia captivorum publice venundata. Quocirca nihil mutandum in Sulpicio. Nam absque dubio secutus hic est Eusebium, non Iosephum. Orofius numerum dispersorum ponit, quem ait fuisse ad CX hominum millia.
units.tr: But the captured, some 97 thousand, were sold: it should be written from Josephus, "about a hundred thousand," for there were 97 thousand. Hegesippus also acknowledges this number. But in Eusebius there is "a hundred thousand captives publicly sold." Therefore nothing should be changed in Sulpicius, for without doubt he here followed Eusebius, not Josephus. Orosius gives the number of those dispersed, which he says was about 110 thousand people.

units.la: Adhibito consilio] ducum aut procerum sex, qui nominantur Αλά[?]. 7.9. inter quos Marcus Antonius Iulianus procurator Iudaeae. ibid. Titus ad consilium vocavit duces exercitus, &c. Hegesippus lib. 5. cap.41.
units.tr: Having taken counsel: with six of the commanders or nobles, who are named in Josephus, book 7, chapter 9, among whom is Marcus Antonius Julianus, procurator of Judea. In the same place: "Titus called the commanders of the army to council," etc. Hegesippus, book 5, chapter 41.

units.la: Nonnullis videbatur aedem sacratam &c.] Titus ipse ita sensebat. Duces conditionem addebant, Si Iudaei illud reliquissent. Vide Iosephum.
units.tr: To some it seemed that the sacred temple, etc.: Titus himself thought so. The commanders added a condition: "If the Jews would leave it." See Josephus.

units.la: Quae servata modestiae R. &c.] Titi haec sententia erat, quam Iosephus his verbis expressit, Neque se unquam tantum opus incensurum: jam enim Romanorum fore hoc damnum, sicut ornamentum quoque fore imperij, si n[?] aneret. In eam iverunt Fronto, Alexander & Cerealis.
units.tr: Which, preserved out of respect, etc.: this was Titus's opinion, which Josephus expressed in these words: that he would never burn so great a work, for this would be a loss to the Romans, just as its preservation would be an ornament to the empire. Fronto, Alexander and Cerealis went along with this.

units.la: At contra alij] Aliis quidem videbatur lege belli utendum esse. Numquam enim Iudaeos a novis rebus posse desinere templo manente, quo omnes ubicunque essent colligerentur. Iosephus.
units.tr: But on the other hand others: Others indeed thought that the law of war should be used. For the Jews could never stop revolting while the temple stood, to which all, wherever they were, would gather. Josephus.

units.la: Et Titus ipse] hoc verum non esse docent ea quae supra ex Iosepho produximus. Iosephus enim scribit invito Tito templum incensum esse. Nec aliter Hegesippus, ad quem te adire volo. Quò plenius Iudaeorum & Christianorum religio tol-leretur] finxit ex ingenio. Nam nihil tale in Iosepho, aut apud alios, quos vidi.
units.tr: And Titus himself: that this is not true is shown by what we have brought forward above from Josephus. For Josephus writes that the temple was burned against Titus's will. Nor does Hegesippus say otherwise; I want you to consult him. In order that the religion of the Jews and Christians might be more fully destroyed: he invented this from his own mind. For there is nothing like it in Josephus, or in others whom I have seen.

units.la: Licet contrarias sibi] non sunt contrariæ, sed eadem. Nam prophetæ, nihil dissident ab Apostolis. Quid igitur diversas, imò contrarias, fecerunt Pharisæi, a quibus populus tum pendebat. Nam traditiones & cæremonias, quas Christus abolevit, mordicus retinuerunt, hodieque adhuc retinent Iudæi: non omnes, fatetor; sed tamen plerique, quos Rabbanijm appellant.
units.tr: Although they were opposed to each other: they are not opposed but the same. For the prophets do not differ at all from the Apostles. Why, then, did the Pharisees make them different, indeed opposed, the Pharisees on whom the people then depended? For they clung tenaciously to the traditions and ceremonies which Christ abolished, and the Jews still cling to them today, not all, I admit, but most of them, whom they call Rabbanites [Rabbanim].

units.la: Christianos ex Iudaeis exstitisse] nam primi Christiani Iudæi erant, ut etiam ipse Christus, cujus illud est, Salus ex Iudæis est. Unde in principio Christiani Iudæi vocabantur. Notum illud Taciti, Iudæos Chresto duce assidue tumultuantes Roma expulit. De Claudio loquitur.
units.tr: Christians arose from the Jews: for the first Christians were Jews, as Christ himself was, of whom it is said: "Salvation is of the Jews" (John 4:22). Hence at the beginning Christians were called Jews. Famous is that saying of Tacitus: "Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome, who were constantly causing disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus." He speaks of Claudius.

units.la: iisdem] ab iisdem Sigonius.
units.tr: by the same: by the same, Sigonius.

units.la: Templum dirutum] imo intensum, quod accidit decimo die Augusti, quo etiam a Babyloniorum rege fuerat concrematum. Urbs post capta fuit, videlicet die octavo Septembris, qui Tbefri Ebræis[?]. De urbe superiore mihi sermo. Nam inferior ante templum capta fuerat. Iosephus a condita primum urbe usque ad excidium ejus putat annos MMCLXXVII. Ἀλώσεως lib. 7. cap. 18.
units.tr: The temple destroyed: indeed burned, which happened on the tenth day of August, on which it had also been burned by the king of the Babylonians. The city was afterwards captured, namely on the eighth day of September, which among the Hebrews is Tishri. I am speaking of the upper city, for the lower city had been captured before the temple. Josephus thinks that from the founding of the city to its destruction there were 2,177 years, Capture of Jerusalem, book 7, chapter 18.

units.la: Capite autem decimo ejusdem libri a prima structione templi usque ad eversionem ejus, quae per Titum facta, numerat ann. MCXXX, menss. VII, dies XV: a secunda vero, quae sub Dario Notho accidit, ann. DCXXXIX, dies XLV. Ceterum excisa fuit urbs anno Vespasiani secundo, qui fuit a nato Christo, secundum supputationem Eusebij, septuagesimus tertius: ab eodem passo quadragesimus: & baptizato XLIII. Vide Chronicon ejus.
units.tr: In the tenth chapter of the same book, he counts from the first building of the temple to its overthrow by Titus 1130 years, 7 months and 15 days; and from the second building, which happened under Darius Nothus, 639 years and 45 days. The city was destroyed in the second year of Vespasian, which was the seventy-third year from the birth of Christ by Eusebius's reckoning, the fortieth from his passion, and the forty-third from his baptism. See his Chronicle.

units.la: Qua extorres patria] Tertullianum, dispersi palabundi & soli coelique sui extorres vagantur per orbem, sine homine, sine Deo rege: quibus nec advenarum jure terram patriam saltem vestigio salutare conceditur. Vide sequentia.
units.tr: Whence exiled from their homeland]: Tertullian says: scattered and wandering, exiles from their own soil and sky, they roam the world without a man or God as king, and not even the right of foreigners grants them so much as a footstep on their native land. See what follows.

units.la: Non ob aliud eos, quam ob illatas Christo manus &c.]
units.tr: Not for any other reason than for laying hands on Christ, etc.

units.la: Sic Prudentius,
units.tr: So Prudentius:

units.la: Exiliis vagus huc illuc fluit antibus errat Iudæus, postquam patria de sede revulsus Supplicium pro cæde luit, Christique negati Sanguine respersus commissa piacula solvit. Sæpe alias, cum propter peccata captivitatibus tradentur] sub judicibus sæpe captivitatem pependerunt, ut cum a rege Mesopotamiæ subacti essent, pag. 40. & alias. Servitus Ægyptiaca non fuit propter peccata: hoc primum, deinde ultra LXX annos ibi servierunt. Quocirca nihil facit ad hunc locum, ut nec ea quam pependerunt sub Antiocho Epiphane. Tum enim lege spoliati fuerunt, non in captivitatem abducti, nisi forte quis dicat ipsorum conscientias tum captivitatis pœnam subiisse.
units.tr: Wandering in exile, the Jew drifts hither and thither, torn from the seat of his fatherland; he pays the penalty for slaughter, and sprinkled with the blood of the Christ he denied, he atones for the crimes he committed. Often at other times, when they were handed over to captivities on account of sins: under judges they often suffered captivity, as when they were subdued by the king of Mesopotamia (p. 40) and elsewhere. The Egyptian servitude was not on account of sins; first this, and then they served there more than seventy years. Hence it has nothing to do with this passage, nor does the servitude they endured under Antiochus Epiphanes. For then they were stripped of the law, not led away into captivity, unless perhaps someone says that their consciences then underwent the punishment of captivity.

units.la: Ultra LXX annos] tot annos duravit captivitas Babylonica, quæ Iudæorum propria, hoc est duarum tribuum. Nam decem tribus in Assyriam abductæ nunquam inde redierunt.
units.tr: The Babylonian captivity lasted so many years; it belonged to the Jews alone, that is, of two tribes. For the ten tribes carried off into Assyria never returned from there.

units.la: Domitianus] cui Neroni cognomentū ob crudelitatem: quem ideo nonnulli credunt Antichristum venturum, ut supra ex Hiero. probavimus.
units.tr: Domitian, who had the surname Nero because of his cruelty; for this reason some believe that Antichrist will come, as we proved above from Jerome.

units.la: Quo tempore Iohannem apostolum, &c.] Chronicon Eusebij, Secundus post Neronem Domitianus Christianos persequitur: sub quo apostolus Iohannes in Pathmos insulam relegatus Apocalypsin vidit, quam Irenæus interpretatur. Consule Polycraticum, lib.8. cap.19[?].
units.tr: At which time the apostle John, etc.: Eusebius's Chronicle: "Second after Nero, Domitian persecutes the Christians; under him the apostle John, relegated to the island of Patmos, saw the Apocalypse, which Irenaeus interprets." Consult the Polycraticus, book 8, chapter 19.

units.la: Iohannem apostolum atque Euangelistam] etiam propheta fuit Hiero. in primo adversus Iovinianum, cap 14. Iohannes & apostolus & euangelista & propheta. Apostolus, quia scripsit ad ecclesias ut magister: Euangelista, quia librum euangelij condidit, quod excepto Matthæo, alij ex duodecim Apostolis non fecerunt: Propheta, vidit enim in Pathmos insula, in qua fuerat a Domitiano principe ob Domini martyrium relegatus, Apocalypsin infinita futurorum mysteria continentem. Refert autem Tertullianus, quod Romæ missus in ferventis olei dolium, purior & vegetior exiverit quam intraverit. Ceterum titulus libri apud Græcos Ἀποκάλυψις Ἰωάννου τῆς θεολόγου[?], id est, Iohannis theologi; non apostoli, non evangelistæ.
units.tr: John the apostle and evangelist: Jerome in the first book against Jovinian, chapter 14, also calls him a prophet: "John is apostle, evangelist and prophet. Apostle, because he wrote to the churches as a teacher; evangelist, because he composed a book of the gospel, which none of the other twelve apostles did except Matthew; prophet, for in the island of Patmos, to which he had been banished by the emperor Domitian on account of the martyrdom of the Lord, he saw the Apocalypse containing infinite mysteries of things to come." Tertullian relates that when he had been put into a vat of boiling oil at Rome, he came out purer and more vigorous than he went in. Moreover, the title of the book among the Greeks is "Revelation of John the theologian", that is, of John the theologian, not of the apostle or the evangelist.

units.la: Ioannem] Ἰωάννης[?]. Græci enim voces in medio raro aut nunquam aspirant. Sed Ebræa consuetudo poscit ut scribamus Iohannem, cum aspiratione, quæ duplex est in hoc nomine.
units.tr: John [Ἰωάννης]. For the Greeks rarely or never aspirate a letter in the middle of a word. But Hebrew usage requires that we write John with the aspiration, which is double in this name.

units.la: In Pathmum insulam] scribo, in Patmum insulam, cum φ[?] simplici: quomodo etiam scribendum putarem in loco Eusebij superius citato. Nam Græce est εἰς Πάτμον[?]. Est autem Patmus una ex Cycladibus, in mari Ægæo, quæ in circuitu patet xxxM passuum.
units.tr: I write "in the island Patmos", with a single, unaspirated letter, as I think should also be written in the passage of Eusebius cited above; for in Greek it is "into Patmos" [εἰς Πάτμον]. Patmos is one of the Cyclades, in the Aegean Sea, and measures about thirty thousand paces around.

units.la: Librum sacrae Apocalypsis] quod alium diceret Apocalypseos, id est revelationis. De hoc libro quae fuerint veterum judicia inveniesapud Erasmum[?] in Annotationibus ad cap. XXII. Vide quoque Theodori Bezae prolegomena in hunc librum.
units.tr: The book of the holy Apocalypse: because it calls itself another Apocalypse, that is, of revelation. On what the ancients thought of this book you will find in Erasmus's Annotations on chapter 22. See also Theodore Beza's prolegomena on this book.

units.la: A plerisque] Graecis praesertim, qui de hoc libro semper dubitarunt, ut Hiero. ad Pardanum scribit. Caius autem quidam eum Cerintho haeretico tribuebat. Eusebius hist. eccles. lib. 7 c. 25.
units.tr: By most: especially the Greeks, who always doubted this book, as Jerome writes to Pardanus. But a certain Caius attributed it to the heretic Cerinthus. Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 7, chapter 25.

units.la: Pag. 139. Tertia persecutio per Traiani m[?] fuit j[?] hanc initam alij scribunt anno Christi 103. alij ann. 108. Biennio post, hoc est, ann. Christiano 110. Simon Cleopae F. qui episcopatum Ierosolymorum tenebat, crucifigitur Eusebius in Chronico.
units.tr: Page 139. The third persecution under Trajan. Some write that it began in the year of Christ 103, others in 108. Two years later, that is in the Christian year 110, Simon, son of Cleophas, who held the bishopric of Jerusalem, was crucified. Eusebius in his Chronicle.

units.la: Qui cum tormentis] nam initio edictum proposuit, ut Christiani ubique conquirerentur, & per tormenta, si aliter non posset, usque ad mortem sacrificare ritu majorum adigerentur. Post cum Plinius Bithyniae proconsul per epistolam eum super hac re consuluisset, respondit, Christianani conquirendi non sunt: si deferantur & arguantur, puniendi sunt. Epistolam hanc ceteris Plinij epistolis, quae nunc in omnium manibus versantur, intextam invenies. Meminit & Eusebius per haec verba, Plinius secundus, quum quandam provinciam regeret, & in magistratu suo plurimos (quosdam est in Tertulliano, & mus in Graecis Eusebij) Christianos interfecisset, multitudine eorum perterritus quaesivit de Trajano quid facto opus esset, nuncians ei, praeter obstinationem non sacrificandi & antelucanos coetus ad canendum cuidam Christo ut Deo nihil apud eos reperiri. Praeterea ad confoederandam disciplinam vetari ab his homicidia, furta, adulteria, latrocinia & his similia. Ad quae commotus Trajanus rescripsit, hoc genus quidem inquirendos non esse, oblatos vero puniri oportere. Tertul. in Apologetico.
units.tr: Who with torments: for at first he issued an edict that Christians were to be sought out everywhere and, if they could not otherwise be dealt with, compelled by torments, even to death, to sacrifice according to the custom of their ancestors. Afterwards, when Pliny, proconsul of Bithynia, consulted him about this matter by letter, he replied that Christians were not to be sought out; if they were denounced and convicted, they were to be punished. You will find this letter woven among the other letters of Pliny, which are now in everyone's hands. Eusebius too mentions it in these words: "Pliny the Younger, when he governed a province and in his magistracy had killed many Christians, terrified by their multitude asked Trajan what should be done, reporting that among them nothing was found except obstinacy in not sacrificing and assemblies before dawn to sing to a certain Christ as to God. Moreover, to bind their discipline together, they forbade homicide, theft, adultery, robbery and things like these. Moved by this, Trajan replied that such people were not to be sought out, but if they were brought forward they ought to be punished." Tertullian in the Apologeticus.

units.la: Saeviri in eos ultra vetuit] anno Christi centesimo undecimo. Eusebius. Quae si vera, duravit haec persecutio annos tres, aut, ut alij volunt, octo.
units.tr: He forbade them to be harried further: in the year of Christ 111, according to Eusebius. If these things are true, this persecution lasted three years or, as others would have it, eight.

units.la: Iudaei rebellare voluerunt] imo rebellarunt, duce quodam Iudaeo, quem Eusebius & alij Barchochabam nominant. Id sonat filius stellae. Nam Chochab stella. De quo R. Aquiba exponebat textum illum, orietur stella ex Iacob. Idem ejusdem armiger fuisse traditur. Meminit Hiero. adversus Rufinum lib. 3 cap. 9.
units.tr: The Jews wished to rebel: nay, they rebelled, under a certain Jew whom Eusebius and others name Barchochab. That means "son of a star", for Chochab is "star". Concerning him, R. Akiba expounded that text, "a star shall rise out of Jacob." He is also said to have been his armour-bearer. Jerome mentions him in the third book against Rufinus, chapter 9.

units.la: Barchochabas autor seditionis Iudaicae stipulam in ore succensam anhelitu ventilabat ut flammas evomere putā-retur. Magnus hostis fuit Christianorum, quod sibi contra Romanos militare nollent. Eusebius, Chochebas dux factionis, Iudaeorum nolentes sibi Christianos adversum Roma-num militem ferre subsidium, omnimodis cruciatibus necat. Iudaei eum nominant Barchoziba, id est, filium mendacij, quod fraudulenter circumvenisset Iudaeos, Mesiam se esse persuadendo. Ejus mentio in Thalmud, traditur Sanhedrin, & in Iohasin Verba Salmanticensis, Filius Chozibae rebellavit in Romanos, surrexitque & profectus est in Cyrenen, quae in Africa, surgentesque Iudaei, qui ibi erant, occiderunt omnes Romanos & Graecos in illis locis, qui arenam matris numero aequabant. Inde abiit in AEgyptum & fecit similiter. Quod cum audirent Iudaei qui in Giphdi, hoc est in AEgypto, interfecerunt omnes gentes usque adeo ut non remaneret residuum. Quo audito Trajanus misit contra eos Adrianum qui subegit eos & posuit legē Romanæ ne quis Iudaeus intraret AEgyptum. Dicunt etiam doctores nostri, quorum fausta fit memoria, Adrianus Caesar occidit multa[?] millia, in Bitther autem occidit duplo plures quam egressi sunt ex AEgypto, anno LII post excidium. Porro regnavit Adrianus post excidium ann. XLV, qui primus Caesarum nutrivit barbam suam, nec totondit eam, ut alij Caesares. Obiit anno LXV excidij. Haec ille, Liber est apud me scriptus Ebraice a nescio quo, cum hac inscriptione, Hypomnema urbis Romae a die quo condita fuit usque ad initium regni Ismaelitarum. In eo scriptum lectum, In diebus Domitiani extitit Choziba, & in diebus Nervae & in diebus Adriani regnavit Choziba & filius ejus neposque ejus: qui bellarunt bella magna cum omnibus gentibus, & subegerunt AEgyptum. Contra hos roboravit se Adrianus & ascendit contra terram Iuda percusitque filium Chozibae & occidit eum. Tum extinctus est populus multus. Non vexavit eos Nebuchodonosor neque Titus, sicut Adrianus Caesar. De hoc nebulone tam multa in monumentis Ebraeorum, ut justus liber confici posset, si quis omnia observavasset. Ac Palaestinam] accidit hoc anno Christi CXXXV. Ad quem annum Eusebius, Iudaei ad arma, inquit, versi Palaestinam depopulati sunt, tenente provinciam Tenio Rufo, cui ad opprimendos rebelles Hadrianus misit exercitum.
units.tr: Barchochabas, the author of the Jewish sedition, blew upon a straw held in his mouth, set alight, with his breath, so that it seemed he was belching out flames. He was a great enemy of the Christians, because they would not fight alongside him against the Romans. Eusebius: "Chochebas, leader of the faction, since he would not allow the Christians to bring aid to him against the Roman soldier, put them to death with every kind of torture." The Jews call him Barchoziba, that is, son of a lie, because he deceitfully ensnared the Jews, persuading them that he was the Messiah. His mention is in the Talmud, tractate Sanhedrin, and in Iohasin; the words of the Salmanticensis are: The son of Chozibah rebelled against the Romans, and rose up and set out for Cyrene, which is in Africa; and the Jews who were there rose up and killed all the Romans and Greeks in those places, who equalled the sand of the mother in number. Thence he went to Egypt and did likewise. When the Jews who were in Giphdi, that is, in Egypt, heard of this, they killed all the nations, so that not one remnant was left. On hearing this, Trajan sent Hadrian against them, who subdued them and laid down a Roman law that no Jew should enter Egypt. Our teachers, of blessed memory, also say: Caesar Hadrian killed many thousands; in Bither he killed twice as many as had gone out of Egypt, in the fifty-second year after the destruction. Hadrian reigned for forty-five years after the destruction; he was the first of the Caesars to grow his beard and not shave it, unlike the other Caesars. He died in the sixty-fifth year of the destruction. Thus he. I have a book written in Hebrew by I know not whom, with this title: Hypomnema of the city of Rome from the day it was founded until the beginning of the reign of the Ishmaelites. In it is written and read: In the days of Domitian there arose Chozibah, and in the days of Nerva and in the days of Hadrian Chozibah reigned, and his son and grandson, who waged great wars with all nations and subdued Egypt. Against them Hadrian strengthened himself and marched against the land of Judah, and struck down the son of Chozibah and killed him; then a great people perished. Nebuchadnezzar did not harass them, nor Titus, as Caesar Hadrian did. There are so many things about this scoundrel in the monuments of the Hebrews that a whole book could be made, if someone had gathered them all. And Palestine: this happened in the year of Christ 135. To that year Eusebius says: "The Jews, turned to arms, laid waste Palestine, while Tineius Rufus governed the province, to whom Hadrian sent an army to put down the rebels.

units.la: In templo ac loco dominicae passionis } Ajunt in loco, ubi Dominus passus fuerat, templum fuisse Domini, quod Hadrianus terra obruit, ac templum aliud Veneri dedicavit. Id mansit eo modo usque ad Constantinum.
units.tr: In the place of the Lord's passion: they say that on the spot where the Lord suffered there was a temple of the Lord, which Hadrian buried in earth, and he dedicated another temple to Venus on it. It remained in that state until Constantine.

units.la: Daemonum simulachra] id est, idola. Respexit ad locum Apostoli, Qui idolo immolat, daemonibus immolat, non Deo. Vide Augustinum de civit. Dei, lib. 2. cap. 17. Quo facit & illud Pfal. 95. ὅτι πάντες οἱ θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν δαιμόνια [?]. Quamquam in fonte אֱלִילִים [?], id est, Dij nihili sive deastri. Clemens Protrept. Οἱ θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν δαιμόνιοι εἰσιν εἴδωλα [?]: Dij gentium daemonum sunt simulachra: Ioh. Sarisberiensis de nugis Curialium, Ad similitudinem ecclesiae (loquitur de Juliano) daemonum templa constituit. Videatur Lactantius lib. 1. cap. 17.
units.tr: Images of demons: that is, idols. He is looking to the apostle's words, "What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God." See Augustine, De civitate Dei, book 2, chapter 17. To the same purpose is Psalm 95: "for all the gods of the nations are demons" [ὅτι πάντες οἱ θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν δαιμόνια]. "But in the source the word is elilim" [אֱלִילִים], that is, "gods of nothing" or "worthless gods." Clement, Protrepticus: "The gods of the nations are demons; they are idols" [Οἱ θεοὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν δαιμόνιοι εἰσιν εἴδωλα]: "the gods of the nations are images of demons." John of Salisbury, De nugis curialium: "In imitation of the Church (he is speaking of Julian) he set up temples of demons." See also Lactantius, book 1, chapter 17.

units.la: Quia Christiani ex Iudaeis potissimum putabantur] Supra, Christianos ex Iudaeis extitisse. Vide quae notavimus ad illum locum, pag. 138.
units.tr: Because Christians were thought to come chiefly from the Jews: above, that Christians arose from the Jews. See what we have noted on that passage, page 138.

units.la: Ex circumcisione] id est, Iudaeum circumcisum. Sacerdotem] episcopum. Praefuerunt autem ibi ex circumcisione in universum episcopi quindecim, videlicet, 1. Iacobus frater Domini ab apostolis ordinatus, quem & Iustum vocabant. 2. Simeon vel Simon. 3. Iustus. 4. Zacheus. 5. Tobias. 6. Benjamin. 7. Iohannes. 8. Matthias. 9. Philippus. 10. Seneca. 11. Iustus alter. 12. Levi. 13. Ephres. 14. Iofes. 15. Iudas. Eusebius in Chronico, Ierosolymis decimus post Philippum constituitur episcopus Seneca. Post quem undecimus Iustus: cui succedit duodecimus Levi. Post quem tertiusdecimus Ephres. Quartusdecimus Iofes. Quintusdecimus Iudas. Hi omnes usque ad eversionem, quam ab Hadriano perpessa est Ierusalem, ex circumcisione episcopi praefuerunt.
units.tr: From the circumcision: that is, a circumcised Jew. Priest: that is, bishop. There were in all fifteen bishops from the circumcision who presided there, namely: (1) James, the brother of the Lord, ordained by the apostles, whom they also called Just; (2) Simeon or Simon; (3) Justus; (4) Zacchaeus; (5) Tobias; (6) Benjamin; (7) John; (8) Matthias; (9) Philip; (10) Seneca; (11) another Justus; (12) Levi; (13) Ephres; (14) Joses; (15) Judas. Eusebius in his Chronicle: "At Jerusalem, Seneca is set up as the tenth bishom after Philip. After him, Justus as the eleventh; he is succeeded by Levi as the twelfth. After him, Ephres as the thirteenth. Joses as the fourteenth. Judas as the fifteenth. All of these, down to the overthrow that Jerusalem suffered at the hands of Hadrian, presided as bishops from the circumcision."

units.la: Quae Iudaeos omnes Hierosolymae aditu arceret] Tertullianus in Apologetico de Iudaeis, quibus nec advenarum iure terram patriam saltem vestigio salutare conceditur. Hunc locum & supra produximus, in quo per terram patriam intelligitur non Iudaea (ita mihi videtur) sed Ierosolyma: a cuius aditu Iudaei arcebantur Romanis interdicti-nibus. Eusebius, Bellum Iudaicum, quod in Palaestina gerebatur, finem accepit, rebus Iudaeorum penitus oppressis: ex quo tempore etiam introeundi eis Ierosolymam licentia ablata, primum Dei nutu, sicut prophetae vaticinati sunt, deinde Romanis interdictionibus. Quo forte consilio Hadrianus imperator, cum Aeliam id est, Ierosolymam instauraret, in fronte ejus portae, quae ad Bethlehem erat, suem in marmore sculptam proposuit, ut Casiodorus in Chronico scribit. Figura enim immundi exosique animantis, quam ne nominare quidem poterant, abigebat & absterrebat eos aditu. Quanquam Eusebius aliam rationem adfert, inquiens, in fronte ejus portae, qua Bethlehem egredimur, sus sculptus in marmore significans Romanae potestati subjacere Iudaeos. Videsis Pithaeum Adverf. lib. 1. c. 3.
units.tr: Which kept all Jews from entering Jerusalem: Tertullian in the Apologeticus, on the Jews, to whom not even the right of strangers is granted to set foot upon their native land. We have also cited this passage above, where by "native land" is understood not Judea (so it seems to me) but Jerusalem, from whose entrance the Jews were kept out by Roman edicts. Eusebius: The Jewish war that was waged in Palestine came to an end, the affairs of the Jews being utterly crushed; from that time the permission to enter Jerusalem was also taken from them, first by the will of God, as the prophets foretold, and then by Roman prohibitions. Perhaps with this in mind the emperor Hadrian, when he rebuilt Aelia, that is Jerusalem, set up a carved marble image of a pig on the front of the gate that led to Bethlehem, as Cassiodorus writes in his Chronicle. For the figure of an unclean and hated animal, which they could not even name, drove them off and frightened them from the entrance. Eusebius, however, gives another reason, saying: on the front of the gate by which we go out to Bethlehem, a pig carved in marble signifies that the Jews are subject to Roman power. See Pithoeus, Adversaria, book 1, chapter 3.

units.la: Quod quidem Christianae fidei proficiebat] locum hunc ita explicat doctissimus Sigonius, Vtile erat Christianae fidei, neminem esse Christianum, nisi qui Iudaeus sub legis observatione vixisset: ita ordinante Deo, ut libertas fidei legis servitutem abrogaret: meo judicio, non recte. Sensus est, Vtile erat Christianae fidei Iudaeos Ierosolyma arceri. Nam ex hac occasione ceperunt primum abjicere jugum legis, cui ad hoc usque tempus paruerant, sub legis observatione Christum venerantes. Iudicent eruditi, & qui judicio pollent.
units.tr: Which indeed was useful to the Christian faith: the most learned Sigonius explains this passage thus: "It was useful for the Christian faith that no one should be a Christian unless he had lived as a Jew under observance of the law, God so ordaining that the freedom of faith should abolish the servitude of the law." In my judgment this is not right. The sense is: it was useful for the Christian faith that the Jews be kept out of Jerusalem. For from this occasion they first began to cast off the yoke of the law, to which they had submitted up to that time, worshipping Christ under observance of the law. Let the learned judge, and those who are gifted in judgment.

units.la: Tum poene omnes Christum Deum sub legis observatione credebant] hos posterior aetas Nazaraeos dixit, cum initio Christiani omnes ita vocarentur: unde euangelium Nazaraeorum, quod & euangelium secundum Ebraeos. Erant autem semi- Iudaei & semi- Christiani, hoc est neque Iudaei neque Christiani veri. Scribit autem Hiero. Iudaeos quotidie sub nomine Nazaraeorum ter Christianis maledicere. Hoc vel ideo verum esse potest, quod Christianos hodieque [illegible, ~5 letters] id est, Nazoraeos appellant.
units.tr: Then almost all believed that Christ was God under observance of the law: the later age called these Nazarenes, though at the beginning all Christians were so called; hence the Gospel of the Nazarenes, which is also the Gospel according to the Hebrews. They were half Jews and half Christians, that is, neither true Jews nor true Christians. Jerome writes that the Jews daily cursed the Christians three times under the name of Nazarenes. This may be true for the very reason that they still call Christians "Nozrim" [illegible, about five letters], that is, Nazoraeans, even today.

units.la: Vt legis servitus a libertate fidei, &c. ] observatio rituum Iudaicorum servitus est legis, quam sustulit Christiana libertas, suos ab omnibus illis caeremoniis liberando
units.tr: That the servitude of the law should give way to the freedom of faith, etc.: the observance of Jewish rites is the servitude of the law, which Christian liberty abolished, freeing its own people from all those ceremonies.

units.la: Ita tum primum Marcus, &c. ] Chronicon Eusebij, Ierosolymis primus ex gentibus constitutus episcopus Marcus cessantibus his qui ex Iudaeis.
units.tr: So then for the first time Mark, etc.: The Chronicle of Eusebius: at Jerusalem Mark was first appointed bishop from among the Gentiles, when those from the Jews had ceased.

units.la: Quarta sub Hadriano persecutio] hujus meminerunt quidem Augustinus & Orosius, sed eam sub Marco Antonino factam scribunt, Eusebius autem refert Quadratum discipulum Apostololorum & Aristidem Atheniensem Philosophum libros pro Christiana religione Hadriano dedisse compositos. Idem, Serenus Grannius, inquit, legatus vir apprime nobilis litteras ad Imperatorem misit, iniquum esse dicens clamoribus vulgi innocentium hominum sanguinem concedi, & sine ullo crimine, nominis tantum & sectæ reos fieri. Quibus commotus Hadrianus Minutio Fundano proconsuli Asiæ scribit, non sine objectu criminum Christianos condemnandos: cujus epistolæ usque ad nostram memoriam durat exemplum. De hoc Hadriano Orosius lib 7. cap. 8. Iudæos sane perturbatione scelerum suorum exagitatos & Palæstinam provinciam quondam suam depopulantes ultima cæde perdomuit: ultusque est Christianos quos illi Chocheba duce (ita leg. vulgo perperam Cotheba) qui sibi adversus Christianos omnes non assentirentur excruciabant; præcepitque ne cui Iudæo introeundi in Hierosolymam esset licentia, Christianis tantum civitate permissa, quam ipse in optimum statum murorum extructione reparavit & Aeliam vocari de prænomine suo præcepit. De eodem Ludovicus Vives in commentaria ad August. de civitat. Dei, col. 1127. Hadrianus ex animo Christianis favit, sed occulte. Quin & molitum ferunt ut Christus pro Deo reciperetur, templaque in eum usum erexisse: deterritum tamen consilio quorundam, qui affirmabant fore ut cultus omnis Deorum periret, si id fieret, quod de Christo cogitabat.
units.tr: The fourth persecution under Hadrian: Augustine and Orosius do indeed mention this, but they write that it was carried out under Marcus Antoninus. Eusebius, however, reports that Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, and Aristides the Athenian philosopher gave Hadrian books composed in defence of the Christian religion. The same Eusebius says: "Serenius Granianus, a distinguished man and legate, wrote to the emperor, saying it was unjust that the blood of innocent men should be yielded to the outcry of the crowd, and that men should be made defendants for a name and sect alone, without any crime." Moved by these things, Hadrian wrote to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, that Christians were to be condemned, but not without the charge of crimes; a copy of this letter survives to our own memory. Concerning this Hadrian, Orosius, book 7, chapter 8: "The Jews, indeed, harassed by the disturbance of their own crimes and laying waste the province of Palestine, once their own, he subdued with a final slaughter; and he punished the Christians whom they, under their leader Chocheba (the reading in common editions, Cotheba, is wrongly printed), tortured because they would not agree with them against all Christians. He ordered that no Jew should have permission to enter Jerusalem, the city being open to Christians only, which he himself restored to its best state by building walls, and he ordered it to be called Aelia after his own praenomen." Ludovicus Vives on the same, in his commentary on Augustine, De civitate Dei, column 1127. Hadrian favoured the Christians from his heart, but secretly. Indeed they say he even planned that Christ should be received as God and had built temples for that purpose; but he was turned from the plan by the advice of some who maintained that all worship of the gods would perish if this were done, which he had been thinking of in regard to Christ.

units.la: Pag. 140. Antonino Pio imperante pax ecclesiæ fuit] Xiphilinus ex Dione, constat inter omnes Antoninum pium probum virum fuisse, neque enim ceteris subditis gravis, neque Christianis infensus fuit: quos vehementer observavit. Apud hunc, nisi fallor, in magno pretio fuit R. Iuda Hannasi, qui vulgo Rabbenu Haccados, id est, doctor noster sanctus. Fuit alius Antoninus cognomento Philosophus, qui & Marcus Antoninus & Lucius Aurelius imperavitque cum L. Vero ann. XIX, mense uno. Hic Ecclesiam vexari sivit, quod significat Sulpicius noster, cum ait,
units.tr: Page 140. Under the emperor Antoninus Pius the Church enjoyed peace: Xiphilinus, from Dio: it is agreed by all that Antoninus Pius was a good and upright man; for he was neither burdensome to his other subjects nor hostile to Christians, whom he greatly protected. Under him, unless I am mistaken, R. Judah Hannasi, commonly called Rabbenu Hakkadosh, that is, "our holy teacher," was held in great esteem. There was another Antoninus, surnamed the Philosopher, who was also called Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius, and reigned with L. Verus for nineteen years and one month. He allowed the Church to be harassed, as our Sulpicius indicates when he says:

units.la: Sub Aurelio deinde Antonini filio persecutio quinta agitata] quæ quarta est aliis, ut Augustino, Orosio & Eusebio: quam perhibent exercitam a Lucio Vero ipsius collega. De hoc tempore Chronicon Eusebij, Persecutione orta in Asia Polycarpus carpus & Pionius fecere martyrium, quorum scriptae quoque passiones feruntur.
units.tr: Under Aurelius, the son of Antoninus, the fifth persecution was stirred up: others, such as Augustine, Orosius and Eusebius, count this as the fourth, and they report that it was carried out by Lucius Verus, his colleague. Concerning this time the Chronicle of Eusebius says: "In a persecution that arose in Asia, Polycarp, Carpus and Pionius suffered martyrdom; their written accounts of suffering are also said to survive."

units.la: Ac tum primum intra Galliàs martyria visa] Idem Chronicon, Plurimi in Gallia gloriosè ob Christi nomen inter-secti, quorum usq; in praesentem diem condita libris cer-tamina perseverant.
units.tr: And then for the first time martyrdoms were seen within Gaul: the same Chronicle: "Very many were gloriously slain in Gaul for the name of Christ, whose contests, recorded in books, continue to this day."

units.la: Serius trans Alpes Dei religione suscepta] hoc parum verum esse putat Sigonius. Nam S. Martialis, inquit, Lemovi-cum, Eucherius Treviros, Fronto Petrogoricas, Sabinus & Potentianus Senonas ad praedicandum euangelium a S. Petro apostolo missi: post sub Nerone passi esse dicuntur.
units.tr: Later, beyond the Alps, the religion of God was received: Sigonius thinks this is hardly true. For, he says, St Martial was sent to the Lemovices, Eucherius to the Treveri, Fronto to Périgueux, and Sabinus and Potentianus to Sens, by the apostle St Peter to preach the gospel; afterwards they are said to have suffered under Nero.

units.la: Sexta deinde, Severo imperante, Christianorum vexatio fuit] hanc Augustinus & Orosius quintam vocant. Augustini locus, ubi hoc dicit, habetur lib. XVIII de civit. Dei, cap. LII. Vide sis Vivem ad illum locum. Orosij verba lib. VII. cap. XI. haec sunt, Quinta post Neronem persecutione Christianos excruciavit: plurimique sanctorum per diversas provincias martyrio coronati sunt. Spartianus de hoc Severo: Christianum fieri sub gravi poena vetuit. Vide quoque Eusebium lib. V. hist. eccles.
units.tr: Then, under the emperor Severus, came the sixth persecution of Christians: Augustine and Orosius call this the fifth. The passage of Augustine where he says this is in book 18 of De civitate Dei, chapter 52. See Vives on that passage. The words of Orosius, book 7, chapter 11, are these: "After Nero, the fifth persecution tormented the Christians, and very many of the saints were crowned with martyrdom in various provinces." Spartianus on this Severus: "He forbade anyone to become a Christian under severe penalty." See also Eusebius, book 5 of the Ecclesiastical History.

units.la: Quo tempore Leonidas] Id Eusebius conjicit in annum Christi CCIV, Persecutione, inquit, in Christianos facta, Leonides Origenis pater gloriosa martyrij morte transfertur.
units.tr: At that time Leonidas] Eusebius places this in the year of Christ 204: "In the persecution raised against the Christians, Leonides, Origen's father, was taken away by a glorious death as a martyr."

units.la: Interjectis deinde annis VIII & XXX] a primo Antonino Caracalla, qui Severo successit, usque ad Decium Eusebius numerat annos XL. Quod ex hac tabella perspici poterit, Antoninus cognomento Caracallas ann. | 6 Macrinus an. | 1 Marcus Aurelius Antoninus ann. | 4 Alexander Mamaea F. ann. | 13 Maximinus ann. | 3 Gordianus ann. | 6 Philippus ann. | 7 Summ. ann. | 40.
units.tr: After the intervening thirty-eight years] From the first Antoninus Caracalla, who succeeded Severus, down to Decius, Eusebius counts forty years. This can be seen from this table: Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla, 6 years; Macrinus, 1; Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, 4; Alexander Mamaea's son, 13; Maximinus, 3; Gordian, 6; Philip, 7; total, 40 years.

units.la: Nisi quod medio tempore Maximinus &c.] Eusebius de temporibus, Maximinus adversus ecclesiarum sacerdotes persecutionem facit. Idem alibi, Maximinus propter gravem invidiam, qua contra Alexandri familiam, in qua complures fideles & Christiani versabantur, acerbam perfecutionem concitavit, jussitque solos ecclesiarum praesides, tanquam autores doctrinae euangelicae, neci dari.
units.tr: Except that in the meantime Maximinus etc.] Eusebius, in his work on the times: "Maximinus stirred up persecution against the bishops of the churches." The same author elsewhere: "Maximinus, out of bitter hatred against the household of Alexander, in which many faithful and Christians lived, stirred up a harsh persecution and ordered that only the presidents of the churches, as authors of the evangelical doctrine, be put to death."

units.la: Mox Decio imperante, jam tum septima persecutione, saevitum in Christianos] de hac septima persecutione videndi sunt Orosius lib.7. cap.14. & Ludovicus Vives ad Augustinum de civit. Dei, lib.18. cap.52. Meminit & Eusebius per haec verba, Decius cum Philippos patrem & filium interfecisset, ob o-dium[?] eorum, in Christianos persecutionem movet, qua diaconus Laurentius Romae martyrium duxit.
units.tr: Soon, under Decius, already then the seventh persecution, the Christians were savagely treated] On this seventh persecution see Orosius, book 7, chapter 14, and Ludovicus Vives on Augustine's City of God, book 18, chapter 52. Eusebius also mentions it in these words: "Decius, after he had killed Philip, father and son, out of hatred for them, stirred up persecution against the Christians, in which the deacon Laurence suffered martyrdom at Rome."

units.la: Inde Valerianus octavus sanctorum hostis fuit] in hac octava persecutione martyrio coronatus fuit D. Cyprianus episcopus Carthaginensis. Vide sis Orosium lib.7. cap.15. Augustinum, loco citato. Eusebium in Chronico, & ipsum Cyprianum.
units.tr: Then Valerian was the eighth enemy of the saints] In this eighth persecution Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, was crowned with martyrdom. See Orosius, book 7, chapter 15; Augustine, in the place cited; Eusebius in the Chronicle; and Cyprian himself.

units.la: Interjectis annis fere quinquaginta] anno Diocletiani XIX coeptum est saeviri primum in Christianos, quae persecutio nona, ab aliis autem decima vocatur. Sunt autem ab obitu Valeriani usque ad annum illum fere quinquaginta anni. Nam ad numerum illum tres quatuor tantum desiderantur. Ceterum ab Augustino & Orosio nona post Neronem referitur persecutio Aureliani: de qua Eusebius in Chronico, Aurelianus cum adversum nos persecutionem movisset, fulmen juxta eum comitesq; ejus ruit: ac non multo post inter Constantinopolim & Heracliam in Coenophrurio viae veteris occiditur.
units.tr: With about fifty years intervening] In the nineteenth year of Diocletian, the persecution against the Christians first began to rage. This is called the ninth persecution, but by others the tenth. Now from the death of Valerian to that year there are almost fifty years, for only three or four are lacking to that number. Moreover, Augustine and Orosius count the persecution of Aurelian as the ninth after Nero, of which Eusebius says in the Chronicle: "When Aurelian had stirred up persecution against us, a thunderbolt fell near him and his companions, and not long after he was killed between Constantinople and Heraclea, at Coenophrurium on the old road.

units.la: Acerbissima persecutio exorta] persecutio Decii fuit maxima, ut haec saevissima & acerbissima.
units.tr: The most bitter persecution having arisen] The persecution of Decius was the greatest, and this one was the most savage and bitter.

units.la: Per X continuos annos] ab anno Christi CCCIII, usque ad annum ejusdem CCCXII Sigonius.
units.tr: For ten continuous years] From the year of Christ 303 down to the year 312, according to Sigonius.

units.la: Omnis fere sacro martyrum cruore orbis infectus est] quippe triginta dierum[?] spatio XVII millia trucidata feruntur. Idem ex Beda & aliis.
units.tr: The whole world was almost stained with the sacred blood of the martyrs] Indeed, in a space of thirty days, seventeen thousand are said to have been slaughtered. The same from Bede and others.

units.la: Quam nunc episcopatus pravis ambitionibus appetuntur] de ambitu[?] e episcoporum illius temporis videndus Ammianus Marcellinus: qui licet a religione, quam nos Christiani profitemur, alienus esset, tamen de primis episcopis, qui persecutionum temporibus vivebant, ita scribit, lib XXVII.
units.tr: How now bishoprics are sought after with corrupt ambitions] On the ambition of the bishops of that time, see Ammianus Marcellinus, who, although he was a stranger to the religion we Christians profess, nevertheless writes thus of the early bishops who lived in times of persecution, book 27.

units.la: Quosdam provinciales antistites tenuitas edendi potan-dique parcissime, vilitas etiam indumentorum & super-cilia humum spectantia perpetuo numini verisq; ejus cultoribus ut puros commendant & verecundos.
units.tr: Some provincial prelates, by their extreme frugality in eating and drinking, by the plainness of their clothing, and by their eyes ever fixed on the ground, commend themselves to the eternal divinity and its true worshippers as pure and modest.

units.la: Qui primus omnium Romanorum principum Christianus fuit] non tam primus Christianus fuit, quam primus imperatorum pacem Christianis dedit. Nam ante illum Philippus Christianus fuerat. Chronicon Eusebij, Philippus Philippum filium suum consortem regni fecit, primusque omnium ex Romanis imperatoribus Christianus fuit. Orofius lib. 7. cap. 13. Philippus primus omnium imperatorum Christianus fuit. Idem lib. eod. cap. 18. Constantinus imperator est creatus primus imperatorum Christianus, excepto Philippo, qui Christianus annis admodum paucissimis ad hoc tantum constitutus fuisse mihi visus est, ut millesimus Romae annus Christo potius quam idolis dicaretur.
units.tr: Who was the first of all Roman emperors to be a Christian. He was not so much the first Christian as the first of the emperors to give peace to the Christians, for Philip had been a Christian before him. Eusebius's Chronicle: Philip made his son Philip co-ruler of the realm and was the first of all the Roman emperors to be a Christian. Orosius, book 7, chapter 13: Philip was the first of all emperors to be a Christian. The same author, same book, chapter 18: Constantine was made emperor, the first Christian emperor, apart from Philip, who seems to me to have been a Christian for only a very few years, and was set up only so that the thousandth year of Rome might be dedicated to Christ rather than to the idols.

units.la: Militia rejiciebat] idem Christianos de palatio suo pellebat. Eusebius, Orofius. Sed vide sodes hoc loco Sigonium.
units.tr: He removed Christians from the army] The same emperor drove the Christians from his palace. Eusebius, Orosius. But please see Sigonius at this place.

units.la: Nec ulterius persecutionem fore credimus] id refutat Augustinus de civit. Dei, lib. 19. cap. 21.
units.tr: Nor do we believe there will be any further persecution] Augustine refutes this in The City of God, book 19, chapter 21.

units.la: Sacris vocibus decem plagis mundum afficiendum esse] ubi hoc pronuntiatum sacris vocibus? vide sis Augustinum de civit. Dei, lib. 18. cap. 52. & Orofium lib. 7. cap. 18. Iam enim vela mihi contrahenda sunt ob properantiam typographi propter instantes nundinas Francfurtenses.
units.tr: That the world is to be struck with ten plagues by sacred voices] Where is this declared by sacred voices? See Augustine, The City of God, book 18, chapter 52, and Orosius, book 7, chapter 18. For now I must draw in my sails, because the printer is in a hurry on account of the approaching Frankfurt fair.

units.la: Cum IX fuerunt] X alij, qui eam, quae sub Antichristo futura est, undecimam appellant. Vsque adeo nihil certi de his, quae conjectura tantum constant. Conjectura enim humanae mentis, si aliquando ad verum pervenit, aliquando etiam fallitur.
units.tr: When there were nine] Ten others, who call the one that is to come under Antichrist the eleventh. So nothing certain is known about these things, which rest only on conjecture. For the conjecture of the human mind, if it sometimes reaches the truth, sometimes also goes astray.

units.la: Pag. 143. Funeris extincti] Sigonius corrigit, funus extincti, & paullo post, funus excitatus est. Vide si habes.
units.tr: Page 143. "Funeris extincti": Sigonius corrects it to "funus extincti", and a little later "funus excitatus est". See for yourself, if you have him.

units.la: Pag. 144. Etenim duobus Arriis] Hunc locum forte an in mente habuit is qui disputationem Athanasij contra Arrium in Latinum sermonem convertit, cum ita scriberet. Sed si illud recolat quod in Chronica sua beatae memoriae Sulpicius Severus posuit, dicens, duo Arrij tanquam duo serpentes, ex uno ore sibilabant: duos Arrios fuisse evidenter reperiet.
units.tr: Page 144. For with two Arii] Whether the man who translated Athanasius's disputation against Arius into Latin had this passage in mind when he wrote thus is perhaps uncertain. But if he recalls what Sulpicius Severus, of blessed memory, wrote in his Chronicle, saying that two Arii hissed like two serpents from one mouth, he will clearly find that there were two Arii.

units.la: Pag. 146. Res ad Constantinum refertur] hoc verum esse sequitur, cum inter mortem Constantini Magni, & Sardicensem synodum anni sint decem. Siquidem Constantinus obiit anno Christi CCCXXXVII. Episcopi autem apud Sardicam congregati fuerunt anno ejusdem CCCXLVII. Vide Sigonium. Sed & Gifelitinum, quiprimus nos de hoc errore admonuit.
units.tr: Page 146. The matter is referred to Constantine] This is true, as follows, since between the death of Constantine the Great and the Synod of Sardica there are ten years. For Constantine died in the year of Christ 337, and the bishops gathered at Sardica in the year 347. See Sigonius. But also Gifelinus, who first warned us of this error.

units.la: Ursatius] scribitur & Ursacius. Si libri variant in Sulpitius & Sulpicius. Hujus Ursatij, ut & Valentis, meminit Hieronymus adversus Luciferianos, cap.7.
units.tr: Ursatius] It is also written Ursacius. If the books vary, Sulpitius and Sulpicius. Jerome, against the Luciferians, chapter 7, mentions this Ursatius, and Valens.

units.la: A Singiduno Ursatius] Ursatius episcopus Singiduni Mysiæ, Pannonius. Athanasius, paginis 570,588 & 670.
units.tr: Ursatius from Singidunum] Ursatius, bishop of Singidunum in Mysia, Pannonia. Athanasius, pages 570, 588 and 670.

units.la: Valens a Mursia] quæ & Mursa Pannoniæ inferioris civitas, ubi olim Vetranio imperator factus & Magnentius victus fuit. Infra Morsa dicitur. Hiero. adverf. Lucif. Valens Mursiensis episcopus.
